paragraph_text: There is a system to assess the use of TRACES in BIPs by means of supervision. At the LVUs level the system of verification does not sufficiently cover the use of TRACES, therefore it is not ensured that deficiencies are detected and corrective actions are implemented when required. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Poland has designated a competent authority for use of TRACES in relation to products of animal origin and live animals. Other competent authorities use TRACES for non-animal origin products for training purposes. In general staff at BIPs and LVUs are qualified and experienced in relation to TRACES activities and use TRACES correctly, with the exception of the controls of live animals at aba

There is a system of supervision developed within the import control sector, which includes verification of the correct use of TRACES. This includes both local supervision by the head of each BIP and central supervision via supervisory visits to each B IP by the Borders Office (4 BIPs are visited per year). However, this supervision mainly focuses on correcting individual mistakes done by BIP staff. Supervision did not identify the shortcomings described in this report (e.g. use of collective user accounts, control of re-entry horses, follow-up at controlled bodies and destruction plants).

The Border Office also carries out periodic reviews of TRACES from central level using 11 data warehouse and Clickview since December 2012 to monitor the confirmation of receipt and takes appropriate actions when receipt is not recorded as required in respect of consignments imported under Articles 8 and 15 of Directive 97/78/EC.

The regional coordinator stated that TRACES was used for management of economic operators at LVUs and statistical information. Requirements for the regional coordinators do not foresee the supervision duties on the use of TRACES for INTRA-CERTS and control of animal by-products issued and received by LVUs .

At LVUs there is no system of supervision or other activity to assess the correct use of TRACES, therefore shortcomings identified by this audit and described under findings have not been noticed. There is no routine or pro-active analysis/verification of data within TRACES. Records are checked only in response to problems identified by the competent authority of the Member State of destination.

label_heading: Conclusion on the resources for the performance
paragraph_text: The competent authority has suitably qualified and experienced staff, facilities and equipment relating to TRACES activities. Different users of TRACES received appropriate training enabling the correct use of TRACES. In some areas where instructions were not sufficiently detailed for both BIPs and LVUs, the relevant official controls are either not recorded or recorded incorrectly in TRACES. 5.3 USE OF TRACES Legal Requirements Decision 2004/292/EC, Commission Decision 2000/571/EC, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Regulation (EC) No 599/2004, Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Decision 93/444/EC, Directive 97/78/EC

In one BIP visited where imported live animals were sent to approved bodies, the confirmation from the place of destination was not received and consignments were not followed-up by BIP staff contrary to the requirements of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. Staff were not aware of this requirement and the instructions do not contain information about it.

GVI provided a number of training courses, as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, relating specifically to the use of TRACES or including it as a part of training themes. Staff also obtain on-the-job training and practice. The training courses were provided to regional services, LVUs and BIPs staff. Evaluation of the training material on control of animal by-products showed that training was sufficient and clear, however training was not effective because it had not improved the awareness of staff on the control of animal by-products at the place of destination and TRACES was not correctly used for those purposes.

Several consignments were sent to customs warehouses located in other Member States, but confirmation of arrival in TRACES was not received from the competent authorities at destination, what is not in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Decision 2000/571/EC. However, the BIP staff contacted the Polish customs authorities, who confirmed that consignments had arrived to the place of destination. The data in TRACES were never confirmed and there is no evidence that the consignment was controlled at the warehouse by the veterinary authorities of destination. The lack of feedback from destination is not notified by the BIP to the GVI, since instructions do not foresee follow-up of non- co

For consignments re-imported, sent for destruction, transiting and others which need to be followed-up, the BIP of entry follows-up those consignments by contacting the customs services in writing. Customs provide confirmation in writing that the consignments in question arrived to the place of destination. Therefore such consignments were regarded as followed- up although confirmation was not recorded in TRACES.

One BIP visited received consignments of live animals destined for approved bodies in accordance with the national legislation, after the GVI issued an import licence for certain animals. CVEDAs issued were entered into TRACES, but part 3 (Control) of the CVEDA was never completed by an official veterinarian responsible for supervision of the controlled destination contrary to requirement laid down in Part 3 of Annex 1 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. 5.3.6.1.2 At destination

LVUs controlling the economic operator at the place of destination do not ensure that the outcome of control on the arriving consignment is correctly recorded in TRACES (this recording is required by Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004). This requires additional follow-up efforts from the BIPs staff. The low level of confirmation of receipt at the place of destination (e.g. re-imported, sent for destruction, approved bodies) in Traces indicates that LVUs have a low level of controls to follow-up consignments at the place of destination. 5.3.7 Animal welfare checks

In relation to exports of live animals to third countries transiting through other Member States, it was noted: · that they are accompanied only by the certificate to export to the third country (in Polish and in the third country's language). The relevant instruction "Exportation of live animals and animal products to third countries" does not require an INTRA-CERT to be issued. Certifying officers entered data related to the consignment into TRACES as soon as possible after the consignment had departed but this could take a few days and the animals may have left the EU by then. Therefore, the requirements of Article 2(1) of Decision 93/444/EEC which requires consignments of live animals to

In relation to consignments of live animals arriving from other Member States, it was noted that: · according to the competent authority, all incoming TRACES notifications are checked to verify that the details they contain are acceptable, however in order to implment Article 5(a) of Directive 90/425/EC on non-discriminatory checks, 5 percent of consignments of live animals are physically controlled at destination often in the case of suspicion. · official controls related to ante-mortem inspections or welfare controls at Control Posts are not routinely recorded in TRACES, contrary to the requirements of Article 3.1 of Decision 2004/292/EC. There are currently no national instructions that r

In relation to the movement of specific animal by-products, it was noted that: · The GVI stated that commercial documents were provided via the INTRA-CERT module of TRACES as required. Neither of the LVUs visited during the audit were responsible for controls on trade that would require issuing documents for the outward movement of such animal by-products to other Member States. · There is a national instruction on the requirements of Article 48.3 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and it was covered in training courses in recent years. However, the GVI did not have an overview to what extent it was being implemented (i.e. the requirement that incoming consignments of certain animal by-products

Instructions on use of DOCOMs does not contain information on the requirement of follow- up of consignments of animal by-products received from other Member States contrary to the requirements of Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

paragraph_text: The competent authority complies with the requirements of communication, training and instructions (with the exception of instructions for control of transhipments and for sampling for microbiological testing) and resources to support the effective implementation of the controls. However, the system does not ensure veterinary checks and certification are only performed by authorised staff which may lead to imports of consignments that do not fulfil the legal requirements related to animal and/or public health. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 System to ensure presentation of consignments for veterinary checks Legal requirements Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article

paragraph_text: Import controls are implemented but the systemic problems identified in previous FVO audits remain unaddressed: pre-notification of consignments does not include all the information required, the competent authority does not ensure that no entry or handling of veterinary consignments occurs in the free zone of the port without their agreement, controls are not implemented by authorised staff (including the issuing of certificates), the monitoring plan has a limited scope. As regards transhipments, the competent authority has access to information (Customs information, manifests) but does not use it to identify the goods and the required controls on consignments transhipping in Malta are not

The competent authority has written job descriptions for the official veterinarians and the veterinary support staff. These include the general responsibilities of the personnel and they do not detail specific tasks and related responsibilities (finding 17) contrary to the requirement of Chapter II(4) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In this context, it was noted that auxiliary staff carry out controls and sign certificates when such activities have not been included in their responsibilities. This shortcoming was reported in the 2010 report and a recommendation (No 3) was consequently issued, which has not been addressed.

Previous FVO audits identified that veterinary checks and issuing of certificates were not always done by authorised staff (see finding 4). After the 2010 FVO audit the competent authority hired an additional official veterinarian but the shortcoming had not been addressed at the time of the 2011 audit (see heading 5.2.1 of the 2011 report). The situation remains unchanged, auxiliary staff carrying out controls when official 6 veterinarians are not present in the BIPs and signing subsequent certificates (CVEDs) in TRACES.

The audit team noted that in the port BIP official controls and the signing/issuing of CVEDs was done by the official veterinarians. In the airport BIP the official veterinarian is present once per week and support staff performs more than 95% of the official import controls, including the signing/issuing of CVEDs. Official veterinarians are not involved in the performance of official controls to ensure that they are correctly implemented. This means that: Official controls are not performed under the responsibility of the official veterinarian contrary to the requirements of article 4(1) of Directive 97/78/EC; The signing of CVEDs, is done by support staff instead of the official veterinari

Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that Customs shall not allow the entry or handling in free zones or free warehouses of consignments subject to veterinary checks without the agreement of the competent authority. This requirement is not included in the memorandum of understanding between the competent authority and Customs. There is no procedure for the enforcement of the requirement and the competent authority cannot ensure that no entry or handling of veterinary consignments occurs in the free zone of the port without their agreement. This shortcoming was noted in previous FVO audits and as recommendation (No 1) in the 2011 report. The recommendation has not been addressed.

Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 requires that the monitoring plan reflects the nature of the imported consignments and the hazards that they represent. The monitoring plan for imports includes sampling for chemical hazards and it is implemented correctly at the BIPs. An average of 3% of the imported consignments is subject to testing. The plan does not cover microbiological hazards and does not include an assessment of microbiological risks that would justify their exclusion from the plan. As a consequence, imported products of animal origin have not been tested for microbial pathogens although relevant commodities have been imported (beef, poultry). These parameters for imported goo

label_heading: Conclusion on the use of TRACES
paragraph_text: TRACES is used for import-related activities. Inaccurate and/or incomplete data in TRACES is linked to shortcomings in the official controls (controls done by non- authorised staff, lack of testing of official samples or controls not implemented, specifically in transhipments), which undermines confidence in the official control system on the whole. 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Article 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

TRACES is not used for transhipped consignments. There are no controls on those movements contrary to the requirements of Article 11 of Council Directive 97/78/EC. The consignments could go on to a non-BIP EU port, where no checks would take place; or if they went to another EU BIP port, the port would not receive information about the transhipment via the TRACES inbox notifications as provided for in the General Guidance for consignments of live animals and animal products from third countries in transit or transhipment. 5.2.3 Veterinary checks

The port is a free zone and operates 24/7 with few exceptions. Imports of products of animal origin are allowed only during the presence of the official veterinarians, but transhipments can happen at any time. This means that those consignments could leave the port without TRACES documents intended for transhipment, which is not in line with Article 3 of the Commission Decision 292/2004/EC. 5

In the airport BIP, checking the arriving consignments and issuing and signing CVEDS in TRACES is normally done by auxiliary staff using a generic TRACES account. The implementation of veterinary checks by auxiliary staff is not in accordance with paragraph 2 of the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC, Article 5(1) of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 4 of Directive 91/496/EEC.

Documentary and identity checks are recorded in TRACES. The audit team evaluated a sample of documents, and found a number of shortcomings, for example: at the airport several CVEDs indicated satisfactory documentary checks even though the data on the health certificate did not match with data declared on the first page of the CVED by the persons responsible for the load; the approval numbers of controlled destinations in the CVEDs were incorrect; many CVEDs are issued by auxiliary staff who sign using a generic password; consignments of live lobsters were certified with CVEDAs instead of the required CVEDPs. In the 2010 report a high number of errors in TRACES data were also reported.

Consignments sampled in 2013 and 2014 under the monitoring plans and subsequently released into free circulation appeared in TRACES as still pending results. The competent authorities confirmed that the tests have not been done yet. This means that in the case of a non-compliant result, it is too late to act ­ for example, no re-enforced check (REC) or Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) notification could be triggered. The significant delay of a year between sampling and testing was already highlighted in the 2010 report.
The results of the tests actually carried out were not entered in TRACES either. This is not in line with Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. 5.2.4 INTRA module

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of the verification activities
paragraph_text: The competent authority is developing the activities for verification of effectiveness of the official import controls including objectives and indicators. The competent authority has not planned to implement such verification activities since 2012 leading to an absence of the evaluation of effectiveness and appropriateness of the official import controls and their compliance with EU legislation. 4 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE VERIFICATION ACTIVITIES Legal requirements Council Directive 91/496/EEC, Council Directive 97/78/EC, Directive 2002/99/EC, Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Commission Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Commission Decision 2001/812/EC, Commission Decision 2004/292/EC. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the verification activities
paragraph_text: The verification activities were not implemented for the last two years, which means that the competent authority cannot ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of the official import controls and their compliance with EU legislation. 5.3 IMPACT OF THE VERIFICATION PROCEDURES Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on the impact of the verification procedures
paragraph_text: The organisation of the verification activities foresees the use of the results of verification for planning and improving the official controls and also the future verification activities. However, in the area of the official import controls this has not been done for the last two years. Regarding verification activities conducted until 2012, improvements in the performance of the import controls were evident, however there were cases in which shortcomigns were not addressed meaning that the verification activities did not ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of the official import controls and their compliance with EU legislation. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authority is de

The SMSD stated that various FVO audit reports recommendations in different departments higlighted the need to develop a new procedure for the verification of effectiveness and appropriateness of the official controls of different sectors in line with Articles 4(2)(a) and 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The SMSD held a meeting with the sectors to provide guidance on the development of the new procedure, in January 2014. The SMSD sent an email providing guidance on the development of the procedure. This includes a SWOT analysis (analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats) of the official controls and the setting of measurable objectives and criteria related to them. The

The certified system (finding 2) includes verification of effectiveness of the audit activities (which also include the central level supervision). After the ISO certification no verification according the new procedure (finding 2) has been followed on the official import controls.
No verification of effectiveness of the official import controls by following the new verification procedures was available at the time of the audit.

The competent authority has last audited in 2011, one of the BIPs' visited by the audit team. Both BIPs visited underwent their most recent supervision from the central level in 2010. Apart from these, the competent authority conducted a supervision on the approved warehouse under Article 12 of Directive 97/78/EC in 2010. All other BIPs last underwent a supervision either in 2010 or in 2012.

There is no head of the BIP in Budapest airport since 2011. No verification (central nor local) activities were followed on this BIP for this period of time. The competent authority issued a decision in March 2014 to have the former head of the BIP once per week to supervise the BIP activities.
No verification has been conducted on the activities of the official import controls sector at central level (LATSTD).

The competent authority does not conduct verification relating to official controls of consignments subject to veterinary inspection in customs warehouses (finding 6). However, the Customs have notified at least in two cases the competent authority regarding consignments subject to veterinary controls that had not been checked in a BIP, and which were found in customs warehouses during clearance procedure. The competent authority stated that those consignments were brought back to a BIP for veterinary inspection. 5.2.2 Veterinary checks

The head of the BIP Roszke stated that he conducts an informal supervision every two weeks on documentary checks, physical checks, sampling, facilities. Once per month he picks files of imported consignments and he assesses the correctness of the controls. He stated that he also checks TRACES on a weekly basis. The audit team noted that there is no written instruction for the supervision and the results of the supervison are not documented, which makes the statement not verifiable.

The head of the BIP Roszke conducts a monthly meeting with the inspectors in which among others, he stated that he is providing feedback on the errors he identifies in the official controls. The audit team assessed the notes and the agenda of three meetings selected by the head of the BIP and these had no information on deficiencies identified during supervision activities.

An annual report follows the verification activities of the NFCSO. The SMSD and the management of NFCSO are using this report to set priorities and directions in the planning of the official controls and also the planning of the verification activities. However, as no verification activities were followed for the LATSTD since 2012, there was no input and impact of this reporting to the official import controls for the last two years.

The BIPs provide reports of the official import controls they conduct on a monthly, quarterly and annual basis to the central level. These include figures of imports. Currently the competent authority does not use this information to verify the effectiveness of the official import controls

The internal audit referred to in finding 14, identified some shortcomings and recommended to have available all relevant documented procedures and to keep staff up-to-date on their tasks. However, the audit report indicated that no action plan was required. There was no follow-up on the recommendations and no corrective actions were implemented contrary to the requirement of Article 8(3)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The system in place to assess the use of TRACES in BIPs and LVUs does not ensure that deficiencies are detected and corrective actions are implemented when required. As a consequence, (i) information in the database does not always reflect accurately the controls implemented and (ii) the system is not used to detect shortcomings in the implementation of controls (e.g. no controls at destination of consignments requiring them) and those remain inadequate. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Responsibilities have been allocated to various levels of the organisation, providing adequate support for a correct use of TRACES. Although there is a provision for training and instructions, a number of shortcomings o

There was one "technical audit"/central supervision carried by NFCSO-DAHAW-LATSTD in March 2014 on ABP legislation which included an assessment of the correct use of TRACES. The report was not available at the time of the FVO audit but preliminary feedback was that no 1 In their response to the draft report, the competent authority noted that CEDs must be issued via the use of TRACES in all DPEs (BIPs) within Hungary as from 1 September 2013. 10 significant issues were detected related to the use of TRACES at the one ABP establishment visited during the audit.

There is a system of local supervision by managers at the two BIPs and two LVUs visited which includes an evaluation of the use of TRACES. There are no instructions to cover local supervision and no specific reports are created. The head of one BIP visited stated that the results of the supervision are discussed during monthly meetings with staff although this is largely undocumented/recorded. The managers at both LVUs stated that they share the relevant outcomes of their supervision activity with appropriate colleagues but that this is largely undocumented/recorded (one LVU started supervision in January 2014). There was no local supervision at one of the two BIPs visited between 2011 to th

None of the issues identified by the FVO (findings 18 to 21, 24, 26 to 31, 36 and 37) had been identified by the various forms of verification being implemented by the competent authority with the exception of the rate of confirmation of receipt at destination for channelled consignments. Conclusion on verification and review

label_heading: Conclusion on the use of TRACES
paragraph_text: Staff at BIPs and LVUs use TRACES correctly for routine activities. However, the receipt at destination of many consignments is not notified to BIPs or Member States of origin (e.g. slaughter animals, animal by-products), contrary to the legal requirements. This means that the traceability of such consignments is compromised and the arrival of the goods at the intended operator is not confirmed to origin. 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal Requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

There is one customs warehouse in Hungary which is approved under Article 12(4) of Council Directive 97/78/EC which stores very small amounts of consignments of non-conforming goods. The last consignment entered into TRACES by the LVU responsible for this warehouse was in November 2012. The LVU has been granted Super LVUs (SLVU) status so that it can issue CVEDs for split consignments. The SLVU used such a collective account where the officials' names were not listed and therefore their names were not recorded individually when they issued CVEDs for consignments split at the warehouses (see finding 34).

Designation of authorities (e.g. regional animal health and public health authorities and BIPs) are well defined. BIPs and regional animal health authorities have proper access to TRACES and use it with regards to imports and intra-Union trade of live animals and animal by-products. However, not all regional public health authorities have access to TRACES, thus they can not exchange information with other Member States in relation to animals sent for slaughter and re-imports. 5.2 RESOURCES FOR THE PERFORMANCE OF THE CONTROLS Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Commission Regulation (EC) No 1152/2009, Commission Implementin

The competent authorities have experienced staff with the exception of the regional public health authorities, who have not been using the system, do not have access to it and have not received training. Therefore, the minimum prerequisites for the use of TRACES by the regional public health authorities are not in place. 5.3 USE OF TRACES Legal requirements Decision 2004/292/EC, Commission Decision 2000/571/EC, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Regulation (EC) No 599/2004, Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, Council Directive 97/78/EC and Council Directive 90/425/EEC. 5 Findings 5.3.1 Management of users and organisations 5.3.1.

label_heading: Conclusions on the verification and review
paragraph_text: There is a system of verifying that TRACES modules are used correctly by the BIPs. However, it does not detect and correct on time repeated errors due to focusing on the implementation of control procedures. Therefore it is not ensured that official controls are effective, deficiencies in TRACES are detected and corrective actions are implemented when required.

label_heading: Conclusions on the verification and review
paragraph_text: There is no system of verifying that TRACES modules used by regional animal health authorities are used correctly (control of DOCOMs, channelled consignments or consignments sent for destruction) and LVUs (control of INTRA-CERTs). Therefore, the deficiencies are not detected and corrected on time. A system to verify that the TRACES control module is used by regional public health competent authorities is not developed since they have no access to TRACES or only have recently received access. Therefore, Spain does not comply with the minimum requirements of the use of TRACES for the recording of controls in abattoirs and re- imported consignments of products of animal origin). 6 OVERALL CONCL

label_heading: Conclusion on the use of TRACES
paragraph_text: Most CVEDs, INTRA-certificates and DOCOMs are issued correctly in Slovakia. However, for many consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination, TRACES is not used in compliance with the legal requirements for ensuring traceability, e.g. consignments arriving from other Member States (slaughter animals, animal by-products) and imports (re- imports and channelled consignments). The best practice approach covered during training for dealing with feedback received from other Member States in Part III of INTRA-CERTS is not being implemented at LVUs. 7 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal Requirements Regulation(EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Figures from the TRACES database indicate that 49 consignments were channelled from EU BIPs to destinations in Slovakia during the 18 months prior to this audit and that receipt at destination was confirmed via box 41 of the CVED in 47 cases. In some cases, box 41 was completed well outside the 15 day limit ­ some more than a year after the consignment left the BIP of entry. The competent authority explained that this was related to LVUs reviewing records in TRACES and updating the system as required.

There were three re-imported consignments during the same period of 18 months, none had been confirmed as being received at destination in box 41. One of these was discussed at one of the LVUs visited and it was explained that the consignment had been controlled at destination 5 but that the relevant official was not aware of the requirement to enter the control in TRACES and did not have access to TRACES. That official has subsequently applied for access.

There is no specific national instruction that official controls related to ante-mortem inspection for animals arriving from other Member States should be recorded in TRACES (59% of such consignments had those controls recorded during 2013 in TRACES). The competent authority did say however, that there is a general instruction which requires that all relevant official controls should be recorded in TRACES which would apply for animals arriving for slaughter from other Member States.

There is a specific national instruction on the implementation of the requirements of Article 48.3 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 (i.e. that categories 1, 2 and processed animal proteins (PAP) from category 3 animal by-products arriving from other Member States should be controlled and confirmed in TRACES as having been received at destination). According to the TRACES database, 36% of arriving consignments of PAP and categories 1 and 2 in the DOCOM module were recorded in TRACES as being controlled during 2013. 5.2.9 DOCOM module

The correct use of TRACES is covered by the verification activities of some sectors/official controls. In the BIPs, repeated deficiencies are detected and corrective actions are implemented as required which is not the case at LVUs. As a consequence, (i) information in the TRACES database does not always reflect accurately the controls implemented and (ii) the system is not used to detect shortcomings in the implementation of controls (e.g. no relevant controls at destination) and those remain inadequate. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authority has provided appropriate resources to support the correct use of TRACES. There is a system of local supervision at LVUs. This is based on a national procedure being adapted at each LVU to fit the local situation/activities. Both LVUs visited had adapted the national procedure. One LVU had implemented supervision on a planned basis (supervision every six months) and supervision reports were created which assessed one or two individual export consignments per certifying officer and no deficiencies were detected. The other LVU stated that they carried out local supervision, however this was not in accordance with their own procedure and no reports were created during the process. label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The system for import controls covers the consignments presented at the BIPs and the official controls are generally performed correctly. However, the competent authority does not use available information (Customs database, manifests) to ensure that all consignments subject to veterinary control are presented to the BIPs and there is partial enforcement of the requirement to notify the goods prior to arrival at the BIPs.

In the airport BIP visited, several consignments were not pre-notified contrary to the requirement of Article 2(1) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. In the port BIP, a full assessment of pre-notification by the audit team was not possible as the individual import files created prior to August 2014 did not contain a part I of the CVED signed and dated by the person responsible for the load. Evidence of pre-notification was available in files created post August 2014. In the road BIP visited, pre-notification was in line with the legal requirements.

label_heading: Conclusion on the use of TRACES
paragraph_text: Most CVEDs, INTRA-certificates and DOCOMs are issued correctly in Romania. However, for many consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination, TRACES is not used in compliance with the legal requirements for ensuring traceability, e.g. consignments arriving from other Member States (slaughter animals, animal by- products) and imports (reimports and channelled consignments). The impact of the shortcomings is limited as some controls are implemented but not recorded in TRACES. The system of randomly checking notifications related to arriving products does not ensure that the LVU is aware of all consignments which require follow-up. Feedback received from other Member States in

Figures from the TRACES database indicate that 24 consignments were channelled from EU BIPs to destinations in Romania during the 18 months prior to this audit. Receipt at destination was confirmed by completing box 41 of the CVED in 12 of these cases.
There were five re-imported consignments during the same period and three had been confirmed as received at destination via completed box 41. 5 5.2.7.2 At the point of introduction

There are three Control Posts approved in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 1255/97 in Romania. There are no instructions for recording official controls carried out at Control Posts in TRACES and officials do not record such controls in TRACES. 5.2.9 INTRA module

There is no national instruction that official controls related to ante-mortem inspection for animals arriving from other Member States should be recorded in TRACES (18% of such consignments had those controls recorded during 2013 in TRACES but according to the competent authority all consignments would have been subject to ante-mortem controls).

A national instruction on the implementation of the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 requires that TRACES should be used to confirm receipt at destination of category 3 animal by-products arriving from other Member States. However, it does not include a similar requirement for Categories 1 and 2 animal by-products which are also included in Article 48(3) of Regulation EC (No) 1069/2009. According to the TRACES database, less than 20% of arriving consignments of processed animal protein and categories 1 and 2 in the DOCOM module were recorded in TRACES as being controlled at destination during 2013. It was not possible to confirm what percentage of consignments were actually contr
Many consignments rejected by BIPs and sent for destruction were not recorded in box 41 of the CVED in TRACES as being received at destination and there is no instruction on this. 5.2.10 DOCOM module

The set-up of the competent authority in TRACES does not correspond to the current structure where local veterinary units of the NVWA following regional division have been removed. Therefore, all INTRA-CERTs in TRACES identify the non-existent local veterinary units. The competent authority has suitably qualified and experienced staff for TRACES activities. 5.2 USE OF TRACES Legal Requirements Decision 2004/292/EC, Commission Decision 2000/571/EC, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Regulation (EC) No 599/2004, Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Decision 93/444/EC, Directive 97/78/EC, Council Directive 2002/99/EC and C

The NVWA is the competent authority responsible for coordination of the use of TRACES in accordance with the requirements of Article 1 of Decision 92/486/EEC. In 2012, the structure of the NVWA was changed, which has led to the removal of the local veterinary units (LVUs) and the regions. The information on the structural changes has not been provided to the Commission in order to amend Decision 2009/821/EC. This has an impact on the use of TRACES. Currently, the official veterinarians issuing INTRA-CERTs access TRACES as the central competent authority (not as local veterinary units listed in Decision 2009/821/EC) in order to reflect the existing structure of the NVWA. The audit team noted

The use of TRACES for routine activities for imports and for intra-Union movements of live animals leaving the Netherlands is in general correct. Lack of records in TRACES reflects lack of controls by the BIPs (e.g. exit of transit consignments) or by the NVWA offices (e.g. re-imported or consignments sent for destruction). In some cases these controls are done, but not recorded in TRACES. The arrival of a number of intra-Union consignments is not controlled at the place of destination (e.g. animal by- products) or the full range of controls are not recorded in TRACES (e.g. slaughter animals). Therefore, the traceability of consignments mentioned above and the communication between the compe

Repeated non-confirmation of exit of transit consignments was noted, even though the work instructions issued by the NVWA require the confirmation of the exit of transit consignments within 30 working days as required by Article 9 of Directive 91/496/EC and Articles 11 and 12(8) of Directive 97/78/EC. In the Rotterdam BIP visited, the transit consignments were followed-up using shipping companies' IT systems to check if they left the port and that information was recorded in TRACES. The Amsterdam BIP visited does not have a follow-up system to track exit transit consignments and does not record them in TRACES.

Commercial operators pre-notify consignments exiting the warehouse using hard copy CVEDs. After veterinary checks, consignments are accompanied using hard copy CVEDs completed and signed manually by official veterinarians. These CVEDs are entered manually into TRACES by correctly using the split function, when the veterinary officials are not overloaded with veterinary checks at the warehouses. This means that some consignments are notified to the BIPs in other Member States via TRACES with a delay. As a result, those consignments can leave the EU territory without the exit BIP being able to perform the controls. The risk is mitigated since the veterinary authorities communicate with other M

National instructions issued by the NVWA require the confirmation of arrival for re- imported consignments in accordance with the requirements of Article 15 of Directive 97/78/EC. However, TRACES-NL does not identify those consignments for follow-up by the veterinary inspectors at the place of destination and it is not recorded in TRACES. Re-imported consignments might be higher risk, especially if they were rejected by the third countries because of bacterial or chemical contamination. The reasons of rejection by third countries of products of animal origin produced in the Netherlands might need to be investigated.

Consignments sent for destruction are not followed up by the veterinary inspectors at the place of destination due to the set-up of the risk module in TRACES-NL. TRACES-NL does not classify those consignments as high risk and does not require them to be followed up at the place of destination contrary to the requirements of Article 17(2b) of Directive 97/78/EC. 5.2.8 Signatures

In relation to the movement of live animals from other Member States: INTRA-CERTs and CVEDs are downloaded into TRACES-NL and are filtered for official controls if this foreseen by the national risk evaluation plan. Approximately 8 percent of consignments of live animals are physically controlled at the destination (except for some live animals from several Member States where controls are carried out on 100 percent of consignments) following the requirements of Article 5(a) of Directive 90/425/EC on non-discriminatory checks. Those controls are correctly recorded in TRACES. Official controls related to ante-mortem inspections are recorded in TRACES following the frequency of 8 percent ident

The instructions mentioned in finding 41 describe requirements on the controls to be carried out at the place of destination when certain animal by-products arrive from other Member States. Those instructions require that the controls of certain animal by- products shall be carried out on an average of 10 percent of consignments contrary to the requirement of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The competent authority stated that the reduction in controls is due to limited human and financial resources, and the high number of animal by-products arriving from other Member States.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of the verification activities
paragraph_text: The competent authority is developing the activities for verification of effectiveness but has not yet set the relevant indicators to measure the extent to which the objectives are met. Currently the verification activities assess the appropriateness of the official import controls only when a shortcoming in the implementation of the controls is identified. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE VERIFICATION ACTIVITIES Legal requirements Directive 91/496/EEC, Directive 97/78/EC, Directive 2002/99/EC, Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 , Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Decision 2001/812, Decision 2004/292/EC. paragraph_text: The verification activities largely ensure compliance, of the official import controls, with legal requirements and planned arrangements. The new procedure foresees setting of measurable objectives for the official import controls and indicators linked to these objectives, however at the time of the audit the strategic objectives were not developed into operational objectives. The procedure uses the verification of compliance as the basis for verification of effectiveness, and highlights the difference between the two concepts. However both concepts get mixed later in the document.

The objectives of the audit activities on official import controls are to assess the activities and their compliance with the relevant procedures. This includes an evaluation of the appropriateness of the official import controls when a shortcoming in the implementation of these controls is identified. In such a case the audit team is conducting root-cause analysis to determine if the procedure needs to be improved.

In both BIPs visited there is cooperation with Customs in respect of Customs nomenclature codes (CN codes) that do not specify the type of commodity. The heads of the BIPs hold regular meetings with Customs officials. A central supervision conducted in October 2013 in both BIPs recommended that these meetings should be documented. These meetings are documented in BIP Gjueshevo but not in BIP Kapetan Andreevo.

The new procedure specifies the measures to ensure that all consignments subject to veterinary checks are identified and presented to the BIP in line with requirements of Article 3 of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 2(1) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. The supervision at local level in BIP Kapetan Andreevo assesses the pre-notifications without following the checklist annexed to the new procedure and the relevant instruction for checking a percentage of CVEDs. In BIP Gjueshevo the supervision assesses the pre-notifications following the checklist and relevant instruction.

The heads of both BIPs visited were aware of how the Customs database flags the consignments, but they did not use all intelligence available (Customs documents and data), contrary to the requirement of Article 6 of Regulation 136/2004 to cross check that no import of a consignment violates the requirements of Article 4(1) of Directive 91/496/EEC and Article 3 of Directive 97/78/EC. The verification activities had not identified this shortcoming either at local (supervision) level or at central (supervision, audit) level. 5.2.2 Veterinary checks

The new procedure for the verification of effectiveness has instructions on what percentage of CVEDs should be evaluated. The supervisors stated that they fill the supervision checklist using the previous knowledge they have on each veterinarian's performance.

The local supervision focuses on the performance of the official veterinarians. Having no overview of the official import controls, the supervision does not detect errors by the persons responsible for the loads (pre-notification) or other BIPs and local veterinary units (LVUs) (related to follow-up of the consignments).

In February 2014 the competent authority conducted an unannounced supervision of the warehouse, using a new checklist that will be incorporated into the procedure referred to in finding 2. The supervision identified the non-confirmation of exit transit in BIP Kapetan Andreevo. However no recommendation was issued and no action plan was implemented contrary to the requirement of Article 8(3)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882

The competent authority does not register in TRACES CVEDs for non-complying consignments intended for other warehouses in different Member States, contrary to the requirement of Article 3(2) of Decision No 2004/292/EC.

A local supervision procedure on the warehouse was launched by the LVU in December 2013. This is not related to the procedure described in findings 2-5. This supervision has not identified major shortcomings. The officials performing the supervision are not kept up-to-date relating to official import control requirements, although this was recommended by a relevant internal audit (finding 23). This reduces the capability to identify shortcomings in the operation of the warehouse. The competent authority performed a reconciliation test for quantities of commodities handled in which they used the information in TRACES. The competent authority keeps a report of monitoring the status of corrective action plans for supervision activities. This does not include the verification activities in the Article 12 warehouse. In the case of the audit activities certain actions planned were not implemented within the deadline and not at the time of the audit (finding 23). There was no follow-up by the time of the audit, contrary to the requirement of Article 8(3)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on the use of TRACES
paragraph_text: Finnish competent authorities are correctly using TRACES, with some specific exceptions (controls on consignments which require confirmation of receipt at destination are not always recorded in the system). This lack of information in the system undermines the communication between competent authorities in relation to the specific controls. 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Regulation(EC) No 882/2004 Findings

All of the re-imported goods via Finnish BIPs are indicated as channelled from the entry BIP to establishment of origin, as required. However, LVUs responsible do not always confirm in TRACES the arrival at destination (TRACES window 41 of the CVED is not filled in for most of them). BIPs staff stated that there is a written agreement of acceptance signed by the re-importer.

A number of consignments of blood products were imported, which require channelling (Annex XIV, Chapter II, Section 2 point 3.2 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011). About 50% of consignments were channelled in TRACES by the entry BIP, as required. Each of those consignments were confirmed by the LVU at destination using TRACES. The instructions for import controls did not cover the controls required for blood products, and the different officials interpreted the requirements of the Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 in different ways. The central competent authorities amended the instructions during the FVO audit and distributed these to the BIPs immediately.

Arrival of (rejected) consignments channelled to an incinerator for destruction was not confirmed in TRACES, contrary to the requirements. The reason is that the notification on the channelled consignment does not reach the environmental authority in charge of controls at the incinerator (who is not a TRACES user). It was noted that, instead of the TRACES confirmation, the system ensures that the BIP receives a paper document confirming the arrival at destination of the consignment. 5.2.8 Animal welfare checks

Some of the CVEDAs issued by BIPs in other Member States, with destination in controlled destinations in Finland, did not include records of the controls at destination in the control part of the TRACES document. 6 5.2.9 INTRA module

The INTRA documents for some consignments sent to control bodies in a different Member State, the "control part" had never been filled in by the authority at destination. One consignment of live animals exported via another Member States had no control part filled in at the point of exit from the EU. The authorities in Finland did not follow-up such cases to verify the reason for the absence of records in that control part.

A national instruction requires the filling in of the control part for documents of consignments of animals arriving for slaughter from other Member States. For other animals, all incoming consignments of live pigs and cattle should also be controlled at destination. However, there is only some evidence in TRACES of controls on such consignments having taken place. The missing information on the required controls did not trigger any action from the competent authority. The checks for other consignments are performed on the basis of risk or suspicion. 5.2.10 DOCOM module

Consignees are instructed to do checks on all consignments arriving from other Member States. If the place of destination is under the control of an official, the veterinarian should ensure that all the checks are done and record this in TRACES. 80% of DOCOMs arriving to Finland have the control part completed in TRACES. 74% of documents going out from Finland have the controls at destination recorded in TRACES.

Daily monitoring on the certificates provided in TRACES is carried out by EVIRA and regional official veterinarians. However, officials met at the LVUs were not always aware that some DOCOM notifications received via TRACES had not been followed up. The period for which the use of medicines should be declared was unspecified in the instructions and the audit team observed that this was interpreted in different ways by farmers. Food chain information and carcase conformation were not considered in relation to the substance(s) the samples would be tested for, although the latter was clearly indicated in the sampling order. There was no batch number of the feed or sampling spot on the farm (shed, silo, trough) indicated.

Representatives of BMG informed the audit team that it was reluctant to register traders of ABP/DP who do not actually receive the products concerned (hereafter: paper traders) owing to difficulties in controlling their transactions. Only one such paper trader has currently been registered in accordance with Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/20091.

Similarly, the registration of carriers of ABP/DP has currently been postponed due to a number of questions regarding the applicable requirements and practical difficulties2. Although this approach is not in line with Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the competent authority expressed concerns that carriers of ABP/DP could use their registration to conceal the origin and/or destination of the products. The system of official controls for the traceability of ABP/DP is negatively affected by an early stage of registration process of transporters of ABP/DP and by the unreliability of the relevant official lists of plants, establishments and operators involved in the chain of ABP/DP.

In France, official lists of approved and registered establishments are managed at regional level and are publicly available. Each region is responsible for updating their official lists on the basis of information provided by each relevant Département by using the national database of business operators (SIGAL). In 2012 an instruction was issued by DGAL highlighting the need to change the previous codification of establishments handling ABP/DP in order to bring it in line with the EU technical specifications for establishments and plants handling ABP. However, the audit team noted that a number of operators included in the SIGAL database did not appear in the official regional lists. This w

As regards registration of transporters and traders, a Ministerial Decree was issued in 2011 highlighting the obligation for these business operators to notify their activities to the departmental authorities and, in 2013, another instruction was issued to remind the local competent authorities to update the lists of establishment handling ABP/DP with registered transporters and traders. Moreover, according to representatives from DGAL, a meeting with various associations of business operators was held in 2011 where, among other things, this obligation was clarified. However, the audit team noted that in many cases, transporters and traders did not appear in the official regional lists or th

The system of official controls covers a number of operators dealing with ABP/DP, however its effectiveness is negatively affected by the following: a) traders and transporters which are not subject to official controls without a risk based justification and, b) organisation of official controls which only allows superficial checks that cannot ensure enough attention to the risk of diversion or misuse of ABP/DP. 6 5.3 TRACEABILITY OF ABP/DP: OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS Legal requirements Article 41, 43 and 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; Articles 17(1), 25 and 32 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011; Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. 5.3.

paragraph_text: Official controls on ABP/DP are carried out in accordance with the national plan and using a standard checklist but, the fact that there is a very limited confirmation of arrival of consignments of ABP/DP traded from other Member States and that checks on traceability requirements are often carried out in a superficial manner or not at all, negatively affects the ability of the competent authorities to detect any diversion or misuse of ABP/DP (see conclusion 16). 5.4 INFORMATION ON THE CHAIN OF PAP TO BE USED IN AQUACULTURE FEED

As indicated in the National Inspection Programme, the frequency of inspections of business operators handling ABP/DP is risk-based. It is determined by applying a formula which, among other things, takes into account the theoretical risk of the plant (on the basis of the nature of the activities and the products handled), the volume of the product placed in the market and the performance of the business operator (determined by the inspector in charge of the official controls). The resulting frequency of inspections may vary from once per year to once every four years. In the Départements visited, the audit team noted that Category 3 processing plants were inspected generally every three yea

In the Départements visited, inspections were carried out at the planned frequencies and were largely in line with the frequency-criteria established by the National Inspection Programme. However, the audit team noted that the National Inspection Programme does 5 not include some registered business operators, namely transporters and traders handling ABP/DP, without any solid risk-based justifications being provided by the competent authorities and, as a result, these business operators are not subject to planned official controls (see also paragraph 20). This is not in line with requirements laid down by Article 3(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

A standard checklist is available for officials to carry out inspections in ABP plants. This checklist consists of a list of generic items applicable to all processing plants. In addition to that, a guide released in 2009 provides further details and legal clarifications. According to the competent authorities the checklist and the guide are going to be updated soon to take into account, among other things, the relevant changes in the legislation. The audit team noted that, although the current checklist (and the draft of the new one) is largely comprehensive, it contains only two-three generic items related to the traceability of ABP/DP. As a result, officials are only required to confirm,

In a trader importing fishmeal visited, the audit team reviewed the documentation of three imported consignments of fishmeal in bulk and noted that for one of them no analysis showing the absence of unauthorised constituents of animal origin accompanied the consignment as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and set out in Section C, Chapter III of its Annex IV. The competent authorities stated that for such consignments of fishmeal, which had been released for free circulation, no analysis was available. The audit team noted that the competent authorities did not know this deficiency because the operator had never been inspected (see paragraph 12). 7 5.3.2 Operator obligatio

However, it was noted the following: a) the points related to the origin and the traceability of ABP/DP were not checked in a regular manner or, when checked, it was done in a superficial way. The system for certificates of competence does provide for the required exam with a good emphasis of practical situations through its use of pictures in the assessment. BOs have used the good practice guides effectively, but both these and the exam are not adequately covering tasks in slaughterhouses which present particular risks for animal welfare such as slaughter without stunning. 5.2 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 3, 41 and 42 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. With the transfer of responsibility for animal welfare to the regions, from 1 January 2015 the regions' animal welfare departments are responsible for organising training and exams and awarding certificates of competence for the activities referred to in Article 7(2) of the Regulation, as envisaged by its Article 21.

Pending this change, national level training and exams were organised as follows: · There is a specific university-level course for AWOs. It was noted that all but one of the AWOs met by the audit team had attended this course. As there is not yet legal basis for this course, the CA are not checking that the AWOs have attended this course. · The other slaughterhouse personnel can undergo training organised by a training institute or in-house training organised by the AWO of the slaughterhouse. In the latter case there has to be an independent exam. For this an online exam programme has recently been created which can be accessed from a computer in the slaughterhouse. It was noted that certificates awarded to those who take the online exam do not differentiate between tasks. A CCA representative explained that the exam covers all activities as it was difficult to make this differentiation using the on line format used to develop the exam. Exam participants have to respond to pictures rather than plain written questions. On exam questions and topics set in Annex IV to the Regulation, it was noted that when an applicant worked in a slaughterhouse that practiced slaughter without stunning there were no precise questions/pictures regarding this practice, where both the practices and the monitoring of the risks for animal welfare are very different compared to

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The checklists for controls are well designed with a weighting factor reflecting the seriousness of non-compliance, however the data produced from the checks is not being adequately used to plan the subsequent controls on the basis of the business operators past records, or to analyse if the weighting factors for the various non- compliances were appropriate.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Centrally, FASFC is not using data such as Foodnet as effectively as it could to ensure requirements are met and to better prioritise checks. In general, analysis of the results of previous checks has not been carried out. In particular, the results of prioritising checks on slaughter without stunning were not available. 6 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON BUSINESS OPERATORS' OBLIGATIONS Legal requirements Articles 8, 9 and 10(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 5(1)(c) of, and Section I of Annex I to, Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Articles 6 and 17 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. Findings

The results of the OVs' official controls were collated in the Foodnet database in such a way that they can be analysed. However, FAFSC has not yet used this data to evaluate and review the system of official checks to ensure that requirements are met and to better prioritise checks on such issues as broiler monitoring, problems reported from checklists and the effectiveness of enforcement in different provinces (see also sections 5.4, 5.5 and 5.6).

Every question on the OV electronic checklist is subject to a weighting factor reflecting the seriousness of non-compliance (see also sections 5.3 and 5.5). 5 · The weighting of the seriousness of non-compliance cases in the checklists triggers action when an individual case of non-compliance scores 10 or when more than 20 % of the items on the checklist are non-compliant. · For example, the lack of signs on lairage pens showing their capacity and the animals' time of arrival scores low in terms of the significance of the non-compliance as there were other ways that the CA checked overnight stays and overstocking.

The competent authorities have the necessary elements to maintain and implement a system of official controls as required by Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 which is enhanced by the implementation of the quality management system in place for official controls and the good co-operation and co-ordination between SFVS and territorial SFVS; however, the effectiveness of the system is negatively affected by a number of transporters or traders not being registered as ABP operators before engaging into activities in the ABP/DP chain and consequently not being controlled. Official controls are well documented, planned on the basis of a risk assessment and executed as planned. Weaknesses arising from t

As regards transporters, the audit team noted that in some cases the transporters indicated on the commercial documents were not identical to the ones indicated on the CMR way bill. Some of the transporters mentioned on the CMR way bills seen by the audit team during the visits to operators were not registered as ABP transporters.

In the pet food plant visited, an inspector had identified during a previous official control that a transporter used by a supplier was not a registered ABP operator. The pet food plant was requested to stop using this transporter. The audit team noted that this approach does not prevent the transporter from continuing to transport ABP for other operators without being registered. The inspector confirmed that this transporter was never used again to deliver products to the pet food plant, however, he could not say whether the transporter is now registered as an ABP operator or not.

In one of the paper traders visited, the audit team noted that the operator engaged in the trade of ABP/DP before being registered by the competent authorities; three consignments 5 were traded prior to becoming registered. In the traders visited for instance, it was noted that in order not to disclose their suppliers of materials, traders were generating a pair of fictitious commercial documents in which they appeared as either the destination or origin of a consignment, although the product neither ever arrived to their premises nor to Lithuania (in cases where the producer was located in another Member State). Information that would allow the origin of the product to be identified (e.g. Producer approval numbers, 8 batch numbers or container seal numbers) was omitted

In one case for instance, the trader included his Lithuanian registration code in the field foreseen for the approval code of the producer. In other cases, commercial documents indicated a different country of destination than the actual plant of destination. In others, a competent authority from a different Member State than the one responsible for the consignor of the product was indicated. Nevertheless, in some cases, in particular in transporters, traders and plants carrying out intermediate activities, these are carried out and recorded rather superficially, which results in non-compliances being overlooked. 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON TRACEABILITY REQUIREMENTS ALONG THE CHAIN Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1

The audit team noted that in some cases, the time spent on individual inspections is reduced in order that the required number of inspections can be carried out, leading to some tasks being completed in a superficial manner or not being completed. For example, in one transporter and two traders visited, the inspection reports indicated less

In the said plant, stock balance checks were almost impossible. The audit team compared the in-coming and the out-going quantities and found that in certain periods of the year the operator appeared to have more incoming material than could be stored on site. National rules foresee dedicated transport for food or ABP/DP. However, in a transporter visited, the audit team noted that it could not be demonstrated that these requirements were fulfilled and that fats considered as food or ABP were actually kept separately, especially during reloading (the operator could not provide any evidence where reloading took place). This increases the risk that ABP could be diverted to the food chain. These findings were overlooked by official controls. In addition, the audit team noted that the official controls in 7 this establishment were particularly short (less than one hour), which would make a thorough covering of all points on the check-list impossible.

According to a trader of fats visited, his company was the only client of a transport company for the transport of fats. The audit team noted that the number of cistern vehicles owned by the specific transport company and registered as ABP vehicles was very high in comparison to the quantities of fats transported for the trader. In light of the national requirement for dedicated ABP vehicles, no plausible explanation could be provided about the usage of all ABP cistern vehicles which appear to be idle all year round. The audit team identified that official controls on ABP in slaughterhouses and cutting plants overlooked that certain slaughterhouses or cutting plants were in several cases issuing commercial documents which are used for food products, although the materials being dispatched were destined for an ABP plant and thus the intended use was ABP and not food. This issue was also identified by an RVI inspector during a supervisory official control over DVI inspectors (who overlooked this issue). The RVI has sent letters to the DVIs concerned requiring the proper use of commercial documents in accordance with Article 17 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

The system in place for the organisation, planning and implementation of official controls of the ABP/DP chain relies largely on the federal states putting in place adequate measures to ensure the relevant EU requirements are fulfilled. However, in the absence of measures to encourage a harmonised approach to these tasks, substantial differences were seen in the two federal states visited. While one (Bavaria) had put in place a mostly satisfactory system of risk-based controls for most operators in the ABP/DP chain, many deficiencies were identified in the effectiveness of the systems put in place by the districts authorities in the other federal state visited (NW) and there were insufficien

Although operators generally make efforts to comply with the traceability requirements for ABP/DP, there is a lack of consistency in the performance of official controls on these aspects, which, in one federal state visited resulted in deficiencies being overlooked. This also applies to the use of TRACES, consignments handled by paper traders or those traded to and from other Member States where there is limited information available regarding their fate. These factors undermine the ability of the competent authorities to ensure that operators fully comply with the traceability requirements for ABP/DP throughout the country. 10 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system in place for the organisation,

The organisation of official controls remains largely as described in the country profile (see section 4.1). Within their territories, each of the 16 federal states has exclusive competence for the organisation, planning and execution of the official controls and supervision of ABP/DP required by Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

There were a number of important differences in the approach taken in the two federal states in the organisation, planning and performance of official controls on the ABP/DP chain and so these are covered separately: The following was observed in Bavaria: a. A system of risk-based official controls for ABP/DP plants and operators has been put in place, as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which takes into account a number of criteria to determine the basic frequency of official controls (above a set minimum) to be carried out. However, in the absence of measures to encourage a harmonised approach to these tasks, substantial differences were seen in the two federal states visited. While one (Bavaria) had put in place a mostly satisfactory system of risk-based controls for most operators in the ABP/DP chain, many deficiencies were identified in the effectiveness of the systems put in place by the districts authorities in the other federal state visited (NW) and there were insufficien

This also applies to the use of TRACES, consignments handled by paper traders or those traded to and from other Member States where there is limited information available regarding their fate. Representatives of BMEL informed the audit team that traders which are shown in the commercial documents as being the final destination for ABP/DP even though they do not actually receive the goods (hereafter: paper traders) have not been registered in accordance with Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 as this activity is considered to be outside the scope of the ABP Regulations. In the federal states visited, such traders were not included in the scope of official controls on the ABP/DP chain.

In all plants visited, operators were aware of the requirements relating to the registration or approval of their suppliers or customers. The inspectors carrying out official controls in the plants visited were actively cross-checking that the operators and plants shown on commercial documents (including those located in other Member States) were approved or registered as required. The audit team checked the registration/approval status of several operators appearing on commercial documents and noted that all but the paper traders were registered or approved in accordance with Articles 23 or 24 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, respectively.

At a storage plant for derived products visited in NW, the audit team noted that several consignments of horn chips which, according to the operator, originated in a third country, were received without being accompanied by a commercial document. These consignments were found to have been imported by a trader based in a federal state other than the ones visited in this audit, and then stored in a different federal state before being dispatched to the plant in NW without commercial documents. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in Annex XIV, Chapter II, Section 12 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. Carriers have been re- classified as low risk and have to be inspected once every three years. In addition, the audit team noted good practices by certain officials, who undertook initiatives to better take into account the risk of diversion or misuse of ABP/DP. Nevertheless, the otherwise robust system ensuring that ABP/DP are only used or disposed of in permitted ways is weakened by i) the fact that the said initiatives cannot be considered an integral part of the system for official controls, and ii) gaps in verifying the arrival of consignments of ABP/DP traded in from other Member States. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Ov

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: The low vaccination coverage on positive holdings in the area of Trás-os-Montes, compromise the overall effectiveness of vaccination in this area. As a consequence the disease frequently occurs in non-immunised animals.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: Lack of reliable information on all locations where animals are kept on a permanent or temporary basis prevents full traceability of animals, as well as enforcement and verification of movement restrictions. As not all common pastures are registered, the enforcement of movement restrictions and verification of their effectiveness cannot be fully ensured. Although tracing of movements of animals to common pastures is part of an epidemiological investigation, this information is of limited value because not all new brucellosis outbreaks have been investigated. Failure to fully inforce the movement 14 restrictions and traceability favours the spread and persistence of infections in areas with h

The CCA has established information systems that support continuous monitoring and evaluation of implementation of the BMEP measures. Desk-top evaluations allow to monitor the indicators of the progress of implementation of the programme (such as number of animals sampled, tested, vaccinated, observation of deadlines). The absence of checks on-the-spot, to evaluate implementation of measures carried out by OPPs (such as sampling and vaccination) as well as lack of verification of implementation of measures such as movement restrictions and cleaning and disinfection on infected holding, preclude the CCA from evaluating the quality, completeness and effectiveness of the specific BMEP measures.
In the area of Trás-os-Montes, on a significant number of positive holdings where vaccination coverage was investigated, animals have not been vaccinated as required by Point 4.4.7 of the BMEP.

Movement restrictions are largely applied according to Point 4.4.9 of the BMEP. However, full control and enforcement of movement restrictions of animals from BMNF herds to common pastures is not implemented in areas where 90% of holdings are dependent on common pastures on a daily basis.

There is a lack of procedures to verify on-the-spot implementation of certain control and eradication measures (for example sampling, vaccination, cleaning and disinfection) in order to evaluate their quality, completeness and effectiveness as well as to ensure corrective actions when needed. Thus, the CA cannot demonstrate that activities and measures are implemented as described in the approved programme contrary to the requirement in Article 15.1(a) of Commission Implementing Decision 2013/722/EU.

label_heading: Conclusion on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The documented procedures and instructions in place are sufficient for BIP staff to perform the controls correctly and consistently once the consignments are notified. However, an internal procedure to ensure that consignments will be presented for veterinary checks is not in place, which increases the possibility of a consignment entering without veterinary checks. 5.2 BIP FACILITIES AND EQUIPMENT Legal requirements Articles 4, 10 and Annex II of Regulation (EC) 882/2004; Article 6(2)(a) and (b) of, and Annex A to Council Directive 91/496/EEC; Articles 3 and 4 of Commission Decision 97/794/EC; Regulation (EC) 1/2005.
