label_heading: Conclusion on BIP facilities and equipment
paragraph_text: The facilities proposed cannot ensure that standards for animal welfare can be maintained for dogs, cats or ferrets, where there is a need for housing. The BIP facilities are adequate for receiving and checking consignments of insects. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The proposed BIP will be integrated into the existing national import control system. Allocation of tasks, responsibilities and duties, training and instructions will support the correct implementation of the official import controls. The absence of an agreement with Customs to ensure that goods will be presented for veterinary checks increases the possibility of a consignment entering without veterinary checks. At the time of the audit,

The inspection room is suitable for different species of animals. However, it is not equipped with the necessary tools that would allow staff to perform identity and physical checks (e.g. refrigerator for storing samples, equipment to restrain, equipment to check their identification i.e. microchip readers), contrary to the requirements laid down in Articles 3 and 4 of Decision 97/794/EC.

The existing isolation spaces (kennels) to detain a typical consignment of the species expected are located outside the BIP facilities, near the tarmac. The distance between the kennels and the runaway of the airport is insufficient to mitigate adequately the noise levels. The kennels are not suitable for puppies, small dogs, cats or ferrets: they do not provide lighting, ventilation and/or temperature control. Overall, the isolation facilities proposed cannot ensure that the environmental conditions are adequate to avoid distress to the animals, contrary to the requirements of Regulation (EC) 1/2005.

Contracts and procedures are in place, as required by points 8 and 10 of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC, as follows: for cleaning and disinfection of the facilities of the BIP, laboratories where the samples have to be sent, disposal of carcasses/dead animals, and additional veterinary surgeon services. There is no contract for pest control in the area where the kennels are located, outside the building (see finding 16).

The legal framework to enable the full implementation of the revised measures introduced by CID 2015/789/EU, and the approval of the revised AP, was not in place at the time of the audit. There is no timeline for its adoption by the MIPAAF, or implementation, although all of the measures in that CID were applicable from 21 May 2015.

The SA stated that a new Decree would need to be adopted, to establish the necessary legal framework for the application of CID 2015/789/EU. They stated that it is intended that the new Decree will contain additional requirements, beyond those in CID 2015/789/EU. A new AP will be issued following the adoption of the Decree. The SA was not able to provide a timeline for completion of the process. In the interim period though, the Decree of 26 September 2014 remains in force, i.e. the measures introduced by CID 2015/789/EU will not be implemented (with the exception of the revision to the demarcation of the area, detailed in paragraph 10 above).

label_heading: Conclusions on Relevant National Legislation and Provisions
paragraph_text: National laws necessary to implement legally binding European Union acts relevant to this audit have been adopted by the CA. However, the fact that the National Regulation does not incorporate all relevant EU requirements creates confusion when it comes to their implementation by CBs. In addition, some of the EU requirements further developed by the National Regulation are not in line with EU Regulations. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent Authorities, Control Authorities and Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 27(1), 27(4), 27(4)(a), 27(14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889

Even though the current version of the National Regulation is dated June 2014, it does not incorporate some of the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, in force since 1 January 2014. Although it is mentioned in the National Regulation that all EU Regulations are directly applicable, this inaccuracy may cause that CBs to not include in their procedures some of the missing EU requirements, as CBs may use the National Regulation rather than the directly applicable EU legislation as a reference when drafting their procedures. This was noted to be the case by the audit team at the headquarters of one of the CBs, which referred in its procedures to the National Regulation and to Regulation

In addition, the National Regulation includes some requirements which are not in line with EU Regulations, such as the delegation to CBs of the power to grant derogations on the renewal of flocks and herds and the possibility to grant derogations on housing conditions and stocking densities, which are already phased out in the EU Regulations since 31 December 2013. Although these derogations had not been granted in recent years, they are not in line with EU Regulations.

label_heading: Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of CBs
paragraph_text: Annual supervision is carried out by the CU on the delegated CBs. However, it is not adequate to verify the effectiveness of controls as it failed to identify and address the systematic severe shortcomings in the performance of the CBs.

label_heading: Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of CBs
paragraph_text: Reports issued by Accreditation Bodies are not taken into account when the CU carries out supervision of CBs.

However, although accreditation is a compulsory requirement for approval, the CU does not take into account the accreditation reports issued by Accreditation Bodies when carrying out the annual supervision to CBs, which is not in line with Article 92c(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. At the time of the audit, the CU had not requested any accreditation reports on the seven CBs whose headquarters are based in other MSs, nor 6 had the CU established cooperation arrangements for supervision with the CAs of those MSs. The CU requested the IABSA to provide, but had not received to date the reports on the four CBs whose headquarters are in Bulgaria (see paragraph 9).

However, the systematic shortcomings observed by the audit team, described in several sections of this report, were not noted by the CU, inter alia: CBs do not appear to have the infrastructure required and sufficient staff to adequately carry out their tasks. Timing and preparation of inspections are often not adequate Documented procedures used by CBs were very basic and checklists did not contain all relevant requirements or criteria to be checked during inspections; Risk analysis applied by both CBs did not serve as an adequate basis to determine the nature and frequency of visits; CB2 did not carry out adequate annual inspections to subcontracted operators. CB2 did not carry out any add

The CU does not adequately assess the information received from CBs in their annual reports. For example, CB1 reported in 2014 that 26 samples tested positive for the presence of unauthorised PPPs, while CB2 reported no positive results. The audit team noted that 60% of the samples were taken by CB2 from the same product, and in most cases, not at operators with high risk profiles. Moreover, CB1 notified in the 2015 annual report a total number of irregularities three times higher than the number notified by CB2, which had not reported any major irregularities in at least the last three years. This obvious difference between the results of controls did not provoke any reaction from the CU.

The exchange of communication between CBs is not always adequate when operators move CB, and it is not ensured that the operator´s control file and the reports referred to in Article 63(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 are transferred from the previous CB to the subsequent CB. In addition, the notification of the changes made by CBs to the CU is not adequate as it cannot be ensured that the CU is aware of such change having taken place.

When operators move CB, the relevant elements of the operators´ file and the reports referred to in the second subparagraph of Article 63(2) must be transferred from the previous CB to the subsequent CB. However, the audit team noted several cases where this relevant information was not transferred. This is not in line with Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The change must also be notified to the CU by the CBs concerned. The CBs do not notify directly to the CU but by uploading the information on the operators onto the list instead. This approach was proved to be inadequate as the CU was unaware of the change. The audit team noted several cases when operators had signed a contract w

label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: CBs do not necessarily require the operators to submit important compulsory information, such as on the precautionary measures, or do not adequately asses it. In addition, the number of staff available for certification and control tasks is very limited. As a result, the timing and preparation of the annual and additional visits are not always adequate, which strongly undermines the effectiveness of controls.

Both CBs doubled the number of operators under their control in recent years. This huge increase was not accompanied by a proportionate readjustment in their resources, including staff, to carry out control and certification tasks. The ratio of inspections per inspector/year is very high, especially in certain periods in the year. The majority of operators in Bulgaria are plant producers, which narrows the timeframe to execute the inspections. As a result, a significant percentage of inspections are not carried out at the most suitable time, which renders these controls ineffective. This is not in line with Article 5(2)(b)(i) and (ii) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted seve

label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: Risk analysis as carried out by CBs does not serve as a good basis to determine the nature and frequency of the visits to operators. Compulsory requirements such as quantities or past records are not adequately taken into account, not all operators are subject to risk assessment and not all subcontracted activities subject to the same level of controls.

CB2 does not carry out the same type of annual inspection to all operators. Subcontracted operators, which carry out important core activities such as production, are not subject to the same level of control from the CB as certified operators. The CB uses a different checklist and carries out only short inspections, with significant scope limitations, in comparison to those carried out on certified operators. The CB stated that they considered subcontracted operators less risky operators as they were under the internal control of the client to whom they sell their products. This is the approach followed by CBs when issuing certification to Producer Groups in developing countries, but in MSs

Both CBs use risk analysis procedures to select the operators for additional visits and sampling. Several criteria are used, such as past irregularities, time in the control system, number and types of crops grown, multiple activities carried out, parallel production and processing of organic and conventional products. The criteria are put together in several groups, which may score a maximum of five points. The scoring of the different groups is aggregated, and according to the final score, operators are allocated into risk groups.

The audit team noted the following weaknesses in the risk analysis implemented by both CBs: Some operators such as small farmers who do not market, and small traders selling only pre-packed products, are not subject to risk assessment by CB2. This is not in line with Article 65(2) and 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, which establishes that the selection of the operators where samples have to be taken and the random control visits shall be based on the general evaluation of the risk of non-compliance with the organic production rules. Quantities produced are not taken into account, which is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EU) No 889/2008. Operators with major non-compliance

At the time of the DG Health and Food Safety audit, less than 0.050% of operators under the control of CB1 and CB2 were classified in the highest risk category. The majority of operators were placed in the second lowest risk category by CB1 while CB2 only had two risk categories, meaning that more than 99,9% of operators were placed in the lowest risk category. The audit team observed a number of cases where operators with low risk profiles (e.g. small fully organic farmer with no past irregularities) were placed in the same risk category as operators with a high risk profile (e.g. large producer and processor of conventional and organic products with past irregularities). label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: CBs do not necessarily require the operators to submit important compulsory information, such as on the precautionary measures, or do not adequately asses it. In addition, the number of staff available for certification and control tasks is very limited. As a result, the timing and preparation of the annual and additional visits are not always adequate, which strongly undermines the effectiveness of controls.

The inadequate timing may also be caused by insufficient knowledge of the operators to be visited. CB1 does not request the operators to submit information on all of their undertakings, but only on the parcels or units subject to organic certification. Precautionary measures, which are important prerequisites to comply with the organic production rules, are not required to be submitted to the CB either. This is not in line with Article 63(1) (a) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. As a result, the CB does not verify the description of the units and the precautionary measures. This is not in line with Article 63(2) of the same Regulation. CB1 had not noted that, for more than one year, on

CB2 receives from their operators the information referred to in Article 63(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. However, the audit team noted cases where it was not used adequately. As an example, the CB manager evaluated the information on the operator and signalled points of attention for the inspector to focus on during the inspection. The annual inspection was planned after both the organic and conventional plots had been harvested. This rendered the inspection ineffective. The inspector was requested to check that the organic operator had sold the harvest as conventional rather than focusing on the only risky point, which was the presence of a conventional neighbouring plot.

label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: The number of additional visits and unannounced visits does not meet the minimum requirements in EU Regulations. The selection of operators for additional visits and sampling is not always carried out risk-based. Moreover, additional visits are not primarily carried out unannounced in all cases and annual visits are always announced, which is not in line with EU Regulations. 13 5.2.4 Controls of Operators Legal Requirements Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Title II of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Title IV of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Article 65 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

CB1 carries out the additional visits primarily unannounced, which is in line with EU Regulations. However, the number of additional visits does not reach the minimum 10% of the total number of operators, which is not in line with Article 92c(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The total number of unannounced visits is also not reached, which is not in line with Article 92c(2)(c) of the same Regulation. Moreover, the audit team noted that most of the additional inspections carried out by CB1 in 2014 were concentrated in November and December. This undermines the effectiveness of the inspections as no relevant activity was carried out at that time in plant producers. CB2 could not provide a

Both CBs have documented procedures in place with the aim of ensuring consistency of controls. However, the level of detail is not adequate to provide inspectors with adequate guidance. Checklists do not include the verification of records showing the effectiveness of cleaning, the results of verification at reception and the balance between input/output. Operators are not required to keep such records and consequently, most operators do not keep them, thus not providing evidence that the relevant requirements have been complied with. In addition, units where non-organic products are produced or kept are not necessarily subject to the minimum control requirements.

Both CBs have documented procedures to carry out controls. The main document used for the inspections is the report template, which also serves as a checklist for the inspectors. A copy of the report is given to operators, including the description of non- compliances and deadlines for the operators to apply corrective measures, which are followed-up by inspectors during the following inspection. However, the checklists used by the CBs did not provide the basis for assurance on the following important aspects as they failed to cover: Records showing the effectiveness of cleaning measures in facilities where parallel processing of conventional and organic foodstuffs take place, as required by

This lack of adequate documented procedures is also not in line with Article 27(6)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, which establishes that the standard control procedure of CBs must contain a detailed description of the control measures and precautions that the body undertakes to impose on operators subject to its control.

When such records or, any other document, such as maps showing the areas surrounding beehives are present, they are not adequately verified by inspectors to ensure compliance of operators with EU requirements. In addition, inspectors do not notice gross non- compliances regarding relevant requirements such as prohibited dehorning practices, inadequate husbandry and animal welfare conditions, proving such inspections to be ineffective. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 23(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Regulation. Title III of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Article 27(13) of Council Regulation (EC) No

When records and accounting documents were available at the operators, inspectors did not adequately check them and other relevant requirements were often overlooked: CB1 inspectors signed and stamped the internal records checked and made a 14 reference in the report and attached a copy of these records to the report. One inspector from CB1 stated that he always stamps and signs on the records. This could be considered as a good audit practice as the performance of the inspectors can be traced back and subject to later evaluation. However, this inspector had not checked the records on the use of fertilizers and PPPs during the previous inspection, as there were no stamps or signatures on any

Labelling and traceability controls are regularly performed by the CA and CBs. Controls carried out by the CA are overall adequate. However, controls by CBs are not always exhaustive. Inspectors do not either require the operators to keep records on the identity checks carried out or to keep the products identified at all times allowing for establishing the link between the processing steps. Nevertheless, the outcome of the traceability exercise carried out during the audit was satisfactory for the products selected. As regards labelling checks, CBs do not systematically verify that the approved labels are used on the final products and it cannot be ensured that labelling of the products com

CBs approved in advance the labels used by operators. CBs receive and assess the format of the labels, which can only be used after the CB notify the operators. However, the audit team noted that in some cases, the labels used were not fully in line with the EU Regulations (e. g. blue logo used on a white background or letters difficult to read due to a transparent background). In two cases, products not satisfying the requirements of the EU Regulations bore labels including the term "bio" in the trademarks, which is not in line with Article 23(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

CBs carry out labelling and traceability checks during inspections at operators. Checklists used by CBs contain a specific aide-memoir for labelling and traceability checks to be performed at operators. However, the audit team noted that checks were not always adequate: Inspectors did not request or did not adequately verify records on the identity checks to be performed by operators. This is not in line with Article 66 of Regulation (EC) 889/2008 which establishes that operators shall keep documentary records proving that they have performed identity checks on the purchased products to verify that the labels or invoices contain the information referred to in Article 33 of Regulation (EC) 88

label_heading: Conclusions on Sampling and Laboratory Analysis
paragraph_text: Not all CBs reach the minimum number of samples to be taken for the analysis of substances not authorised in organic production.

label_heading: Conclusions on Sampling and Laboratory Analysis
paragraph_text: It cannot be ensured that the selection of the operators to be sampled is risk-based, that the quantities sent to the laboratories are sufficient and that samples are preserved, at least in the case of perishable products for the detection of PPPs. These deficiencies undermine the reliability of results. 5.2.7 Exceptional production rules and other derogations. Legal Requirements Article 29 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and Annex IX of the same Regulation. Sections 2 to 4 of Chapter 6 of Title II of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Article 22(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Findings

The selection of the operators by CB2 was not risk-based because there are only two operators in the highest risk category and the operators in the lower risk categories are randomly selected. The audit team noted several cases where samples were taken from operators with a low risk profile. In addition, around 60% of samples in 2014 and 40% in 2015 were taken from the same product, which is not representative of the activities controlled by the CB. This is not in line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) 889/2008, which establishes that the selection of operators for sampling shall be based on the general evaluation of the risk of non-compliance with organic rules.

The audit team noted that in several cases, CB2 took a good number of samples at one processor on the same day and counted them as having been taken from the suppliers of the raw materials concerned. As a result of this practice, the total number of samples was artificially increased by 50% in 2014 and 2015. Without this practice, the CB did not reach the minimum number of samples required. In addition, six out of 11 CBs reported to the CA that they had taken during 2014 a number of samples which did not reach the minimum required, with two CBs not taking any sample at all. This is not in 20 line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2004, which establishes that the number of samples

paragraph_text: It cannot be ensured that the selection of the operators to be sampled is risk-based, that the quantities sent to the laboratories are sufficient and that samples are preserved, at least in the case of perishable products for the detection of PPPs. Instructions by CB2 refer to the fulfilment of the requirements of Directive 2002/63/EC, which establishes the methodology to be followed for the testing of PPPs, including quantities to be sent to the laboratory for each type of product and conditions for the preservation of samples. However, the audit team checked several files and noted that the CB often did not follow its own procedure. Samples were sent to laboratories in quantities smaller than indicated in the Directive. In addition, samples were not preserved, which is not in line with Section 4.6

Instructions issued by CB1 specify the equipment to be used and also the techniques to ensure the representativeness of the sample. The instructions do not require that the samples of perishable products are kept cool when delivered to the laboratories, which is not in line with Section 4.6 of the Annex of Directive 2002/63/EC. The audit team observed the procedure for taking samples followed by CB1. The inspector stated that a cooling box is used to transport the samples to the headquarters of the CB. However, the sample had to be sent to a laboratory in another MS and the CB does not use specific containers to preserve the sample cooled. In addition, the inspector used a plastic jar provid

label_heading: Conclusions on Sampling and Laboratory Analysis
paragraph_text: CBs have sampling programmes in place for the detection of substances not authorised in organic production. Action is taken by CBs in all cases where analytical results show any presence of unauthorised substance. Laboratories used are accredited to ISO 17025. However, laboratories are not designated by the CU, who does not check during supervision whether the analytical scope of the laboratories used by CBs is adequate. In addition, it is not ensured that laboratories carrying out official controls take part on the proficiency tests organised by the National Reference laboratory.

Laboratories are not designated by the CU in advance and during the supervision of CBs, the CU does not check that laboratories have the appropriate scope to carry out the tests requested by CBs. The CU argued that the only requirement established in Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 is that laboratories used by CBs operate in accordance with the standards referred to in Article 12(2) of the same Regulation (ISO 17025). However, the same Article also establishes that these laboratories may only be designated by the CU if they operate and are assessed and accredited to that standard. In addition, Article 12(3) establishes that such accreditation and assessment may relate to individu

As the CU does not designate the laboratories analysing official samples, it does not notify them to the National Reference Laboratory, thus not ensuring that the laboratories take part in the proficiency tests organised at national level, as indicated in Article 33(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on Sampling and Laboratory Analysis
paragraph_text: In addition, the delegation of tasks to CBs does not define who is responsible to decide on the minimum range of products to be tested. As a result, the CBs do not request 22 laboratories to test PPPs which are commonly used in the EU.

CB1 only requests the laboratories to use multi-residues methods. This is not adequate as some PPPs commonly used in the EU (for example Glyphosate and Chlormequat) can 21 only be detected by using methods that are specific for the relevant PPP. The sample sheet used by CB2 caters for other PPPs but Glyphosate is not included either. The delegation of tasks to CBs does not describe who is responsible to decide on the range of PPPs to be tested, taking into account relevant information available. This is not in line with Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Both CBs use laboratories accredited to ISO Guide 17025, which establishes the general requirements for the sampling and calibrating laboratories. The audit team checked several laboratory results and noted that the scope of the laboratories was adequate for the methods used and substances tested. However, CB2 does not systematically check that the scope of the chosen laboratory is appropriate. The audit team noted that CB2 kept an old version of the accreditation certificate of the laboratory often used by the CB. The audit team also noted that in one case, the results submitted by the laboratory referred to physical-chemical analysis, which had not been requested. This was not noted by the

label_heading: Conclusions on Exceptional Production Rules and Other Derogations
paragraph_text: The National Regulation establishes the derogations and exceptions to organic rules to be granted by the CU and CBs. It also includes provisions for certain derogations which, although not granted in recent years, are not in line with, or already phased out in EU Regulations.

label_heading: Conclusions on Exceptional Production Rules and Other Derogations
paragraph_text: The CU correctly grant derogations for the applications received. However, it cannot be ensured that operators use conventional seeds only after a derogation is granted by CBs. Moreover, CBs often do not request operators to prove the unavailability in the market of the same organic variety.

According to the National Regulation, the CU has the competence to grant derogations, except derogations on the use of conventional seeds and propagating material, which had been delegated to CBs, in line with EU Regulations. The National Regulation also includes provisions for certain derogations which, although not granted in recent years, are not in line with, or already phased out in EU Regulations. For example, CBs may grant derogations for the renewal of herds and flocks and for the introduction of non- organic female mammals, which is not in line with Article 42 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The National Regulation also foresees the possibility to grant derogations on housing condit

All derogations granted by CBs concerned the use of conventional seeds. When examining applications submitted, CBs must check whether operators justify the use of the conventional seed and also prove that no organic seed was available at that time in the market. At the time of the DG Health and Food Safety audit, there were eight organic suppliers registered in the seed database to supply organic seed and other 23 propagating material (see paragraph 105). The audit team noted that in several cases, operators had used a conventional seed without applying for a derogation, contrary to Article 45(6) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The audit team also noted that some derogations were granted in

label_heading: Conclusions on Exceptional Production Rules and Other Derogations
paragraph_text: CBs do not adequately check that operators applying any exceptional rule have been authorised in advance, and do not check the conditions under which the rules are 24 implemented in practice. 5.2.8 Imports of Products from Organic Production Legal Requirements Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Chapter 3 of Title III of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008. Annexes II, III, V and VI of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008. Findings

In cases where operators apply any exceptional rule, CBs must check whether they have been granted any derogation in advance, and also whether the derogation is adequately applied (e.g. to use only conventional seeds not treated with PPPs). However, the audit team noted that, in some cases, the inspectors were not aware of any derogation having been granted and did not adequately check whether operators apply any exceptional rule (see last bullet point in paragraph 48 related to systematic dehorning in a dairy farm). label_heading: Conclusions Measures in cases of irregularities and infringements
paragraph_text: The CU has adopted and notified to CBs a catalogue of infringements and corresponding measures to be applied by CBs. However, most of the measures applied are neither dissuasive nor proportionate, and therefore ineffective to ensure compliance of the 28 operators with organic requirements.

The CU has adopted and notified to CBs a catalogue of enforcement measures to be applied in cases of non-compliances, in line with Article 92(d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, although its adoption was late3. The measures are contained in Annex III to the National Regulation.4 The measures range from a simple remark or warning to total withdrawal of the operators from the system, depending on the severity of the non- compliance. However, most of the measures foreseen are not adequate to ensure compliance of operators with organic requirements. For the following non-compliances, operators will only receive warnings with no suspension of the certification, even if no corrective action is take

The sanction catalogue does not adequately take into account the repetition of non- compliances, and for some of them (for example dehorning without prior authorisation) operators may receive a "remark" the first year, a "corrective instruction" the second and a "warning" the third. After 24 months with no repetition of the irregularity, past records are disregarded. No monetary sanctions are foreseen, even in cases where no corrective action may be taken (for example when non-compliant product has already been sold as organic and it cannot be recalled from the market).This is not in line with Article 55(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, which establishes that measures must be proportionate

CBs follow the national sanction catalogue. For the non-compliances noted by the audit team during the visits at operators (see bullet points in paragraph 48) CB1 only reported remarks to the operators concerned and the certification was granted in all cases with no need of corrective measures to be applied by the operators. The CB stated that the non- compliance would be followed-up during the annual inspection in 2016.

One of the few measures found to have consequences for the operators´ certification were those applied by CB1 concerning the use of unauthorised PPPs (see paragraph 71). However, the sanction catalogue only foresees the prohibition of operators from marketing any organic products for short periods (up to 12 months) if they are found to use unauthorised substances during several consecutive years.

label_heading: Conclusions Measures in cases of irregularities and infringements
paragraph_text: The CU has not established documented procedures to ensure the communication of irregularities between CBs and the CU and among CBs, and irregularities affecting the organic status of the products are not immediately notified. As a result, the CU cannot take adequate action to either prevent non-compliant products being marketed or to follow-up the accuracy of the actions taken by CBs.

CBs notify the CU of the irregularities found during the year by means of their annual report. The national legislation does not require CBs to notify the risk or suspicion of non-compliance as they occur. Major irregularities affecting the organic status of the product are not immediately notified, either to the CU or to other CBs. In fact, the standards procedures of CB2 envisaged such notifications "if necessary". This is not in line with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. The audit team noted that there are no documented procedures to ensure this exchange of communication to happen, which is not in line with Article 92(5) of Regulation 889/2008. The audit team noted that, duri

label_heading: Conclusions Measures in cases of irregularities and infringements
paragraph_text: OFIS cases are not always adequately followed up and the CU does not sufficiently evaluate the actions taken by CBs. In addition, the CU does not usually meet the 30 days deadline to reply in OFIS. 5.3 SEED DATA BASE Legal Requirements Articles 48 and 49 to 56 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

However, the audit team noted that follow-up was not carried out to operators at all stages of production and that not all necessary documents were submitted. For example, in one of the cases observed, the actions focused exclusively on the exporter, who had only relabelled the final product. The CB visited neither the wild collection area nor the processor involved and the documents submitted did not include cleaning records from the day when the notified batch was processed. In another case, the CB had correctly determined the reason which caused the irregularity but the corrective action taken was not adequate. The operator had accepted certain raw material without adequately checking its

The role of the CU was found by the audit team to be insufficiently active. According to the National Regulation, the CU may also carry out inspections to operators on its own initiative, but to date no such inspections have been carried out, even in cases where the same operator had been involved in several OFIS notifications. The CA waits for the CBs to submit information on the measures taken by CBs, but there is a lack of evaluation by the CU of the effectiveness of such measures. In addition, it normally takes more than 30 days for the CA to send a reply in OFIS, which is not in line with is not in line with Article 92(a)4 or Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

There is an adequate system in place for the registration of operators and overall it is effectively implemented. The CAs publish and keep an updated list of operators, in line with EU legislation. However, DAFA does not publish the documentary evidence and the documentary evidence issued by DVFA to the operators does not follow the model of Annex XII of Regulation (EC) No 899/2008.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning and prioritisation of controls
paragraph_text: Controls on organic operators are in most cases annually carried out in line with Article 65(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. However, the frequency of control on a defined group of small farmers that do not place products on the market is not in line with the above-mentioned article.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning and prioritisation of controls
paragraph_text: Additional visits are primarily unannounced and based in most cases on risk assessment as established in Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. However, the risk assessment carried out to select additional visits to organic farms is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 5.2.4 Controls of Operators Legal Requirements Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 9 Titles II and IV and Article 65(1) and 65(3) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. label_heading: Conclusions on sampling and laboratories analysis
paragraph_text: Both DVFA and DAFA had planned for 2014 an adequate number of samples to be taken. As a general rule, sampling is risk based. However, the selection of operators (which does not include farmers) by DAFA is not based on the general evaluation of risk of non-compliance with the organic production rules at all stages of production, preparation and distribution, which is not in line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

label_heading: Conclusions on exceptional production rules and other derogations
paragraph_text: Generally, derogations granted comply with specific EU requirements. However, dehorning is carried out routinely and without prior authorisation by the CA which is not in line with Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 899/2008. 5.2.8 Imports of Products from Organic Production Legal Requirements Articles 32 and 33 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. A number of arrangements have been put in place to facilitate the communication between and within CAs, CtrlAs and CBs. The audit team saw several minutes of biannual meetings between the CAs (including Customs) and the CBs aimed at improving and harmonising official controls in the organic sector. Moreover, the NFA has recently launched an electronic platform to facilitate the communication with other CAs, CtrlAs and CBs. However, it was observed that the NFA does not have sufficient information on whether and how the MUNs implement controls to verify the conditions for exclusion of certain retailers from the obligation to be subject to controls by the CBs, because, as stated by representat

label_heading: Conclusion on Control Bodies: approval, supervision and withdrawal
paragraph_text: In general, despite the lack of written procedures, there is an effective system for the approval of CBs, the delegation of controls on organic production to the CBs, and for their supervision. However, some requirements in force from January 2014, namely the requirements for additional, unannounced visits and the number of annual samples to be taken by the CBs, had been overlooked during the supervisory activities in 2014 and, partly, in 2015. The plan of the SBA and NFA to be more actively involved in such activities should strengthen the supervision process. 5.2.3 Registration of operators Legal Requirements Articles 28(1), 28(2) and 28(5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. label_heading: Conclusion on the registration of operators
paragraph_text: There is a system which is partly effective in ensuring that operators which produce, prepare, store or import organic products or who place on the market such products are registered and subject to controls. In particular, operators are neither yet obliged to notify their activity to the CAs, nor are included in a publicly available list and this might hamper the traceability of the organic products. Moreover, the operators' commitment to follow the applicable provisions of the organic legislation and the information concerning the description of their activities and the relevant precautionary measures, are not consistently required by the CBs when the operators are first included in the sy

The audit team noted that the delegation decisions issued by the CAs require the CBs to ensure that operators (wishing to produce, prepare, store or import organic products or placing on the market such products) notify their activity to them. In both the CBs visited, the audit team noted that this was clearly described in their websites. However, it was noted that, although an amendment of the legislation is in the pipeline, the current legislation does not include the obligation of these operators to notify their activities to the CAs. This is not in line with Article 28(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

According to representatives from both the CBs visited, during the first control, the inspector is requested to check, among other things, the appropriateness of the relevant precautionary measures put in place by the operator and the outcome of this evaluation is indicated in the report which is left with the operator. However, the audit team noted that CB1 does not require the operator to sign the declaration containing the operator's commitment to follow the applicable provisions of the organic legislation, the description of its activities and the relevant precautionary measures, contrary to the provisions laid down by Article 63(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

According to the information provided by the CAs, no lists of operators are publicly available yet. The audit team noted that every CB has its own list of operators but such lists are not accessible to the public. This is not in line with Article 92b of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. An amendment of the national organic legislation is in the pipeline in order to facilitate the publication of these lists. According to the information provided by the CAs, its publication is expected by the end of 2015.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and prioritisation of controls
paragraph_text: The measures put in place by the CBs for the planning and the prioritisation of controls are, in general, effective, although the new requirements related to the additional and unannounced visits, in force from January 2014, have been implemented by the CBs with a delay and they do not always carry out unannounced visits as required. 5.2.5 Controls of operators Legal Requirements Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Titles II and IV and Article 65(1) and 65(3) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Representatives of the CBs visited stated that the aforementioned unannounced visits are in general carried out without prior warning to the operator, although, in both cases, a prior notification of not more than 24 hours is allowed in case of particular circumstances. In this regard, the CAs have slightly different positions: according to representatives from the NFA and Swedac, no exceptions are allowed for the "unannounced" visit; on the other hand, the SBA's position allows a prior notification (of not more than 24 hours) when this notification could not jeopardise the possible outcome of the control. label_heading: Conclusion on the controls of operators
paragraph_text: The CBs have set up broadly adequate systems to ensure effective controls of operators. However, the provision for food and feed processors to carry out a risk analysis to identify the critical steps and relevant precautionary measures for the production of organic food/feed is not regularly required by the CBs. This may affect the overall performance of the controls since additional efforts are required for the CBs to identify the areas which require more attention during their controls. 5.2.6 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Articles 23, 24 and 27(13) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Title III of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

The audit team noted that the operators visited were largely in line with the relevant organic production rules. In a number of cases the inspectors of the CBs rightly identified a number of non-compliances (e.g. expired certificates of suppliers and the lack of notification to the CB of the conventional production, in the case of the farm). However, the audit team noted that the food processors visited, certified by CB1, were not required to document a risk analysis indicating the critical steps for the production of organic food and relevant precautionary measures (see finding 18). This is not in line with Article 26(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 8 Conclusion on the controls of operat

label_heading: Conclusion on measures in cases of irregularities or infringements
paragraph_text: Various measures have been put in place by the CAs, CtrlAs and CBs to manage irregularities and infringements. Those related to the obligations of communication between CBs and CAs are effective. However, the lack of a national harmonised sanction catalogue negatively affects the effectiveness and consistency of the measures taken in case of irregularities and infringements throughout the country. 5.3 SEED DATABASE Legal Requirements Articles 45(5) and 45(8), 48 and 49 to 56 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Moreover, no national catalogue of measures in case of irregularities and infringements, as required by Article 92d of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 has yet been adopted in Sweden. Order No 3D-352 of 17 May 2012 describes the procedure for official controls on imports of organic products. There is a well-developed catalogue of sanctions for non-compliances but in some cases the cumulative nature of the non-compliances detected is not taken into account resulting in an incorrect perception of the severity of the non-compliance and, consequently, enforcement measures that are neither proportionate nor dissuasive.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls
paragraph_text: The system of official controls is in place as described in the Country Profile for Spain. Within the scope of the audit, the official control plans are implemented as foreseen and official controls are carried out in accordance with documented procedures. Despite systems being in place, there are some shortcomings in their thoroughness and follow-up. Systems for training varied between ACs, with no training on the use of additives being provided in one etc. Some of the deficiencies identified could directly be contributed to insufficient training. 5.2.2 Implementation of official controls

In one AC, the FVO audit team noted that most inspection visits in one establishment visited were planned instead of being unannounced. The CA of the AC stated that visits in large-scale establishments are usually announced in advance. Provided the nature of the control permits and the inspector knows that the presence of a particular member of the business is advisable, visits to large-scale establishments may be arranged according to the CA, at the shortest notice possible.

label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: The significant non-compliances in one establishment raises question as to the efficacy of the official controls in this particular case. Concerning the many non-compliances relating to the incoming goods, while none of them can be considered as critical, their range and frequency indicate that, notwithstanding the official system in place, controls are superficial and unable to detect any systemic non- compliances regarding traceability (particularly with regard to quantities) and labelling. A contributing factor is the insufficient time allocated for checks on traceability during official controls. No systematic official controls are performed on the use of food additives by FBOs.

label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: The absence of official controls on the flow of product through establishments undermines the effectiveness of the overall system of traceability. 5.3. Miscellaneous 5.3.1. Mechanically Separated Meat

Specific checklists for controls on traceability and labelling are in use. However no checklists or sampling reports of meat products were available on the use of additives. The V&I checklist for traceability and labelling (effective from 15-02-2015) does not 4 contain detailed questions on internal traceability and quantitative traceability (mass balance). In-depth verification of traceability within establishments is rarely performed.
The CA did not have a special checklist or instructions for checking the use of additives. Evidence of official sampling was not available in the establishments visited.

The Dutch CA has clarified their position in a note to the DG Health & Food Safety dated 3 June 2015 concerning internal traceability, pointing out that neither Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 nor the Commission Guidance on the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 European law imposes any obligations on FBOs to have an internal traceability system, and that, as a consequence, the NVWA cannot impose requirements in this regard. The only exception concerns the traceability of beef.

The requirement that FBOs must be able to demonstrate from whom products are received and to whom products are delivered is checked and enforced. However, if the mass balance (correlation of quantities received with output of final product, quantities in-storage and production losses) is not correct, or absent, no follow-up actions are taken and no sanctions can be imposed.

label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: In one establishment the audit team identified the presence of eight bags of dried blood without identification. The provider of dried blood had a procedure to remove all labels (including identification marks, process codes, use-by-date, etc.) from product supplied. The CA informed the DG Health & Food Safety that, while a warning had been issued to the provider of the dried blood, no further action had been taken. (see also paragraph 39 fourth sub indent).

label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: Control of incoming goods: In three establishments visited, some meat and meat products had been accepted without the required health mark or identification mark. In one of them (a large distribution centre), in the reception area three consignments out of six were not compliant. In a cutting plant, the individual commercial documents of the incoming consignments from one supplier did not correspond with the content of the corresponding truck. A difference of 200 half pig carcasses was noted on three consignments. The FBO control at entry did not identify these discrepancies. Although during a previous inspection, the CA had identified that traceability was inadequate, no follow-up on this non-compliance had been carried out. During the visit the CA stated that a fine would be issued for this non-compliance. In several establishments, some products were unidentified and there were open packages without identification. label_heading: Conclusion on official controls on food processing chain
paragraph_text: Use of additives: In one establishment, according to the recipe of one non-heat treated meat product, the content of nitrite to be used was above the legal limit set out in Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008. Specifications, on several additive pre-mixes seen, did not mention the content of the additives for which a maximum limit is established and consequently this does not allow calculation of the maximal amount to be used. Official controls do not include checks on the use of additives.

The Dutch CA considers that for the production of MSM ("type 4") with reference to point 4 Chapter III, Section IV of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, there is no time limit between deboning and production of MSM. The FBO producer of MSM visited restricts the use of the poultry carcasses to five days after slaughter because they produce only "type 4", but has no indication if the three days between slaughter and cutting had been respected in all cases. In addition, the use by date (three days) of the 11 deboned poultry carcasses fixed by a German supplier was ignored by this FBO and had expired. The CA undertook to follow-up this issue.

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: In all the establishments visited, the FBOs stated that a traceability system was in place. However, the evaluation of these systems revealed a less positive picture concerning traceability in general and quantitative traceability in particular. In one cold store a robust system was in place. Two establishments were making good progress towards implementing a good system but the others still had significant progress to make. Two establishments had yet to start work on implementing a traceability system.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls
paragraph_text: The only cold store visited had a robust system in place based on the bar coding of any single entering pallet of meat. This bar code is scanned and registered in the system as well as the physical location of any bar coded pallet. As soon as an order is received for exiting goods, the system designates the palettes to be extracted from the cold store using the first in first out principle. The exiting goods are scanned allowing the cold store to have an ongoing permanent state of play of all goods stored. The exercises carried out by the FVO team revealed only one minor deficiency relating to one tray of meat.

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: In all the establishments visited, the FBOs stated that a traceability system was in place. However, the evaluation of these systems revealed a less positive picture concerning traceability in general and quantitative traceability in particular. In one cold store a robust system was in place. Two establishments were making good progress towards implementing a good system but the others still had significant progress to make. Two establishments had yet to start work on implementing a traceability system.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls:
paragraph_text: A system of official controls is in place and performs effectively. Documented procedures are established and applied. Some checklists are not complete as they do not contain relevant questions on controls on traceability, labelling and use of additives for establishments in the case of establishments under the control of the DGSAPVS and on the use of food additives in the case of the EFET. Both CCA indicated that the checklists will be reviewed in this regard.

The checklist issued by the EFET for controls in establishments producing meat and meat products thereof includes controls on general hygiene requirements, FBOs' HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) based systems and contains questions on traceability, labelling and sampling for additives. Traceability controls and the checklists used are focused on one step forward and one step backward in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Nevertheless, in some establishments, particularly those which export products, official controls on internal traceability are effectively performed. The CCA confirmed that the checklist does not contain specific questions on the us

The checklist issued by the DGSAPVS is mainly focused on general hygiene and does not contain questions related to traceability, labelling and use of additives. However, in one establishment visited, the local CA used the EFET checklist related to traceability, but not related to labelling and use of additives. The CCA stated that this checklist will be reviewed. 5

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls:
paragraph_text: A system of official controls is in place and performs effectively. Documented procedures are established and applied. Some checklists are not complete as they do not contain relevant questions on controls on traceability, labelling and use of additives for establishments in the case of establishments under the control of the DGSAPVS and on the use of food additives in the case of the EFET. Both CCA indicated that the checklists will be reviewed in this regard.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on food processing chain:
paragraph_text: The authorities identified some minor non-compliances in the traceability and labelling that had no impact on food safety for the eleven traceable samples. The authorities did not identify some non-compliances related to the use of food additives, in particular, the use of nitrites and nitrates. The information referred to in Article 3 of Regulation (EU) No 931/2011 was not available for a particular ingredient used. 5.2.2.2.Official controls on food business operators' obligations Findings

The checklist issued by the EFET for controls in establishments producing meat and meat products thereof includes controls on general hygiene requirements, FBOs' HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) based systems and contains questions on traceability, labelling and sampling for additives. Traceability controls and the checklists used are focused on one step forward and one step backward in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Nevertheless, in some establishments, particularly those which export products, official controls on internal traceability are effectively performed. However, in one establishment visited, the local CA used the EFET checklist related to traceability, but not related to labelling and use of additives. The CCA stated that this checklist will be reviewed. 5

The audit team verified the documentation relating to these 12 cases. The outcome of this exercise was as follows: The observations made by the authorities regarding tracing (one step forward ­ one step backward) could be confirmed for all cases regarding meat and meat products thereof. For the samples, in particular, for meat and products thereof, produced and traded within Greece, not all suppliers provided information in trade documents on food supplied with a reference identifying the lot, batch or consignment, as appropriate. Instead in most cases this information is retrieved on arrival by the receiving FBO from the labels attached to the meat. For the 10 cases seen, for which the auth

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls:
paragraph_text: The annual control plan was not documented in some regional EFET and local CAs. In most cases the frequency of minimum controls established at central level was followed. As regards follow-up of non-compliances, in some cases deadlines for corrective actions by FBO were not provided, and/or no documented evidence for such corrective action was available. 5.2.2. Implementation of official controls

Depending on the non-compliances found, follow-up normally takes place during additional controls or during the next planned inspection if it does not concern food safety. This could take up to one year. Reports were seen where no clear deadline was given to the FBO to correct the deficiencies identified. In some cases no written evidence was available of following up previous non-compliances found.

The sampling design is generally in line with EU requirements and ensures the collection of isolates from all bacteria species for monitoring of AMR in the food producing animal populations and food categories set out in EU legislation. Nevertheless, improvements could be made with regard to the collection of Salmonella isolates gathered under the FBO's own-check programmes, in the proportional allocation of samples and in the random selection of batches at slaughterhouses.

In SN the audit team was informed that the isolates gathered under SNCP in 2014 (1 official and several from FBO) were available at the official Länder laboratory and were only submitted to the BfR in the few cases when clarifications regarding serotyping were needed. The laboratory representative stated that as no information from the BfR about the total number of isolates available for AST at national level was received, these isolates were not submitted in order to achieve the 170 foreseen in the legislation. Therefore, not all the Salmonella isolates available at the end of 2014 were included in AST and reported to EFSA as foreseen in Article 2(2)(a) of Decision 2013/652/EU.

The sampling design is generally in line with EU requirements and ensures the collection of isolates from all bacteria species for monitoring of AMR in the food producing animal populations and food categories set out in EU legislation. Nevertheless, improvements could be made with regard to the collection of Salmonella isolates gathered under the FBO's own-check programmes, in the proportional allocation of samples and in the random selection of batches at slaughterhouses.

The audit team noted, in both Länder visited, that samples were allocated to the slaughterhouses of higher capacity. Nevertheless, this allocation for both 2014 and 2015, despite the 2015 updated instruction, was based on the total number of animals slaughtered and not on the specific domestic population as foreseen in the third paragraph of point 2.3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.

label_heading: Conclusions on assessment and reporting of AMR
paragraph_text: The annual report includes all the mandatory information for each individual isolate reported under harmonised monitoring. However, improvements could be made in order to ensure the reporting of the overall description of the implementation of AMR monitoring and assessment of results.

The collection form used for the reporting of "generic description of the implementation of the AMR monitoring" was not submitted to EFSA. Therefore, the description on the sampling designs implemented and on stratification and randomisation procedures per animal populations as well as results of the AMR monitoring assessment were not included in the reporting of data related to the 2014 monitoring programme as required in Part B (2) of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. 2 Web interface through which data providers can submit their files. 18

CAs are designated for the official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG for the verification of compliance with the product specification and are adequately staffed. However, ACCAs are not designated in all Autonomous Communities to carry out checks for the surveillance of the use of the names in the market place. and therefore it cannot be ensured that controls based on risk analysis are carried out in all Autonomous Communities. This lack of designation is not in line with Article 36 of Regulation (EC) No 1151/2012. 5.2.2 Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 39(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. label_heading: Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls
paragraph_text: Although PDO/PGI/TSG feature in the risk classifications, currently official controls focus on food safety which means that, in practice, official controls on PDO/PGI/TSG are not undertaken.

label_heading: Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls
paragraph_text: No controls relating to verification of compliance before placing the product on the market were undertaken, although procedures exist for such activities. 5.2.3 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 12, 13(1), 23, 24(1), 36(3), 44 and 46(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. label_heading: Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls
paragraph_text: CBs may grant authorisation to new operators joining the production scheme without an inspection visit being carried out by the relevant CB to verify compliance with the product specification.

label_heading: Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls
paragraph_text: Official controls for verification of compliance with the product specification prior to placing on the market of PDO/PGI/TSG products are not always adequately planned and implemented as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In particular, the selection of operators to be visited is not always based on risk assessment and the frequency of visits does not always ensure that all operators are regularly inspected. Moreover, inspections are not always carried out without prior warning.

Most aspects of official controls are adequately undertaken at producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG to verify compliance with the product specification. Market controls are adequate overall. However, there are no documented procedures to ensure that the requirements of Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 664/2014 and Article 4 of Regulation (EU) No 668/2014 (which had not yet been included in all relevant control plans) are verified during inspections at PDO/PGI/TSG operators. 5.2.5 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

label_heading: findings to the DVO of the farm of origin for necessary action.
paragraph_text: The system that has started being implemented for the monitoring of welfare indicators of broilers at slaughterhouses takes into account the main animal based indicators but there is a risk of having only limited impact on the welfare conditions in farms. This is due to the high trigger values for the CDMR and the lack of availability of this data at the CAs where this matters, namely the DVO of the farm of origin and the CCA. 5.5 ACTIONS TAKEN IN CASE OF NON-COMPLIANCE Legal requirements Articles 22 and 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. Findings

The CCA had very recently issued detailed instructions for OVs working in poultry slaughterhouses to monitor animal welfare indicators in broilers as required by Point 2 of Annex III of Directive 2007/43/EC. These instructions include the evaluation of samples of chicken's feet for footpad dermatitis and a relevant scoring system with two trigger levels of action depending on the severity of the welfare conditions of the birds: A trigger level for average welfare conditions, in which the OV at the slaughterhouse reports the findings to the supervising DVO. This information is kept at the supervising DVO and only communicated to the DVO of the farm of origin if a second notification is made.

label_heading: findings to the DVO of the farm of origin for necessary action.
paragraph_text: A cumulative daily mortality rate of more than 5% triggers a notification of poor welfare conditions. This value is significantly higher than the maximum permitted CDMR in poultry flocks being kept at stocking densities between 39 and 42 kg/m², as indicated in Point 1(c) of Annex V of Directive 2007/43/EC.
