Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on evaluation and review of official controls
paragraph_text: Regional and district CAs are effectively carrying out the evaluation of official controls on compliance with the Regulation. The CCA has put in place a system to collect results of official controls for the purpose of further analysis and review. The process of data collection aggregates data in two phases and as a consequence, some information is lost in the process. From the aggregate data reaching the CCA, it is not possible to effectively analyse certain aspects of compliance e.g. trends in non-compliances or recurring issues. This undermines the CCA's ability to achieve the objectives laid down in point 2(b) and 9.2 of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/654/EC (to outline progress a

The CCA had very recently issued detailed instructions for OVs working in poultry slaughterhouses to monitor animal welfare indicators in broilers as required by Point 2 of Annex III of Directive 2007/43/EC. These instructions include the evaluation of samples of chicken's feet for footpad dermatitis and a relevant scoring system with two trigger levels of action depending on the severity of the welfare conditions of the birds: A trigger level for average welfare conditions, in which the OV at the slaughterhouse reports the findings to the supervising DVO. This information is kept at the supervising DVO and only communicated to the DVO of the farm of origin if a second notification is made.

label_heading: findings to the DVO of the farm of origin for necessary action.
paragraph_text: The data collected in the slaughterhouses on the welfare indicators of broilers is kept at the slaughterhouse unless this requires action according to the trigger system. Conclusions on monitoring of broiler welfare at the slaughterhouse and follow up

When analysing these reports it is not possible to identify repeat offenders, trends in non-compliances in slaughterhouses of specific characteristics (throughput, species slaughtered, stunning method, etc.). Furthermore, these reports are not accompanied by any data analysis that could have made by the reporting DVO.

Similarly to the reports sent by the DVOs to the RVOs, these are not accompanied by any data analysis that may have been carried out by the reporting RVO. Furthermore, the format adopted by the CCA for the collection of data, including the data categories selected by the CCA, does not allow the CCA to carry out an effective analysis of the results of official controls (e.g. trends in non-compliances detected and repeat offenders). This notwithstanding that Section 9.2.2 of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/654/EC provides guidance on the analysis of non- compliances for the submission of consistent annual reports to the Commission as required by Article 44 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on training activities in the live animal transport sector
paragraph_text: National legislation recognises some academic courses as equivalent to training courses although assurances that the training required by Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 is included in these academic courses is not always provided. 6 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Training courses in Austria are of high quality and are using a quality system to deliver and regularly assess suitability and effectiveness. This has been achieved by underpinning training in the Federal Animal Welfare Act and a high level of commitment by CAs and training bodies to promote awareness of animal welfare due to the inclusion of this principle in national legislation. CAs and training bodies are providing several training activities

label_heading: Conclusion on the controls on transits of non-EU goods
paragraph_text: The controls at the entry and exit BIPs on transits of non-EU goods comply with the EU requirements and provide guarantees that only eligible goods are accepted into the EU and they always leave the territory. The controls at the warehouse are weakened by the poor checks on traceability and the inadequate physical checks of the goods. 5.3. EXTERNAL TRANSITS OF EU GOODS Legal requirements Article 6(1) of Council Directive 89/662/EEC; Article 7(1) of Council Directive 90/425/EEC; Article 12 of Regulation (EC) 206/2010. Findings

label_heading: Conclusion on the controls on external transits of EU goods
paragraph_text: The competent authority was unaware of the requirement to control EU goods re-entering from external transits, and controls are not done. Consignments that should not have been allowed re-entry to the Union were not rejected, even though they did not fulfil the animal health requirements, which may pose an animal health risk in the EU. 9 5.4. VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Articles 4 and 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

label_heading: Conclusion on controls at the exit BIP
paragraph_text: The official controls of exit transit consignments are correctly implemented in the vast majority of cases ensuring that consignments leave the EU territory as required by EU legislation, except for the Rijeka BIP. The different, undocumented implementation of instructions on exit transit controls at this BIP level cannot ensure that the exiting consignments are checked to confirm that they have not been manipulated during transit. 10 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS IMPLEMENTED ON SPECIFIC TRANSITS 5.3.1 Derogations for consignments from Bosnia and Herzegovina and destined to third countries. Legal requirements Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; Regulation (EU) No 553/2013, Regulation (EU) No 5

In April 2014, the central competent authority in cooperation with Customs approved an instruction for exit checks made by Customs officials outside the working hours of BIPs. Following the newly approved instruction, the BIP staff perform the exit checks of transit consignments during the working hours of the BIPs. Customs are responsible for 9 the exit checks of transit consignments outside the working hours of the BIPs. The instruction is prepared following the requirements of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2000/208/EC.

In those cases where the transit checks are done by the BIP staff the seal check is done at the BIP facilities. Outside of working hours, the seal check is done by Customs officials at the Customs control post. In both cases these controls are done following the requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC. The port BIPs visited keep track of exiting transit consignments until they are unloaded into ships for dispatch outside the EU.

The audit team noted that none of the BIPs visited follow the above-mentioned work instruction: a. In the Ploce port, Customs authorities always send the exit transit consignments to the BIP for checks even if the BIP is not working. The consignment then waits until the BIP is open. b. In the Rijeka port, the exit transit checks are always performed by Customs even when the BIP is open. The local agreement to divert from the national instruction (finding 44) is not documented. Central Customs officials confirmed that Customs are obliged to check veterinary seals only in cases defined in the national instruction. This means there is no legal obligation for Customs to check the veterinary seal

There are controls at the warehouses, but identity checks upon arrival at the warehouses do not ensure that mismatches with the certificates are identified. The mismatch with the original certificate means that those goods are (i) accepted for transit without adequate guarantees and (ii) are re-certified incorrectly by EU officials at the time of dispatch. The risk to animal health is mitigated since currently only canned fishery products are stored in the warehouses. Furthermore, the traceability system put in place by the operator allows for the reconciliation of the goods. 5.2.5 Controls at the exit BIP

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: A consignment split in the warehouse visited had been rejected by the third country of destination due to a mismatch between the lot number on the boxes and the lot number on the health certificate accompanying the consignment from origin. The competent authority interpreted that there is no legal requirement to check/record the lot numbers of the consignments during the full identity check. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 4(4)(a)(ii) of Directive 97/78/EC. The operator of the warehouse stated it had taken corrective actions and strengthened controls during loading, cross-checking the lot number to match with the information on the health certificate.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The audit team conducted traceability exercises both to trace back and trace forward a randomly selected product in the warehouse. The data from TRACES matched precisely the info provided by the competent authorities' and the operator's records. However, the lot number of the consignment examined did not match that indicated in the original health certificate which accompanied the consignment. This had not been detected during the checks upon arrival at the warehouse, which is not in line with the requirements of Article 4(4)(a)(iii) of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 4 of Decision 2000/571/EC.

label_heading: Conclusion on the official controls on non-conforming goods
paragraph_text: There is currently no formalised system in place to ensure that consignments of EU origin which move between two points in the EU via a third country and re-enter the EU via Latvia are controlled as required under EU legislation. However, due to a combination of factors the probable level of trade is low and the competent authority has begun the process of establishing a system. 5.4 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

The competent authority has implemented the requirements for communication, cooperation and training to support the overall functioning of the controls on transits, except in regard of transits of live animals (which was a recommendation of the 2013 FVO audit) and controls on external transits (which are not included in the planning of controls). 5.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON TRANSITING GOODS Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Regulation (EC) No 282/2004, Council Directive 97/78/EC, Council Directive 91/496/EC, Commission Decision 2000/571/EC, Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 of the European Parliament and of the

The audit team noted that the competent authority made available to the staff of the BIPs visited the procedures related to transit movements (i.e. controls of transits at entry and exit BIPs and at Customs warehouses). The available procedures were up-to-date in the BIPs visited and staff also has access to the internal IT network of the competent authority which includes the entire documented system for the official import controls. 3 This is used by staff in order to be kept up-to-date in the area of their competence as required by Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted the following exceptions: a. previous FVO audit report (2013-6962) recommended that the compe

The competent authority stated that the port and rail BIPs visited conduct manifest checks (with a view to identifying possible cases of consignments not presented at the BIPs) on an ad hoc basis and there is no recording of these controls. The road BIP visited does not monitor incoming consignments in order to identify cases that should be subject to veterinary controls, contrary to the requirements of Article 7 of Regulation (EC) 136/2004 and Article 6 of Regulation (EC) 282/2004. The audit team noted that the procedure for controls of transits does not refer to the above-mentioned requirements. 5.2.1.2 Veterinary checks

The audit team noted that the instruction for the controls of transits at entry BIPs is not sufficiently clear on the different cases faced by officials. In particular it is not clear when the BIP staff need to perform a full identity check and whether consignments that have been rejected should leave the BIP sealed (a case was noted in which the rail BIP performed a full identity check on a consignment and rejected it unsealed). The above may lead to a lack of consistency in the related controls among the different BIPs.

The specific conditions for transit via the EU territory between Kaliningrad and mainland Russia are implemented following the requirements of EU legislation, with some weakness in the identity checks ­ which are limited to tail checks ­ that may lead to the non-detection of consignments that do not tally exactly with the description in the accompanying document. 5.4 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Decision 2000/571/EC, Articles 12 and 17 of Regulation (EC) No 206/2010. Findings

paragraph_text: There is a system in place to verify official import controls which includes consignments in transit. label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The veterinary checks for transit consignments at the entry BIP are implemented ensuring that consignments in transit fulfil the necessary animal health guarantees. The fact that the NVWA accepts explanatory letters when discrepancies are found during documentary checks weakens the effectiveness of the documentary controls. 5.2.2 Controls at warehouses and ship suppliers 5.2.2.1 Approval and listing of the warehouses/ship suppliers and specially approved warehouses

The audit team noted that Customs officials perform the documentary checks using a database which contains up to date and relevant information on requirements for transit consignments. The models of transit/storage veterinary certificates uploaded in the above-mentioned database are correct and comply with the model established by EU legislation. However, the audit team noted that a number of these certificates additionally bear the footnotes referring to the draft document number provided during the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed. This leads to discrepancies between the certificates accompanying the consignments and the model in the database. There is no documented pro

BIP staff stated that, when officials detect errors in the certificates, explanatory letters from the third country competent authority were routinely requested. The NVWA 4 confirmed that replacement certificates are rarely requested. Despite the absence of EU legislation on this matter, the Guidelines for Design, Production, Issuance and Use of Generic Official Certificates (CAC/GL 38-2001), issued by the Codex Alimentarius Commission, indicate that, for certain administrative corrections or if the certificates are lost or damaged, replacement certificates are foreseen. This is also reflected in the Guidance on transit. The BIP operational procedures do not indicate when explanatory letters

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at warehouses and ship suppliers
paragraph_text: There is a well-functioning system of official controls on consignments in transit upon entry or exit from warehouses and ship suppliers which ensures that if a consignment has been manipulated during transit or does not arrive at the warehouse, this will be detected. Consignments ready for dispatch are subject to official controls. The controls during the storage are limited and do not include reconciliation exercises, which may potentially compromise the overall system of official controls at the warehouses. 5.2.3 Controls at the exit border inspection post

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The warehouse operators identify each box of the consignment stored in the warehouse with a label with the reference number of the arriving CVED, in accordance with the requirement of Article 1(5) of Decision 2000/571/EC. In addition, the information on the consignments stored in the warehouse is recorded in the operators' databases, in accordance with the requirements of Article 3(1) of the same Decision. Nevertheless, the audit team noted discrepancies in the traceability of consignments stored (see finding 36).

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The audit team conducted traceability exercises both to trace back and trace forward a randomly selected consignment stored in the warehouse. The audit team noted the following: In one warehouse, the warehouse operator incorrectly recorded the country of origin of the product stored in the warehouse (i.e. the country of origin of the product was Canada, but it was recorded in the operator's database as Argentina). In the other warehouse, the records were correct but the boxes stored displayed labels with an incorrect CVED number.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at the entry BIP
paragraph_text: The official staff responsible for the official controls at the warehouses perform weekly verification of the consignments stored in the warehouse concerned. The audit team noted that during these verification visits the information on the selected consignments 8 is obtained from the warehouse operators' databases and it is cross-checked with the number of boxes stored in the warehouse. Official staff do not compare the data of the operator with official data available (e.g. amounts entering and exiting the warehouse). Therefore, the verification activities are not appropriate to identify the deficiencies described in finding 36, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at entry Border Inspection Posts
paragraph_text: The official control system of transit consignments at the entry BIPs ensures that only consignments eligible for transits are accepted as required by EU legislation with the exception of specific shortcomings on (i) the screening of available information on arriving consignments in the road BIPs that reduce the ability to detect consignments that should undergo border controls, and (ii) the identity checks, which are limited to tail checks, therefore do not ensure that the consignment tallies exactly with the description in the accompanying document. All consignments were confirmed at exit. 5.2.2 Controls at the exit Border Inspection Posts

The competent authority informed the audit team that none of the BIPs visited had direct access to information available in Customs contrary to the requirement of Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 and Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 (see finding 5).

The staff at Pireas port BIP stated that they carry out manifest checks (to identify possible consignments not presented for controls at the BIPs) on an ad hoc basis. There is no record of these controls, contrary to the requirement described in the BIP manual. The road BIPs visited do not implement any checks to identify such cases, contrary to the requirements of Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. The procedure for controls of transits described in the BIP manual does not refer to the above-mentioned requirements for the road BIPs.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at entry Border Inspection Posts
paragraph_text: The official control system of transit consignments at the entry BIPs ensures that only consignments eligible for transits are accepted as required by EU legislation with the exception of specific shortcomings on (i) the screening of available information on arriving consignments in the road BIPs that reduce the ability to detect consignments that should undergo border controls, and (ii) the identity checks, which are limited to tail checks, therefore do not ensure that the consignment tallies exactly with the description in the accompanying document. All consignments were confirmed at exit. 5.2.2 Controls at the exit Border Inspection Posts

In all the BIPs visited, staff perform identity checks for all transit consignments to ascertain that the products correspond to the information given in the accompanying certificates or documents, , as required in Article 4(4) of Directive 97/78/EC. In Pireas BIP these checks consist of a tail check, also in containers that include several commodities. Tail checks do not fulfil the definition of "identity checks" laid down in Article 2(2)(c) of Directive 97/78/EC (i.e. a check by visual inspection to ensure that the veterinary certificate(s) or veterinary document(s) tally with the product itself). Such tail checks may lead to consignments that do not tally with the description in the accom

The official controls do not ensure that if there are movements of EU consignments through third countries into Greece the EU animal health requirements are met. 9 5.4 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Article 6(1)(a) of Directive 89/662/EEC and Article 7(1) of Directive 90/425/EEC, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 206/2010, Articles 4 and 8(3)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Customs stated that all EU goods including food of animal origin and live animals arriving from third countries are always accompanied with customs documents and are subject to a Customs documentary check. There is no arrangement with the veterinary service or any instruction on what checks need to be done for the consignments of veterinary interest when these are of EU origin. The audit team noted that the competent authority is not enforcing the requirement to control EU goods re-entering from external transits as provided in Article 6(1)(a) of Directive 89/662/EEC and Article 7(1) of Directive 90/425/EEC.

The audit team found cases of Intra-trade animal health certificates (INTRA) consignments issued by Greece for which the route is not defined/entered as required in the notes for guidance for intra-Community certification in Commission Regulation (EC) No 599/2004. This hinders notification to the relevant authorities and compromises the capability of the officers at exit points to identify the consignments and perform official controls at the exit contrary to the requirements in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 206/2010. The same appears on consignments destined to Greece certified in other Member States.

The audit team found no cases of checked consignments in external transit. It is yet unknown whether such movements exist due to the lack of controls (see finding 27) and incomplete registration of intra-trade movements in TRACES (see finding 28).

label_heading: Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: Whilst there is a monitoring plan in place, the absence of a risk-based rationale for the design and content of the plan does not ensure that the plan covers all relevant commodities and the related risks. 5.1.2 Implementation of the monitoring plan

The Veterinary and Import Division and the Consumer and Safety Division of NVWA are responsible for the planning of the monitoring plan on imported food of animal origin. The NVWA described that both divisions meet after the drafting of the monitoring plan and agree on the implementation at the BIPs. The NVWA stated that for the preparation of the following year's monitoring plan it takes into account RASFF information, quantities of imports, requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, general information on problematic products and advice of the Office for Risk Assessment within the NVWA. There is no evidence that non-compliances not recorded in RASFF (e.g. consignments rejected at the bo

The monitoring plan includes residues of veterinary medicines, contaminants and microbiological examination (mainly Salmonella). The NVWA could not demonstrate that its controls are risk-based and did not present any risk assessment or other rationale for the design of the plan (e.g. for testing Trichinella in horse meat, beta-agonists in chicken meat or for excluding from testing honey or egg products, for which the Netherlands is the main country of introduction into the EU). In the absence of any such assessment, the NVWA is not in position to ensure that official controls are carried out on a risk basis as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (see finding 1).

label_heading: Conclusion on actions in case of suspicion
paragraph_text: There is a system in place which could allow BIP staff to take samples in case of suspicion. However, in practice, cases of suspicion where samples are taken are limited only to consignments which are already subject to EU safeguard decisions. The absence of sample collection in regard to any consignment other than the ones subject to EU safeguard decision, together with the limited scope of the monitoring plan, undermines the effectiveness of the official control system. 5.3 RASFF Legal requirements Article 5 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 16/2011. Findings

label_heading: Conclusion on the implementation of the re-enforced checks regime
paragraph_text: The competent authority's decision not to apply re-enforced checks on consignments falling between the 11th to 30th is not in line with the Guidance on re-enforced checks and does not fulfil the objective of the legislation to confirm or rule out suspicion. This approach also has an impact on the consistency of the controls at EU level, as consignments that would normally undergo detention, and possibly testing, in the rest of the Member States do not undergo these controls in the Dutch BIPs. 5.5 COMPLIANCE OF THE FACILITIES, EQUIPMENT AND HYGIENE CONDITIONS OF THE INSPECTION CENTRES VISITED Legal requirements Article 6 of, and Annex A to Council Directive 91/496/EEC, Articles 3 and 4 of Com

label_heading: Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: Samples under "special projects" (see finding 5) are taken during physical checks at the BIPs, but they are not recorded in TRACES. The NVWA informed the audit team that these samples give an overview for specific commodities, and there are no enforcement actions in case of non-compliances (e.g. rejections, recalls, RASFF notifications). The reason presented was the big delay between the sampling and testing and the limited possibility of the product still being present on the market. BIP staff are not made aware of the results of these tests or of the outcome of the project. This lack of information undermines the ability of the BIP staff to use the intelligence gathered to better inform th

The procedures in place allow for the possibility of BIP staff to take actions in case of suspicion (including detention and sampling) in accordance with Article 20 of Directive 97/78/EC. However, in practice this is limited to the consignments which are subject to various EU safeguard decisions. These controls are correctly recorded as "Suspicion" in box 28 of the CVEDPs and consignments are detained until the laboratory test results are received.

The instruction on re-enforced checks issued by the Veterinary and Import Division of the NVWA requires that BIP staff take samples following the requirements of re- enforced checks for the next ten consignments as required by Article 24 of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 30 of Council Directive 96/23/EC. The instruction explicitly excludes any further sampling of subsequent consignments (i.e. from the 11th to 30th consignment). This policy decision is contrary to the objective of Article 20 of Directive 97/78/EC which requires the competent authority to carry out any veterinary checks that it deems appropriate in order to confirm or rule out suspicion. 8

label_heading: Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: Basically in compliance with the legal requirements, there is a monitoring plan in place to be implemented at the BIPs. The plan is prepared on the basis of risk management in order to ensure that it covers all relevant commodities and the related risks. The plan has not been reviewed/amended since 2011, therefore does not take into account the results of previous monitoring or emerging risks. This means that its ability to detect hazardous goods may be compromised. 5.1.2 Implementation of the monitoring plan

The monitoring plan was last made available to the BIPs and to the authorised island entry points listed in Annex I to Decision 94/641/EC in 2011. Since then it has not been reviewed/amended. The competent authority stated that this was due to a lack of human resources. In this way, the results of previous years are not taken into consideration, contrary to the requirement of paragraph 1 of Annex II to Regulation No 136/2004.

label_heading: Conclusion on actions in case of suspicion
paragraph_text: There is a system in place which allows BIP staff to take samples in case of suspicion. The system works correctly as per EU legislation and planned arrangements. However, the system does not ensure that the operator responsible for the consignment or its representative is liable for the costs incurred by the competent authority for the actions in case of suspicion. 5.3 RAPID ALERT SYSTEM FOR FOOD AND FEED Legal requirements Article 5 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 16/2011. Findings

At the Pireas and Peplos BIPs, the cost of all laboratory tests (including those under re- enforced checks or suspicion) is covered by the State. In the other BIPs visited, depending on the laboratory in which the analysis is performed, some test costs are borne by the operators and others by the State. The cases in which economic operators are not charged for the cost of controls (e.g. sampling and testing) in case of suspicion or re-enforced checks are not in line with the requirement of Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

paragraph_text: Recommendation No 2 from DG(SANCO)/2013-6977 is addressed. However, appropriate actions have still not been taken as regards recommendations 1 and 5 of the same report. In addition, the system does not ensure in some cases that staff at the LVUs in the Greek islands gather and analyse relevant information to ensure that eligible consignments are subject to veterinary checks under Decision 94/641/EC and that imported consignments are only handled at approved operators' facilities. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The monitoring plan generally contributes to ensuring that imported goods comply with EU requirements but it has not been updated since 2011, therefore its effectiveness is undermined as it doe

However, although it foresees the granting of access of the official veterinarians at the BIPs to the Customs database, this is not implemented. The competent authority confirmed that none of the BIPs and the LVUs visited had direct access to information available in Customs contrary to the requirement of Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. In addition, the competent authority at central level has not considered using data available in the Customs database to verify the correctness of the controls laid down in Decision 94/641/EC.

label_heading: Conclusion on the official controls at exit Border Inspection Posts
paragraph_text: The system for official controls at exit BIPs for consignments in transit leaving the EU is not effective at identifying all relevant consignments and therefore implementing the required controls which ensure that consignments have not been manipulated during transit. 5.3 VERIFICATION AND REVIEW Legal requirements Articles 4 and 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

label_heading: Conclusion on the official controls at entry Border Inspection Posts
paragraph_text: All consignments in transit entering Italy are checked at BIPs although not all requirements related to pre-notification are enforced. Veterinary checks are carried out in line with the requirements of EU legislation ensuring that only eligible consignments are accepted for transit. 7 The system to promptly identify and follow-up consignments for which no confirmation of receipt at destination has been received by the entry BIP is not effective, reducing the ability of the system to identify non-conforming consignments that have not left the Union as planned. 5.2.2 Controls at approved warehouses 5.2.2.1 Approval and listing

label_heading: Conclusion on the official controls at approved warehouses
paragraph_text: Official controls on transiting consignments stored in warehouses are implemented but their compliance with EU legislation is compromised by the decision of the competent authority to issue single CVEDs for consolidated consignments, which does not permit effective traceability of the goods and cannot ensure the effectiveness of the controls up to the point of delivery. 10 5.2.3 Controls at the exit Border Inspection Posts 5.2.3.1 Documentary, identity and physical checks

Article 11(2) of Directive 97/78/EC requires BIP staff to ensure that they receive confirmation of arrival (from an approved warehouse) or confirmation of exit from the EU (from the exit BIP) within 30 days after a transit consignment leaves their BIP. If no confirmation is received within 30 days then official staff should seek confirmation either by contacting the officials in charge of controls at the warehouse or the BIP), or by asking Customs. The audit team noted that: At one of the BIPs, confirmation from destination was received for the vast majority of consignments. However, the system to promptly identify when confirmation of receipt was not received within the 30 day legal time li

paragraph_text: Before non-conforming consignments can leave the approved warehouses, the operator must submit a request to the competent authority who subsequently checks the consignment, seals the means of transport after loading and issues the CVED (linked with the original CVED via box 24) or the document for the Captain's Declaration. The audit team noted the following at the two approved warehouses visited: Approved warehouse A ­ for ship supplies, a register is in place to verify that confirmation of receipt by the ship is received back, and that follow-up action is implemented if required. The warehouse had only issued two CVEDs during 2014 for which box 41 was completed for one within 30 days and f

label_heading: Conclusion on the verification and review
paragraph_text: The verification system of official controls related to non-conforming transit consignments is based on a combination of internal audits and a performance reporting system. The detection and correction of shortcomings is not ensured because official controls at approved warehouses are not covered by internal audit and not all types of transit controls are checked within the performance reporting system. 5.4 FOLLOW-UP The table below summarises the follow-up to recommendation number 1 from FVO report DG(SANCO)/2011-8964: Number Recommendation Assessment 1 "To ensure that verification of the controls Partially addressed performed at Italian BIPs is carried out in accordance with "Linea Guida"

Approved warehouses are currently not included within the scope of internal audits by the central competent authority. One of the warehouses visited had an internal audit by the regional level in 2013, but there is no formalised plan for internal audits at approved warehouses at any level.

The main elements of the performance reporting system with relevance for transits is the requirement to check the compliance of a percentage of the certificates that are issued. The overall target was 5% at both BIPs visited due to a high throughput of consignments. The audit team noted that: Genoa Port BIP: checked no transit related documents based on a risk assessment (these were regarded as low risk consignments because they were not destined for EU market). Livorno Port BIP: checked 100% of transit related documents based on a risk assessment (these were regarded as high-risk consignments which should be prevented from reaching the EU market). These checks had identified similar issues

The audit team noted that the following issues identified during the FVO audit were not identified by the national verification system: issues with pre-notification (as described in finding 8); issues at entry BIPs with confirmation of receipt at destination (finding 15); issues with exit controls (finding 26). The current performance reporting system checks a percentage of the documents issued by the location being assessed. Recording the controls referred to in findings 15 and 26 usually involves completing box 41 in TRACES on a CVED issued by a location other than the one carrying out the follow-up control. Therefore these controls are not checked as part of the current performance report

Verification of the official import controls is implemented in recent years by the Ministry of Health via a system which evaluates its activities and objectives in accordance with Public Administration rules, i.e. "System for measuring and evaluating the performance". This system is implemented at BIPs and according to the competent authority, verifies official import controls by amongst other things, setting the following objectives for each BIP: to plan and carry out inspections of the structures of the BIP/Inspection centre; to respect the sampling activities for laboratory checks according to the percentages established by monitoring plan (3%); to verify the compliance of the certificate

label_heading: Conclusion on the implementation of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: The monitoring plan is implemented in accordance with the planned arrangements. In general, staff at BIPs use TRACES correctly. However, the exchange of information in TRACES is compromised by officials not filling in all results of laboratory testing in a timely and complete manner. Thus correct and relevant information is not provided on time to other Member States and the Commission. Equipment for handling of samples is not calibrated and monitored regularly. 7 5.2 ACTIONS IN CASE OF SUSPICION Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004; Articles 3, 18 and 28 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; Articles 4 and 20 of Directive 97/78/EC. Findings

label_heading: Conclusion on the implementation of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: The ability of the monitoring plan to detect goods not complying with the required guarantees is undermined by the clustering of sampling in a limited period and the inability of the competent authority to ensure availability of laboratory capacity in time. The long storage of samples and the delays in obtaining results compromise the ability of the competent authority to take immediate action in case of animal or public health risk. The verification activities have not acted upon the problems encountered with the availability of laboratory capacity. 7 5.2 ACTIONS IN CASE OF SUSPICION Legal requirements Articles 18, 28 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Articles 4, 7, 20 and Annex III of Direct

label_heading: Conclusions on Designation of CAs and Resources for Official Controls
paragraph_text: The CAs in the context of this audit are designated. 5.2.2 Registration/Approval of Establishments Legal Requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 2 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 210/2013, Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings 5.2.2.1 Registration of Food Establishments

The NVWA is an independent agency commissioned by the VWS and the MEA. It is under the administrative responsibility of the MEA but functions as an executive delivery body for both Ministries. The NVWA is subdivided into seven divisions. The Agriculture and Nature division is responsible for the official controls of FNAO relating 5 to plant protection products (PPPs). However, the official controls do not cover microbiological contamination at primary production of FNAO.

There is a system in place for registration of food establishments. However, the lack of information on the crops grown by primary producers weakens the effectiveness of the risk based planning of official controls as required by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on Organisation and Scope of Official Controls
paragraph_text: Official controls on primary producers were not in place to target crops with higher microbiological risks and this may compromise the ability of the CA to detect non- compliances with the food law and verify that unsafe food is not placed on the market. 5.2.4 Implementation of Official Controls over FBO's Obligations Legal requirements Article 10(2)(b)(i), Article 10(2)(c), Article 10(2)(d) and Article 15(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 4(1), Article 7, Article 8 and Part B of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 3 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 208/2013, Regulation (EU) No 211/2013 and Annex I of Commission Reg
The controls on primary producers are not effectively planned to address the risks on microbiological contamination.

According to the data provided by CAFIA, the number of registered primary producers has increased from 1 281 in 2012 to 2 019 in May 2015. The CA explained that the reason for this increase is mainly due to the fact that since CAFIA was delegated to conduct inspections on behalf of the payment agency for Cross Compliance (CC), more FBOs have become known to CAFIA. In relation to primary production, the registration database contains details whether the FBO is dealing with fruit and/or vegetables, but there is no information available on the specific crop being grown which precludes the possibility of planning official controls on an appropriate risk basis as required by the Article 3 of Regu

CAFIA informed the FVO audit team that primary production sectors are included in the scope of the current risk assessment for inspections. However, individual primary producers are currently not entered in the database that is used for the selection of FBOs to be audited. Consequently primary producers have not been subject to risk based controls at the time of the audit as required by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The CA informed the FVO audit team that the database would be adapted in June 2015. The regional inspectorates of CAFIA are responsible for planning of "ad hoc" inspections to primary producers. The FVO audit team was informed that the same principles for the risk assessment are a

In one of the Regional Inspectorates visited during the audit, roughly 400 FBOs were registered for primary production and 6 so-called comprehensive inspections were conducted in 2014. The crops involved were combinable crops, sugar beet and potato. Additionally two inspections were conducted in 2014 based on consumer complaints related to crops like garlic, onion, potatoes and apples. The comprehensive inspections were not targeting high priority crops identified by the EFSA Opinions on the matter.

CISTA informed the FVO audit team that the inspections conducted at growers were under three different inspection frameworks, CC, Delegated Inspections and National Controls. The inspections conducted for CC and National Control schemes control contamination arising from fertilisers (as defined within Annex I Part A, II, point 3 (a) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004) such as the use of manure and sewage sludge which is banned for use in soil where vegetables and fruits are grown. The inspections for CC were planned to reach 1% of the registered growers and for National Controls between 400 and 500 inspections were conducted each year. However, the CISTA representative stated that the risk asses

label_heading: Conclusions on Designation of CAs and Resources for Official Controls
paragraph_text: Staff performing official controls in sprouting establishments and at primary producers of FNAO did not receive specific training in this area and were not adequately aware of any potential source of contamination at farm level. 5.2.2 Registration / Approval of Establishments Legal Requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/204, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings 5.2.2.1 Registration of Food Establishments

Procedures are in place for the registration of establishments. However, the retailers of seeds for sprouting are registered only if their activities regarding food are considered as a major part of their business. Registration of primary producers of FNAO does not include all relevant information to allow CAs to perform risk based official controls effectively.

label_heading: Conclusion on Organisation and Scope of Official Controls
paragraph_text: Official food hygiene controls relating to microbial contamination of FNAO are carried out. There is an effective risk based system of official controls in place for sprouting establishments and the trade chain for seeds for sprouting. However, for other type of primary production operators, the lack of use of the information by the CA limits the ability to implement a risk based system of official controls to prevent microbiological contamination of FNAO. 5.2.4 Implementation of Official Controls over Food Business Operator's Obligations Legal Requirements Article 10(2)(b)(i), Article 10(2)(c), Article 10(2)(d) and Article 15(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 4(1), Article 7, Artic

The CA did not ensure that approved sprouting establishments fully comply with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 210/2013. 7 5.2.3 Organisation and Scope of Official Controls Legal Requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings
A general guide to GAP is available to primary producers. However, its dissemination and use was not encouraged by the CAs.
No major deficiencies were noted in visited establishments. All observed inspections correctly covered traceability, labelling requirements and cleanliness of establishment.
The official controls at farm level did not cover all food hygiene requirements to prevent microbiological contamination of FNAO and some were not assessed correctly.
The requirements on obligatory testing of seeds for sprouting and sprouts, laboratory results, personal hygiene and equipment were not assessed correctly by official controls.

There is in place system for follow-up of RASFF notifications however, the RASFF notifications concerning microbiological contamination of produce of Danish origin are not followed through to the producer level except for sprouting establishments. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is in place a system of official controls at all stages of primary production of FNAO to prevent microbiological contamination. However the effectiveness of the risk based system is limited by incomplete information available to CAs about primary producers of FNAO with the exception of sprouting establishments and seeds for sprouting chain. The NRL in the context of this audit is active and the microbiological laboratori

label_heading: Conclusions on Organisation and Scope of Official Controls
paragraph_text: While official controls on primary producers of FNAO cover the risk of microbiological contamination of irrigation water, the remaining major microbiological risks identified by EFSA are not considered (with the exception of one region visited) in the planning of official controls. This circumstance, coupled with the fact that the design of official controls does not make specific provision for targeting the high priority crops identified by EFSA as particularly prone to microbiological contamination, weakens the effectiveness of official controls in this area. 5.2.4 Implementation of Official Controls over Food Business Operators Obligations Legal requirements Article 10(2)(b)(i), Article 1

The risk ranking set out in the EFSA scientific opinion was not taken into account in the framework of the above-mentioned exercise. This negatively affects the effectiveness of official controls as the major risks identified in EFSA scientific opinion do not contribute to the risk basis for those controls, contrary to Article 3.1(a) and 4.2(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, the CCA, regional CAs and local CAs informed the audit team that microbiological hazards will be considered in the risk based planning for 2016. The CAs are planning to evaluate the risk assessments by the end of this year in order to take into account the microbiological risks identified in scientific opinions

In addition, in September 2015 the regional authorities in Calabria started to develop a new procedure for the official control on primary production of FNAO with relevant checklists containing certain microbiological risks. In 2015, the authorities were responsible for controls on approximately 2400 farms producing FNAO and they carried out approximately 200 inspections at those FBOs. However, at the time of the audit, inspections did not consider any microbiological risks except for contamination of water used at primary producers. Moreover, at the time of the audit, microbiological risks (other than relating to water) identified by EFSA concerning FNAO were not included in the risk-based
The development of national guides to good practice is not encouraged as required by Article 7 and Annex 1 to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

Currently there are no national guides to good hygiene practice for the control of hazards in primary production of FNAO in Bulgaria. The CA didn't provide evidence that the development of such guides is encouraged.

The two inspectors checked the documentation of the company, including test results of water analysis (twice a year), results of testing the hygiene of the equipment and rooms, cleaning and disinfection using swab tests (twice a year), pest control, labelling and traceability. The information regarding accreditation of the laboratory and the method used for STEC were not available on the certificates provided. There was no indication that the seeds were intended for sprouting.

paragraph_text: Risks of microbiological contamination in primary production were not included in the risk analysis at the time of the audit. Controls by the PPCD on farms are risk-based. The audit team was informed that at the time of the audit the risk-assessment was mainly based on the use of pesticides.

label_heading: Conclusions on official control of production and placing on the market
paragraph_text: Official controls on production and placing on the market cover all stages of production and are in general implemented in accordance with EU requirements. However, for certain requirements (e.g. use of food additives), officials over-rely on statements and declarations provided by FBOs without actually verifying actual compliance. Thus, in those cases official controls do not provide guarantees that fishery products and FBO comply with relevant Union requirements.

label_heading: Conclusions on official control of fishery products.
paragraph_text: Official controls of fishery products are carried out according to EU requirements. The weaknesses detected regarding official checks on the operators' control of parasites indicates that fishery products reach the market with insufficient treatment to kill viable parasites. 5.4 FOLLOW-UP OF RASFF NOTIFICATIONS Articles 50 and 52 of Section I, Chapter IV to Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. paragraph_text: There is a system in place to investigate problems that occur and to take action in response to RASFF notifications. However, the over-reliance on statements and declarations provided by FBOs described in conclusion 27 has also had an adverse impact in the follow-up of RASFF notifications. 5.5 LABORATORIES Legal requirements Articles 11, 12 and 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 1 and 5 and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and Article 2 and Section II of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005. According to national procedure, FBOs do not have to document good manufacturing practices (GMPs) if they are not linked to food safety. Official assessment of GMPs, as required by Article 10.2.d of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, is restricted to the explanation of the modus operandi by FBOs to official inspectors. The audit team noted that in one of the establishments visited testing of ready-to-eat products was not documented. This lack of documentation had not been acted on by officials during previous control visits4.

In some cases, deficiencies noted by the audit team during the visits had already been identified during official controls or were detected by official inspectors during the Commission services visit (e.g. shortcomings on traceability or lack of temperature records). However, this was not always the case5, for example: Regarding general hygiene, in one establishment visited there was no physical separation (i.e. some space) between raw material and products ready to be smoked. Stagnant water on the floor after washing whole and gutted fish was also noted that could splash the products ready to be smoked which were kept nearby. Testing for parasites takes place randomly by visual inspection. In addition, during official controls, official inspectors focus on FBO own-checks and, in particular, if fishery products are intended to be consumed raw or subject to any other treatment that is insufficient to kill viable parasites, FBOs must have adequate procedures in place. These procedures shall include freezing of fishery products derived from wild caught fish or, in the case of farmed fishery products, a certificate to guarantee the requirements of Section VII, Chapter III.D.3.d of Regulation (EC) No 853/200411. label_heading: Conclusions on measures in cases of pesticide residue detections
paragraph_text: The national Guidelines will help harmonising investigation procedures across CBs. Files for pesticide residue detections in 2014 show the different approaches taken by CBs at the time. This demonstrates the need for further harmonisation through the new Guidance, in order to achieve consistent investigation procedures compliant with Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

Both CBs visited had included in their Manual of Procedure a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for inspectors on the risk assessment for prioritising samples for pesticide residue analyses. There were also detailed sampling instructions. CB1 requires a laboratory sample of 500 g only, which is less than the 1-2 kg required for fresh fruits and vegetables in the national Regulations. The SOP of CB2 correctly implemented the national sampling provisions, but two laboratory files for samples of leaves indicated a weight of 32 and 107 grams, respectively, which is less than the 200 grams required for leaves in the national Regulations, and which may not be sufficient for a representative sample

A file for pesticide detection in 2014 was examined by the audit team at CB1. The producer had been informed of the decertification of her field based on a pesticide residue detection of 0.03 mg/kg of the pesticide pendimethalin. There was no evidence of consultation of the producer concerned, contrary to Article 91(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Neither follow-up inspection nor re-sampling was performed. In 2014, a total of 146 samples of organic products had been taken and in two cases only there were pesticides detected. In a further eleven cases, the producer admitted the use of unauthorised pesticides without samples being taken. Conclusions on measures in cases of pesticide residue

The laboratories and an NRL have been adequately designated in line with Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. There were no official criteria for the CBs on the laboratory checks to be carried out, contrary to Articles 5(2)(a) and 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Consequently, the performance of the analysis is compromised. This affects the range of pesticides checked and the quality control procedure applied.

The MIAFQI Guidelines (see point 7) specifies that the scope of laboratory analyses should not focus on the price, but on the likelihood to find pesticides. The analyses should also take into account the type of product, the risk of infringement and plant protection measures in conventional farming. The Guidance does not explicitly specify which pesticides should be checked, and the sensitivity of methods as expressed by the Limits of Quantification (LOQs) to be applied by the laboratory. Consequently, the private laboratory visited did not sufficiently apply these procedures. label_heading: Conclusions on Competent Authorities and Control Bodies
paragraph_text: As laboratories for analysis of organic samples under Regulation 834/2007 are not designated by CA and communicated to the NRLs, they are not included in the co- ordination of and supervision by NRLs and EURLs, which can influence the quality of analytical results. 5.2 SAMPLING FOR DETECTING UNAUTHORISED PESTICIDES AT ORGANIC OPERATORS Legal Requirements Article 65 (2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 on control visits. Findings

In Germany, organic samples taken by CBs are analysed in laboratories for pesticide residues. There is no legal obligation for CBs to notify these laboratories. Therefore, this is not a pre-condition for their approval. As part of the approval, CBs are only requested to inform the CA about laboratories they use, but these are not officially assessed by the CA. Furthermore, no legal requirements are in place for these laboratories to be officially designated. As a result, their use for purposes within the scope of the audit is not communicated to the NRLs, and, thus these laboratories are not subject to supervision by either the NRLs or the approving CA.

There is a system is in place to ensure that no consignment from a non-EU country is introduced into EU territory without being subjected to veterinary checks, although the system did not work for consignments transhipped via other Member States during 2015 at Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP. 5.3.2 Veterinary checks and the decision on the consignment Legal requirements Articles 4, 8, 15 and Annex III of Directive 97/78/EC, Article 4(1) of Directive 91/496/EEC, Article 27(2) of Commission Regulation 142/2011, 4(2)(d) of Commission Decision 2001/812/EC, Annex II of Commission Decision 97/794/EC and Commission Decision 94/360. There were four transhipment consignments of products during 2015 which were destined for the Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP. This BIP had not detected the relevant TRACES notification sent from the first EU BIP although staff stated that TRACES notifications are checked twice per day. The competent authority contacted Customs who confirmed that all four consignments had been released for free circulation as they had CVEDs (see finding 10). A similar finding was reported in report DG(SANTE) 2014-7012 but corrective actions have not been implemented. Conclusions on the system to ensure presentation of consignments for veterinary checks

label_heading: Conclusions on veterinary checks and the decision on the consignment
paragraph_text: In general, veterinary checks and decisions on consignments are correct but there are several issues which undermine the effectiveness of the system. The most significant of these is at Röszke BIP where the system to implement physical checks does not comply with national or EU requirements. Appropriate corrective action was not implemented in response to a related finding in report DG(SANCO) 2014-7008. This means that CVEDs do not reflect the reality of the controls done at the BIPs and the competent authority does not ensure that corrective action is taken when needed.

In relation to the implementation of physical checks on consignments (products), the audit team noted that: Röszke BIP received 82% of consignments presented at Hungarian BIPs in 2014. Staff at Röszke BIP stated that physical checks are often carried out without unloading any of the consignment from the means of transport and can be based on only a visual examination of the boxes. This approach does not comply with the requirements of Section 3.4 of the BIP Manual. It also does not comply with Annex III of Directive 97/78/EC which describes the aim and types of physical checks to be conducted at BIPs. This also means that CVEDs do not reflect the reality of the controls done at the BIPs. Fin

label_heading: Conclusions on the controls of transit/non-complying consignments
paragraph_text: Veterinary checks carried out at entry BIPs on consignments in transit comply with EU requirements and ensure that only eligible consignments are accepted. The system to promptly identify and follow-up consignments for which no confirmation of receipt at destination has been received by the entry BIP was not being implemented as planned, reducing the ability of the system to identify non-conforming consignments that have not left the Union as planned. 5.5 COMPLIANCE OF THE FACILITIES, EQUIPMENT AND HYGIENE CONDITIONS OF THE BIPS VISITED Legal requirements Article 6 of Directive 97/78/EC and Articles 1-5 of, and the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC for products and Directive 91/496/EEC concernin

Only Röszke BIP has received incoming transit consignments in recent years, e.g. 628 consignments during 2014. Details on non-confirmed consignments were sent about every two months to the central competent authority for further investigation. The audit team noted that the BIP did not consult with local Customs before consulting the central competent authority. This is not in line with internal procedures and causes unnecessary delays. It was clarified during the audit that the central office was not aware that Röszke BIP had not been contacting local Customs before it forwarded the list to them.
At Záhony BIP 20 out of 21 consignments were checked in 2014. In Röszke 4 out of 13 consignments were checked during 2014. Neither BIP followed-up the consignments not presented for checks.

There was one consignment in TRACES which indicated Eperjeske as the exit BIP (notified in December 2013). The BIP had not detected the notification via their daily screening and therefore had not informed Customs. The CVED indicated that the consignment was being transported by road. The competent authority confirmed that it had exited via BIP Záhony without being checked by the BIP. The same staff is responsible for import controls at the BIPs Eperjeske and Záhony, yet the consignment had not been detected. Transits of live animals

There were no entry transits and only four exit transits via Hungarian BIPs during 2014 and 2015. No Part IIIs of the CVEDs were completed by the exit BIPs in TRACES. One 11 consignment was discussed during the audit, i.e. a cat which entered via Budapest-Liszt Ferenc and with Röszke as the exit BIP. The animal was destined for Serbia and the CVED did not contain any details for the means of transport after the entry BIP and therefore the exit BIP could not detect it. Budapest-Liszt Ferenc did not receive any confirmation of exit via TRACES and did not follow this up with Customs. Controls on free and customs warehouses

Findings

Eperjeske BIP Facilities, equipment and hygiene conditions are compliant with the exception of: Facilities are shared for checks on consignments destined for human and non-human consumption but there is no documented risk assessment contrary to Article 4(5) of Decision 2001/812/EC. There is currently no system to ensure that equipment is calibrated as required. 12

Kelebia BIP Facilities and equipment were found to be sub-standard due to their poor maintenance (in addition to the main deficiencies identified in the other BIPs, at Kelebia, the most serious included broken doors preventing access to the unloading area) and hygiene conditions were poor.

Röszke BIP Facilities, equipment and hygiene conditions are compliant with the exception of: The storage room for frozen consignments destined for human consumption was being used to store paper files and office equipment at the time of the audit and was therefore unavailable for its intended use. The BIP staff stated that this situation had existed for about one year and no specific deadline for resolution was available. Although a written procedure exists to ensure appropriate cleaning and disinfection of the entire BIP, no records were available of its implementation. There is currently no effective system to ensure that equipment is calibrated as required.

Záhony BIP Facilities, equipment and hygiene conditions are compliant with the exception of: There is currently no system to ensure that relevant equipment is calibrated as required. Conclusions on the compliance of the facilities, equipment and hygiene conditions of the BIPs visited

label_heading: Conclusion on general issues on SNCPs
paragraph_text: The CA has tools in place to facilitate the monitoring of the implementation of the official and own-check sampling (database, auditing and reporting system) and review and evaluate the progress of the SNCPs. However there are weaknesses in the system as it does not allow the central level to monitor CSVFSDs and CSVFSLs performance and consequently to guarantee that the activities contained in the SNCPs are implemented as described in the programmes themselves. In fact, shortcomings related to sampling frequency and sampling procedures in own-checks detected by the audit team had not been identified/recorded by the official staff at county level and therefore they were not communicated from

Procedures are in place for the rejection of non-compliant samples collected under the programmes. However, at county level, there are shortcomings in their implementation and this has entailed as a consequence that non-compliant samples have been accepted by the laboratories for analysis. This is not in line with EU requirements and with the approved SNCPs. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION SNCPs are implemented in Romania and cover all relevant poultry populations. An effort has been made by the CA to improve the situation since the last FVO audit in 2010. label_heading: Conclusions on Controls at farm level
paragraph_text: The interpretation of the term flock used by the German authorities does not always match the definition set down in EU legislation. As a consequence, the testing scheme in place cannot ensure that the sampling protocols applied always meet EU requirements.

label_heading: Conclusions on SNCP for laying hens
paragraph_text: The implementation of the SNCP for the laying hens is, in general, carried out in accordance with the programme and EU requirements, in particular concerning sampling frequency of the official controls and of the own-checks and sampling protocol used during routine official sampling. However, the sampling protocols applied by FBOs when the holding consists of different populated houses are not always in line with EU requirements, particularly due to the actual interpretation of flock's definition.

The identification of the bids of a holding is based on the specific populated house of the holding (house number) and the date it is populated or the age of birds. Under the actual interpretation of a flock, even where birds are kept in different houses on a holding, in some instances they can be considered as a single flock equating with one epidemiological unit. The audit team noted that usually all the birds of the populated houses of the same holding being in the same location are considered as one epidemiological unit and so as one flock (e.g. 7 houses with a common egg belt of a laying hen farm were documented as one flock). This does not match with the EU definition of a flock which

In particular, the CAs at Länder level explained that in order to establish the size of a flock, several factors are taken into consideration (e.g. common equipment used among holding's houses, common hygiene facilities and common entrance into the houses, other risks of cross-contamination). Based on this, the CA representatives in NI informed the audit team that in the majority of cases each holding represents a single flock. 9

However, the audit team noted during its visits to different holdings that in some cases houses equipped with their own hygiene facilities (separate entrances for each house of the holdings, separate ventilation systems, separate silos for storage of feed and feeding systems) and located close to each other were considered as one flock.

In relation to the actual interpretation of flock, when the audit team reviewed the implementation of the SNCP during its visits in the different districts offices and poultry farms, it was noted that: in the majority of cases reviewed, the sampling protocols applied by the FBOs were in line with EU requirements. In these instances, even if all the houses of the holding had been considered as one flock, the sampling protocols of own-checks were applied per house. in a small number of cases reviewed, the interpretation of flock led to less samples been taken by FBOs. In three holdings examined (one turkey fattening farm and two laying hen farms) the own-checks sampling comprised one pair of b

The audit team visited two laying hen holdings. The first one consisted of two houses keeping two different flocks: one free range and one in enriched cages. The second holding consisted of three houses, with a barn farming system, considered to be one flock according to the actual interpretation of flock definition. During the visits at the local CAs of both Länder visited the audit team also reviewed documentation related to other laying hen farms. During these visits and the reviews the audit team, noted that: · the sampling frequency of official and FBO sampling were in compliance with EU legislation with the exception of one case where the first sampling of the adult laying hens had bee

The confirmatory sampling policy applied in holdings is not in compliance with Point 2.2.2.2 (c) of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 200/2010 as it is carried-out without any specific reason to doubt the validity of the initial results (false positive or false negative results). In addition the sampling protocol used is not in line with Point 2.2.2.2 (b) of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 200/2010, particularly concerning the lack of furter testing when the presence of relevant Salmonella serotypes is not confirmed. 4.5 SNCP FOR LAYING HENS Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 517/2011. Findings

Under federal legislation and SNCP rules, confirmatory testing must be always performed when own-check tests, taken at the holding or hatchery, result positive for the targeted Salmonella serotypes. The practice of performing routine confirmatory sampling when own-checks results of sampling at the holding are positive is not in line with Point 2.2.2.2 (c) of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 200/2010 which establishes that this should only be done in exceptional cases, when the CA has reason to question the test results (e.g. false positive or false negative results).

Under federal legislation and according to the information given to the audit team by the CA, confirmatory sampling (at holding level) is carried out in accordance with Point 2.2.2.2 (a) of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 200/2010 (i.e. sampling protocol provided for official routine sampling) by taking one set of samples in accordance with Point 2.2.2.1 of the Annex to the Regulation. However, the Regulation states that in the exceptional cases described in Point 2.2.2.2.(c) of its Annex the sampling should be carried-out in accordance with Point 2.2.2.2.(b) (i.e. official protocol for confirmatory sampling following detection of the relevant Salmonella serotypes from sampling at the 17 hatcher

label_heading: Conclusions on SNCP for laying hens
paragraph_text: A small number of holdings under the framework of SNCPs (with number of birds <1000) can under certain conditions be excluded from the Salmonella sampling frame. This could have an impact on the level of Salmonella prevelance reported by Germany as the number of these holdings is not always reported by the local CAs and there are no data on sampling results.

label_heading: Conclusions on SNCP for laying hens
paragraph_text: The confirmatory sampling policy applied in Germany, which is performed routinely without any specific reason to doubt the validity of the initial test results is not in line with the relevant EU legislation. In this regard the sampling protocol used does not comply with Point 4, Part D of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003, in particular concerning the method used, which is less sensitive than the one required in this Regulation. Furthermore the actions taken for verifying the absence of the use of antimicrobials potentially affecting the results of the analysis of the confirmatory sampling do not comply with EU rules either. 4.6 SNCP FOR BROILERS Legal requirements Article 5 of Regul

In both Länder visited the audit team was informed by the CAs that specific criteria had been developed for the assessment of these quality systems implemented at farm level. The CCA informed the audit team that the GflSalmoV requires also authorities at district level to report the data (e.g. the number) of these holdings. However, in two of the four district offices visited the audit team noted, that this data was not reported and that official controls to verify/monitor the implementation of the conditions to be met in these holdings had not been performed. The audit team further noted in the districts visited that the number of these holdings were in general low. The fact that the sampli

According to the GflSalmoVand the SNCP, an official confirmatory sample has to be always carried out in case an own-check sample results positive for the Salmonella targeted serotypes (or if there are sufficient grounds for suspecting a Salmonella infection for the targeted serotypes e.g. after the detection of relevant serogroups). This is not in line with EU legislation (Point 4, Part D of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003) as it should only be carried out in exceptional cases in order to exclude initial false-positive results.

In two of the districts visited the audit team noted that the sampling protocol applied during the confirmatory sampling was the same as that for routine official sampling (three pair swab tests instead of five boot swabs plus two dust samples analysed separately) and so it is not in line with Point 4, Part D of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003.

The audit team further noted, in all the positive cases examined, that the serotyping (for both own check and official samples) was always carried out officially in the NRL, which needed a usually long time to provide official results (see also paragraph 61). 20

In all the Salmonella positive cases examined by the audit team, it was noted that no laboratory tests for verification of the absence of use of antimicrobials was performed by the CA when confirmatory sampling resulted negative. This is not in line with Point 4, Part D of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003 which requires CAs to verify11 the absence of use of antimicrobials, potentially affecting the results of analysis of the sampling. The CA informed the audit team that this verification is based on documentary checks. In one of the districts visited the CA informed the audit team that it is not foreseen, as part of the SNCP, to take samples for detecting the use of antimicrobials. C
The confirmatory sampling policy in place, which is performed routinely, is not in line with the relevant EU rules.

According to federal legislation, confirmatory sampling must always be performed in case of results of own-check sampling being positive for relevant Salmonella serotypes. This is not in line with EU requirements.

The control system in place does not ensure that the relevant information concerning Salmonella in broilers is provided as required along the food chain through in particular the FCI and the health certificate accompanying birds to the slaughterhouse which are found to be Salmonella positive. 4.7 SNCP FOR TURKEYS Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003 Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 1190/2012. Findings Breeding turkeys

In the districts visited, the audit team reviewed documentation on broiler flocks found positive for relevant Salmonella serotypes. The CA informed the audit team that: · In one case, the FCI and the health certificate (signed by the official veterinarian when the AMI was carried out at the holding of provenance) did not contain information on the Salmonella status of the flock despite the laboratory results being positive for Salmonella targeted serotypes, and · In a second case, in another district, despite a routine official sample result being positive for Salmonella spp, neither the FCI nor the health certificate contained this information. The flock was slaughtered as Salmonella negati

The CAs explained to the audit team that the health certificate template does not contain a specific point for reporting information on Salmonella results /status of the flock12. The CA also added that the FBO is obliged to include positive laboratory results in the FCI. It may include negative results at its discretion.

The above mentioned findings are not in line in particular with: · third paragraph of Point 4.2 of Regulation (EU) No 200/2012 which states that the results of the tests shall be considered relevant for the FCI as provided in Section III of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, and · The requirement of Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 which requires the official veterinarian who carried out inspection tasks to take appropriate measures as regards the communication of inspection results..
