label_heading: Conclusion on general issues on SNCPs
paragraph_text: The routine confirmatory sampling and the reporting policy applied in Poland has an impact on the calculated prevalence of Salmonella compared to other Member States. In particular regarding flocks of breeding Gallus gallus, laying hens and broilers, given that routine confirmatory sampling is applied and that flocks are deemed positive only after official confirmation of positive own-checks. 5.4 SNCP FOR BREEDING HENS Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 200/2010. 12 Findings

The audit team was informed by the CA that, under the SNCPs for all poultry populations, a flock is only considered positive when a relevant Salmonella serotype has been isolated either during official sampling or when positive own-check sample has been confirmed by official sampling and analysed by the official laboratory.

When reviewing the information provided by the CCA the audit team noted that in breeders of Gallus gallus, laying hens and broilers, positive FBO samples are reported as negative flocks if the routine official confirmation is negative. In breeders of turkeys and fattening turkeys, flocks are reported as positive when the own-check result alone is positive. 11 The CCA informed the audit team that the prevalence in 2014 in breeding flocks of Gallus gallus was recorded as 1.54 % (25 positive adult flocks out of 1,627 flocks tested). Seventeen flocks tested positive for relevant Salmonella serotype in the FBO own-check sampling and nine of these seventeen flocks proved negative in confirmatory s

With the exception of the absence of residue monitoring in the first two months of the year and the lack of verification on how control bodies implement suspect or targeted sampling, the residue monitoring plan is implemented effectively. 5.1.4 Other residue monitoring programmes Legal Requirements Articles 9 and 11 of Directive 96/23/EC; Articles 8 and 10 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

In 2014, RMP sampling started in the second half of March, as the planning process was not finalised earlier. In 2015, VMPRMD had forwarded the first set of sampling requests to the regional coordinators in the week preceding the FVO audit. An investigation was performed in the laboratory but the reason for the samples going missing was not identified1. In two of the slaughterhouses visited, official residue samples were kept in unsecured fridges and freezers, either in storage rooms within the slaughterhouse's own laboratory area or in an unlocked fridge in a room with no access restriction for personnel. The temperature of one freezer was also not monitored. Such unsecured storage is not in line with the requirements of point 2.9 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC regarding suitable storage to ensure analyte stability and sample integrity or the requirements of Article 11(7) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 that samples must be handled in such a way as to guarantee both their legal and analytical validity.

Although samples are effectively sealed, such storage does not fully ensure that all samples remain under official control from the time of sampling through to analysis. If such samples were removed by a third party and this was noticed at the end of the day or the next day before samples were to be collected, although the animal carcase would likely still be available for sampling in the slaughterhouse, many of the original matrices which may have been subject to sampling would not be (e.g. 1 In their response to the draft report the competent authorities clarified that a human error seems to be the most plausible reason for the missing samples. Veterinary medicinal products 5.2.1. Competent authorities

The method for quinolones (in operation since 2006) has been validated in accordance with the requirements of Article 3 of Decision 2002/657/EC in bovine muscle. No other muscle matrices (for example pig, poultry, fish and rabbit) have been validated (though there were satisfactory results in proficiency tests for oxolinic acid and difloxacin in rabbit meat in 2009). There are no instructions on how to address possible matrix effects in the general SOP on method validation.

The LC-MS method for sulphonamides in muscle was recently validated at 20 µg/kg (screening) and MRL level (confirmation) in line with the requirements of Article 3 of Decision 2002/657/EC. While the screening method was validated in muscle of different animal species, confirmatory method validation was carried out only in pig muscle samples. No muscle of other animal species (e.g. cattle, fish, and rabbit) was included in the validation study. 9

As described in the 2009 FVO report, a special form called document d'administration ou de fourniture (DAF) is used to document veterinary treatments on holdings. Veterinary practitioners are obliged to record on DAFs both medicines personally administered by the veterinarian to animals on the farm during the risk period and those delivered from the veterinary depot to the farmer. The DAF forms seen by the audit team did not include the identification of specific/ individual animals to be treated4. Therefore the DAF form cannot be considered as equivalent to treatment records as required under Article 10 of Directive 96/23/EC and Article 69 of Directive 2001/82/EC. At all three farms visited

For recording treatments administered to food-producing animals by a farmer, a standardised form (administration/ supply record) is distributed by the Flemish association (Dierengezondheidszorg Vlanderen -DGZ) and the Walloon association (Association Régionale de Santé et d'Identification Animales -ARISA), with the provision that treatment records have to be maintained for each animal species separately (i.e. separate records for cattle, sheep etc.). As recording of withdrawal periods is not foreseen in this form, the content of the form is not fully in line with Article 10 of Directive 96/23/EC and Regulation 852/2004 (Annex I, Part A III, point 8(b))5. The competent authority stated that consultations with stakeholders are on-going and that a task force to draft a new legislative act on veterinary medicines records on farms was formed with the target to have the Belgian legislation compliant with EU rules by 1 January 2016. The system in place for controls on the distribution and use of veterinary medicinal products is well designed, notwithstanding the fact that the simplified food chain information introduced for bovines in the form of a farmer declaration is not in line with EU requirements and weakens the effectiveness of said system as regards investigations of non-compliant results. As regards equidae, the system for the identification of horses is in place and controls on slaughtered horses are being effectively implemented. 5.3. paragraph_text: The follow-up of the relatively few non-compliant results to date has been done in a timely and effective manner. paragraph_text: As regards biosecurity standards, the CA does not ensure that official controls on biosecurity measures applied in the poultry holdings are carried out at the established frequency based on risk analysis in accordance with Article 3.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and in line with the SNCPs.

A standard checklist was introduced by the CA in 2011 for verification of the biosecurity measures applied on-farm to prevent the introduction of Salmonella. paragraph_text: The official controls in place do not guarantee FBO compliance with all the general hygiene provisions laid down in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 for primary production, in particular concerning water quality and cleaning and disinfection practices. Therefore the CA does not fully ensure that appropriate measures are in place to prevent Salmonella contamination at farm level. 7 5.3 GENERAL ISSUES ON SNCPS

Under the SNCPs, FBO compliance with biosecurity conditions has to be checked annually by officials and when a farm is found positive for relevant Salmonella serotypes. According to the CA the frequency has been determined on the basis of a risk analysis which takes into account the data obtained through the SNCPs implemented the preceding year. A standard checklist was introduced by the CA in 2011 for verification of the biosecurity measures applied on-farm to prevent the introduction of Salmonella. In two out of three farms visited municipality water was used. The CA informed the audit team that when the supply of water is from private boreholes, analysis to ensure water quality is performed by the FBO on a voluntary basis. In one of the farms using well water, the audit team was informed by the CA that water analyses for some 6 parameters were performed by the FBO. However, analyses results were not available to the audit team. Cleaning and disinfection

Under the SNCPs and as required by national legislation, after depopulation of a positive flock an effective cleaning and disinfection should be carried out by the FBO. The audit team was informed by the CA that the effectiveness of such cleaning and disinfection must be verified by official environmental samples. Under national legislation, the CA can permit restocking only once no Salmonella spp. is isolated from these environmental samples. However, in two positive farms visited (broiler holdings) this procedure was not followed as permission for restocking was granted by the CA although such samples had not been taken. label_heading: Conclusions on general issues on SNCPs
paragraph_text: The CA has tools in place to facilitate monitoring the implementation of the SNCPs. However, when issues are detected corrective actions for remedying the situation are not taken. Therefore the CA does not ensure that all the activities contained in the SNCPs are implemented as described in the approved programmes, in particular concerning the sampling (insufficient number of samples and incorrect sampling). Audit findings

In 2013 an internal audit was carried out by the VRD to verify the correctness of the implementation of the SNCPs. The majority of the shortcomings highlighted in the resulting audit report are similar to those detected by the FVO audit team during the course of this audit. The deadline set for the verification of the corrective actions required in the 2013 report was April 2014. The CA informed the audit team that the deficiencies found during the internal audit had not, at the time of the current FVO audit, been addressed or followed-up. The CA explained that the appointed auditor had left and is still to be replaced (see also Chapter 5.3). 4 Conclusions on competent authority

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: In addition, some practices which deviate from the approved Programme (such as movement restrictions applying only to positive animals, absence of testing of all eligible animals on positive holdings, absence of bacteriological testing on positive holdings, no investigation of abortions, application of EU non-compliant testing scheme to classify a holding as BMOF, no restrictions of use of pastures used by infected animals). These practices have an adverse effect on elimination of the infection and hamper achievement of the Programme objectives to the detriment of the overall cost- effectiveness of the Programme.

According to the Ministerial Decision Ref 4888/130873 as well as Official Decisions on measures to be implemented on infected holdings in the vaccination zone, verified by the audit team on the spot, restrictions on movements apply to positive animals only. This is not in line with the Point 4.4.9 of the BMEP nor with the Article 3(13)(a) of Council Decision 90/242/EC, where the prohibition of exit and introduction of animals (except movements for immediate slaughter) applies to the infected flock.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: In addition, some practices which deviate from the approved Programme (such as movement restrictions applying only to positive animals, absence of testing of all eligible animals on positive holdings, absence of bacteriological testing on positive holdings, no investigation of abortions, application of EU non-compliant testing scheme to classify a holding as BMOF, no restrictions of use of pastures used by infected animals). These practices have an adverse effect on elimination of the infection and hamper achievement of the Programme objectives to the detriment of the overall cost- effectiveness of the Programme.

The Ministerial Decision Ref 4888/130873 does not require application of measures to infected pastures. Pastures that held infected animals are not forbidden to be used for at least two months, which is not in line with Article 5(1) of the Council Decision 90/242/EC. None of the Official Decisions verified by the audit team included a requirement as regards pastures used by animals from infected herds. 5.3.6.2 Slaughter of positive animals

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of the eradication measures
paragraph_text: The absence of measures as regards the use of milk from animals in an infected holding on the same or on another holding in the vaccination zone, prevent minimisation of possible risk of infection of humans or animals. This is in particular relevant for infected herds where vaccination coverage is low.

Milk from vaccinated animals on infected holdings is considered as milk from non- infected animals. According to the Article 16(7) of the Ministerial Decision Ref. 4888/130873, milk from non-infected animals from an infected holding has to be used according to the provisions of Annex III, Section IX, Chapter I, Paragraphs 3 to 5 of the Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. However, no Official Decisions reviewed by the audit team, imposed restrictions or requirements regarding the use of milk from animals from the infected holding on the same or other holdings. Also, Official Decisions reviewed, did not specify any restrictions as regards the use of milk from infected animals as mentioned in Point 4.

Samples submitted for laboratory analysis for SCC and TPC showed evidence of having been manipulated in order to obtain satisfactory results. Contributing factors are the lack of standard procedures for collection of samples by FBOs and the absence of official controls on sample collection. The integrity of samples as required by Article 11.7 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 has not been achieved.

Some of the results of raw milk analysis of samples taken on the holding visited were shown to the FVO audit team. For the reasons given in paragraphs 40 ­ 42 below, these cannot be considered plausible. Conclusions on Official Controls over Food Business Operator's compliance

The laboratories visited could provide the results for all the samples delivered to them and these were evaluated by the FVO audit team. For the reasons mentioned below, the results were not credible. Only one laboratory provided credible results. While this had been identified in a number of laboratories, only one (NRL) had documented these anomalies. However, no follow-up action had been taken by the official services and official controls had not detected problems with the lack of credibility of analysis results.

The results of the tests carried out in different public or private laboratories differed very significantly, with some public laboratories identifying high or very high numbers of unsatisfactory results, while the private laboratories identified hardly any non- compliance even when performing a high number of analyses including in the same geographical areas. The range went from zero to 30% for TPC and SCC.

In a high proportion of cases raw milk samples taken by an official or the FBO at holding level had been manipulated. They had been diluted before being submitted for analysis: this was evident when the values for fat content and/or freezing point were taken into consideration. For example, many examples were seen where the fat content was lower than 1%. This was also the case for official samples taken in the framework of the process for the classification of holdings. As a consequence the results for TPC and SCC were deemed satisfactory whereas, in reality, they would have been unsatisfactory if they had not been diluted prior to analysis.

When subjected to statistical analysis, it was found that the results of samples collected by specific FBOs on different holdings were lower than or approaching the limits of repeatability of the methods (for example 6,6 % at a level 140 000 cells where the acceptable variation limit was 10 % when analysing the same samples twice). Usually, results showing 50% to 90% (depending of the level of TPC or SCC) of variation are expected with such microbiological reference methods. This was the case for one laboratory, in particular, where a high number of analyses had been carried out. In such cases, it cannot be excluded that the sampling supposed to come from different holdings came from one sin

The method in place for detecting inhibitors is not suitable for detecting certain categories of inhibitors which has the potential to allow non-compliant milk to enter the food chain. The number and range of laboratory ring test organised by the NRL is insufficient to provide assurance of adequate performance by laboratories.

All four laboratories visited during the FVO audit were accredited for the analysis carried out. Nevertheless one of the laboratories visited was accredited for the reference method (ISO 13336-1) but was using an automated variance of this reference method without any internal or external validation having been carried out.

The analytical performance of laboratories is assessed by inter-laboratories tests (Ring tests) organised by the NRL for Total Plate Count (TPC), Somatic Cell Count (SCC) and residues analysis for inhibitors. It is compulsory for the public laboratories to take part in these ring tests and all private laboratories are invited to participate. Most private laboratories do so and the four laboratories visited by the FVO audit team had participated on a regular basis or at least partially (one laboratory had not participated in 9 the ring test in relation to SCC). Ring tests are not performed sufficiently frequently to allow a reliable assessment of the performance of laboratories. In addition,

Concerning inhibitors, the Bulgarian standard method was used in all laboratories visited, but its application varied between laboratories, in particular, concerning the cut off (time or acidity range) between compliant and non-compliant results. More generally, it should be noted that this method is insufficient to detect certain categories of inhibitors. This was confirmed in an evaluation carried out by the NRL and this could 10 also explain the almost complete absence of the detection of inhibitors in official and own check samples. The manual on phytosanitary import control has an attachment with 12 sampling tables for visual inspection for different types of commodities prepared on the basis of ISPM 31. These tables define the number of units for sampling e.g. fruits, sachets, bunches of flowers, to be selected for visual inspection. For each type of commodity, a sampling matrix at confidence level of 95% and 99% is set as per ISPM 31. The sampling size i.e. the column to be used depends on the level of risk established for the lot or consignment. Default sampling rate for all types of c

The FVO team witnessed plant health checks of fruit (pomelo and lime), vegetables (green chillies and bitter gourd) and cut flowers (gypsophila) and noted that: Inspectors had appropriate technical competence regarding the detection of HOs in commodities which they regularly inspected; Inspections witnessed were meticulous. Inspectors checking cut flowers were shaking bunches above a paper sheet for the detection of thrips. All the bunches were opened for additional examination of the leaves under the illuminated magnifying lens; The inspection of fruit consisted of random selection of the required number of fruit from different boxes to meticulously inspect them with a magnifying glass. 10%

The definition of the "unit" to be sampled for visual inspection in the FASFC guidelines is not appropriate for some commodities e.g. a single fruit of small green chilli counts as a unit. For a large consignment of chillies the sampling size would be 60 pieces for low risk or 150 pieces for high risk consignment. The sample size inspected for large consignments of fruit and vegetables is not in line with ISPM 31 and cannot be considered as a representative sample. This does not comply with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC. In view of ISPM 31, the sample size should be big enough to result in a satisfactorily probability for finding pests. 13

The FASFC does not have a procedure for monitoring of non-regulated commodities, irrespective of risk. There is not a procedure in place for monitoring of non-regulated products. They are checked only if presented in mixed consignments, in consignments of fruits and vegetables which are subject to marketing standards quality controls and in consignments of non-animal origin in case of suspicion of the presence of HOs. The FVO team noted that articles on the Alert list are considered as high risk for the inspection but there are no procedures in place to enable the inspection of high risk non-regulated products. The plant health inspectors did not monitor them, this is not in line with provisions of Article 16(2) second subparagraph of Council Directive 2000/29/EC.

The FASFC stated that the procedure applied when non-compliances are detected during an import check. Internal procedures require that inspectors have four days from the date of receipt of laboratory analysis to report interceptions to DG Control who is then in charge of validation and entering the interception in EUROPHYT within one day. label_heading: Conclusions on on official controls on traceability of ABP/DP
paragraph_text: The checks carried out by the competent authorities to confirm the arrival and dispatch of consignments of ABP/DP in Portugal, combined with the attention paid to traceability and documentation requirements during official controls of most operators in the ABP/DP chain, provides adequate assurances that ABP/DP is used or disposed of in accordance with EU requirements. However, the lack of checks on these and other relevant issues carried out during controls of transporters of ABP/DP undermines the ability of the competent authorities to ensure that the EU requirements are fulfilled throughout the distribution chain. 6 5.3 FOLLOW-UP The table below summarises the follow-up to the relevant rec

Transporters of ABP/DP are inspected annually in order to authorise the containers or trailers used to carry such products, in accordance with national requirements (see finding 8). However, these controls do not include checks on relevant EU requirements including traceability and documentation systems (see finding 23). This is not in line with Article 32 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

At the transporter of ABP/DP visited, the audit team confirmed that the main focus of the annual official controls is the authorisation of containers and trailers used to carry such products, in accordance with the national rules (see findings 8 and 13) and in practice, no checks are carried out to verify that the relevant EU requirements are fulfilled as required by Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and Article 32 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The audit team confirmed that the operator had maintained a comprehensive documentation and traceability system which satisfied the requirements of Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and also recorded the sequence of different loads

label_heading: Conclusions on the official control systems
paragraph_text: Business operators, establishments and plants along the chain are subject to risk-based official controls; however, the competent authorities have not yet put in place the necessary arrangements (notably, updated checklists/guidelines) to ensure that: a) the checks along the chain of the production and use of PAP for aquaculture purposes are carried out and recorded on a regular basis, and b) that the process for the authorisation of operators handling products of ruminant origin is followed in a consistent manner. Although no sampling plans to detect the presence of ruminant proteins in PAP and aquaculture feed containing such PAP were organised in 2013 and 2014, a plan has been developed f

Operators along the chain are mostly checked according to the planned frequencies and non-compliances are followed in a structured and systematic manner. However, the absence of evidence of checks on the relevant feed ban requirements (notably, when an authorisation is required) and a low attention paid to the risk of cross-contamination during transport, undermines the overall reliability of the official controls. This weakness is mitigated by largely comprehensive own-control systems put in in place by the operators. 8 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a system of official controls in place which ensures all relevant operators, plants and establishments in the animal by-products / feed chain

The audit team visited two establishments, located in two different Regions, which required an authorisation because they were handling ruminant and non-ruminant materials, and noted the following: In one case the establishment is a processing plant producing blood products of porcine origin to be used for the manufacture of feed for aquaculture. It was noted that, although the establishment largely fulfilled the necessary conditions to obtain 4 an authorisation, there was no evidence available to demonstrate that these conditions had been actually checked during official controls (see paragraph 16). In the second case the establishment is a feed manufacturer (see paragraph 19). It was noted

Slaughterhouses/cutting plants, processing plants handling ABP destined to be used in the aquaculture feed and transporters of ABP and derived products are subject to inspections according to risk-based frequencies which are determined taking into account the recommended frequencies decided at central level and the specific risks identified at local level. In the feed sector, the PNAA valid from 2015 to 2017, highlights the need to inspect all feed business operators according to risk criteria and provides comprehensive explanations on, among other things, the risk factors to take into account. In both sectors (i.e. the ABP and the feed sector) guidelines and checklists to carry out official

The audit team visited a processing plant supplying PAP of poultry origin in big-bags or bulk for aquaculture feed. The operator had devised a largely comprehensive own-control system based on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles and regular samples from the final products are analysed to detect the presence of ruminant DNA (always resulted negative). However, the audit team noted that the risk of cross- contamination during the transport of incoming ABP was not considered in the hazard analysis and had not been included in the agreements with outsourced transporters even 6 though it is one of the conditions laid down in Section D of Chapter IV of Annex IV to Regulat

In the second processing plant visited the products placed on the market for aquaculture consist of whole dried blood and dried haemoglobin both of porcine origin, dispatched in big-bags or in bulk. The whole blood is processed in a dedicated production line physically separated from another line which processes blood of other species (including ruminants), whereas the haemoglobin is purchased, as such, stored in dedicated silos and dispatched. Although satisfactory arrangements were in place to avoid the risk of cross- contamination and these were verified by sampling final products, there was no evidence these had been checked during official controls, as the checklist used does not yet in

The audit team visited two transporters, located in two different Regions, one handling ABP and the other PAP, both of poultry origin, for aquaculture. Both of them had been authorised as transporters of ABP or derived products, according to a national rule and were subject to planned official controls (although in one of the three Regions visited the competent authorities declared that no checks of transporters were planned due to the lack of resources). According to the aforementioned national rule, the authorisation is granted by the local competent authority for each individual truck owned by the transporter and the transport of ABP/DP and feed in the same truck is prohibited. The audit

The audit team visited a trader of, among other things, PAP, and two feed manufacturers producing feed for aquaculture using PAP as raw material, one of which produced for both aquaculture and other farmed animals (including ruminants). All of them had largely comprehensive own-control systems and were subject to official controls (once or twice per year) according to the risk-based criteria set up by the central competent authority. However, the audit team noted that no evidence of the official checks on the relevant feed ban requirements, as required by Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, could be provided by the local competent authorities.

A system of official controls on the requirements concerning the ABP legislation and the general feed ban is in place in slaughterhouses, ABP plants, transporters of ABP and PAP and in feed manufactures producing feed for aquaculture animals. This also includes a sampling plan to detect ruminant DNA in feed for aquaculture animals. However, no specific checks on the new requirements pertaining to the use of derogated PAP in aquaculture feed have been organised yet. As a consequence, although the competent authorities undertook some immediate actions to address some of the issues identified, they are not yet in position to ensure that only eligible PAP is used for the production of feed for a

Official controls carried out in slaughterhouses, ABP plants, transporters of ABP and PAP and in feed manufactures producing feed for aquaculture animals, do not yet include regular checks on the new requirements pertaining to the use of derogated PAP in aquaculture feed. This limits the ability of the competent authorities to ensure that only eligible PAP is used for the production of feed for aquaculture animals. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system of official controls already in place in slaughterhouses, ABP plants, transporters of ABP and PAP and in feed manufacturers producing feed for aquaculture animals has not been extended yet to include the requirements related to the use of derogated

In the slaughterhouse, in the processing plants and in the transporter visited, the audit team noted that, although checks on requirements of the ABP legislation were carried out during official controls, these had never included the specific requirements applicable to sourcing and transport of ABP to be used for the production of derogated PAP for aquaculture feeding. Moreover, it was noted that neither guidelines nor checklists were available to the inspectors to assist them in verifying compliance with these requirements. As a result, official controls overlooked a number of deficiencies (see points 11, 12 and 13). This is not in line with the requirements on official controls laid down i

Official controls in manufacturers of feed for aquaculture cover aspects related to the feed ban in general. A specific checklist, which includes feed ban related issues, is available, 4 although it is officially no longer in use because it needs to be updated in order to include the specific requirements for the use of derogated PAP for aquaculture feeding. In this respect, the audit team noted that some requirements related to operators' own checks and their procedures for sourcing eligible PAP had been overlooked during official controls (see points 14 and 17). This is not fully in line with the requirements on official controls laid down in Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation

However, the audit team noted that the DVFA laboratory did not always use the Standard Operating Procedure describing the operational protocols for the combination of light microscopy and PCR, developed by the EURL-AP, although this procedure is a binding complement of the requirements laid down by Annex VI to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. All samples were first submitted to screening by the light microscopy method irrespective of the nature of the concerned sample. It was noted that aquaculture feed samples containing blood meal were not submitted to PCR, contrary to the aforementioned Standard Operating Procedure, because the light-microscopy method did not detect any particles from terrest

In one of the processing plants visited, the transport of ABP was outsourced to an external ABP transporter, who was also authorised to transport Category 2 and Category 3 ABP with no limitations in terms of animal species. This transporter was also providing the reusable containers. The audit team noted that the processing plant operator did not have any measures in place to ensure that the reusable containers were either dedicated exclusively for transport of eligible ABP or were cleaned by means of an authorised cleaning procedure prior to being used for the transport of ABP destined for production of 6 derogated PAP as required by Chapter IV, Section D, point (b) of Annex IV to Regulatio

The audit team noted that in one of the two processing plants visited consignments of PAP were dispatched without the required warning sentence in the commercial documents, as laid down by Chapter IV, Section D, point (e) of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. This was not identified during official controls. 5.2.2 Use of PAP for producing compound feed

Both fish feed producers visited in Denmark were dedicated to the production of fish feed. According to the feed business operators, the only information required to their suppliers of PAP was an evidence of approval/registration in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and a written declaration of the origin of PAP in terms of animal species. The audit team noted that no further information to confirm the origin and the eligibility of the PAP had ever been requested by the feed business operators. This issue was not checked during official controls.

The fish feed manufacturers visited used labels on the products containing information in several languages. In order to accommodate the information required in all languages, the operators made use of very small fonts difficult to read. Moreover, it was noted that in feed containing fish meal and other PAP, the operators used at the same time the warning sentence required for fish meal and the one required for PAP. As a result there was a risk of misinterpretation because fish meal can be fed to all farmed animals except ruminants, whereas PAP can only be fed to aquaculture farmed animals. This issue was not checked during official controls. 5.2.3 Actions in case of non-compliance

label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring, awareness and surveillance
paragraph_text: Passive and active surveillance programmes for rabies are in place. However, the effectiveness, in particular of passive surveillance, varies between the counties and is inadequate in several counties. This means that surveillance results are not sufficient to reliably assess the rabies incidence in all regions. Furthermore, the surveillance data reported to central level are not detailed enough to allow the identification of potential risks to the overall success of the eradication programme.

All foxes submitted to the laboratory under the vaccination monitoring programme, are tested for rabies virus before any other tests are carried out. The audit team noted that: In 2014, 2,269 foxes have been examined for the rabies virus, including foxes tested under active and passive surveillance. One of the national measures taken in the protection zone around rabies cases is to request additional samples of foxes for virus detection. paragraph_text: Once the vaccine has been accepted upon delivery to the cold store the responsibility for the implementation of an oral vaccination campaign rests with private operators (subcontractors) who are neither supervised by the main contractor nor subject to unannounced official controls by competent authorities during the campaign. This system is not effective as illustrated by the fact that deficiencies in the cold chain during 2014 had neither been corrected by the contractor nor reported at the time to the competent authorities.

There are no documented procedures containing information and instructions for officials carrying out inter alia controls on storage conditions, transport and handling of vaccine baits1. Such procedures are required under Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and are aimed at ensuring the quality and consistency of official controls that is required under Article 4(4) of the Regulation. label_heading: Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: Even though the monitoring plan requires the taking of samples for microbiological examination, the BIPs visited did not have proper equipment (see section 5.5) to implement the physical checks and the sterility. label_heading: Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: The competent authority has developed a monitoring plan to monitor conformity of goods with the requirements of EU legislation. However the lack of communication between those involved in the development and implementation of the monitoring plan, combined with the lack of a mechanism to ensure flexibility in its implementation, reduces the effectiveness of the monitoring plan in overseeing that imported goods comply with EU requirements. 5.1.2 Implementation of the monitoring plan

The Trade, Import, Export, BIPs Directorate (hereafter ­ the Import Directorate) within the NSVFSA is responsible for the planning of the monitoring plan on imported 3 products of animal origin. The representatives of the Import Directorate informed that they revise the monitoring plan on an annual basis without consulting other Directorates of NSVFSA or Romanian laboratories. This can lead to shortcomings such as possible lack of laboratory capacity or incorrect interpretation of legal requirements (see findings 5 and 6). This has an impact on the implementation of the monitoring plan.

The audit team noted that the monitoring plan is very prescriptive and it does not foresee adjustments during the year to take into consideration the changes of import patterns, in particular the plan does not cater for the possibility that BIPs may not receive the commodities specified in the monitoring plan. This, in turn, can lead to not targeting the correct consignments or to not sampling at all (see finding 16) resulting in weak implementation of the monitoring plan which is contrary to the requirements of Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusion on the development of the monitoring plan
paragraph_text: Romanian national legislation requires that the person responsible for the load covers the costs of the transportation of samples to the laboratory, as required by Article 27(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, the person responsible for the load collects the official samples from the BIPs and delivers them to the laboratories concerned, contrary to the requirement of Article 11(7) of Regulation (EC) 882/2004 since the official services can no longer guarantee the legal and analytical validity of the official import samples.

The audit team noted that the economic operator is also responsible for financing the transportation to the laboratories of official samples taken in case of suspicion (see finding 17). 8 Conclusion on actions in case of suspicion

label_heading: Conclusion on actions in case of suspicion
paragraph_text: Sampling in case of suspicion is limited to following safeguard measures and imposed checks subject to EU safeguard decisions. There are no instructions on actions in case of suspicion. The absence of further sampling under suspicion, together with the limited implementation of the monitoring plan, undermines the ability of the competent authority to detect consignments for which the veterinary legislation might have been not complied with or for which there is doubt. 5.3 USE OF THE RAPID ALERT SYSTEM FOR FOOD AND FEED Legal requirements Articles 2 and 5 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 16/2011. Findings

paragraph_text: The use of RASFF by the Import Directorate and BIPs is limited, therefore it cannot be used for consultation to identify the possible suspicious consignments.

There is no instruction in place which would prompt the BIP staff to take actions in case of suspicion (including detention and sampling) in order to follow the requirements of Article 20 of Directive 97/78/EC. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Furthermore, the BIP staff does not have direct access to RASFF (see finding 34). In practice, BIP suspicions are limited to the tracing of the consignments which are subject to various EU safeguard decisions or imposed checks following information in TRACES. These controls are correctly recorded as "Suspicion" in box 28 of the common veterinary entry document for products (CVEDPs) and consignments ar

The representatives of the Import Directorate confirmed that there is no system in place for consultation between the national RASFF contact point and the Import Directorate before the information is provided to the Commission, contrary to the requirements of Article 2(5)(b) of Regulation No 16/2011.

The BIP staff do not have direct access to RASFF and they are not able to get the detailed information for all the consignments which might be of interest to import controls. This issue limits the ability of the BIP staff to be proactive in case of suspicion or obtaining more information on consignments rejected by other Member States (see finding 25). 9

label_heading: Conclusion on the official controls at entry Border Inspection Posts
paragraph_text: In the three BIPs visited, consignments in transit are checked as required but in Frankfurt/Main BIP staff have no access to the information from the relevant databases which would enable them to verify that consignments are always presented for the controls. Veterinary checks generally ensure that only eligible consignments are accepted for transit.

label_heading: Conclusion on the official controls at approved warehouses
paragraph_text: Compliance with the requirements and effectiveness of the controls differ between the warehouses visited: In one of them the official controls comply with the EU requirements and the competent authority was acting to improve their effectiveness. In the other warehouse, the control system failed to comply with the minimum requirements (verification of traceability, labelling, and certification) and could not provide guarantees that products reached their intended destination. The warehouse is not approved/authorised as a customs warehouse, but it is under Customs supervision (on the basis of the particular provision of Customs law related to the foreign military forces). This supervision coul

paragraph_text: The actions proposed to address recommendation No 1 from DG(SANCO)/2013-6901 have not been effective and the recommendation remains unaddressed. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The responsibilities of competent authorities have been designated and communication, cooperation and coordination exist between veterinary authorities and Customs at national and Länder level. These systems, combined with the provision of a range of resources including appropriate written procedures and relevant training, support the implementation of the official controls on transits. 14 The three Länder visited have set up systems for official controls at BIPs which generally ensure that only consignments eligible for transi

The competent authority presented to the audit team the missing functionalities in TRACES as the reason for failing to use it.

In relation to the issuance of subsequent CVEDs in the warehouses, the audit team noted that: in warehouse 1 the exiting consignments were not accompanied by subsequent CVEDs, therefore there was no documentary traceability of the goods. This is a consequence of the absence of an official control system in warehouse 1 contrary to the requirements of Article 12 of Directive 97/78/EC; in warehouse 2 the consignments were intended for ship supplies and left accompanied by the veterinary certificates in compliance with the requirements of Article 5 of Decision 2000/571/EC; the representative of another Land, in which the audit team did not visit a warehouse, stated that the subsequent CVEDs acco

label_heading: Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results
paragraph_text: A detailed surveillance protocol and good inspection guidelines have been elaborated in Spain for the detection and identification of PFB. However, the percentage of ware and seed potato producing areas inspected and sampled in annual official surveys varies widely between the ACs and is, in many cases, significantly lower than required in the National Contingency Plan and is insufficient to reliably identify or rule out the actual presence of PFB.

label_heading: Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results
paragraph_text: The suspected occurrence of PFBs triggered increased surveying activities in both recently affected ACs. However, the implemented intensity of surveillance does not provide sufficient information about the actual distribution of the harmful organism in these ACs. 5.3 CONTROL MEASURES WHERE THE PRESENCE OF EPITRIX SP. IS CONFIRMED 5.3.1 Demarcation of Epitrix sp. infestation Legal requirements Article 5 of Decision 2012/270/EU. Annex II Section 1 of Decision 2012/270/EU. Findings

Data in Tables 2 and 3 indicate that for the vast majority of the ACs, there was practically the same overall level of implementation of the surveillance in 2013 and 2014. However, there was a significant increase in the area inspected and the number of inspections carried out in Galicia in 2014. In addition to potatoes, 40 ha of tomato crops were also inspected in 2013 and 20 ha in 2014. The average inspected area of the total ware potato production in 2013 represented 4.8 % and in 2014 3.8 %, which is in accordance with the required 3 % in the National Contingency Plan. However, there was very significant variance between the ACs from 0.5 % to 100 % of fields inspected. In Andalucía the pr

Another way of evaluating the inspection data is looking at the number of fields inspected compared with the total production area which gives an indication of the 8 inspection density. As shown in the last column of Tables 2 and 3 above, the average inspection density in Spain was 96 ha and 48 ha of potato production per inspection in 2013 and 2014 respectively and varies very much between the ACs. In Andalucía there were 311 ha of potatoes per one inspection in 2013 and 339 ha in 2014 which is significantly below the national density average. It indicates that large but few potato plots were inspected there and consequently a very low density of inspection. The inspection density in Asturi

Seed production in Spain is concentrated in three ACs, namely in Castilla y Leon with the largest share of production of around 68 %, followed by Basque Country and Navarra. In 2013 and 2014 on average some 30 % plots of seed potatoes were surveyed for PFB with some 1,300 visual inspections of seed potato fields per year. However, in the largest seed producing, AC Castilla y Leon, there were only 56 visual inspections carried out and 7 plots inspected each year covering an area of 12 ha in in 2013 and 13 ha in 2014. Furthermore, in the same AC there were no lot inspections carried out in 2014, although in total 515 lot inspections were carried for domestic seed produced in Spain. The intensi

Taking into account the high proportion of inspected fields found infested in Asturias and Andalucía, the high proportion of unregistered producers of potatoes, the lack of systematic surveys of other cultivated host plants and vegetable hobby growers, the intensity of survey is not considered sufficient to determine the actual distribution and spread of the pest. Furthermore there is a very low intensity of surveys for PFB carried out in some other key potato producing ACs in Spain which does not provide sufficient information of the presence of the organism. This is not in line with Article 4 of Commission Decision 2012/270/EU. Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results

label_heading: Conclusions on control measures for Epitrix sp.
paragraph_text: The establishment of demarcated areas in Asturias and Andalucía were notified immediately in line with EU requirements. However, due to uncertainty regarding the actual spread of PFB, the establishment of infested zones and buffer zones was not carried out taking into consideration the sound scientific principles required by Decision 2012/270/EU. In particular, geographically close demarcated areas were not merged. This is not in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, Annex II, Section 1, points 2 and 3.

The representative of Asturias also stated that they establish a demarcated area and designate an infested zone and a buffer zone around each infested plot according to the minimum required by Decision 2012/270/EU of a 100 m width from the infested plot. The geographically close demarcated areas were merged. However, where the 100 m radius intersects plots, the entire plot is not added to the demarcated area, which is not in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, Annex II, Section 1, point 1.

label_heading: finding of PFB in Andalucía on 28 May 2015 and MAGRAMA notified the
paragraph_text: When delimiting the size of the buffer zone, the minimum required by Decision 2012/270/EU was always applied in Andalucía and Asturias. There was a very high proportion of inspected fields found infested in Asturias (some 50 %) with a high level of infestation, fragmented cultivation of host plants and presence of host weeds. Due to the recency of the outbreaks in Andalucía and insufficient intensity of surveillance, there was uncertainty about the actual spread of the pest. Thus the plant health services in both ACs did not take into consideration other elements for delimitation, such as, the presence of other cultivated or wild PFB hosts in the area and the capacity of the pest to spread n

label_heading: Conclusions on control measures for Epitrix sp.
paragraph_text: Official control measures put in place in demarcated areas were generally in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, however, confirmation of the outbreak did not trigger intensive monitoring or additional investigation in the demarcated area or its vicinity. Not all necessary measures were put in place like prohibition of planting of host plants and alternative measures are not equally effective to achieve eradication. This is not in line with Article 5 of Decision 2012/270/EU and the requirements for official measures to be taken within demarcated areas as laid down in Section 2 of Annex II to the same Decision.

label_heading: Conclusions on control measures for Epitrix sp.
paragraph_text: Control measures in place for commercial scale movement of potato tubers outside demarcated areas are adequate, however, surveillance is not carried out for non- commercial movement of potatoes. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The potato flea beetle has spread further in Galicia and to Asturias, possibly due to natural spread. Therefore the implemented control measures seem to be able only to slow down but not prevent further spread in these two (neighbouring) Autonomous Communities (AC) and eradication of the pest there is now very unlikely. Authorities in Andalucía have made significant efforts to prevent further spread and the initial control measures are broadly in line with the minimum requiremen

The FVO team visited five demarcated areas in Andalucía and met plant health inspectors, owners of the infested fields and of fields in the buffer zone and noted that: All the fields visited were tilled and without any potato debris left and clean of weeds, including along the field's borders. Owners of the infested fields and of the fields in the buffer zone confirmed the receipt of the official demarcation notice and were aware of the harmful organism and imposed control measures. They intended to plant other crops in the next growing season. Professional farmers have their own technical staff responsible for the management of the crop production and protection. They confirmed regular and

The representative of Galicia stated that five warehouses in the demarcated areas comply with the requirements for the marketing of potatoes outside demarcated area, including the management of waste. Potatoes are inspected in the warehouses after washing. In Asturias all infested plots identified by the regional authorities so far were intended for own-consumption or at most for local market and surveillance of the movement of potato tubers out of the demarcated areas was not carried out. Thus, the control activities in Asturias do not ensure that all potatoes produced in the demarcated areas comply with the requirements for movement laid down in Annex I to Decision 2012/270/EU.

National control programmes for implementing the requirements laid down in relevant EU legislation have been established. However, discrepancies exist between Slovakian SNCPs and EU requirements as regards sampling at the initiative of the FBO in the rearing phase in breeding and laying hen populations.

The audit team noted that some discrepancies exist between the SNCP for breeding and laying hen flocks and relevant EU legislation, in particular sampling at the initiative of the FBO is not mandatory in the rearing phase. This is not in line with Annex II, Part B, Point 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. The CA explained that since 2014 this sampling is no longer a FBO's obligation for financial reason. For more details see paragraph 75 and 91.

label_heading: Conclusions on management of LSD crisis
paragraph_text: The failure to activate and make the NDCC fully operational prevented the maximum use of resources and the responsibility of crisis management was not shared among all relevant stakeholders. The fact that not all stakeholders exercised their advisory or management role, as foreseen in the contingency plan, resulted in additional pressure and responsibility on veterinary staff who mainly worked alone and under difficult circumstances. The absence of strategic planning at central level and of emergency funds, together with the inadequate preparedness for emergency vaccination, imposed additional burden on local services and other staff directly involved in the crisis operations and delivery on
The NDCC was not formally established as a crisis unit after the confirmation of the first LSD outbreak, contrary to provisions of Article 8 (2) and Point 1 of Annex IV to Directive 92/119/EEC.

Several measures related to hunting wild boar included in the 2016 national programme for the control and eradication of ASF submitted for obtaining EU co-financing are not being implemented as stated in the plan and they might have negative impact on stopping the spreading of the disease.

The audit team noted that section 4.3.8 of the 2016 national programme states that: "Wild boars which are shot for hunting purposes are kept in refrigerated cooling places which 10 belong to hunting organisations until lab results. When test results are positive then carcasses are taken to above mentioned containers. If the tests results are positive then storage place, all equipment and transportation means are disinfected under the supervision of veterinary inspector/official veterinarian." Via discussions with the VFB and hunters, it was established that not all aspects of the above plan are being implemented, e.g.: Only about 25% (80/318) of hunting grounds in Parts II and III have "refr

The pre-movement certification of all live pigs provides, in principle, guarantees of compliance with movement rules and thus reduces the risk of disease spread between holdings. However, as authorised veterinarians do not perform pre-certification checks correctly (i.e. sampling procedures and verification of residency periods) and the verification system does not pick-up failures in the system, the measure is not very effective, which hinders this reduction of risk. 5.3 BIOSECURITY MEASURES Legal requirements 9 Article 8 of Directive 2002/60/EC. 5.3.1 Biosecurity in relation to wild boar

paragraph_text: For pig meat, the reliability of this system is undermined by the insufficient assurance that pigs comply with residency and standstill requirements. 17 5.6 FOLLOW-UP OF OPEN RECOMMENDATIONS FROM DG(SANTE)/2015-7563-MR FINAL

All holdings in Part II or III that send pigs to either an abattoir or to another holding have to obtain a certificate for the movement, usually issued by an authorised veterinarian, i.e. a "9T" in the case of animals moving from a holding to an abattoir or a "7E" in the case of animals moving between holdings. Both certificates are used to demonstrate compliance with the requirements of various Articles in Decision 2014/709/EU, e.g. articles 3 or 4. These certificates provide information on the ASF testing history (either on a holding or consignment basis) and confirmation of the clinical health of the animals in the consignment. However, there is no certification of compliance with other r

All live pigs arriving at an abattoir are accompanied with a "9T" health certificate as described in finding 29. The official vet in an abattoir relies on the "9T" and the list of holdings which comply with Article 3, 3a or 4 of Decision 2014/709/EU in order to assess whether pigs are eligible for the derogations under this Decision. If deemed eligible, a triangular national health mark is used for fresh pig meat, pig meat preparations and pig meat products from III which allows circulation on the national market. Eligible pigs from Part II receive the oval health mark and can circulate on the EU market.

The system for managing suspicions of ASF on holdings is not being implemented as intended and ASF diagnostic samples are submitted without any involvement or knowledge of the local veterinary office. This might impair the quick containment of the disease in new outbreaks as officials cannot impose restriction of movements before results are available.

Veterinary practitioners submit blood samples and organ samples from dead pigs to the official laboratory for ASF testing without informing the local official vets and the holdings may not be subjected to any restrictions or recorded as suspicions.

A special system for notifications was implemented in 2016 in which seven holdings were recorded as official suspicions following phone/e-mail contact with the competent authority. Four of those seven holdings received official restrictions before the laboratory results arrived.

There is a national instruction which states that organ samples should be taken from dead suspects and blood from live ones in line with the requirements of point A.4 of chapter IV of the Annex to Commission Decision 2003/422/EC. Official and authorised veterinarians were reminded of the national instruction during training in September 2016 as this had not been followed in two outbreaks in July and August 2016. 5.4.3 Laboratory testing

In general, the national system for holding registration, animal identification and movement controls provides a solid basis to support ASF-related controls. The fact that movements of pigs to abattoirs do not have to be notified to the national database decreases the amount of information in the database available to the competent authority and makes the forward tracing of pigs difficult.

Pig keepers must provide census information on numbers of pigs kept on an annual basis (1st May). There is a requirement for both the seller and the buyer to notify the database within 7 days when pigs move between holdings. There is no requirement for notification when pigs move from a holding to an abattoir which does not comply with the requirements of Article 18(c) of Council Directive 64/432/EEC. 6

label_heading: Conclusions on the organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Some procedures and contracts were still under preparation at the time of the audit and were therefore not possible to evaluate. Some procedures were missing altogether and others were insufficient, e.g. procedures for cleaning, disinfection, pest control and sampling of the imported animals. Such gaps could affect the implementation of official controls if they are not resolved before the BIP is approved.

A sampling procedure to ensure risk-based testing of imported animals through the Airport Bucharest Henri Coand in accordance with Part III of Annex II to Decision 97/794/EC had not been developed at the time of the audit although the staff was aware about these requirements. This is not in line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on BIP facilities and equipment
paragraph_text: In general the BIP facilities are ready for receiving and checking consignments of live animals. However, the facilities proposed do not fully ensure the standards for animal welfare during unloading and for isolation, whenever such need arises. In addition, a shower for the BIP staff should be made available. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The proposed BIP is integrated into the existing national import control system. Allocation of tasks, responsibilities and duties, training, instructions and the cooperation agreement with Customs will support the correct implementation of the official import controls. At the time of the audit, facilities were ready to use but several shortcomings were noted with

The BIP has a sufficiently large changing room and washbasin with cold and hot water at the disposal of staff responsible for carrying out veterinary checks of live animals. However, a shower is not available in the BIP facilities for live animals contrary to the requirements of point 4 of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC. 3

The unloading area is adequate for the animal species expected, as required by point 2 of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC. Horses are transported to the BIP in boxes which are placed on the platforms pulled by the airport trailer. The equipment for the unloading (step-down) of horses from the above-mentioned platforms onto the rubber floor was not available, and needs to be procured. The airport operator provided assurances that the unloading equipment will be provided within the month after the audit.

The inspection area is suitable for carrying out the checks required. However, it is not fully equipped with the necessary tools that would allow staff to perform identity and physical checks (e.g. equipment to restrain, thermometer), contrary to the requirements laid down in Articles 3 and 4, and Annex II (parts I and II) to Decision 97/794/EC. The microchip reader was available during the audit. The competent authority informed that sampling for registered horses will be carried out only in suspicious cases following the derogation foreseen in Annex II (part III.1) to Decision 97/794/EC.

The animals' housing and isolation facilities are easy to clean and disinfect. However, the walls in the isolation facilities had gaps in them allowing communication with the outside that impedes the correct isolation of animals, when necessary.

The eight RCPPQCs are tasked with the coordination of the DREVs in their jurisdiction. The RCPPQCs draw up the annual programme of regular on-site inspections jointly with the competent DREVs. However the audit team was informed that such activities had not yet been implemented at the time of the audit (see paragraph 17). Conclusions on Competent Authorities

The national legislation requires that in relation to PGI wines, at least 20% of applications for certifications have to be sampled and analysed as well as at least 20% of the total production quantity of the PGI wine in the relevant regional unit. Given that there is no coordination being undertaken by the RCPPQCs, the audit team could not determine whether or not these requirements were met. In the particular DREVs visited, the inspectors met stated that these requirements had not yet been met.

Although the majority of inspectors met were knowledgeable on oenology, at the time of the observed inspections, there were no obvious guidelines or checklists used by the inspectors. Subsequently, the CCA stated that guidelines and checklists were provided by an implementing circular to the DREVs which were provided to the audit team. There was however no further explanation provided to the audit team as to why these guidance documents were not used by the inspectors observed. During two site visits the audit team requested traceability exercises to be performed. Although these were undertaken satisfactorily, the information of the producer, both in electronic and paper format, were fragmen

The RCPPQCs visited had not implement a risk based approach to controls and neither was there any coordination of the DREVs in place. In addition, any communication between DREVs was informal and undertaken on an ad hoc basis. Controls on the Market: (visit to supermarket)

In relation to the PDO/PGI wine sector products selected for this audit, procedures in terms of guidelines, checklists and reporting procedures were not used by the inspectors observed. The effectiveness of inspections, in particular the checking of each element of the Product Specification could not be assessed fully due to the lack of records and inspection reports. In addition, market controls were not in place. 5.2.4 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 19 of Regulation (EC) No 607/2009. 8 Art 103 of Regulation (EC) No 1308/2013. Findings

During this audit, the audit team visited the production sites of two PDO and three PGI wine sector products in three different regions. All inspections were undertaken by official control staff from the respective DREVs. In all site visits, it was noted that for the majority of inspections, no inspection reports were drawn up making it impossible to determine if all elements of the Product Specification were checked.

Where inspection reports had been issued by the DREVs, they contained very little detail of the site visit and the activities carried out and whether or not all elements of the Product Specification were checked. In addition, there was no documentation attached to the report to substantiate any checks that had taken place. 7

label_heading: Conclusions on national measures and sampling design
paragraph_text: The competent authority has documented procedures in place to support the implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, delays in the inception of the sampling plan, shortcomings in the proportional allocation of samples and in the selection of the epidemiological units to be sampled, undermine the representativeness of the samples taken. 5.2.2 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC; Article 4 and Annex Part A.5 of Decision 2013/652/EU. Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

In 2014 and 2016 the number of caecal samples to be taken from turkey slaughterhouses was not calculated correctly. This is because for this calculation, the only turkey slaughterhouse in the country was treated as a broiler slaughterhouse. As a result, the number of samples allocated for turkey ceca was significantly lower than the one necessary to obtain the required isolates. This does not meet the requirements of point 2.2 of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.

label_heading: Conclusions on national measures and sampling design
paragraph_text: The competent authority has documented procedures in place to support the implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, delays in the inception of the sampling plan, shortcomings in the proportional allocation of samples and in the selection of the epidemiological units to be sampled, undermine the representativeness of the samples taken. 5.2.2 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC; Article 4 and Annex Part A.5 of Decision 2013/652/EU. Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Contrary to the requirements set out in part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, the AMR monitoring programme did not ensure that samples were distributed over each month of the year. Instead, monthly sampling took place from March to December in 2014 and from May to December in 2015 and 2016. The competent authority informed the audit team that the monitoring plan was issued only when the Grant Decision, which details the EU funds that would become available for co-financing of the plan, was published. NSVFSA stated that they will consider the possibility to have bi-annual financial plans to avoid this issue reoccurring.

The annual Service Notices state that sampling days should be limited from Monday to Wednesday to ensure that the laboratory starts processing the samples within 48 hours of collection. In the slaughterhouses visited, officials took most of the samples on Mondays. This cannot be considered random and therefore is not in line with point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU.

The Service Notices state that repeated epidemiological units cannot be sampled. Nevertheless, the epidemiological unit definition given therein is not fully in line with Decision 2013/652/EU. As a consequence, in two of the three slaughterhouses visited, the audit team noticed a few examples of repeated epidemiological units sampled. This is not in line with point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.

According to the explanation provided by NSVFSA on this issue, the decision to select these counties was mainly based on the consumption of fresh meat therein. However, 6 the competent authorities did not present any consumption data to show that the actual county selection ensured representativeness. Moreover, the audit team noted that the population in the selected counties was far below the 80% required by EFSA guidance document 2014 representing 54% and 49% for 2015 and 2016, respectively. Therefore, it cannot be concluded that as required by Article 2.2 and point 1 of part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, the isolates obtained were representative.

A laboratory network of designated official laboratories is in place for official monitoring of AMR. Laboratories are accredited and participate regularly in proficiency tests with satisfactory results. Whilst considerable improvements were noted since the implementation of the monitoring plan, some weaknesses of the quality control system in place, notably the insufficient use of reference strains and some deviations to the standard procedures, could undermine the reliability of the monitoring results obtained. 5.3 ASSESSMENT AND REPORTING OF AMR Legal requirements Article 9 and Annex IV of Directive 2003/99/EC and Article 5 and the Annex of Decision 2013/652/EU. Findings

While the procedures in place were generally in line with the relevant standards, the audit team noted the following: County laboratory: o There were no procedures in place to perform regularly colony counts on inoculum suspensions as requested by ISO 20776-1:2006 and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) M07, which are the standards required by point 3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, in order to ensure that the required final inoculum concentration was obtained and therefore the test wells contain an adequate number of cells. o Incubation time and temperatures for MIC determination were not performed fully in line with ISO 20776:2006 or CLSI standards. The time/

The lack of powers of the designated laboratory staff for accessing slaughterhouses and perform sampling has an impact on fulfilling the Decision requirements regarding the poultry population to be covered by the sampling design. 5.2 ORGANISATION OF THE MONITORING SYSTEM 5.2.1 NATIONAL MEASURES AND SAMPLING DESIGN 5.2.1.1 National measures

In 2014, staff from this laboratory were not allowed to enter a significant number of broiler slaughterhouses initially included in the work plan. The figures on slaughter production used for the sample allocation corresponded to two years before the sampling year and not to the previous year as recommended in EFSA 2014 guidance document. label_heading: Conclusions on SNCP for Breeding Flocks of Gallus gallus
paragraph_text: The implementation of the SNCP for the breeding hen population is not fully satisfactory as regards own-check and official sampling frequency while the related protocols in both rearing and adult phases are applied in accordance with EU requirements and the relevant SNCP.

label_heading: Conclusions on SNCP for Laying Hens
paragraph_text: The implementation of the SNCP for laying hens is satisfactory as regards routine own-check sampling; in particular the frequency of own-checks applied goes beyond EU requirements. Concerning routine official sampling, this is not fully in compliance with EU requirements as regards both sampling frequency and protocol applied.

While interviewing both the AVs and VIs, the audit team noted that in general they were aware of the tasks to be performed, the requirements contained in SNCPs and the procedures to be followed. However some difficulties concerning the implementation of official sampling, in particular as regards the sampling frequency and/or protocol in the breeding and laying hen populations, was observed by the audit team (for more details see paragraphs Nos 68 and 69). Supervision and Audit

The audit team was informed by the VFSD that in the 2015 annual plan for official controls they forgot to include Salmonella official sampling for all the various poultry populations. However they detected the problem in the course of the year and to remedy the situation a complementary document was prepared. The document indicated the poultry holdings where Salmonella sampling had to be performed in the second half of 2015 and was sent by the VFSD to the regional offices and from there to the branch offices in order to be implemented. The CA informed the audit team that this document could partially cover the official sampling required by the SNCPs in 2015. However, due to limited time avai

In the branch offices visited the audit team had the opportunity to confirm that, for the reasons explained above, the official sampling was not carried out with the required frequency in particular in breeders and in laying hen population (see also paragraphs Nos 90 and 103).

During the on-the-spot visits the audit team noted there were some problems concerning the implementation of the official sampling, particularly in the breeding hen population as regards the sampling frequency and in the laying hen population as regards the sampling frequency and the protocol. The audit team also noted that the difference between own-check and official sampling was not very clear to the staff responsible for implementing the SNCPs.

In this regard the VFSD informed the audit team that prior to 2015 all samples taken in the framework of the SNCPs were considered as official samples. However, since 2015 a distinction has been made by the CA between own-check and official sampling in national rules and the SNCPs because the relevant EU legislation stipulates that poultry populations should be sampled at the initiative of the FBO and as part of official controls. The CA explained to the audit team that due to the fact that these changes have taken place recently, the staff is still encountering difficulties in differentiating between the sampling for own-checks and the sampling for official controls and it therefore may hap

The audit team noted that although the CA is aware of the issue concerning official sampling i.e. through the supervision of VIs carried out by the CA from central level and heads of regional offices and the monthly reports of Salmonella analysis results sent by the NRL to the CA at central level (see paragraph No 79), and that some corrective actions have been put in place to remedy the situation detected, problems were still present at the time of the current audit.

The audit team noted in all the farms visited that official sampling had not been carried out in 2015 and that one official sample taken in 2016 was analysed in a designated laboratory instead of being tested in the NRL as required by the SNCP.

The audit team was provided by the CA with the data of official sampling performed in 2015. According to this data the frequency for official sampling was not in line with EU requirements (six official samples were tested while there were 64 holdings with more than 1,000 birds). The audit team noted in one of the laying hen farms visited that no 17 official samples had been taken in 2015. The CA explained that this fact was due to the mistake made in the 2015 annual planning (see paragraph No 65).

In the majority of cases reviewed by the audit team, the protocol used in official sampling was not in line with point 2.2.2 of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 517/2011 (e.g. in a caged laying hen farm two faecal samples were taken instead of the required three faecal samples and in a free range farm two faeces samples were taken instead of three pairs of boot swaps). In practical terms, the protocol for own-checks was used instead of the official one in both type of production due to the confusion between own- check and official sampling (see paragraphs Nos 68 and 69).

label_heading: Conclusions on Organisation and Scope of Official Controls
paragraph_text: A control system of primary producers covering the verification of microbiological risks was in place, however, the controls only started in 2016 and were not planned taking into account the risks posed by pathogens that may contaminate FNAO.
By the time of the audit there were no direct imports from third countries of seeds for sprouting in Romania. Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over FBO Obligations

For 2016, controls are planned for producers of fruits and vegetables that also have storage and/or processing activities of FNAO and are registered as such. These FBOs will be visited once in 2016. A risk-based control system, taking into account the EFSA scientific opinions on the public health risk posed by pathogens that may contaminate FNAO, is not in place. This is not in accordance with Article 3.1(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. For 2017 a risk-based control system is planned to be developed.
None of the three FBOs were ever inspected before the audit concerning the risks of microbiological contamination of FNAO, as identified by EFSA, only their storehouses had previously been inspected.

The CCA confirmed that being not aware of any Hungarian producers of seeds for sprouting, these producers are not controlled as such (see paragraph 15 and 48).
