paragraph_text: Official controls at sprout-producing establishments, contrary to what is required by Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, do not consistently enforce the requirements laid down in Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of the said Regulation (as regards preliminary testing of seeds intended for sprouting and sprouts). Enforcement of such requirements had only been initiated recently in the establishments visited.

The inspector verified the sampling plan of the FBO, specifically the results of the preliminary tests for seeds for sprouting and the tests of final products (sprouts). Seeds for sprouts are not tested before use (preliminary tests). The CAs allowed the FBO to use, instead of preliminary tests for seeds, the analytical reports on the seeds provided by the supplier. Moreover, the tests of the final products (sprouts) were available, but the frequency was not respected and samples were not analysed for STEC. In the previous reports there was no evidence of non-compliances regarding analytical frequency and parameters. The inspector informed the audit team that she was aware from previous insp

The CAs confirmed that this second sprout-producing establishment (not visited) complied with the frequency for preliminary tests on seeds for sprouting and final tests on sprouts. However, STEC was not tested as required by Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of the Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The CAs informed the audit team that the inspector of this second facility was aware from previous inspections that also this FBO did not comply with the requirements laid down by Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of the Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. However, the high price and the limited availability of STEC analyses was the reason for not requiring this.

The inspector verified the sampling plan of the FBO, specifically the results of the preliminary tests on seeds for sprouting and the tests on final products (sprouts). Seeds for sprouting were regularly tested according to Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 before growing. All the results were compliant. The tests of the final products (sprouts) were available and the frequency had been respected. However, samples of final product were not analysed for STEC. This non-compliance had been identified in previous inspection reports and a deadline (not yet expired at the time of the audit) had been given to the operator to address the situation.

For virus analysis in soft fruit, the method used does not follow the applicable international rules. It can prevent official controls from reliably detecting viral pathogen in official samples while these pathogens are considered relevant hazards by the CAs. 5.2.7 Procedures for Performance and Reporting of Control Activities Legal Requirements Article 8, and Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

The laboratory runs molecular methods to detect norovirus and hepatite A virus in food using some principles of EN ISO/TS 15216-2:2013 and reports results. These methods do not fall within the laboratory's scope of accreditation.

The main principle of virological analysis of soft berries lies in the virus concentration from 25g of berries. The most reliable method is the Polyethyleneglycol Precipitation. This method is part of ISO 15216-1 and 15216-2 and has been successfully tested in an inter-laboratory trial. Other methods for virus concentration are so far not as efficient and this has been shown in the Norovirus outbreak 2012 in Germany. The results are published and available as open access (Mäde, D.; and collaborators. Detection and Typing of Norovirus from Frozen Strawberries Involved in a Large-Scale Gastroenteritis Outbreak in Germany. Food and Environmental Virology. Volume 5 (2013), Issue 3, pp 162-168).

label_heading: Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of CBs
paragraph_text: CBs are accredited and approved in accordance with national and EU rules. CBs are subject to effective annual supervision by the CA which includes office and witness audits as well as direct inspections at operators selected based on relevant risks. The sampling activity outsourced to the NRL has however so far not been subject to supervision by the CA. 5.2.2 Registration of Operators Legal Requirements Article 28(1), (2) and (5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92(2) and 92b of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

The CBs have subcontracted the sampling activity to the National Reference Laboratory (NRL). The contract covers the main requirements for the testing of organic samples. 5 The CA stated that, so far, the sampling activity carried out by the NRL has not been subject to supervision. The NRL has also been designated for the testing of organic products by the CA (see also chapter 5.2.6).

Both CBs have well developed and comprehensive documented procedures in place providing good guidance to inspectors to achieve a high level of consistency and effectiveness of controls at operators. Comprehensive information is generally available to the inspectors in advance of the controls allowing them to prepare well and to acquire a good understanding of the situation on the spot. One CB does not require farmers to provide all compulsory information in advance of the controls (such as precautionary measures), but nevertheless verifies it on the spot. 10 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 23(1) of Regulation

The two CBs have procedures in place requiring the operators to submit a full description of their activities, including a description of precautionary measures put in place to avoid potential contamination of organic products. CBs' inspectors have to verify the implementation of these precautionary measures when visiting the operators. However, the audit team noted that CB1 does not require farmers to maintain a description of precautionary measures contrary to Article 63(1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Nevertheless, inspectors observed during inspections verified the precautionary measures put in place by the operators.

However, other aspects such as planning and preparation of inspections and control measures to be applied by CBs were not verified in this supervision. As no office audits had been carried out since 2011, the CCA had not verified whether both CBs had incorporated some relevant requirements of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, as amended by Regulation (EC) No 392/2013, in force since 1 January 2014. The lack of adequate verification of the internal procedures used by CBs for the controls is not in line with Article 92c(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The audit team identified several shortcomings in the office audits carried out to both CBs (e.g. inadequate selection of operators for additional

However, the CCA only evaluates the topic covered by the supervision, and the overall performance of the inspectors is not evaluated. This is not in line with Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. As a result, the supervision by the CCA did not identify the systematic shortcomings observed by the Commission audit team during the inspections witnessed. (see findings 54 and 55). 7

However, the report on the result of the supervision carried out in early September 2015 was submitted to CB1 only on 20 April 2016. At the time of the present audit, the report had not been submitted to CB2. As a consequence, both CBs had not yet implemented corrective actions to address the shortcomings identified by the supervision. Some of the shortcomings described in the CCA reports were again observed during the inspections observed by the audit team. This delay in the communication of the results of supervision undermines its effectiveness, as it does not ensure that corrective actions are taken by CBs in a timely manner. Conclusions on Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withd

A system of controls is in place in accordance with Article 27(4) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. CAs responsible for controls in organic production are designated with a clear distribution of tasks and responsibilities among the CAs and the delegated CBs. There is good communication and co-operation between the different CAs, and regular meetings are held between DAFM and the CBs. However, due to limited staff resources, the CA does not adequately supervise CBs controls in the area of processing which reduces the effectiveness of the system in place (see also conclusion no 23). 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal Legal Requirements Articles 5(2) and (3) of Commissio

label_heading: Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of Control Bodies
paragraph_text: There is a system of approval, annual supervision and withdrawal of CBs in place in Ireland, which includes the withdrawal of the CB's approval by the CA in case a CB fails to fulfil its obligations. Regular coordination and communication between CAs and CBs is established aiming at harmonising organic controls. The effectiveness of the CA's supervision of CBs is however reduced because the CA does not effectively supervise CBs' controls in the area of processing (due to staff shortage). The system is further weakened by the fact that the CA does not take all relevant information into account when supervising CBs located outside Ireland and that several systematic shortcomings in the perform

There are six administrative staff in the Organic Unit assisted by two inspectors and one technical officer charged with, inter alia, organic controls of organic production. In addition, there are 30 technical officers who undertake controls at local markets and retailers. All DAFM staff met by the audit team were experienced in the area of organic production and were found to be knowledgeable for the tasks assigned. DAFM staff attend regular training on organic production and meetings, including the Committee on Organic Production held in Brussels. However, DAFM informed the audit team, that due to the limited resources, no dedicated staff member is allocated to supervisory activities in th

Furthermore, as these CBs do not have a branch office in Ireland, the office audits are carried out at the home of the CBs´ inspectors, where all information necessary for supervision might not be available. Moreover, DAFM does not notify the result of the supervision to the CB headquarters, but only to the inspector. Therefore it cannot be ensured that the management of the CB is aware of any non-compliance and that effective corrective measures are taken as necessary.

In addition to office audits, DAFM carries out witness audits to observe the performance of the CBs´ inspectors. According to the information provided to the audit team, eight witness audits were carried out in 2015 at farm level. No witness audits were carried out to observe the performance of controls at processors. The inspections at processors by CBs observed by the audit team were overall superficial and not all relevant requirements were checked by inspectors (see finding 54). The failures in the performance of CBs were not identified by DAFM inspections described in paragraph

The audit team reviewed a number of reports issued by DAFM following witness audits and re-inspections. Several shortcomings were identified and the overall performance of inspectors was evaluated. The shortcomings were notified to the CBs concerned with a delay of several months. This delay in the communication of the results of supervision undermines its effectiveness, as it does not ensure that corrective action is taken by CBs in a reasonable time.

Moreover, corrective measures proposed consisted only in re-inspecting the operator where the supervision had taken place. No corrective measures were proposed by DAFM to or required from CBs to avoid the repetition of the shortcomings related to the performance of the inspectors. Some of the shortcomings described in the reports issued by DAFM were repeated during the inspections observed by the audit team (e.g. no identification of individual animals present on the fields, no measurements of stables in every inspection). The lack of corrective action to address the root cause of the problem detected does not fully ensure the effectiveness of the controls carried out by CBs. This is not in

The system however does not ensure that all operators, in particular wholesalers, are registered. Moreover, the fact that the list of operators does not include all required information and is not regularly updated, reduces the tool's functions for effective verification of the status of organic operators.

Although the CA conducts inspections at retailers to verify fulfilment of conditions for exemptions of retailers from organic controls, the limitation of the inspection scope to plant products only, fails to ensure that all relevant retailers are covered by the CA inspections. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Articles 3, 41 and 92f of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the 9 Council. Article 27(3) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Articles 65(1), (4) and 92(c)(2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

According to DAFM, Ireland requires the registration of operators as indicated in Article 28(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Any operator who produces, prepares, stores, places organic products on the market or import/export from/to non-EU countries shall submit his undertaking to the control system. Subcontracted operators are also subject to the control system. The audit team reviewed the agreements for the delegation of tasks signed between DAFM and the CBs and noted that the requirement regarding operators who place products on the market was not explicitly included. The audit team noted that wholesalers dealing only with pre-packed and labelled feed were not subject to the control sy

Since 2012, the Horticulture and Plant Health Division is responsible for inspections at retailers (which were previously inspected by technical staff of the Agricultural Environment and Structure Division). The fulfilment of conditions for the exemption of retailers from official controls is usually checked during these inspections. However, the audit team noted that the scope of these inspections focus on plant production only, and do not cover products of animal origin, providing information to the CA which is insufficient to satisfactorily assess whether retailers exempted under Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 (continue to) fulfil conditions for exemption.

The system however does not ensure that all operators, in particular wholesalers, are registered. Moreover, the fact that the list of operators does not include all required information and is not regularly updated, reduces the tool's functions for effective verification of the status of organic operators.

However, the list does not contain updated documentary evidence issued by CBs using the model set up in Annex XII to Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, including at least the range or types of products certified. In addition, although the DAFM register is updated to reflect changes in the organic status of operators, the changes are not necessarily fed into the list kept on the website. This lack of complete information is not in line with Article 92(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: Incomplete operator files and the fact that CBs do generally not require operators to notify changes in their activities hamper the effective planning of controls as well as verification of relevant requirements on-the-spot. Moreover, CBs do not necessarily carry out prior inspections when notified by an operator of a new activity.

However, the information submitted is not always complete or not adequately verified by CBs. The audit team noted that at two farmers, not all CB inspectors observed were aware of all the activities carried out and of precautionary measures taken by the operators. This was not checked in previous inspections. At one grower, the CB inspector did not pay attention to the processing steps which took place on the farm (drying of cereals) and the subcontracting activity (transport of organic feed in bulk, traceability and records of cleaning of the vehicles). At another grower, the CB3 10 inspector had never checked the transport of the product to costumers, which was a subcontracted activity. Th

However, the audit team noted during visits to processors that these procedures were not followed by one CB. The CB did not inspect and authorise new products /production lines before the production start. The failure of operators to notify such new activities to in advance of the production start to the CB was not considered a non-compliance by the CB, contrary to its procedure. The verification of such a scope extension was only done later, during the next inspection visit, with the risk that potentially non-compliant products might have already been placed on the market by the time of this inspection (see finding 53).

label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: Generally, CBs plan and prioritise controls of operators at a sufficient frequency, including unannounced inspections. However, the effectiveness of the system is reduced as CBs do not consider the quantity of products handled per operator in their risk evaluation and high risk operators are not necessarily subject to additional controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: While inspections at farm level are generally allocated with sufficient inspection time, there is a risk for inspections at processors to remain rather ineffective as allocated inspection time per operator is too short to allow adequate verification of relevant requirements and / or inspections are not always conducted when organic products are processed. 5.2.4 Controls of operators Legal Requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Titles II and III of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Titles II and IV and Article 65 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

However, the time allocated to inspections at processor level is very limited, even in the case of processors handling large quantities of organic and conventional products. As observed by the audit team during the inspections, not all relevant requirements were checked by inspectors and not all premises were fully inspected, which is not in line with the procedures of the CBs (see finding 54). In addition, CB2's procedures require inspectors to observe the production lines during the production of an organic product once every three years, which means that inspections are not always scheduled to allow verification of conditions under which processing of organic products takes place. This is

However, CB1 does not take into account for the risk analysis, the quantities produced by operators, which is a compulsory criterion according to Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. In addition, the results of the risk analysis carried out by CB1 and CB2 do not serve in practice as an adequate basis for the planning of annual and unannounced inspections (less than 10% of operators are differentiated by this method). In the case of CB1, the majority of operators were classified in the lowest risk category, while only 2.5% of operators were classified by CB2 as high risk operators. This is not in line with Article 92c(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

The audit team reviewed the list of operators selected by CB1 and CB2 for additional controls, and noted that only a small number of operators visited were selected based on their risk category. CB1 and CB2 carried out most of the additional inspections to new 11 operators and also to follow-up on non-compliances detected during the previous annual inspection. This is not in line with Article 92c(2) (b) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls

The effectiveness of controls at operators was however reduced as checklists used were incomplete and relevant requirements sometimes incorrectly and/or superficially verified by CB inspectors. This concerned in particular inspections at processors where relevant premises were not always fully checked by CB inspectors and stock and financial records not sufficiently verified when performing the calculation of the input/output balance. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Articles 23, 24 and 27(13) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Title III of Commission Regulation (EC) N

However, the checklists used are not sufficiently detailed and do not include some relevant requirements of EU Regulations. This lack of detailed documented procedures is not in line with Article 27(6)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. During the inspections observed, the audit team noted that inspectors did not check certain requirements that were not included in the checklists, in particular: CBs do not require operators to keep records on the results of verification on reception of organic products as required by Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and do not adequately check records. Inspections witnessed by the audit team at processors were overall superficial with no in-depth verification of all information provided by operators The following aspects were not adequately checked by inspectors: not all premises were checked by inspectors, even though the CB´s procedures indicates that all premises of an operator must be inspected. The lack of adequate verification of premises is not in line with Article 67(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. CBs did not systematically verify the results of operators´ own quality assurance programs referred to in Article 67(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Although the checklist used by CB2 included a specific question on the check

The system in place provides for a regular verification of labelling of organic products and their traceability by CBs and the CA. However, the system has so far failed to effectively rectify recurrent non-compliances with regard to compulsory labelling requirements, including the list of ingredients. 5.2.6 Sampling and laboratory analysis Legal Requirements Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Article 65(2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

According to the CBs´ standards, operators must ensure that products are clearly and accurately labelled in order to comply with all relevant requirements. However, labelling checks at processors carried out by CBs are not effective (see finding 54). As a result, CB1 did not note the use by a processor of a label which had not been approved by the CB. The label used indicated the use of a non-organic ingredient of agricultural origin while in the approved label it was indicated as organic. Furthermore, according to the recipe, the ingredient used was 6.7% of the weight of the product, which is not in line with EU Regulations.

In addition, the audit team noted several non-compliances with Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 concerning the labels (e.g. small size or no presence of the EU logo, ingredients of agricultural origin not indicated as organic, non-use of the code of the CB or of the operator who carried out the last operation on the product, etc.). These non- compliances had not been noted by CBs during controls. 15

Moreover, CBs do not adequately follow-up on the use of non-compliant labels. For example, DAFM notified CB1 of a complaint received from a client regarding a label where the main ingredient was not indicated as organic. CB1 informed DAFM on 12 August 2016 that the operator had been asked to change the label. However, the CB did not require the operator to stop using the non-compliant label. The audit team noted that the label was still used for the production of the same product on 18 August 2016. In addition, the CB did not require the operator to demonstrate the organic origin of the ingredient. There was also no request to evaluate if other products in the range could also be subject to

However, the audit team noted that the organic nature or the lot number of products supplied was not indicated on all accompanying documents. This lack of relevant information did not permit the linking of raw materials supplied with the accounts of the supplier, who also handled similar conventional products. The lack of this information is not in line with Articles 31(1)(b) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Moreover, in the case of the chicken breast, the documents provided by CB2 were not sufficiently detailed to trace the product throughout all the processing steps (slaughter, cutting, packaging and distribution) and therefore it was not possible to track the product back to the fa

In addition, the information on the labels was not supported by the documents kept by operators. In the two multi-ingredient products, the information concerning the place where the agricultural ingredients had been farmed (EU/non-EU agriculture) did not match with the information on the documents provided by suppliers. CBs permit processors to always use the reference to EU/non EU agriculture, regardless of where the agricultural products have been farmed, which is not in line with Article 24(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

Moreover, the trader who distributed two of the products was not registered for products of animal origin and CB1 had failed to detect this shortcoming. This also indicates that controls carried out by DAFM at retail level do not ensure that operators verify the documentary evidence of suppliers, which is not in line with Article 29(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 16 Conclusions on Labelling and Traceability

CBs sampling policy ensure that the required minimum samples are taken based on an appropriate risk assessment of operators as well as provide for sampling in cases of suspicion. Although CBs use accredited laboratories for the testing of organic products, these laboratories are not designated by the CA with the risk that relevant requirements and rules are not defined and hence laboratories results inadequate to provide the basis for the enforcement of organic rules. CB sampling procedures are not always adequate, which could reduce the validity of the testing results. Moreover, CBs do not always take appropriate measures in case of positive samples to identify the reason for contamination,

However, the sampling procedure used by CB1 is not in line with horizontal and national requirements. The audit team noted that the CB, in accordance with an "informal" procedure, had taken samples, but not provided for counter samples, which prevents the taking of any enforcement measures against the operator concerned in case of dispute. "Formal" samples are only taken when a first positive result is found or when a suspicion exists. This shortcoming, which is not in line with Articles 12(1) and (2) of statutory instrument 112/2004, had not been noted by DAFM supervision.

DAFM has not designated any laboratory for the testing of organic samples which is not in line with Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted that analytical reports from the main laboratory used by one CB did not indicate whether results presented in the reports related to the limits of detection or the limits of quantification, which is an important quality requirement. This shortcoming had been raised by INAB during the previous audit carried out to the CB, but DAFM did not request the CB the correct this shortcoming.

label_heading: Conclusions on Exceptional Production Rules and Other Derogations
paragraph_text: The system in place generally ensures that derogations are granted by DFMA and CBs based on a thorough evaluation of the operators request. There is good cooperation between CA and CBs and appropriate procedures are in place. However, the fact that dehorning and similar operations do not require prior-approval by the CA and conditions under which they are carried are not verified by CB inspectors during on the spot controls constitutes a major weakness of the system in place. 5.2.8 Imports of Products from Organic Production Legal Requirements Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Chapter 3 of Title III of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008. Annexes II, III, V and VI of Regulation (EC) No 123

DAFM issued guidance according to which operations such as dehorning of young animals, attaching elastic bands, tail docking of bovine animals and cutting of teeth are carried out routinely, which is not in line with Article 18(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. CBs do not check conditions under which these operations are carried out by the operators. During inspections observed, all farmers explained that no anaesthesia or analgesia was used, even for the castration of animals, which is not in line with Articles 18(1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Exceptional Production Rules and Other Derogations

label_heading: Conclusion on Imports of Products from Organic Production
paragraph_text: An import control system is in place in Ireland, consisting of documentary checks adequately carried out by the CA. However, the decision on the nature of controls, in particular to carry out physical checks on imported products, is not based on an assessment of the risk of occurrence of irregularities and infringements. The effectiveness of the system is further reduced due to the fact that importers are not required to notify the arrival of consignments to CBs in due time and non- compliances identified at operators by CBs are not notified to the CA to be taken into account for the CA's planning of import controls. 5.2.9 Measures in cases of irregularities and infringements Legal Requireme

Import controls consist of the verification of the Certificate of Inspection accompanying the consignments. So far, no physical checks on consignments have been carried out by DAFM before they are imported. However, no risk assessment was ever made by the DAFM to justify the absence of physical checks which is not in line with Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. DAFM informed the audit team that new procedures in co-operation with the Customs are being developed, which will require importers to notify DAFM 10 days in advance of the arrival of a consignment and the performance of risk-based physical checks by the Organic Unit.

CBs do not require importers to notify in due time the arrival of consignments to be imported, contrary to Article 84 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Visits and sampling at importers is planned based on risk by CBs, but, as indicated in findings 53 and 54, CBs do not systematically check how importers verify consignments at arrival. Therefore, CBs are not necessarily aware of any non-compliant product received by importers. Moreover, CBs do not always inform DAFM of non-compliances detected at importers, in particular when the operator concerned is not directly responsible for the non- compliance (see finding 85). This information can therefore not been taken into account for the planning of

However, the audit team noted that not all severe irregularities are notified by CBs, but only the ones classified as "manifest infringements", which need the agreement of DAFM for suspending the license of the operator concerned. Generally, non-compliances are only notified to DAFM after the procedure of appeal has finished and the certification decision has been confirmed by the CB which is not in line with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 requiring immediately notification of such non-compliances. label_heading: Conclusions on Measures in Cases of Irregularities and Infringements
paragraph_text: The system in place does not ensure that adequate and harmonised measures are taken in cases of irregularities and infringements. Although OFIS notifications were timely followed up, there was no evaluation by the CA of the actions taken by the CBs. Moreover, CBs do not always and immediately notify the CAs of irregularities, which is, in particular with regard to severe irregularities, undermining the effectiveness of the actions taken by the CA. 5.3 SEED DATA BASE Legal Requirements Articles 48 to 56 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

According to the CBs procedures, actions are taken by CBs in all cases where analytical results show the presence of unauthorised substances. CBs visited confirmed during the office audits that the likelihood of a non-compliance (i.e. detection of a traces of unauthorized plant protection product) is not notified, and even if the non-compliance is confirmed, it is not always notified to DAFM (see finding 85). Conclusions on Sampling

At the time of the present audit, DAFM had not adopted a catalogue of measures as required by Article 92(d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. At the opening meeting, DAFM presented the audit team with a draft statutory instrument for DAFM to apply 20 sanctions to operators in cases where they are found to commit an offence against the organic regulations. However, this legal act has to do with the role of DAFM regarding monetary sanctions applied to operators, and not with the measures to be applied by CBs.

The Organic Food and Farming Standards classify non-compliances in three categories according to the severity of the non-compliance and the certification decision to be taken (corrective action for deviations not affecting the organic status of the products, de- certification of product for irregularities affecting the organic status of the product and suspension of the operator´s licence for severe infringements or with a prolonged effect). However, the classification is not pre-defined for specific requirements of EU Regulations. In addition, no other measures are pre-defined either by CBs for particular cases of non-compliance. Generally, non-compliances are only notified to DAFM after the procedure of appeal has finished and the certification decision has been confirmed by the CB which is not in line with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 requiring immediately notification of such non-compliances. paragraph_text: The system in place does not ensure that adequate and harmonised measures are taken in cases of irregularities and infringements. Although OFIS notifications were timely followed up, there was no evaluation by the CA of the actions taken by the CBs. Moreover, CBs do not always and immediately notify the CAs of irregularities, which is, in particular with regard to severe irregularities, undermining the effectiveness of the actions taken by the CA. 5.3 SEED DATA BASE Legal Requirements Articles 48 to 56 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

The cases reviewed demonstrated that there was good communication and co-operation between DAFM and CBs. While measures by CBs were generally appropriate to identify the origin of the contamination, there was no evaluation by DAFM of these CB actions before the documentation of the investigation was uploaded onto OFIS. In one case when an antibiotic was found on marketed frozen fish, the CB first suspended the licence of the operator and then lifted the suspension based on a second sample which tested negative for the presence of the antibiotic. Laboratories for pesticide residue analysis in organic products have been designated. However, the lack of clear instructions from the CA for designated laboratories with regard to the methodology and implementation of laboratory analysis results in weaknesses in the implementation of routine pesticide residues analyses and may reduce the reliability of analytical results.

In Finland, three laboratories are designated to perform pesticide residue analysis in organic products. In order to be designated, laboratories have to be accredited for pesticide residue analysis under ISO/IEC 17025, as required by Article 12 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Another criterion, taken into account by EVIRA for designation of laboratories, is the number of analytes sought. However, the scope of accreditation is not a criterion for designation. In addition, there are no clear instructions for designated laboratories with regard to methodology and implementation of laboratory analysis in order to detect and quantify substances not authorised for organic production, as requir

In the first laboratory, a quality management system for routine pesticide residue analyses is in place. However, the audit team observed some weaknesses, including the following: 9 for standards, standard solutions and working solutions, records were available, but inconsistent labelling of standard solutions does not allow for a proper traceability; testing and replacement of standard solutions is performed by only a single injection and application of deviation criteria for comparison of old and new standards could not be demonstrated; requirements for identification and confirmations, i.e. application of acceptable deviations in retention time and ion ratio could not be demonstrated, whi

The overall performance of the second laboratory is generally good. Some weaknesses were identified in the implementation of routine pesticide residue analyses, such as: sample homogenization performed at room temperature, in-house validation data for some of the commodity groups was incomplete and traceability for calculation of analytical results could not be demonstrated comprehensively clear.

The lack of clear official criteria on sampling procedures for products other than those of plant and animal origin covered by Royal Decree No 290/2003 poses a risk that the interpretation of laboratory results is affected by a sampling procedure which is not representative for its purpose.

The lack of clear official CA criteria for the scope of analyses to be carried out (in particular, as to gas and liquid chromatographic techniques) impacts negatively on the control system: as gas chromatography is used as the only laboratory detection technique in many cases, the data on pesticide detections is likely to represent an underestimation of the true presence of pesticide residues in organic produce. 5.3 LABORATORY PERFORMANCE Legal Requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on delegation of specific tasks related to official controls; Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on official laboratories; Article 33 of the Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 on national reference

Weaknesses exist in the system to issue equine identification documents. These do not contain all the required information and are frequently issued with no regard to the lifetime treatment of horses with veterinary medicinal products or the animals' age. Together with incomplete FCI, this results in ineligible animals entering the food chain. Additionally, late identification results in an unknown number of horses not being tested for EIA in accordance with national surveillance programme requirements.

ANZ confirmed it is not currently possible to print a replacement identification document from database. Consequently, equidae not identified by 12 months of age are issued a standard identification document with no associated restrictions.

Equidae which are issued a duplicate or replacement identification document are not excluded from the food chain contrary to the requirements of Articles 29(2)(c) and 32(2)(c) of Regulation 2015/262. Identification verification (Transponder)

The audit team reviewed two veterinary health certificates (from the previous week) for movement of horses from traders to the slaughterhouse visited, covering 20 and 11 animals respectively. 15 animals in the first, and six in the second, had consecutive transponder numbers. Seven consecutive numbers were checked on ANZ database and all of them had corresponding identification documents issued 1-2 days before slaughter of which two were issued to horses greater than 2 years old. CA agreed that horses with consecutive numbers had been identified at traders holding and had moved there from holding of birth with no identification.

The audit team reviewed 10 passports returned from equidae slaughtered in March 2016 from the slaughterhouse visited. Three were duplicate passports and two were "original" passports (issued for the first time). The ages of the animals ranged from 1 to 15 years old. In eight of the ten, the outline diagram had not been completed and no photograph or print depicting the animals was available.

The CA is actively involved in measures that improve the welfare of cattle on dairy farms. Official controls provide satisfactory assurances of compliance with animal welfare requirements for cattle in dairy farms. Awareness levels on national legislation prohibiting tail docking are not high and, despite some preventive measures, there is an apparently low but continuing level of the banned practice of mutilation (tail-docking) of dairy cows.

label_heading: Conclusions on indicators of animal welfare
paragraph_text: Improving trends are perceived in the majority of welfare indicators, particularly those which are being promoted by several actors from the industry. Actions for the management of mastitis, through the control of somatic cell count in milk, are strongest since most actors are addressing this issue. Actions addressing tail-docking are weakest, as they are being addressed by only one actor other than the CA. 15 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The measures in place generally ensure that cattle on dairy farms are not caused unnecessary pain, suffering or injury. The Irish national strategy for dairy farming actively involves the CA and all other actors in managing animal welfare on dairy farms including

National legislation on animal welfare is found under the Animal Health and Welfare Act of 2013 which prohibits persons from doing, or failing to do, anything or causing or permitting anything to be done to an animal that causes unnecessary pain, distress or suffering.
