One farm had less than 50 cattle in total (dairy cows, calves and heifers), kept tethered when indoors but grazing at pasture at the time of the visit, and produced milk exclusively for direct sale. The other had over 1000 dairy cows kept in loose housing conditions: In the smaller farm the cattle stalls were too short for the length of the animals present but, although both the AV and the County veterinarian agreed with this assessment, neither the County veterinarian nor the AV had reported it as a non- compliance nor required in writing any actions to rectify the problems (which i

Official controls on animal welfare of dairy cattle are performed on a regular basis, based on risk-assessment (see also paragraphs 16 and 17): by County veterinarians on the welfare of calves, in the case of farms with more than six calves; by AVs for all other types of cattle, so all of both dairy and beef cattle of all ages. 8 Or ad-hoc, by County veterinarians: to follow up on reported non-compliances by the AVs who are not empowered to impose sanctions. Due to that, if sanctions are envisaged, any non-compliance with animal welfare requirements reported by an AV must be confirmed by a County veterinarian; or as a consequence of complaints.

County veterinarians informed the audit team that the ad-hoc control focuses in principle on confirming the presence of the reported non-compliance, or the cause of the complaint. A full animal welfare control (which would use the instruction and checklists for County veterinarians that has the complete requirements for cattle instead of only those from Directives 98/58/EC and 2008/119/EC) may be done during these ad-hoc visits but usually only if additional non-compliances are noticed during the visit.

The number of animal welfare non-compliances in dairy farms reported by the AVs and County veterinarians is low: out of 2006 controls in 2013 and 1487 controls in 2013 in cattle farms (dairy and beef cattle) there were respectively 51 (2.5%) and 30 (2%) animal welfare non-compliances reported. Additionally, in the two Counties visited there were almost no complaints related to animal welfare issues in dairy farms within the last three years. Since the regular controls of dairy cattle other than calves are carried out by the AVs and their instructions and checklists do not include the complete cattle requirements (see also paragraph 13), there is no regular verification of compliance with 9 t

label_heading: Conclusions on pig identification and registration
paragraph_text: The existence of uncontrolled pigs in some parts of Sardinia compromises the reliability of pig population data and undermines the traceability of pig movements on the island.

label_heading: Conclusions on pig identification and registration
paragraph_text: Under-registration/under-notification of the number of piglets and movements of pigs, hampers the confidence in the data stored in the database. As a consequence, the pig identification and movement registration system does not fully support planning and implementation of ASF eradication measures. It also does not fully allow for reliable/targeted planning of official controls, taking into account risks associated with, for example, movements of pigs from infected to non-infected parts of the island.

The CCA does not have an up-to-date list of all the holdings and keepers which keep pigs in Sardinia, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(a) of Directive 2008/71/EC. The authorities provided data on pig farms and number of pigs (see Annex II). Those data do not describe the full pig population because a number of pigs are still kept uncontrolled in some parts of Sardinia, which is illegal according to national law. The regional authority estimates that there are still "3000 to 4000 uncontrolled pigs in nine to ten municipalities, and may be on a few more locations". The majority of such pigs are in the ASF infected area. There is no estimation of the number of keepers of such pigs. 5

A significant number of pig movements are not notified and registered in the national pig database (Banca Dati Nazionale dell'Anagrafe Zootecnica), contrary to the requirement of Article 18(c) of Directive 1964/432/EEC. Pig movements are not registered into the database within seven days. The audit team visited two provinces and selected movement documents randomly in the ASL. In one, all movements were registered in the database; in the other, none of the movements selected for verification were registered in the database (the movements took place in June and August 2016 - two to four months before the audit). Slaughterhouses do not always notify the slaughter of pigs within 7 days. In one

Exclusion of male animals from testing in some areas on mainland Portugal may have compromised the maintenance of the OTF herds in these areas in 2015. Also, exclusion of 25% of herds on the mainland from field testing, decreases the ability of the system to detect and eliminate the infected animals as early as possible. As a consequence, the time window for the infection to find another susceptible animal is prolonged as well as the time to finally eliminate the infection. This to some extent explains the continuous persistence of Mycobacterium infection in some areas. This approach decreases the confidence in the true level of bTB infection in cattle population on mainland Portugal and mos

In 2015, all male animals were systematically excluded from bTB testing for the purpose of maintenance of OTF herd status in some parts of the country (e.g. where the prevalence of bTB is between 0.2% and 1%). This was not in compliance with the requirements of points 3 and 4.4.2 of the 2015 bTB Programme nor with Annex A(I)(2)(c) to Directive 64/432/EEC. For the purpose of maintenance of OTF herd status, the 2015 national operational instructions on bTB testing requested, for these areas, to test only female animals older than 6 weeks.

The 2016 bTB Programme modified this point. It requires testing of males not intended for fattening and females older than 6 weeks (for the maintenance of OTF herd status in areas where herd prevalence is between 0.2% and 1%). This measure is not fully in line with the requirements of Annex A(I)(2)(c) to Directive 64/432/EEC. For these areas, the 2016 operational instructions on bTB testing instruct that males for breeding older than 6 weeks should also be tested. In one region visited, the OPP coordinating veterinarian stated that only male animals that will, according to the keeper, be kept for breeding will be subject to bTB testing.

In case of disease outbreak, the existing weaknesses in pig identification would lead to an increased number of herds being restricted and investigated in order to determine the route and source of infection. Consequently, this would result in increased demands on official services and likely delay in implementing control measures. The necessary backward tracing using holding registers would not be possible where pigs had no identification or illegible identification.

The Polish Act of 2 April 2004 on the identification and registration of animals requires pigs born in Poland to be identified with an ear tag or tattoo bearing the 12 digit holding number of birth. If pigs move to another holding, there is no requirement for them to be marked with the 12 digit holding number of the second holding when they leave. This is not in accordance with the requirements of Article 5(2) of Directive 2008/71/EC.

In one pig slaughterhouse visited, carcases observed were identified in a number of ways including : single illegible plastic ear tags, single fully legible ear tags, fully legible 12 digit tattoo of Polish holding number, single fully legible ear tag from another Member State but no tattoo/ear tag with a Polish holding number (even though it arrived at the slaughterhouse from a Polish farm) additionally carcasses were seen with no eartag or tattoo.

Regulation (EC) No. 853/2004, Annex III, chapter IV (3) requires the food business operator (FBO) to ensure animals sent for slaughter are identified so their origin can be traced. In the case of carcases with no ear tag or tattoo, this had not been detected by the operator at ante-mortem examination or by the OV during their verification.

In the slaughterhouse visited, FBO operated an internal traceability system whereby all pig carcases were identified with a FBO batch code which related to the supplier. One batch code reviewed by the audit team demonstrated that pigs presented by one supplier had been sourced from 11 other holdings. The operator was in possession of holding numbers for these 11 suppliers but it was not possible, with the information available in the abattoir, to determine the holding where each pig had been consigned from; for this, as a minimum, each holding register for the 11 holdings would have to be examined.

There is a weak system of certification of live bovine for intra-union trade from assembly centres. As all relevant available information is not reviewed by certifying officers prior to issuing veterinary certification, the system does not provide the necessary guarantees and illegible animals (i.e. animals that did not stay 30 days prior to loading or since birth in holding of origin) are certified and traded, which increases the risk of spreading diseases through the EU. 5.3 REVIEW / CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT Compliance with minimum legal requirements requires significant investments but doesn't guarantee efficient and effective functionalities for the various services provided. In order to b

In the assembly centre visited, the audit team selected and reviewed a sample of certificates from the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES) and supporting documents for consignments of bovines certified for intra-EU trade and noted the following: one calf had pre-certification from its birth herd and a passport showing it left its birth herd at 21 days of age and arrived at the assembly centre three days later. The passport confirmed the calf had been registered in three holdings before arriving at the assembly centre. records for a second calf showed it arrived at the assembly centre, at 23 days of age, having been registered in three other holdings before arriving at the assembly centr

The audit team reviewed approximately five intra-trade certificates selected from TRACES and issued from an assembly centre in a different region of Poland and cross checked animal movements in the ARMA database. One calf left its holding of birth at 21 days of age, spent three days at a second holding before moving to an assembly centre and being certified for intra-EU trade the following day. This, along with point (43) above, is not in compliance with the requirements of Article 6 to Council Directive 64/432/EEC. In the final meeting, the competent authority provided a copy of a letter dated 25 January 2016 and addressed to all regional veterinary inspectorates. This letter stated that al

GVI and ARMA are directing significant resources to implementation of official controls on identification and registration of animals and the verification of data quality in the database. Timeliness of data reporting is improving but despite efforts, weaknesses remain with data quality and actions taken don't appear to be significantly improving data quality.

Data provided by GVI for 2012 - 2014 demonstrated high levels of non-compliance in bovine and ovine holdings inspected. 7 Percentage of holdings where non-compliance found during inspection: Bovine 2012 2013 2014 Ovine 22.5% 39.9% 37.7% 14.5% 27.8% 19.6% GVI confirmed they had not considered increasing the minimum rate of checks in subsequent years where a significant degree of non-compliance exists as required by Article 2(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 and Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006.

The ARMA database does not include a geographical indication of the holding nor data on ASF restrictions. Holdings could include non-contiguous parcels of land. Thus, the process for tracing back animals is burdensome and time-consuming (e.g. to ascertain whether pigs come from holdings in restricted areas due to ASF, officials would need to cross check manually data from the land register and EU legislation listing restricted districts). 5.2 USER INTERFACES User interfaces provide the various user-groups with relevant information from the database. The needs of users vary depending on the user-group and the use-case-scenario. For the purposes of this audit, three use-case-scenarios were use

The database does not contain the geographic co-ordinates or equivalent geographic indication of the holding as required by Section D(1)(b) of the Annex to Regulation 21/2004 ( sheep and goats) and Article 1(d) of Decision 2000/678/EEC (pigs).

The incomplete official template for flock register on sheep farms has no big impact in the day-to-day business (small sheep population) but could delay traceability in the case of emergencies (e.g. Foot-and-Mouth disease outbreak).

The CA has designed a template for holding register for sheep to be used by the farmer. Not all data required by EU legislation are included in the template, e.g. the result and date of last inventory, the name of transporter, the registration number of the vehicle or date of identification of new-born animals. On the sheep farm visited by the audit team those data (with exception of the result and date of last inventory) were not recorded by the keeper. This is not in line with Article 5 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 21/2004. 5.1.3 Correspondence with reality

On a sheep farm visited, all animals, including lambs for slaughter were tagged with two earmarks, one of them electronic. The flock register was updated in a timely manner by the owner. But not all data required by the EU legislation were included (for more see point 22). The sheep off movements were notified in a timely manner to the CHR (as batch movement). The result of the latest animal inventory was updated into the CHR in January 2016, but the number of animals recorded was significantly lower than the number of animals present on the farm at the time of audit team visit. The reason provided for the discrepancy was a mistake made by farmer's consultant when updating the CHR. 17 Conclu

The central database is only partially used for certification purposes; instead the certification at assembly centres relies on a system of pre-certification statements, some of which are not verified as should be. As a result, the existing weaknesses negatively affect reliability of the certification process for intra-EU trade. 5.3 MONITORING AND REVIEW Compliance with minimum legal requirements requires significant investments but doesn't guarantee efficient and effective functionalities for the various use-cases. In order to bring the systems up to a level where users get real benefits and return for investment, more than minimum compliance is needed. Review and continuous improvement are

At the assembly centre visited, the audit team noted shortcomings related to the certification procedures, in particular that the official veterinarian accepted incomplete information or unsigned statements by the owners of the animals. Furthermore, the farmers' statements that animals stayed for 30 days in their holding (for pigs) and no 20 animals were imported during the same period (for pigs and bovines) were directly accepted as the basis for certification without any additional verification (e.g. validated against data in the CHR)1. This is not in line with point 2, Article 3 of Directive 96/93/EC. The same shortcomings were detected during an internal audit in 2012, but no actions hav

The current system of directly linking each on/off notification prevents keepers from making notifications in certain situations where the connected buyer or seller has not completed their part in the notification process. It is very difficult for the competent authority to detect if the buyer fails to submit a notification on behalf of the buyer and the seller.

The fact that 100% of on/off paper notifications (over 150,000 in 2015) include the same date of signature for both the buyer and the seller may indicate that in some instances keepers insert an incorrect date on the notification which affects perceived compliance levels and merits further investigation by the competent authority. For electronic notifications, the date of notification by the buyer is also recorded by the database as the date of notification of the seller.

Various events such as births, deaths and movements must be notified by the keeper to database within specific deadlines, e.g. movements between holdings of bovines, ovines/caprines and porcines have to be notified within 7 days according to national legislation which implements the requirements of Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 of the European Parliament and of the Council. All national deadlines for notifications either comply or go beyond EU requirements.

Data provided by the competent authority shows that average notification times have improved during the past five years for all types of notifications in bovines as follows: Bovines - Percentage notifications of: Birth within 7 days of tagging 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 within 14 days of tagging 49.49 52.94 54.77 63.32 77.56 85.52 within 21 days of tagging 70.15 72.76 73.27 80.71 87.00 88.84 78.28 80.22 80.16 86.74 90.10 90.04 Death on farm within 7 days 94.38 96.68 94.98 96.48 96.65 97.15 within 14 days 95.66 98.44 96.92 98.48 98.52 98.94 within 21 days 96.22 98.91 97.50 99.02 99.03 99.33 Slaughter within 7 days 64.69 66.59 67.65 69.01 75.07 84.12 within 14 days 76.32 77.55 77.75 78.34 8

The competent authority stated that both the buyer and seller each have a legal responsibility to notify the FACR within 7 days of bovine movements under national legislation. Notifications between holdings can be notified in two ways, i.e.: a) in hard copy: where the seller (holding of origin) completes a section on a paper form and gives the form to the buyer (holding of destination). According to the competent authority the form usually accompanies the animal. The buyer completes their section and forwards it to the FACR, or b) electronic: where the seller notifies the database and a message is forwarded to the buyer to confirm receipt of the animal on-line. This option is only possible w

In both of the above options, the database will only accept movement when both the seller and the buyer complete the notification. The competent authority stated that the decision to link the notification from the seller and the buyer in one common notification to the database had improved overall compliance, and in particular data coherence. However, the current notification system has potentially negative impact on data completeness in FACR as described in findings 6 and 7.

For paper notifications, if a buyer fails to notify the database then the seller, through no fault of their own, has also failed to meet their legal obligation to notify. As indicated in finding 55, over 50% of movements are notified via paper. The only way to detect if the buyer fails to report the movement is through official controls on site, by matching movement documents with the database entries or when the seller becomes aware that the database has not been updated and they contact the competent authority. For electronic notifications, the buyer is prevented from making the notification for the on- movement if the seller fails to notify the off-movement.

In 2015, there were 845 movements of bovines where the destination holding did not notify the arrival (floating animals). This figure is based only on electronic notifications because there is no systematic way to know if a buyer does not notify a movement and no figure is available for the number of movements for which the buyer did not notify via hard copy.
The database does not flag "floating" animals if the buyer does not confirm receipt by a certain period or trigger any follow-up action by the competent authority.

The template paper notification form includes the date of movement, a date of signature for the seller and a date of signature for the buyer. The date of signature is accepted as the date of notification and is used to calculate compliance with legal deadlines. According to the competent authority, buyers and sellers always insert the same date of signature on the paper notification form. Therefore, the same date of notification for on and off-movements is always recorded in the database. For electronic notifications, the date when the buyer notifies the on-movement is used as the date of notification for both the on and the off-movement. 6

Based on the figures in finding 3 for 2015, the vast majority (98%) of notifications are received within the 7 day legal deadline which relates to 300,722 notifications. About 50% of these (or about 150,000) were via hard copy and according to the competent authority, all were signed by both the buyer and the seller on the same day. 2% of notifications were over the 7 day legal deadline (i.e. 3,493), which means that both the seller and the buyer signed the same non-compliant date for about 1,700 notifications. The buyer's signature (responsible for notifying on-movement) cannot pre-date the seller's (responsible for notifying the off-movement). Therefore, if the seller signs late then the b

Target figures for on-the-spot controls comply with EU requirements but the selection process for holdings is not based on the criteria in relevant EU legislation. A new risk analysis currently being developed will form an important part of rectifying this situation and better target holdings with higher risks of being non-compliant.

Article(2)(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006 require that the selection of holdings to be inspected by the competent authority shall be made on the basis of risk analysis. The two articles go on to specify the criteria that the risk analysis shall take into account. The competent authority stated 8 that although there had been a risk analysis in the database for several years to select holding for inspection that it could not be used by DVFA's because it did not provide appropriate data/results. Therefore, a new one was being developed which should be available in the near future.

The audit team visited two DVFAs and discussed how holdings were selected for on- the-spot inspections. Discussions focused on 2015 as an example year because the new risk analysis was discussed at national training in April 2016 and was subsequently implemented which meant that two systems were applied during 2016. In DVFA 1, staff were aware of the new methodological instruction but the annual plan for IRS inspections was based on the annual plan for Cross Compliance (CC) controls, i.e. in May 2015, the 12 holdings selected to be visited for CC checks were also selected for IRS controls. Subsequently, another 15 holdings were inspected for IRS controls during 2015 based on a number of crit

Although some criteria used for the selection of holding to be visited for CC controls may be the same as those for selecting holdings for IRS controls, they are not all the same, e.g. disease history and therefore the 3% holding selected may not represent the highest risk based on purely IRS criteria. Also CC controls are only carried out on holdings which receive subsidies and therefore not all holdings are included. The CA stated that CC controls are generally notified in advance (up to 48 hours) to the keeper. This presents difficulties for complying with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 which states that in general on-the-spot checks shall be unannounced.

The competent authority has not increased the minimum rate of checks in subsequent years where a significant degree of non-compliance existed as required by relevant EU legislation which could lead to an improvement in accuracy of the database.

The SVFA confirmed they had not considered increasing the minimum rate of checks in subsequent years where a significant degree of non-compliance existed (see finding 16) as required by Article 2(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003 and Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006.

The movement of live sheep to "temporary holdings" which are not registered on the central database and which are not subject to the normal legal requirements or official controls results in significant numbers of sheep moving outside the official control system and lost traceability.

National legislation allows sheep less than 12 months of age to move to "temporary holdings" where they should be slaughtered within 7 days of the move. A generic code in the database captures all off-movements to "temporary holdings", of which there were 4,044 in 2015. However, the "temporary holdings" are not registered on the national database as required by Article 7 of Council Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 and do not have to comply with the normal legal obligations of a holding. EU legislation does not include the concept of "temporary holdings". All slaughters associated with these movements should be notified to the DVFA's but DVFA staff confirmed that this does not always happen and the
There were non-compliances related to information recorded in the holding registers for sheep which can affect identification/traceability of animals.

The audit team visited three farms (bovine, ovine and porcine) and examined the IRS on each, including reports from the last on-the-spot official controls. In general, the level of compliance was high and the reports from the last official controls on each holding indicated that a comparative examination between individual identifications on animals, holding registers and the national database was carried out during the visit. No non- compliances were detected on any of the three holdings during those controls. But the audit team noted that the national template for the sheep holding register does not 11 include the following information required in point B of the Annex of Regulation 21/2004

label_heading: Conclusions on Organisation of Official Controls
paragraph_text: Official controls on both marketing and use of PPPs are performed in accordance with written instruction, in a uniform manner, which ensures consistency and operation of PPP wholesalers and professional users to the same standards. However, the complications for ASTA staff to take enforcement measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in the case of irregularities identified at pesticide distributors, small scale growers and landscapers could compromise the effectiveness of official controls. 5.3. IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1. Controls on the Marketing of Plant Protection Products Legal Requirements Article 28 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 on the authorisatio

For official controls on the use of PPPs, a system is in place for decision making on compliance with national and EU legal requirements, including enforcement measures and sanctions. However, this is not the case for official controls on the marketing of PPPs and for professional users with no extensive use of PPPs (landscapers and small scale growers), where there is a risk that non-compliances are not remedied by infringing operators, as no corrective measures are recommended to non-compliant operators and due to the absence of verification by any of the CAs. The complications with regard to imposition of penalties is one further complication. As a result of all these, the effectiveness o

In addition to the responsibilities stated under paragraph 7, ASTA is the CA in charge of decision making with regard to compliance or non-compliance of pesticide wholesalers, as part of official controls on the marketing of PPPs. ASTA staff are also responsible for carrying out of ad-hoc inspections at small scale growers and landscapers (see paragraphs 36 and 74 below). ASTA stated, however, that their staff do not have the status of "judicial police officers" ("officier de police judiciaire" (OPJ)). In order for ASTA staff to take any of the measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, they have to be accompanied by police officers. Once the Regulation, listed under parag

ASTA staff do not have the OPJ status allowing them to take enforcement measures (see paragraph 8 above), unless accompanied by police officers. However, there are provisions in the PPPA, allowing the Minister of Agriculture to take a number of administrative measures, which correspond to some of these, laid down in Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. According to information provided during the audit, in the case of irregularities identified and reported by ADA, ASTA staff could only recommend non- compliant operators as to what corrective measures to take in order to remedy the situation. There are no other follow-up actions by any of the CAs in order to verify that adequate act

According to information provided by ASTA, at the time of the audit, national legal provisions and rules regarding penalties applicable to infringements of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and Directive 128/2009/EC were laid down in the PPPA. For the same reasons, as listed above (see paragraphs 8 and 70), ASTA staff are not allowed to impose penalties. At the time of the audit, imposition of penalties, as well as any further measures in the case of serious infringements, were the responsibility of the Court of Justice. Once the Regulation, listed under paragraph 2, has been adopted, ASTA staff will have the powers to enforce the imposition of the penalties referred to in the final bullet points

At grower level, in the case of ad-hoc inspections by ASTA, the situation with regard to enforcement measures is similar to that described under paragraph 70 above. The reason is the same; ASTA staff do not have the OPJ status to apply any of the measures under Article 54 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, or to impose sanctions. Conclusions on Enforcement Measures

label_heading: Conclusions on measures in the demarcated areas
paragraph_text: No surveys were carried out in 2015 in the BZs in PACA. In Corsica the intensity of the surveys in the BZs is lower than that required by Article 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU. As a result there is no comprehensive information available about the infection status of the BZs.

label_heading: Conclusions on measures in the demarcated areas
paragraph_text: The sampling and testing practice within a radius of 100m around the infected plants is not in line with the provisions of Article 6(3) of Decision 2015/789/EU. Therefore, the real extent of the spread of infection is not known in each outbreak site.

The audit team noted that due to sampling and laboratory capacity problems, especially immediately after the first outbreaks, it was not possible to sample and analyse all the specified plants in the 100m area around the IZ. Instead, the area of 15m around each IZ was prioritised. In this area the specified plants were sampled and tested in line with provisions of the Decision.

In PACA the majority of the outbreaks were discovered in the last months of 2015 or in 2016, therefore no surveys had been carried out in the BZs at the time of the audit, which is not in line with the provisions of the Decision. In Corsica, due to the numerous recent outbreaks, the CA stated that it was not in a position to carry out surveys in line with the provisions of the Decision (i.e. visual inspections and sampling of plants with 18 symptoms based on a 100m x 100m grid). At the time of the audit, the entire BZ area was 380,100 ha; therefore the same number of visual inspections would be required annually to fulfil the requirements of the Decision.

The audit team was informed that visual inspections were and will be carried out in the BZs based on a grid split into 1km x 1km squares. The CAs noted that the proper implementation of the plan could be hindered by the inaccessibility of some areas. 5.3.4 Tracing back and forward of infection sources

label_heading: Conclusions on measures in the demarcated areas
paragraph_text: The measures taken in the DAs show the commitment of the French CAs to eradicating Xf, in order to protect major crops and environmentally and economically important areas. Specific efforts were made to implement appropriate measures. The demarcation of the affected areas, the eradication of infected plants and hosts (known at the time of detection) in the 100m radius and the trace back and forward of the infections was carried out in line with the provisions of Decision 2015/789/EU. However, as outbreak sites where eradication activity had been completed were not revisited after new hosts were identified, there is a risk that infected plants remain in those areas.

In the case of the first three outbreaks in Corsica it was assumed that the infection was caused by Xf subsp. pauca, therefore in the 100m area around the IZ, hosts plants of that subspecies and all symptomatic plants of other species were removed. Later, based on the assumption that Pm was the prominent source of infection, each plant of this species was removed. The audit team noted that due to capacity problems, Corsica SRAL could not return to all the outbreak sites where removal had been completed, to check for the presence and order the removal of plants of newly identified host species. For all outbreaks in PACA, immediate removal of host plants (known to be hosts at the time that the

The audit team visited nurseries in the DAs in Corsica and PACA, to whom derogation B had been granted and noted: They keep records on entries and sales. In the case of private clients the name, address and telephone number is recorded; Plants are treated with pesticides at least once a month; They are inspected by the SRAL regularly; In the nursery in Corsica, host plants (Lavandula sp.) were present, although this species was not considered as a host plant at the time of the demarcation. SRAL informed the audit team that the lot was put on hold and sampled, and that destruction was planned in the case of positive results; 5.3.6 Other measures to prevent the spread of Xf

label_heading: Conclusions on measures in the demarcated areas
paragraph_text: Nurseries located in DAs are allowed to move non-host specified plants outside their DA without fulfilling all requirements of Article 9(2) of Decision 2015/789/EU. It creates a potentially high risk as the plants spend time in the nursery, surrounded by potentially infected plants without any protection against transmission by vectors.

DGAL stated that it interprets the provisions of Article 9 of Decision 2015/789/EU as providing the possibility to grant three different types of derogations to nurseries in the DAs. SRAL authorises the movement of host and specified plants within and outside of the DAs according to the scheme outlined in paragraphs 72-75 below. In general, the applicable derogation depends on the type of plants and the length of time they spend in the DA. Derogation A is applied to nurseries who deal with marketing of plants which are in pots or containers and the premises are not considered as growing fields (i.e. plants are not multiplied and kept on solid surface). It is granted for non-host specified pl

Derogation A is granted if the nursery Carries out an inventory on the stocks; Carries out permanent insecticide treatment of the plants against insect vectors; Keeps a record on sales and keeps a register of observations any disease symptoms; Receives prior authorisation of the stocks from SRAL; Subscribes for the BSV and follows training on Xf organised by an expert body.

Derogation B is granted if the nursery Keeps a record on entries (date, supplier, quantities) per plant species; Carries out permanent insecticide treatment of the plants against insect vectors and keeps a record of the treatments; 20 Keeps a record on sales (date, client, quantities) per plant species and keeps a register of observations of any disease symptoms; Subscribes for the BSV and follows training on Xf organised by an expert body.

The audit team noted that derogations A and B are not in line with provisions of Decision 2015/789/EU. However, DGAL stated that based on the French language version of the Decision, it interprets that the movement ban of Article 9 refers to plants which have been cultivated in the DAs and does not include those that are kept on premises for wholesale and retail purposes only. The CA considers that the measures, linked to derogation A and B provide the necessary guarantees of not distributing the pest through sales of planting material. The CA has also emphasised that the approach was developed based on the need to allow trade of planting material without pronounced risk while taking efforts

The audit team visited nurseries in the DAs in Corsica and PACA, to whom derogation B had been granted and noted: They keep records on entries and sales. In the case of private clients the name, address and telephone number is recorded; Plants are treated with pesticides at least once a month; They are inspected by the SRAL regularly; In the nursery in Corsica, host plants (Lavandula sp.) were present, although this species was not considered as a host plant at the time of the demarcation. SRAL informed the audit team that the lot was put on hold and sampled, and that destruction was planned in the case of positive results; 5.3.6 Other measures to prevent the spread of Xf

In 2015 France carried out a comprehensive and risk based Xf national survey as required by EU legislation. The surveys outside the DAs in Corsica took into consideration the new risk elements identified as a result of the outbreaks. In PACA, as the outbreaks were detected recently, there was no time for comprehensive surveys outside the DAs. In both regions, the limited accessibility of private properties, scrublands or other natural sites compromise the surveys. The lack of movement controls of specified plants beyond the controls related to the implementation of the plant passport system outside the DAs does not increase the risk of spread substantially as there is limited trade of plants

Outside the DAs, surveys in the two regions targeted nurseries and public places, where there were reports about the presence of Pm plants or symptomatic plants. The audit team was informed that in both regions, there are numerous private properties where Pm and other host plants are present. Accessing these properties for surveillance purposes is very difficult. In Corsica many private properties are second homes of residents in continental France and the owners are not present for much of the year. Therefore in many cases it is difficult to obtain the consent of the owner/tenant for the survey.

In some areas, especially in Corsica, Pm has become part of the wild flora and is commonly found in scrublands (in French - maqui). The audit team was informed that there are signs that some of these wild plants exhibit symptoms of Xf. However, the majority of these plants are located in sites that are difficult to access in order to take samples and practically inaccessible for the implementation of eradication measures, if necessary. SRAL Corsica surveyed some scrublands with a drone and confirmed the presence of symptomatic Pm plants. SRAL intends to contact the National Botanical Conservatory of Corsica, who are involved in flora mapping of wild areas, in order to collect information abo

The audit team was informed that visual inspections were and will be carried out in the BZs based on a grid split into 1km x 1km squares. The CAs noted that the proper implementation of the plan could be hindered by the inaccessibility of some areas. 5.3.4 Tracing back and forward of infection sources

label_heading: Conclusions on surveys for the detection of Xf
paragraph_text: The surveys were carried out at times not being the most appropriate for certain specified plants or even inappropriate for some other specified plants. Therefore the effectiveness of the visual inspections as a means of identifying symptomatic plants and suspected cases of infection were compromised. The impact of this could be mitigated to some extent by the 2016 sampling and testing regime, which goes beyond EU requirements.

Although EU and Italian legislation established the current BZ in May 2016 (see chapter 5.1.2) the full scale 2016 surveys started there only in August after the Prosecutor's ban was revoked (see chapter 4.2) and the necessary financial and human resources were put into place including the training of the surveillance staff.. The work was being carried out by ARIF, based on a 100m x 100m grid approach, as required by the EU legislation. It was decided to start the work at the northern border of the BZ and to move progressively southward in order to first detect any infection situated farthest from the IZ (see figure II).

After recruiting and training the necessary personnel, the survey started on 29 August 2016 and full capacity was reached in September, involving 172 ARIF agents working in 86 teams. ARIF agents have the status of public agents and Ministerial Decree 2014/2005 gives them the right to enter private property. Each team has an average capacity of 20 squares per day enabling ARIF to check around 1,500 squares and collect 2,000-2,500 samples daily. A complex and sophisticated IT system supports the activity.

The visual inspection and the sampling are carried out following a very detailed guideline. ARIF regularly controls the quality of the work of its agents. The guideline lists the main elements of the methodology as follows: The survey team shall identify the physical borders of each grid square with the help of orthophotos, high resolution satellite images and by using GPS coordinates. The system ensures that there is no overlap of the inspected squares and that no gaps are left uninspected in the territory; The entire area of the square shall be scouted and checked visually. The host and specified plants shall be identified with particular attention to visible symptoms. As the first symptom

The audit team observed a survey carried out by an ARIF team and noted that: The agents were experienced and had good knowledge about the legislation and about the host and specified plants; ARIF organises the sampling properly; the activity of the teams and the logistics of the samples are fully coordinated; The IT system used ensures the proper identification of the squares and the host and specified plants present. The electronic report, which is prepared according to a template, contains all information necessary for the authorities and for other statistical and analytical purposes; The agents carried out the visual checks and the sampling fully in line with the provisions of the guideli

From September 2016 onwards, ARIF started its activity also in the "20km zone". First they checked some high risk spots while the systematic survey with the method described in chapter 5.2.2 started in October after the work in the BZ was largely completed. At the time of the audit, in the "20km zone" 11.6% of the area had been checked and sampled. The work started at the border of the BZ and was to continue at the rate of 1,500 squares a day until completed. RPS expects the completion of the work in January 2017 (see table III). label_heading: Conclusions on specific surveys and information campaigns
paragraph_text: The surveys for Japanese beetle in Italy are organised appropriately, however, they are unevenly distributed between both affected regions and the implemented intensity does not provide sufficient information about the actual distribution of the pest.

Visual inspections were concentrated in the areas not infested by Japanese beetle, i.e. the buffer zone, and were carried out between mid June and mid August 2016. The three km buffer zone is subdivided in three concentric bands of one km in width within which a 1000 m square matrix grid is used and the sites for inspection were as equally distributed as possible. This density of survey points is significantly lower than that required in EU legislation in other outbreaks, e.g. for buffer zone surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa (100 x 100 m), however, the RPSs performs more dense visual inspections in the area closer to the infested zone. The sites contained preferred host plants on which th

In 2016 the RPS in Lombardy carried out 1 825 visual inspections and the RPS in Piedmont 430. With the recent update of the demarcated area in the summer 2016, the area of the buffer zone was extended and is very large. As mentioned above, a 1 000 m x 1 000 m survey grid is not very dense for a secure delimitation of the infestation and the number of inspections indicates that Piedmont in 2016 was far from achieving even that coverage. Thus the authorities might not obtain sufficient information on the current distribution of the pest and may not delimit the outbreak adequately. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC that all necessary measures mus

The containment control measures taken are considered to be appropriate to suppress the population and slow the natural spread of the pest. However, since the measures aimed at eradication are not applied in the buffer zone, containment of the pest is unlikely.

Movement of plants for planting and lawn turf is adequately regulated. However, the prohibition on selling plants outside of the demarcated area is not officially enforced and there is potential risk of spreading the pest outside demarcated area. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC that all necessary measures must be taken to eradicate, or if that is impossible, inhibit the spread of the pest. 5.7 RESEARCH Findings

However, given the relative low level presence of the host, particularly in Piedmont and Lombardy, where outbreaks have occurred, the variation in susceptibility, as well as the issue of latency with respect to delayed symptom expression, the current level of monitoring intensity of timber producing trees is inadequate to reliably delimit for the presence of Thousand canker disease.

Similarly, in Veneto, despite a higher presence of host trees, predominantly plantations of J. nigra, and based on the same issues with respect to susceptibility and latency, the current level of monitoring intensity there is also inadequate to reliably delimit the disease.

Insufficient monitoring is carried out for mono-cultures of J. regia in commercial walnut fruit production in all of the regions, and for which no contingency plan exists. Such absences pose particular potential challenges with respect to disease management and further control should Thousand canker disease enter the fruit production industry.

Despite a high degree of homogeneity with respect to the monitoring approach and overall surveillance strategy, the level of monitoring intensity varies between regions but, in each case, is considered insufficient to reliably delimit the presence of Thousand canker disease and provide for the protective measures required by Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC (see paragraphs 40 to 52). Veneto

Veneto manages a total of 50 strategically positioned monitoring sites across its region. Identified from the public nursery database (of Veneto Agricultura) and the regional register (see also paragraph 33), the sites are also selected, as much as is practically possible, to a defined geometrical grid.
Trees at all 50 sites are subject to visual inspection. Thirty of the sites are complemented with a pheromone trap. Sites are inspected on a monthly basis.

In addition, the RPS stated that one trap is positioned in one plantation which is also subjected to monitoring. No Thousand canker disease has been observed there to date. Furthermore, both producers and an industry association met during the audit stated they have never witnessed Thousand canker disease, nor the vector, in their plantations. Piedmont

Piedmont has a total of 15 strategic monitoring sites across its region. Of the four pheromone trap deployments, two are located at each of the notified outbreak sites. Eleven other sites are subject to visual monitoring only. Sites, as well as traps, are inspected on a monthly basis.

From their observations, Piedmont stated that no Thousand canker disease has been observed on varieties of J. regia for walnut fruit production. Therefore, the commercial walnut fruit plantations to the South east and south west of the region have not been included in their monitoring regime.

Lombardy monitors 10 strategically selected sites with pheromone traps within its region each year. Each site typically comprises up to 20 trees. Each site is visited on a monthly basis during which the traps and trees are checked for the vector and 12 Thousand canker disease, respectively. This regime, in place since 2014, was preceded by a less stringent preliminary monitoring approach in 2013 following notification of the first outbreak case in Veneto. The location of some of the monitoring sites are changed each year.

In addition to selected sites for visual inspections, Friuli Venezia Giulia originally deployed 21 pheromone traps in 2016 (on loan from the University of Padua), 16 of which are currently operational as five were removed for operational reasons. Deployment is partially random, but some are strategically positioned close to road and railway lines, the others in small young commercial timber plantations of typically 0.5 to 1 Ha. Sites are visited once per month.

As commercial walnut fruit plantations of J. regia are limited in Friuli Venezia Giulia they are not included in the RPS monitoring regime. 5.2.5 Commercial availability of Thousand canker disease pheromone

label_heading: Conclusion on situation of Trioza erytreae
paragraph_text: The outbreaks of T. erytreae have been notified to the European Commission and other Member States, but after a significant delay. That is not in line with Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC nor Article 2 of Decision 2014/917/EU; it also hinders the response of other Member States, in particular in adapting their official controls as necessary.

The notifications provided the information required by Decision 2014/917/EU, however the long delay, between confirmation of the presence of the pest and its notification to the Commission and other Member States in both cases, is not in line with Article 2 of Decision 2014/917/EU, which provides for a maximum of eight working days for the provision of at least a preliminary notification. 5.2.2 Surveys for Trioza erytreae and Ca. label_heading: Conclusion on control measures for Trioza erytreae
paragraph_text: However, the application of authorised plant protection products, which is the only measure aimed at inhibiting the further natural spread of the pest, is not carried out systematically, particular in those areas bordering the remaining free areas of the AC of Galicia. The further spread of T. erytreae is therefore inevitable. It cannot therefore be concluded that all necessary measures have been taken to inhibit the spread of the pest, at least in those areas, as required by Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.4 CONTINGENCY PLAN FOR CANDIDATUS LIBERIBACTER SPP Legal requirements There are no EU requirements for contingency plans for harmful organisms Article 16(1) to Directive 2000/29/

The audit team observed the application of a pesticide treatment to a recently identified infested tree, on the boundary of the infested zone close to Santiago de Compestela, within the area targeted by the official pesticide treatment programme. label_heading: Conclusion on control measures for Tecia solanivora
paragraph_text: The objective of the control measures for T. solanivora in both Galicia and Asturias, is its eradication, however the measures, as applied, are unlikely to achieve this.

The control measures taken following a finding of T. solanivora focus on infected tubers or the field or store in which the trap on which the moths were caught was placed, which is not necessarily their source. This means that the measures are unlikely to result in the eradication of the pest from the infected area, however they should at least inhibit its spread in line with Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.6.2 Control measures for Tecia solanivora in Asturias

The competent authority has elaborated control measures that should, if applied systematically, inhibit further spread of the pest in line with Article 16(1) of the same Directive. However, these measures are not systematically applied or their enforcement within the infested zone of the demarcated areas is not efficient and the pest continues to spread. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 16(1) of the same Directive 15 that all necessary measures must be taken to eradicate, or if that is impossible, inhibit the spread of the pest. 5.4 CITRUS GREENING 5.4.1 Follow up action of the Algarve case

paragraph_text: The delayed elaboration of the national Xf contingency plan may impact negatively on the implementation of the necessary measures in the case of possible future outbreaks. 5.2 NOTIFICATION OF THE OUTBREAK, ESTABLISHMENT OF THE DEMARCATED AREA Legal requirements Article 2 (1) of Commission Implementing Decision 2014/917/EU. At federal level, preparatory steps have been made under the leadership of the JKI for developing a contingency plan for Xf. A working group was set up with participation of diagnostic and plant health control experts from Bavaria, Thuringia, Brandenburg, Baden-Württemberg, North Rhine-Westphalia and Lower Saxony.

However, the plans cannot be considered as meeting the requirements of the Decision; It is unlikely that the national contingency plan will be finalised by 31 December 2016, the deadline set by Article 3a of Decision 2015/789/EU. 5.1.4 Communication and cooperation within the plant health services and with other authorities involved in controls

paragraph_text: The presence of Xf in the BZ was monitored with a methodology, in line with EU provisions and the most risky sites were prioritised. However, as the entire territory of the BZ was not checked, the absence of Xf has not yet been fully verified. 5.4 ERADICATION MEASURES Legal requirements Article 6 of Commission Implementing Decision 2015/789/EU. ISPM 9, ISPM 14 and ISPM 31 as referred to by Article 6 (3) and (10) of the Decision. Findings 5.4.1 Trace back and forward of possible infection

The LPPS of Saxony and Thuringia carried out surveys in the BZ, based on a grid split into 100 x 100 m squares, as required by Article 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU. At the time of the audit, Saxony had inspected 1,394, while Thuringia 2,535 squares, 9% and 16% of the squares in the BZ in their territory, respectively.

label_heading: Conclusions on the movement control of specified plants
paragraph_text: The implementation of movement restrictions relies mainly on public awareness. Little actual control of the sale/movement of specified plants takes place and the level of guarantee foreseen in the Decision 2015/789/EU may not be achieved. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS With comprehensive assistance of the federal CAs, Saxony and Thuringia implemented appropriate measures with the aim to eradicate Xf following a confirmed finding in May 2016. Human and financial resources were mobilised to address the outbreak. A robust information campaign channels all necessary information to the relevant producers and traders and to the general public. An adequate laboratory regime was established for testing Xf wi

The audit team noted during visits in nurseries and garden centres in the BZ that the operators: All have stocks of specified plants and market them all year around; Grow or keep the specified plants in open field or in non-vector-proof establishments; Do not carry out vector controls, the applied chemicals target the main pests of the plants, but not the xylem feeding vectors; Usually do not have detailed inventories of the specified plant stocks, their origin and time of arrival; Do not register their customers, however they stated that they are usually from the area and are informed about the movement restrictions; Are fully aware of the details of the EU legislation, including the list o

The audit team also noted that: LPPS inspectors of Saxony and Thuringia carry out some controls on the movement of specified plants in the nurseries and garden centres in the BZ; The customers of the nurseries and garden centres are not checked and no road controls are carried out; The implementation of movement restrictions relies mainly of the extensive public awareness measures (see chapter 5.5.1 and 5.1.5). The audit team therefore considers that the official controls cannot ensure that plants which have been grown for at least a part of their life in the DA are not moved out of that area. paragraph_text: There is a clear organisation of the controls related to PWN and there is a good cooperation and communication between the entities involved. label_heading: Conclusions on organisational aspects of controls
paragraph_text: The current Action plan for the demarcated area of As Neves is not fully in line with Decision 2012/535/EU as it limits the intensive survey to the surroundings of the new finding although such an intensive survey was still required around the initial outbreak. 5.2 ANNUAL SURVEYS OF THE TERRITORY OUTSIDE DEMARCATED AREAS Legal requirements Article 2 of Decision 2012/535/EU 7 Findings

Control measures have been taken to address the new detection of PWN based on the assumption that this is a new outbreak linked to a new incursion from Portugal. However, this is not based on evidence and the extension of the outbreak of 2010 cannot be excluded. This risk is not addressed by control measures taken so far.

The delays in felling and removing the infested symptomatic tree and the absence of preventative measures resulted in a risk of further spread of PWN. These risks would have been significantly less if control measures had been implemented in accordance with Point 7 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU. The inadequate implementation of the clear-cut following the finding of PWN further adds to this risk. 5.4 CONTROL MEASURES IN THE DEMARCATED AREA Legal requirements Article 6 of Decision 2012/535/EU Points 6 to 10 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU Findings 5.4.1 Annual surveys in the demarcated areas

However, despite of the fact that the demarcated area had been in place since the end of 2010, the regional service had not set up a system ensuring the timely implementation of PWN control measures as required in Decision 2012/535/EU, the Regional legislation and the Action plan for the demarcated area. In particular, In 2016, the resources allocated to the surveys, identification of dead trees or trees in decline and sampling activities were insufficient for the work to be completed in the whole demarcated area at the frequency and within the required deadlines; (see also section 5.4.1) In 2015 and 2016, the work of felling and removal of identified dead or declining trees in the demarcate

The audit team noted that the sample taken from the symptomatic tree in Salvaterra do Mino on 18 February 2016 was confirmed to be infested with PWN by the regional laboratory on 2 May 2016 i.e. 2,5 months after the sample was taken. Although the symptomatic tree was in a demarcated area where there was a requirement to fell and remove identified dead or declining trees before the 1 April, the tree was not felled until the diagnostic was confirmed. Although the confirmation by the National Laboratory is a prerequisite for taking official measures, the handing of the infested wood sample by the Regional laboratory was not done so as to minimise the delays in getting the results confirmed: the

The audit team noted that the surveys of trees in the 20 km zone along the border with Portugal and the demarcated area are performed by the same two people from Tragsatec. The map above shows that the work is conducted starting from the border with Portugal and progressing Northward in accordance with the regional service's assessment of the highest risk for PWN infestation. The results of the intensive surveys conducted in this 20 km zone along Portugal since 2010 have demonstrated that PWN is not present outside the existing demarcated area of As Neves. This is confirmed by the preliminary results of the surveys conducted in 2016. Conclusions on annual surveys of the territory outside dem

The audit team noted that Tragsatec staff involved in these felling and sampling activities did not check for the presence of signs of vectors' activity either in the infested tree or in the dead or declining trees and branches surrounding it. There was no assessment of the risk of further spread from this site before the felling and removal of the susceptible trees. Based on the interviews held by the audit teams, staff involved in these activities and in their supervision had a limited knowledge of the biology of the vector and ways of spreading PWN and could not explain the signs of vector activity.

The audit team noted that there was no investigation of the possible origin of the PWN infestation. The regional service considered that this new finding was a new incursion from Portugal, either by dispersal flight of the vector or human assisted dispersal. However, they had not identified any particular risk in the surroundings or any evidence for two such incursions at short distance despite intensive surveys showing that the 20 km zone along the border with Portugal is free from PWN (see section 5.2). The audit team noted that while there was no evidence of a new incursion from Portugal, the following facts points towards an extension of the outbreak detected in 2010: The two infested tr

The action plan dated May 2016 further specifies the different zones comprising the Buffer Zone and control measures to be implemented in each of these: Zone A: clear-cut zone of 100 m radius around the new infested tree; Zone B: a 100 m to 3 km zone around the new infested tree where intensified surveys of susceptible trees and vectors are conducted; Zone C: the remaining part of the buffer zone also referred to as 3-20 km zone.

The audit team noted that the order delegating the work of felling and removing trees to Tragsa was signed mid-July i.e. at the end of the period given to private owners to organise their sales of wood. Consequently the clear-cut zone was implemented from end-July to September, which is after most of the vectors would already have emerged from trees and branches. These measures were therefore implemented too late to be effective in preventing PWN spread and are therefore not in line with point 2 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU.

According to the regional service, 1,282 susceptible trees were felled in the clear-cut zone. A total of 17 samples were taken from symptomatic trees which were sampled. Only one sample was taken from asymptomatic trees without this being justified based on the risk of spread of PWN which is not in line with point 2 of Annex I. This requires that a number of asymptomatic trees be sampled selected based on the risk of spreading of PWN. All samples tested negative for PWN.

The audit team visited the infested site and the clear-cut zone and noted that the stump of the infested tree was marked with a red ring and was located in an uneven and rocky terrain on a steep slope. The representative of the regional service who had supervised the work stated that after the felling and removal of trees, the branches and cutting remains had been crushed on-site by a tractor and that the result had been judged satisfactory given the characteristics of the area. The audit team noted that on such terrain the method implemented could not be effective and indeed spotted the presence of some branches big enough to contain pupae of the vector. label_heading: Conclusions on development of the programme of audits
paragraph_text: The CAs have developed and implemented processes for establishing annual and multiannual audit programmes. The processes are not adequately documented and had not considered all relevant areas to be audited in the last five years. The methodology applied for risk based prioritisation of audit planning is still under ongoing development with the aim of addressing this shortcoming.
