AFSVSPP does at present not have a system in place for independent scrutiny.
IRSAFHF is in the early stages of planning for independent scrutiny.

HIRS has a quality system in place that gives limited assurances to the management on the audit processes' achievement of the objectives of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex of Commis
AFSVSPP had at the time of the audit not made plans for independent scrutiny.
IRSAFHF has not engaged in independent scrutiny so far. One external audit is planned for 2018, but at the time of this audit, no terms of reference for this external audit had been determined.

HIRS is subject to an external evaluation every year, as part of its ISO accreditation. These external evaluations focus on compliance with ISO standards and cover a much wider scope than their official controls which fall under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The external evaluator gives an opinion on the independence of the audit body/auditors in the context of the Quality Management system, but does not demonstrate that Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) 882/2004 has been taken into consideration. However, as the evaluation reports identify areas for improvement and best practices, they can provide for some aspects of independent scrutiny. Conclusions

The range of official controls that must be covered by audit programmes has been adequately identified and considered by two of the three audit bodies. IRSAFHF does not include relevant activities at central level.
AFSVSPP has a system in place for development and approval of audit programmes. However, all areas cannot with current arrangements be covered in a reasonable timeframe.

AFSVSPP establishes its programme based on specific food and feed risks. There are documented procedures for development and approval of audit programmes. A risk assessment with risk analysis and its impact, considering "effectiveness" and "sensitivity", has been done with participation of the Director of Food Safety, Veterinary and Plant Health Inspection; the Heads of Professional Divisions and the Heads of Regions. The participants did their assessments on their own and separately for each area/topic. The total results were compiled and the areas/topics with highest scores were prioritised for audits. The Director General approves the plan and can propose areas to include. Recommendations

IRSAFHF has a plan for internal audits of all inspectors working with official controls falling under Regulation No 882/2004 for 2013 ­ 2016, but do not include in their audits the activities of central level such as development of documented procedures, and planning and co-ordination of official controls. Audit topics are selected for each inspector from the cases that have been handled by them. Cases that contain non-conformities, sampling, penalties, complaints, etc. are prioritised. The Head of the Agriculture Service approves the plan. All inspectors are audited within a four year period (2013 ­ 2016).
In AFSVSPP the impact of the audits is undermined by the failure to address recommendations in a systematic and timely fashion.

AFSVSPP follow-up procedures include the role of management and state: 'If the auditee does not follow the recommendations and not implement corrective or preventive measures or improvements, the Director of the Internal Audit Office informs the Director General of the AFSVSPP by means of a written report'. There is no clear indication at what point after the deadline for submission of an action plan, or after deadlines for completion of actions proposed in the action plan, the Director General should be informed. The audit team noted that actions to address the audit recommendations are still awaited in: Two of the three AFSVSFF audits in 2014 where clarification of the action plan has not

AFSVSPP indicated that certain audits (e.g. border inspection posts) lead to recommendations which are focused on the inspection level and follow-up is easier than when audits identify certain policy measures which need to be improved. When recommendations address policy level issues it is sometimes less clear who should take responsibility to develop an action plan.

For DGCCRF, independent scrutiny of the current audit processes has not yet been carried out. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex of Commission D

For DGCCRF, even if some potential mechanisms exist (the Ministerial Audit Committee) that could be suitable to undertake independent scrutiny of the audit processes, these mechanisms are not being used for this purpose at present.
At the time of the DG SANTE audit, no decisions had been taken as to when and how independent scrutiny of the DGCCRF internal audit processes would be achieved. Conclusions

A system for training of officials and for keeping their competence up-to-date is in place and the knowledge of the officials met was in general satisfactory, with the exception of HACCP-based programmes. 5.1.9 Enforcement measures Legal requirements Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Official controls do not sufficiently verify the implementation of HACCP-based procedures by the FBOs, thus possibly overlooking incompletely designed and implemented HACCP-based procedures. 5.2.3 Microbiological criteria for foodstuffs Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

The audit team noted that the officials met during the visits in the dairy processing establishments had a limited knowledge with regard to evaluation of FBOs' HACCP- based procedures (see paragraph No 60); The CCA stated that no specific training on HACCP-based procedures has been provided so far. Conclusions on training

The documented official controls seen by the audit team showed that, in some cases, non-conformities such as non-updated procedures, absence of action thresholds for certain microbiological criteria to be set by the FBO, corrective actions not reflected in the real activity of the establishment (e.g. acceptance of raw milk exceeding the limits for TPC/SCC and notification to the CA, potable water treatment, etc.), were not properly identified and evaluated by the CA.

The evaluation of FBOs' HACCP-based systems is included in the inspection checklist for processing establishments. However, the checklist includes a generic reference to the existence of HACCP-based systems and to their evaluation. No instructions on how to evaluate HACCP-based programmes had been provided to official staff at the time of the audit. The audit team noted that some of the official staff interviewed had a limited knowledge in the matter. Conclusions on HACCP based systems

No arrangements have been put in place, contrary to the requirement of Article 4(6) of Regulation 882/2004/EC, to ensure independent scrutiny of the audit process. This means that the competent authorities missed an opportunity to receive inputs for promoting continuous improvement of the audit process. 5.2.3 Auditor competence Legal requirements and other audit criteria Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently"

The MCCAA audit system achieved ISO 9001 certification in 2004 (by an accredited certification body) and is subject to certification assessment every year. The audit team discussed with the competent authorities the extent to which this assessment covers the internal audit activities. Whilst this assessment is independent and covers inter alia the internal audit activities, it is limited to the requirements of the ISO 9001 standard and does not focus on the aspects of the audit process (such as programme development, independence etc.). This means that the certification assessment does not provide information on whether the audit process is achieving its objectives therefore does not serve a

VRD and EHD have no arrangements in place to perform independent scrutiny of the audit process contrary to the requirement of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 9 Conclusions on independent scrutiny

label_heading: Conclusions on follow-up of audit recommendations
paragraph_text: The competent authorities have put in place systematic arrangements to ensure that appropriate corrective actions are proposed and implemented and that these actions have been effective at ensuring deficiencies are addressed. However, the lack of a procedure to systematically "escalate" cases where audit recommendations are not addressed means that deficiencies in the performance of the official controls may remain outstanding/reoccur for a long period of time contrary to the objectives of Article 4 (6) of Regulation 882/2004. 5.2.7 Transparency Legal requirements and other audit criteria Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires, inter alia, that "audits ........shall be carried

While all competent authorities have taken steps to ensure independent scrutiny: in two competent authorities the arrangements had only very recently been put in place; in another two competent authorities the arrangements were insufficient to achieve the objectives of the process either because the whole audit process was not included in the scrutiny or because the arrangements for such scrutiny did not involve individuals with sufficient relevant experience in the field of audits conducted in accordance with Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In DAFM, the audit charters of both VIAU and IAU state that independent scrutiny shall be carried out by the Audit Monitoring Group. In practice, this group is one person: both VIAU and IAU have for a number of years used an external expert to scrutinise and provide feedback on their audit programmes, in particular to ensure that appropriate risks were considered. This same individual is a co-signatory of their audit charters.
While this process adds value to the audit programmes, it does not consider other aspects of the audit process and no particular feedback on these aspects has been received.

SFPA has recognised that some adjustments will be necessary to enable the committee to discharge this newer responsibility: The current audit committee membership was set up before the inclusion of audits conducted in accordance with Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in its remit. As a result its membership was established with a focus on financial auditing and internal controls. The SFPA representative met by the DG SANTE audit team stated the reinforcement of the committee with additional external members with specific expertise relevant to the internal audit of fisheries control and food safety of fishery products was under discussion; The terms of reference for the committee in

The charter states that its scrutiny should have a particular focus on ensuring that the audit process "is capable of producing objective results and meeting its obligations under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004". At the time of this DG SANTE audit, the terms of reference for the independent scrutiny had been drafted, based on the NAS Network document on Independence and Independent Scrutiny. A suitable individual to carry out independent scrutiny had just been identified and it was intended to finalise the terms of reference with this person over the following weeks.

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: National legislation and guidelines necessary to implement EU requirements relevant for the sector audited have been issued and, from a preliminary analysis, they are in line with EU legislation with the exception of the national measures applied to FBOs who 4 process their own milk at farm level. These latter measures are not in line with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 as they provide for placing products on the national market with the application of an identification mark which does not comply with the requirements of Annex II, Section I of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

Ordinance on special conditions for approval of certain establishments dealing with food of animal origin (OJ 100/15) sets out the requirements for FBOs processing their own milk on the holding and selling their dairy products on farm, markets, exhibitions, restaurants and retailers in the country. The Ordinance establishes that the products must be marked with a round identification mark bearing the same approval number (see paragraph 39): this is not in line with the requirements of Annex II, Section I of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, prescribing an identification marking of foodstuffs of animal origin, when manufactured in the EU by an approved establishment, of oval shape. Conclusions on

The Ordinance on special conditions for approval of certain establishments dealing with food of animal origin covers specific requirements to be complied with by facilities processing milk at the farm of origin for direct supply of dairy products, marked with a special identification mark, to final consumers at the place of production and at markets and exhibitions in the whole country. These requirements are related to layout, equipment, operation and hygiene and provide that dedicated spaces must be arranged for equipment destined for collection/storage of raw milk and for by-products not intended for human consumption, rooms must also be dedicated for milk processing and for maturing of d

label_heading: Conclusions on registration/approval of food business establishments
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for the registration and approval of establishments that allows the CAs to keep them under official controls. However, the system in place does not require the approval of all MCCs, contrary to the requirements of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

label_heading: Conclusion on controls on HACCP-based systems
paragraph_text: The control system in place includes official controls for verification of FBO compliance with HACCP-based procedures. However its effectiveness is compromised as controllers are not able to identify some non-compliances in the design and implementation of the HACCP-based procedures and therefore cannot verify that FBOs identify the risks associated to their production, via CCPs, have them 19 under control and take appropriate corrective actions when necessary. 5.4.6 Microbiological criteria for foodstuffs Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

A training system aimed at ensuring that official staff is able to carry-out its tasks adequately is in place. However, based on the findings noted during the audit, it does not seem to be effective. 5.1.8 Enforcement measures Legal requirements Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

label_heading: Conclusion on registration / approval of FBOs
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for approval and registration of establishments. However, the implementation of the approval procedure is not satisfactory as it does not ensure that approved establishments fulfil all the relevant EU requirements.. 5.1.4 Prioritisation of official controls Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 4 Findings

label_heading: Conclusion on general and specific hygiene requirements
paragraph_text: Official controls for verification of FBOs compliance with the general and specific hygiene requirements are in place. However, the controls are not effective as they are not able to identify significant problems at establishment level. As a consequence the system in place does not satisfactorily verify that the establishments comply with the relevant EU requirements. 5.2.2 Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points based systems Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Articles 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. 11 Findings

This establishment was fully approved by the CA on 11 September 2015 as fulfilling all the structural and operational requirements. However, on 14 March 2016, the CA carried out a comprehensive inspection and a list of 15 shortcomings was noted. This list contained among others shortcomings related to Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP), labelling, traceability, cold chain, food contact materials, water quality and other prerequisites.

The audit team visited three small establishments and noted they did not meet all the relevant EU requirements. Two establishments in particular had significant shortcomings related to structure and lay-out (see chapter 5.2.1) Conclusion on registration / approval of FBOs
Nevertheless several shortcomings identified by the audit team, mostly related to approval and pasteurisation procedures/process had not previously been identified by the CAs.

In two of the four counties visited, the official reports did not reflect the non- compliances identified by the audit team in the four establishments visited. The officials in charge of the establishments concerned completed the control checklists without identifying any relevant shortcomings present in the establishments. Also the approval of three establishments visited in these counties had not been carried out correctly (establishments approved without fulfilling all the relevant requirements, see paragraphs 19 and 20)

The audit team noted in particular:- - In two milk processing establishments, none of the lay-out and structural shortcomings had been identified by the CA. Lay-out and structure did not prevent crossing of flows of operations and possible cross-contamination of raw/pasteurised and packed/unpacked products. In one of these establishments, the critical control point for pasteurisation was not properly identified and not properly monitored. In the other establishment, evidence could not be provided to the audit team that the time-temperature combination (67o-69o for 10 minutes) applied by the FBO had an equivalent effect to those indicated in EU legislation for achieving pasteurisation. The CA

In one establishment visited, the flow and space available for crates used for finished products was not satisfactory. Dirty crates were used for packing of products. The CA had identified the problem with storage, but had not drawn any conclusions or made written recommendations for the correction of the problem.
In one establishment, with limited space and with intermediate products exposed to cross-contamination, black mould was noted on wooden support structures in the maturation room.

In two establishments visited, the water sampling plan had, according to the local CA, been approved and is controlled by the Health Board. The FBO had implemented the water sampling in accordance with their plans. However, in both cases the monitoring for chemicals, under this sampling plan, did not cover all the parameters foreseen in Directive 98/83/EC, and in particular acrylamide, vinyl chloride, and bromate. The CA referred to an explanation provided by the Health Board, according to which analyses of these parameters was found to be unnecessary in dairy establishments and as such, these were not required.

In one case, based on the establishment's water consumption, organoleptic and microbiological parameters (check monitoring) should have been checked quarterly and all parameters in Article 5 of Directive 98/83/EC (audit monitoring) annually. Instead, the check monitoring had been carried out by the FBO once a year and the audit monitoring every ten years. The CA and the FBO were unable to explain the reason for this reduced frequency. Conclusion on general and specific hygiene requirements

label_heading: Conclusion on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points based system
paragraph_text: The official controls cover the HACCP systems applied by the FBOs. However their effectiveness is compromised as the CA had not identified some non-compliances in the design and implementation of the HACCP-based procedures. As a consequence FBOs who had not identified properly all relevant critical control points were not monitoring all risks associated with production and were not in a position to take appropriate corrective actions when necessary. 5.2.3 Microbiological criteria for foodstuffs Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 Finding

However, in five plans reviewed by the audit team significant risks and corresponding critical control points had not been identified by the FBO and this situation was not noted by the CA (see paragraph 63).

In several cases, the FBO did not follow the procedures as described in the HACCP programme. In particular, for pasteurisation procedures, where a certain amount of unpasteurised milk could go for products supposed to be made exclusively from pasteurised milk. This was not identified by the CA.

In one establishment records on the pasteurisation and the cleaning programme were kept both on paper and on computer. However, the times recorded did not reflect in all cases the action being carried out. Thus, for example, the time of pasteurisation as recorded on paper could be logged as cleaning time in the computer. Based on these records it was impossible to determine if the current activity at any given time was pasteurisation or cleaning. This brings confusion concerning the amount of milk really pasteurised. Conclusion on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points based system

paragraph_text: However there are concerns regarding its effectiveness as the CA was not able to detect some important shortcomings during the official controls, in particular concerning the inaccuracy of own-checks test results transmitted by the laboratory to FBOs, and does not guarantee that appropriate actions are taken by FBOs when non-compliances are detected during the controls. 5.2.7 Animal by-products Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. In relation to the handling of samples: a. In Le Havre and Marseille BIPs, officials used tamper-proof seals and the samples were transported under the responsibility of the competent authority. This was different in BIP Roissy-CDG, where the bags for the samples were not closed with a tamper-proof seal5. This was already noted during the previous audit DG(SANCO) 2010-8554. 4 In their comments to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that, after satisfactory documentary checks, the second consignment was released. 5 Immediately after the audit, the SIVEP informed the audit team of the corrective actions implemented to eliminate this shortcoming: the "Inspection Guide" has been am

Controls on food of non-animal origin, under the responsibility of DGCCRF, are performed in temporary storage facilities where hygiene conditions are only verified after the goods arrive. This arrangement does not ensure that goods are handled hygienically.

DGAL uses BIP facilities for the controls under their responsibility (products of animal origin and feed). For the controls on food of non-animal origin, identity and physical checks are implemented in interim storage facilities operating under Customs supervision. The importers propose on a case-by-case basis the storage facility, chosen amongst any operator (not necessarily food or feed operator) functioning in the area2. The competent authority underlined that this practice is not a use of the derogation provided under Article 19 of Regulation (EC) 669/2009. They also stated that they are satisfied with the guarantees provided by the current arrangements.

The system described in the previous paragraph does not ensure that the facilities used for identity and physical checks are hygienically adequate to store food. The registration as food operators of these interim storages is not a pre-requisite, so operators are not necessarily subject to the obligations laid down in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Verification of the hygiene conditions is done when the officials go on-the-spot to implement the import controls. This arrangement does not ensure that products are always handled hygienically (which is required by Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004). 5.1.3 Fees

In compliance with the EU legal requirements, staff are appropriately qualified to perform their job, and instructions are available. The communication between and within the competent authorities functions well, which contributes to the effectiveness of the controls.

In response to the recommendation of the audit DG(SANCO) 2010-8596 on the fees borne by the operators, DGCCRF introduced the Statutory Order of 16 August 2013, 2 In their response to the draft report, the competent authority noted that currently there is no specific registration system for bonded warehouses where food of non-animal origin can be presented for checks and stored while awaiting the result of the testing. If the premises have a food storage activity, they are registered in the food sector and subject as such to hygiene rules. There is currently no link between the enhanced import controls and the hygiene controls in these establishments. 5 setting the amounts of the fee for impo

Regarding emergency measures taken under Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, the French authorities amended the Customs Code in 2014 to provide a national legal basis for charging operators the costs of import controls. Nevertheless, the implementing decree has not been drafted yet, and the requirements of Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014, Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 885/2014 and Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 2015/175 are not complied with (all costs resulting from the official controls including sampling, analysis, storage and any measures taken following non- compliance, shall be borne by the feed or food business operators). Conclusions on the general requirements

The cooperation between Customs and the two sanitary authorities ensures that the relevant consignments are presented for sanitary controls. For products of animal origin, the lack of manifest checks at the BIP Roissy-CDG opens the possibility that mis- declared or non-declared consignments enter the Union without the prescribed controls. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE IMPORT CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 1(1) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. Article 8(1)(b) and 9(2) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009. Articles 3(1), 11(7), 16(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 4(3) of Directive 97/78/EC. Commission Regulation (EC) No 401/2006. Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014. Findings 5.3.1

At the BIP Roissy-CDG, staff from SIVEP explained that manifest checks have not been carried out since 2013. The competent authority explained that (a) the resources required for manifest checks are disproportionate to the number of undeclared consignments detected, (b) the non-declared consignment ­ if any ­ would have left the airport by the time staff has time to check the manifests, and (c) data in the manifests are often difficult to interpret. This position does not comply with the requirements laid down in Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, to gather all pertinent intelligence for the purpose of detecting consignments not presented for controls3.

paragraph_text: There is a system for providing information and instructions to BIPs and DPEs, which supports the implementation of the enhanced controls. paragraph_text: The required sampling frequency is not always respected in DPEs and BIPs. paragraph_text: Minor deficiencies were noted in the BIP facilities visited. The official controls of products of non-animal origin subject to enhanced controls are not always carried out under appropriate hygiene conditions. 5.2 MECHANISMS TO ENSURE THAT CONSIGNMENTS ARE PRESENTED FOR IMPORT CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) No 882/2004 Article 3(3) of Directive 97/78/EC Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 Article 7(2) of Regulation (EU) No 885/2014 Article 7(2) of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 Ar

At Peplos BIP/Kipi Evrou DPE: The BIP facilities for identity and physical checks of products for non-human consumption are also used to carry out checks on products of non-animal origin subject to enhanced controls, thus applying the possibility granted by the provisions of Article 15(5) of Regulation (EC) 882/2004. A very low number of consignments of products of animal origin for non-human consumption are introduced into EU via Greece (only six consignments in 2015 and one consignment in January ­ March of 2016). The appropriate measures for cleaning and disinfection after each inspection are in place. The measures put in place by the competent authorities rectify the deficiencies noted d

At the Thessaloniki port BIP the competent authority has taken corrective actions to rectify deficiencies in the facilities reported in 2015: the changing room and ceiling in the unloading room for products for non-human consumption have been put in place, and the walls have a hygienic slope finish. The audit team noted that the BIP staff do not follow the hygiene requirements to steer the flow of personnel (risk of cross- contamination) in the area for products for human consumption.

At Athens airport BIP: The changing area is located in the office. The location of the changing area does not allow the BIP staff to enter directly to the unloading area, contrary to the requirements of the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC. The audit team noted that the access to facilities for the veterinary checks of products for non-human consumption is only possible via the facilities for the veterinary checks on products for human consumption, which can lead to cross- contamination, and is contrary to the requirements of Article 4(4) of Decision 2001/812/EC.

label_heading: Conclusions on the training, supervision and audits
paragraph_text: There are eight DPEs in Denmark, six of which are local FCOs which are approved only for documentary control and they are not located at the specific points of entry in the Member State's territory which is in contradiction with the definition provided in Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009.

label_heading: Conclusions on the training, supervision and audits
paragraph_text: In the list there are two private food and feed business operator facilities approved as DPEs. They are located in the port territory and they accept to store consignments for identity and physical checks, including laboratory analyses from other FBOs. At the same time they are approved as DPIs as well. However, documentary checks for these consignments are carried out at local FCOs instead of DPEs.

Where a rejected consignment of products of non-animal origin is re-dispatched, the operator is not requested to submit any evidence that the consignment left Denmark for an approved destination. This does not ensure that the deadline established in EU legislation has been respected and opens up the possibility that the consignment may have been illegally placed on the EU market. 13

Regarding both products of animal origin and products of non-animal origin, if the result shows a non-compliance, the consignment is rejected and can be destroyed or re- dispatched. In the case of re-dispatch, the DVFA requires confirmation from the country of destination that they agree to receive non-compliant consignments as required by Article 21 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. A 60-day deadline is given to food business operators to destroy or re-dispatch non-compliant consignments. The audit team noted that where the consignment of products of non-animal origin is re-dispatched, the importer is not required to submit evidence to ensure that the 60-day limit is respected as foreseen in

Mechanisms are in place, supported by the system applied by the Customs authorities, to ensure that consignments requiring enhanced controls are presented for official controls. In one BIP visited such a mechanism is still under development and does not yet ensure that all consignments subject to enhanced controls will be identified. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE IMPORT CONTROLS 5.3.1 Documentary checks Legal requirements Article 4(3) of Directive 97/78/EC, Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009. Findings

At BIP (and DPE) Leipzig, 98% of consignments are handled by the same operator who provides information concerning consignments prior to arrival for both products of animal and non-animal origin. For this operator, import manifests are checked by the official staff on a daily basis. No checks of manifests by the official staff or alternative systems are in place at the BIP for consignments handled by the other operators, which is not in line with Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) 136/2004. The competent authority informed the audit team that corrective actions will be initiated to include these checks on the consignments handled by the other operators (2%).3 2 In their response to the draf

At BIP Munich, checks of manifests have not been carried out by the official staff since 2014 contrary to the requirements laid down in Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. The competent authority stated that a new IT tool is being developed to include such checks. It is planned that this system will be finalised and implemented by end 20164. Conclusions on the mechanisms to ensure that consignments are presented for import controls

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of identity and physical checks
paragraph_text: There is an established system that allows identity and physical checks of consignments subject to enhanced controls to be carried out as required and which ensures that 9 consignments are not released before satisfactory laboratory tests results are received. 5.3.3 Decision on the consignments and enforcement measures Legal requirements Articles 19, 21(3) and 54(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 5(1) of Directive 97/78/EC, Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014, Articles 8(2) and 13 of Regulation No 669/2009, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, Article 12 of Regulation (EU) No 885/2014. Findings

There is adequate cooperation with Customs authorities ensuring that consignments requiring enhanced controls are presented for official controls. For products of animal origin, staff do not have access to information about arriving consignments contained in the databases of Customs or port/airport operators (except for Brussels-Zaventem BIP) which would enable them to verify that consignments are always presented for controls. Thus, the BIP staff are reliant on Customs for identifying consignments. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE IMPORT CONTROLS 5.3.1 Documentary checks Legal requirements Article 16(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 4(3) of Directive 97/78/EC Article 1(1) of Commission Re

The FASFC explained that BIPs do not have access to and have not carried out manifest checks since 2013. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 6 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. The FASFC stated that the discussion on access to the relevant databases is ongoing. Meanwhile, the FASFC receives from Customs all data about consignments controlled by Customs during the previous month. This information is distributed to the BIPs. Antwerp BIP staff stated that this information is not used since it is time-consuming to review and does not allow staff to make proper searches for non-declared consignments.

label_heading: Conclusions on the general requirements regarding the control system
paragraph_text: The current facilities at the DPEs/DPIs visited are not appropriate to undertake the necessary checks and to handle food of non-animal origin hygienically, leading to a risk of contamination or spoilage.

In the three DPEs/DPIs for food of non-animal origin visited, the audit team noted non-compliances concerning the structure of the facilities that negatively impact on the hygienic handling and storage of the consignments, contrary to requirements of Article 4 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Article 8 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In the DPE/DPI Genova, the DGISAN informed the audit team that they have accepted plans for new DPE/DPI facilities. The current facilities are of a non- permanent nature (a marquee located in a customs warehouse) and are not appropriate to undertake the necessary checks and to handle the food hygienically. It is foreseen that the new facilities will be in place by March 2017.

In the DPE/DPI Ravenna, the competent authorities gave a very short deadline to the operators of the DPE/DPI to rectify the non-compliances identified during official controls in order to ensure that the facilities have the basic structures for the hygienic handling and storage of the consignments. At the time of the audit, the shortcomings had only been partly addressed, and based on the letter of the 6 operator to the competent authorities, the audit team considered that the guarantees provided by the operator that a permanent solution would be in place in spring 2017, were not sufficient. Conclusions on the general requirements regarding the control system

There is an adequate mechanism (including good cooperation with Customs) to ensure that consignments requiring enhanced controls are presented for official controls. However, the competent authorities do not systematically implement measures to ensure that food and feed business operators or their representatives provide prior notification before physical arrival of the consignments in the BIPs and DPEs, which potentially can have an impact on the planning and organisation of the official controls. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE IMPORT CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 1(1) of, and Annex I to Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 Articles 16(1) and 24(3) to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article

The person responsible for the load submits to the BIP staff part 1 of the CVED for food and feed of animal origin using TRACES as well as in hard copy to notify the consignments prior to their physical arrival. However, the audit team identified that a significant number of consignments subject to enhanced controls are not notified prior to the physical arrival in the BIPs visited. Out of 36 files verified, 9 were not notified before physical arrival (25%), which is not in compliance with the requirements of Article 3(3) of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 2(1) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. The audit team noted that for the files assessed, official controls were performed as requ

The competent authority at the DPEs/DPIs visited received prior notification of the physical arrival of food of non-animal origin in the form of part I of the CED from the food business operators or their representatives through the database NSIS as well as in hard copy. However, the audit team identified that a significant number of consignments subject to enhanced controls are not notified at all prior to the physical arrival in the DPEs/DPIs visited. Out of 24 files verified, 18 are not notified before physical arrival (66%), which is not in compliance with the 8 requirements of Article 17(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 6 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Article 7 of

In BIP Genova, the competent authorities stated that they took some measures to discourage the late prenotifications of the consignments but with partial success. Conclusion on the mechanisms to ensure that consignments are presented for import controls

paragraph_text: The facility visited (BIP Milano Malpensa ­ facilities of the inspection centre "ALHA Airport MXP SpA", currently approved for categories "U" and "E") fulfil the requirements laid down in the legislation for registered equidae ("E"), enabling the implementation of effective controls, but not for ungulates ("U"). 5.5 FOLLOW-UP OF PREVIOUS RECOMMENDATIONS

Following the information provided by the competent authority the recommendation No 2 of the audit report DG(SANCO) 2012-6501 is partially addressed in relation of the BIP facilities at Ancona port and Milano Malpensa airport. label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The competent authority does not carry out manifests checks. Those controls are still essential because of the limitations of the INTERTRACE in using the data provided by Customs, and consignments intended for import or for transhipment can move undetected when they should undergo controls. 5.3 VERIFICATION ACTIVITIES Legal Requirements Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Finding 10 of report 2014-7003 described how checks on manifests had stopped in March 2014 according to the competent authority due to a lack of human resources. The 4 situation remains the same and this activity is not systematically performed contrary to the requirements of Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Articles 5 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. The audit team noted that, however, manifests checks would still be necessary because the INTERTRACE application works with complete Customs nomenclature (CN) codes to identify consignments subject to checks, and Customs do not require a CN-code in their pre-notifications. In cases where CN- code information is absent or

The lack of corrective actions following the internal audits, combined with a lack of documented procedures to perform specific supervision activities does not allow the competent authority to identify gaps in the system for controls and opportunities for improvement, in particular as regards transhipments by using the features of INTERTRACE. 5.4 FOLLOW-UP OF PREVIOUS RECOMMENDATIONS 5.4.1 Follow-up of recommendations from report DG(SANTE)/2014-7003 No Recommendation Assessment 1 To ensure that the veterinary checks in the BIP Addressed. See finding 4. are implemented under the responsibility of the official veterinarian as required by Article 4(1) of Directive 97/78/EC and that, after compl

An internal audit performed at the Maltese BIPs in September 2015 recommended putting in place verification activities on the official controls at BIPs. The competent authority started conducting supervisions after this internal audit with the aim of verifying the effectiveness of the official controls in line with Article 8(3)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The supervisions included the assessment of documentary checks, correctness of CVEDs and correct use of TRACES. The audit team noted that these activities were not based on a written procedure and were discontinued. The competent authority stated this was due to the increased workload put on the official inspectors at the BIPs.

The deficiencies identified during this audit (e.g. limitations of INTERTRACE, poor enforcement measures, incomplete pre-notifications) were not identified by the verification activities. The lack of effective verification procedures in Malta has been highlighted in several reports of the Directorate General for Health and Food Safety. 10 Conclusions on the verification activities

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Import controls are generally implemented in line with the legal requirements. For consignments in transhipment, since May 2015 the competent authority has used the data from Customs, the agents responsible for the consignments and the port operator to identify and control consignments where required. Some deficiencies still exist i.e. the competent authority: does not use the available data if consignments are pre-notified with two digit CN-codes or no CN code, or when the format of the documents from Customs is not compatible with INTERTRACE. does not enforce the requirement for operators to provide information on the next BIP of destination when transhipments are destined to be imported i

The pre-notification is done via INTERTRACE (table 1). The shipping agents provide most of the data required in part I of the CVEDs, but the next BIP of destination is not required by the competent authority and is not provided by the shipping agents, contrary to the requirement of Article 1 of Decision No 2011/215/EC. This repeated non- compliance was already identified in report 2014-7003 (findings 13 and 14) and still remains to be addressed as the competent authority has not foreseen actions to enforce this requirement. Finding 19 of report 2014-7003 described that the monitoring plan did not include microbiological hazards and that the risk assessment was not documented. The audit team noted that risk-based planning for microbiological testing is still not documented and the decision on hazards/commodities to be tested or to be excluded from testing is not justified.

The documented procedures and instructions in place could ensure adequate implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, the delays in the implementation of the sampling plan, the exclusion of some months of the year and, notably, shortcomings in the allocation of samples to slaughterhouses calls into question the representativeness of sampling.

The requirement set out in point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU that caecal samples collected at slaughterhouses shall be distributed evenly over each month of the year was not adhered to in 2014 or 2015 and will most likely not be achieved for 2016 for the following reasons: 5 The SVFA annual instructions (see point 10) were not introduced timely enough. Notably the 2015 instruction was introduced in June and therefore sampling did not cover the previous months of the year. The officials interviewed stated that sample delivery to the laboratory during the summer months and December was problematic. As a consequence, in the two slaughterhouses visited December was not i

SFVA made the initial allocation on the basis of the total annual throughput of the slaughterhouse and not to the throughput of animals of domestic origin as required by point 2.3.1 of part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU (for example, in the pig slaughterhouse visited 30-35% of pigs slaughtered originated from other Member States). This inadequate allocation design, and the lack of oversight of sampling by SVFA, prevented achieving the samples outlined in the sampling plan and resulted in only 131 of the 150 required pig caecal samples taken in 2015.

For 2014, not all of the Salmonella isolates available were tested for antimicrobial susceptibility even though the minimum number required for each combination of bacterial species and type of sample had not been achieved.

In 2015, the competent authority did not gather (for the purpose of antimicrobial susceptibility testing) isolates from samples taken by food business operators in the context of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, even though the minimum 85 Salmonella isolates from pig carcasses had not been achieved. 5.2.3 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC; Article 4 and Annex Part A.5 of Decision 2013/652/EU; Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

In 2014, contrary to point 2.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, only 100 Salmonella isolates (including the 12 non-mandatory isolates obtained from poultry meat) were subject to AST and reported to EFSA; this was despite the fact that additional isolates were available. For laying hens only 4 isolates were tested and reported despite another 2 isolates being available for testing. In the case of broilers at farm and slaughter levels, only 19 and 58 isolates, respectively, were subject to AST and reported, whereas another 44 isolates obtained at farm level and enough isolates to complete the minimum 85 at slaughterhouse level were available. SVFA stated that only 100 Salmonella

In relation to the above point, the audit team noted that Salmonella isolates originating from samples collected by food business operators in the context of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 were available in the corresponding private laboratories. Despite the minimum required number of isolates not being achieved, the competent authority did not make use of the possibility of using these isolates for AST, as set out by Article 3 of Decision 2013/652/EU (see point 27). According to the competent authority this was because there are no national provisions requiring these private laboratories to submit the isolates for this purpose (see section on Closing Meeting). 5.2.2.2 Representativeness of sa

Regarding the selection of Salmonella isolates for AST, in 2014 not all isolates available from different epidemiological units were tested (see point 16). The selection of isolates for AST made by the Veterinary and Food Institute (VFI) in Bratislava, which is the national reference laboratory (NRL) for Salmonella, was aimed at covering different serotypes, ensuring an even distribution throughout the year and representativeness in the geographical origin.

Due to the low prevalence of Salmonella in Slovakia, the minimum 85 isolates were not available for each population of laying hens, broilers and fattening turkeys. Nevertheless not all eligible isolates available from different epidemiological units were subjected to AST (see point 16). Isolates from carcase samples collected at slaughter

For the year 2015, the competent authority gathered 13 Salmonella pig carcase isolates. The minimum 85 isolates were not achieved due to the low Salmonella prevalence in pig carcasses. Nevertheless, in the pig slaughterhouse visited the audit team noted that despite 1 positive result from a food business operator being communicated to the competent authority at local level, the collection of this isolate from the private laboratory did not take place. The competent authority confirmed that similar situations occur in other slaughterhouses (see point 17).

An appropriate laboratory network for official monitoring of AMR is in place. Laboratories are properly designated and operate in accordance with the EU requirements. The NRL for AMR has been proactive in identifying and correcting shortcomings affecting the reliability of results. Nevertheless, further weaknesses identified during this audit could negatively affect the reliability of AMR results. These concern a number of inadequate documented procedures and, notably, weaknesses in the coordination role of the NRL for AMR. 5.3 ASSESSMENT AND REPORTING OF AMR Legal requirements Article 9 and Annex IV to Directive 2003/99/EC and Article 5 and the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. Findings

During the annual meetings of Slovakian microbiological NRLs, technical issues related to the official laboratory activities are presented and discussed. Nevertheless, SVFA during the last control visit to the NRL for Salmonella in January 2016 identified that the NRL for AMR did not fulfil its obligations in relation to coordination of activities in the AST area. In particular the NRL for AMR did not disseminate information supplied by the EURL and did not coordinate, for the AST area, the activities of the NRL for Salmonella. Some corrective actions had been implemented already with a successful inter-laboratory proficiency test on Salmonella AST organised by the NRL for AMR at the NRL for

The audit team noted that there was still room for improvement in the cooperation between these two laboratories and in the coordination role of the NRL for AMR. In particular, there was still a lack of dissemination of information provided by the EURL on AST. Similarly, there was no feedback from the NRL for Salmonella to the NRL for AMR on the results of participation in the relevant proficiency tests.

Laboratory procedures were available on the spot and generally followed the relevant international standards. However, the following was noted by the audit team: NRL for AMR The new procedures introduced for sample acceptance after the problems identified in 2014 were not documented and samples rejected were not adequately recorded. 11 The laboratory procedures for Campylobacter MIC determination were not based on the M45 standard from the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) as required by point 3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. In particular, the time/temperature defined for incubation was not in line with the relevant standard and included deviations by up to

Both laboratories have the necessary equipment to freeze isolates at temperatures below -80°C and to store them for at least 5 years. Nevertheless, the audit team noted that in the NRL for AMR the procedures in place required isolates to be stored at -70ºC. Back- up equipment and an emergency plan in case of equipment malfunction are available. Conclusions on official laboratories

The competent authorities responsible for the monitoring of AMR are clearly designated, adequately organised and have the necessary powers for the implementation of the harmonised monitoring of AMR. Nevertheless, there are gaps in the allocation of tasks and in the information available to the different authorities involved in the gathering, selection and testing of Salmonella isolates. These gaps had a negative impact on achieving the Decision 2013/652/EU targets for these bacteria. 5.2 ORGANISATION OF THE OFFICIAL MONITORING SYSTEM 5.2.1 NATIONAL MEASURES AND SAMPLING DESIGN 5.2.1.1 National measures

label_heading: Conclusions on national measures and sampling design
paragraph_text: Nevertheless, and due to deficiencies in the organisation, including the information flow of the Salmonella isolates gathering by the competent authority, the minimum numbers required were not achieved and reported accurately.

Nevertheless, the methods used to allocate responsibilities to the different competent authorities and laboratories involved, and the information available to the laboratories and reporting officers, did not allow the gathering and identification of the relevant Salmonella isolates for the populations required by point 1(a) of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. As a consequence, the available Salmonella isolates were not tested and/or reported (see points 22 and 25) in order to achieve the minimum number required. 1 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=NL 3 Conclusions on the competent authority

In 2014, the competent authority did not report any Salmonella isolates obtained at farm level for the three categories requested by Decision 2013/652/EU (broilers, laying hens and turkeys), despite their availability. The competent authority stated that some of the reported isolates may have originated from samples taken in the context of the SNCP but the flow of information does not allow distinguishing them from isolates from other origins.

Data on the isolates provided by the RIVM do not include information regarding the sampling programme/context, which does not allow the NRL for AMR to ensure that an adequate selection of isolates is subject to AST. As a consequence, all the reported Salmonella isolates were identified as obtained from caeca at slaughterhouses while their origin was unknown.

The RIVM is responsible for the selection of isolates that are submitted to the NRL for AMR for AST. However, the RIVM only gathers a small amount of isolates obtained under the SNCP. This is not in accordance with the technical requirements of point 2.3.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU as, if available, Salmonella isolates obtained in the framework of the national control programmes shall be collected to achieve the minimum number required.

The Agriculture and Nature division of the NVWA oversights the SNCP. The official samples taken within the SNCP are tested in the Animal Health laboratory. The isolates obtained have not been subject to AST so far, since the NVWA staff with responsibilities over the SNCP were not aware, before this audit, of the provisions of Decision 2013/652/EU that requires subjecting these isolates to AST. 2 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=3245 6

The Salmonella isolates obtained from the official samples taken in the context of testing and verification of compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 were gathered and subject to AST but the results were not reported to EFSA, as required by points 1 (a) and 2.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. The NVWA stated that the AST results for these Salmonella isolates were excluded from reporting to EFSA because the isolate information available in the database to the reporting officers was insufficient to allow, for example, the exclusion of repeated epidemiological units.

In the three slaughterhouses visited the audit team noted that the food business operator's private laboratories regularly obtained Salmonella isolates. Contrary to point 2.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, these isolates were not gathered by the competent authority despite the fact that the official isolates available were not sufficient to achieve the minimum required (see point 11). paragraph_text: Weaknesses in the procedures in place ensuring a proportional sample allocation to slaughterhouses based on the throughput of domestically produced animals, sample randomisation design and avoidance of sampling repeated epidemiological units undermine the representativeness of the samples taken. 5.2.2 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC; Article 4 and Annex Part A.5 of Decision 2013/652/EU. Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Nevertheless, and contrary to point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU, the allocation was not made on the basis of the annual throughput of domestically produced meat. For example, in the poultry slaughterhouse visited the audit team was informed that over 60% of the broilers slaughtered originated from other Member States.

In accordance with the procedures in place, samples were generally taken on the same day of the week. This is contrary to point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU that requires that the AMR monitoring programme should be randomised. The audit team noted that there was sufficient sample transport services available to allow a better sample randomisation.

label_heading: Conclusions on assessment and reporting of AMR
paragraph_text: The annual report includes all the mandatory information for each individual isolate reported under harmonised monitoring, and a significant amount of information reported on a voluntary basis which exceeds the current mandatory monitoring under EU legislation. There are though some weaknesses in the completeness and quality of information provided for some isolates and the lack of overall description of the implementation of AMR monitoring that have an influence on the harmonised reporting of AMR data. 13 6 GOOD PRACTICES AND DEVELOPING AREAS Findings

The veterinary and imports division of the NVWA is responsible for reporting AMR data under Decision 2013/652/EU to EFSA. The verification of the reported data, prior to their uploading, is minimal. As a consequence, the omission of some compulsory reporting areas, such as Salmonella isolates at farm level and in the context of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, was not noticed.
In the case of the Salmonella isolates reported in 2014 and 2015 the sampling stage and the matrix was reported incorrectly.

Also incorrect isolation dates were reported for the ESBL-producing E. coli isolates tested in 2015 by the NRL for AMR where different isolation dates were reported for the first and second panel testing of the same isolate.
The ESBL-producing E. coli identified in 2015 from bovine and pig meat retail samples were not reported. The competent authority stated that this was due to a mistake.
The competent authority could not exclude that isolates from repeated epidemiological units were reported, which is requested by point 2.3 Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.
The collection form used for reporting the `generic description of the implementation of the AMR monitoring' was not submitted to EFSA. Conclusions on assessment and reporting of AMR

label_heading: Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results
paragraph_text: Variability in the comprehensiveness of registration of both producers and pack houses exists between the various RCAs visited/consulted. Registration is particularly incomplete in two ACs where considerable surface areas of ware potatoes are grown but the growers are not registered or known to the relevant RCAs. This undermines fundamentally the overall effectiveness and reliability of surveillance efforts and ultimately any control measures in place.

All RCAs consulted use the CAP register as a basis for their respective official records of professional potato producers. Typically this is further supplemented with industry information on an on-going basis. However, the team noted that in certain ACs registration is incomplete.

The Valencian RCA stated that registration of pack houses only started there in 2015. So far 19 premises have been registered, but the total number remains unknown. There is no single register. This also applies in the case of growers. In Andalucía, the previous audit reported 91 ware potato wholesalers/packing stations and 195 seed potato wholesalers. The Andalucía RCA reported there are now 280 registered ware potato wholesalers. However, despite the progress observed regarding increased registration of ware potato wholesalers in Andalucía, recent interceptions of potato consignments from this autonomous community in two Member States and follow up investigation during this audit (see also

All RCAs acknowledged difficulties in dealing with the generic issue of small private growers. As there are no legal requirements, small non-professional growers are not registered, and normally produce for private consumption within the immediate locality of production. RCA inspections are largely conducted at random or guided by local knowledge. 5.2.2 Surveillance strategy

label_heading: Conclusions on control measures for Epitrix sp.
paragraph_text: In Andalucía, the recognition of E. papa as the causal organism has led to the emergence of a parallel risk management approach. Management of existing DAs established under Decision 2012/270/EU are only partially compliant with the Decision, whilst new outbreak sites, notified under Article 16.2 were, at the time of the audit, neither demarcated, nor, in the absence of the anticipated regional 17 Resolution, subject to any further measures. Orders prohibiting harvest and movement of two potato fields from the eight new outbreak sites in the province of Seville had been violated.

label_heading: Conclusions on control measures for Epitrix sp.
paragraph_text: Merging of geographically close DAs, in line with Annex II section 1 (2) of Decision 2012/270/EU, has not taken place (see section 5.4) with risk(s) as regards the further spread remaining as movement of potatoes from the area between them is not restricted.

At the time of the audit, the regional resolution necessary to deal with this new situation was still in draft format. Consequently, a precautionary approach, based on prohibition orders on the harvest and movement of infested potato crops, was adopted. However, this approach did not include demarcation, or the associated risk management obligations, as required by Decision 2012/270/EU.

The four closely located DAs, of the eight DAs originally established under Decision 2012/270/EU had not been merged within the scope of Annex II section 1 point (2). The RCA of Andalucía does not consider that the distance of approximately 2 km from one another is sufficiently close to merit such action. These four DAs have been merged under a parallel regional "vigilance zone" concept, which is identical to the requirements of a DA as outlined in Annex II Section1, with the exception that potatoes can be moved without washing or brushing. label_heading: Conclusions on the development of the programme of audits
paragraph_text: The process for the audit programme development is not well-documented or transparent and it does not follow risk-based prioritisation, which means that it does not result in programmes that could achieve an appropriate risk-based coverage of relevant official control activities. The development of the audit programme is further constrained by the lack of stable and sufficient resources without which the continuity in the provision of audit services cannot be ensured. 5.2.5 Implementation of the audit process 5.2.5.1 Legal requirements Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that "Audit" "means a systematic and independent examination to determine whether activities and related re

The audit activities have consisted of one pilot project per year since 2014 and each project covers a specific area of the official controls. Plant health, the residue control programme for food of animal origin, and the Salmonella control programme are the three projects that have been carried out so far. In 2017, an audit project on the control of fertilisers will be carried out. The competent authority has prepared a multi-annual audit programme for the period 2015-2018 that includes areas based on the choices made by the Directors of Evira in the context of the pilot phase of the audit function. The purpose was to have audits in sectors that could be used for modelling and further devel

The audit programme is planned based on the resources available (capability of two audit projects per year) and it is considered that in five years there will be five projects on food safety and two or three projects on plant health and production and an equal number on animal health and welfare.

The audit system has not defined the audit universe and as regards the audit programme development, the process is not well-documented and transparent, and it does not include risk-based prioritisation.

The audit team noted that the extended scope and time-consuming nature of the audit programme and its execution combined with the limitations in the availability of human resources, makes it unfeasible to cover all relevant areas of official controls in a five- year period. paragraph_text: The implementation of documentary checks is generally carried out correctly in BIPs and DPEs and performed using all available information, with some exceptions. The non-compliances identified by the audit team in relation to documentary checks of racing pigeons and food of non-animal origin weaken the system of import controls and may endanger animal and public health.

When the DPEs and BIPs identify non-compliances during the documentary check, they take appropriate action. However, in some notable cases, consignments were accepted without the required health guarantees, which could lead to the import of live animals, food and feed which does not comply with the EU health requirements, potentially causing a risk to public and animal health. 5.4 THE USE OF TRADE CONTROL AND EXPERT SYSTEM Legal requirements Article 3(2) of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC Findings

In addition, there is no evidence that the development of the audit programme has considered all relevant areas, and it is not evident how this results in risk based prioritisation and effective coverage of all areas in a reasonable timeframe.

label_heading: Conclusions on the development of the programme of audits
paragraph_text: The approach to risk-based planning is inadequately documented and defined. There is no recorded risk analysis methodology to describe the areas in sufficient detail, and the relevant process is not documented or transparent. Therefore, the TAS could not demonstrate the risk basis for the frequency of auditing some areas nor justify the exclusion of other areas.

The audit procedure developed by the TAS (Code PS-01-DATC) sets out how to develop the multi-annual / annual audit programme. The main criteria taken into account for its development are as follows: - the areas of NSVFSA competence (the competent authority has defined 33 areas of official controls but this list does not appear in the audit-related procedures) 12 - the results of internal and external audits conducted in previous years - changes in legislation - changes in the organisation of structures involved in the control systems - the national and international epidemiological situation in the area of animal health - the evolution of various animal diseases - NSVFSA policies on the erad

Whilst the audit universe has been defined (albeit not well-documented), the risk universe has not. Out of the 33 areas identified in the audit universe, 16 of these are related to specific animal health issues, two are related to animal welfare issues, and the remaining 15 cover very broad categories such as border inspection posts, food hygiene under Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, poultry meat and derivatives thereof, etc. When the official control areas have not been subject to a detailed breakdown, as is the case with all the areas identified in the audit universe excepting animal health, it is difficult to properly define the risks, as different aspects (e.g. product, process, establishme

The TAS had planned to audit some areas more than once in the five year audit programme cycle but could not demonstrate why some areas were prioritised over others, except for the ad-hoc audits ordered by the President of the NSVFSA. The concept of 'adequate coverage of all relevant areas of activity' of point 5.1 of Decision 2006/677/EC was taken to mean 'audit' of all relevant areas, rather than risk-based consideration of all relevant areas. 14

The NAO concluded in their 2014 review of arrangements for food controls that NAO audits did not satisfy the requirement for independent scrutiny. The NFA has subsequently worked together with colleagues in the other countries of the Nordic Council (Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway and Iceland) on a project "The Nordic cooperation on independent scrutiny". This project has not yet been carried out in Sweden. The NFA hopes that the project may give rise to a permanent arrangement for independent scrutiny.

The SBA Internal Audit Unit carries out an annual evaluation with an external evaluation every fifth year, following the International Professional Practices Framework (IPPF). This also includes areas outside Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 for which this Unit is responsible. The unit is scrutinised on the basis of international auditing practices, national rules for agencies to do internal audits and its obligations under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The external audit, which takes several weeks, includes verification of a self-evaluation report through review of certain audits of official controls, including working documents and interviews with auditees (heads of unit).

The SBA's animal control has an arrangement for self-evaluation by reviewing audits of official controls, including the working documents. However, the unit has no arrangement for independent scrutiny. Conclusions

paragraph_text: The veterinary checks at the BIP are mostly carried out correctly and the decisions taken on the consignments are generally appropriate to satisfy the import control requirements. In some cases of live animals, BIP staff accepted consignments with inappropriate veterinary certificates and documentation related to the animal welfare of live animals which might lead to non-compliant consignments of live animals being accepted or animal welfare requirements not being respected.

Detailed documented procedures are in place to carry out the official controls and take samples correctly for live animals, products of animal origin and non-animal origin. The audit team noted one exception regarding the instruction for the controls of live animals, which does not require a check of the route plan for animals going on to travel long distances to ensure that proper resting times have been scheduled in order to respect animal welfare requirements during transportation (see findings 14 and 32). Conclusion on the organisation of the competent authorities and of official controls

The audit team noted several shortcomings in relation to the documentary checks of live animals: Several consignments of live animals were accepted when certificates did not comply with the detailed rules for documentary checks for live animals laid down in Annex I to Commission Decision 97/794/EC. In particular, several non- conformities were noted where the veterinary certificates were accepted without evidence that the certificate consisted of a single sheet or two or more pages that were part of a single and indivisible sheet of paper containing a sequence of numbered pages. paragraph_text: There is a system in place to carry out controls of food of non-animal origin following the EU requirements at the DPE.
