label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of documentary checks
paragraph_text: In general, the documentary checks are performed correctly in order to ensure compliance with the requirements of the legislation. However, as none of the BIPs visited have access to the ship and aircraft manifests and other sources of information, this impairs the ability of the competent authority to correctly identify consignments which have not been presented and should be subject to official controls.

The BIPs visited had no access to the ship, boat and aircraft manifests or other sources of information required to ensure that all consignments of live animals are presented for veterinary control. This is not in line with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004 (see finding 23).

The BIPs visited had no access to the ship, boat and aircraft manifests or other sources of information required to ensure that all relevant consignments are presented for veterinary control. This is not in line with Article 6 of Commission Regulation (EC) 136/2004 (see finding 17). For ports, access to manifests was terminated after the introduction of the new "Customs One-Stop Shop" system.

label_heading: Conclusions on the control of consignments at the BIP
paragraph_text: Although the BIP staff interviewed demonstrated good knowledge of Union legislative requirements for imports and transhipment of goods (with the exception of some aspects pertaining to non-harmonised species), other VRD staff have occasion to work in the BIPs after normal working hours and, for them, the absence of adequate instructions for conduct of checks and taking decisions on consignments militates against consistency in approach.

label_heading: Conclusion on the implementation of documentary checks
paragraph_text: There are adequate mechanisms in place to ensure that consignments are presented for official controls and with few exceptions (in DPEs), the implementation of documentary checks was carried out correctly in the BIPs and DPEs visited, being performed using all available information.

On the whole, actions taken when non-compliant goods are detected during documentary check, are appropriate and, with few exceptions, are in line with Union rules. 5.4 THE USE OF TRADE CONTROL AND EXPERT SYSTEM Legal requirements Article 3(2) of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC 9 Findings

The audit team checked a total of 33 files related to import of products of non-animal origin and noted that the documentary checks had been performed correctly using all available information with the following four exceptions: 1 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that during the checks, it informed the operators which, under current EU legislation, were supposed to pre-notify consignments at the required time. The operators informed the competent authority that in some cases they were not able to prepare the common entry documents (CED) in advance because the requisite documents whose numbers they needed to enter in box I.10 of the CED were not available. I

However, in some cases of imported food of non-animal origin the competent authority did not take the appropriate actions, which is contrary to the requirements of Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (see finding 33).

label_heading: Conclusion on the implementation of documentary checks
paragraph_text: The lack of sampling of products of non-animal origin from Japan as required by EU legislation could lead to the import of products which do not comply with the EU health requirements. 2 After the audit and in advance of the production of the draft report of the audit, the competent authority provided additional information on 28 November 2017 indicating that it had already taken some measures to rectify the deficiencies described in the fourth bullet point of finding 33 and finding 34. 8 5.3 ACTION TAKEN IN CASE OF NON-COMPLIANCES RELATED TO DOCUMENTARY CHECKS Legal requirements Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

The audit team noted that none of the consignments imported from Japan in last three years in the visited DPEs and falling under provisions of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2016/6 had been sampled as required by the Article 10(1)(b) of said Regulation2. Conclusion on the implementation of documentary checks

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of documentary checks
paragraph_text: Documentary checks for products of non-animal origin are not implemented in line with EU requirements; therefore such checks cannot ascertain if, where relevant, consignments are accompanied with authentic or appropriate health certificates, results of analyses performed and other relevant documents. 8 5.3 ACTION TAKEN IN CASE OF NON-COMPLIANCES RELATED TO DOCUMENTARY CHECKS Legal requirements Articles 8(1), 19, 20, 21 and 54(2)(g) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Annex III to Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 Findings

No documentary checks are carried out for the products covered by Commission Regulation (EC) No 669/2009. The importers submit data in the Client-VGC and the computerised system checks automatically that all necessary boxes have been filled in. After this, consignments are selected randomly for identity and physical checks or released. The data in the Client-VGC is not verified against any certificates (e.g. phytosanitary) or commercial documents accompanying the consignment, which is not in line with Article 8(1)(a) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 and the definition of documentary checks in Article 2(17) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

For consignments covered under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 885/2014, the persons responsible for the load do not have to provide Customs with the original health certificate. It is sufficient to email a scanned copy of the certificate to Customs. This does not make it possible to ascertain the authenticity of the health certificates contrary to the requirements of Article 9(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 8(1) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 885/2014.

label_heading: Conclusions on National Legislation and Provisions
paragraph_text: Regional provisions are in place to implement legally binding Union acts. However, some of these provisions and / or their implementation are not in line with requirements of the EU organic regulations. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF CONTROLS 5.2.1 Competent authorities and Control Bodies Legal Requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council Article 27(1), (4) and (14) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Article 92 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

The system in place generally ensures that operators are registered and that key information about their organic activity is made publicly accessible by CAs. However, there is no system in place to verify whether exempted retailers fulfil conditions for 6 exemption. Moreover, documentary evidences issued by CB do not necessarily follow the model provided for in the EU regulation. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Articles 3 and 41 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 27(3) and 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Articles 65(4) and 92c(2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: CBs' control plans are based on an assessment of the risk which is generally adequate and efforts are made to increase the effectiveness of controls by improving the planning of visits to processors. CBs conduct a high number of controls which potentially compensate the risk related to the fact that not all CBs directly consider production quantities in their risk evaluation of operators. Some key information is not yet reported in the framework of the MANCP. 5.2.4 Controls of operators Legal Requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Title II and IV of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Article 65 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 8

Controls at operators were overall effective although some shortcomings were observed with regard to the control of labelling of organic products, the calculation of input/output and the records of the verification of the organic status of products when received by operators. label_heading: Conclusions on Exceptional Production Rules and Other Derogations
paragraph_text: Some of the regional provisions for exceptional production rules and other derogations, as well as their implementation, are not in line with EU rules. 5.2.8 Imports of Products from Organic Production Legal Requirements Articles 32 and 33 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Chapter 3 of Title III and Annexes II, III, V and VI of Commission Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008 Findings

Some requirements in the regional legislations and / or their implementation are not in line with EU rules. This mainly relates to exceptional production rules (see chapter 5.2.7), conditions for the grazing of cattle (paragraph 40) as well as the exemption and control of retailers (see paragraph 27 and 30). Conclusions on National Legislation and Provisions

All three Regions made use of Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and exempted retailers selling pre-packed products to the final consumer. According to Article 4.2 and 4.3 of the Decree of Wallonia and Article 4.2 and 4.3 of the Decree of Bruxelles-Capital the exemption from official controls is limited to retailers with an annual turnover of less than 5,000 Euros (of sales of organic products) in these two Regions provided conditions laid down in Article 28(2) of the above mentioned regulation are fulfilled.However, CAs confirmed that no controls are undertaken to verify whether exempted retailers fulfil conditions for exemption from official controls provided for in Article 28(2)

All operators certified by the CBs visited receive at least one annual control. However, Article 17 of the Decree of the Flemish Government referred to in paragraph 2 provides for partial annual checks on retailers provided that controls cover all aspects during a period of three years. This is not in line with Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 which requires that operators, with the exception of wholesalers and operators selling to the final consumer or user as described in Article 28(2) of the same regulation, must be subject to a verification of compliance once a year.

At a dairy farm, the audit team noted that the CB accepts that operators may keep animals permanently indoors up to an age of six months, even during the grazing period. The responsible CA confirmed that the CB follows relevant instructions adopted by the advisory committee referred to in paragraph 22. This is not in line with Article 14(2)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 14(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which stipulates that herbivores shall have access to pastures for grazing whenever conditions allow. Conclusions on Controls at Operators

As regards dehorning of animals, derogations granted by CAs to individual operators are valid for one year and for an estimated number of animals. In the case of CB1 applications by farmers are accepted before animals are born. This is not in line with 11 Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which does not provide for routine dehorning, but requires a case-by-case assessment before derogation can be granted. The CB assesses the case and forwards a proposal for decision to the CA. However, no documents are provided to the CA to support the CB proposal.

CB1 stated that dehorning has to be done within seven days of birth of the animal. In the case of CB2, the audit team noted that derogations were granted for the dehorning of animals of up to 6 months of age and more. During inspections observed, it was not verified whether animals when dehorned were of appropriate age and subject to application of appropriate anaesthesia/analgesia as required by Article 18(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

During witness audits, it was noted that a conversion period of three months was granted to an operator who produces vegetables in glasshouses. The CB stated that it followed relevant instructions provided by the CA (Flanders) on its website. This was confirmed by the relevant CA. The CA further stated that pesticides which were not authorised for organic production were previously used on production in hydroculture and that the soil, at that time, was covered with plastic film which prevented contamination. This was confirmed by a soil sample (no residues) before the three months conversion period was granted to the operator. This is not in line with Article 36(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 8

Regional legislations (see paragraph 2) allow for the tethering of animals in holdings having less than 50 animals. However, no evidence was provided to the audit team demonstrating that all other specific conditions laid down in Article 39 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 are verified by CAs before the derogation is granted. Conclusions on Exceptional Production Rules and Other Derogations

paragraph_text: The control system for organic production is only partially in place. Although competencies and related obligations are well defined at regional level, no CA is responsible for import controls of organic goods (see also chapter 5.2.8). 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal 4 Legal Requirements Articles 5(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Articles 27(5) to (9) and 27(14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Articles 92c and 92e of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on Imports of Products from Organic Productions
paragraph_text: Import controls may take place on an ad-hoc basis in Belgium. However there is no CA responsible for import controls and it is currently not ensured that relevant control requirements are implemented. 5.2.9 Measures in cases of irregularities and infringements Legal Requirements Articles 54, 55(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 27(5)(d) and 30 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Articles 91, 92, 92(a) and (d) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

Customs is responsible for general import controls. There is however no CA responsible for import controls of organic goods and the implementation of relevant EU requirements. This is not in line with Article 27(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 which requires EU MSs to designate one or more competent authorities responsible for controls in respect of the obligations established in the EU organic regulations (see also chapter 5.2.8)

The regional CAs stated that a protocol is being developed between the Regions and Customs for the implementation of the electronic certification via the Trade Control and Expert System New Technology (TRACES NT) applicable as of October 2017. However, neither a draft nor a deadline for finalization of such a document could be provided by the regional CAs or Customs to the audit team. This, together with the fact that no CA is currently responsible for import controls, puts at risk the timely implementation of the electronic certification system.

Files reviewed confirmed that good communication is in place between the regional CAs and the paying agencies concerning irregularities relating to EU organic rules and the exchange of other relevant information such as the list of land parcels managed by an organic farmer. However, irregularities related to imported goods are not shared in a systematic manner by the regional CAs with Customs (see paragraph 62). Conclusions Competent Authorities and Control Bodies
There is no CA designed for import controls of organic products in Belgium, contrary to Article 27(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 12

Provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008 in relation to the EU import of organic products such as the risk assessment to determine the frequency of physical checks or the sampling of consignments of organic products before they are released for free circulation into the EU by Customs are not implemented.

Customs may receive, on an ad-hoc basis, information from regional CAs as regards organic consignments entering into the EU via Belgium. The audit team was presented some examples showing that organic consignments from Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan were sampled. However, the CAs could neither present an overview nor could they provide evidence to confirm that all organic consignments from Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan had been subject to the reinforced control measures adopted by the EU.

In a case reviewed by the audit team, an organic consignment was imported into Belgium without a Certificate of Inspection. This was discovered by the CB during control at the importer who had imported this consignment. The CB notified the regional CA, but the irregularity was not shared with Customs. A calculation of the balance of input and output was conducted during all inspections observed. The exercise was mainly based on documentary checks and often did not include the verification of the real situation on the spot. At the egg producers visited, the input/output calculation focused on feed consumption per hen per day for a randomly selected hen house. The data related to an appropriate period, starting from the stocking day of the house with hens up to the inspection day. Inspectors took data from records such as the volume of feed in stock, but did not verify the real amount of the feed still in stock on the day of inspection. This had never been raised as non-compliant by the CBs in the past. The CBs visited confirmed that operators are not required to record the verification of the organic status of the goods at reception which is not in line with Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

As regards the labelling, a number of labels on packaging of organic products were seen which included a reference to both, EU and non-EU agriculture, on the same label despite the fact that ingredients were of either EU or non-EU origin. The CAs stated that such reference, i.e. EU / non-EU on the same package, is considered acceptable mainly for practical reason, even if this reference does not always fully reflect the content of the product. This is not in line Article 24(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. label_heading: Conclusions on Sampling and Laboratory Analysis
paragraph_text: The high number of samples annually taken by the CBs is based on an adequate risk assessment and laboratories used by CBs are accredited. However, laboratories are not designated by the CA as required by EU legislation. 5.2.7 Exceptional production rules and other derogations. Legal Requirements Article 29 and sections 2 to 4 of Chapter 6 of Title II of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

The two CBs visited have a list of laboratories which are used for the testing of organic samples. These laboratories are accredited to ISO 17025, but they are not designated by the CAs for the testing of organic products as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The CAs of Flanders and Wallonia stated that the scope of active substances tested by the laboratories in the case of organic samples is verified during supervision of CBs. However, the audit team noted that result of such verification was not reported by the CAs in the relevant supervisory reports.

The CBs visited, stated that, in relation to the scope of active substances analysed for, they relied on the fact that the laboratory was accredited. In their view, accreditation implied that the laboratory would be aware of the appropriate testing scope for organic samples. Nevertheless evidence was seen that CBs request single residue methods when required, for example when substances such as glyphosate have to be tested for.

label_heading: Conclusions on Measures in case of Irregularities and Infringements
paragraph_text: The CBs visited apply a "soft" approach with regard to enforcement measures in particular in cases of severe and recurrent irregularities. This, together with the fact that not all irregularities are either reported to relevant CAs or fully investigated by CBs, reduces the effectiveness of the control system. 5.3 SEED DATA BASE Legal Requirements Articles 48, 49 and 56 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

The catalogues of measures are overall comprehensive and the files reviewed by the audit team confirmed that the CBs apply measures in line with the catalogues. However, 13 the majority of measures provided for in these catalogues consist only of light action such as "observation", "comment", "warning", "a request for improvement" and enhanced controls". Moreover, operators who use conventional seeds without prior approval receive a "warning" in Flanders and a "request for improvement" in Wallonia.

Files reviewed and inspections observed during the audit confirmed that measures imposed by CBs in particular in cases of severe and/or recurrent non-compliances were not sufficiently effective to ensure compliance with Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007: An organic operator was only issued a "request for improvement" for the recurrent use of conventional seed without prior-derogation from the CB. The field in question was only declassified after the operator was found to have used conventional seeds without prior-approval for the fifth time. Moreover, the CB confirmed that the producer of the raw material would not necessarily be informed of the incidence, which is not in line with Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 requiring the CB to inform without delay the CB of the operator who had pro

Regional legislations require immediate notification of irregularities in cases (i) which involve operators controlled/certified by other CBs, and (ii) when products, plots, or operators are to be decertified by CAs. In Flanders, such notifications have to be done within three working days. In the other two regions, no deadline is imposed, which means that immediate notification is required according to the understanding of the two CAs concerned.

Both CBs confirmed that CAs are formally notified when irregularities involve operators in non-EU countries. This is not in line with Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which requires that CBs, when identifying irregularities with regard to products under the control of other control bodies, shall inform those control bodies without delay. Nevertheless, CBs copy, on an ad-hoc basis, CAs into email communication by which operators are informed of irregularities. Moreover, CBs confirmed that the likelihood of irregularities are not required to be notified to CAs, which is not in line with Article 27(5)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

Files reviewed by the audit team confirmed that findings of residues of non-authorised pesticides below the limit established in the regional legislations are not notified by the CBs to the relevant CAs. Moreover, CB2 did not notify cases of samples which showed multiple residues of non-authorised pesticides, neither was a case notified to the CA where a feed sample showed pesticide residues beyond the above mentioned limit. The 15 CB stated the case was not notified because no feed was left to be decertified. Conclusions on Measures in case of Irregularities and Infringements

label_heading: Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of CBs
paragraph_text: CBs are accredited and approved in accordance with national and EU rules. CBs are generally subject to effective annual supervision by the CA which includes office and witness audits. However, the CA neither takes into account the reports of the accreditation body audits nor requires the CBs to submit their risk analysis procedures before supervising CBs which may undermine the effectiveness of the CA supervision. 5.2.2 Registration of Operators Legal Requirements Article 28(1), (2) and (5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92(2) and 92b of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 6 Findings

The SAB notifies the AFSVSPP of the results of the accreditation audits carried out on CBs. However, this information is not taken into account for their supervisory task which is not in line to Article 92c(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Moreover, The AFSVSPP does not require the CBs to submit their risk analysis procedure which is not in line to Article 92c(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. This may reduce the effectiveness of supervision as any deficiency related to the CBs' risk analysis may only be detected post factum.

Findings

The two CBs have procedures in place requiring the operators to submit a full description of their activities, including a description of precautionary measures put in place to avoid potential contamination of organic products. CBs' inspectors are required to verify the implementation of these precautionary measures when visiting the operators. However, the audit team noted that in relation to both CBs, the operators did not submit the description of precautionary measures contrary to Article 63(1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The CBs stated that precautionary measures put in place by operators are verified during the inspections. The audit team noted, during the inspections obser

There is an adequate system in place for the registration of operators and overall it is effectively implemented. The CA makes available to the public regularly updated relevant information on organic operators. However, the list of operators as such, is not publically available which is not in line with EU legislation. The system in place also ensures that exempted retailers continue to fulfil the conditions for exemption. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Article 41 and Article 92f of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Articles 65(1) and (4) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/

The registration of organic operators is managed by the MAFF. The MAFF prepares a list of organic operators taking into account all information provided by the CBs. This list is updated daily. However, the list of operators as such, is not publically available although a search facility on the MAFF webpage permits searches for specific operators which is not fully in line with Article 92b of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which require the list of operators to be made public by MSs. All the relevant information, including documentary evidence is present when/if one has a specific name to undertake the research.

paragraph_text: However, the effectiveness of the system is reduced as there is a risk that not all high risk operators may be selected for additional inspections.

label_heading: Conclusions on Sampling and Laboratory Analysis
paragraph_text: However, the limited scope and testing methods used for organic samples and the inappropriate selection of operators for sampling carried out by one CB may reduce the effectiveness of the sampling programme. 5.2.7 Exceptional production rules and other derogations. Legal Requirements Article 29 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and Annex IX of the same Regulation. Sections 2 to 4 of Chapter 6 of Title II of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Article 22(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Findings

The two CBs have procedures in place for the selection of operators for additional controls and sampling. Both CBs apply these procedures when selecting operators for sampling and additional controls. Scores are given for each criterion and a final score is given to each operator which allows the CB to rank operators according to their risk profile. However, the system applied by CB1 does not ensure that operators with several past non-compliances are classified as high risk. In relation to the risk 8 assessments prepared by CB2, the procedure in place to select operators for additional visits does not ensure that most of the additional visits are carried out at high risk operators. Conclusi

The audit team reviewed the scope of the PPP residues that can be analysed at the one designated laboratory. It was noted that some substances commonly detected by MSs in organic products were not included in the analytical scope (such as anthraquinone, piperonyl, 2,4D). Moreover, substances that can only be detected when using single methods and which are frequently notified in the Organic Farming Information System (OFIS) are also not included (such as Glyphosate, Chlormequat). This is not in line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

Although inspections observed were overall effective, some important aspects were not sufficiently covered during the visits which may undermine the effectiveness of the inspections. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. paragraph_text: However, the CA delegated to the CBs the competence for authorisation to tethering of animals which is not in line with EU requirements. 5.2.8 Imports of Products from Organic Production Legal Requirements Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 14 Chapter 3 of Title III of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008. Annexes II, III, V and VI of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008. Findings

According to the national organic rules, the MAFF has the competence to grant derogations, except for the use of conventional seeds and propagating material, which has been delegated to the CBs. However, the derogation for tethering of animals had been delegated to CBs which is contrary to Article 27(7) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

label_heading: Conclusions on Measures in cases of Irregularities and Infringements
paragraph_text: The system in place is effective as it is based on a catalogue of measures providing a framework for harmonized and adequate measures in case of irregularities and infringements of EU organic rules. However, major non-compliances are not immediately notified between CBs and the CAs and other bodies involved, which may not allow the relevant bodies to take enforcement actions in a timely manner.

Generally there is good communication between the CAs and CBs with regard notification of irregularities. CBs notify the AFSVSPP of irregularities found during the year by means of their annual and weekly reports. Major and severe irregularities affecting the organic status of the product are weekly notified by the CBs to the AFSVSPP which is not fully in line with in line with Articles 27(5) and 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 92(4) of (EC) Regulation 889/2008 which prescribe that irregularities or infringement affecting the organic status of the product shall be immediately notified by the CBs to the CAs. The procedures of CB2 require inspectors to immediately inform the C

label_heading: Conclusions on Measures in cases of Irregularities and Infringements
paragraph_text: However, the CA does not always respond on a timely basis to OFIS notifications to 17 the EU as there is not a procedure in place to properly follow-up in a timely manner which may prevent MSs involved taking appropriate actions. 5.3 SEED DATA BASE Legal Requirements Articles 48 and 49 to 56 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

The audit team reviewed two cases notified in OFIS. In both cases the CA launched an investigation. The CA, for different reasons, were not able to upload the results of the investigations in OFIS within 30 days as required in Article 92a(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. In one case, the regional office took more than 3 months to respond to the CA (then the CA took one more month to reply to the notification), in the other case, the CA uploaded the notification in OFIS in October 2017, seven months after having the relevant information collected (by 31.03.2017). The CA acknowledges the lack of written procedures to deal with these matters. Conclusions on Measures in cases of Irregularities

The CAs are designated for the official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG and are adequately staffed and trained. However, the exchange of information between regional and/or central level was not always effective. This increases the risk that non-compliant products continue to be marketed. 5.2.2 Control Bodies

label_heading: Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls
paragraph_text: There was no systematic risk based approach to market controls in place at the time of the audit which fails to ensure that PDO/PGI/TSG on the market are in compliance with the requirements of the legislation. 5.2.4 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 12, 13(1), 23, 24(1), 36(3), 44 and 46(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 664/2014, in particular Article 1. Commission implementing Regulation (EU) No 668/2014, in particular Article 4. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Articles 8(1), 9 and 10(2)(b)(vi) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 Findings

In all Länder visited the market controls of PDO/PGI/TSG are undertaken by the local level food safety inspectors. These market controls are focussed on food safety issues and PDO/PGI/TSG is a relatively low priority. There was no systematic risk based approach to market controls in place which is not in compliance with Article 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012.

The CA delegates certain official control tasks to CBs which are accredited to ISO17065. Supervision of the CBs by the CA is not fully effective as the supervisory process does not include witness inspections, which is not in line with Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Articles 22(1) and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Findings

The CA confirmed that they do not undertake any shadow audits of the CB inspectors as part of their supervisory activities. A representative of MARD may occasionally attend the RENAR accreditation audit of a CB as an observer. An accreditation audit occurs once every four years for each CB. However, as no judgement is made by the CA in these observation roles, it cannot be considered to be part of the supervisory activity of the CB. 5

The audit team reviewed a number of the reports prepared by the CA relating to the CB office audits. These mainly describe the findings that the CBs have observed during producers/processor inspections during the previous year. However, the CA does not evaluate the activities of the CB.

The fact that the CA does not carry out any witness audits of the CB inspectors at the operator level does not permit the CA to evaluate the effectiveness of inspections carried out by CBs. This lack of supervisory activities by the CA is not in line with Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted some systematic shortcomings in the inspections carried out by the CBs (see paras 33, 34 and 35). Such shortcoming could only be detected through carrying out such witness inspections. Conclusions on Control Bodies

paragraph_text: All annual official controls of producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks are announced which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004

Although official controls are undertaken at an agreed frequency at producers/processors, the inspections are announced, superficial and do not always include each element of the Product Specification/Technical Files. Consequently, this approach does not provide the necessary level of assurance that producers/processors are fully compliant. 5.2.6 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 Findings

Given the relatively small number of producers/processors of PDO/PGI agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks in Romania the approach taken has been to subject all producers/processors to an annual official control. At the time of the audit the official controls for agriproducts and foodstuffs were delegated to CBs whereas official controls of spirit drinks were undertaken by the CA. The CCA confirmed that all annual official controls at producers/processor level for both types of registered names are announced. 6 This is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which states that official controls shall be carried out without prior warning.

The audit team visited two producers of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and three producers of GI spirit drinks. In all cases, a series of inspection reports were available which illustrated that all producers/processors were subject to an annual official control. The audit team was informed that all inspections at operators whether carried out by CAs (spirit drinks) or CBs (agriproducts and foodstuffs) are announced. The CA stated that this approach ensured that inspections take place at the time of processing and that all relevant documents are prepared by the operators. 8 Agriproducts and Foodstuffs ­ Controls Undertaken by CBs

paragraph_text: Routine risk based market controls of PDO/PGI/TSG agriproducts and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks were not included in the prioritisation of official controls at the time of the audit. 5.2.4 Procedures and Performance of Official Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 12, 13(1), 23, 24(1), 36(3), 44 and 46(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. A number of case studies were described by the NACP which illustrated their competence to investigate and to sanction where appropriate. One complicated investigation related to a registered name from a non-EU country. The NACP had received a complaint that coffee which was not the genuine article had been traded in Romania. The NACP successfully identified the source of the problem and implemented the relevant enforcement measures. 7 Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls

paragraph_text: The lack of official sampling and laboratory analysis of spirit drinks means that the requirements of Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 are not met.

Although official controls are undertaken at an agreed frequency at producers/processors, the inspections are announced, superficial and do not always include each element of the Product Specification/Technical Files. Consequently, this approach does not provide the necessary level of assurance that producers/processors are fully compliant. 5.2.6 Enforcement Measures Legal Requirements Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. In relation to spirit drinks, the annual official control at producers/processors did not include the checking of all elements of the technical file and neither did it include, sampling, for laboratory analysis. This could not ensure compliance with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008.

It was noted that raw materials were accepted on the basis of a general declaration by the supplier, that the raw materials complied with the requirements of the Product Specification. As an example, the CB never raised a non-compliance regarding the absence of labelling of a specific raw material. This acceptance signifies a lack of control measures.

In the spirit drink producers visited, although the operators kept records as regards the production, as well as purchase and sales records, no verification of the information in these were made by the inspectors. The inspectors stated that such controls were undertaken by the revenue authorities. 9

There has been inadequate progress in rectifying the deficiencies reported during the Commission audit to Hungary DG(SANCO) 2011/6045 on animal welfare during transport. Actions taken by the Hungarian authorities to rectify the deficiencies were ineffective as the same deficiencies were found at district level in 2017.

Official controls at district level do not ensure transporter's compliance. This together with the absence of verification in a number of key areas might cause unnecessary pain or suffering to animals during long distance transport by road to non-EU countries. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 18 and 26 and Chapters II, III and VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings

The County offices provide training for district offices mainly on certification of animals but also on welfare issues. During 2016 NÉBIH required all counties to give training on animal welfare requirements to those district official veterinarians dispatching consignments for long journeys. NÉBIH supplied training materials (including the elements in paragraph 3 a-g above) and all officials were trained by December 2016.

Most officials at district level did not take into account the training or instructions regarding the time taken to cross the border at Turkey and the working hours of Turkish veterinary authorities there, in their verification of journey log planning (see paragraphs 26 to 28 below). This resulted in incorrect journey planning and animals subjected to routinely longer journey times.

Staff at district level generally did not know how to check certain requirements requested by NÉBIH, e.g. approving vehicle deck surface areas and suitability of drinkers or analysis of retrospective satellite navigation system or temperature records from long journeys (see paragraphs 10, 11, 12, 26 27 and 28 below). This is despite training and guidance from both central and county level. This lack of knowledge or competence in carrying out tasks at district level is not in compliance with Article 6 of Regulation 882/2004.

There has been inadequate progress in rectifying the deficiencies reported during the Commission audit to Hungary DG(SANCO) 2011/6045 on animal welfare during transport. Actions taken by the Hungarian authorities to rectify the deficiencies were ineffective as the same deficiencies were found at district level in 2017.

This together with the absence of verification in a number of key areas might cause unnecessary pain or suffering to animals during long distance transport by road to non-EU countries. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 18 and 26 and Chapters II, III and VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings

Most officials at district level did not take into account the training or instructions regarding the time taken to cross the border at Turkey and the working hours of Turkish veterinary authorities there, in their verification of journey log planning (see paragraphs 26 to 28 below). This resulted in incorrect journey planning and animals subjected to routinely longer journey times.

Staff at district level generally did not know how to check certain requirements requested by NÉBIH, e.g. approving vehicle deck surface areas and suitability of drinkers or analysis of retrospective satellite navigation system or temperature records from long journeys (see paragraphs 10, 11, 12, 26 27 and 28 below). This is despite training and guidance from both central and county level. This lack of knowledge or competence in carrying out tasks at district level is not in compliance with Article 6 of Regulation 882/2004.

There is no verification of the district level work due to budgetary constraints, though a framework for doing so is in place. The district levels could not demonstrate adherence to documented procedures and this was not known to higher levels. This is not in compliance with Article 8 of Regulation 882/2004. District officials at times took decisions based on discussions with transporters rather than confirming themselves that requirements are met or following NÉBIH guidance. 4 Conclusions on Official Controls

The poor standard for approval leads to a risk of inadequate space allowances and unsuitable drinking devices, during long journeys and thus to welfare problems for the animals transported. The inadequate measuring of deck floor surface areas and assessment of drinking devices at the time of approving the vehicle leads to incorrect calculations on stocking densities ­ as they are based on the deck surface area indicated in the vehicle approval certificate. Therefore, reductions in stocking density indicated in most journey logs for summer consignments are often inaccurate.

Vehicle approval renewals are subject to the same process as new vehicles. There is extensive written guidance available for consultation for district official veterinarians (OVs) who approve vehicles for long journeys. This includes specific guidance on suitability of drinkers but not on measuring vehicle space allowances. There is no systematic training for OVs, but some have taken part in Better Training for Safer Food courses and meetings between counties and districts allow dissemination of this information. A note from NÉBIH also draws attention to the need for accurate vehicle deck areas to calculate appropriate stocking densities and to verify the suitability of drinking devices for

The audit team reviewed vehicle approval certificates. All but one of them were inaccurate with regard to the calculation of deck surface area: many listed only an overall area for multi-deck vehicles, or the same deck surface areas for multi-deck trucks, including those with goose-neck decks at the front. This is not in compliance with the requirements necessary to correctly issue the vehicle certificate in Article 18 of Regulation 1/2005 and the specifications required to be completed in the certificate listed in Annex III Chapter IV of Regulation 1/2005. District officials relied upon the figures provided by vehicle manufacturers' which were not always accurate.

Vehicle drinking devices were not physically verified at the time of approval by the district OVs. They assumed vehicle manufacturers' would fit suitable drinkers for the species that the vehicles was listed as being capable of transporting. This is not in compliance with Article 18 of Regulation 1/2005 or in line with NÉBIH guidance. Vehicles approval certificates were issued for different species and ages of animals which would require different non-compatible drinking systems e.g. horses, rabbits, 5 calves and pigs on one certificate and would lead to some animals being unable to drink during rest stops due to the unsuitability of drinkers.

The requirements for adequate headspace and therefore ventilation provision for large adult cattle in two-tier vehicles is not respected causing unnecessary suffering to these animals during long distance transport by road to non-EU countries. The actions 7 proposed in response to previous DG SANTE recommendations on these issues were not effective as they have not been properly implemented at district level.

Officials at district level did not recognise the physical limitations imposed by vehicle design height restrictions and the carriage of two decks of average height large adult cattle. There was a recent instruction issued (see also paragraph 3c above) but no clear practical guidance (vehicle and animal schematics) from NÉBIH on this. Adequate headspace and therefore ventilation was not ensured when large adult cattle (over 500kg) were transported e.g. the guidance from NÉBIH for 20cm space requirement above the withers of large bulls on two decks (which must be stacked in some way) on conventional trucks would require a minimum2 vehicle height of over 4.8m. i.e. it is not possible to load l

The current system for certification of approved vehicles does not sufficiently distinguish the types of vehicle appropriate for weaned and unweaned animals. As a result unweaned animals may not have access to liquid and be if necessary fed during long distance journeys. The risk of unweaned animals being transported in these unsuitable vehicles is sufficiently mitigated in the Netherlands by systematic controls at the moment of loading. However, this shortcoming may negatively impact journeys starting from another Member State, where the suitability of the vehicles may not be systematically verified at the moment of loading as in the Netherlands. 5.3 RESTING Legal requirements Articles 14,

This implies that unweaned animals may be transported on vehicles that are inadequate for this category of animals with the biggest risk being the inability to access liquids due to unsuitable drinking devices (Point 2.2 of Chapter VI, Annex I of Regulati

label_heading: Conclusions on unexpected delays at the EU border
paragraph_text: Contingency plans, set up by transporters as required by Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, do not include measures to provide bedding, feed and water to the animals in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at the EU border. There are therefore inadequate assurances that the needs of animals blocked at the border can be met and that these animals are not caused unnecessary suffering. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The measures in place provide satisfactory assurances that exports of live animals operate 10 smoothly and that these journeys are correctly planned and carried out in line with animal welfare requirements to prevent causing unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to the animals. label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring, awareness and surveillance
paragraph_text: The under-implementation of the monitoring programme, the sometimes inappropriate age groups tested, and the uneven spatial sample distribution add a high level of uncertainty to any assessment of the effectiveness of the oral rabies vaccination campaigns. The lack of active promotion of this programme from the Ministry of Environment and Energy makes it more difficult for the local veterinary services to engage the local forestry services and hunters in fox hunting, which is not part of their normal activities.

The CCA provides each Regional Unit with a target number of foxes to be sampled for the monitoring programme. The aim is to test 2 foxes/100 km2 after each ORV campaign, as described in the approved programmes. The hunters are reimbursed with 30 EUR for each fox, but the sampling is far from reaching the target levels and the implementation varies among the Regional Units. In 2016, approximately 9% of the planned foxes were shot and submitted for analysis under the monitoring programme. Monitoring results from Regional Units for the three ORV campaigns from autumn 2015 to spring 2016 showed that, six of the 27 Regional Units involved in one of more of the campaigns had not submitted any moni

Monitoring results between the first spring campaign (2016) and the 2016 autumn campaign show that a large proportion of the foxes submitted for testing were less than one year old. This age group is not a good indicator for the effectiveness of ORV when tested between birth and their first autumn ORV campaign. Although these cubs would still have been inside their dens during the spring campaign a large proportion showed evidence of bait contact. It is not known if fox vixens are likely to bring vaccine baits into the den to feed their cubs. Some cubs were positive for rabies antibodies but it is not possible to establish if these fox cubs had maternal antibodies or had actually been vaccin

The way the laboratory reports the age of the tested foxes makes it difficult for the competent authority and the Commission to evaluate the effectiveness of the rabies vaccination campaigns. The practice of reporting as positive only tetracycline lines from the most recent vaccination campaign, excluding evidence of bait contact in previous years, may assist the authorities in evaluating the vaccine distribution in the most recent campaign but it distorts the assessment when compared to the sero- prevalence, which is based on antibodies from any vaccination campaign. This practice may explain the consistent reporting from Greece of foxes that are seropositive without evidence of bait contac

When determining the age of foxes the laboratory would differentiate between several age groups and the same animal shot after an autumn campaign would end up in 20 different age classes, depending on whether it was shot before or after 1 January during its first and second winter. This classification follows the instructions from the EURL.

Only foxes with tetracycline lines that can be referred to the most recent vaccination campaign (excluding lines indicating bait contact in previous campaigns) are reported as positive, even if other tetracycline lines show that the fox had been in contact with vaccine baits earlier6. This could be the reason why, in Greece, the results reported to the Commission in 2014, 2105 and 2016 show that certain foxes (5-14%) have antibodies to rabies virus but are reported as negative for contact with vaccine baits (as described in finding 38), which is unexpected considering the nature of the infection and the vaccine baits.

The diagnostic pathway for confirming rabies cases, particularly in the case of suspected human exposure or inconclusive FAT results, does not follow international standards. The alternative method currently used to confirm the result of the accredited FAT method is not subject to the same quality assurance as the FAT method. This increases the risk of an incorrect overall test result which may have implications for post-exposure treatments of human patients. None of the rabies cases detected in 2012- 2014 had been caused by vaccine virus. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a sound legal basis for all aspects of the rabies eradication, a clear chain of command, clear distribution of responsibili

Methods for virus isolation in cell culture or mouse inoculation test are not available in the NRL. No other laboratory has been subcontracted to carry out these tests. Current international standards (Manual of Diagnostic Tests and Vaccines for Terrestrial Animals of the International Organisation for Animal Health, Chapter 2.1.17.) stipulate that one of these tests should be used as a complement to the FAT (referred to as the "gold standard") in case of human exposure to rabies or an inconclusive FAT result. Another alternative is to repeat the FAT test on other tissue samples. Instead, the NRL is using a non-validated, non-accredited real-time PCR method for this purpose.

label_heading: Conclusions on surveillance, controls on domestic pigs
paragraph_text: Although with regional variations, the active surveillance programme for domestic pigs provides substantial guarantees that the CSF virus is not circulating in commercial holdings. The system gives more limited guarantees for holdings with low biosecurity, where shortcomings in holding registration and records undermine the ability to fully assess the CSF epidemiological situation but the sharp drop in the number of backyard holdings following comprehensive verification by the competent authority mitigates the significance of this weakness.

label_heading: Conclusions on surveillance in wild boars
paragraph_text: The active surveillance system for wild boars has significantly improved since the authorities issued guidelines on the targeted sampling of wild boars for the CSF surveillance programme in 2013. The programme, as implemented, has adequate sensitivity for confirming absence of CSF virus circulation in wild boars. The significant under-performances in some regions lead to uncertainty regarding the disease status of these zones, especially for peripheral regions, where a vaccination programme has been implemented until recently. There are no procedures in place to confirm or rule out the presence of the disease when a wild boar is tested seropositive.

Based on the data provided by the competent authority, they surpassed the total target set for industrial and type A holdings where animals had to be clinically examined, but not all regions achieved the targets set for them. In 2015, authorised veterinarians had to inspect 100% and official veterinarians 10% of backyard farms; in 2016, the surveillance scheme changed to 10% and 5% respectively.

The team noted the following: The active surveillance system for wild boars has significantly improved since guidelines on the targeted sampling of wild boars have been issued and implemented. label_heading: Conclusions on Animal health controls on meat production and EU trade
paragraph_text: The authorities certify and dispatch to other Member States live pigs, fresh pig meat, meat products and meat preparations which do not comply with the requirements set for Bulgaria for intra-Union trade. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authority cannot properly assess the sensitivity of the surveillance programme. Although there is a system in place for verification and supervision of official controls, they do not carry out an epidemiological analysis of CSF data collected. The central database offers a more accurate picture of the pig farming sector in Bulgaria than before. paragraph_text: The authorities certify and dispatch to other Member States live pigs, fresh pig meat, meat products and meat preparations which do not comply with the requirements set for Bulgaria for intra-Union trade. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authority cannot properly assess the sensitivity of the surveillance programme. Although there is a system in place for verification and supervision of official controls, they do not carry out an epidemiological analysis of CSF data collected. label_heading: Conclusions on verification, supervision and expert group
paragraph_text: The system of internal audits, supervision and analysis contributes to the harmonisation of official checks and to the detection of weaknesses in the implementation of disease control measures. There is a limited quantitative analysis of the results of official controls by both central competent authority and ASF expert group which limits the capacity to ascertain the effectiveness of the implemented activities. This analysis at central level is particularly weak in assessing the effectiveness of biosecurity measures implemented by hunters and, to a lesser extent, by pig holdings. This hinders the central authority's ability to identify potential gaps and to fine-tune its measures. 5.7 FOLLO

In general, the ASF expert group exercises the functions set out by the ASF control Directive. In particular, the expert groups did assist the competent authorities in defining infected areas as required by the EU legislation and in defining additional control measures to combat ASF disease. The members of expert groups receive regular updates on the evolvement of ASF epidemiological situation. However, the ASF group had not yet received the results of some official controls (e.g. on compliance with biosecurity measures for hunting and on pig holdings) in a manner that would allow them to fully evaluate the effectiveness of those additional measures, although this is required by Article 15(2

The strengthened controls on the movements of live pigs reduce the risk of disease spread between holdings. Pre-movement testing is inadequately targeted, and thus provides less guarantees than it could in reducing the spread of diseases due to the movement of pigs from the infected area. 5.2 EARLY DETECTION AND SURVEILLANCE Legal requirements Articles 4, 14, 15, and 18 of Directive 2002/60/EC, Commission Decision 2003/422/EC; articles 4 to 10 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; the approved national programme (based on ASF strategy for Eastern Part of the EU (SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 4) 5.2.1 Surveillance in wild boar

When pigs were moving from the infected area, the veterinarian performed pre-movement ASF testing, selecting pigs randomly instead of considering whether there had been a recent occurrence of sick animals. This is the same finding noted in the 2014 Commission report (DG(SANCO) 2014-7294).

The existence of two pig databases complicates the proper planning and implementation of official controls. The amendment of functionalities of the ARMA database should address the majority of the problems, but it will take more than one year to implement.

Commission audit reports (DG(SANCO) 2014-7294 and DG(SANTE) 2016-8776 describe the identification and registration system for pigs in Poland, highlighting the 4 following: there were two pig registers/databases in the country, with different systems for entry and control of information and managed by different authorities ­ a pig database required by EU legislation and maintained by Agency for Restructuring and Modernising Agriculture (ARMA) and the registers required by national legislation kept by individual District Veterinary Offices (DVOs). Both of them had limitations in their use as a disease management tool. Since then this situation has not changed as was evidenced during this audit

The Polish authorities had already scheduled the development of the new system called e-IRZ to address the limitation of the ARMA database and a tender for this system has been prepared. The new system should include functionalities to fulfil the new requirements for identification and registration introduced in 2016, enhance support to the veterinary services, improve the efficiency of electronic data exchange between the authorities involved, and provide for implementation of two-way communication with the livestock owners. The timeframe to have e-IRZ ready is a year after the tender is awarded.

label_heading: Conclusions on early detection and surveillance
paragraph_text: The effective and well implemented passive surveillance in wild boar provides assurances that new cases of ASF will be detected at an early stage. The competent authority has access to updated data on the epidemiological situation and geographical spread of the infection. The system benefits from good cooperation between hunters and competent authorities and the active role of the ASF expert group. However, the insufficient serological tests performed reduce the amount of epidemiological information available to follow the evolution of the disease in the region.

Antibodies have been tested only in 6,876 wild boars which represent 68.80% of hunting bags which is not line with the national ASF eradication programme and ASF Strategy for Eastern Part of the EU (SANTE/7113/2015-Rev 4) that require testing of all shot wild boars in ASF restricted areas for antibodies against ASF virus. The partial testing hinders from drawing conclusion on the apparent increase of seropositivity rate between 2015 and 2016. The central CA is aware of this last weakness and as remedial action updated (at the end of 2016) procedures for sampling of wild boar. 5.2.2 Surveillance in pig holdings

The reserved rendering capacity should allow Hungary to cope with depopulation in an outbreak situation. However, in the event of confirmation of ASF, due to limitations of the database performing a census of pigs will be more time consuming and demand increased resources to localise holdings in restricted areas. In addition, there is no verification of the availability of adequate county contingency plans by the CCA. This may delay containment of disease in an outbreak scenario. 5.4 VERIFICATION, SUPERVISION AND EXPERT GROUP Legal requirements Articles 4 and 8 of Regulation No 882/2004; Directive 2002/60/EC (Articles 15, 16 and 22, Annex VI) Findings 17 5.4.1 Supervision by line management

label_heading: Conclusions on verification, supervision and expert group
paragraph_text: The competent authority has not fully engaged the ASF expert group is to provide assistance with the control of ASF and to verify the effectiveness of eradication measures.

The competent authority confirmed that the expert group membership was changed in May 2016 and currently includes veterinarians, wildlife biologists and epidemiologists but no hunters which is contrary to Article 15(2) of Directive 2002/60/EC. The authorities indicated they have plans to expand group to include hunters and representation from the Ministry of the Environment.

The re-established expert group has not met formally and there were no records to confirm the informal meetings /contacts between group members which had taken place. The competent authority confirmed that the expert group has been invited to prepare a report on wild boar management covering improvements in hunting ground biosecurity, wild boar census and hunting quotas. To date, the expert group has not verified the effectiveness of the measures adopted to eradicate ASF from the infected area, which is not in line with Article 15(2)(a) of Directive 2002/60/EC.
The identification and registration deficiencies in some non-commercial farms significantly weaken the tracing of pigs and makes the containment of disease difficult in an outbreak.

The audit team reviewed one epidemiological investigation on a non-commercial holding. The authorities could not establish the origin of the two pigs on the outbreak holding as they were not identified as required by article 5(2) of Council Directive 2008/71/EC. The authorities confirmed that census performed in this District, following six further outbreaks of ASF in 2017, disclosed a further two non-commercial holdings where origin of pigs was unknown and two pig keepers who had not declared pigs. 5.1.3 Movement restrictions

This produces less guarantees than it could in reducing the spread of disease due to the movement of live animals from the infected area.

The private veterinarian of the consigning holding confirmed that he, rather than the official veterinarian, randomly selected healthy pigs for ASF sampling when required for intra-Union trade. As there has been no systematic vaccination of calves since 15 July 2016, there is a serious risk of an ever increasing number of susceptible animals in Bulgaria which could become infected if/when virus circulates. This risk would be addressed if the instruction issued on 13 February to vaccinate all calves over 4 months of age with immediate effect and to continue this on a weekly basis is implemented.

There has been no systematic vaccination of calves since 15 July 2016. The policy to vaccinate calves was amended at a meeting between the CCA and all RFSD's in December 2016 when the age limit was reduced from 6 to 4 months of age. However, apart from the minutes of the meeting no specific instruction was issued to RFSD's and at the time of this audit, no systematic vaccination of calves had commenced.

The current multi-annual programme requires sampling and laboratory analysis of domestic pigs found sick or dead, from non-commercial holdings across the entire territory of Romania, where classical and ASF could not be ruled out (passive surveillance). This surveillance does not apply to commercial holdings.

In two industrial commercial farms visited by the audit team, the private veterinarians providing a service had both submitted in 2016, pig carcases to regional laboratories for post mortem examination. In both cases the veterinarian had requested classical swine fever testing but not ASF testing. The authorities confirmed that samples submitted for classical swine fever testing were paid by the authorities but ASF analysis in commercial industrial farms had to be paid by farmer. In contrast, backyard holdings do not have to pay for ASF testing.

The current multi-annual programme (2016 - 2018) for the surveillance and control of ASF requires sampling and laboratory analysis of all wild boar found dead or sick and those killed in road traffic accidents from the entire territory of Romania (passive surveillance). In normal conditions it is expected that the minimum number of wild boar to be found in a given area is ~ 1% of wild boar population at risk. Finding dead wild boars is a challenge due to the large numbers of natural predators, cannibalism by the wild boar themselves and the tendency for dying wild boar to seek secluded areas where it is difficult to find them. Currently, there are no incentives encouraging hunters to overcome this challenge, on the contrary (a) hunters are expected to transport found dead wild boar to the nearest laboratory at their own expense and (b) hunters lose one animal from their hunting bag for each found dead wild boar reported.

The competent authority plans to incentivise reporting of found dead wild boar but cannot implement financial incentives until the budget is approved in line with National Decision 1156/2013 which lays down the budget for all animal disease control in Romania. They indicated this would take at least 60 days.

This increasing population will favour the spread of ASF and create difficulties in its elimination and control should the disease reach Romania.

Six out of the eight counties at risk have wild boar densities between 0.25 ­ 0.5 / km². The two remaining counties have wild boar densities between 0.5 ­ 0.75 / km² (see map below). The current ASF strategy for the eastern part of the EU considers a wild boar density of 0.5 wild boar / km² or lower as optimal to reduce the spread of ASF.

However, District Forestry Offices recommend that hunting ground users can allocate up to one percent of total hunting ground area for growing crops to sustain wildlife (including wild boar) - crops include oats and maize.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of plant health import controls
paragraph_text: The sampling methodology applied for plant health checks of aquatic plants, fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, is not based on the risk of the presence of harmful organisms. It is not therefore ensured that it can be concluded, as a result of these checks, that the lot is not contaminated with harmful organisms. 5.2 COOPERATION AND COMMUNICATION WITH CUSTOMS SERVICES AND STAKEHOLDERS Legal requirements Articles 2(1) and 13(1) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC Article 6 of Commission Directive 2004/103/EC. Findings 5.2.1 Customs

All plants intended for planting (other than aquatic plants), including seed, are categorised as high-risk. Low-risk plants include all aquatic plants; and fruits, vegetables and cut flowers imported between October and April. All other plants and plant products fall into the medium-risk category.

The BAES explained that aquatic plants are categorised as low-risk due to the intended use of these plants (presumed to be placed into aquaria), which means the likelihood of any harmful organisms which may be present transferring to other host plants is low. The BAES also explained that seasonality is a key criterion in determining the risk of fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, because of the cold climatic conditions in Austria between October and April, which means that any harmful organisms present would not be able to establish in their territory. The BAES went on to explain that these types of products were, to the best of their knowledge, always destined for customers in Austria.

During a visit to Vienna airport, the audit team observed an inspection being carried out of a consignment from Thailand containing mixed plant produce, including three regulated articles, aubergines (Solanum melongena); mangoes (Mangifera indica); and 6 orchid cut flowers (Dendrobium sp.). All three regulated lots were categorised as 'low- risk' for the purpose of determining the size of sample to take for visual checks. However, at the time of the audit, orchid cut flowers featured on the non-EU trade Alert List3 due to repeated interceptions notified by EU Member States. The BAES inspectors stated that based on their own experiences of regular consignments of the same exporter and the sam

The sampling methodology applied for plant health checks of aquatic plants, fruits, vegetables and cut flowers is determined according to the risk posed to the Austrian territory by any harmful organism which may be present, rather than the risk of the lot being contaminated by harmful organisms. This is not line with Article 13(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

paragraph_text: The survey system, applied by France in the BZs is not in line with the provisions of the Decision. It does not provide the required level of meticulousness and territorial coverage and therefore, the information collected about the infection status of BZs is inadequate and unreliable.

In 2016, the surveillance in the BZs started in August and the activity was carried out according to a protocol, developed by DGAL. The audit team noted that: There were over 300 BZs in Corsica, the majority of which consisted of natural scrubland and/or mountainous area with difficult access; The 20 BZs in PACA were mainly situated in urban areas with numerous private properties and not always easily accessible. Taking into consideration these and the available resources France applied a specific system in 2016 as follows. In PACA a survey grid of 100m x 100m was used in the inner 1 km part of each BZ, while in the 1km ­ 10km part a grid of 1km x 1km was applied; In Corsica a grid of 1km x

In each grid square, two observation points were designated. The surveillance team checked the vicinity of the observation point for the presence of specified plants and took samples in the case of the presence of symptoms or any suspicion. The plants were sampled individually, composite samples were not collected. The CA informed the audit team that for better coverage of the areas, in the future new observation points will be selected each year. The audit team noted that the use of grids larger than 100m x 100m, in combination with the applied survey method, which does not include entering private gardens and natural areas difficult to access, was not suitable to obtain comprehensive information about the infection status of the area. The visual checks in the randomly selected observation points provided information only about a small part of a grid which was not representative and the vast majority of the area remained unchecked. Such surveillance is also not in compliance with the requirements of the Decision, which requires, in the BZ, that the surveyed area be based on a grid split into 100m x 100m squares.

Recommendation No 1 of the 2016 audit report recommends France to ensure that the monitoring in the BZs is implemented in line with Article 6(7) of the Decision. This recommendation has not been addressed. 15

Recommendation No 4 of the 2016 audit report recommended France to ensure that surveys in the DAs take into consideration the presence and biology of the specified plants, and in particular the accessibility of hosts in private gardens and in remote areas. The audit team noted that due to climatic conditions and composition of the flora in the BZs in Corsica and PACA, the survey period of August-December 2016 was suitable as practically all host plants of Xf subspecies multiplex and the vast majority of specified plants could be visually checked (being in full vegetation with leaves) and duly sampled. However, as it is explained above (see paragraph no. 45) there were no attempts made to acc

The eradication measures in PACA are largely in line with the provisions of the Decision. However, some delays in removal of the host plants in certain IZs and the non-removal of olive trees in the case of the Menton IZ compromise their efficiency. The use of protective netting is not in line with the Decision.

The eradication measures in Corsica are not in line with the provisions of the Decision and do not ensure the elimination of the bacterium from the IZs. 20 5.4 Movement control of specified plants Legal requirements Article 6(8) (road signs), Article 9 (movement ban), Article 10 (traceability) and Article 11 (official checks) of the Decision. The outbreak in Menton was treated as a special case for the DRAAF/SRAL for the following reasons: The first laboratory tests in 2015 identified the presence of Xf subspecies multiplex on some Polygala myrtifolia plants, which were removed and destroyed already in 2015; EU host plants of the subspecies multiplex known at that time, were also removed and destroyed; During the first laboratory test, a PCR method (Hernandez-Martinez et al., 2006) was used which could not detect Xf subspecies pauca; After the recent version of the EPPO Xf diagnostic protocol was published, the DNA extract of the positive sample was re-tested with a different method (Pooler and Hartung, 1995) and found positive f

The audit team noted that eradication measures in PACA, in particular the removal of host plants in the IZ, were generally in line with the provisions of the Decision, except for: Delays in removal and destruction of the host plants due to problems with identification and notification of the land owners and The non-removal of olive trees in the Menton IZ.

In Corsica, eradication measures, fully in line with provisions of the Decision were implemented only in the case of the first outbreaks, identified in 2015. The audit team noted: The number of outbreaks is very high; 237 were identified until February 2016 and a further 104 in the period February 2016 ­ March 2017; The number of host species, found positive increased rapidly and at the time of the audit there were 36; A part of the IZs are located in areas with difficult access where the removal of any plant is sometimes very difficult; A considerable part of the IZs cover natural land or abandoned agricultural land, where, after the removal of the hosts, no agricultural activity is expecte

Due to the above mentioned concerns and due to the limited accessibility, in newly established IZs in Corsica removal and destruction of all host plants is not carried out. The following plants present in the IZ are removed and destroyed: Until May 2016: plants which were tested positive or showing symptoms and all the Polygala myrtifolia plants, regardless of their health; Since May 2016 in addition all plants of the species, which tested positive, are also eradicated.

The audit team was informed by the CA that although numerous new host species were identified in Corsica in 2016, only about 25% of the IZs, established in 2015 and about 75 % of the IZs established in 2016 were revisited. During these inspections over 1,000 samples were taken and about 0.6% of these tested positive.
The CA stated that the immediate removal and destruction of the host plants in Corsica was not possible due to the large number of outbreaks, in particular in South Corsica. 19
On the basis of the above the audit team noted that in Corsica, the eradication measures were not in line with the Decision and therefore there is a continuous presence of the bacterium in the IZs.

The audit team furthermore noted that although there is no comprehensive information available about the range of vectors and their transmission potential, related to Xf subspecies multiplex, results of insect collections showed the continuous and high presence of cicadas in the IZs of Corsica.
