label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of plant health import controls
paragraph_text: Two newly recruited staff at Sofia Airport are not technically competent to carry out plant health checks, as a result, their checks cannot be considered as reliable. The same staff were unaware of interceptions made in other Member States. Furthermore, whilst staff are familiar with most official instructions, there are instructions on certain topics, which inspectors are generally unaware of. As a result, plant health checks are not always carried out in line with the BFSA's work instructions which, compromises the reliability of these checks. The system of internal audits has not been effective in identifying and addressing this.

The audit team confirmed with inspectors met during the audit, that they had undergone training as described by the BFSA. However, the audit team noted that two inspectors at Sofia Airport, who had recently completed their induction training, did not carry out an effective inspection of basil (see section 5.4.4 below). All other staff met by the audit team appeared to be fully technically competent.

Two staff at Sofia Airport, responsible for performing import checks for plant health, are not technically competent and cannot therefore be considered as qualified, at least to perform plant health checks, which is not in line with Article 1 of Directive 98/22/EC, in particular Point 2 of the Annex to that Directive. 4

The BFSA stated that they have issued official work instructions (see section 5.1.3 below) to ensure that, if followed, controls are performed appropriately and in line with Directive 2000/29/EC. However, at least in the case of sampling (see section 5.1.3) and dealing with soil attached to imported produce (see section 5.1.6 below), staff were generally not aware of these work instructions. The lack of awareness of official work instructions means that staff are not necessarily able to ensure the proper application of the Directive, and cannot therefore be considered as qualified, which is not in line with Article 2(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

Whilst observing an inspection of cut basil (Ocimum sp.) from Israel, inspectors stated that they were unaware of any interceptions having been notified on this trade elsewhere in the EU. In fact, at the time of the audit, basil was the second most frequently 6 intercepted commodity from Israel which in turn was the non-EU country with the fourth highest number of interceptions for harmful organisms in the EU1. These inspectors did not have available information on interceptions made by other Member States. This is not in line with Point 1 of the Annex to Commission Directive 98/22/EC. 5.1.4 Planning of official controls

The audit team noted that, at least in the case of fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, the work instructions on sampling are generally not applied in practice (see section 5.1.3 above). It was also noted by the audit team that RFSD inspectors operating at approved places of inspection were not aware of sampling instructions for fruits, vegetables and cut flowers. The senior official from the region concerned confirmed that she was aware of such instructions but considered them to be out of date and no longer relevant. The BFSA later confirmed that the instructions were current and should have been known by the RFSD.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of plant health import controls
paragraph_text: The work instructions provide for sample sizes which, in some cases, are too small to be considered representative of the lot and the sample sizes applied in practice are sometimes even smaller. Therefore, the resulting checks are not reliable in determining the pest status of the lot. 5.2 COOPERATION AND COMMUNICATION WITH CUSTOMS SERVICE AND STAKEHOLDERS Legal requirements Article 6 of Commission Directive 2004/103/EC. Findings 5.2.1 Customs

The audit team noted that, if applied, the sampling rates in the work instructions would, according to ISPM 31, provide an appropriate probability of detecting harmful organisms in small and large lots of fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, and plants intended for planting. However, for mid-sized lots, the sample size would, in many cases, provide a confidence level significantly below 80% of detecting even a 5% level of infestation and this reduced level of confidence was not justified based on risk. The work instructions on sampling do not therefore provide for a sample which is large enough to be considered as representative, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2

The audit team noted that the work instructions on sampling are not generally applied in practice in the case of fruit, vegetables and cut flowers. All inspectors met by the audit team, other than those at Sofia Airport who followed the work instructions on sampling, stated that they sample 200 individual fruit, vegetables or stems, selected at random from 10 boxes, which is not in line with the work instructions.

The audit team observed an inspection of citrus from Turkey and noted that: the lot consisted of 2 200 boxes, each weighing 10 kilograms; the BCD inspectors selected 10 boxes from five different pallets and inspected 20 fruit from each box; according to the work instructions, the sample size should have been 88 boxes. The sample size taken in this case was therefore lower than that provided in the work instructions, which already provides for too low a confidence level. The sample was not therefore representative of the lot, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

Inspection facilities are of a good standard, although with somewhat inadequate lighting. However, the facility at Sofia Airport did not meet all of the minimum conditions for carrying out plant health checks. These shortcomings make it difficult for inspectors to carry out appropriate checks.

Facilities at the land border crossing and seaports visited by the audit team were generally in line with EU requirements, although the lighting at the seaports was not appropriate as the light source was fixed behind the location where inspectors stand whilst carrying out their visual examinations, casting a shadow over the inspection area.

At Sofia airport, the audit team noted that the inspection facility lacked appropriate lighting and the inspection table was located immediately adjacent to the loading bay of the warehouse facility where there was a significant level of forklift traffic. This was not a suitable area for inspection since it did not provide any protection from the risk or noise of industrial traffic. This facility does not therefore meet all of the minimum conditions for carrying out plant health checks specified in the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC as required by Article 1 of the same Directive.

label_heading: Conclusions on action taken in case of non-compliance
paragraph_text: Interceptions of 'non-commercial' consignments, in particular those imported in passengers' luggage, are not notified to the Commission and other Member States. This does not enable the Commission and other Member States to evaluate and potentially mitigate the risk posed by such imports. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Bulgaria has established a comprehensive system of import controls for plant health, which is generally in line with EU requirements. Checks are carried out on all regulated plants and plant products as well as high-risk wood packaging material. The system includes some examples of good practice, in particular, the systematic sampling of high-risk plants and plant products for laborato

At Sofia Airport, BCD inspectors stated that they work daily with the Customs Services in the passenger channels. Customs officers identify passengers for inspection and in the event that they are carrying any quantity of plant material, BCD inspectors are engaged to determine whether the material is compliant with import requirements. BCD inspectors stated that, at the time of the audit, two seizures had resulted from these passenger baggage controls so far in 2017, in both cases the quantities detected were in excess of the small quantity concession and no accompanying phytosanitary certificate was present. The BCD inspectors stated that they do not notify such interceptions through the EU

The audit team studied notifications submitted by Bulgaria and noted the notification procedures laid down in Commission Directive 94/3/EC are generally complied with. However, the BFSA do not notify interceptions related to passenger baggage (see section 5.3.5 above). Failure to notify these interceptions is not in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Directive 94/3/EC.

The effectiveness of checks carried out at the PECs visited is reduced however, by the lack of facilities to ensure that the sample taken from containerised consignments is representative, as required by EU legislation.

The phytosanitary certificates are not endorsed with an entry stamp as required by EU legislation, however the risks arising from this are mitigated by the secure storage of the original documents, which effectively prevents their misuse. 5.5 WOOD PACKAGING MATERIAL Legal requirements Article 13(3) and Annex IV, Part A, Section I, point 2 of Directive 2000/29/EC. The DPPP has not issued comprehensive national inspection guidelines for import controls. The DPPP stated that, since inspectors were highly qualified and well trained, there was no need to provide detailed guidance documents, and that, moreover, the specific details of the implementation of import controls was left to the discretion of the regional and local services. The DPPP have issued translations of relevant ISPMs, notably ISPM 23 and 31, which inspectors are instructed to follow. In addition, some specific guidance documents have been issued by the DPPP, which deal with controls of Egyptian potatoes, collecting and dispatching samples for laboratory analysis and record keeping.

The audit team noted that many of the tasks and procedures involved with import controls are not covered by the guidelines prepared by the DPPP, for example, no 5 specific guidance is available on the procedure to follow when carrying out documentary, identity or plant health checks, or the process to follow in the case of non- compliance.

At Thessaloniki seaport, the RCPPQC had prepared a local guidance document on import procedures, the DPPP stated that it had not been approved centrally. At Evzonoi (the land border crossing with the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia), the RUDREV explained that they were planning to prepare their own inspection guidelines in order to ensure consistency of approach by different inspectors.
Inspectors carrying out import checks do not have available, written, up-to-date national inspection guidelines, which is not in line with paragraph 1 of the Annex to Commission Directive 98/22/EC.

The DPPP stated that this was due to limitations on the number of user credentials which had been setup by the DPPP for the EUROPHYT system. label_heading: Conclusion on handling of suspected and confirmed Cms and Rs outbreaks
paragraph_text: The action taken to enforce eradication and prevent re-occurrence of ring rot is only occasionally effective. Following ring rot findings, contaminated warehouses, storage crates and agricultural machinery are subject to decontamination measures. However, this may take place too late in the season as in most cases contaminated or probably contaminated material in practice remains within the premises of the place of production 19 without being controlled. Furthermore, the inappropriate designation of demarcated areas and extent of contamination and probable contamination together with the lack of adequate follow up measures observed in some places of production undermines the efforts to conta

However, the audit team also noted that the action taken by VIPHSI to enforce and prevent re-occurrence of ring rot is often not effective and in particular: In a place of production following a ring rot finding, no further testing of other potato lots to fully determine their plant health status and the extent of contamination was carried out. Other potato lots having clonal links with contaminated material were only assumed being probably contaminated without testing; In the same place of production this resulted in pronouncing two fields, the contaminated and a neighbouring one operated by the same machinery, as contaminated whilst all other fields of the same place of production were dec

paragraph_text: The system is undermined by human resources available which are too limited to ensure that all PWN-related control measures are implemented throughout the buffer zone in accordance with the national plan or guidance (see sections 5.2.3 and 5.4). 5.2 Annual surveys in the demarcated area Legal requirements Article 7 (1) of Decision 2012/535/EU Point 2 of Annex II (control measures in the infested zone) Point 3(a) of Annex II (surveys in the buffer zone) Findings 5.2.1 Surveys of trees in the infested zone

The identification of trees dead or in decline and their sampling is largely performed in accordance with point 3(a) of Annex II of Decision 2012/535/EU. However, the fact that human resources are not sufficient to allow the identification, recording and sampling of all dead or declining trees 1) to always be done as soon as they are noticed by the staff involved and 2) throughout the buffer zone during the Autumn-Winter, prevents the timely elimination of these trees and therefore lead to a risk of PWN spreading into the buffer zone.

Based on data provided by the ICNF, the audit team estimated that overall, one FTE was responsible for the survey and monitoring of more than 100,000 ha. The ICNF staff involved in these tasks confirmed the difficulty in doing everything in a timely manner in such a big area, especially for those who were also responsible for other tasks. The audit team indeed noted that despite the motivation of staff, they had difficulty to keep up with all their tasks in the territory they were responsible for (see section 5.4). 5.1.4 Laboratories

In the two Regions visited, the regional service of the ICNF informed that the territory of the buffer zone had been divided up and allocated to different teams of one or two staff members. They stated that all the territorial units were visited at least once a year and that a number of them were visited more than once (see also section 5.2.2). Although their objectives was to identify as many trees dead or in decline in Autumn- Winter with a view to "clean" the buffer zone before the start of the flight season, the ICNF staff stated that it was not possible to visit all the territorial units during this period. Some of them were using printed maps to mark those territorial units monitored over a certain period. The audit team visited the buffer zone in two Regions and noted that forest areas were in good condition, with the exception of areas affected by fire in the Region North. The audit team noted the presence of some declining trees in different locations. In a number of these locations, these trees had already been identified and sampled. In some other locations, only a portion of the trees had been identified and the ICNF stated that the additional trees would be identified (i.e. recorded in FITO) and sampled at felling. paragraph_text: With regard to feed, excluding GMO containing feed from testing for non-EU- authorised GM events has the potential to reduce the effectiveness of the official controls. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Controls of the authorised deliberate release of GMOs Legal requirements Articles 4(1), 4(3), 4(5), 6, 8, 9, 10 and 31(3) of Directive 2001/18/EC. Findings

Evira informed the audit team that it does not consider surveillance of national production through sampling and testing necessary, because the Customs' checks on incoming food ingredients (used by domestic producers) is considered to provide sufficient safeguards since GMOs are not commercially grown in Finland. According to Evira no food items containing GMOs are produced in Finland and consequently as the customs already checks the imported potential GM ingredients, there is little need to check potential cross contamination again at the national production level. Annual tests carried out up to 2013 did not, according to Evira, give any non-compliant test results. However, due to the subs

Evira classifies feed business operators into risk categories. The classification determines the frequency of inspection. Production of medicated feed, use of animal proteins and production volume are the main factors determining the risk category. As regards GMOs, Evira has chosen to almost exclusively sample and test (for authorised and non-EU-authorised GMOs) feed that is not labelled as containing GMOs (not supposed to contain authorised GMOs above a 0.9% level). However, there is no evidence that feed containing authorised GMO above 0.9% (and labelled as such) is less 7 likely to contain non-EU-authorised GMOs supporting its exclusion from sampling and testing.

Concerning paragraphs 24 and 25, Article 9.1 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 requires Member States to ensure that inspections and other control measures including sample checks and testing (qualitative and quantitative), as appropriate, are carried out to ensure compliance with the Regulation while Article 4.2(a) of Regulation (EU) No 882/2004 requires CAs to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls.

The CAs have access to a broad scope of accredited analytical capability for GM events, which underpins the effectiveness of the control system. However, current contractual arrangements, or the absence of those, leave room for the use of non-accredited methods and this has the potential to undermine the reliability of analytical test results. 5.3.7 Enforcement measures Legal requirements Articles 4(5) and 33 of Directive 2001/18/EC. Articles 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003. Findings

Evira has a framework contract with its laboratory for the GMO analysis of feed samples. The contract is flexible with regard to the GM events covered. It is stipulated that methods must be accredited or the validity of the method must be demonstrated otherwise. The contractual turnaround time of samples is two weeks for obtaining quantitative results for EU ­ authorised GM events.

The Customs Laboratory and the Evira Laboratory have been accredited to standard ISO 17025:2005. Both laboratories operate analytical methods for an adequate range of GM events. All methods of the Evira Laboratory for GM events in feed and 64 out of 68 methods of the Customs laboratory for GM events in food were included in the scope of 14 accreditation. The methods of the Customs laboratory have not been specifically accredited for seed. Since some of the accredited methods for feed apply to seed as a feedingstuff, the practical implications could be minor. However, the use of methods not included in the scope of accreditation, for testing of official samples, is not in line with the requir

Recent improvements in the coordination between the competent authorities have had a positive impact on the achievement of the objectives of Decision 2013/652/EU, although there are still gaps in in this respect which limit the number of Salmonella isolates available for AST (when the minimum numbers are not achieved), and in the supervision of the implementation of the sampling plan, which negatively affect sample representativeness 2,3. 5.2 ORGANISATION OF THE OFFICIAL MONITORING SYSTEM 5.2.1 NATIONAL MEASURES AND S

label_heading: Conclusions on national measures and sampling design
paragraph_text: The documented procedures and instructions in place could ensure adequate implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. The competent authorities have over time improved the design and implementation of the sampling plan addressing some issues that weakened this plan in the past. However, the gathering of AMR monitoring data in Italy is still not fully comparable with those obtained by other Member States. This is because further strengthening of the procedures is necessary, notably to verify that the minimum required slaughtered population is covered by the sampling and that an even distribution of sampling takes place during all months of the year.

The audit team noted that in 2016 over 90% of sampling was completed for all categories. The achievement of the targets set in the sampling plan improved from 2014 when only 83% and 66% of the planned caecal samples were achieved for broilers and turkeys respectively. Regarding 2015, the competent authorities achieved over 95% for all categories except for bovines under 1 year of age where only 74% was achieved.

The central competent authority has introduced in the 2017 AMR monitoring plan a new supervisory element that consists of the obligation for the regional authorities to submit the regional sampling plans for review to central level. Nevertheless, the audit team noted that the instruction does not specify the different elements to be included in the information provided in order to verify effectively compliance with certain elements of 2 In their response to the draft report the competent authority provided information on actions taken after the audit to address this issue. For more information please see the action plan presented by the competent authority to address the recommendations made

The audit team noted that the central competent authority did not verify if the slaughterhouses included by the regions in their sampling plans covered at least 60% of the domestic population which is the minimum percentage required by point 2.3 Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. During the audit and at the request of the audit team, the competent authority performed an evaluation of the 2015 sampling plan concluding that for bovines under 1 year of age 69.2% of the population was covered by the regional sampling plans while for pigs the figure amounted only to 47.1%. The data available did not enable the competent authority to perform the same exercise for poultry for 2014 and 201

The requirement set out in point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU that caecal samples collected at slaughterhouses shall be distributed evenly over each month of the year was not adhered to in 2014 and 2015 when sampling took place from May to December. The situation improved for 2016 and 2017 with sampling commencing in February and January respectively. The audit team noted the following: The time of approval of the AMR monitoring plans, which for 2014 and 2015 was March and for 2016 and 2017 late December of the previous year, did not allow the regions to design and issue the plans at regional level early enough to ensure that all months of the year were covered evenly

In the two regions visited, samples were generally taken on a Monday and Tuesday and on a few occasions on a Wednesday. This approach reduced the randomisation of the sampling days. The audit team noted that the NRL for AMR accepted samples until Friday which implies, with the sample delivery service available, that sampling could be routinely randomised from Monday to Thursday to fulfil the requirements of point 2.3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU and the EFSA guidance document 2014 9.

In the bovine slaughterhouse visited, samples were taken randomly selecting the day, with the constraints described above, and the animals to be sampled using an IT programme. In the poultry slaughterhouse visited, on the selected sampling dates most of the available lots were sampled in order to fulfil the required number of samples. In the pig slaughterhouse the sampling days and the carcasses to be sampled were selected by the sampling officer for reasons of convenience, which is not fully random 9.

label_heading: Conclusions on surveys for the detection of Xf
paragraph_text: Surveys in the BZ and IZs are not in line with the provisions of the Decision and do not provide a comprehensive picture of the territorial spread and extent of the infection and of the host range. This seriously compromises the eradication measures and has a negative impact on the implementation of other measures, required by the Decision.

Directly after the presence of Xf was confirmed in a nursery in Mallorca the ACCA the ACCA established a BZ of 10km radius and commenced surveying it, based on a 100m x 100m grid as required by the Decision. As this survey quickly resulted in numerous positive findings the CA decided to extend the BZ to the entire territory of the Balearic Islands (see chapter 5.3.1). Due to the available limited human resources and laboratory capacities, it was then decided to carry out surveys in the BZ, based on a 1km x 1km grid. The work started in parallel on each of the four islands. The main aim was to swiftly obtain comprehensive information about the outbreak situation.

The audit team observed inspections carried out by inspectors of the Plant Health Service and by employees of a public company specialised in providing emergency services in agriculture, rural development and nature conservation (TRAGSA) in the DA and noted that the survey teams: Identified the position of the 1km x 1km grid square to be checked with the help of GPS data and with a specific application on their computer tablets, which used satellite pictures indicating the already inspected squares; 13 Attempted to check visually at least 50% of the surface of the square. In order to achieve this goal they drove along all available roads in the square and walked into the fields where possibl

The ACCA informed the audit team that, at the time of the audit overall 62% of the squares had been surveyed; the coverage was higher in Mallorca and Ibiza. Samples for laboratory analysis were taken from only 15% of the inspected squares (see table III.). Table III. The audit team noted that the intensity and territorial coverage of the surveys in the BZ is not in line with provisions of Article 6(7) of the Decision and consequently cannot provide a comprehensive picture about the territorial spread and extent of the Xf infection. The number of positives and their territorial distribution (see figure I in chapter 4.2) already indicate that Xf is widespread throughout the three islands, in cultivated and abandoned agricultural land, natural and urban areas.
The audit team considers that the current survey results do not provide a comprehensive picture of the host range of Xf in the BZ. 5.2.3 Surveys in the Infected zones

The currently applied measures do not ensure the eradication of the pathogen. Given that Xf is widespread on three of the Balearic Islands on a wide range of host plants and different subspecies of the pathogen are present in the infected area, eradication will be very difficult to achieve.

After numerous positives were identified in the Balearic Islands in the period December 2016 ­ January 2017, Spain decided not to eradicate the outbreaks fully in line with the provisions of Article 6(2) of the Decision. In the vast majority of the IZs only the host plants, which were tested positive, were removed or intended to be removed. All host plants in the 100m radius of the positive plants, regardless of their health status and other specified plants, showing symptoms were not considered subject to eradication measures. Table VI and VII show details of the eradication work. Table VI. Eradication measures in the Balearic Islands (as of 9 June 2017) Island Positives Positives Positives

At the time of the audit, about half of the positive plants had been removed. Felling orders were issued in general two-to-three weeks after the final laboratory result was available. None of the proprietors has appealed against the official decision. 18 Thereafter, it usually took two-to-three weeks to complete the felling. Nevertheless, there were significant delays in certain cases due to difficulties in identifying the owner (e.g. holiday homes, abandoned land). (see table VI).

The audit team visited IZs in Mallorca and Ibiza, where positive plants had been removed and noted that: In the 100m area of the removed plants, there were numerous host plants, which were not removed (olives, almonds etc.). Many of them showed symptoms of decay to varying degrees. Only some of them had been sampled and found negative; In the IZs, an inventory was not made to identify the (non-host) specified plants and no samples were taken from those plants present; The IZs were not revisited to remove newly identified host plants.

The audit team considers that the current measures are not in line with the Decision regarding eradication, as some of the plants tested positive were removed with delay and the host plants regardless to their health status and other plants showing symptoms were not removed in the IZs. The CAs did not express a clear position about their future intention regarding the removal of host plants other than those tested positive in the IZs. 5.3.3 Agricultural practices

paragraph_text: The controls in the nurseries provide a level of guarantees that specified plants are not leaving the demarcated area and also that a possible outbreak is quickly detected. However, despite the wide-ranging information campaign it cannot be excluded that tourists or other individuals intend to export specified plants bought in the nurseries. Therefore there is a pronounced plant health risk related to the possible transport of specified plants in the luggage of private persons leaving the islands.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The competent authorities have a risk-based control plan in place covering feed additives, their ingredients and traceability, but their failure to consistently adhere to 7 planned arrangements and select establishments for inspections on the basis of established risk criteria weakens the efficiency of the control system.

The audit team noted that the number of planned routine controls had not been reached for at least the previous three years. As explained by the competent authority, this was due to human resource constraints, structural changes, the processing of available data, and outstanding inspection cases from previous years. Consequently the stated risk- based frequency of inspections is not being met. Furthermore, official controls that are performed at feed establishments no longer follow the planned risk-based criteria.

In the case of comprehensive inspections, the frequency is set once every three years but solely applying to the higher two categories of producing FeBOs and all feed additive producers, and only the higher category of non-producing FeBOs. As with routine controls, examples were seen of comprehensive inspection frequencies not being met. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The appropriate level of competency and knowledge were shown by all relevant competent authorities. Official controls targeted the relevant areas of feed business operators' obligations such as the implementations of HACCP based procedures, own control programmes including traceability, labelling and sampling. However, official controls did not verify that feed business operators met their obligation as regards the retention of samples. This weakens the effectives of the system of official feed controls. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

FeBOs' retained samples are labelled to enable appropriate traceability and stored for at least as long as the given shelf-life of the product. However, only a minority of FeBOs visited had retained samples which were appropriately sealed to avoid the possibility of tampering. In addition, in the majority of FeBOs visited there were no adequate written procedures to take such samples. The BAES inspections covered the issue of retained samples, however, in none of the establishments visited had the absence of appropriate sealing been identified as requiring corrective action. This is not in line with the section "QUALITY CONTROL"(4) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 5.2.1.2.2 Labell

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of sampling
paragraph_text: Planning of official sampling is risk-based and the implementation, for the most part, is adequate, being carried out by staff with the requisite competence and expertise. label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The audit team presented the BAES inspectors with various sampling scenarios and in all instances, they were able to quickly analyse the situation, and upon consulting the legislation, present the correct sampling procedural plan. Nevertheless, a systemic shortcoming was noted, in that the preparation of final samples from the aggregate sample was performed by simple manual mixing. This practice cannot ensure the appropriate homogenisation as required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The sampling equipment observed, whilst appropriate for sampling in certain conditions, did not allow sampling throughout the sampled portion when the product is stored in large bags or in bulk form. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by part 4 and 5 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

label_heading: Conclusion on actions taken on non-compliances
paragraph_text: Whilst there is a well-structured system for the identification and categorisation of non- compliances and initial communication to FeBOs requesting corrective action, its effectiveness is undermined by either an absence of monitoring or a much delayed follow-up of such non-compliances. paragraph_text: The audit team saw several examples of such warning letters for minor and major non- compliances. The FeBOs visited were able to demonstrate that, following their internal analyses and investigations, corrective actions had been taken.

paragraph_text: With regard to the BAES' monitoring, follow-up and escalation of enforcement of unaddressed non-compliances, the audit team observed that in the case of the three major non-compliances presented as examples, in two of these, four weeks were given to the FeBOs to take appropriate action, with the follow up inspection only taking place around one and a half years after the original inspection visit. In the third case from the latter months of 2016, no date for corrective action had been given nor had follow-up yet taken place. label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of sampling
paragraph_text: In the case of minor non-compliances, for which a time-scale for corrective action is, as defined in the BAES procedures, not given to FeBOs, there is no reporting mechanism, either by the FeBOs or the BAES inspectors, on corrective actions (if any) being taken. In relation to the ICQRF, audit programming is based on covering the full range of official control activities of each Territorial Office within a five-year cycle rather than on a risk-basis. label_heading: Conclusions on the development of the programme of audits
paragraph_text: Whilst OSQCA did not carry out audits for several years, it is now on track to audit the horizontal aspects of all 21 official control areas in the 2017-2019 cycle. However, given the scarce resources, the scope and depth of these audits is limited to evaluating compliance with the horizontal requirements of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on the development of the programme of audits
paragraph_text: A procedure for determining the risks associated with each official control system has been recently developed but is not sufficiently detailed to identify risk-based priorities, nor does the planning cover the actual performance of official controls and diversity of sectoral requirements. The impact on the current audit cycle is limited, however, given that a) OSQCA's aim is to gain a quick overview of all official control systems after a long period without audits, and b) there are currently only resources available to audit horizontal requirements. 5.2.5 Implementation of the audit process 5.2.5.1 Legal requirements Article 2(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that "Audit" "means a

A recently developed procedure has been adopted to determine the main risk associated with each official control system, which identifies certain areas of the food chain (e.g. production, processing, transport etc.) where controls are carried out. This approach to risk-based planning is a starting point but does not reflect the diversity of official controls and sectoral requirements within each of the 21 official control areas. As the broader official control areas have not been subject to a more detailed breakdown, the risks relating to the different aspects have not been explicitly identified (e.g. product, process, establishment type etc.). Furthermore, there is no methodology in place t

The strategy for the current three-year cycle is to audit each control system at least once to gain an overview of the state of play of official controls. This means effectively that risk prioritisation is limited to the order in which the official control areas will be audited. The concept of 'adequate coverage of all relevant areas of activity' of point 5.1 of Decision 2006/677/EC was taken to mean 'audit' of all relevant areas, rather than risk- based consideration of all relevant areas. OSQCA stated that this would be considered for the next audit cycle and that it would also reflect on lengthening the audit cycle to five years to facilitate more in-depth audits.

There is a regular feed training programme whereby the representatives of the NFCSO organise training for the county and district feed safety officers on different topics. In the last three years training was provided on traceability, evaluation of laboratory results, implementation of official inspections, assessment of labelling, and implementation of official sampling. In the period 2015-2018, the central competent authority organised seven training courses per year for county and district officials in different regions. The audit team interviewed officials who had participated in these training courses but their knowledge on certain topics (e.g. labelling and official sampling) was not s

Despite the fact that training had been provided on the legal requirements of feed labelling (see finding 4), county feed inspectors were generally unable to apply this knowledge during official inspections, and thus to undertake their duties competently, (see finding 33 and 34) which is not line with requirements of Article 6(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The audit team noted that, in spite of the centrally-developed guidance document on the practical aspects of official sampling (see finding 42) and training provided (see finding 4) on the legal requirements of official sampling, county feed safety inspectors, as opposed to the performance of official sampling carried out by the Food and Feed Safety Directorate of the NFCSO, were not aware of the guidance document with the result of them failing to follow the requirements on official sampling laid down by Commission Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. This calls into question the appropriateness of the training provided under the requirements of Article 6(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

However, the facilities were not well-maintained (flaking paint in the unloading area for products of human consumption due to an old leak and a damaged unloading ramp) and equipment unrelated to the performance of import controls was kept in the facilities.

In addition, the facilities were used for purposes other than those intended e.g. storage facilities at ambient temperature were used to store office supplies. In the facilities rodent pellets for pest control were exposed.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls on imported goods
paragraph_text: The implementation of the import controls on live animals and feed and food of both animal and non-animal origin was generally in line with EU legislation, though there were shortcomings in the implementation of documentary checks on some consignments of live animals and products of animal origin, weakening assurances that only compliant consignments are imported into the EU via the BIPs in question.

The controls on live animals were, based on the documentation checked by the audit team, in general well-implemented with a few exceptions: the Combined Nomenclature - CN code mentioned in part I of some common veterinary entry documents for animals (CVEDAs) did not cover all fish species, crustaceans, molluscs or corals; the catch area of wild fish was not mentioned on some other health certificates examined by the audit team. These omissions had not been noticed by the BIP staff. The audit team noted that in 2017 some registered equidae had entered Austria from Serbia as temporary admissions. Some of the animals had been converted into permanent imports contrary to the declaration in part

The audit team noticed the following shortcomings related to the documentary checks of products of animal origin: a) A consignment of raw hides from a non-approved establishment was allowed for further processing. This is not in line with point 2(f) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. b) One consignment of casings was imported, but the accompanying health certificate differed from the model health certificate. This is not in line with point 2(c) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. 8 c) A consignment of a blood preparation was exported from Austria to a third country without an export certificate. The consignment was re-imported without the original export certificate containing

A number of CVEDPs examined by the audit team had been accepted even though there were discrepancies in the content of the health certificate e.g. chilled instead of frozen meat, carcasses versus packed meat. There is a system in place for channelling of products according to Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. Confirmation of arrival at the establishments of destination is received via e-mail and thereafter registered in 9 TRACES by BIP staff. The audit team identified some shortcomings regarding the channelling of products, in particular related to the awareness of the approval of the physical place of destination within Austria or in another Member State.

The FASFC has prepared guidance on sampling requirements for imported PAP. Samples for microbiology have to be taken from the first 6 consecutive bulk consignments of PAP from each third country. The audit team identified that in some cases only 20% of the imported PAP consignments in bulk had been sampled without any evidence that analyses on the first 6 consignments had been carried out as required by point 2, Section 2 of Annex XIV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.4

However, the lists of plants in the chain of production and use of non-ruminant PAP for the aquaculture sector are not sufficiently accurate. This weakness hampers the competent authority's overview and has resource implications for officials who have to investigate each case when a decision on the presence of ruminant protein in a given consignment of PAP has to be taken. Moreover, certain inaccuracies identified in the approval and registration of some ABP plants and operators partly undermine the overall effectiveness of official controls. 8 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Articl

The audit team noted some inaccuracies in the official lists of plants along the chain of production of non-ruminant PAP to be used in the aquaculture sector, as follows: a. The list of food plants contained a very limited number of plants and in one case a plant approved for cutting bovine, ovine and caprine meat was wrongly listed in such list. b. The list of ABP processing plants did not contain several plants which were included in another official list containing ABP processing plants eligible to export non-ruminant PAP (see finding 16). c. The competent authorities confirmed that the above-mentioned lists could not be considered realistic, although in July 2017 the DGAHVM and DGFHFSN r

As a consequence of the previous finding (No 15), whenever an export/trade certificate of non-ruminant PAP has to be issued, or an ABP operator wants to have confidence that his suppliers are eligible for the production of non-ruminant PAP, it is necessary to contact the authority in charge of controls on the supplier and request an official declaration. The Ministry of Health keeps a list of operators, mainly processing plants, 6 which are eligible for the export of non-ruminant PAP, but this list does not cover all types of establishments covered in Section A, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 (see also finding 35). 5.1.3 Planning of official controls Legal requirements

The competent authority was unable to meet its planned targets for official controls in the ABP sector in 2016 and 2017 due to a spike in unscheduled approval visits and the limited time available to inspectors to carry out official controls. This indicates a weakness in the official control system given the resources available are insufficient to carry out the number of planned inspections and there is no built-in contingency to be able to absorb ad-hoc requests such as new establishment approvals. As official controls on registered operators will also have to be factored in from 2018 on, the implementation rate of inspections will almost certainly decrease further, weakening the system ove

The implementation rate of the scheduled inspections of approved ABP operators was 62% in 2016 and 58% in 2017 (174 out of 298 scheduled controls was actually carried out). The competent authority explained this low implementation rate by the fact that there had been an increase in the request for approval of composting plants and biogas producers, due to a national programme in this sector, and therefore, 215 approval visits had to be carried out in 2017. As these approval visits have to be prioritised and are time-consuming, scheduled official controls often have to be postponed to the following year. As inspections of registered operators will have to be considered in the future planning,

Routine official controls still need to be strengthened as they did not detect a number of shortcomings, in particular with regards to the issuing of commercial documents. Inaccuracies and information gaps in commercial documents used for domestic trade weaken the competent authority's ability to verify the traceability of certain ABP and PAP and to verify whether they are used in accordance with their intended purpose. The implementation of official controls in relation to hygiene requirements was in general satisfactory.

The audit team visited a storage plant which stored PAP on behalf of two processing plants. The establishment had been approved for the storage of PAP in big bags in 2016 and has never been inspected since. The audit team noted that the establishment has not been well maintained and at the time of the visit did not comply with legal requirements laid down in Section 1 of Chapter III, Annex IX to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 anymore. The operator declared that they are currently planning a comprehensive refurbishment of the storage premises. Moreover, in addition to the storage of PAP in big bags for which it was approved, the establishment is storing also a liquid product (poultry fat) in tan

In general, checks on commercial documents accompanying consignments of derived products were regularly carried out during inspections and these checks were recorded in the relevant points of the checklist. The officials met were largely familiar with relevant requirements; however, some of them mentioned difficulties in assessing commercial documents as they were not familiar with the model for intra-EU trade. In France, for national trade, there is no specific form required, but any document is accepted which includes the relevant information, in line with point (4a), Chapter III, Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. In all premises visited during the audit, the audit team checked a

Contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, TRACES notifications relating to intra-EU trade were not made for these products. The competent authority stated that such notification is not required by the relevant internal instruction (see finding 21). The percentage of PAP consignments arriving to France from other Member States which are notified back to the competent authorities in the Member State of origin is still wholly inadequate (approximately 4%), impacting on the fulfilment of traceability requirements in intra-EU trade.

The audit team reviewed the notes and determined that there is a detailed description of how the French competent authority has to notify the competent authority of origin via the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES) about the arrival of the consignments as required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In particular, note 590 is very detailed and includes also a comprehensive annex with a list of specific cases. However, OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM are not listed as requiring notification. 8 This is not in line wi

The audit team noted that, although training and instructions had been provided (see findings 5, 7, 21), in the vast majority of cases arrivals of consignments of PAP were not confirmed by the French competent authorities to the competent authorities of the Member States of origin by means of TRACES, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017, according to figures of the competent authorities, arrival of only 7.37% of such consignments was confirmed, and in 2018, 4.45%.

The reduction of seal checks of consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein exiting the EU from 100% of all consignments to just 3% chosen on a random basis is not implemented in accordance with the procedure developed for this purpose. The BIPs do not receive documents confirming the exit for all consignments which have been notified to them, the target of 3% seal checks of consignments is not being met and the competent authority is not consistently reacting to failures of the operators to confirm the arrival of the consignments at the port and their ultimate departure from the EU. Taken together with the fact that not all BIPs have access to the tracking 16 application that would enab

When, following the amendment of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, exports of consignments of PAP derived from ruminants started in July 2017, the BIPs in France implemented the instruction communicated by SIVEP (see finding 22). In the BIP visited, the procedure for export checks established by the BIP included a verification of the arrival of the consignment in the port via an extract of the tracking application "AP+" including the seal number, which the operator has to provide as the BIP only has limited access to this application. In addition, a second extract from the application is required when the container has been loaded and the ship has left the port, which usually is sent seven days a

In this way, the BIP visited by the audit team verified the exit of all 24 consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein in 2017 and 43 in 2018 notified to them via TRACES, until the exit of consignments via this port stopped in February 2018. Since the SIVEP procedure TI 240 was issued only in March 2018 (see finding 23), no seal check was ever carried out at this BIP.

According to the evidence provided by the competent authority, in another BIP, through which the majority of consignments were exported from France, the information that the consignment actually left the EU was received in relation to around 99% of consignments in 2017 and around 94% in 2018 up to the time of the audit (for 2018: 1049 out of 1139 valid commercial documents). Around 70 consignments were still under verification at the time of the audit, as the departure of these containers had not yet been confirmed via the extract of the tracking application. Evidence was received after the audit that these 70 consignments had exited the EU. In some cases, the operators had created the comme

This was the case for 270 consignments which were notified by operators via commercial documents in TRACES in 2017 and 653 consignments in 2018 up to the time of the audit. This is not in line with point 1(c), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Following the audit, the BIP confirmed the exit of the 653 consignments in 2018 by providing extracts of the tracking application "AP+". The audit team verified a random sample of these co

The audit team noted that in several cases different points of exit were selected in the corresponding box in TRACES (the BIP, but also the port as designated point of entry for phytosanitary controls). Neither the operator, nor the competent authority could provide evidence that the seals of these export consignments had been checked at any BIP, contrary to the requirements of point 1(c), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Operators producing insects or insect PAP for animal feed are subject to official controls which, inter alia, provide a basis for their registration, approval and listing. In one of the two plants visited by the audit team, there was sufficient evidence to support the approval. This was not the case for the second plant where approval had prematurely been granted without relevant EU requirements being fulfilled, indicating that the approval process is not consistently applied by the competent authority. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE PRODUCTION, PLACING ON THE MARKET AND TRADE OF INSECT PAP AND INSECTS AS FEED Findings

On the basis of the information provided by the operator of the second plant, although the main final product was dried larvae of Black Soldier Fly, the intention was to place on the market insect PAP. The audit team noted that the full approval had been granted recently (July 2018) without the testing of the final product over a period of 30 production days being completed, as this period only started on 1 November 2018. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of residue monitoring
paragraph_text: Whilst sampling in 2017 was implemented as planned, the inordinate delay in laboratory testing of samples taken in 2017 has substantially weakened the effectiveness of the residue monitoring plan for that year. Even if those samples are eventually analysed, there is a possibility that time-dependent analyte instability will invalidate the results (i.e. samples which were truly non-compliant at the time of sampling will test as false-compliant) and, in the event that non-compliant results would be found, the delay between sampling and analysis will militate against identification of the cause of the residue and effective follow-up investigations. 5.1.3. Other residue monitoring programmes Leg

Recommendation 2 of the 2011 report requested the competent authority to ensure that the length of time between sampling and laboratory results would be sufficiently short to allow for effective follow-up in case of non-compliant results 16. In 2017 the tendering procedure to contract an external laboratory failed and, as a result, half of the samples taken in 2017 had not been analysed at the time of the audit, remaining in the freezers of the NVL waiting for new arrangements to be put in place with subcontracting laboratories. The competent authority can largely have confidence in the laboratory performance and the reliability of analytical results as all laboratories are accredited, methods are generally appropriately validated and staff well-trained. However, a few factors weaken the system, such as the long sample analysis turnaround times, the non- adequate validation for a few rare matrices/species combinations and the fact that the NRL for residues of veterinary medicinal products does not completely meet its NRL obligations and has deficiencies in its quality assurance procedures. 5.2. Veterinary medicinal products 5.2.1. Competent authorities

The national residue monitoring plan stipulates that the sample analysis turnaround time is 10 working days for Group A substances and 30 working days for Group B substances . The audit team noted that these turnaround times count from the moment the sample arrives at the laboratory which analyses the sample. In many cases IZS laboratories (IZSs) sent samples to another IZS laboratory for analysis (see also findings 32 and 45), which leads to the fact that the turnaround times from sampling to finalising the laboratory report are longer than 10 or 30 days.

The audit team was provided with sample analysis turnaround time statistics. These showed that 80% of all samples analysed by the IZS laboratory were processed within the required turnaround time. However, 49% of the samples to be analysed for beta-lactam antimicrobials exceeded the 30 day turnaround time and were analysed within 70 days, and one sample within 165 days. Samples sent by the visited IZS to other IZS laboratories exceeded the 30 day deadline for 81.4% of all samples and 4.2% of samples had a turnaround time of 91 to 218 days. The long processing times may affect the analytes' stability and sample integrity (in particular for beta-lactam antimicrobials), which is not in line wit

The competent authority can largely have confidence in the laboratory performance and the reliability of analytical results as all laboratories are accredited, methods are generally appropriately validated and staff well-trained. However, a few factors weaken the system, such as the long sample analysis turnaround times, the non- adequate validation for a few rare matrices/species combinations and the fact that the NRL for residues of veterinary medicinal products does not completely meet its NRL obligations and has deficiencies in its quality assurance procedures. 5.2. Veterinary medicinal products 5.2.1. Competent authorities

The Italian laboratory network comprises five NRLs and 10 regional laboratories. Four NRLs belong to the National Health Institute (ISS) (residues of veterinary medicinal products, mycotoxins, heavy metals and pesticides) and one NRL (dioxins/Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs)) plus the 10 regional laboratories belong to the Experimental Animal Health Research Institute (IZS). All the laboratories are accredited to ISO 17025 by the Italian accreditation body Accredia.

The NRL has created and maintains a database which includes the information on, inter alia, CC-alphas and CC-betas of the methods applied by the IZSs. The information provided in the database is periodically evaluated and discussed within the IZS laboratory network, which was demonstrated in the form of minutes from two recent annual workshops between the NRL and the IZSs.

The competent authority can largely have confidence in the laboratory performance and the reliability of analytical results as all laboratories are accredited, methods are generally appropriately validated and staff well-trained. However, a few factors weaken the system, such as the long sample analysis turnaround times, the non- adequate validation for a few rare matrices/species combinations and the fact that the NRL for residues of veterinary medicinal products does not completely meet its NRL obligations and has deficiencies in its quality assurance procedures. 5.2. Veterinary medicinal products 5.2.1. Competent authorities

The audit team observed the standard operating procedure for the validation of methods and found that it was in line with the relevant provisions of Commission 8 Decision 2002/657/EC. Staff of the NRL stated that a software-based validation protocol will in future be applied for all method validations. The envisaged validation protocol is based on the approach outlined in part 3.1.3 of the Annex I to Decision 2002/657/EC.

The audit team examined the validation files and reports for the analysis of chloramphenicol in muscles and found that the validation plan was adequate and included all relevant provisions laid down by Decision 2002/657/EC. The validation process was adequately presented in the validation report. However, quality assurance documentation for routine samples was not available, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5 of Decision 2002/657/EC.

paragraph_text: The specific checklists provided for plastic do not include all the legal requirements of the DoC as listed in Annex IV of Regulation (EU) No 10/2011 to the point that most of these DoCs examined by the inspectors would not meet all the criteria set out in the legislation.

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs and FBOs
paragraph_text: The effectiveness of the controls in place is hampered by the fact that inspectors are not suitably trained or experienced to evaluate compliance of FCM legislation, including a detailed analysis of the DoC and supporting documentation. Such expertise is not always sought or cannot be provided by the CA. However, when sought or provided, the performance of the inspectors is largely enhanced. 5.2.5 Official Sampling Procedures and Laboratory Performances Legal Requirements Article 4(2)(c), Article 11, Article 12(1), (2) and (3) and Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

SFVS is aware that for the assessment of complex supporting documentation specific knowledge (i.e. chemistry education) is essential to verify the statements given in the DoC. At the time of the audit, such expertise is available at the NRL and at the CCA.
In addition, at central level, CAs in 2017 assessed a number of DoC and supporting documentation and only in 10% of cases, were DoC and supporting documentation in compliance with legislation.

At the second plastic manufacturer (also distributor), the inspectors moved one-step further assessing the contents of the DoC. The inspectors succeeded to a certain extent but deficiencies including information on dual use substances, a missing statement about Non-Intentionally Added Substances (NIAS) and incompleteness in the evaluation of migration from the printed surface were not identified. Inspectors also had difficulties in assessing EU requirements relating to GMP on inks.

Moreover, the audit team observed that the DoC provided by this manufacturer had some inconsistencies compared to the DoC prepared by its supplier. For example regarding specific migration limits (SML ­ i.e. for monomers and others starting substances) the manufacturer gave information not consistent with the information provided by the supplier. The point had not been identified by the inspectors during official control.

At the third plastic manufacturer, the inspectors asked for DoC and, as supporting documentation, they asked for starting materials (pellets) and migration test for suitable use for food. The inspectors assessed the DoC as in compliance without asking for evidence regarding GMP, specific migration test (verification of the compliance with SMLs), information about the process (re-use of cut off materials) and the risk analysis done by the BO to evaluate NIAS, theoretical calculation for migration limits and organoleptic tests.

The audit team noted that official controls on plastics, in most cases, do not include sufficient checks on the supporting documentation for statements in the DoC (final product). In particular, the following were missing: An assessment of the supporting documentation relating to the completeness of laboratory results in matters of SML or organoleptic tests; An assessment of NIAS ­ e.g. impurities, reaction products and decomposition that can be formed during the processing of a granulate into the final product; A verification of the BOs' risk assessment required under Article 19 of Regulation (EU) No 10/2011.

Concerning DoCs, the audit team observed that the inspectors relied on the information provided by the BOs. The inspectors have limited expertise for evaluating the formula of a product and for assessing the documents provided by the BOs.

The audit team observed that the inspectors, after requesting the help of a more experienced staff member of the CCA, were able to carry out an in-depth evaluation of the DoC documents provided and furthermore, completed the evaluation in a shorter time. The outcome of their inspection was also communicated to the FBO more accurately and clearly. However, deficiencies in the DoC regarding NIAS information were not identified by the inspectors.

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs and FBOs
paragraph_text: Official controls largely focus on the presence of a DoC presented by the BOs and did not sufficiently verify the completeness of the DoC. Limited controls were made on the completeness of supporting documentation for the DoC, which would lead to inadequate or incomplete risk assessments/DoCs being overlooked. Thus, non-compliant products might go undetected and correct application of the relevant legislation would not be enforced.

Moreover, those non-compliances have to be placed in the context where DoCs are not checked for their completeness but only for their presence or absence. This means that, regarding DoC, no non-compliances have been identified because the official control, so far, focused on the DoC presence and whether it was suitable for the intended purpose of use. At the time of this audit there was no evidence that supporting documentation has been systematically required.

GMP is controlled based on a checklist prepared by SFVS, which reflects the basic requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2023/2006. Inspectors rely mainly on what the BOs provide to them during the inspections concerning manufacturing procedures and risk analysis. Moreover, the risk analysis documents were never asked for nor verified by the inspectors.

One of the official work instructions contains a checklist, which prompts inspectors to examine the requirements of the DoC e.g. "does the declaration meet the established requirements?" However, at the first plastic manufacturer (also distributor) the representative of the RO and the inspectors informed the audit team that regarding DoC the inspection is limited and focuses on its presence or absence. An assessment of DoC and supporting documentation was not carried out at the time of the audit.

The inspectors informed the audit team that during inspection the assessment of DoC is not done. Regarding DoC, they limit the verification to its presence or absence. However, the CCA informed the audit team that the inspectors may, to some extend but not systematically, verify the statement regarding the intended use reported in the DoC.

The CCA informed the audit team that the risk assessments done by FCM manufacturers for substances referred to in Article 19 of Regulation (EU) No 10/2011 had to date not been requested and therefore not evaluated by the SFVS. Inspectors accept the DoC and supporting documentation without verification of completeness of the information given, which does not help identify cases where risk assessments should have been carried out. FBOs

Concerning plastic packaging, the fact that some elements of the DoC were missing (producer, dual use substances, overall migration and surface/volume ratio) was not identified by the inspectors, which stated that, at the time of the audit, they only seek for presence of the DoC without assessing such document.

The reports of the previous three years were available, checklists had been completed and annexes to trace the controls were available. From the previous reports, it was clear that up to now, regarding official controls on FCM, the inspectors focus on traceability, labelling and hygiene conditions (storage and use). Concerning DoC, inspectors limit themselves only to register its presence or absence. Moreover, in the reports reviewed by the audit team, there was no evidence that manufacturing and processing equipment had been controlled.

Concerning non-compliances, the SFVS provide figures (see paragraph 43 and 44) on their number, type and severity. During the visits to the two FBOs, the audit team reviewed four official reports and confirmed that non-compliances regarding DoC relate to its absence and that no verification had been made regarding its content. Importers/Retailers

The audit team observed an inspection to a retailer classified as low risk. The inspectors informed the audit team that, regarding DoC, they limit their inspection to verifying its presence without verification of the content. However, during this inspection they moved one-step further and attempted to assess the DoC. The inspectors succeeded to a certain extent but deficiencies such as dual use of substances, missing statement about NIAS and incompleteness regarding the intended use were not identified by the inspectors.

The three previous inspection reports, completed checklists and annexes to trace the controls were available. The reports indicated that, up to now, regarding official controls on FCM, the inspectors focused on traceability, labelling and hygiene condition (storage and use). Concerning DoC, inspectors limit themselves only to record its presence or absence. Moreover, in the reports reviewed by the audit team, there was no evidence that manufacturing and processing equipment had been controlled. The audit team was informed that at retailer level, manufacturing and processing equipment is checked only if there is a consumer complaint or suspicion.

The audit team observed one inspection at an importer classified as high risk. The high risk ranking was due to a RASFF notification. Compared to the previous controls, the inspectors moved one-step further and they performed an in-depth verification of the DoC. The inspectors informed the audit team that generally they limit the verification to the presence or absence of the DoC. However, the fact that reference to GMP was not mentioned in the DoC, was not identified by the inspectors. Moreover, the inspectors accepted the statement in the DoC regarding the intended use even if they did not properly verify the test provided. label_heading: Conclusions on Designation of CAs and Resources for Official Controls
paragraph_text: Although the CA acknowledge the relevance of staff with a chemistry background for in-depth FCM controls, current rules of engagement prevent their recruitment into the RPHA, thus limiting in-depth knowledge to a limited number of NRL personnel. 5.2.2 Registration / Approval of FCM Business Operators Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs
paragraph_text: Although DVFA inspectors have stated that they have not received adequate training on FCM legislation, they performed the appropriate checks. However, unlike PHA, SVFA has provided generic checklists that do not fully cover the legal requirements of the DoC to the point that most of these DoCs examined by the inspectors would not meet the criteria set out in the legislation.

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs
paragraph_text: Official controls rely on BOs' risk assessment, instead of verifying if these risk assessments are fit for purpose. This result in limited controls being made on the completeness of supporting documentation in the DoC, which implies that inadequate or incomplete risk assessments/DoCs are being overlooked. Thus, products which present a potential health risk could be placed on the market.

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs
paragraph_text: The effectiveness of the controls in place is hampered by the fact that inspectors are not suitably qualified to evaluate specific details of DoCs as required by legislation, for which they rely on expertise to be provided by others, but such expertise may not always be sought.

The PHA and SVFA are aware that for the assessment of complex supporting documentation specific knowledge (i.e. chemistry education) is essential to verify the statements given in the DoC. At the time of the audit, such expertise is available at the NRL and inspectors on the spot could ask for technical support. However, the NRL stated that, caused by a shortage of staff (one person in charge), they are able to address a limited number of requests.

Furthermore, based on the national legislation, in order to be employed as an inspector at the PHA, an education in the field of public health, including food safety, is required. A Degree in Chemistry, on its one, is not enough as a requirement. 4

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs
paragraph_text: Centrally, CAs do not keep data regarding non-compliances. Inspectors did not systematically record and did not systematically address the detected non-compliances. This leads to the loss of an element of risk-based planning (i.e. the history of compliance). 5.2.5 Official Sampling Procedures and Laboratory Performances Legal Requirements Article 4(2)(c), Article 11, Article 12(1), (2) and (3) and Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

Indeed, in four cases out of the five reviewed on the spot 3 In their response to the draft report the CAs noted that in light of the audit findings, measures will be taken for more consistent requirements for the DoC and supporting documentation. 9 which were under RPHA responsibility, no measures were taken after deadlines had expired and enforcement procedures were not initiated.

At one producer visited, the audit team noted that, based on the last reports for 2017 and 2016, the DoCs were not in compliance and in none of the cases were measures taken by the CAs to ensure compliance (i.e. correction of the deficiencies noted).

At the second manufacturer the last report available was for 2017 and no non- compliances had been detected. For this manufacturer no audit or other inspection regarding FCM was carried out. An audit covering GMP was planned for 2015 but never carried out, according to the RPHA, due to limited staff resources.

At the same RPHA the audit team also checked official documentation regarding a plastic bottle manufacturer. This manufacturer was audited for GMP in 2017 and no non-compliances were identified. This was the only official control carried out in the last six years to this FCM producer.

Concerning non-compliances the DVFA are not able to provide figures on their number, type and severity. During the visits at the two FBOs, the audit team reviewed six official reports and none of them contained non-compliance.

There is a system of national enforcement measures in place. However, no evidence was provided that these measures are consistently implemented or applied following inspections. In this way official controls lose they effectiveness in raising/maintaining levels of compliance and, in addition, it could result in products which present a potential health risk being placed on the market. 5.3 RAPID ALERT SYSTEM FOR FOOD AND FEED Legal Requirements Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Article 19(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
