Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs 13

At the RPHAs visited, the audit team investigated cases of non-compliant DoCs and the RPHAs follow-up of the cases and the measures (sanctions such as penalties and in two cases withdrawals of FCM related products from use before 2010). However, the follow-up at the BOs, in the majority of the cases was not in line with the procedures in place.

However, the audit team noted a number of shortcomings, where recommendations from the CAs were not followed up and no further action was taken regarding non-compliant BOs. Conclusion on National Enforcement Measures

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs and FBOs
paragraph_text: During official controls inspectors are able to verify the presence of DoC and, to a certain extent, to assess the completeness of those declarations. Limited controls were made on the completeness of supporting documentation for the DoC, which would lead to inadequate or incomplete risk assessments/DoCs being overlooked. Thus, non- compliant products might go undetected and correct application of the relevant legislation would not be enforced.

label_heading: Conclusions on Implementation of Official Controls over BOs and FBOs
paragraph_text: The effectiveness of the controls in place is hampered by the fact that inspectors are not suitably trained or experienced to evaluate compliance of FCM legislation, including a thorough analysis of the DoC and supporting documentation. Expertise available at central level is rarely sought3. 3 In their response to the draft report the CCA noted that concerning two DRAPs visited, whenever doubts are raised, an official request for support is sent to the Directorate-General for Food and Veterinary Matters - Department for Nutrition and Food. Different situations may result from the fact that the level of knowledge differentiation among the technicians carrying out the checks is still such that

At the first FCM manufacturer (producer of PET bottles) the inspectors verified the DoC of the ready-to-use bottle, asked questions regarding the raw materials used, identified an issue with regard to surface/volume ratio and also requested to see the supporting documents. The inspectors confirmed that they were not able to go further on what is already stated in the DoC since more expertise is needed. 13

The second FCM manufacturer (PET bottles blower) was inspected for the first time in relation to FCM. DoCs concerning raw materials and final products were requested and evaluated by the inspectors. However no further supporting documentation was requested and the inspectors did not ask for the risk assessment performed by the BO concerning the blowing procedure in order to evaluate the effect of the process.

At the third manufacturer, the inspectors carried out a verification check in relation to FCM (see paragraph 31). The inspectors examined additional documents provided and decided for which areas action was still required by the BO. They stated that they do not have the expertise to evaluate the completeness of the DoC and the supporting documentation. They informed the audit team that they can only evaluate what the BO provides to them. If a substance is not mentioned in the DoC they do not have the expertise to find out if such a substance is not present in the formula or is not mentioned for whatever reason.

The audit team observed that inspectors rely mainly on what the BOs provide to them during the inspections concerning manufacturing procedures and risk analysis including the presence of non-intentionally added substances (NIAS). The inspectors have limited expertise to evaluate the formula for a product or to identify if information concerning certain substances is missing. There was no documentary evidence that they systematically requested organoleptic test results from BOs.

The audit team noted that official controls on plastics, in most cases, do not include sufficient checks on the supporting documentation for statements in the DoC (final product). In particular, the following were missing: An assessment of the supporting documentation relating to the completeness of laboratory results in matters of SML or organoleptic tests; An assessment of NIAS ­ e.g. impurities, reaction products and decomposition that can occur during the processing of a granulate into the final product; A verification of the BO's risk assessment required under Article 19 of Regulation (EU) No 10/2011.

At one DRAP visited the audit team noted that the evaluation of DoCs covers the formal aspects. The inspectors stated that they do not have the expertise to evaluate the formula of the product and thus they are not able to determine if a substance is not present in a product or if the DoC is incomplete. In a particular case, and although the DoC was forwarded to the NRL and DGAV for their opinion on whether to carry out sampling, neither provided feedback advising DRAP's inspectors that the specific DoC was incomplete (substance missing), since they also rely completely on the information provided by the BO.

The CCA informed the audit team that the risk assessments carried out by FCM manufacturers and/or processors, for substances referred to in Article 19 of Regulation 14 (EU) No 10/2011 had to date not been requested and therefore not evaluated by the inspectors since that requires specific knowledge and expertise and support from central level. However, such a support was not available (and it had never been sought) at the time of the audit.

Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points (HACCP) plans are evaluated by the inspectors also in relation to the chemical hazards associated with FCM used. However, concerning FCM, the inspectors during the documentary checks relied on the information provided by the FBO rather than checking whether chemical risks associated with FCM foreseeable use are adequately identified and managed by the FBO2. 2 In their response to the draft report the CCA noted that relevant questions of this topic can be raised during the visit to the facilities. 15

Regarding this specific case the audit team requested that the inspectors sought an expert opinion. Based on the information they collected on-the-spot a draft expert opinion was prepared by central level identifying certain non-compliances related to the articles/ FCM selected. Some non-compliances not related to the DoCs had not be identified by the inspectors during their control but were mentioned in the expert opinion. The expert opinion drafted contained information on what the inspectors should additionally request of the FCM retailer to be able to conclude whether the article/FCM in question complied with the legal requirements.

ASAE informed the audit team that FCM controls were not a priority at the time of the audit and therefore advice/guidance from central level was rarely sought. It was explained that in 2016, and although a few non-compliances were identified related to the DoC, the possibility of requesting an expert opinion was not availed of.

The audit team examined a case of such a documentary check and saw that the relevant information DoC and supporting documents were attached to the file. The analysis mentioned on supporting documents related to ceramic material whereas the actual import concerned a plastic material. This was not identified by the inspectors during the import control.

In relation to its NRL duties, the laboratory has not undertaken coordination activities with the other official laboratories dealing with FCM, including organising comparative tests, which is detrimental to enhanced high quality and uniformity of the analytical results. 5.2.6 Procedures for Performance and Reporting of Control Activities Legal Requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team visited a freezer vessel in the Azores approved in February 2010 (date of attribution of the approval number). During the audit team visit, the inspectors indicated that a Hazard Analyses and Critical Control Point (HACCP) plan was not in place in January 2017 during an official inspection to maintain the approval and that it had taken one year for the operator to correct the non-compliance. The audit team while reviewing the official report on the 2017 visit, noted that this finding was not recorded and that the approval was not questioned. The next official control report dated October 2018 and indicated that a HACCP was implemented. During our current visit, the audit team

The situation described above, i.e. approval without an HACCP plan in place, is not in compliance with Article 31 (2) (c) and (d) Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusions on registration/approval of food business operators' establishments.

In most of the cases, the approval procedures implemented, which commence after food business operators are registered with the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Siret number), are fit for purpose and in line with the EU rules.

However, there are exceptional circumstances where different units of a same business operator can have the same unique approval number. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 2(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 which leads to the requirements of Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 not being met. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Official control of the production chain Legal requirements Article 17(2) of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Chapter I of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings General description of the official control syste

In the first case, during the approval procedure, the authorities approved as a single establishment and assigned a unique approval number to a set of four individual facilities located adjacently or near to each other. During the visit the audit team identified two different units (buildings adjacent and with a direct communication between them being considered one unit) physically separated, with independent entrances, different operational staff and, in one of them, performing different operations. These two units are located in a public common area which cannot be considered as a unique area under the full control of the food business operator. The authorities informed the audit team tha

Therefore, the approval procedure implemented by the French authorities allows the existence of exceptional cases in which Article 2(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 is not respected. As a result the requirements of Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 6(1) to (3) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 are not met.

label_heading: Conclusions on official control of the production chain
paragraph_text: The official control system in place covers completely the production chain of tuna fishery products and is globally implemented as planned. However, the audit team noted instances where the defined procedures were not adhered to, e.g. inspection frequencies for establishments on land and freezer vessels, and completion of the inspection within the defined timeframe.

With regard to the 15 tuna freezer vessels controlled by the department visited during the audit the audit team noted that all of them had been approved after an on-the-spot inspection and that after the approval several control visits were made. Using the period 2010 to 2017 as reference, the audit team noted that the defined minimum frequency for (8) Two approved facilities located within a wholesale market were visited during the audit. However, those visits did not cover the wholesale market as an approved facility. 11 the inspections under the SRN (once every two years ­ for freezer vessels considered as risk class I) was not achieved (see table below). (Number of vessels) Within Within

The audit team visited two freezer vessels outside metropolitan France and noted that they had been inspected by the relevant departments in accordance with the set procedures, although the minimum frequency of once every two years has not been followed.

The audit team visited eight processing establishments in five French departments and the authorities of those departments provided detailed information concerning the inspections of the approved establishments. During the visits the audit team noted that, with regard to the DGAL controls, the defined inspection frequencies (based on the risk category) were not respected in two out of six establishments (the remaining two establishments have been recently approved). These two establishments were located in two different departments. The audit team also noted that the frequencies for the inspections within the scope of DGCCRF were respected in the establishments visited.

The authorities of the two departments where the frequencies were not respected informed the audit team that another establishment also had not been inspected within the set frequencies. They attributed this to staff shortage (sick leave and transfer of staff), additional tasks acquired that were not initially foreseen (new approval, follow- ups, investigations of alerts) and increased export certification tasks.

label_heading: Conclusions on official control of the production chain
paragraph_text: In general the operations carried out by the operators were broadly in line with the EU rules with the exception of the freezing process in one establishment on land ("static freezing") and in one freezer vessel (double step freezing). The authorities deem these processes as in accordance with the EU requirements, which the audit team finds as not respecting the conditions set in Chapter I(I)(C)(1) of Section VIII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 14 5.3.2 Official control of the products Legal requirements Article 17(2) of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Articles 4 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Chapters II and III of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Findings
One of the vessels was a brine freezer while the other was a brine freezer with a second step of blast freezer (for fish not intended for canning).

label_heading: Conclusions on official control of the production chain
paragraph_text: In general the operations carried out by the operators were broadly in line with the EU rules with the exception of the freezing process in one establishment on land ("static freezing") and in one freezer vessel (double step freezing). The authorities deem these processes as in accordance with the EU requirements, which the audit team finds as not respecting the conditions set in Chapter I(I)(C)(1) of Section VIII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 14 5.3.2 Official control of the products Legal requirements Article 17(2) of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Articles 4 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Chapters II and III of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Findings

However, in one establishment the audit team noted that the competent authorities approved a freezing process that is not in accordance with the EU requirements. The audit team noted that a part of a cold storage room had been dedicated to freeze fishery products and the duration of the freezing process was set at 72 hours. The audit team checked the relevant production records and noted that, at the start of the freezing process the products were at 2°C, after 48 hours were at -11.5°C and after 72 hours were at -18°C.

The competent authorities informed the audit team that this type of freezing, "static freezing", is allowed in France and is documented in the Technical Instruction DGAL/SDSSA/2015-807 of 12/11/2015 and provided the audit team with a copy. The audit team informed the French authorities that the practice and the instruction do not respect the EU rules, namely the requirements of Chapter I(I)(C)(1) of Section VIII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on official control of the products
paragraph_text: The official controls of tuna fishery products are broadly carried out adequately and in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

Findings

paragraph_text: The official controls of tuna fishery products are broadly carried out adequately and in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on official control of the products
paragraph_text: However, those controls are not fully in line with Chapter II(C) of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Chapter 1(1.26) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) no 2073/2005 because samples are only taken at retail level (not random).

The plans mentioned above generally cover the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 in relation to environmental contaminants and parasites. However, they do not include testing of relevant fishery products for tin. Additionally, sampling for histamine carried out for product in the internal market, which only covers the retail level, is not implemented as required by Chapter II(C) of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and by Chapter 1(1.26) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 ­ random testing, which if it is carried out outside retail would require nine sample units.

DGCCRF also samples fishery products in the framework of its national tasks (see paragraphs 36 and 37). In 2017 fishery products were sampled (one sample unit and usually at retail level) to determine the levels of additives and in 2018 two specific tasks targeting tuna were executed. One (TN 273 KA) focused on the use of vegetable extracts and the other (TN 273 KH) on tuna loins (chilled/fresh). According to the authorities 64 samples were taken in tuna loins and 24 of these showed abnormal results for ascorbic acid (22 samples with values ranging 351 mg/kg to 3 500 mg/kg) and nitrates/nitrites (two confirmed cases with nitrosylated pigments). Non-conform results for histamine were not dete

However, although REGEPA is in operation since 2015 a substantial number of farms were not yet registered in several of the AC visited. This is not in line with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and could result in numerous farms, producing high risk produce, not considered for official controls. 5.2.3 Organisation and Scope of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

The CCA stated that roughly 95% of primary producers are registered in REGEPA. However, the respective AC visited estimated that approximately 95% in Galicia, Catalonia and Andalucía, 70% in Comunitat Valenciana and 60% in Murcia of farmers were registered in REGEPA at the time of the audit. The number of unregistered farms was mainly linked to the farm size and farms not receiving CAP subsidies. According to the CA a significant number of these unregistered farms could be involved in the production of very high risk products.

Representatives of the AC of Galicia informed the audit team that for the planning of official controls information from additional databases were used to capture the majority of farms in the AC. The Comunitat Valenciana initiated awareness campaigns among farmers to increase the registration rates in the database. In the Autonomous Community of Catalonia, information on REGEPA was circulated in order to increase registrations. 6 Approval of Food Establishments

label_heading: Conclusions on relevant national legislation and guidelines
paragraph_text: The legal provisions in place designate and empower CAs at central and provincial level for the implementation of official controls on microbiological risks in the whole production chain, including primary production. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Designation of competent authorities and resources for official controls Legal requirements Article 4(1) Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 Designation of competent authorities

There are central and regional CAs designated by national legislation regarding official controls on microbiological risks at all stages of production. However, the central and regional CAs did not act to implement such controls before and during harvest, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Therefore, a considerable part of the FNAO production is not covered by the official control system.
The CA stated that they can apply penalties to operators as imposed by the LMSVG, but this is restricted to food after harvest. Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations

The main national legislation in the context of this audit is the Food Safety and Consumer Protection Act (LMSVG), Federal Law Gazette of the Republic of Austria (BGBI) I No. 13/2006.3 This act covers the EU food law and Hygiene Package. The scope of the Law is described in paragraph 1(1) and comprises the requirements for food, water for human consumption, utensils and cosmetic products and the associated responsibility of the FBO. It applies to all stages of production, processing and distribution. It does not apply to primary production for private domestic use or to the domestic processing, handling or storage of food, commodities and cosmetic products for domestic private consumption. P

Several BMASGK guidelines are in place, in particular regarding: health requirements for persons handling food after harvest; staff training handling food after harvest; fruit processing at farms after harvest.
The Chamber of Agriculture of Austria has published guidelines on hygiene and own controls for direct suppliers after harvest. Conclusions on relevant national legislation and guidelines

The audit team visited five growers in two different Provinces. All growers had packing facilities and were direct sellers or distributing to retailers. In all visited premises, inspectors stated that they only carry out inspections if the primary production is linked to direct sales or the distribution to retail chains.

The inspections took place at the facilities where produce was received, cleaned, packed and stored. The inspectors followed the four modules of the checklist "producer" which cover facilities and equipment, produce and handling, hygiene and training and documentary checks.

During the audit visit, some inspectors asked questions regarding the use of field toilets during harvest and the protection of crops against pets and wild animals. The inspectors declared that this would not be part of their routine controls.

Staff performing official controls are trained on food safety in general, but there is no training regarding the reduction of microbiological risks and sampling for microbiological testing at primary production level and at sprouting premises. which is not in line with Article 6 and Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.2 Registration / approval of food establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings Registration of primary food producers 6

Food inspectors have at least a secondary school education with an additional training for specific food safety subjects. All staff met by the audit team has received training on food hygiene related issues, but no specific training for microbiological risks at primary production stage or for sampling for microbiological risks.

The audit team noted that the sampling procedure is very general and does not instruct the inspectors to foresee specific measures to ensure that the sample is not contaminated during sampling (e.g. no provision to use sterile tools and bags for loose produce). The inspectors did not receive specific training for sampling.

The inspectors met in the establishments informed the audit team that no specific training has been provided to them regarding the detailed legal requirements for the production of sprouts and seeds for sprouting. A few inspectors participated at BTSF training for FNAO. The knowledge gathered there, however, has not been shared between the inspectors.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and scope of official controls
paragraph_text: There is no official control system in place covering microbiological risks before and during harvest. The system in place for controls of primary production after harvest is not risked-based. This is not in compliance with the provisions of Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The audit team noted that the sampling procedure is very general and does not instruct the inspectors to foresee specific measures to ensure that the sample is not contaminated during sampling (e.g. no provision to use sterile tools and bags for loose produce). The inspectors did not receive specific training for sampling.

Official controls at farm level concerning microbiological contamination at primary production of FNAO were not defined in the planning process in any Province of Austria. The method for risk ranking set out in EFSA's scientific opinion (see above Section 4 Background) was not taken into account. BMASGK stated that the EFSA document will be used as base for a future risk assessment.

There is a system of risk categorisation included in ALIAS. It comprises of 10 steps, from 0 (lowest) to 9. FNAO primary producers with the exception of sprouting establishments are categorised in step 0 "other". The CAs should carry out controls every ten years. The frequency can be changed according to the specific situation at an establishment and the outcome of the official controls. The microbiological risk of the different FNAO products, e.g. ready-to-eat or soft berries is not taken into account for this risk categorisation and no routine control system is in place.

A sampling plan is developed each year by the BMASGK in co-operation with AGES. In addition to the risk-based plans, targeted national or provincial priority actions are carried out each year. Samples can be taken in the case of suspicion. The plan includes the scope of possible tests for each group of foodstuffs but does not specify for which parameters the sample shall be tested.

The CA has documented procedures, instructions and checklists to enable the CA to perform official controls at primary production level of FNAO after harvest. Regarding sprout-producing establishments the procedures, instructions and checklists are too general to achieve an adequate level of controls which is not in line with Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.8 Follow-up of former audits of DG Health and Food Safety The table below summarizes the follow-up to the relevant recommendations made in report DG SANTE 2013/6663-MR Final No Previous Assessment 1. Procedure VA-K 020A describes the planning preparation and execution of controls. It refers to the relevant paragraphs of the LMSVG. It does not contain provisions for primary production before or during harvest.

The checklist CL-K020A is annexed to the procedure. It is divided in chapters and modules which cover the different stages from production until distribution. The modules for the official controls start at the FBO controls on incoming goods (see paragraph 8).

Inspectors used the same general check-list as for FNAO. The checklist gives no guidance concerning specific sprouting issues. The inspectors checked the documentation of the FBO, including results of sprouts analyses, water analyses, cleaning and disinfection. The facilities visited complied with good hygiene standards in general; some minor shortcomings were detected by the inspectors and noted in the inspection report.

In both establishments, raw material was tested before use and monthly samples were analysed during production. However, regarding the testing requirements of sprouted seeds, the audit team observed that both operators did not follow the procedures as described in Annex 1 Chapter 3, point 3.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The CAs accepted these sampling procedures but did not follow the rules for granting derogations as set out in the same Regulation. The operators and the CA presented to the audit team some communication with AGES on this topic, but there was no formal decision taken. One establishment did not let analyse for Salmonella spp. as required by the Regulation.

At the second sprouting establishment the audit team noted that the batch identification number on the health certificate of a third country consignment of mung-beans did not correspond with the number printed on the labels fixed to the bags of the consignment. 10 Moreover, the checks on incoming goods did not comprise the check of batch numbers. One consignment of mung-beans did not bear identification marks or labels. These non- compliances were not spotted by the operator or the CA.

Procedures are in place for the registration of primary producers in a national electronic database at CAB level and for the registration of all other food establishments at MUP level. However, by estimation on a national level, at least 13.5% of primary producers, including FNAO, are not registered and not all garden centres selling seeds for sprouting are registered yet. Thus, not all FBOs are under official controls.

From the data obtained by NFA from the CABs, in 2017 there were 1,371 primary producers of FNAO registered in PRIMÖR, in the scope of this audit. At CAB level it is estimated that 13.5% of all primary producers are not registered yet, including primary producers of FNAO. The CABs stated that mainly small producers are not registered. The NFA informed the audit team that missing registrations are caused by uncertainty of the CABs which primary producers would need to be registered or not. Therefore, NFA plans to improve current guidance regarding registration of primary producers and make it more detailed.

The NFA confirmed that internet sellers of seeds for sprouting and garden centres selling seeds for sprouting are obliged to be registered as FBOs. The NFA has made an investigation regarding current registrations at the level of MUP. Currently 21 out of 26 identified sellers of seeds for sprouting are registered. 5.2.2.2 Approval of Sprout-Producing Establishments

There is an official control system in place along the FNAO production chain. The implementation at primary production, however, shows a number of gaps, notably related to provision of training and specific instructions (i.e. what are relevant non- compliances regarding the hygiene of staff, safe handling of food and suitable facilities). Therefore, significant non-compliances were not detected. Thus, non- compliant products might be undetected and the correct application of the relevant legislation might not be enforced.

Regarding the sprouting businesses the inspectors did not verify effectively compliance of import certificates because they were not familiar with the certification and traceability requirements established in Regulations (EU) Nos 208/2013 and 211/2013. Furthermore, inspectors did not verify that the own checks contained the analyses of sprouts for Listeria monocytogenes and STEC. Thus, the implementation of official controls on sprout producers is not sufficiently effective in verifying and, as appropriate, enforcing applicable hygiene rules.

The CA did grant informally derogations for the pre-testing of seeds of sprouting without any conditions which is not in line with the rules and criteria laid down in Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 for seeds for sprouting. Thus, non-compliant products might be placed on the market and could pose a health risk for the consumers. 5.2.5 Official Sampling Procedures Legal requirements Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Annex I, Chapter 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on Competent Authorities and Control Bodies
paragraph_text: A system of control is in place in accordance with EU provisions. CAs are designated with a clear division of responsibilities and tasks between CAs and CBs. There is good communication between the CAs and the CBs and other involved parties which includes the regular exchange of relevant information on the results of controls. However, in cases where operators change their CB, the exchange of information between the two CBs involved does not cover all relevant elements of the control file. 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal Legal Requirements Article 5(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 27(5) to (9) and (14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92

The CBs have procedures in place for certification of operators who move between CBs. The audit team reviewed one file related to transfer of operators and noted that not all relevant information related to the operators concerned was exchanged between the CBs involved. The CB just informed the other CB that the relevant operator had irregularities and was no longer covered by that CB as the certification was not renewed. This is not in line with Article 92(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which requires that the previous CB must hand over all the relevant elements of the control file and reports referred in Article 63(2) to the subsequent CB.

label_heading: Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of CBs
paragraph_text: CBs are accredited and approved in accordance with national and EU rules. CBs are generally subject to effective annual supervision by the CCA which includes office and witness audits. However, the CCA neither takes into account the reports of the accreditation body audits nor requires the CBs to submit their risk analysis procedures in advance of annual supervision which may undermine the effectiveness of the CCA supervision. In addition, the CCA did not establish deadlines for the CB to correct deficiencies detected during supervision. 5.2.2 Registration of Operators Legal Requirements Article 28(1), (2) and (5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92(2) and 92b of Commission Re

RENAR does not notify the CCA of the results of the accreditation audits carried out on CBs. So, this information is not taken into account by the CCA for their supervisory task which is not in line to Article 92c(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Moreover, the CCA does not require the CBs to submit their risk analysis procedure which is not in line to Article 92c(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. This may reduce the effectiveness of supervision as any deficiency related to the CBs' risk analysis may only be detected post factum.

The CB plan additional inspections and sampling of organic operators based on a risk assessment. The CB visited uses criteria to classify operators into high, medium and low risk categories. Different criteria to classify operators are used depending on the type of activity carried out by the operator (primary production, processor, importer etc.) which include inter alia previous non-compliances, the size of the business, the risk for exchange of products or the complexity and type of activities. According to the CB's procedure, all operators classified in high risk and 80% of operators classified in medium risk must be selected for additional visits. However, the audit team noted that the selection of operators for additional visits for 2017 was not in line with the described procedures. Only 47% of high risk operators were visited and around 60% of medium risk were visited (specifically 18 of additional audits took place in high risk operators, 238 in medium risk operators and 144 in low risk operators). A significant number of low risk operators were also selected for additional visits. The CB

However, in 2017 the CB did not fully follow its procedure for the selection of operators from sampling as 10 low risk operators were sampled while not 100% of high risk operators and 50% of medium risk operators were subject for sampling. paragraph_text: CBs are approved by the CA and subject to annual supervision in line with EU rules. However, the supervision carried out by the CA, did not fully consider all aspects of risk assessment and its overall impact on selection of operators for sampling and additional controls. 5.2.2 Registration of operators Legal Requirements Articles 28(1) 28(2), 28(5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Article 92b of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

The CB met described in detail how it had now changed its approach to handling risk assessment in order to address Recommendations No 1 and No 4 of audit report 2014- 7098. Previous non-compliances detected by the CB are now taken into account. However, the audit team still has concerns on the appropriateness of the overall risk categorisation of operators. The current approach is complex, utilising 20 criteria to calculate the risk score to categorise an operator. More significant is the realisation during this audit that the criteria and the scoring applied is contradictory in some instances and potentially leads to the CB targeting the incorrect operators for additional controls and sampl

The planning of the allocation of CB inspectors commences in mid-December and is finalised in April. At the time of the audit, the CB confirmed that the planning for 2018 in terms of inspection dates was not yet available. The CB explained that they inform the CA on a weekly basis of their inspection plans.

Since the previous audit, and in order to address recommendations Nos 1 and 4 from audit report 2014-7098, previous non-compliances are now factored into the risk assessment calculation. The audit team thoroughly reviewed the approach to risk assessment and noted a number of contradictions. The CB met has a highly complex approach to calculate the score to allocate an operator to a specific risk category which requires 20 criteria to be addressed. Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 specifies three criteria which have to be taken into account for the risk assessment. These are (i) results of previous controls, (ii) the quantity of products concerned and (iii) the risk for exchange o

Each of the 20 criteria is reviewed separately by the CB when it performs the risk assessment of each operator. In relation to the first of these criteria, previous non- compliances, the following approach is used. The number of points attributed to an operator when a non-compliant result is confirmed with regard to unauthorised substances is 25 points. These 25 points remain on the record of the operator for the purpose of calculating the risk categorisation of the operator for the subsequent five years. A similar approach for carrying over risk points is applied when complaints from other CBs are received relating to a specific operator. If this occurs, an additional 10-30 risk points coul

The second criterion, the quantity of products produced by the operator is only indirectly considered. One of the 20 criteria refers to the size of the operator's holding which only applies to primary producers. As an example, a holding the size of 1000 ha receives one risk point. This approach does not factor in the type of production, whether it is vineyard, tillage, or pasture and how such different production activities give rise to different quantities. The risk assessment criteria make no reference to the quantity of product produced for any other activity.
Regarding the third risk criteria, that associated with exchange of products (organic and non-organic), at mixed operators, a risk score of two points is allocated.

The CB stated that there were five other criteria which indirectly assessed the issue of quantity. However, the audit team noted that all of these criteria would only add one or two points per criteria. This would not ensure that such significant risks are taken into account in a proportionate manner.

The handling of other risk criteria also raised concerns for the audit team. Examples include the situation where more points are allocated to operators who have a greater number of species of animals on their land than those with a single species. This leads to a situation where an operator with 1000 cattle gets one point however an operator with two goats and two sheep got more points. The audit team also noted that when an operator complied with the requirement to obtain a derogation for the use of non-organic seed, an additional risk point was added.

Official controls at producers/processors of PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs are undertaken on a regular basis by following documented procedures and they are overall effective. However it cannot be ensured that all of the relevant elements of the product specification are checked by the CBs for all products

The audit team noted that not all the elements necessary to verify compliance with the product specifications were contained in the checklists, and therefore were inadequately checked, even if records were available at the operators´ premises. For example, the control plans for PDOs of animal origin did not cover verification that the feed came from within the same geographical area (which is also a requirement established in Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 664/2014). The CA stated that so far it has been satisfied with the statements made by operators that such feed is sourced from the geographical area specified in the product specification.

The CB records also demonstrated that the planning was followed. All users of the registered names were inspected at least once a year and other stages of the production, including producers supplying the products, were also subject to inspection in the period of three years foreseen in the control plans. However, as described in the previous paragraph, as the origin of feed is not verified, no separate inspections are planned to feed mills supplying to the producer to cross-check the invoices and delivery notes provided. label_heading: Conclusions on early detection and surveillance
paragraph_text: Although not all home slaughter in Part II receives official inspection, surveillance arrangements for domestic pigs in this area should make early detection of ASF possible. Outside the infected area, passive surveillance for early detection of ASF in domestic pigs is weakened by the fact very few samples are tested. This will hamper the early detection of ASF in this population should it occur.

Between June 2017 and February 2018, 373 and 109 domestic pigs were tested in Part II under active and passive surveillance respectively. In Part I, 129 and 255 pigs were tested under active and passive surveillance respectively. In the remainder of the country, only 5 pigs were tested for ASF under passive surveillance during the same period (see Annex 2). This is not in accordance with the ASF Strategy for Eastern part of EU which recommends enhanced passive surveillance in the whole country.

The fact that holdings with more than one pig are not registered, and consequently are not under official control represent a weak point in the control system. Outside of Part I and II, these non-registered holdings are unknown in terms of number and location. This, along with incomplete holding registers, will represent a challenge in tracing pigs and containment of disease in the event of an outbreak. 11

Holding registers were available on the three holdings visited by the audit team. These registers followed a national template and recorded number of pigs present and dates of events e.g. date of movement on / off and slaughter for own consumption. In both the large commercial farm and one of the smaller holdings visited, entries to holding registers recorded that more than one pig (between 2 - 8 pigs) had moved to non- registered holdings in single movement events. label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: Movement controls for live pigs within Estonia allows pig meat from Part II to be dispatched to other Member States and third countries. However, there are weak points regarding how pigs should be selected for ASF sampling and on the application of standstill requirements. These may increase the risk of spread of ASF infection.

On another holding visited, the team noted that pigs were moved to slaughter 4 days after a consignment of pigs were introduced from an area listed in Part II. This holding did not fully comply with the requirements necessary to avoid a standstill period e.g. the implementation of the biosecurity plan was checked every 6 months rather than every 3 months as required by both Article 3b of Decision 2014/709/EU and the authorities staff guidance. 5

The authorities confirmed that they do not require all holdings on the high biosecurity list to observe the 30 day standstill required for movement to slaughter ­ contrary to what is required by Article 11(3) of Decision 2014/709/EU.

label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: The surveillance implemented for domestic pigs, with holdings regularly submitting samples from dead pigs for ASF testing, contributes to the early detection of ASF. The delays observed in transporting some samples to the laboratory may weaken this early detection and delay measures to control the spread of ASF.

Holdings reviewed by audit team had records to demonstrate weekly submission of samples from dead pigs for ASF testing in conformity with ASF Strategy for the EU. In one county, turnaround time between sample submission and reporting of test results was 1 ­ 2 days. In two other counties visited, turnaround time within the reference laboratory was usually one day but in some cases it took an additional 4 ­ 7 days to transport the samples to the laboratory. Sampling is performed by the herd owner and the regional veterinary office despatches samples to the laboratory. The authorities confirmed that samples are sent to the laboratory using a bus service and the frequency of bus service impacted

There are satisfactory supervision and verification measures in place related to ASF controls in domestic pigs, which contribute to the effectiveness and consistency of the official checks. The weakest points in the verification relate to how authorised veterinarians deliver their controls and the disposal of ABPs. This prevents the authorities from detecting possible inconsistencies and preventing their recurrence.

In two counties visited by the audit team, authorised veterinarians performed the bi- annual sampling for ASF. There is no national guidance available for them to assist in the interpretation of Chapter IV of the Annex to Decision 2003/422/EC (ASF Diagnostic manual) and no official supervision of their performance. In a third county visited, the official county veterinarian selected pigs to be sampled and oversaw holding employee taking the samples.
The authorities confirmed there is currently no supervision of authorised veterinarians performing ASF sampling duties (see finding 13).

label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: The ARIB database is used by the competent authorities to record movements of pigs between holdings and can be used for tracing these animals. However, movements of pigs to slaughter are not recorded making it more difficult for the authorities to carry out forward tracing. The absence of a field to record sanitary information makes e.g. routine verification of movement restrictions difficult.

The audit team reviewed a selection of holdings in ARIB, both commercial and non- commercial, and confirmed the timely recording of farm to farm movements. The authority confirmed there was no field for entering sanitary information as required by Article 1 (1)(e) of Commission Decision 2000/678/EC.

Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: Each CA has put in place a system of risk based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by procedures and covering relevant aspects of the legislation. Most establishments producing RTE products are placed in the "high risk" category, reflected in a higher frequency of controls which is largely achieved by the CAs, except SFPA.

All CAs reported a shortage of resources over recent years, which according to the CAs and the internal audit reports seen led to not achieving the target for planned controls and occasionally to reducing the official samples for process hygiene criteria (limited staff at laboratory level as well). All CAs reported progress in hiring new staff after the ban on recruitment of public servants in Ireland was lifted. Currently, most CAs achieve targets above 90% of the planned controls with efforts being made to ensure a swift handover and training of new staff.

In contrast, certain difficulties in this respect are still encountered in SFPA. Figures emanating from the new quantification system (see paragraph 20) indicate that SFPA achieved 71% of the overall planned official controls, and 60% of the controls in high risk RTE food producing FBOs. The figures indicate that the two regions with the 7 highest number of FBOs have the lowest rate of implementation of controls (43% and 57%).

The same quantification system highlights that the FBOs producing high risk RTE fishery products have amongst the lowest rates of implementation of SFPA controls (between 29% and 39%) compared to other types of FBOs in the regions with the highest number of FBOs. The highest rate of implementation of controls concerned FBOs producing low risk non-RTE foods, which was explained by the lower number of scheduled controls. In most cases, FBOs had been subject to controls at a minimum of once per year in 2017, with only a small number of RTE food producing establishments receiving no official controls in 2017

The SFPA resource challenge had been identified by FSAI in a 2016 audit and work has been done to quantify it through the new quantification system, resulting in the data provided in paragraphs 10 and 11, but the corrective action is outstanding. SFPA attributed this to a lack of staff, difficulties in recruiting also due to budgetary constraints as well as the fact that SFPA is undergoing a management reorganisation.

The controls are largely implemented by the CAs as planned, with the risk based frequency, mainly without prior warning. However, in the case of SFPA, while the planned frequency of controls in establishments producing high risk RTE fishery products is three times per year, the implemented frequency in 2017 was approximately once per year - the same as for establishments producing low risk RTE - in the regions with the highest numbers of FBOs.

The similar level of implemented controls for all types of FBOs in these two regions, despite having been assigned different inspection frequencies on the basis of identified risks, together with the limited attention given to new approvals in another region (see also paragraph 30) suggest that SPFA, in the face of dealing with limited resource and with multiple tasks may have to look again at the prioritisation process to ensure resource for higher risk facilities within and between regions. 4.4.1.2 Procedures for official controls

SFPA highlighted that the joint controls between SFPA official controls staff support the identification of shortcomings and gave an example of one region where 80% of the inspections are joint inspections. However, in one of the regions with the highest number of FBOs, 1% of the inspections were explained by the CA to be joint inspections. The CA highlighted a constant increase in the number of fishery establishments in the busy regions.

No official control officer was assigned to one of the fishery establishments visited by the audit team. No official controls had been carried out in this establishment in the past year, although three were planned. Several non-compliances were noted on the day of the audit team visit, including some long standing ones.

Challenges were identified in particular in relation to the availability of personnel resources, aspects of training and verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings which identified some of these issues, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods, to a greater extent for SFPA. 4.3 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FBOS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The official controls over FBOs compliance with the EU food hygiene requirements are largely satisfactory, in particular in large establishments subject to DAFM controls. The unsatisfactory elements concern mainly the controls over FBOs compliance with Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 (a.in particular for the use of flexibility options and avoidance of cross-contamination in small establishments (LA and Dairy Certification), establishments with multiple activities (HSE) and establishments subject to SFPA control; b. for the use of food additives and flavourings, including smoke flavourings in their production), as well the controls over FBOs sampling and testing methods.

Some CAs aim to cover compliance with all legal requirements within two to three years (with two visits per year), while others aim to achieve the same in one year with a range between two to twelve visits per year, depending on the CA. The depth and thoroughness of the controls vary between CAs. The DAFM checklists for HACCP tend to focus on the main activity and due to the infrequency of the marginal activities the related controls focussed on the main production in the small dairy establishments visited. Marginal activities are subject to official sampling and the food safety management system that manages all activities is subject to audit (see also paragraph 47e).

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The official controls over FBOs compliance with the EU food hygiene requirements are largely satisfactory, in particular in large establishments subject to DAFM controls. In some of the establishments visited (producing fishery, dairy and meat products able to support the growth of Listeria), CAs accepted that FBOs do not carry out sampling for the detection of Listeria in the processing area and equipment during processing, but only after cleaning and disinfection, to assess its efficiency. This does not take into account the EURL Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes which recommends sampling during processing. Sampling only after cleaning and disinfection makes the detection of the pathogen difficult and can lead to a false sense of security.

paragraph_text: Comprehensive official sampling and testing of RTE food is in place with a largely satisfactory outcome, in particular at production level. paragraph_text: The contingency plan is outdated and thus it does not reflect the current structure and competences of both central and local veterinary services. This precludes better identification of rules and responsibilities of all services in delivery of the on-the-spot operations. As stated in the 2015 Commission report, it also resulted in the absence of 8 involvement of most major stakeholders during epidemic situation.

The Commission audit report DG(SANTE)/2015-7508 MR Final states several deficiencies related to the contingency plan, e.g. it does not contain: all relevant provisions to ensure the legal powers necessary for its implementation, detailed information on staff involved in control measures, their skills and their responsibilities, a register of staff that may be called upon nor a clear procedure for emergency staffing to deal with an animal disease crisis. These deficiencies have not yet been addressed.

label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring and sampling scheme
paragraph_text: The fact that during the 2016 Salmonella outbreak some serotyping test results were issued with delays of up to 3 weeks, indicates that the system in place did not satisfactorily deal with high demand on its capacities in crisis times, in particular to assure timely testing. The measures implemented still prevented additional risk to consumers, nevertheless, without the serotyping result, the competent authorities could have faced legal difficulties in imposing the necessary marketing restrictions.

During the 2016 outbreak this laboratory needed additional days (up to 3 weeks) from the detection of Salmonella to provide the results on serotyping. This was caused by different factors including the very high number of additional samples to be serotyped at this crisis period and to exhausting the stock of reagents. In both laying hen holdings visited affected by the 2016 outbreak and with samples tested at this laboratory, the measures restricting marketing of eggs from these holdings as class A eggs (for direct human consumption) had been implemented at the time of Salmonella detection (without waiting for serotyping) therefore preventing additional risk for consumers. 5.2.3 SNCP for bre

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The fact that the authorities do not request journey logs for most consignments, as these start mostly in Spain, prevents them from ensuring that journeys are realistic and have been planned in line with the requirements, in particular to avoid unnecessary waiting times at the port and the identification of a person or entity responsible for the sea leg of the journey.

The large majority of consignments arriving at the port are accompanied by a national movement document instead of a journey log (see also finding 18). This movement document is not nationally harmonised. In the different versions seen by the audit team, the declaration of fitness for transport was always signed by either the transporter or the farmer at the place of departure.

For the few trucks that arrived after long road journeys, the official checks do not detect the absence of a transporter for the sea journey on the journey log (which should have been indicated in box 6.4 of Section 1). Copies of tachographs are not collected, as required by Article 21(2) of the Regulation, to verify journey times from the place of departure to the port.

The competent authorities follow the instructions of the national protocol and do not request journey logs for animals travelling short road journeys before reaching the port. This is not in line with the Zuchtvieh judgement4, which indicates that these should also be considered as long journeys since it takes more than 8 hours to reach the destination in the non-EU country. In 2015 the Spanish authorities asked the Commission in writing about this issue and they proposed means of addressing it (see also finding 22); they have received no reply to date.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The new documented procedures could ensure ­ when fully implemented ­ that in general, animals are spared unnecessary suffering during the journey.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The lack of appropriate facilities at ports for checking the animals in the trucks and of no permanent veterinary presence during loading of the livestock vessels, combined with the absence of an official veterinarian at the place of departure to certify fitness for transport5 create a risk of unfit animals being transported. The system is further weakened by the lack of registers at the ports about the animals' fitness for transport.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The official veterinarians seen carrying out pre-loading inspections of livestock vessels were competent in this task and this provides a good level of assurance that livestock vessels inspected in this way are suitable to prevent unnecessary animal welfare problems notwithstanding the poor quality of records kept. However, the poor conditions on a livestock vessel which was allowed to load at one of the Spanish ports earlier in 2018 indicates that some pre-loading inspections are insufficient and do not ensure that essential systems for animal welfare are in place. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authority has recently updated its procedures which, if properly implemented, should ensure

The national protocol: Does not indicate the need to identify a transporter for the sea leg of the journey, required by Article 6(1) of the Regulation, nor their responsibilities (see also findings 17 and 35); Indicates that a journey log is only required if the time taken to reach the exit point is more than 8 hours.

The national protocol also includes sections indicating legal requirements and additional instructions. They both go into more detail than that the Regulation for both the approval of livestock vessels and their inspection prior to loading. It also includes relevant checklists. The pre-loading inspection checklist (Annex 5D) is incomplete, e.g. it does not include checks that the equipment listed in Chapter IV of Annex I of the Regulation is in good working order.

The competent authority indicated that the above-mentioned national protocol has not yet been fully implemented. Namely, the central competent authority has not yet verified how the measures prescribed in the protocol translate into practice, and how they are being applied. Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the competent authority to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT Findings

During the audit, the competent authorities at the two ports exporting animals could not provide annual data on the number of animals for which they had refused loading due to the animals being unfit or having arrived dead at the ports.

The national protocol procedures are in general sufficient for inspections to livestock vessels, but have not yet been fully implemented. These procedures include many of the criteria contained in the Network Document on livestock vessels agreed by the National Contact Points' network, and were well-known by the personnel met by the audit team.

The competent authority provided the information in the table below. This shows the total number and outcome of livestock vessel inspections at the time of loading (Article 20 of the Regulation) between January 2015 and June 2018. The type of deficiencies detected included: non-operational drinkers, presence of rust, lack of identified "hospital/isolation pens", dirty or poorly maintained feeders, no first-aid kits/supplies for the animals, lack of alarms at the wheelhouse for the systems for ventilation, light and water production, and lack of stunning equipment. The competent authority informed the audit team that all deficiencies could be corrected prior to loading and there was no need t
The competent authorities at both ports are not using the pre-loading checklist that is included in the national protocol.

During the audit, the officials described and demonstrated pre-loading animal welfare controls of livestock vessels carried out at the port visited. They were correct and well- performed. Regarding documentation: Records indicate that controls are carried out on ventilation (Point 2 Section 1 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation), cleaning and disinfection, watering equipment (Point 4 Section 1 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation) and ramps; Records also indicate that calculation is made to evaluate the stocking density (Chapter VII Annex I of the Regulation) and the amount of water and feed necessary for the animals (Section 2 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation); There are no records ind

The available documentation of those controls in the port which was not visited was very poor, indicating only that a control according to Article 20 of the Regulation had been carried out but without giving details on what had been checked.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The absence of facilities to unload the animals at the port might lead to welfare problems, particularly if a delay occurs with the loading of the animals. Although this is 5 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that at the place of departure there is an official veterinarian who issues health attestations, although these do not always include an attestation of fitness for transport. 8 mitigated by provisions in the contingency plans, the feasibility and suitability of the arrangements have not been fully verified by the relevant authorities. 5.5 WELFARE OF ANIMALS DURING SEA TRANSPORT Legal requirements Article 3, 7(2), 19 and 20 of the Regulation. Findings

Both ports lack appropriate facilities to rest, feed and water the animals outside the means of transport. This would not allow the authorities to fulfil the requirements in Annex I, Chapter III, Point 1.2(a) of the Regulation in the case, for instance, where unloading and loading of the animals from each truck requires more than four hours. The competent authorities require organisers to plan the arrival of trucks at the port in a way that avoids unnecessary waiting.

In one port there are no plans to add such facilities. In the other, there is a project to build a facility, with an estimated capacity for 600 cattle and a covered area with a capacity to park 40 trucks in the shade. The authorities will discuss this project for its approval in November 2018. 5.4 DELAYS AT THE BORDER Findings

The competent authorities require organisers to submit contingency plans for each shipment, which must include providing for a situation where the loading of animals is not authorised. At the port visited, the operator, as part of its contingency plan, has an agreement with a holding, located 60 km from the port, to use it for unloading the animals in case of need. According to the operator, the holding has capacity for 5600 cattle or 15000 sheep. The competent authorities have not visited this holding to confirm whether it would be feasible to use it at short notice, and its suitability.
The other port has not identified nearby facilities in which to unload the animals in case of need. Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The official controls at the port are insufficient to minimise the risk of welfare problems for the animals involved in the journey. These are the result of under resourcing, insufficient planning (e.g. no sufficient time for vessel inspection), absence of detailed instructions and verification to trigger improvement.

label_heading: Conclusion on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The port veterinarians do not have the sufficient technical knowledge to perform a proper inspection of the livestock vessel and thus they do not assess effectively all the necessary elements. This, together with the short time allocated for the inspections, the absence of an approved classification society to verify the strength calculations of pen rails and decks indicates that the Croatian system to approve livestock vessels for transport in the EU and for inspecting them subsequently before each loading is insufficient to guarantee that animal welfare requirements are respected.

The procedures did not indicate that there needs to be a transporter for the sea journey who is established, or in the case that the applicant is established in a non-EU country, represented in the Member State (Article 10(1) of the Regulation). As a result port inspectors did not detect the absence of an authorised transporter responsible for the journey by sea (which should be in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey logs). In practice, the port veterinarians make all requests regarding fulfilling the legal requirements for the export of animals to a forwarding agent, or the captain of the livestock vessel, although the competent authority has not defined if either of these actors have any l

The written procedures did not include instructions to take into account the judgement of the European Court of Justice in case C-424/13: Zuchtvieh3 (hereafter "the Zuchtvieh ruling") when checking journey logs; i.e. the organiser of the journey has to submit a journey log which is realistic and compliant with the Regulation up to the destination, including the stages of the journey which take place outside the EU.

The officials did not receive sufficient information in advance of the arrival of a livestock vessel, thus they had to assess everything (e.g. stocking density plan and feed plan for the sea journey) once the vessel was in the port.

The authorities have procedures for approval of the livestock vessels. Although these procedures include the network document translated to Croatian language, this has not been adapted to create suitable procedures and instructions to officials at the port. The instructions for staff to perform the vessel approval are not sufficient, which is not in line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The audit team noted that on 31 July 2018 the port veterinarians completed in one hour the preloading inspection of a large vessel used to carry over 3000 bovine animals (see also paragraph 23). For that vessel, it was unrealistic to complete a preloading inspection in just one hour.

The port veterinarians checked 78 loadings in 2017 and 40 loadings in the first semester of 2018. The reports of inspections did not indicate any deficiencies for vessels in the port in the last three years.

The veterinary inspector did not check the water production records or the working order of the drainage pump, alarms of the ventilation, fresh water and lighting systems5. This is not in line with Article 20(1)(c) of the Regulation. The procedures indicated the legal requirements for ventilation and alarms but did not indicate how to check these. The inspectors admitted that they were not competent to assess some of the "non-veterinary" requirements of the Regulation, such as the number of air exchanges required to provide sufficient ventilation.

The procedure indicates also the need for assessing the amount of feed, but not how to do it, conclude, record and report. The veterinarians generally relied on the agent's statement 5 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that " Inspection of the ventilation, alarm system, fresh water system and lighting system is carried out by the engineer of Ministry of Transport and infrastructure, Port authority-Pula at least 2 times a year, and when approving the ship jointly in cooperation with veterinary inspectors. After these checks, the veterinary inspector checks the functionality of all systems before loading, but does not perform detailed technical checks" 8 for t

The inspectors confirmed to the audit team that they assess ventilation subjectively, based on their experience, and did not verify the air changes per hour required by Annex I Chapter IV, Section 1 point 2(a) of the Regulation.

All this hinders continuous improvement to ensure the welfare of an

The competent authority did not provide evidence that it has a procedure to verify the effectiveness and appropriateness of the official controls at the exit point, which is not in line with Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The majority of shortcomings detected during this audit were unknown to the authorities, e.g. that port veterinarians did not detect systematic deficiencies in journey logs (see paragraph 18) and procedures with insufficient detail for carrying out a practical assessment of requirements (see paragraph 34). 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT

There were no reports on checks performed before November 2017. From November 2017 to May 2018 10 consignments were the subject of reports to the Member States of origin: one without one hour rest in the journey log, four that did not provide temperature records, three animals unfit for transport (two mastitis and one sick animal euthanised), one dead animal with no water in the vehicle and one with unsuitable dividers in the vehicle.

The audit team reviewed documentation of consignments arriving from five other Member States. None of them indicated who the sea transporter was. The audit team noted that: 5 In all journey logs seen, only organisers from one Member State had indicated the transfer of animals to a livestock vessel in box 6.1 of section 1. The logs from all other countries indicated the journeys ended at the port. However, in some journey logs the organisers indicated the name of the livestock vessel ­ so they had considered the journey out of the EU. But they failed to indicate the name and number of the authorised transporter responsible for this stage of the journey in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey l

During four days, 101 trucks from five Member States arrived at the port during a heatwave to load cattle in a vessel that departed in August 2018. For those 101 trucks, veterinary inspectors detected that: in 26% of the trucks, animals had been exposed during the journeys to temperatures above 35oC; 6 16% of the truck drivers did not provided temperature records of the vehicles and 7% did not provided the journey logs; the journey planning, which is responsibility of the organisers, did not avoid the arrival of vehicles at the same time; daytime temperatures were well over 30oC, and thus the loading of vehicles at departure should not have been carried out if authorities there had checked t

In that incident, the port veterinarians and representatives from the central authority did not have a clear course of action to follow to deal with the animals already in the port and those on their way4. After this incident the Croatian authorities notified three Member States by e-mail and for the other two Member States issued section V of the journey logs. Only one Member State replied to the Croatian contact point.

The central authority indicated that they did not impose sanctions in relation to this incident. In their opinion, the detected infringements were caused by the lack of proper planning in the countries of departure of the consignments. They indicated they have a procedure that allows any vehicle to be detained until the fine is paid.

After this incident the Croatian authorities requested better coordination, scheduling and communication to all interested parties (shipping agent, port operator and main road transporter). During the closing meeting of this audit, the central authority stated that they will improve the related procedures.

The authorities provided a document with the financial penalties for infringements to the Regulation. These range from HRK 10,000 (EUR 1,347) to HRK 100,000 (EUR 13,476). The average daily rental of a livestock vessel is EUR 25,000. The central authority indicated during the closing meeting that they plan to have new rules for sanctions next year. Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The current arrangements do not guarantee the welfare of the animals if there is a delay in loading a vessel. Neither the organisers, nor transporters, nor the authorities had contingency plans for this eventuality.

At the port, there was a single veterinary official in charge of many tasks, some of which occurred simultaneously, e.g inspection of the ship, control of documents from arriving trucks, assessment of fitness of animals. As result, not all tasks were completed properly and with the necessary attention.

The capacity of the assembly centre is not sufficient to accommodate all the animals loaded onto certain livestock vessels. In most cases, this is not a problem as the authorities co-ordinate the arrival of the trucks to the port and there are no major delays in transferring animals from road vehicles to the vessels. However, this can constitute a major problem in a case where the authorities refuse the loading of a big vessel. The authorities did not have arrangements to unload, accommodate, feed and water the animals in such cases and safeguard their welfare. This is not in line with Article 22(2) and Article 23 of the Regulation. 5.4 DELAYS AT THE BORDER

Poland has detailed documented procedures for official controls on animal welfare at all stages of transport and on animal health certification, even though with a few shortcomings. Some instructions for those procedures are also not sufficiently clear and thus differently understood by the different districts resulting in a non-harmonised approach in carrying out official controls.

Although the central competent authority indicated that the journey plan must be until the final place of destination in the non-EU country and that this has been always their interpretation, this was not clear to all DVOs and therefore there is a risk that travelling times are sometimes exceeded once past the EU border.

There is a system in place to assess planned and actual resting and travelling times before and after the journey. Assurances given by this system are nevertheless weakened by the failure to ensure that all journey plans cover the full journey until the final place of destination in the non-EU country and by the lack of evidence that the prescribed retrospective checks have been carried out.

Some points in the animal welfare instructions are unclear, such as: The instruction to check that journeys are planned until "final place of destination".
