Organisers notify the DVO well in advance of the intention to transport animals over long distances. This notification: Indicates the date and place of departure, the place of destination, the number of animals to be transported, the transporter and the vehicle number plate; Does not include a properly completed signed copy of Section 1 of the journey log, contrary to the requirements of Point 3(b)(ii) of Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. The OVs therefore cannot check in advance if the planned journey is realistic and complies with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, in particular with travelling and resting times.

Certificates of approval of vehicles for long distance journeys do not distinguish between adult and unweaned animals. As a result unweaned animals may not have access to liquid and be if necessary fed during long distance journeys. This shortcoming may negatively impact journeys starting from another Member State, if in that Member State the suitability of the vehicles is not also systematically verified at the moment of loading. 5.3 RESTING Legal requirements Articles 14, 15, 19, 25 and 26 and Chapter V, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Articles 1 and 2 of Commission Decision 2013/188/EU. Findings

Certificates of approval of vehicles for long journeys do not distinguish between adult and unweaned animals, contrary to Chapter IV Annex III of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. This implies that unweaned animals may be transported on vehicles that are inadequate for this category of animals with the biggest risk being the inability to access liquids due to unsuitable drinking devices (Point 2.2 of Chapter VI, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005).

The regions' ineffective verification of the reports submitted on the number of checks during transport can undermine the validity of the data collected and negatively affect the analysis of data that the GVI is required to perform. 5.4 UNEXPECTED DELAYS AT THE BORDER Legal requirements Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Returned journey logs were available for all exports examined by the audit team. The audit team saw evidence of retrospective checks carried out on those journeys for which notifications of non-compliances had been received. paragraph_text: Port inspectors carry out official controls in accordance with Article 21(1)(a),(b) and (c) of the Regulation, and the results of these checks confirm that the majority of animals arrive at the port in good condition, and where necessary, the port inspectors take action to ensure that any unnecessary suffering is dealt with. label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: The authorities deal with situations such as their refusal to allow the loading of a livestock vessel on a case by case basis; however, there is a risk that animal welfare may not be safeguarded if there is a delay in a sailing and the capacity of the control post is exceeded as the authorities have not determined any options for the arrangements they are required to make in such situations. 5.5 WELFARE OF ANIMALS DURING SEA TRANSPORT Legal requirements Articles 3, 7(2), 19 and 20 of the Regulation. Findings

The capacity of the control post is not sufficient to accommodate all the animals loaded onto certain livestock vessels. Co-ordination of the arrival of animals has taken place so that this has not been a problem; i.e. there have been no major delays in transferring animals from road vehicles to livestock vessels. However, the authorities had no arrangements to care for animals where they refused the loading of a livestock vessel and where the number of animals exceeded the capacity of control post. Article 22(2) of the Regulation requires the competent authority to ensure that appropriate arrangements are made to care for animals, and if necessary to unload, accommodate, feed and water them

The audit team saw that when the port inspectors refused the loading of a ship (see section 5.5) they had ad hoc discussions with their national contact point, who accompanied the audit team, regarding who to consult and what actions to take and 5 https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/animals/docs/aw_list_of_approved_control_posts.pdf 8 initially they did not have a clear course of action to follow regarding how to deal with consignments in the port and those on their way to the port. The audit team also noted that the transporter responsible for the road transport did not have a contingency plan to put into operation in the event that the authorities refused the loading of animals onto

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The competent authority had not provided sufficient information, instructions or access to suitably qualified staff, contrary to Article 4 and 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, to support port inspectors in checking the technical requirements of Section 1, Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, such as air changes per hour on board a livestock vessel. Therefore, the competent authority has not ensured adequate inspections of livestock vessels, as required by the Regulation, and has been repeatedly recommended in previous DG Health and Food Safety audit reports.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: Procedures include the relevant legal requirements but do not provide instructions for inspectors on how to verify these requirements as part of a practical inspection of a livestock vessel. Inspections of livestock vessels are therefore based on the experience of the inspectors, but not all requirements are adequately verified, which could have major implications for animal welfare during sea journeys. The competent authority had not ensured the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, contrary to Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The central authority has given repeated commitments, first given in 2009, that a system was being devised which included sufficient competence for inspection of livestock vessels. The central authority did give port inspectors opportunities to acquire knowledge and skills, by allowing them to take part in study visits and to take part in drafting the network document on livestock vessels. However, this knowledge was not transferred to create a system which adequately covered the requirements for livestock vessel inspection. 2 Judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union (Fifth Chamber) of 23 April 2015 ­ Case C424/13 see: http://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=C-424/13 4 5.2 T

The competent authority indicated in response to a recommendation in report 2012/6375 and again as part of an action plan for 2015 that they would provide a manual to support inspectors in this task. This has not been provided. The competent authority also failed to deliver on commitments made in response to a recommendation in report 2009/8241, and repeated in report 2012/6375, to set up a system so that the port inspectors would have sufficient professional support for carrying out inspections of livestock vessels. The only evidence of close cooperation between the port inspectors and the Slovenian Maritime Agency was in relation to an incident in 2017 where a livestock vessel loaded with

The port inspectors concluded that this livestock vessel was deficient regarding points 2(a), 4, 5, 6 and 7 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, i.e.: ventilation, the fresh water system, drainage, lighting, no alarms for these systems and no fire alarms in the decks accommodating animals. However, they had not identified these system failures in their report of their inspection of this vessel in 2017 and admitted that they were not competent to assess some of the "non-veterinary" requirements of the Regulation, such as the number of air exchanges required to provide sufficient ventilation.

In the last five years, the competent authority approved one vessel, according to Article 19 of the Regulation, for the transport of cattle and sheep. Prior to the approval inspection, the forwarding agent submitted certain documents: A declaration from the ship's master that the vessel was a suitable means of transport; A plan of the ship including the animal accommodation, disinfection certificates; A list of crew members; and A list of the last ten ports visited. The competent authority indicated in a checklist that various legal requirements, including those for generators, ventilation and alarms, were compliant. label_heading: Conclusions on registration and approval of food business operators
paragraph_text: The comprehensive approval procedure supports official control staff in their work and several elements of it are implemented satisfactorily. Nevertheless, staff's lack of correct understanding of certain provisions thereof as well as the less strict national rules do not ensure that compliance with the EU legislation is routinely achieved. 4.4 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OF FBOS PRODUCING RTE FOODS 4.4.1 Organisation and implementation of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Articles 3, 4(2)c, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Articles 1 and 5 of Regulation

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The differences in the development of the control systems for the different sectors suggest a missed opportunity for sharing good practices and exploiting synergies within and between DGCCRF and DGAL with a view to providing comparable support for staff carrying out controls in establishments with similar risks, further strengthening the control systems and their consistencies as well as ensuring a uniform control approach towards all FBOs. 4.4.3 Challenges encountered by the CA in the organisation and performance of controls over the production of RTE foods

Both administrations have systems to ensure officials have access to training, amongst other, on relevant RTE topics. a. DGAL training includes food technology, inspection of food safety management systems, HACCP based procedures, microbiological criteria, alerts and outbreaks management and auditing. In this regard the audit team noted that while the training for most of the above technical topics was delivered to a large number of officials, this was not the case for audit training, although national control procedures require local CAs to carry out audits or to use auditing techniques routinely in their controls in RTE producing establishments. b. DGCCRF training includes Hygiene Package

Both DGAL and DGCCRF staff have access to the "Better Training for Safer Food" (BTSF) initiative and the "resource persons" met participated in BTSF sessions. The official control staff met was in general experienced and knowledgeable for their work. Some support/training needs were identified during the audit, mainly in relation to: a. CAs' assessments and audits of good hygiene practices and HACCP, grading of non-compliances and enforcement and follow-up action (see paragraphs 11, 58-62 and 88 - 93). b. approval of establishments and keeping it under review (see paragraphs 25 to 28) linked mainly to the staff understanding of the rules. c. CA's controls over sampling and testing procedures

This suggests that the official control staff is not adequately kept up-to date in their area of competence as required by Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 for the areas highlighted above. The audit team did not note any problems related to facilities and equipment for the performance of official controls.

DGAL's had recently updated the approval procedures. The general inspection handbook instructs inspectors to check that the activities carried out by the establishment correspond to those covered by the approval. The FBOs visited by the audit team were in most cases approved for the activities they carried out. However, the audit team noted in four of the six approved establishments visited instances on non-compliance with the provisions of Article 31(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and/or the national procedures explained by the CCA as local staff's apparent lack of awareness of the rules.

label_heading: Conclusions on registration and approval of food business operators
paragraph_text: Both CAs have procedures in place for registration of RTE producing establishments and in the case of DGAL also for approval. However, the registration system does not favour the correct identification of production activities, including ready-to-eat, for all types of establishments. This has an impact in the DGCCRF's ability to organise the related risk based official controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: Each CA has put in place a system of routine risk based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by comprehensive procedures and covering relevant aspects of the legislation. The procedures for organisation of controls are currently under review for further fine-tuning the risk determination for the RTE sector. While some of the national provisions and procedures provide clarification for aspects that go beyond the EU requirements, other are less strict and if applied as such may potentially provide a lower level of safety than the EU requirements, in particular as regards Listeria, Coagulase-positive Staphylococci and controls for parasites in fishery products.

All FBOs are required to register with the Business Formalities Centres to enable the company to be created and be assigned a SIREN (business) number and a SIRET6 number. The FBO declares the main activity performed in accordance with the French Administrative Nomenclature (NAF) codes drawn up by the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE). The Business Formalities Centres are obliged 6 In their comments to the draft report, the CAs noted that a SIRET number is assigned to any primary or secondary establishment within the meaning of Article R123-40 of the Commercial Code, i.e. `any permanent establishment, distinct from the registered office or principal establishment a

The lack of clarification on what constitutes RTE which takes account of national consumption habits and FBOs' approaches as well as the lack of guidance for the composite products RTE sector do not support the related official controls and uniformity thereof. 4.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITY Legal requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings
An array of sector specific support mechanisms and access to several technical training, aid the CAs in their controls on production of RTE food, but to lesser extent for composite products.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The controls on Hygiene Package requirements in establishments producing food of animal origin are well developed. This was noted to a lesser extent for establishments producing composite products in particular in the case of DGCCRF, with an unknown percentage of registered establishments not subject to such controls on a scheduled basis.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the Hygiene Package, with some areas for improvement in relation to FBO's measures for prevention of cross- contamination and sampling and testing procedures. The CAs' ability for detection of the 23 non-compliances and assessment of the impact thereof is sometimes hindered by the current system for targeting controls and the limited use of systematic reviews.

National legislation applicable at retail, in particular for storage and transport temperatures for food of animal and non-animal origin. The national federation for trade and distribution also adopted guidance on microbiological criteria applicable at retail. b. The official controls over FBOs compliance with the microbiological sampling and testing requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 are limited. CAs are not 17 required to verify FBOs' sampling methods. In the case of alerts, CAs verify the testing method indicated in the laboratory test results. Nonetheless, official control decisions are taken on the basis of FBOs' test results. The CCA clarified that CAs have the option of taking official samples from time to time to provide clarification to the inspector, guide his/her work and determine the measures taken following the inspection.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The effectiveness of the control and enforcement system is also weakened by the fact that some long-standing deficiencies detected and classified by the CAs as medium or major ones are not adequately followed­up and enforced by the CAs to ensure the FBOs swiftly remedy the situation.

The procedures also establish deadlines for finalising the controls, reporting and following-up of non-compliances. Within the current establishment rating system, these deadlines do not support swift FBO action to address non-compliances when such non 7 In their comments to draft report, the CCA noted that the threshold of 1 000 cfu/g was set instead of 10 000 cfu/g for the other products to be consumed cooked, in order to take into account the risk of minced or thinly sliced products being insufficiently cooked through. In some cases, products labelled as `to be cooked' have been considered `ready-to-eat', either because the instructions on the label were not specific enough for the consum

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: Official sampling and testing of RTE food is in place. Official laboratories are accredited and subject to NRL coordination. The organisation of the official sampling for RTE food of animal origin prepacked by the producers, with a view to testing for Listeria, suggests a discriminatory approach focusing more on RTE food produced in other countries, including other MS.

Between 2013 and 2017 DGAL took 2167 RTE samples. From 2013 to 2016 the sampled matrixes only included unpasteurised dairy products and sausages while in 19 2017 sliced pig meat products were targeted. During this period the testing focussed on Salmonella and Listeria testing (STEC in 2014). Sampling of RTE for microbiological criteria does not take place every year at production level. The non-compliance rates identified range from zero in 2017 for Listeria in sliced meat products to 2.25% in 2016 for Listeria in unpasteurised dairy.

A training system, also covering issues related to the RTE food sector, aimed at ensuring that official staff can execute their tasks effectively is in place. However, the system could not ensure in some cases that official controls are carried out in a consistent manner; in particular, weaknesses were noted in the knowledge of SSI staff on the procedures and guidance for official controls to verify the FBOs' compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE food
paragraph_text: The CAs put in place a system of risk based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by comprehensive documented procedures and guidance. Although these procedures do not fully take into account the specific risks related to RTE food (in particular those identified by the CAs as high risk RTE), the impact is mitigated by the frequent and efficient controls in place. Some inconsistencies in the implementation of GSI procedures for risk assessments to determine inspection frequencies were noted.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE food
paragraph_text: Official controls and enforcement actions over RTE foods were satisfactory. However, shortcomings in the official controls to verify FBOs' compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 were noted in particular for GSI.

Although in each establishment visited, PSES inspectors provided the audit team with evidence (i.e. training certificates) on their participation in training sessions relevant to official controls of RTE food, these were not effective as the audit team noted some 8 weaknesses in their knowledge regarding the relevant requirements. For example: in one establishment visited, the audit team noted that when carrying out verification on the FBO's own-check sampling programme for microbiological analyses, the PSES inspector was not familiar with the existing CCA Order on this subject (see paragraph 64). The inspector attributed the lack of knowledge of the CCA Order to the absence of adequate trai

The audit team noted disagreement between GSI and VSES/PSES officials regarding the interpretation of the CCA procedure to be followed. GSI informed the audit team that frequency of inspections should be determined based on the result of the risk assessment (as described above). However, the VSES visited informed the audit team that when calculating the frequency of visits PSES inspectors should take into account further risk elements (e.g. volume of production, if the establishment is one of the major producers in the district, etc.).

The cases reviewed by the audit team showed an adjustment of inspection frequency by the PSES inspectors, resulting in a higher frequency of planned visits than based solely on risk assessment. However, in the absence of clear CCA procedures on determining the frequency of inspection, this result is not guaranteed in the future. Nevertheless, GSI informed the audit team of their commitment to review the risk assessment procedure in the light of the findings and conclusions of this audit (see Chapter 7). 5.4.1.2 Procedures for official controls VI

In one of the establishments visited (under the control of SSI) that produced certain RTE products able to support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes, the food safety criterion of point 1.2, Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 was applied, with the limit to be 100 cfu/g during the shelf-life of products. The audit team noted however, that the CA inspector accepted the use of this limit without the FBO's adequate demonstration that the product will not exceed the limit 100 cfu/g throughout the shelf- life, which is in breach of footnote 5 of point 1.2, Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (see paragraph 96).

The audit team noted in one establishment visited under SSI supervision that the FBO took one sample from RTE products instead of the required five for microbiological 16 analysis without being able to demonstrate to the CA by historical documentation that it has effective HACCP-based procedures (which is in breach of Article 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005).

Moreover, in two establishments visited under SSI supervision, the FBOs regularly took swab samples from processing areas and equipment and analysed them for Listeria monocytogenes. However, all these samples were taken after cleaning and disinfection. This is neither in line with SSI guidelines on this issue nor with the guidelines of the EU Reference Laboratory (EURL) (Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes) which recommends (in order to increase the probability of detecting a persistent strain) that the sampling should be carried out during processing. The system in place also includes reporting of and supervision over the activities carried out by official staff with the objective of verifying the implementation of official controls and the performance of the OV of the official controls. However, this system was not fully effective in detecting certain gaps in the controls, and therefore not capable of prompting appropriate corrective action in these instances. 5.2 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. label_heading: Conclusions on controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: Official controls are in general organised in line with EU requirements, their frequency 15 is risk-based and they follow specific documented procedures including those related to enforcement. However, the lack of resources, the time limitations to perform in-depth checks, the lack of details in the reports and the delegation of certain tasks to the FBOs without effective oversight, affects the overall efficiency of the official controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: While the system of official controls includes checks on FCI and animal identification, these are not fully reliable and are not sufficient to guarantee that any non-compliances are detected.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: CAs follow-up on identified non-compliances, but the measures taken did not address the cause in some cases.

The audit team was informed that in order to ensure that controls are carried out adequately, the following measures were put in place: On a regular basis, in each region a verification is undertaken to check that, at team level, planned controls are being carried out, non-compliances are followed-up within deadlines set, and that control reports are sent to FBOs within 14 days. Starting from 2018 all CAs (CABs, regional NFA and MCAs) must report to the central NAF office on the controls performed, which establishments have been controlled, the legislative scope of the controls, and on the non-compliances found. The intention is to collect better data in order to support determining the focu

The control staff organise the work, including how often to go on-the-spot, depending on the number of hours assigned to each establishment. The frequency of controls is related to the number of allocated hours (e.g. a registered cold store receives one hour per year which results in visits on the spot every few years when sufficient hours have accumulated, while a stand-alone meat establishment which receives more hours, may receive several control visits per year). These hours include preparation for the control, carrying out the on-site control and drafting the report (one third of the allocated time for each of these activities), which are then charged directly to the FBO concerned. 5

The hours allocated to perform certain controls might not support an in-depth evaluation in all situations. For example, a large meat products establishment with several production lines received 15 hours/year for controls, of which five hours occur on the spot; for one the biggest cutting plants, also producing meat preparations and minced meat, 39 hours for controls per year had been allocated; while for a medium sized meat preparations and meat product establishment ­ 20 hours had been assigned for the year.

All establishments visited had established HACCP-based systems. Official controls include as part of the routine controls and/or during audits the verification of these systems and the evidence available showed that the controls had been carried out as described and, in general, did identify very few shortcomings. The official controls also covered checks on pre-requisite programmes such as potable water, cleaning, disinfection and pest control.

The system in place also includes reporting of and supervision over the activities carried out by official staff with the objective of verifying the implementation of official controls and the performance of the OV of the official controls. However, this system was not fully effective in detecting certain gaps in the controls, and therefore not capable of prompting appropriate corrective action in these instances. 5.2 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. While detailed procedures exist for the approval of establishments, in practice new establishments are approved without their compliance having been verified under operational conditions. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS AT ESTABLISHMENT LEVEL 5.3.1 Organisation of official controls Legal requirements Articles 3, 8, 9, 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

The approval procedure foresees that establishments are given a conditional/provisional approval. In practice, however, and due to the system related to the recovery of costs for official controls through fees, de facto approval is granted without actually seeing an establishment in operation and without eg. the verification of the implementation of the Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points (HACCP) system; subsequent controls/routine inspection may only take place the following year. The CA informed the audit team that the legislation on fees is under review. 4

An effort has been made to keep the establishment list published on the NFA website, and fewer discrepancies -compared to the situation during the previous audit- were noted. Nonetheless, some differences were still found between the approved activities and the information appearing on the establishment lists published on the NFA website: The list of approved establishment indicates in some cases the postal address of the business which differs from the geographical location of the establishments. Two meat product establishments visited had been approved for activities, e.g. re- wrapping, that were not included in the published establishment lists. This deficiency has also been identified du

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: While the system of official controls includes checks on FCI and animal identification, these are not fully reliable and are not sufficient to guarantee that any non-compliances are detected.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: Although official controls related to identification marking, labelling and traceability had been carried out in line with EU requirements, these controls did not identify the types of shortcomings that were identified by the audit team during the on-site visits.

For each of the areas of controls assessed, instruction and guidance for controls had been issued by the NFA and made available by NFA both on their website in the "Kontrollportalen", which is available to all control authorities, as well as in "Kontrollwiki" which is also available to FBOs and consumers. For the areas assessed, the control staff is made aware of the legislation relevant to the area of control, and suggestions for questions to the FBOs are prepared.

National instructions on the identification of animals for slaughter (2015-09-04/BMODA) lay down the responsibilities of animal keepers, transporters, FBOs and the OVs. However, the verification of the identification of animals is done by the FBO after slaughter and not on the live animals, which is not in line with EU requirements or with point 5, third paragraph, of this instruction. Implementation of controls and resources

In the majority of the cases, official controls had been carried out according to the plan, with an exception for the region Central-North which continues to encounter difficulties with staff recruitment despite efforts to improve manpower levels. In this region, and depending on the time of year, a shortfall of up to 10 % in required numbers was noted for 2017;there is a need to employ nine additional staff in 2018. One additional staff member was recruited in 2018. As a result of staff shortage, not all the planned controls can or have been done. e.g. in one large establishment packing products for consumers, only 40% of the attributed and planned hours for 2017 for official controls (20.5

In the northern part of the country, the CAs faces challenges for the implementation of the controls due to the great distances between establishments, the concentration of the slaughter in certain times of the year and the lack of internet connection (all CA documents are in electronic format).

In the same region, it is planned that staff working in slaughterhouses carry out other controls in the months of the year with low slaughter activity. A system is in place to 7 appoint OVs on a temporary basis for the times of the year with higher volumes. These veterinarians, already employed by the SBA, are appointed by the NFA on a yearly or once every two years basis. For new temporary recruits a permanently employed OV from NFA provides induction training, all the required information and on-the-job training related to OV's specific duties. It is only when the latter is satisfied that the temporary OV is allowed to carry out his assigned official tasks independently. 5.3.2 Reporting of

Starting from 2018 a new report template is in use in several MCAs, including Gothenburg and Stockholm. The use of the new template by all NFA staff is delayed pending the organisation of training courses on how to write the reports. The template provides for the inclusion of all items checked during the controls - the previous system reported only on identified non-compliances- and includes details on the FBO's corrective actions in response to non-compliances from previous controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: Ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection are generally carried out and documented in a satisfactory way. However, the CA does not ensure that post-mortem inspection in low throughput slaughterhouses is done without delay as required in Chapter II, Section I (D,1) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. In addition, the final check of absence of contamination prior to health marking is still not considered the responsibility of the OV, which is not in line with Chapter V, 1.(s) Section II of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

In response to recommendation No 5 of report 2014-7229 relating to delayed post-mortem inspections in low through-put slaughterhouses, the CCA stated that the NFA has chosen not to proceed with the adoption of national measures in accordance with Article 17(3) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: Ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection are generally carried out and documented in a satisfactory way. However, the CA does not ensure that post-mortem inspection in low throughput slaughterhouses is done without delay as required in Chapter II, Section I (D,1) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. In addition, the final check of absence of contamination prior to health marking is still not considered the responsibility of the OV, which is not in line with Chapter V, 1.(s) Section II of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

The system in place to guarantee absence of contamination on carcasses is still not in line with Chapter V, 1.(s) Section II of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 indicating that "soiling, faecal or other contamination" are reasons to declare meat unfit for human consumption. The NFA considers it to be the responsibility of the FBO to verify absence of contamination and takes no responsibility prior to the health marking as part of the post 9 mortem decision. Checks for contamination of carcasses are not part of the CA's post- mortem inspection before health marking. The OV checks every day a random sample of carcasses, depending on slaughter volume. e.g. in a slaughterhouse processing 1

All competent authorities have arrangements in place for developing audit programmes and these reflect responsibilities and areas of official controls laid down in the Slovak MANCP. The DAC representative stated that, although it is planned, there is currently no methodology in place demonstrating how the risk criteria are applied through the risk universe to result in the audit programme. These are selected following the occurrence of claims notified to PHA, the number of notification of infectious diseases, e.g. hepatitis, or particular interest in some specific areas, e.g. production of baby food. label_heading: Conclusions on Biosecurity in pig holdings
paragraph_text: The many backyard holdings (~ 535,000 containing just under half the domestic pig population) and Type A holdings, with rudimentary biosecurity, represent the most likely route for the introduction of disease to the domestic pig population.

label_heading: Conclusions on Biosecurity in pig holdings
paragraph_text: The risk of spread of disease is much greater from Type A holdings as they breed pigs and can have commercial activity (sale of live pigs). 5.3 SURVEILLANCE IN DOMESTIC PIGS Legal requirements Council Directive 2001/89/EC; Commission Decision 2013/722/EU. Findings

In the Type A and backyard holding visited by audit team, biosecurity was rudimentary and there was no availability of disinfection facilities at the entrance to holding as required by Article 6 of Implementing Decision 2013/764/EU. 5 Conclusions on Biosecurity in pig holdings

label_heading: Conclusions on surveillance in domestic pigs
paragraph_text: The fact that there was no suspicion on CSF reported in the country in the past two years indicates lack of awareness of both pig keepers and veterinarians towards this disease. This weakens the field surveillance and thus the capacity to detect early the introduction of the virus.

The competent authority confirmed that in 2016 and 2017 there had been no suspicions of CSF reported in domestic pigs ­ this despite clinical signs of African swine fever recorded in two holdings in December 2017 which were subsequently confirmed as African swine fever outbreaks in January 2018.

In one county visited, the competent authority had recently investigated a pig herd where clinical signs included an increased number of abortions, dullness and discolouration of ears. In a second county, a circumscription veterinarian submitted samples from five backyard holdings in the same locality, at the same time, with no indication on submission forms there may be a common disease problem or that the samples should be processed as a priority. Neither event was treated as a suspicion of CSF.

The import checks in Germany are carried out meticulously, in line with either national or local guidelines. The effectiveness of the plant health checks carried out at the two main points of entry for plants and plant products is compromised though, by the size of the samples taken for 'non-ISPM 31' checks at Frankfurt Airport, which significantly reduce the probability of detecting any harmful organisms that are present, and the reduced checks of regulated commodities at peak times, at Hamburg port, which is not in line with EU legislation.

In most cases, the sampling methodology provides an adequate level of statistical reliability, according to ISPM 31. paragraph_text: The 2018 annual monitoring in the BZs was partly in line with provisions of Article 6(7) of the Decision as certain parts of of the BZs were not checked and the applied system of two observation points does not ensure that specified plants present in each grid are visually inspected. Therefore symptomatic plants could be overlooked and not sampled. Consequently the monitoring cannot fully confirm the status of Xf in those areas.

In the PACA region, in the period April-October 2018, FREDON carried out monitoring in the circles of 5km radius around the established IZs according to the DGAL work instructions (see blue circles in Figure IV). paragraph_text: The authorisation of movement of vine bud-wood produced in Corsica for thermotherapy in mainland France is not in line with provisions of Article 9 of the Decision.

label_heading: Conclusions on movement controls of specified plants
paragraph_text: The frequency of official controls in the nurseries together with the limited information about the final destination of the plants do not ensure that specified plants, which have been grown for at least part of their life in a DA, do not move out of those areas. In particular in the DAs of the PACA region there is a risk that specified plants leave the DA which could contribute to the spread of Xf.

There are many nurseries in the DAs, especially in the Department Alpes-Maritimes. FREDON agents are responsible for controlling the movement of specified plants within and out of the DAs. The audit team was informed that the nurseries are inspected generally twice annually during the vegetation period. One of the visits is the annual 21 plant passport control. Besides the producer and trader nurseries, inspections are carried out at the markets of national interest (MIN), at florists and at hyper- and supermarkets dealing with plants.

label_heading: Conclusions on movement controls of specified plants
paragraph_text: Although road signs provide certain indication about the Xf risk, they cannot inform the public effectively about the delimitation of the DAs.

In 2018 the SRAL of the PACA region placed signs at some petrol stations of a retail chain located inside the DAs. The signs provide information about Xf and the associated plant health risk in a visually attractive form. The audit team noted that the signs are not placed at the border of the DA. Although the format attracts attention, it is difficult for the bypassing drivers and passengers to read the entire text. The CAs consider that the current signs provide information for a broader range of recipients and can be better protected from vandalism than any sign erected at the border of the DA.

Recommendation No 3 of the 2017 audit report requested France to ensure that road signs are set up, indicating the borders of the DAs as required by Article 6(8) of the Decision. The CA stated that these types of samples ("prospective samples") are sent for analysis to the regional laboratory in another AC for screening of two elements (p35S and 14 tNOS). According to their workflow, in the case of a positive screening, they would repeat sampling and would take an official sample, in three repetitions and send these for analysis to an accredited GMO laboratory. So far, they have not used that option for additional sampling.

The audit team noted that the scope of accreditation for some of the regional official laboratories is very narrow. For example, the public laboratory in Cantabria, authorised for GMO analysis of food and feed samples, is accredited only for two screening elements, p35S and tNOS and for three event-specific qualitative methods; and in Aragon only two screening elements, p35S and tNOS were used which means that only certain relevant GM events can be detected (e.g. in soya bean some 50 % of events cannot be detected).

For example, one food sample (snack) tested positive for both p35S and tNOS and tested negative for Roundup Ready soya bean, maize Bt11 and MON810. During the recent potato crop production periods, the NPA and its regional county offices had not organised information campaigns, conferences or any other events on potato bacteria. Extension and/or consultation services to producers or other operators of the potato production and marketing sectors are provided occasionally at the beginning of the potato surveillance period or after ring rot outbreaks.

Non-registered growers usually state that they do not grow potatoes for commercial purposes but only for their own needs or limited local circulation (family consumption or animal feed). According to the data provided, in 2017 there were 49,125 small scale and 5,547 larger scale (more than one ha) producers who were receiving subsidies from 7 the APIA but were not registered with the NPA. This is not in line with the national requirement for registration with the NPA of potato producers with more than 0.5 ha and Article 6.6 of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The audit team came across cases of small scale non-professional producers growing potatoes on more than 0.5 ha who, despite being registered with APIA, stated that they were not aware of the obligatory registration with the NPA or that, in any case, they could not afford the registration fees imposed by the NPA.

Data from the National Statistics Service of Romania indicate that during 2017 ca. 133,600 ha were cultivated with ware potatoes. However, despite a collaboration agreement between the NPA and APIA, there is no consistent access by the NPA to the database of APIA. The producers with ware potato areas totaling more than 0.5 ha who do not comply with the requirement of registration in the phytosanitary database are not known by the NPA. Overall, producers registered with the NPA correspond only to ca. 9.5% of the total ware potato producing area; the majority (ca. 70%) of the area of ware potatoes is grown by operators who are not registered either with the NPA or APIA. The Single Authority stated that the concession applies to all 'non-commercial' imports, which includes imports by passengers, by post and courier. Due to the relatively large quantity of plants to which the concession applies, most non-commercial imports fall within its scope, and do not therefore need to be accompanied by a phytosanitary certificate or be subjected to systematic inspection.

In addition, the Single Authority, and the RPS visited by the audit team, stated that the small quantity concession prevented the effective control of passenger, postal and courier imports. They elaborated that this was because the scope of the concession, in terms of both maximum weight and modes of entry it applies to, means that it effectively captures all such non-commercial consignments. Consequently, the controls of these modes of entry were focused almost exclusively on detecting prohibited articles, rather than controlling regulated commodities.

Furthermore, the Single Authority stated that the scope of the concession was historic and that they were not aware of any risk-assessment used to arrive at the maximum quantities or the modes of entry it applies to. It has therefore not been established that there is no risk of harmful organisms spreading in the Community as a result of this concession, which is not in line with Article 13b(3) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

paragraph_text: A control system is in place with clearly defined responsibilities for CAs and CBs. There is good cooperation among these players and regular reporting of control results. However, there is delayed notification of major irregularities (see also chapter 5.2.7) and of operators changing their CB. 3 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal Legal Requirements Article 5(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 27(5) to (9) and (14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 92c of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Findings

Evidence presented by CB1 confirmed there was delayed notification to MARD and other CBs of operators who moved from CB1 to other CBs. This is not in line with Article 92(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Competent Authorities and Control Bodies

label_heading: Conclusions on Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal of CBs
paragraph_text: MARD annually supervises CBs visited. Reports issued are comprehensive and clear deadlines are indicated for CBs to rectify shortcomings. However, the number of witness and review audits by MARD is low in relation to the number of operators controlled by CBs in Romania. Hence, there is a risk that relevant information is not available to the CA for its evaluation of CBs' performance. Moreover, MARD does not verify whether CBs' risk analysis procedure is fit for purpose (see chapter 5.2.3). 5.2.2 Registration of Operators Legal Requirements Article 28(1), (2) and (5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. label_heading: Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls
paragraph_text: Both CBs visited undertake a risk assessment to prioritise controls to their operators and had fully implemented their planned controls in 2017. Both CBs exceeded by far the minimum level defined in the EU regulation for additional and unannounced controls. However, the CBs risk analysis can lead to some high risk operators being incorrectly categorised and hence not being subject to the required control frequency. 5.2.4 Controls of operators, traceability and labelling Legal Requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Article 23 and 27(13) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 65

Both CBs visited have procedures in place for the planning and prioritisation of controls of their operators. These procedures require that all operators receive at least one annual control and that at least 10% of these operators are subject to an annual additional control based on risk evaluation. Risk criteria defined in the CBs procedures in principle include those referred to in Article 65 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

A significant weakness was noted in the risk assessment methodology used by CB1. It turned out that an operator with parallel production of annual crop having a previous major non-compliance could still be categorised as a low risk operator. This has never been contested by the MARD during its supervision of this CB.
It was also noted that the risk assessment undertaken by one individual in CB1 was not supported by documentary evidence and the approach used was considered to lack transparency and objectiveness.

Both CBs visited define the size of farms by only considering the hectares of land under organic management and leave aside the non-organically managed land. Files reviewed by the audit team confirmed that operators with land under organic management had substantially more land under non-organic management and that this situation was not taken into account for the CBs' risk assessment. CB1 classifies processors into small, medium and big operators. However, there is no quantitative measurement of what defines the CB's understanding of a small, medium and big processor in its procedures.

Several files were reviewed by the audit team at CB2. A number of the cases related to parallel production, i.e. the growing of the same annual variety as organic and non- organic which is contrary to Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. The CB, in line with its catalogue of enforcement measures, downgraded the affected parcel and the related harvest had to be sold as non-organic which was confirmed during the following inspection. The CB confirmed that this type of non-compliance is frequently detected during on-site inspections. This CB does not require its operators to notify the annual schedule of production of crops prior to its on-site visit (as required in Article 71 of Regulati

Although there is a publicly accessible register of all organic operators, the absence of information relating to some operators' non-organic activities is a weakness. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Article 41 and Article 92f of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 5 Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Articles 65(1) and (4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Article 92c(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

Documentary evidence issued by the CBs visited does not contain information relating to the non-organic activity carried out by their operators. This is not in line with the model of Annex XII to Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Registration of Operators

The absence of reliable data on the location and movement of pigs within the non- commercial sector means that it is often not possible to trace animals that could have carried ASF virus to or from outbreak holdings. It also means that it is not possible for the veterinary authorities to enforce the prohibition to dispatch live pigs originating from the areas included in the Part III territory in the case of non-commercial holdings.

The veterinary authorities carried out a preliminary study in 18 counties at highest risk of ASF introduction to assess the impact and feasibility of implementing the new biosecurity rules. Key findings and conclusions reported include: a. A lack of awareness of the new biosecurity requirements among pig keepers, particularly on non-commercial holdings that have infrequent contact with veterinarians; b. Unregistered movements of live pigs between non-commercial holdings without notifying the authorised free practice veterinarian; c. Practical difficulties for veterinary inspectors to distinguish non-commercial holdings that engage in local trading activities from those that keep pigs solely
Prior to the introduction of the new biosecurity rules referred to above (paragraph 1), biosecurity controls on non-commercial holdings were not performed.

According to information provided by the veterinary authorities, approximately 47% of the total pig population (approximately 4.3 million head) are kept by non-commercial keepers on 630 000 holdings. Most of these keepers own less than five pigs, which are kept for personal consumption. However, there is no legal limit and significantly larger numbers of animals may also be kept.

To illustrate this, ADNS reports indicate that at least 1 095 ASF outbreaks occurred on non-commercial holdings between June and November. The vast majority of these outbreaks occurred in holdings keeping one or two pigs. However, 136 outbreaks occurred on non-commercial holdings keeping between 21 and 100 pigs and 15 outbreaks occurred on non-commercial holdings keeping more than 100 pigs.

High levels of non-compliance with Union pig identification, registration and movement notification requirements on non-commercial holdings have been reported in several Commission audit reports. Most recently, mission report DG(SANCO) 2014-7045 included a specific recommendation4 on the subject.

The veterinary authorities have not taken appropriate actions to enforce the legal requirements nor to apply proportionate and dissuasive sanctions in cases of non- compliance, as required by Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 respectively.

The lack of thorough epidemiological inquiries on non-commercial holdings, which account for more than 90% of all ASF outbreaks, means that opportunities are missed to intercept infected live animals and contaminated products before they spread disease to previously uninfected areas.

The operational manual provides instructions on the completion of the epidemiological inquiry: a. Detailed templates (Forms B.7 and B.8) should be used to prepare the initial and final epidemiological inquiry in the case of larger outbreaks (typically on holdings keeping more than 20 pigs). b. In the case of smaller outbreaks an abbreviated epidemiological report template (Form A.4) should be used. It collects contact details for the holding and records basic information about the farm collected during the initial interviews with the animal keeper and local free practice veterinarian.

The audit team reviewed the epidemiological inquiries carried out for several outbreaks on non-commercial pig holdings. In no case did the veterinary authorities trace the movement of persons, vehicles, pigs, carcases, semen, meat and other materials which could have carried the virus to or from the holdings in question, which is not in line with the requirement established in Article 8 of Council Directive 2002/60/EC.

Live pigs and their products coming from non-commercial holdings located in the areas defined in Part III of the annex to Commission Implementing Decision 2014/709/EU are entering the national market. This has allowed the disease to spread long distances to counties that were previously free of disease. 5.5 COORDINATION Legal requirements Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, particularly Articles 4 ­ 10 Council Directive 2002/60/EC, particularly Annex VI (c) Findings

However, they do not specify the checks they should be made to verify compliance with the conditions (30 day residency, negative laboratory test results or regular holding inspections) that the live pigs must satisfy in order for their meat to be placed on the national market.

Furthermore, the service notes do not require official veterinarians responsible for holdings of origin to declare that these conditions have been verified in the documents that accompany the animals to the slaughterhouse. Consequently, official veterinarians responsible for applying health marks and/or certifying that the fresh meat has been produced from eligible animals are not in possession of all necessary information.

The audit team examined the documents that accompanied slaughtered pigs originating within the Part III territory. They had been completed in accordance with the service notes and did not include all necessary information concerning the eligibility of the animals.

label_heading: Conclusions on management of official controls
paragraph_text: The competent authorities' approach to the setting of objectives and the planning and reporting of official controls is mainly operational "business as usual" with no targets, indicators or measurement of progress, nor any prioritisation of controls or allocation of resources and as such is insufficient to bring measureable change.

The Länder working group on animal welfare (LAV-AGT) has identified seven general strategic and operational objectives for the areas of food and feed safety, animal health and welfare. The first relates to optimising the quality management system (QMS) for official controls across all competent authorities and sectors including verification through appropriate audit systems. This should, by default, improve consistency and efficacy of controls, i.e. have an impact on animal welfare. However, there is no baseline set or operational objectives laid down to measure if projected outcomes for animal welfare are successful or not.

The second and third "strategic" objectives relate to improving procedures and are, as such, operational rather than strategic objectives. There is no link between the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect these objectives. Article 42 (2) (a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect the strategic objectives of the MANCP.

In addition, these are not measureable objectives on what Germany wants to achieve for animal welfare. There are no specific strategic objectives indicated in relation to animal welfare outcomes e.g. reduce incidence of tail docking by x%, improve FPD levels by x%, decrease lameness levels in cattle by x % through official controls and related actions in the MANCP such as training, targeted enforcement campaigns on certain issues, liaison with sector to set agreed targets etc. For instance, considering the amount of resources devoted to the development and drafting of an Action Plan on tail docking of pigs there is no mention of it as either a strategic or an operational objective (with meas

Documentation related to the Action Plan on tail docking of pigs is included in the QMS documentation of the Land (Federal State) visited but only for information purposes. A strategic objective is a long-term objective, setting out what an official control system and its priorities intend to achieve. St

Previously there had been animal welfare objectives set in the Land visited, such as, on group housing of sows where the local level (Kreis - district or county) were asked to carry out specific controls. However, currently as there is no legal spur for such a focus, there are no specific objectives set for animal welfare controls at Land level, nor were any specific reports received at Land level on local level objectives or activities.

The Annual Report on implementation of the MANCP and the report on animal welfare required under Commission Decision 2006/778 give at best a superficial analysis of the results of official controls on animal welfare. Official control results are simply reported in terms of compliance/non-compliance.

There is insufficient analysis on the results of controls to enable authorities at different levels to have a clear picture of the animal welfare situation on farm and to assist them in developing strategies to address the major issues.

The annual report on the MANCP gives statistics on compliance for each of the areas covered by Decision 2006/778 and Article 27 of Regulation 1/2005. Nonetheless, it does not indicate whether the actions taken are contributing to improvements, whether compliance/detection is improving/decreasing and whether the activities are suitable to reach the objectives and ensure effective operation of the MANCP, including enforcement action and its results as required under Article 44 (1) (d) of Regulation EC No 882/2004.

There are output indicators such as the quantity of inspections and non-compliances detected per inspection but these do not give an outcome for animal welfare. The outputs are not linked to the existing strategic objectives.

The reports sent to the Commission by Germany on Decision 2006/778 give only a collation of non-compliances with no analysis at any level of the significance of the findings or the root causes or any influencing factors. Article 8 of the Decision requires an analysis of the most serious findings of non-compliance and a national action plan to prevent or decrease their occurrence for the forthcoming years. The reports merely list essentially the same findings and actions to address them each year.

For example an extract from the German 2006/778 report for 2018 indicated: Free Barn Enriched Unenriched Calves Pigs range cage cage 6,108 67,223 Holdings subject to inspection 8,002 840 147 0 101,844 5,129 867 Inspected holdings 78 0 6,541 818 Production sites without non- 747 65 0 5,110 3.521 compliance These inspections resulted in the following enforcement action being taken: Non-compliance A 46 100 15 0 2,266 2,702 Non-compliance B 0 112 271 Non-compliance C 4 16 1 0 389 470 2 15 1 There is no analysis available on why the inspections on pig or calf farms resulted in much higher rates of non-compliance detected on farm (31% pigs, 22% calves) than on barn holdings for laying hens (11%) f

There is potentially useful data within this framework but the reporting is not reliable in certain cases or analysed to any degree e.g. mutilations on pigs were reported as 99% compliant, although this is not the case as approximately 95% pigs are routinely tail docked. The guidance for inspectors on this issue relates to whether the mutilation was carried out correctly and does not question whether the mutilation should have been carried out in the first place according to the legislative requirements in Point 8 of Annex I, Chapter I to Directive 2008/120/EC.

The Land level authority knew very little about the type of issues or their significance reported from the local level to them under Commission Decision 2006/778 as neither they nor the local level had analysed the results of inspections reported from local level before sending on the information to BMEL. The lack of Land level knowledge on the outcome of controls was noted in previous Directorate F audits (DG SANTE report 2018-6445 on pigs).

There is no specific report on broilers produced as required in Article 7(2) of Directive 2007/43/EC. Data on inspections on these farms was available in the Land visited, but there is no aggregated report for the whole country and no analysis of the non- 7 compliances generated. Animal based indicators are well established in the broiler sector, where the data is collected at slaughterhouses and used to select the highest risk farms for inspection. Although this is a robust system of control it does not make use of certain indicators which are required by EU legislation, i.e. verification of daily mortality rates and the limit for cumulative daily mortality rates for broiler flocks operating at the higher stocking densities.

However, the passive surveillance has been under-reported by ca 50% to the Commission so the coverage has been better than reported, but it is still poor in certain important border areas where the competent authority considers the risk for incursion of rabies to be high. 15

Through the misclassification of samples and results, due to unclear information on the submission forms, the NRL has provided the competent authority with misleading results for rabies surveillance and monitoring of the effectiveness of the oral vaccination.

Hunted foxes and golden jackals, as well as the occasional wolf, from areas outside the ORV areas are subject to rabies testing under a national active rabies surveillance programme. The BFSA has previously informed the Commission services that, until 2017 these tests were included in the applications for co-funding from the EU, but this would not be the case in the application for co-funding of the 2018 programme. Therefore, the summary results provided to the BFSA and the Commission have been misleading. The submission form used by the official veterinarians is the same irrespective of whether the sample is for the monitoring programme, for active surveillance outside the ORV area, or for the passive surveillance (suspect cases, animals killed in road traffic, animals found dead). A description of the sampled animal in free text on the submission form intends to guide the laboratory's classification

The NRL did not have sufficient test material to carry out serological analyses on a large proportion of the blood samples they received for the monitoring in 2017 and 2019. In addition, the low sensitivity of the serological method used in the NRL provides the competent authority with results that likely err towards a lower sero- prevalence in foxes(4). These weaknesses undermine the evaluation by the competent authority of the effect of the oral vaccination on the immunity of the target animal (fox) population. In addition, the laboratory does not have any confirmatory test method for rabies, which may delay important test results, especially in cases of suspect human exposure.

Despite the lack of sufficient supplies of test kits, the NRL used many of the available kits to analyse samples from golden jackals, a species for which the method's reliability is unknown. It is therefore not possible for the competent authority to investigate the possible reasons for the low sero-prevalence but high bait uptake reported by the NRL for golden jackals. 4 In their comments to the draft report the competent authority noted that in 2019 there is a new tender for diagnostic tests for serological analyses and FAT. 19 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is sound legal basis for all aspects of the rabies eradication. paragraph_text: The current practice of performing confirmatory sampling when the FBO requests it for breeding and laying hen flocks without good reason to suspect false positives is not in line with the requirement for it to be done only in exceptional cases such as those. This can have negative impacts when Salmonella is present but not detected with the confirmatory test, resulting in a continued contamination and mistakenly reporting lower Salmonella prevalence. The relatively high levels of lesions detected during a survey in two slaughterhouses indicate serious animal welfare problems in a significant number of French farms and a need for an enforcement strategy aiming at improved compliance with minimum requirements as well as serious improvement measures to reduce the incidence of tail biting.

The sector has started to record evidence of tail/ear biting lesions. However, procedures for the assessment of lesions are incomplete. Farm risk assessment tools are still being developed and there is no robust framework in the Action Plan for improvement measures or when farms should transition to rearing pigs with intact tails. These last three components need to be put in place quickly in order to start making tangible progress to improve compliance with the Directive. In addition, the extended CA deadlines (end 2022 to 2024) mean that without a focus on shortening deadlines and sufficient priority, full compliance with legal requirements will not be reached within the next four years.

An error in the interpretation of legal requirements in official guidance and inspection checklists means that the legal requirement for all categories of pigs to have access to enrichment materials is not being enforced.
There are no specific programmes in France for animal welfare measures on pig farms currently financed or co-financed by the European Union Fund for Rural Development (EUFRD).

Official controls have not yet started to enforce compliance criteria for legislative requirements related to risks for tail biting though this is planned for 2020 once guidance is revised. Whilst the premises visited complied with the existing vademecum, they did not comply with existing legislative requirements on enrichment material and the requirements prohibiting routine tail docking.

Mistakes in the interpretation of legal requirements for enrichment material and interpretation of requirements on mutilations mean that animal welfare and cross compliance inspections massively underreport the high rates of non-compliance for these two items with serious implications for cross compliance payments.
The provision of water through liquid feeding systems does not ensure that all pigs over two weeks of age have permanent access to a sufficient quantity of fresh water.

It is unlikely that corridors can provide suitable accommodation for sick and injured pigs in most building and management scenarios. Blanket acceptance of the use of corridors by the CA without strict conditions and a case-by-case assessment intended to ensure that these areas are suitable for all the objectives specified in the relevant legislation is not in accordance with these legal requirements.

DGAL has worked with stakeholders to implement an Action Plan on tail docking as part of the overall animal welfare strategy. It has taken actions to develop criteria for certain legal requirements that are related to tail biting risk factors on tail docking of pigs to enable inspectors and farmers to make a judgement on whether individual farms comply with EU requirements but these have not yet been implemented. Tail docking is still routinely carried out and the CA is not yet enforcing the corresponding legal requirements.

label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: The existence of two pig databases complicates the proper planning and implementation of official controls. The fact that the pig holding data is not accurate in the ARMA database for the ASF free area of the country will slow down the application of control measures should the disease spread to it.

The identification system for pigs and the Agency for Restructuring and Modernisation of Agriculture (ARMA) database are described in reports from previous Commission audits related to this area, i.e. DG(SANTE)/2017-6114-MR, DG(SANTE)/2016-6114- MR and DG(SANTE)/2014-7294-MR.

In response to Recommendation No 3 from report DG(SANTE)/2017-6114-MR, i.e., "To improve the accuracy and quality of the tools for the traceability of pigs, in order for them to be effective tools for animal health controls", Poland proposed a public procurement procedure for the design and development of a new database, i.e. "e-IRZ Plus". ARMA informed the audit team that a tender process had been opened in 2017 and then cancelled. A decision was taken during 2018 to modify the existing database and create "IRZ Plus". This modification improved electronic data exchange with livestock owners. However, it did not improve the functionality for adding animal health information and official vete

As described in previous reports, the GVI maintains its own separate database ("Vetlink") which includes animal health information and is used to support District Veterinary Offices (DVOs) to manage disease control programmes including ASF. There is limited access to data on Vetlink from areas outside the region in which holdings are located. The GVI have plans to expand the capabilities of the system.

The high number of visits to holdings in the ASF affected area has provided an up-to- date picture of pig numbers on holdings. This has allowed a cross check with the information on the central database and the removal of many holdings that no longer 5 keep pigs which has also contributed considerably to the reduced numbers of pig holdings. (A similar exercise has not taken place in the ASF free area and therefore the accuracy of pig holding information in the database would be lower.)

DVOs produce annual reports on how many such visits are carried out and the main non-compliances detected. They do not confirm the extent to which the target of twice annual visits was achieved, e.g. percentage of holdings visited twice. The reports do not include data on the number of holdings that should have been inspected and the reasons why inspections did not take place as planned. The competent authority did say that many holdings on the list may not have pigs when contacted to arrange a visit but records viewed by the audit team in DVOs did not include this information.

label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: The absence of a national template for reporting on the implementation of biosecurity measures at hunting grounds made the system ineffective, as the ASF expert group cannot compare the information and use it to provide further advice.

In response to Recommendation No 5 from DG(SANTE)/2017-6114-MR, i.e., "To ensure that all measures under the ASF approved programme, including the feed ban are subjected to official controls in order to ensure their effective implementation.", Poland proposed that the Polish Hunting Association (PHA) would supervise the activities of hunting clubs including compliance with the biosecurity rules. The PHA would provide the GVI with reports on those checks and a summary of those reports were to be submitted to the ASF expert group for evaluation.

According to the competent authority, the PHA checked the implementation of the biosecurity rules by hunters in 371 hunting clubs during the 2017/2018 hunting season. The PHA forwarded reports to the GVI but in the absence of a national template, the 9 reports varied greatly and the information they contained could not be compared or assessed by the ASF expert group. The audit team was informed that a proposal for a national template for reporting inspections on hunting grounds/carcase collection points is being discussed between the PHA and the GVI with June 2019 as the current target for agreement and subsequent use.

This intermediate stop of animals from infected area increases the risk of spreading the disease within the country.

However, there are instances where wild boar carcases go out to the free area and then return back again, increasing the risk of introducing the disease.

The audit visited a game collection centre in Part I where wild boar carcases from Part I are stored after they receive a negative result for ASF (was previously stored in a "carcase collection centre" ­ see finding 31). The centre was also used to store wild boar carcases from the free area and the carcases from Part I and the free area were destined for a game processing establishment in the free area. Based on discussions with the operator of the game collection centre, only about 5-10% of hunted wild boar carcasses were sent to game processing establishments with the rest being consumed locally. label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: There are official controls at pig holdings and they are effective. However, there are a significant number of un-registered backyard holdings and as demonstrated by the last ongoing census, counties do not apply a consistent classification of pig holdings and 9 there is outdoor access for pigs at small commercial and backyard holdings. This hinders the possibility to trace those animals, the likelihood to detect the disease at an early stage, and increases the risk of the infection entering into the herds.

To ensure that all holdings comply with registration requirements, the central competent authority had requested a new census survey, in order to remove registered holdings where no pigs have been kept for the previous three years and to register all new pig holdings or holdings that were previously unregistered. The Ministry of Agriculture is implementing a number of supporting actions to further improve the effectiveness and impact of this latest census (e.g. no fees for registering holdings, information campaigns, and enhanced cooperation with municipalities). 4

label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: The controls over live pigs moving within Lithuania allows pig meat from Part II to be 9 dispatched to other Member States and third countries, and for pig meat from Part III to be limited to the Lithuanian market with very low risk of spreading the disease. However, these guarantees are weakened by the inconsistent application of standstill requirements and the absence of verification on channelling for pig meat coming from Part III.

The audit team reviewed documents for movements of pigs from Part II to a slaughterhouse. Two holdings had supplied pigs for slaughter. These holdings received multiple consignments of pigs from an area listed in Part II within the previous 30 days. The widespread labelling deficiencies observed in combination with the apparently good knowledge of the inspectors on the topic raise some questions on whether the official control system is suitable to verify operators' compliance with labelling requirements. 7 Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official sampling
paragraph_text: The system in place for planning of official sampling is effective and risk-based. However, the effectiveness of this element of official controls is weakened by the competent authorities' failure to adhere to planned arrangements and by the fact that the representativeness of sampling, and thus samples' legal and analytical validity, is not ensured for substances with a non-uniform distribution.

paragraph_text: The interpretation of the analytical results does not take into account all required parameters thus weakening the legal validity of the decisions made by the competent authority on compliance. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: A systemic shortcoming was noted by the audit team in terms of the preparation of final samples from the aggregate samples for control of substances where non-uniform distribution of the analyte/substance is presumed. The inspectors would normally use simple manual mixing to ensure appropriate homogenisation rather than special equipment (e.g., mechanical or automatic dividers) which is required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. For substances with a non-uniform distribution, simple manual mixing alone cannot ensure complete homogenisation of the aggregate sample.
