paragraph_text: The audit team examined a number of laboratory reports and noted that not all of the parameters (i.e. expanded measurement uncertainty, correction for recovery and moisture content), necessary for interpretation of the results in accordance with the requirements laid down by part C(6) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, had been reported and thus could not been taken into account by the DAA when making its decision on compliance. In addition, the laboratory reports seen did not provide an unambiguous statement that the number of analytical determinations for non-compliant results had been in accordance with the requirements laid down by part C(3) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152

label_heading: Conclusion on the actions taken on non-compliances
paragraph_text: The fact that the competent authority (DGAV) does not ensure that the operators identify the reason(s) for all non-compliances identified and remedy those weakens the effectiveness of the overall control system. 5.2.4 Establishments producing/trading non-authorised (in the EU) feed additives and exporting or re-exporting them from the EU to a third country

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official sampling
paragraph_text: In every region visited, the audit team studied a number of non-compliances from previous controls (DGAV's area of responsibility). Examples included deficient labelling, HACCP-related deficiencies, and non-compliant sampling results. While follow-up of deficient labelling and HACCP-related deficiencies was largely adequate and effective, the audit team noted that, for non-compliant results on carry-over and exceeding maximum permitted levels for certain trace elements, the communication with the FeBOs had not contained an unambiguous request for corrective action and consequently no timeframe had been specified for the FeBO to remedy the deficiency(ies). paragraph_text: The audit team noted that there was reasonably detailed and adequate guidance on how to deal with non-compliances and the relevant actions to take ­ but only for Salmonella, processed animal proteins and forbidden substances (as per Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009). label_heading: Conclusions on the bovine identification and registration system
paragraph_text: While official controls on the identification and registration of bovine animals are carried out as planned and identified shortcomings are subsequently followed up, these controls have, to date, not identified some non-compliances related to the identification of bovine animals and notification of births of calves at holdings.

label_heading: Conclusions on the bovine identification and registration system
paragraph_text: A lack of effective action by the competent authority to enforce the operators' obligations to notify all events at holdings has contributed to a situation where the information in the national database for registration and identification of bovine animals is unreliable. In addition, due to limitations in the database's functionality, information that would be relevant for the planning and implementation of official controls on BSE and ABP cannot be easily extracted. Overall, these deficiencies cumulatively undermine the reliability of the BSE monitoring programme. 5.3 BSE MONITORING SYSTEM, LABORATORY NETWORK AND TESTING ARRANGEMENT

Despite the above, the audit team noted in the holdings visited ­ which had been subject to official controls - that the records of these controls did not show that the following issues (which were seen by the audit team during the audit) had been identified: a. In two out of four holdings visited, operators had not: (i) recorded in holding registers, (ii) notified, and (iii) identified newborn calves; (for example, in one holding visited, 17 cows had 17 calves in the last 12 months, none of which had been registered). 6 b. In two out of four holdings visited, animals that had died on farm (fallen stock) and/or were emergency slaughtered had not been recorded as such in the holding register

For example: a. Contrary to Article 4a of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 which requires identification of bovine animals within a maximum of 20 days from the birth of the animal and in any event before the animal leaves the holding on which it was born, in one of the holdings visited, six bovine animals out of 43 kept had no ear tags, and approximately 50% of those remaining ones had only one tag; b. Contrary to Article 7 of Regulation

While checking the bovine identification documents in the visited premises, the audit team noted that there had been significant delays in issuing passports. In particular, in one of the slaughterhouses visited, bovine animals presented for slaughter were accompanied by passports that had been issued (for the first time) on the day prior to slaughter or on the day of slaughter. These animals were aged between 18 and 24 months. 7

The audit team analysed the data on the location and the number of bovine passports issued in comparison with the location and the number of registered new-born calves born in the country and noted a lack of correlation between the figures. In nine regions, differences between passports issued and animals born ranged from approximately 1,000 to almost 9,000. The officials in charge of conducting official controls did not pay attention to these discrepancies, which could indicate non-compliances related to animals' individual identification and movements, namely unregistered movements of unidentified young calves (see findings: 18.a, 24 and 25). 5.2.4 Computerised database

According to the data from VetIS, in the period from 2014 to 2018, the population of bovine animals has steadily increased from approximately 721,000 to 765,000. However, the audit team noted that there was a large cohort of bovine animals missing from the database. For example in 2018, the difference between the number of animals born and traded (into Bulgaria) and the number of animals slaughtered, dead, traded and exported (out of Bulgaria), resulted in a surplus of approximately 34,000 animals, without a known (confirmed) history (3). This represents approximately 4.5% of the bovine population in the country.

The owners of bovine holdings visited stated that their main activity is production of milk, and their cows calve every year. The audit team noted that except for two regions where the numbers of new-born calves registered in VetIS were plausible, in the remaining 26 regions registered calves represented from 17% to 30% of the expected number.

In one of the holdings visited, the owner stated that there were 17 calves born within the last 12 months ­ all were sold aged one to two weeks old. In another holding visited, the animal keeper confirmed that his cows calved annually and that he retained a few heifer calves for rebuilding the herd. The audit team cross-checked the situation on that holding with the VetIS data and noted that: a. The calf retained in the herd had no ear tags and was not identified by any other means. b. For 17 cows, ranging in age from 14 to 19 years old, only one to three calves per cow had been notified in VetIS during the entire cows' lives; the owner retained the notified calves in the herd, and during th

The BFSA has granted access to VetIS to officials from the central and regional level, official veterinarians in slaughterhouses and to registered veterinarians. One person at central level (VetIS administrator) has access to all the information, whilst other users are only allowed to see information limited to an individual animal or a holding. These users have limited possibilities to correct or edit data in the event they see a non-conformity. Slaughterhouse operators, those collecting and disposing of fallen stock and animal (3) Data by BFSA (VetIS) and from TRACES. 8 keepers, have no access to VetIS. The BFSA stated that it is preparing a new functionality for animal keepers to allow th

In light of the above, VetIS does not meet the requirements of Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 as it neither reflects the actual population of bovine animals in Bulgaria nor does it facilitate the supply of the required items of information set out in Article 14 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC.

The quality and quantity of samples, once collected, are able to ensure sufficient material for BSE testing. However, the method of identifying samples does not guarantee to trace back to the sampled animal in the event of a positive result.

Despite the fact that the NRL-TSE and regional BSE laboratories are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025, use the approved test kits listed in the Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and have performed satisfactorily in proficiency tests for BSE, both the competent authority and the NRL-TSE have consistently failed to ensure the availability of a sufficient number of diagnostic tests to analyse all the samples taken. This has resulted in an unsatisfactory situation where large numbers of samples from high-risk sub- 16 populations have either not been analysed or their analyses had been delayed for months, further weakening the reliability of the BSE monitoring results.

The audit team noted that the information provided by the competent authorities on monitoring in this sub-population is incomplete. There are significant discrepancies between the number of bovine animals from the sub-population of emergency slaughtered animals and found sick at ante mortem inspection reported by FCD and AHFCD (see Appendix, Tables 6 and 7). Data presented by FCD, AHFCD and those sourced from the BSE testing laboratories differ and cannot be reconciled (see Appendix, Tables 8 to 10, and Tables 16 to 18).

The audit team saw evidence of situations where cows emergency slaughtered at holdings had been classified as healthy/slaughtered for own consumption. The opposite was the case in one of the BSE testing laboratories visited where all bovine animals sampled for BSE and notified as healthy/slaughtered for own consumption had been reclassified by the laboratory to the sub-population of emergency slaughtered. In this laboratory, the approach has been in place for at least four years and concerned samples were collected from eight regions.

Due to the limited availability of testing kits, BFSA decided that samples collected from fallen bovine animals were of a low priority and delayed their testing. This resulted in a situation where samples from a group, which would ordinarily be considered as being a high risk (of BSE), were kept for several months before being tested (see findings 55 and 56).

The NRL-TSE is responsible for ensuring that there is a sufficient availability of BSE diagnostic tests for itself and for the regional BSE laboratories. The audit team noted that the arrangement for acquiring tests did not work effectively in 2018 as the regional laboratories and the NRL-TSE did not have sufficient tests available. This resulted in over 18,000 collected BSE samples (and an additional 11,000 for Scrapie) not being analysed. Due to this shortage of testing kits since August 2018, the samples from the sub- populations of bovine animals slaughtered at holdings as healthy, in emergency and dead were categorised as low priority and collected, but not tested. With respect to the arrangements for BSE testing, the audit team noted that the NRL-TSE did not overcome difficulties in ensuring availability of sufficient BSE test kits in 2019 and the backlog of untested samples is growing. At the time of this audit, there were 6,500 samples awaiting BSE testing (and 5,500 for Scrapie).

Samples of brainstem seen in the laboratories visited were placed in individual sampling containers, which were identified by either labels or a consecutive sequential number written with a marker. While the information from labels (date of slaughter, the 15 slaughterhouse number and the slaughter number of the animal or the ear tag number) could ensure traceability to the bovine animal sampled, the sole consecutive sequential number could not; especially if more samples with the same number were delivered for examination. This is not compliant with the provisions of Point 1 of Chapter C of Annex X to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, which requires that the samples should be marked correctly as

The samples are not taken from all animals that should be tested in the relevant sub- population. A significant proportion of eligible healthy bovine animals, mainly slaughtered outside slaughterhouses, which should have been tested for BSE, have not been sampled. Likewise, sampling of eligible animals emergency slaughtered or found sick at ante mortem inspection is limited to very few regions, whereas the majority of such animals have not been notified or sampled. In comparison with other Member States and even with the competent authority's own estimates, the number of fallen bovine animals sampled remains extremely low.

The CAs have not demonstrated that they have put in place actions that would effectively address recommendation 4 of audit report DG(SANCO)2011-8944. This additionally undermines Bulgaria's request for a relaxation of the frequency of testing for BSE.

The implementation of the actions to address recommendation 6 of audit report DG(SANCO)2011-8944 has not been effective. Collection of SRM produced as a result of on-farm slaughtering of bovine animals in backyard holdings continues to be inexistent.

The population of bovine animals aged over 30 months in the last five years in Bulgaria amounts to approximately 0.5 million heads (VetIS: 521,759 animals in 2018). In its TSE monitoring and eradication programme submitted to the Commission, the BFSA estimated that the number of fallen bovine animals eligible for BSE testing should amount to at least five thousand, representing 1% of this population. The audit team noted that apart from this estimate, there are no countrywide data on mortality at holdings and accordingly, the BFSA has no information on the number of bovine animals from the sub- population of dead bovine animals aged over 24 months. label_heading: Conclusions on the bovine identification and registration system
paragraph_text: While SNIRA is operational and available to all relevant users, the data available therein is incomplete for backyard holdings (retaining over 90% of the bovine population) in relation to the sub-populations relevant for the BSE monitoring and as such does not support the BSE monitoring and eradication system.

label_heading: Conclusions on the bovine identification and registration system
paragraph_text: Official controls on identification and registration of bovine animals (inventory checks) are carried out as planned and are able to detect non-compliances, which are subsequently recorded in SNIRA. However, the lack of regular follow-up of these non-compliances weakens the effectiveness of official controls and in turn does not result in any improvement of the reliability of the national database, in particular, with respect to the absence of recorded movements of animals and of notification of newborn calves. 10

label_heading: Conclusions on the bovine identification and registration system
paragraph_text: There is an increasing trend in the number of notified dead animals, indicating growing awareness of this obligation amongst the bovine animal owners; nonetheless, the mortality rate is still just above the half of the lowest expected. 5.3 BSE MONITORING SYSTEM, LABORATORY NETWORK AND TESTING ARRANGEMENT

In the commercial holdings visited, the audit team noted the following: a. The majority of adult bovine animals had two ear tags, some had one ear tag and, in one holding, only one animal was without both ear tags. This animal, however, had an electronic collar allowing linking of the animal with the holding register. Moreover, the holding operator had already in his possession ear tag duplicates also for this cow. b. With respect to young calves, in one of the holdings, all the young calves had ear tags while in another at least 10 (out of approximately 200 bovine animals) had not. The veterinarians met kept the stock of new ear tags and maintained identification documents. However, the audit team noted the following: a. Out of the five backyard holdings visited, only one had fully completed passports and a complete set of movement documents. In this case, the situation on the holding also matched up the information from SNIRA and both cows had ear tags. b. In another

On a monthly basis, each CSVFSD verifies the reports of these controls submitted by the authorised veterinarians. The controls by authorised veterinarians take place regularly, every year and cover at least 3% of holdings in the counties. b. The analysis of the available data from GDFS, SNIRA and the Laboratory Information and Management System (LIMS) on the sub-population of bovine animals slaughtered as healthy and eligible for BSE testing shows that: a. The number of bovines slaughtered in slaughterhouses reported by GDFS is lower than bovines notified to SNIRA (see Tables 1 and 2). b. Almost all bovine animals sampled as healthy slaughtered originate from slaughterhouses, while the vast majority of these slaughtered outside slaughterhouses (at holdings) are not sampled (see Tables 2, 3 and 4). c. The number of animals slaughtered outside slaughterhouses (at holdings) and not sampled continuously grows (see Tables 5, 6 and 7)

Overall, the system of collection and disposal of ABP, including of the fallen bovine animals from backyard holdings, has deteriorated since the previous audit. Therefore, recommendation 2 of audit report DG(SANCO)/2011-8941 remains unaddressed. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS With regard to Romania's application for review of its BSE monitoring programme it is concluded that, despite some positive trends observed, there are yet no grounds to allow for received 180 days of transitional period to comply with the requirements. 24 the frequency of testing to be relaxed. With the exception of the facilities for live animals ­ category E (registered horses) in the BIP Oostende, the facilities, equipment and hygiene of both BIPs/DPEs were in general fit for purpose for undertaking import controls. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authority has established an adequate framework for carrying out official controls on animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin intended for import into the European Union. The implementation of import controls of animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin, including goods subject to specific import conditions, was generally in line with EU legislation and could ensure that only compliant consignments were introduced

In the facilities for animals ­ registered horses (category E), good hygiene conditions had not been maintained; however, these had not been used in five years. The surrounding area was not kept clean, there was no cover for the drain and the unloading/loading ramp was no longer fit for purpose due to disuse and exposure to bad weather. 15 Conclusions on suitability of facilities

The implementation of the import controls on animals, food and feed of animal origin and of goods subject to special import conditions is generally in line with EU legislation. The competent authorities ensure that documentary, identity and physical checks on animals and goods are carried out as required and that only compliant goods may be imported into the EU. Regular checks of airplane/shipping manifests contribute to ensuring that consignments requiring veterinary import controls do not escape such controls. Some weaknesses were noted in the documentary checks on re- imported consignments (for which the DVFA initiated corrective action) and those intended for ship supply, which weakens t

The procedure applied in one seaport BIP in case of direct movement from the BIP to ship supply or to further storage facilities - one CVED for several consignments (and several veterinary certificates) in one means of transport - is not in line with the requirements of Directive 97/78/EC. On arrival at the BIP, consignments accompanied with several certificates, transported in the same means of transport were presented at the BIP by the operator with one CVED only. Consequently, not all certificates and not all commodities were mentioned on the CVED and thereafter recorded in TRACES.

Exit controls by BIP officials regarding transit consignments leaving the EU through the road BIPs Evzoni and Peplos are carried out outside normal working hours by BIP officials. It is common for the transits between BIPs Evzoni and Peplos and vice versa that the exits take place after working hours when there are no BIP officials available. This results in a situation where the exit of most consignments transiting between the BIPs Evzoni and Peplos and vice versa cannot be declared in TRACES as, in line with Article 11 (2)(e) of Council Directive 97/78/EEC, only BIP officials are allowed to do this. However Customs confirmation of the exit was available (see finding 26).

paragraph_text: All facilities visited with the exception of the BIP facilities at Venezia Port, did not meet the operational hygiene standards resulting from either lack of maintenance and/or inappropriate cleansing and disinfection. Whilst some facilities are being reconstructed to comply with Regulations (EU) 2017/625 and (EU) 2019/1014 there is, however, no plan to upgrade the substandard facilities and equipment at Civitavecchia Port BIP.

paragraph_text: In relation to import controls on food of non-animal origin, DGISAN has not made available to the public a list of points of entry with suitable designated DPE/DPI facilities. DGISAN does not ensure that documentary checks are done at the DPE and that physical checks, including sampling, are carried out at the DPE/DPIs. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The responsibilities of the competent authorities for the official import controls are clearly defined. paragraph_text: USMAF-SASN do not check the originals of certificates or other relevant documents and therefore are not in a position to ascertain their authenticity. Furthermore, the way in which the system for documentary checks on consignments of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions has been set up at the designated point of entry in Venice Port (checks are being carried out at local office level instead of at the entry point at the border) is contrary to EU requirements.

label_heading: Conclusions on suitability of facilities and equipment
paragraph_text: In relation to import controls on food of non-animal origin, DGISAN has not made available to the public a list of points of entry with suitable designated DPE/DPI facilities. The list of DPEs only erroneously refers to local offices of DGISAN and the published list has not been updated since 2016. DGISAN does not ensure that documentary checks are done at the DPE and that physical checks, including sampling, are carried out at the DPE/DPIs. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The responsibilities of the competent authorities for the official import controls are clearly defined. The Italian authorities have established a comprehensive framework for official controls on imported animals and goods, supporte
The controls on food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions were not implemented in line with EU rules in several cases below.

At Venice port, documentary checks on food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions took place at the local USMAF-SASN office instead of in the port of (2) In its response to the draft report the competent authority noted that the BIP staff of Civitavecchia carry out the identity checks of the containerised frozen and chilled goods and collect the packages selected for physical checks at the BCP facilities. 12 entry where physical facilities are in place (see related finding point 82). This arrangement is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 8(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 8(1) of Regulation (E

USMAF-SASN staff carry out documentary controls based on copies of original certificates and/or laboratory test results. This hinders the verification of the authenticity of the health certificates, declarations and the laboratory results due to the reliance on copies. This procedure is not in line with the requirements laid down in Articles 4, 5 and 9(2) of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Articles 4, 5 and 8(1) of Regulation (EU) 2015/175.

In addition, in one port visited, DPE/DPI staff could not provide copies of the certificates and laboratory test results for one out of three consignments of peanuts from Egypt and one consignment of guar gum from India verified in order to demonstrate that the requirements laid down in Articles 4 and 5 of Regulations (EU) No 884/2014 and (EU) 2015/175 respectively were met.

The official samples, taken by DPE/DPI staff are sent to the designated laboratories for analyses. The consignments were detained awaiting results. The results of the laboratory tests were available in all cases verified, but in one case there was no link between the sampling and the consignment due to absence of the lot/batch number. 5.2.5 Decision on consignment and its follow-up

In case consignments are selected for official sampling, the consignments are forwarded to the inspection facilities for food of non-animal origin, which are located in the port of entry. In Venice port, physical checks and sampling takes also place in customs warehouses, which are not designated by DGISAN as DPIs. Carrying out physical checks at these warehouses is not in line with Article 9(2) of Regulation EC) No 669/2009, Article 8(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 8(2) of Regulation (EU) 2015/175.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls on imported goods
paragraph_text: The guarantees in response to recommendation 1 of a previous audit report in relation to entering required data into TRACES by the local veterinary units, confirming the arrival of consignments at destination have not been effectively implemented.

Regarding records of supplies of goods from the customs warehouse to cross border means of sea transport checked by the audit team, the certificate referred to in Article 1(3) of Decision 2000/571/EC (the model certificate being laid down in the Annex thereto) was issued by the BIP staff. However, the audit team noted that in a few cases, operators had not provided the BIP staff with the completed certificate confirming the delivery of goods on board the vessel within the deadline of 30 days, which is not in line with Article 2 of that Decision.

The BIP staff issued a similar document for delivery of goods from the warehouse to NATO/US army bases, and validated thereafter the CVEDs in TRACES. The proportion of cases where confirmation of arrival at NATO/US army bases within the deadline of 30 days varies significantly between bases, ranging from 99,6% to as little as 13.4 % confirmed. DGSAF stated that further action is still needed to ensure that this legal obligation is satisfied in all cases. 5.2.4 Documentary, identity and physical checks 5.2.4.1 Checks on animals

The audit team carried out a desk review of 50 consignments of animal origin which were allowed entry and must be channelled to their destination in line with the requirements of Articles 8(4), 12(1) or 15(1) of Directive 97/78/EC. DGSAF and BIP staff provided evidence that the local veterinary units had been informed of the dispatch and had reported the arrival of such consignments at destination. However, local veterinary units did not enter in TRACES the completion of part III of the CVEDs in 16 of the cases, but used instead other means to report the arrival e.g. by email. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls on imported goods
paragraph_text: The way in which the system for documentary checks of the consignments of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions has been set up (checks are being carried out centrally instead of at the entry points at the border) is contrary to EU requirements. Furthermore, Customs do not check the originals of certificates or other relevant documents and therefore are not in a position to ascertain their authenticity.

The authorities have not put in place appropriate physical facilities within the listed DPEs, and there is no list of DPIs and control points available. The system in place does not satisfy the EU requirement that documentary checks should be performed at the border and cannot ensure that checks on consignments of products of non-animal origin subject to special import controls are carried out under the suitable and hygienic conditions expected of DPEs and DPIs. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authorities have set up an adequate framework for carrying out official controls on animals and products of animal origin intended for import into the EU. This framework is supported by good cooper

The documentary checks of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions are carried out at the Customs Electronic Centre (at central level) and not in the listed DPEs. The listed DPEs are "virtual" with neither physical facilities nor personnel available on-the-spot to perform the documentary checks. This procedure is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 8(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009, Article 9(1) of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014, Article 8(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2015/175 and Article 10(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2016/6.

The operators comply with the obligation to pre-notify the arrival of their consignments: those that use TRACES e-mail scanned copies of the Common Entry Documents (CEDs) to Customs, and where required, scans of the certificates, declarations, laboratory test results and other required documentation, e.g. invoices, prior to the physical arrival of the goods. Customs verify the scanned documents but never request originals of the certificates or laboratory result reports. This hinders the verification of the authenticity of the health certificates, declarations and the laboratory results due to the reliance on scanned documents, which is contrary to the requirements of Article 5 and 9(2) of C

The listed DPEs have no facilities for carrying out identity and physical checks. The identity and physical checks are performed upon request of the Customs Electronic Centre at the Customs' authorised warehouses by trained Customs staff.

The seven listed DPEs have no dedicated facilities for carrying out the import checks (documentary, identity and physical checks, including sampling). The identity and physical checks are performed upon request of the Customs Electronic Centre at the Customs' authorised warehouses (for details, see section 5.2.4.3) and no list is available of DPIs and control points. Contrary to the requirement of Article 8 of Regulation (EU) No 884/2014 and Article 19(2) of Regulation (EC) 669/2009, Customs has not published a list of DPIs and control points as the goods must be inspected in Customs authorised warehouses. Information on the warehouses can be obtained through the warehouse search at the foll

However, inaccuracies identified in the list of operators eligible to supply ABP and produce PAP to be used for aquaculture weakens the reliability of the feed ban measures in this area. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Articles 4(3), 21, 22, 41, 43, 45(1), 46, 48 and 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Articles 8, 17(1), 20, 21, 31, 32 and Annexes IV, VIII, IX, X, XV and XVI to Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 Article 7 and Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings

Listing of food establishments authorised to deliver raw materials for production of non- ruminant PAP and ABP, and feed operators authorised to produce feed materials and compound feed with PAP for aquaculture animals, is a federal responsibility. Each Land has to communicate the list of these establishments to the federal level. These lists are available on the BMEL website. The audit team identified that in Bavaria several food establishment (slaughterhouses, cutting plants) slaughtering and/or cutting bovine and porcine animals were listed. The competent authorities stated that some of these establishments had not provided evidence of having an effective system in place to prevent cross-

The processing plant visited delivered poultry PAP for feed production for aquaculture animals. This processing plant was not listed on the BMEL website contrary to the requirements of point 1(d), Section A, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 While this processing plant was subject to regular official controls, the competent authority has not detected this non-compliance.

Official inspections on operators' HACCP systems are carried out adequately, however problems identified regarding official validation of processing method 7 and official sampling weaken the effectiveness of these controls.

Three processing plants visited were using processing method 7, which had been authorised by the competent authority. In one processing plant during the 30 days validation period microbiological samples were taken (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium perfringens) directly after the treatment. This is not in line with the legal requirements for the testing of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae in PAP. The problem was identified by the competent authority and the sampling was repeated for Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae two weeks later. During the repeated sampling the operator increased the minimum temperature in the drier and reduced the speed of the conveyor screw which may increas

In another processing plant visited using method 7, during the 30 days validation period samples were taken for microbiological controls (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae and Clostridium perfringens). However, for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae only one sample of each were taken contrary the requirements of point G 1(c) (ii) of Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The competent authority did not note this problem and approved the validation of the processing method. In the third processing plant visited using method 7 the validation documents were comprehensive and complete as required by the legislation. 2 In its response to the draft report the competent auth

Official inspections on operators' HACCP systems are carried out adequately, however problems identified regarding official validation of processing method 7 and official sampling weaken the effectiveness of these controls.

Two of the four processing plants visited were located in Bavaria. In one plant, official samples for microbiological analyses were not taken between 2011 and 2018 because the competent authority stated they did not identify in this plant any relevant problem during official controls that would require official sampling (see finding 19). In 2018, two samples were taken for Salmonella detection from PAP as feed material by the feed control authority. Non-compliance was not detected in these samples. In the other plant visited, official microbiological samples were taken for the verification of the heat treatment in 2018. Microbiological contamination was not detected in these samples, however

In two processing plants visited located in Lower-Saxony, official microbiological samples were taken for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae from PAP. However, in several cases the number of samples sent for laboratory tests was lower than that required by Chapter I, Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

In all processing plants visited, regular microbiological samples were taken by operators for microbiological control of produced PAP. In one plant, samples were always taken from the production line not from the storage of final product; in another plant, only 1-1 samples were taken from each production batch for control of Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae. While these plants were subject to official inspections, the local inspectors had not identified that such sampling is not in line with the requirements of Chapter I, Annex X, of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

Inadequate checks on the implementation of requirements concerning confirmation of TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI negatively affect the reliability of the flow of information on the intra-EU trade of such products.

A number of guides are available to support the use of TRACES: - The FLI has prepared a guidance document with the most important questions and answers relating to the use of TRACES and a general instruction on the use of the DOCOM (commercial document) part of TRACES in case of trade in Category 1, 2 and 3 ABP and derived products. - In Bavaria, chapter 13.2 of the ABP manual gives detailed instructions on the use of TRACES in case of intra-EU trade of PAP including the obligatory notification back to the place of origin. Chapter 14.3 gives detailed instructions on the use of TRACES in case of export of PAP containing ruminant protein. There is no instruction on the requirement for TRACES n

The audit team noted that, although guidance/instructions (see finding 22) were established to this effect by the competent authorities, arrivals of consignments of PAP were not systematically confirmed by the German competent authorities to the competent authorities of the Member State of origin by means of TRACES, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017 and in 2018, around 23% and 30%, respectively, of such arrivals were not notified back.

Inadequate checks on the implementation of requirements concerning confirmation of TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI negatively affect the reliability of the flow of information on the intra-EU trade of such products.

Chapter 14.3 gives detailed instructions on the use of TRACES in case of export of PAP containing ruminant protein. There is no instruction on the requirement for TRACES n

The federal competent authority confirmed that intra-EU trade of consignments OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM must be notified in TRACES, based on Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In one Land visited, the competent authority stated that this requirement was not clear for them and they started to implement it only recently. In 2018, the majority of consignments of OF/SI containing PAP traded to other Member States were notified in TRACES. 5.2.3 Exports and imports of PAP

Considering the high number of missing confirmations on the arrival of consignments containing ruminant PAP from points of exit in Germany and in other Member States and the lack of control mechanisms in PAP processing plants to verify that the confirmation of the seal check at the point of exit had been received through TRACES, the German competent authorities could not always ensure that the channelling 14 procedure for export of PAP containing ruminant protein is adequately implemented. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The structure of the official control system and the planning of official controls along the chain of production and trade of PAP provides a good basis for implementation of official

The audit team visited a paper trader (see finding 10). The trader started its business in 2008 and it was registered based on Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 in December 2016. In 2018, the arrival to the BIP of approximately 10% of the export consignments containing PAP with ruminant protein traded by the operator was not confirmed in TRACES and no information was available on the seal check, contrary to the requirements of Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Local official controls had not detected this problem during the last official inspection in January 2019. The audit team reviewed the documentation provided by the operator (invoice, bill of loadi

The audit team identified several systematic shortcomings relating to TRACES notifications of consignments containing ruminant PAP intended for export from Germany to third countries and to the official controls in this regard: 11 Contrary to the requirements of fourth sentence of point 1(c) of Section E, Chapter V, of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, the arrival of significant numbers of consignments intended for export at the point of exit notified in TRACES was not confirmed by the relevant BIP in Germany. In cases where the consignments were intended for export via another Member State and the authorities of the exit point did not confirm the arrival of these consignments at thei

Significant numbers of consignments of PAP which did not contain ruminant proteins were notified in TRACES (as "Mammalia-Ruminantia") although such consignments are not subject to official control in this regard at the point of exit. In several cases consignments produced in processing plants which are not approved for production of PAP containing ruminant protein (for example processing plants with only pig PAP processing lines) declared the species as Mammalia. These inconsistent declarations of the goods (animal species) in TRACES by the business operators created confusion at the points of exit, because based on the TRACES notification it was not clear to the relevant authorities whether

In 2018, 14 Category 3 export consignments were notified in TRACES as Category 1 and Category 2 products. The competent authority had identified these mistakes although the TRACES notifications were only corrected during the audit.

Inadequate implementation of EU requirements concerning transmission of information to the competent authority of the Member State of origin or destination via TRACES relating to intra-EU trade of PAP undermines the reliability of information on the intra- EU trade of such products.

The audit team noted that, contrary to the requirements of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the NVWA does not systematically confirm the arrival of consignment of PAP to competent authorities of the Member State of origin by means of TRACES. The system of checks in place is based on random selection of certain consignments in TRACES and a cross-check of these data on the spot. Only 10% of required confirmations took place in recent years. The frequency of confirmation to the place of origin did however increase to 20% in 2019 (see also finding 20).

Inadequate implementation of EU requirements concerning transmission of information to the competent authority of the Member State of origin or destination via TRACES relating to intra-EU trade of PAP undermines the reliability of information on the intra- EU trade of such products.

The competent authority stated that trade of consignments of OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM is not notified in TRACES. This is not in line with Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 5.2.3 Exports and imports of PAP

The lack of an adequate control mechanism in place to verify at the point of exit that all consignments of ruminant PAP exported from the Netherlands and other EU Member States have actually left the EU territory undermines the effectiveness of official controls in place. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS As regards implementation of official controls requirements regarding the hygiene, traceability and the trade of PAP in the Netherlands, the overall picture is mixed. On the positive side, the system of official controls is underpinned by comprehensive establishment listing, well-managed cooperation and communication within the competent authority, and comprehensive instructions and guidance for inspec

Checks on exports of consignments of ruminant PAP via the port of Rotterdam are is carried out in accordance with the internal instructions of the NVWA. The competent authority stated that there are two types of official controls on exported consignments from the Netherlands, namely administrative and physical controls. Administrative checks on consignments with the origin in the Netherlands are carried out in the processing plants, including check of data in TRACES. Following the pre-notification via e-mail the local inspectors can carry out a random check of the containers at the point of exit. However, the audit team noted that the pre-notification via e-mail from the operator to the comp

Physical controls (seal checks) are carried out at an inspection centre of the BIP Rotterdam approved for import of liquid fats, oils and fish oils at Maastank B.V. No seal checks are carried out on consignments with origin in other Member States (Belgium, United Kingdom). This is not in line with point 1 of section E of Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. As regards consignments from Ireland, the competent authority stated that these consignments are only being transhipped in the port of Rotterdam.

The NVWA inspectors who do not have access to TRACES carry out seal checks on a certain proportion of consignments intended for export. There is no procedure in place to require that the competent authority responsible for the exit point (border inspection 10 post) informs via TRACES the competent authorities of the processing plants about the arrival of the consignment at the exit point and such notifications are not made by the inspectors. This is not in line with point (c) of section E of Chapter 5 of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

However, problems identified regarding operators' validation of method 7 in the 11 processing plants and the official assessments thereof, undermine confidence in the reliability of the results of official controls on this aspect of PAP production.

Three processing plants visited during the audit use processing method 7, which had been authorised by the competent authority. In one processing plant, during the 30 day validation period microbiological samples had been taken (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium perfringens) by the operator. The audit team noted that the sampling frequency and laboratory results were in compliance with EU legislation.

In another processing plant visited, the validation report provided by the operator to the competent authority at the time of validation did not contain all of the processing 8 parameters required by point G 2, Chapter III, of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) 142/2011. The competent authority had not noticed this shortcoming.

However, problems identified regarding the official inspection of commercial documents, limited controls of transporters transporting ABP for the production of PAP for aquaculture, and the authorisation of validation of processing method 7 weaken the effectiveness of these official inspections.

In the two Regions visited some transporters transported ABP to processing plants authorised for the production of PAP for feeding aquaculture animals. These transporters were registered for transport of Category 3 ABP from all kind of species including ruminant and non-ruminant animals. In accordance with point (b) Section D, Chapter IV, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 the animal by-products of non- ruminant origin intended for production of PAP for feeding aquaculture animals should not be transported in vehicles and containers used for the transport of ABP of ruminant origin unless these vehicles and containers have been cleaned beforehand in order to avoid cross-contamination in

However, problems identified regarding the official inspection of commercial documents, limited controls of transporters transporting ABP for the production of PAP for aquaculture, and the authorisation of validation of processing method 7 weaken the effectiveness of these official inspections.

Two processing plants visited were using processing method 7, which had been authorised by the competent authority. In one processing plant, during the 30 day validation period microbiological samples had been taken (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium perfringens) by the operator. The local inspector was not present during this sampling. The operator could not demonstrate that there was a sampling procedure in place at the time of the validation and the operator also could not demonstrate the place of the sampling. The operator sent these samples to a laboratory which was not accredited for testing Clostridium perfringens. The operator stated that the sampling protocol did not accom

In the other processing plant the whole validation procedure was well documented, and the microbiological results were adequate. The official inspector was not present when the samples were taken. The operator had a written sampling procedure in the HACCP plan following the legal instructions. When the operator explained to the auditor his sampling procedure during validation, he stated that the samples were taken at the border of the end of the processing line and the place of storage. The samples for Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae were taken only 3-4 hours later than the end of the production. This very short time after a relatively high temperature (80 C) heat treatment does not give s

However, problems identified regarding the official inspection of commercial documents, limited controls of transporters transporting ABP for the production of PAP for aquaculture, and the authorisation of validation of processing method 7 weaken the effectiveness of these official inspections.

Checks on commercial documents accompanying consignments of raw ABP and derived products is part of the routine official inspections and these checks should be recorded in the relevant checklists. The auditor identified a significant number of commercial documents at processing plants, transporters, and storage plants visited that did not contain information on the sub-category of ABP, contrary to the requirement of Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, and/or without information on the species despite the fact that these consignments of ABP were sent for the production of feed. Several commercial documents of intra-EU trade of Category 3 ABP originating from Spain did not contain info

In some cases local inspectors stated that they orally communicated non-compliances relating to commercial documents to the operators or they sent emails informing the operators on these non-compliances, however these were not recorded in official inspection reports. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2204. The auditor saw evidence of email notifications. A similar problem was identified by an internal audit in 2016 (see finding 8).

Inadequate implementation of requirements concerning information to be transmitted back to the competent authority of the Member State of origin via TRACES relating to intra-EU trade of PAP negatively affect the reliability of the flow of information on the intra-EU trade of such products. 14 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The system of official controls is underpinned by comprehensive internal listing of ABP operators, well-managed cooperation and communication within and between the different competent authorities and comprehensive instructions and guidance for officials. Generally, the official controls carried out on-the-spot provide a good basis for assuring that operators and products satisfy E

The central competent authority has prepared a procedure for the notification of intra- EU trade of PAP and MBM in the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES). Point 3 of this procedure describes the obligation of the Spanish competent authorities to inform the competent authority of Member State of origin of the arrival of each consignment. Based on this procedure the Spanish competent authorities have two options of how to inform the competent authority of origin. The first is via TRACES, which is the requirement of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; the second is to send back the fourth copy of the commercial document from the receiver business to the producer business based on

The auditor noted that the Spanish competent authorities did not systematically inform via TRACES the competent authorities of the Member State of origin of the arrival of consignments of PAP, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017 and 2018, no information was sent to the Member State of origin in relation to around 80% of such arrivals. The auditor also noted that most of the operators visited used the second option of the procedure described in finding 23.

The process for granting approval ensures that insect PAP placed on the market complies with microbiological safety criteria, but was insufficiently robust as regards the assessment of the validation of the processing method and of the HACCP-based procedures; this however did not affect the safety of the product.

The audit team noted that two of the operators visited had received approval for using processing method 7 in a continuous system, however: a. One operator, despite being approved for processing in a continuous system, had carried out validation for the processing method in a batch system with single loads of material ranging from 80 to 120 kg while the targeted operational capacity of the system was up to two tonnes per hour. This way of processing was neither reflected in the operators HACCP-based procedures nor in the approval document issued by the authority; b. Neither of the two operators explained in the validation file the way they measured the feeding rate to demonstrate the minimum

Whilst an arrangement for listing and maintaining the list of approved ABP operators is in place, it is not publicly available and is not updated promptly. This limits the possibility of the public, authorities from other Member States and other operators to verify if a given operator placing its products on the market is approved or not. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE PRODUCTION, PLACING ON THE MARKET AND TRADE OF INSECT PAP AND INSECTS AS FEED

The DGAL website contains the link to the lists of ABP-approved and registered establishments and personnel responsible for official controls have access to these lists. The audit team noted that the link restricts external access and therefore, neither the public nor operators can access the lists. Moreover, the list for Category 3 ABP processing plants (relevant for this audit) held by the authority was outdated (October 2018) and, as a consequence, did not contain information on one of the two approved operators visited. This is not in line with Article 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 requiring that Member States shall keep up-to-date lists of approved or registered establishments, pla

At the wholesaler and the veterinary practitioner of the para-pharmacy visited by the audit team, an electronic system was in use, which fulfilled the record-keeping requirements and the annually required comparison between incoming and outgoing medicinal supplies, as foreseen in Article 65(3) of Directive 2001/82/EC.

Methods are validated according to an in-house validation procedure, which is based on requirements laid down in Decision 2002/657/EC. The samples are required to be spiked at three concentration levels with six repetitions as required in point 3.1.2.2 of the aforementioned decision, thus recommendation No 4 of the 2011 audit report has been addressed. However, one parameter, the within-laboratory reproducibility, is not part of the formalised validation plan, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in point 3.1.2.3 of the Annex I to Commission decision 2002/657/EC. Nonetheless, the competent authority can have confidence in the reliability of the result given the other quality

For all confirmatory methods, as ongoing quality assurance, two calibration curves are included in each analytical series (one at the beginning, one at the end). Furthermore quality control samples, blank samples and fortified samples are run with each sequence and internal standards are used regularly as far as possible. This is in line with the requirements of point 2.3.1 of Annex 1 to Decision 2002/657/EC. The recovery from the fortified samples is used for a recovery correction. Newly prepared standard solutions are checked against old standard solutions. The spiking solution for recovery control samples are different from those used for the preparation of the calibration curves. Quality

paragraph_text: The residue monitoring plan is generally implemented in accordance with planned arrangements. In many cases, the inspectors stated that the samples on the farms would be taken randomly thus underestimating the importance of targeted sampling, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in points 2.1 and 2.3.2.1 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC). The audit team noted that the same establishments (e.g. farms and slaughterhouses) had been sampled for several substance groups on the same day, in some cases even for the same substances. In some cases, this was because the number of samples to be taken was higher than the number of establishments to be sampled. However, in other cases, although the number of samples was limited and much smaller that the number of establishments to sample, several samples were taken from the same establishment. This contradicts the DVFA's own sampling procedure and is not in line with the sampling strategy and targeting criteria laid down in point 2.1, 2.2, 2.3.2 and 2.3.3 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/E

Although instructions and documents seen by the audit team unambiguously require official samples to be sealed, the audit team observed a number of cases where no official sealing had been performed, or performed in a way not ensuring the custody chain and such samples (e.g. from small slaughterhouses) had been kept/transported by a third party service provider. paragraph_text: The standard of record-keeping of treatments on farms was not in line with EU requirements, with the potential consequence of an increased risk of placing on the market animal products within the withdrawal periods. In the event that such violations would occur, the incompleteness of the records hampers the effectiveness of any follow-up investigations.

Such inventories were kept at the farms visited, but contrary to the requirements in EU legislation 49 (where keepers of food-producing animals need to maintain treatment records for a period of five years after the treatment), the registration of use of veterinary medicinal products (treatment records) presented deficiencies as follows: at the dairy farm the treatment records detailed the individual animals, the dates and the withdrawal periods. paragraph_text: There is a system of official controls in place supported by procedures and applied as required by performing inspections and sampling. The approach followed by the inspectors regarding purity criteria does not correlate completely to what is prescribed in the relevant guide which might lead to misinterpretation as to what is required to be checked during official controls. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Official controls consist of sampling and analysis of products destined for the final consumer for FIAs and of on-the-spot controls to verify the FIAs' correct use and labell

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls of FBOs providing or using FIA
paragraph_text: Official controls at FIA users' level are lacking in completeness and depth resulting in an insufficient verification of the compliance with FIA legislation. The absence of specific guidance or instructions creates inconsistencies in the approach followed by the inspectors (i.e. omission to ask for the recipe of the product being examined in relation to FIA used, define the product category and examine the specifications of all the raw materials used in the production of a that product). Adding to that, the limited hands-on experience of the inspectors leads to the oversight of certain issues regarding FIA during such controls. 16

There is no common checklist or guidance at national level to control FBOs regarding FIA use, hence the local authorities using different approaches for these controls (documents to be requested, aspects to be covered, controlling FIA either during inspection or audit). In one of the Regions visited, the local authorities prepared a detailed checklist which acts as guidance for those controls. In the other Region, officials are advised to use a checklist prepared for the controls of FIA in approved establishments handling food of animal origin, also in controls at registered establishments. The depth of the controls also depends on the expertise and knowledge of the individual inspectors. Di

Regarding the FIA users, local authorities in the first Region visited explained that they have recently prepared a pilot checklist which will allow them to cover the aspects not covered to date. The audit team noted that, since this is a relatively new development, inspectors do not follow a structured approach, and sometimes rely solely on the information provided by the FBOs. Some of the elements that the inspectors omitted to examine were: the specifications of raw materials for possible presence of FIA, the recipe of the product examined (which should be the starting point of such controls), the identification of the correct food category; in addition, no requests were made for addition

With regard to FIA users, as indicated at regional level, there is no specific checklist for registered establishments. The approach followed by the inspectors during controls of FIA users was, in the majority of the cases, not consistent (as to what, when and how to 10 check) and not well structured. Some of the inspections were detailed and complete (checking specific requirement for labelling, knowledge of Aluminium-lakes requirements for colours) whereas in others certain elements were not addressed.

Some of the omissions observed by the audit team were: absence of checks of the specifications of the different ingredients to see if some additives could be present, and which of these additives could have a technological function in the final product; failure to note that the specifications regarding purity criteria were incomplete; and conduct of calculations using the weight of the intermediate product (dough) and not of the final product, as appropriate. Nevertheless, when asked by the audit team, in all cases the inspectors were able to re-evaluate or seek for more information for those aspects.

In the second Region visited the audit team was informed that inspectors cover the topic of FIA at FIA users' level during audits. Only in one case the inspectors confirmed that they would start using the dedicated checklist for approved establishments, also for registered establishments as recommended by the regional authority.

The CAs are designated for the official controls throughout the whole production chain (including those at the "green line"). The structures, organisation, powers, staff knowledge and procedures in place (with the exception of those for landing sites and associated operations, small fishing vessels and public health aspects of aquaculture 6 farming), support the implementation of official controls and provide a good basis for meeting EU requirements.

The official control system is implemented in land-based establishments, RVs and certain fishing vessels but excludes smaller primary production fishing vessels, most landing sites/fishing shelters and harvesting of aquaculture products (public health aspects) which is not in compliance with EU requirements.
The Animal Health and Welfare Division (AHWD) of the VS is responsible for aquaculture farms (animal health issues).
Since the 2013 financial crisis, the number of VOs has been reduced by approximately 50% and 30% for Veterinary Inspectors.

Overtime is limited, making inspection visits out of working hours problematic. This is particularly relevant for inspections on vessels where operations such as landing of fishery products, may be outside normal office hours. 5.1.4 Training and knowledge of staff performing official controls

The audit team noted that: The checklists for aquaculture farms are restricted to animal health issues to the exclusion of public health issues. The vessel checklist in use (form for the unloading of fishery products) focusses on the general hygiene and organoleptic characteristics of fishery products at the time of unloading and onward transport. It does not make reference to the detailed vessel requirements laid down in Section VII, Chapter 1 of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. A new VS manual of staff instructions is under development containing operational guidelines, instructions and procedures to better guide inspectors. 5.1.7 Control activities, methods and techniques

There is a procedure for risk categorization of land-based establishments producing food, which are subject to inspection (including an inspection report template). This procedure is used by the officials when determining the frequency of inspections. In practice, official controls are carried out twice/year but sometimes more frequently, if the risk assessment requires this. Larger vessels (i.e. more than 12 meters in length and fishing for more than eight hours) are now inspected annually (previously up to four times per year) and there is a proposal (not yet adopted) to inspect RVs once every four years. They primarily look at veterinary medicinal products' residues, biosecurity and animal movements. VS officials have generally not been present at the slaughter/harvesting of fish.

Any horse entering the country as part of intra-community trade is covered by a health certificate and is registered in TRACES. It must be registered in the CBC within 30 days and in any case before any change in keeper. Where no health certificate can be submitted to the CBC at the time of the registration request or where the health certificate is non-compliant, an approved veterinarian must perform a clinical examination of the animal and a blood sample is taken to test for the absence of specific diseases, such as Infectious anemia at the keeper's expense. In practice, very often the health certificate is kept by the first keeper (most commonly a dealer) and is not available to the owner

The OVs met, in general, are capable of detecting deficiencies and are aware of legal requirements. Nonetheless, the audit team noted certain non-compliances during the on- site visits not detected and / or recorded by the officials.

In one slaughterhouse visited, the audit team noticed non-compliances related to stunning (level of water in electrical water bath did not allow immersion of the birds up to the base of the wings) which was not noted by the OV during a daily control. In addition, when the FBO staff demonstrated the check on stunning, the person took a bird from the line after stunning and explained that the bird should wake up in 90 seconds. When the person was advised to check e.g. cornea reflex by the audit team, the person did not perform the check correctly. The OV did not correct the person and explained later that the person was not the animal welfare officer.

The audit team noted non-compliances in the abovementioned slaughterhouse related to PMI. The birds fallen from the line before PMI, are not presented for PMI as required in point 1, Part B, Chapter V, Section IV of Annex 1 to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, but are disposed as unfit for human consumption. Furthermore, all carcases are washed after evisceration before entering PMI (the same non-compliance was detected by the audit team also in another slaughterhouse visited). These non-compliances related to PMI were not noted by the OVs or by the RVA inspectors during their audits.

The audit team noted in the same establishment that, due to current reconstruction works on that day, the cutting room has no hand-washing facilities. FBO explained that the cutting room is being reconstructed due to the age of the facilities and increased slaughtering capacity. Therefore, personal hygiene is organised in other ways and the OV was aware of this exceptional procedure. The audit team noted in the cutting room 5 that knife disinfection is done by using alcohol spray, in accordance with the FBO's HACCP plan. Washing instructions of knives before disinfection are not included in the plan. The official staff had not noted/recorded this deficiency. During the visit, the hand washin

The audit team reviewed some OV records of temperatures of the cold storage rooms in the same slaughterhouse. The audit team saw evidence that the OV had detected a deficiency in cold chain in one freezer (temperatures between -9,6 and -11,9 for five hours as the minimum should be -18) and had informed the FBO. The FBO had explained to the OV that air temperature in this freezer fluctuates when the door is open. The OV had not recorded this non-compliance in a logbook and therefore, there was no evidence if any corrective action had been requested and / or taken.

In the abovementioned slaughterhouse, the inspection frequency is six times per year (the baseline frequency). However, the audit team saw deficiencies in hygiene (as listed above but also due to ongoing reconstruction) that might indicate higher risk and therefore should result in increased inspection frequency.

The audit team noted in two out of three slaughterhouses visited that washing of carcases takes place after evisceration and before PMI. This non-compliance was not detected by any level of CAs. This is a repeated finding from the audit carried out in 2010 when measures were not taken during slaughter to prevent contamination of meat, in particular, the spillage of digestive tract contents during evisceration, as required in point 5, Chapter IV, Section II of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

In general, the establishments visited comply with EU requirements or the corrective actions have been taken and are in place to reach the adequate compliance level. The control procedures are adopted by officials. Nonetheless, the audit team detected during the on-site visits certain non-compliances which are described in detail in chapter 5.2. 11

The audit team noted in one slaughterhouse visited that the premises need reconstruction due to the age of the building and the increased production capacity. The audit team saw the FBO's reconstruction plan and some of those planned changes had started by the time of the audit. In another slaughterhouse, speed of the slaughter line in relation to the capacity of chilling and cutting of carcases had a negative impact on progression of cutting and maintenance of the required temperature in meat (the same non-compliance was noted during 2010 audit). label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls are planned on the basis of the risk categorisation of FBOs, which does not give the necessary weight to the key elements supporting the categorisation. As a consequence, the frequency of controls and follow-up of previously detected non- conformities may be not appropriate.

Risk classification is determined by DGAL by the application of a formula which comprises the outcome of the last inspection and the volume, type and target of production; the reliability of the FBOs, in performing their own-checks and informing the CAs of any real or potential risk, is not weighted appropriately in this formula. It is noted that the highest risk class IV does not necessarily include insufficiently performing FBOs; FBOs with high volumes of production, or targeting highly sensible consumers, may also be included in this class. On the other hand, a very negative notation of one of the elements of the formula does not necessarily lead to an increase in the risk classification

After each inspection a report with the findings is created and signed by the official. The FBO receives the report with an accompanying letter containing the final decision, signed at Department level. The findings are recorded in the RESYTAL database and are scored, according to their seriousness, within the formula used for the risk classification of FBOs for the following year (see paragraph 43).

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The CA in the slaughterhouses carries out the verification of the eligibility of horses for slaughter for human consumption in a meticulous way, allowing the detection non- compliances and irregularities. The system ensures that only horses with correct identification and clearance for slaughter enter the food chain. However, the virtually complete absence of records of the medical treatments in the passports, together with the scarce verification of compliance with the requirements on prescription and correct recording of the applied treatments in the horse passports, reduces the confidence that only horses which are eligible for human consumption are presented for slaughter.

During the on-site visits, the audit team was able to verify the implementation of the requirements, both with regard to the obligations of the FBO and of the duties of the OVs. Documented evidence was available, confirming that deficiencies are identified and that action is taken, including destruction of carcases with missing identification or for issues related to passports. Treatments were hardly ever recorded in the passports of horses that remain eligible for slaughter.

During the visit to the horse clinic, the audit team also collected information that almost every serious treatment of horses performed due to the absence of specific medication destined for horses, results in the exclusion of these horses from the food chain. Typically, that information is introduced in the passport, if the passport is available, or if this is not possible then that is communicated in a documented way to the owner who then has the responsibility to sign the passport and inform the CBDK about the exclusion of the horse from the food chain.

The audit team checked over 100 passports at the different locations visited (i.e. slaughterhouses, horse dealer, assembly centres). With very few exceptions, no medical treatments were recorded, even when horses were more than ten years old. In the audit team's view, this near-absence of records appears very unrealistic, even if the EU legislation requires that only certain veterinary medications must be recorded in the passport. The CA acknowledged the finding.

To date, there is no cross-reference to verify that the treatments indicated in the records kept by the clinics were transferred when required to the passports and if this is communicated to the CBDK in cases where the treatment would exclude the horse from the food chain. Additionally, it was explained that the RVI do carry out inspections in holdings, during which the treatments records are checked but that those controls focus only on poultry, pigs and cattle.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: Official controls for verification of FBOs' compliance with the relevant EU requirements (including: hygiene, HACCP, own-check sampling, animal welfare, traceability, labelling, food additives, identification marking, etc.) in PM/PMP establishments are in place and in general can provide guarantees that the establishments meet those requirements. However, there were two exceptions, where establishments presented serious structural and hygiene requirements which had not been detected by any level of the CA controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls at establishment level
paragraph_text: Ante-mortem and post-mortem inspections are, in general, carried out in compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, with the exception of significant failure in performing post-mortem inspection in one establishment visited.

The audit team was informed by the DVOs in the districts visited that all AVs are paid from the state budget and that no direct payments from FBOs occur. However, their remuneration is based on the number of animals inspected or on the amount of meat introduced to the cutting plant they supervise. If the activity of the establishment where they perform their duties is stopped for any reason, they are not paid for the period concerned. Therefore, this payment system undermines the AVs' independence in those situations where the required enforcement measures to be taken on the spot would imply or include e.g. stopping of the slaughter operation (see paragraphs 77 and 92).

The CCA informed the audit team that the total number of AVs involved in official controls of meat establishments (including slaughterhouses) was 3,318 in 2018. The audit team noted that this number remained constant between 2016 and 2018 (3,320 in 2016 and 3,279 in 2017). However, during the same period the number of permanent official veterinarians decreased by 141, most of them (90) in the districts, from 2,172 (1,638 in the districts) in 2016 to 2,031(1,548 in the districts) in 2018.

In particular, in 2018, in all 305 districts, there were 396 full time employed official veterinarians in charge of food safety. In each district visited, the audit team noted that there are vacant posts (in some cases for years) which cannot be filled in the absence of applicants, due to non-competitive salaries. In at least two districts visited, only one Food Safety official was available, while there were two posts assigned for the performance of the planned activities.

Despite the shortage of permanent staff declared in all of the districts that were visited, the audit team was informed and saw evidence that the DVIs were able to achieve the number and scope of controls for the establishments visited. Nevertheless, this did not always result in reaching the quality of controls necessary to verify compliance of the FBOs concerned (see Chapter 5.4.2.1). 5.2.4 Training
