label_heading: Conclusions on Registration / Approval of Food Establishments
paragraph_text: Procedures are in place for the registration of primary producers in a national electronic database. However, to date not all FBOs within the scope of this audit have met their obligation to be registered. Thus, not all FBOs are under official control.

The CAs informed the audit team that the verification of the registration of primary producers in operation is done by cross-checking data with controls on retail level, especially on local markets. However, in one RO visited the number of primary FBOs registered in the scope of this audit moved from 3 in 2017 to 46 in 2019 indicating that there may still be a significant number of unregistered primary producers in the country.

The ROs and the CCA informed the audit team that during controls at retail level, non- registered primary producers of FNAO are still being identified. The CCA concluded that at the time of the audit not all primary producers of FNAO were registered. FBOs involved in the "sprout chain"

In the first RO visited, there were 46 primary producers of soft berries of which 33 registered in 2019; at the time of the audit, none has been inspected. The CA informed the audit team that based on its interpretation of the national law, all primary producers have to be classified as "Very Low Risk" which implies inspection within 6 years after registration. As a consequence, no inspection reports were available.

In the second RO visited there were 26 primary producers, 19 of which having been registered in 2019. Seven inspection reports for 2018 were available, none indicating non-compliances related to the scope of this audit. The head of service and the inspectors informed the audit team that those primary producers have to be inspected at earliest after 6 months but within in one year from the registration, in line with the national law. label_heading: Conclusions on Organisation and Scope of Official Controls
paragraph_text: There is an official control system in place covering FNAO. However, contrary to the requirements of Article 3(3) of Regulation (EU) No 882/2004, primary production before and during harvest is not under official control and this weakens the effectiveness of official controls related to FNAO.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: Due to the fact that in practice all primary producers are classified in the "very low risk category", the risk based categorisation cannot prioritise primary producers of FNAO with higher microbiological risks for official controls. This weakens targeting, and thus the effectiveness of the official control system.

Important factors such as size of the plant and production volume are not taken into account for the risk categorisation. The CCA agreed that adding this relevant information would improve the risk based plan.

SFVS has the legal power to perform inspections at all stages of production. SFVS is the CCA in charge for official controls pre-, during and after harvest. However, all the inspectors met informed the audit team that inspections are performed at the level of the premises (storing and/or packing area). Primary production before and during harvest is not subject to official controls. 9

The audit team visited two ROs. Both heads of the service informed the audit team that official controls take place at the premises, after harvest. Inspections at field level before and during harvest are not carried out, as confirmed by the inspectors met.

Requirements such as workers' hygiene, use of fertilisers, irrigation waters, and facilities were addressed by the inspectors without going into the field. Inspectors confirmed that official controls take place exclusively at the premises. 11

The leafy green vegetables primary producer visited was classified as "medium risk", but when asked about this classification, inspectors informed the audit team that it was related to premises (trading of imported leafy green vegetables, packaging and labelling). The inspectors informed the audit team that the right risk categorisation, including only the primary production on the field and greenhouse, will be assessed as "very low risk", contrary to the national law.
This last FBO was already inspected but inspections never took place in the field. This was the first inspection performed by inspectors on the field regarding microbiological risks.

For another three processing establishments, documents related to the risk categorisation were asked. This information established that for one of them, the risk categorisation was not done yet, and that these establishments had not been assessed in respect of all their activities (processors, wholesalers) contrary to national law. 12

This is of particular relevance given that staff numbers had not increased in parallel to the increased work load in recent years.

A uniform model to register is used in Poland for FNAO. The data requested by the model requires general information of the primary producers, e.g. name, official identification numbers and some regarding the crop. The number of registrations of primary producers increased from around 57 000 in 2016 to 85 000 in 2019; 43 000 of these were primary producers of FNAO intended to be eaten raw. CSI has no access to other official databases of primary producers. The CSI stated that the total number of primary producers in Poland is estimated about 700 000 (animal holdings and non-food producers included).

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: Both CAs have put in place a system of routine risk-based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by procedures and a comprehensive network of accredited laboratories under national coordination. Inspections, official sampling and in the Cataluña also audits cover relevant aspects of the legislation. The procedures for organisation of controls are currently under review in Navarra for further fine-tuning the risk determination for the RTE sector, for deciding the frequency for controls over FBOs HACCP based procedures, currently limited, and specific sector requirements and for starting to implement audits of FBOs' procedures and practices.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the "Hygiene Package", although there is scope for improvement in the controls over FBO's measures for prevention of cross-contamination and verification within the HACCP-based procedures, including the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and of the EURL guidelines. The CAs' ability to detect relevant non-compliances and require adequate corrective actions is hindered by the fact that the control focus does not or not necessarily target (all) the areas relevant for food safety, whether by design or at the time of their implementation, and by some gaps in the knowledge of control staff.

The CAs met reported certain human resources challenges over recent years, which in some cases - together with organisational changes, information technology (IT) systems changes and resources allocation - were highlighted by the CAs met as the cause for reduced implementation of certain controls (e.g. on FBOs HACCP based procedures in Navarra, and supervisory controls in both regions visited).

However, some recommendations dating from 2015 such as putting in place audits of FBOs and an internal (CA) verification/supervisory system had not been closed to date. This is not in line with Article 4, Paragraph 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The ACCA took some actions to address them, though limited for the RTE sector. The CA cited IT - and staffing issues (see paragraph 14), but indicated that these recommendations would be addressed this year.

In Navarra, the risk-based criteria are used for establishing the frequency for general hygiene controls for new FBOs and new activities. For other cases, the frequency is every five years. The risk- based criteria are not used for establishing the frequency of controls over FBOs own controls including HACCP- based procedures, nor for controls on specific sector requirements (e.g. raw milk criteria). In Cataluña, the frequency of all types of controls is established on a risk basis.

In Navarra, CAs are required to carry out controls over FBOs HACCP-based procedures at approval, for expansion of activity, and in the case of alerts. Individual inspectors decide when to carry out controls on specific sector requirements. In the dairy establishment visited in Navarra the last control for specific requirements was carried out in 2014. In the same establishment, the last control related to FBOs HACCP- based procedures took place at the time of approval (in 2007) despite expansion works and changes in production.

The CA prioritisation of the controls for an FBO with multiple-activities and more establishments with the same approval (in Cataluña) did not allow an adequate focus on the risk areas. Consequently, the high-risk area visited by the audit team was not subject to recent controls. This prevented the CA from detecting several non-compliances noted during the audit team's visit, some of them long-standing. 4.4.1.2 Procedures for official controls

Each CA has procedures and instructions for staff performing official controls that apply to RTE food production. To the extent assessed by the audit team, these procedures are facilitating the official controls and are in general known and used by the staff met during this audit. The inspectors met considered them as supportive to their work. The procedures cover inspections and sampling, and in Cataluña also audits. Navarra does not have procedures for audits of FBOs' practices and procedures as required by Article 4, Paragraph 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

In Navarra the procedures are under review to ensure that a frequency for certain controls (e.g. on routine controls for FBOs HACCP based procedures and on sector 13 specific requirements) and for the use of related checklists is defined. Certain aspects (e.g. some provisions of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, the use of identification marks) that are mandatory for official controls, were not included in the checklists. This led to a lack of related controls. The regional CA undertook to include them during the revision of the checklists.

The CAs produce reports on the official controls carried out. In line with Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, these reports include a description of the purpose of official controls, the methods applied, the results obtained and action to be taken by the FBO concerned. The FBOs receive a copy of the report. The audit team noted, in some of the reports in both AC, limited evidence that all aspects included in the scope of the control were covered, as required in the ACCAs control procedures. 4.4.1.3 Scope/coverage of official controls

Official controls are performed in Programmes that are grouped together in blocks. The following Programmes, particularly relevant for the scope of this audit, and the related implementation data provided by the CCA are summarised below: a. Programme 1 - general control of food establishments - include hygiene inspections. The MANCP data indicate that this Programme is applied yearly in all ACs and that the ACCAs implemented approximately 85% of the 435 809 scheduled controls under this Programme for the country in 2017 and detected non-compliances in 26 % of these controls. b. In establishments (excluding retail) in the meat, dairy, fishery and composite products/prepared dishes sectors - i

Challenges were identified in particular in relation to aspects of training, efficient cooperation and coordination in practice, and the verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods. 4.3 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FBOS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 9 Findings

While an overall good number of inspectors receive yearly relevant training, there are differences between the AC in the array of training topics offered to their staff, and in the percentage of inspectors participating to training. Limited training was offered for controls over microbiological criteria in some AC.

The official control staff met was in general trained and knowledgeable for some parts of their work within the scope of this audit. The audit team identified training needs, mainly in relation to: a. the approval of establishments in Cataluña (see paragraphs 31-35). A new training session on this topic was ongoing at the time of the audit; 7 b. the focus and depth of the controls, and the assessment of the flexibility options and HACCP-based procedures implemented by FBOs, including compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 in both AC visited (see paragraphs 53-62, 66, 88.e, f and g); c. the evaluation of the gravity of certain non-compliances in both AC and taking the required actions i

The findings above suggest that while a wide range of training is offered to staff, the systems in place for identifying and addressing training needs do not adequately capture the individual needs that arise, in particular considering the wide area of official controls over production of RTE food, in order to ensure that staff is kept up-to date in their area of competence as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The procedure for adding new approved activities in Cataluña emphasised that the official controls should not verify FBOs HACCP based procedures, but focus on infrastructure. The ACCA explained that this approach was intended for particular situations. However, its wording led to some confusion amongst control staff on the requirements in the case reviewed by the audit team. The ACCA swiftly modified this procedure during the audit and provided examples of reports of approval visits demonstrating that the approval visits check FBOs' compliance with all relevant requirements of the applicable legislation.

These reports indicated delays of days or months for the approval visits in five out of eight cases (e.g. nine months conditional approval; five months between the first and second approval visit). The district team carrying out controls in the newly approved 10 establishment visited during the audit considered that six months between the first and second approval visit complies with the rules in place. These examples are contrary to the provisions of Article 31, paragraph 2(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and of the regional procedures.

In the case of a recent approval assessed by the audit team, the district CA evaluated FBOs HACCP-based procedure solely during the visit for full approval contrary to the regional procedures. The duration of the full approval visit did not allow a thorough check of FBOs HACCP-based procedures. Consequently, the inspector had not evaluated certain elements thereof, like its validation and verification, as required by the regional procedures.

The CA acknowledged that the extent to which FBO's own procedures are evaluated depends on the background of the inspectors, and some aspects may be overlooked. The inspectors met had not received training in relation to the approval of establishments. A new training session on this topic was ongoing at the time of the audit.

The audit team noted during another visit that more establishments of the same group, located over a few km radius, with public roads between them, have the same approval number. The CCA clarified this is not in line with the legislation. The ACCA indicated this as a particular case due to historical reasons and that work was ongoing to address it. The ACCA started an investigation during the audit to confirm that this was not the case with other establishments in the AC.

The inspectors were in general able to detect non-compliances during the visits carried out as part of the current audit, in particular as regards the general hygiene requirements. While several aspects were adequately covered by the official controls, some aspects were missed and/or not addressed: a. In three establishments (two dairies and a fishery) CA challenges concerning the implementation of flexibility measures led to acceptance of cross-flows in the absence of adequate mitigating measures, as well as to under-detection of some unhygienic practices (e.g. in relation to unpacking, cleaning during production) with potential for cross contamination; b. In one of these establishments (in

The CAs met required the FBOs to take corrective action once they understood the potential impact on the safety of the product and provided the audit team with official control reports of swift follow-up controls. In an establishment producing RTE fishery involved in several alerts in another AC, not visited by the audit team, the official control report immediately prior to the alert suggested a fully compliant FBO. The control reports related to the alerts indicate several non-compliances including structural, hygiene, temperature controls and shelf-life studies. The ACCA reported to have replaced the inspector in the meantime (see paragraph 80).

The approach to controls over FBOs HACCP-based procedures differs between the ACCAs. In Navarra, these controls are comprehensive at the time of approval (except for validation and verification of HACCP based procedures), but they are limited afterwards (see paragraphs 49 and 51d). In Cataluña these controls are part of the routine controls carried out within the risk-based frequency, but limited as regards certain elements of FBOs' HACCP-based procedures. In particular: 15 a. in a multi-activity establishment, FBOs' practical implementation of the critical control point cooking validation and the reprocessing activity had not been part of CA controls for one of the production lines consider

The official controls over FBOs' compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 are part of Programmes 1 and 2. In Cataluña, these controls are part of the routine risk-based controls. In Navarra, these controls check if the FBOs implement the sampling plans described in their HACCP based procedures (evaluated before starting operation). Nonetheless, FBOs further changed the procedures after approval, as noted in the establishments visited, and the CA did not evaluate if the changes ensure continued compliance with the above Regulation.

In the cases assessed by the audit team, the CAs checked whether FBOs implement their sampling and testing plans for food safety criteria. In one case, the CA accepted the limit of 100cfu/g Listeria monocytogenes at the end of production for RTE sushi with a shelf- life of five days, in the absence of adequate FBO demonstration that this value would not be exceeded throughout the shelf-life of the product. This is not in line with Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The CA acknowledged challenges with the controls over FBOs' compliance with this Regulation and the lack of related training.

As regards process hygiene criteria, the controls had not been satisfactory in one of the three cases evaluated by the audit team. The CA considered the process hygiene criteria in Chapter 2, Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 as a FBO's choice and did not require the FBO to include in their procedures the compliance limits for these criteria and the action to be taken in case of non-compliance, as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The controls as regards the number of sampling units were in most cases satisfactory. In the relatively recently approved establishment visited, the CA accepted the FBO's reduction of sampling units from five to one in the absence of historical documentation proving effective HACCP-based procedures, contrary to the requirements of Article 5.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. FBOs' testing methods had not been subject to official controls in the cases assessed. This is not required by the procedures in Navarra.

FBOs' shelf-life studies for RTE food able to support the growth of Listeria are required to be verified by the CAs routinely in Cataluña, but not in Navarra. The cases assessed by the audit team, both in Cataluña and in Comunidad Valenciana, revealed that in 16 general the CA asks for FBO shelf-life studies for Listeria monocytogenes or checks them thoroughly at the time of alerts, but not beforehand or routinely otherwise.

The provisions of the EURL Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes and of the EURL Technical Guidance Document for conducting shelf-life studies on Listeria monocytogenes in RTE foods were in general not known, and not taken into account by CAs met which had not dealt with Listeria alerts.

Consequently, CA accepted that FBOs sampling only after cleaning and disinfection, which makes the detection of the pathogen difficult leading to a false sense of security. In one case where the CA evaluated the FBOs studies as satisfactory, the studies did not demonstrate that the food safety criteria applicable throughout the shelf-life of the products can be met under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Also, the CA did not detect the lack of shelf-life studies for some product classes. In other cases, the CA accepted shelf-life studies based solely on organoleptic properties.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The CAs met during the audit highlighted different challenges in the organisation and performance of controls over the production of RTE food: a. assessing FBOs decisions to classify different types of food as RTE or not considering production product characteristics, heating/cooking instructions, national or regional consumption habits; assessing FBOs shelf-life studies and the limit applied for Listeria monocytogenes, in the absence of more specific guidance and reference persons/experts; b. limited knowledge of some FBOs producing high risk RTE food, especially small ones challenge CAs in their work with these FBOs, in particular in relation to the implementation of own controls including

label_heading: Conclusions on registration and approval of food business operators
paragraph_text: The ACCAs have systems in place for registration and approval of establishments producing RTE foods which for several aspects are supportive of achieving compliance. The ACCAs visited in general apply the related procedures, to a larger extent in Navarra. However, the procedure in Navarra and the implementation of the procedure in Cataluña, connected with training needs, do not ensure full and consistent compliance with the provisions of establishments' approval as provided for in Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 4.4 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OF FBOS PRODUCING RTE FOODS 4.4.1 Organisation and implementation of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002,

Nonetheless, Navarra AC grants full approval after the first on-site visit, without seeing the FBO in operation and without being able to check the FBOs' validation and verification of its HACPP-based procedures. In addition, limited controls on FBO's HACCP-based procedures are implemented in this AC (2% of the establishments in 2017), and the audit team found that some aspects of FBOs validation and verification of HACCP based procedures are missed by these controls.

The procedure for adding new approved activities in Cataluña emphasised that the official controls should not verify FBOs HACCP based procedures, but focus on infrastructure. The ACCA explained that this approach was intended for particular situations. However, its wording led to some confusion amongst control staff on the requirements in the case reviewed by the audit team. The ACCA swiftly modified this procedure during the audit and provided examples of reports of approval visits demonstrating that the approval visits check FBOs' compliance with all relevant requirements of the applicable legislation.

These reports indicated delays of days or months for the approval visits in five out of eight cases (e.g. nine months conditional approval; five months between the first and second approval visit). The district team carrying out controls in the newly approved 10 establishment visited during the audit considered that six months between the first and second approval visit complies with the rules in place. These examples are contrary to the provisions of Article 31, paragraph 2(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and of the regional procedures.

In the case of a recent approval assessed by the audit team, the district CA evaluated FBOs HACCP-based procedure solely during the visit for full approval contrary to the regional procedures. The duration of the full approval visit did not allow a thorough check of FBOs HACCP-based procedures. Consequently, the inspector had not evaluated certain elements thereof, like its validation and verification, as required by the regional procedures.

The CA acknowledged that the extent to which FBO's own procedures are evaluated depends on the background of the inspectors, and some aspects may be overlooked. The inspectors met had not received training in relation to the approval of establishments. A new training session on this topic was ongoing at the time of the audit.

The audit team noted during another visit that more establishments of the same group, located over a few km radius, with public roads between them, have the same approval number. The CCA clarified this is not in line with the legislation. The ACCA indicated this as a particular case due to historical reasons and that work was ongoing to address it. The ACCA started an investigation during the audit to confirm that this was not the case with other establishments in the AC.

The audit team noted difficulties with ensuring that approvals are kept updated in relation to activities no longer carried out by FBOs. In Navarra, one of the 11 establishments visited had approval for an activity not performed in ten years. In Pais Vasco, a dairy FBO informed the CA that the production ceased and the business was intended to be sold or rented. This type of information does not trigger temporary suspension of activity. The CA became aware that production restarted with a new owner due to an alert caused by detection of 100 000cfu/g Listeria monocytogenes in a RTE food produced in the establishment. The CA's visit on-the-spot identified serious non-compliances and the establ

The national measures in place support both FBOs in addressing the microbiological hazards and control the production process of RTE foods, as well as CAs in performing the related official controls. Advice for consumers aiming to prevent food borne outbreaks is also available. There is scope for reviewing the regional measures to support a harmonised and correct implementation by the dairy industry of the measures for verifying the effectiveness of pasteurisation and related official controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on the production of RTE foods
paragraph_text: The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the "Hygiene Package", although there is scope for improvement in the controls over FBO's measures for prevention of cross-contamination and verification within the HACCP-based procedures, including the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and of the EURL guidelines. The CAs' ability to detect relevant non-compliances and require adequate corrective actions is hindered by the fact that the control focus does not or not necessarily target (all) the areas relevant for food safety, whether by design or at the time of their implementation, and by some gaps in the knowledge of control staff.

The regional guidelines for dairy production in Cataluña do not require FBOs to ensure the alternative methods used for alkaline phosphatase testing to verify the effectiveness of the pasteurisation process, are validated against the ISO method provided in Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005. As the guidance is used by both FBOs and CA staff, this aspect was not checked by FBO and not subject to official controls in the case assessed by the audit team. Conclusions on national measures

In the cases assessed by the audit team, the CAs checked whether FBOs implement their sampling and testing plans for food safety criteria. In one case, the CA accepted the limit of 100cfu/g Listeria monocytogenes at the end of production for RTE sushi with a shelf- life of five days, in the absence of adequate FBO demonstration that this value would not be exceeded throughout the shelf-life of the product. This is not in line with Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The CA acknowledged challenges with the controls over FBOs' compliance with this Regulation and the lack of related training.

As regards process hygiene criteria, the controls had not been satisfactory in one of the three cases evaluated by the audit team. The CA considered the process hygiene criteria in Chapter 2, Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 as a FBO's choice and did not require the FBO to include in their procedures the compliance limits for these criteria and the action to be taken in case of non-compliance, as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The controls as regards the number of sampling units were in most cases satisfactory. In the relatively recently approved establishment visited, the CA accepted the FBO's reduction of sampling units from five to one in the absence of historical documentation proving effective HACCP-based procedures, contrary to the requirements of Article 5.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. FBOs' testing methods had not been subject to official controls in the cases assessed. This is not required by the procedures in Navarra.

FBOs' shelf-life studies for RTE food able to support the growth of Listeria are required to be verified by the CAs routinely in Cataluña, but not in Navarra. The cases assessed by the audit team, both in Cataluña and in Comunidad Valenciana, revealed that in 16 general the CA asks for FBO shelf-life studies for Listeria monocytogenes or checks them thoroughly at the time of alerts, but not beforehand or routinely otherwise.

The provisions of the EURL Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes and of the EURL Technical Guidance Document for conducting shelf-life studies on Listeria monocytogenes in RTE foods were in general not known, and not taken into account by CAs met which had not dealt with Listeria alerts.

Consequently, CA accepted that FBOs sampling only after cleaning and disinfection, which makes the detection of the pathogen difficult leading to a false sense of security. In one case where the CA evaluated the FBOs studies as satisfactory, the studies did not demonstrate that the food safety criteria applicable throughout the shelf-life of the products can be met under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Also, the CA did not detect the lack of shelf-life studies for some product classes. In other cases, the CA accepted shelf-life studies based solely on organoleptic properties.

paragraph_text: In those cases where the potential risk associated with non-compliances considered as "minor" is not adequately assessed, this impacts on both the necessary requests for corrective action, as well as on the timeliness of their implementation. The action in case of non-compliance differs between the regions visited and the action in relation to the products is in general limited to instances of confirmed non-compliant official test results. 5 In their comments to the draft report the CA noted that under the procedures corrective measures must always be taken in case of non-compliance, whether minor, serious or very serious. The procedures do not set deadlines for the corrective measures to be

The actions taken in the cases of alerts related to RTE food assessed by the audit team showed a mixed picture. In Navarra, the CA carried out a swift visit on-the-spot and had verified and documented, in subsequent visits, a rapid tracing back, recall and destruction of the merchandise. Contrary to the national procedure for alerts, an official control to ascertain that the measures put in place by the FBO adequately address the cause(s) and prevent its(their) reoccurrence, does not take place. In Cataluña, the CAs carried out on-site visit and investigated the possible causes of RASFF alerts in the cases assessed by the audit team. 19

In Cataluña, the CA releases the detained product involved in a RASFF alert following detection of Salmonella by a molecular method in an outbreak investigation in the absence of apparent causes at establishment level, according to the official control reports carried out at the time and with negative official test results, Subsequently, the confirmation for Salmonella presence using the ISO method and information that the same strain had been involved in an outbreak was received via the RASFF network.

The new information received resulted in the CA questioning the FBO's food safety management system, called for more thorough official controls and CA requests for adequate shelf-life studies. Nonetheless, the CA had accepted that the FBO uses Salmonella-positive ingredients, in the absence of an indication of the level of contamination, provided 15 samples of the final products were negative. According to the FBO demonstration made available to the CA, the respective production process ensures one log reduction.

The ACCA stated the approach taken by the district CA in managing the RASFF alert above is not the routine one. In addition, following the audit team's visit, the CA requested the FBO to review their HACCP based procedures and to demonstrate that the processing is eliminating the hazard in question as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The action taken by the CA in Comunidad Valenciana in relation to several alerts concerning the same establishment producing RTE fishery products revealed also difficulties in ensuring that the contaminated foods are traced and recalled in a timely fashion, and that the actions put in place by the FBOs prevent recurrence. a. Some of the CA on-the-spot visits took place with one and two weeks delay that could not be justified. The control reports indicate delays in tracing back the product until the product had expired and a recall was not needed, and delays in addressing the root cause (sanctioned with 1000 penalty). b. Seven months after the first alert of these series, based on the outcome

The ACCAs stated to have realised that the case could have been handled better, and to have taken action to address the control weaknesses. As a result, and for the year following this series of alerts, the monitoring system for on-the-spot visits following food incidents indicated a rapid response (see paragraph 54).

When the inspectors do not consider the non-compliances to be serious, the measures taken do not ensure that these are corrected routinely and in a timely fashion. In most of such cases seen by the audit team, the potential for product contamination was not adequately assessed, and CAs in general did not request action in relation to exposed products: 20 a. the CAs had given the same importance and same deadline (e.g. between seven days and 3 months) to maintenance non-compliances like peeling rust and peeling paint, irrespective of whether they could impact on exposed product or not (e.g. in the establishments producing composite products in Navarra, and in the fishery establishments in Cat

In Cataluña, the CAs met by the audit team explained that they are not required to give a deadline for the FBO to rectify minor non-compliances. The CA is required to request action from FBO only in case of serious non-compliances5. This resulted in either non- compliances repeatedly recorded in control reports (e.g. meat establishment) without adequate action (this was the case also for the fishery establishment Comunidad Valenciana) or lack of recording of non-compliances considered to be of minor nature (e.g. fishery establishment).

The national measures in place support both FBOs in addressing the microbiological hazards and control the production process of RTE foods, as well as CAs in performing the related official controls. Advice for consumers aiming to prevent food borne outbreaks is also available. There is scope for reviewing the regional measures to support a harmonised and correct implementation by the dairy industry of the measures for verifying the effectiveness of pasteurisation and related official controls.

There is scope for further exploring in the national or regional measures the options to address the hazards stemming from the highest number of outbreaks, human cases and hospitalised persons following consumption of RTE food in recent years, according to the national data, and for sharing relevant regional measures where available. 4.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITY Legal requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The measures targeting a specific pathogen are more developed as regards Listeria monocytogenes. National or regional measures aiming to support FBOs and CAs in addressing the main cause of outbreaks, human cases and hospitalised persons 5 (Staphylococcus in dairy products) according to the national data (see chapter 3) have to date not been adopted.

Cataluña was implementing an initiative to address the main cause of food alerts due to pathogenic microorganisms (Salmonella detection in meat products) at the time of the audit. This initiative includes relevant guidance for official control staff, based on expert advice. Relevant information of this initiative, from which the control staff in other AC might benefit, has not been shared between ACs.

Each AC may have other guidelines in place. label_heading: Conclusions on Prioritisation of Official Controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at producers/processors are announced which could reduce the effectiveness of the control system.

The CAs had a system in place for undertaking initial verification of compliance prior to placing on the market for producers of PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks. 5.2.3 Prioritisation of Official Controls Legal requirements Articles 37(1) and 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. Articles 22(1) and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008. Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings Agricultural products and foodstuffs

CAs are designated for the official controls of PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks and the distribution of tasks is clearly defined. Training has been provided to official staff. However, the level of information provided by regional/local authorities to the NFA is not sufficient to properly monitor and coordinate their control activities. The CAs control activities are not included in the annual report as established in Article 40 of Regulation (EC) No 1151/2012. 5.2.2 Verification of compliance prior to placing on the market Legal requirements Article 37(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 Articles 22(1) and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 Findings

The Annual Report on the implementation of the MANCP in 2017 was submitted to the Commission. However, this report did not include specific sections on PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs or GI spirit drinks control activities. This is not in line with Article 40 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012. The 2018 annual report is under preparation. The CA informed the audit team that it does not contain reference to controls carried out of PDO/PGI/TSG agricultural products and foodstuffs and GI spirit drinks.

The 2017 annual reports submitted by MUPs and CABs to the NFA did not contain any specific data related to controls on GIs. The procedure has changed, and from 2018, CABs and MUPs report on activities carried out on GIs. However, the information provided is very basic and only relates to the number of controls carried out. It does not include specific information on the operators and GIs subject to controls. Therefore, the NFA cannot have an accurate overview of the inspections carried out or monitor that the CAs involved achieve the frequency of controls planned. This is not in line with Section 3 of Ordinance 1425/2009.

Furthermore the reporting from MUPs to the NFA does not provide clear information on the type and number of products and operators covered by controls and the NFA does therefore not have an overview of the controls carried out by the MUPs. So while ad-hoc controls are carried out, Sweden cannot ensure that risk-based controls take place in a systematic manner in the country as there is no coordination among the CAs involved at market level. This is not in line with Article 4.3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and with Article 38 of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012

The CAs' control activities and results are not all included in the annual report and in the MANCP submitted by Ireland to the European Commission. 5.2.2. Verification of compliance prior to placing on the market Legal requirements Article 37(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 Articles 22(1) and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008 Findings

The audit team noted that while the MANCP and annual reports include elements on official controls for PDO/PGI/TSG, no elements are included on the planning and performance of the official controls of GI spirit drinks.

label_heading: Conclusion on the situation of T. erytreae, D. citri and HLB in Spain
paragraph_text: The initial outbreaks of T. erytreae were notified to the European Commission and other Member States, however, the pests' continued spread into new areas of Galicia was not notified, which hinders the ability of other areas of Spain and the other Member States, in adapting their official controls as necessary.

MAPA and the ACPHS for Galicia confirmed that no further notifications had been provided since 2016, although the T. erytreae had since continued to spread in Galicia, including into the Province of Lugo. The distribution of T. erytreae in Galicia is illustrated in Figure 1 below, which also indicates the year in which the pest was first found in each municipality. Figure 1: Distribution of T. erytreae in Galicia in 2019 10

The data in Figure 1 above indicates that T. erytreae was found in a number of new areas only in 2019 or 2018, in particular in the Province of Lugo and eastern parts of the Province of A Coruña. Neither the new information concerning the spread of the pest into a new area, nor the change of control strategy for T. erytreae detailed in section 5.3 below, were notified to the Commission and other Member States, as required by Article 2(5) of Decision 2014/917/EU.

label_heading: Conclusion on control measures for T. erytreae, D. citri and HLB
paragraph_text: The control measures have also not been fully applied in Galicia, in particular in those areas in which T. erytreae occurs, but that have not been demarcated, as required. That undermines confidence in the guarantees, and pest-free status of host plants, which are intended to be provided by the national and regional legislation and EU legislation, and poses a risk for the further spread of the pest in trade.

As noted in section 5.2.2 above, the ACPHS has not legally revised the demarcated areas for T. erytreae since 2016. Instead, the ACPHS stated that it implements a 'flexible demarcation' in the event that T. erytreae is found in a new area. In practice, this means that the movement of host plants from nurseries in areas, or even places, where T. erytreae has been found is not prohibited. The infested plants identified in the places must either be destroyed or heavily pruned and treated with a plant protection product, but other (un-infested) host plants on the site may be moved within the demarcated area. However, such an approach is not in line with EU requirements for the production and movement of host plants in item 10.1 of Annex IV Part A Section II to Directive 2000/29/EC, nor is in line with the national or regional legislation for the pest, which undermines confidence in the guarantees, and pest free status of host plants, that are intended to be provided by that legislation. paragraph_text: However, the legislation and contingency plans have not been reviewed in light of experience, in particular the proven ineffectiveness of plant protection products, which play a key role in the control measures, which undermines confidence in the ability of the proposed control measures to ensure the prompt and effective eradication of new outbreaks of those pests.

The National Contingency Plans establish the means for implementing the measures required by the Royal Decree. MAPA confirmed that there have been no changes to those plans since the previous audit, and the plans have not been reviewed or tested through test-exercises.

MAPA and the ACPHS of the Canary Islands and Galicia provided details of their experience with the use of plant protection products as part of their control measures for the eradication or containment of T. erytreae, which were initiated following the first findings of the pest in those Autonomous Communities. The report of the previous audit provides a detailed description of the area-wide pesticide applications by TRAGSA in Galicia at that time, which were based on the initial experience in the Canary Islands. Although the treatments had proved effective at protecting individual host plants, the ACPHS stated that they had proved ineffective at preventing the spread of the pest or even in s

MAPA highlighted the continued withdrawal of authorisation of a number of the plant protection products since the previous audit, including for neonicotinoides14. MAPA stated that they would not grant emergency authorisation under Article 53(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1107/2009, for the use of such plant protection products.

MAPA and the ACPHS also highlighted the problem with false-positives in the initial laboratory screening tests for HLB. That can lead to a significant number of results, which must subsequently be confirmed, or refuted by further laboratory analysis. MAPA stated that the additional tests may take a long period of time and are resource intensive and that this complicates the surveys and means that it is legally difficult for the authorities to take action, based on a possibly false preliminary positive result for HLB.

There were no requirements for the establishment or review of contingency plans in the EU legislation applicable at the time of the audit. MAPA informed the audit team that National Contingency Plans had not been reviewed or evaluated in light of experience, as recommended by point 12 of EPPO Standard PM9/10(1).

Temperatures inside the houses were 35°C and higher (with only a few animals in a few pens showing signs of discomfort, panting), and a number of pigs were concentrated around the bowl drinker in most pens and episodically competed for access to it. Despite a legal requirement and an intensive awareness campaign since 2015, only a limited number of non-commercial holdings are registered which makes it difficult for the authorities to detect promptly the disease and to control its spread. The proactive measures taken by the authorities to depopulate backyard holdings in high-risk areas are likely to significantly reduce the risk of disease introduction and spread. However, there is uncertainty about how this limitation of the risk will be maintained when the defined period for the non-population expires, and about how the authorities will monitor these holdings in particular when they are going to restock.

Private registered veterinarians are complicit in maintaining the unregistered pig population as they do not actively support the registration of non-commercial holdings but rather continue to provide service to unregistered holdings.

Despite the recent efforts to reduce the number of non-commercial holdings and to bring them into compliance with biosecurity requirements, it is very likely that there still exits a considerable number of unregistered backyard holdings in the country. The absence of reliable data on the location and movement of pigs within the non-commercial sector means that it is often not possible to trace animals that could have carried ASF virus to or from outbreak holdings. label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring and sampling scheme
paragraph_text: The FBO monitoring and sampling schemes are implemented in line with the approved SNCPs. The central level has tools to monitor and continuously review the progress of the programmes, including official actions. However, some RVAs did not fully respect the planned official sampling frequency in the last two years, in particular for laying hens and broilers.

However for official samples the data and results since 2016 show that not all holdings with more than 1,000 birds were sampled and tested for Salmonella (see tables under Point 5 in Annex 2) contrary to the requirement in point 2.1 of the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 517/2011. According to the SVA analysis, in 2017 only 56 out of 71 eligible holdings were officially sampled. This issue was discussed in one RVA visited where in 2017 no official sample was taken, and in 2018 only some eligible holdings were officially sampled; in that period the RVA diverted available resources to other more urgent issues.

The audit team reviewed results since 2016 (see tables under Point 6 in Annex 2) and in general the number of holdings officially sampled and tested for Salmonella reached the targets in the SNCP. However, in 2018 in two of the 14 regions the RVA had not reached that target (sample 10% of broiler holdings); in one region only two holdings were tested instead of five; in another region instead of two none were officially sampled. The CCA was aware of this deficiency, but since the overall number of planned official samples for the whole country had already been achieved it instructed the RVA not to take the samples.

The central level has tools to monitor and continuously review the progress of the programmes. Results and their analysis are discussed during the regular meetings with the RVAs. Despite this, some RVAs, responsible for implementation of the programmes, did not fully respect the planned official samplings in the last two years, in particular for laying hens and broilers (see findings 34 and 44). These failures in implementation of the official sampling were either not detected at an early stage or were detected but not swiftly addressed.

Since 2016, confirmatory sampling was carried out in 15 of 21 laying flocks that had FBO samples with results positive for Salmonella. Only two confirmatory samples returned positive for relevant Salmonella serotypes with the remaining 13 reported as negative. The impact on Salmonella prevalence rate in laying hens is that if the FBO positive results had been included (instead of discarded after the confirmatory sampling 8 returned negative for 13 out of 15 flocks) in 2016 the prevalence rate in Czech Republic would go above the 2% EU target.

For confirmatory sampling the CA is required (point 2.2 of the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 517/2011) to carry out further checks namely by laboratory tests or documentary checks to ensure that the results are not affected by the use of antimicrobials. The RVAs did not take additional samples of birds for antimicrobial residues or bacterial growth inhibitors in any of the confirmatory samplings reviewed. Instead in all cases they relied on the results of documentary checks on the holdings - verification of treatment records - that showed no antimicrobial treatment of birds. Although EU legislation allows using documentary checks the use and results from laboratory tests can significantly cont

Test results provided by the CA for 2018 show that when comparing results of official sampling with FBO sampling,, the detection rate was approximately 15 times higher from official samples,of 3.48% (3 of 86 tests) versus 0.22% (1 of 453 tests). The CCA accredits the higher prevalence in official samples to the higher detection sensitivity of official sampling (additional faecal sample taken). The CCA had decided not to replace one faecal sample or one pair of boot swabs with a dust sample as allowed in point 2.2.2. of the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 517/2011; inclusion of dust in the official sampling would provide the CA with a more sound basis to establish if the difference in detection r

The CCA provided their view on potential reasons for the increasing prevalence trend in recent years and the above target prevalence in broilers in the last two years as being: feed for parent flocks had not been heat treated (only acidity used); in some instances a lack of adequate biosecurity measures had been applied on the holdings and a recurrence of Salmonella infection; in particular rather small holdings seem to be more vulnerable to the infection.

Test results for 2018, show a Salmonella positive detection rate approximately five times higher than official samples of 8.1% (4 of 36 tests) versus 1.6% (75 of 4 667 tests) from FBO samples. The CA has been aware of this difference in detection rates for several years but cannot identify a reason. To some extent this difference may be explained by the selection of broiler holdings with a high risk for Salmonella in official controls (holdings with recurrence of Salmonella).

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port
paragraph_text: Port inspectors are aware of the official controls they are required to do, but the absence of any records for these checks and for any subsequent action that might have been taken does not make it possible to verify whether they were in fact performed, their quality or 5 effectiveness.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The insufficient information and instructions for port inspectors together with the absence of suitably qualified staff for assessing technical requirements for livestock vessels translates into a poor evaluation of technical requirements (such as air changes per hour on each deck of a livestock vessel, and the equipment used for watering and drainage systems on board a livestock vessel) during the approval and inspection before 8 loading. Therefore, official controls do no contribute to minimise the animal welfare risk linked to facilities and equipment.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: Procedures include the relevant legal requirements but do not provide instructions for CSVFSD official veterinarians and port inspectors on how to verify these requirements as part of a practical inspection of a livestock vessel. Inspections of livestock vessels are therefore dependant on the experience of the inspectors, but not all requirements are adequately verified, which could have major implications for animal welfare during sea journeys.

The documented procedure for the inspection of a livestock vessel prior to approval is substantially a checklist which is part of Order 16/2010. This checklist covers all points included under Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, with the exception of drainage systems (Point 5).

The documented procedure for the inspection of a livestock vessel prior to loading animals is substantially in the form of another checklist: As already described in report 2015/7425, this checklist includes instructions to calculate and record the minimum required quantities of water and feed and available stocking density on board the vessel in order to verify compliance with these three requirements (see also paragraph 27). This checklist was last modified after July 2018 in response to the follow-up action by the Commission's auditing services on a vessel which was seen during the audit to Slovenia to evaluate animal welfare during transport to non-EU countries (report DG(SANTE)2018-6449

There is no documentary guidance or instructions explaining how to verify compliance with specific technical requirements which are not of a veterinary nature, e.g. ventilation capacity, functioning of emergency systems, and water and drainage pumps.
ANSVSA is drafting a checklist for the inspection of vehicles arriving at the port. This document has not been finalised yet. 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT

There was however no documentation to support this decision. The official veterinarians could not explain how they calculated the ventilation capacity on each deck without this documentation. Port inspectors inspect vessels prior to loading animals. Procedures for this control, to verify that the equipment referred to in Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation is in good working order, do not provide the port inspectors with guidance on how to physically carry out these controls (e.g. how to verify that drainage tanks from where sewage is discharged are functioning properly).

All pre-loading checklists seen by the audit team indicated that the vessels inspected complied with the requirements of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, with the exception of the missing check for drainage systems (see also paragraph 1). The port inspectors were however unable to explain how they verify that certain systems and the relevant equipment (forced ventilation systems, drainage systems and pumps, alarms, back-up generators, etc.) are in good working order.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The VIS perform various controls regarding bovine identification, checks on the FCI and on hygiene requirements during slaughter, including AMI/PMI and record their findings in the CA's information systems. Regarding the AMI of bovine animals, the implementation of the central level instructions does not ensure the required (supervisory) presence of OV in the slaughterhouses at all times required by EU legislation. Similarly, the PMI of bovine animals is not performed at all times under the OV supervision in slaughterhouses slaughtering more than 1000 LVU per year.

In the second slaughterhouse reviewed, also slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year it was explained that it is possible that on certain days, the OV is not permanently present throughout the day. Therefore, it is possible that the OA can carry out the AMI of bovine animals which do not present any abnormalities and those animals to be slaughtered. This is not in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 which requires that this task must be carried out under the supervision of the OV (that is, with the OV present in the premises). Animals presenting abnormalities are detained by the OA and undergo a second-level AMI, performed by the OV. This issue regarding the absence of the OV during A

It was also explained by the CAs that in the specific case where an animal is obviously in distress when the OV is not present at the premises, the OA informs the OV as quickly as possible and directly makes an appropriate decision, which may be: the immediate slaughter of the animals fit for human consumption (for example, an animal which has just been injured either in the lairage or during transport and is obviously in distress), retaining the carcase and offal for inspection by the OV. This practice is not in line is with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624; the emergency killing of the animals unfit for human consumption (for example, a sick animal in obvious distress).

The audit team was informed that at local level, the local organisation and the priorities defined by the departmental authority may explain why the AMI might be carried out by 19 an OA under the responsibility and not under the supervision of the OV as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation 2019/624.

Based on the information provided by the CCA for bovine slaughterhouses, the staff of the VIS is systematically present during slaughter. The OV is present for decisions linked to the PMI and systematically validates this decision by signing the slaughterhouse seizure certificates. If the OV needs to be absent, including in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year, carcasses suspected of presenting abnormalities during the PMI are detained by the OA to be inspected at a later stage by the OV (see paragraph 87).

One OV in charge of a slaughterhouse slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year stated that it is possible that the OV might not be present at all times during slaughter since he/she might be assigned to other tasks elsewhere, during this period the OV can be reached by phone if needed. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 that requires that PMI must be carried out under the supervision of the OV in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 1000 LVU.

The OV can carry out the PMI of slaughtered animals or entrust part of this task to one or more OAs under his supervision. If it is not the OV who directly performs the PMI, the OA performs the PMI of the animals after slaughter (first level of PMI). The OA sorts the animals depending on whether or not they present abnormalities. Animals presenting abnormalities are retained. The abnormalities might be pathological lesions, abnormalities requiring further investigations or inspection (e.g. identification or FCI issues, known health risks etc.) by the OV either on the same day or early the next day. 21 Due to the lack of continued presence of the OV highlighted in the paragraph above this pro

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There are procedures and guidelines in place for official staff for the relevant controls, which provide guidance on how to act in different scenarios regarding the handling of cull cows (i.e. emergency slaughter, identification of unfit animals for transport and/or slaughter). The controls system identifies relevant non-compliances, which are followed up satisfactorily. Yet, as already identified in a previous DG Health and Food Safety audit, bovine animals that have suffered an accident are transported to the slaughterhouses accompanied by a CVI, without all EU requirements being met.

The following are (non-exhaustive) examples of animals considered unfit for transport: serious open wound; animal suffering from a severe prolapse; animal unable to move by itself without suffering (example: dairy cow with spread legs); newborn whose navel has not healed; calves less than 10 days old, transported over 100 km; pregnant female ready to give birth (more than 90% gestation)/or having given birth less than a week before transport.

It was evident from the documentation reviewed by the audit team that bovine animals that had suffered an accident (including a non-open fracture) or had a non-serious prolapse were transported to the slaughterhouses accompanied by a CVI document signed by a private veterinarian, provided that they were able to move independently/unassisted. In the CVI the private veterinarian attested their capability of transfer, the fulfilment of the requirements of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 and indicated which additional measures should be taken in order to ensure that no additional suffering is caused during transport. This practice is permissible under DGAL's relevant guidance document contrary

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The number of available official staff and the procedures in place for their deployment while on operation do not ensure in 880 poultry slaughterhouses (30 % of total national production) compliance with the requirements of Article 18(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 regarding the presence of official staff, of Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 regarding the practical arrangements of the PMI of poultry and the supervision requirements of Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and of Articles 3(2) and 7(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. 5.5. Similarly to domestic ungulates, there are no provisions in place to carry out AMI for poultry at the holding of provenance, therefore the AMI must be carried out at the slaughterhouse by or under the supervision of the OV, in line with Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The requirement that the OV is present during slaughter activities is implemented only in those poultry slaughterhouses slaughtering more than 15,000 tonnes per year (34 out of 914 slaughterhouses covering 70% of production).

In 17 slaughterhouses with an annual throughput between 10,000 and 15,000 tonnes the procedures in place require the permanent presence of at least one member of official staff (OV/OA) during slaughter activities with a daily supervisory visit by the OV in case not permanently present. In the remaining 78 slaughterhouses (with a capacity ranging from 300 to 10,000 tonnes per year), at least one member of official staff (OV/OA) is present for certain days each week. These arrangements in place do always ensure that the AMI/PMI is carried out under the supervision of the OV. Article 7(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 requires that PMI can only be performed by an OA under the responsibilit

In the low-capacity slaughterhouses, the VIS is not present throughout the slaughter activities and only visits the slaughterhouses with a minimum frequency of two visits per year while the slaughterhouse is in operation. Besides the AMI issue highlighted in paragraph 95 the current arrangements are not in line with Article 18(3)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which allows slaughterhouse staff to assist in the performance of official control tasks in poultry and lagomorphs slaughterhouses when the task is carried out in the presence of the OV or the OA and following their instructions.

When permanently present at the slaughterhouse or during visits/inspections, the OV or OA carries out a PMI, which includes an inspection of the viscera and body cavities of a representative sample of each flock and an inspection of the poultry declared unfit for consumption by the slaughterhouse staff. The latter is not in line with Article 25(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 according to which the OV/OA shall inspect the viscera and body cavities of a representative sample of each flock, on a daily basis. In France, the derogation of Article 25(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 has not been applied to date.
Staff shortages have an important negative impact, at all levels of the CAs, on the overall delivery of the official control system, in particular on frequency of inspections on FBOs.

All levels of the CA are affected by staff shortages, as several officials are either on unpaid leave or maternity leave, whilst all but one of the Heads of the VRD Units posts are vacant, as well as the post of CVO. As a result, several officials cover and share the tasks from the colleagues above mentioned between different Units and services, while completing their workload, without having been provided with specific training for those tasks.
Field services of the EHD are also understaffed, which impacts on the number and on the extent of their inspections over retailers' activities.

The CCA stated that the last two competitions for recruiting OVs resulted in only one suitable candidate being selected; this person is in the process of being recruited and will take up the position in April 2020. Six Maltese veterinarians will be graduating from a University in Europe, and the CCA is expecting that at least some of these new graduates may be interested in participating in the forthcoming competitions for the recruitment of new staff. The CCA explained that the reasons for such low interest might either be because of the level of salary that is offered to junior OVs, or the requirement of knowledge of the Maltese language in order to qualify for the post. The shortage of staff impacts on the effectiveness of official controls performed: the frequency of official controls in approved establishments, set by the CA on the basis of the specific criteria laid down by Article 9(1) of OCR, is not followed. The audits carried out by central level do not cover all requirements, and some administrative tasks (e.g. updating approval and inspection files) are not completed. A similar issue was brought to the attention of the audit team by representatives of the EHD: due to staff shortage, inspections in retail shops like butchers are performed at a much lower frequency than planned, and does not always cover all items present in the inspection checklists

The VRD has a post dealing with policy and internal audit: however, this post (shared with the Policy and Enforcement Unit) is currently not operational as the relevant official is on unpaid leave. The programme for internal audits for 2018-2020 has not been implemented: the follow-up audit on animal identification and the registration system, scheduled for 2018, was not carried out.

The audit team visited a poultry slaughterhouse to collect information on procedures implemented for ante-mortem inspection. The four approved poultry slaughterhouses carry out their operations daily at the same time: due to staff shortages, ante-mortem inspections are solely performed by a roving OV; four VSOs (one per slaughterhouse) and one senior VSO also provide support in inspection activities (mainly for post- mortem inspections and administrative tasks). The ante-mortem inspection includes an evaluation of the FCI documents accompanying the animals. The audit team noted that certain mandatory information were not indicated on such documents (e.g. number of animals included in the loa

Not all officials performing the controls have sufficient knowledge/experience to perform them adequately, and no specific training arrangements are in place when staff is given new responsibilities or has to cover tasks from other colleagues or vacant posts. Given the number of incidents where staff were found to lack appropriate training to enable them undertake their duties competently, there is clear evidence of non-compliance with Art 5(4) (a) of the OCR.

Specific training for junior OVs was not always delivered; in one slaughterhouse, the recently recruited OV was not aware of (and did not verify) the requirements concerning microbiological testing of cattle carcases (see paragraphs 31 and 77); this same OV's knowledge of the criteria for the assessment of animal welfare at slaughter was also not sufficient (see paragraph 69). Some OVs have participated in different sessions of the 5 Commission's Better Training for Safer Food initiative. The audit team had been provided with documentation on the training for some official staff that was planned and carried out in 2019.

Training was not provided to official staff that had moved to another position and were carrying out new tasks. For instance, an OV was recently moved from the Trade Unit (dealing with border controls) to the SFCU at poultry slaughterhouses (see paragraph 53) with no training having been provided on the specific elements of these new responsibilities.

In the second slaughterhouse visited, no slaughter activities were being carried out at the time of the audit, but the audit team's discussion with the OV highlighted its insufficient knowledge of animal welfare indicators in relation to slaughter activities (e.g. 15 seconds considered by the OV as a satisfactory stun-to-stick interval, not taking into account that, as general practice, the time needed to stun the animal, to unload it from the stunning box and to hoist it before sticking is usually between 45 and 60 seconds). 5.4.5 General and specific hygiene requirements Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. The staff's management verification carried out on the ground is rare or inexistent: consequently, a reasonable level of assurance that controls are carried out uniformly, correctly and consistently, allowing the CA to take corrective actions if needed, cannot be ensured.

The VRD has a post dealing with policy and internal audit: however, this post (shared with the Policy and Enforcement Unit) is currently not operational as the relevant official is on unpaid leave. As a consequence, no support for OVs is provided as no particular lack of knowledge is identified.

paragraph_text: Concerning emergency slaughter, the system in place is in general in line with Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. However, for a small number of emergency slaughtered animals the diagnosis reported in the AMI certificates calls into question the reliability of the statements contained in these certificates declaring that the animals are fit for slaughter and therefore eligible for emergency slaughter.

The CCA informed the audit team that they have recently started to collect information about the diagnosis reported in the AMI certificates accompanying the cattle that have been emergency slaughtered. The data shows that: the majority of animals fall into the category "an otherwise healthy animal which has suffered an accident that prevents its transport to the slaughterhouse for welfare reasons" and for a small number of animals the diagnosis was a disease (e.g. pneumonia) and/or specified that the animal could not stand. This situation raises clear doubts about the health status of the emergency slaughtered animal and, therefore, its eligibility for slaughter for human consumption, becaus

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: In addition, the system in place is not in line with Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 because it does not require persons killing animals in case of emergency slaughtering on farms to have the appropriate level of competence.

The CCA explained that the veterinarians performing AMI at holdings can carry out the stunning and bleeding of animals. Other people can also perform these activities. In this regard, the CCA explained that no specific requirements are necessary. This is not in line with Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1009/2009, which requires that killing and related operations shall only be carried out by persons with the appropriate level of competence to do so without causing the animals any avoidable pain, distress or suffering.

The 2018-2020 MANCP is incomplete regarding official controls in the animal welfare area. The absence of animal welfare objectives together with the absence of information from regional authorities to the progress report make it impossible to 10 assess whether the authorities are directing their efforts effectively or efficiently.

Belgium's 2018-2020 Multi-annual national control plan (MANCP) describes the protocol signed between FASFC and the three regions on delegation of responsibilities on animal welfare, providing the general framework. The MANCP (Section 3.2.11.15.6) states that the competent regional authorities undertake to periodically provide a contribution to MANCP and to the MANCP annual progress report. The audit team noted that information on the planning regarding animal welfare checks was very general, and it did not include objectives for animal welfare for any of the three regions. The MANCP is available at: http://www.afsca.be/apropos/mancp/mancpbelge/default.asp.

The responsibilities for animal welfare at slaughter are clear, but Belgium has not ensured efficient and effective coordination between all authorities involved. This translates into suboptimal cooperation and insufficient sharing of information between the federal and regional competent authorities. The high dependence on the federal checks in the slaughterhouses is more relevant for the Walloon region, where the shortage of resources limits their activities. The checklists filled in by federal official veterinarians do not add much value to the official system.
