The Flemish competent authority explained that, as FASFC is under the Federal competent authorities, it is difficult to cooperate without updating and improving the protocol signed with them. The Walloon competent authority agreed with that view and added that the non-optimal sharing of information with FASFC is mainly due to the institutional set up and they always try to achieve a good direct communication with the slaughterhouse official veterinarians.

The audit team requested an overview of the results of one of the points in the FASFC checklist from the Flemish competent authority. The competent authority indicated that, since 2018 the FASFC had not been entering the checklists into their electronic system, but instead sent either hard paper copies or e-mailed scanned copies to the regions. This makes it difficult for the regions to provide an overview and for their Animal Welfare Inspection Units to assess the findings. For this reason, the regions stopped using the FASFC findings for prioritising which slaughterhouses they visit.

The Flemish competent authority indicated that its Animal Welfare Unit has prepared new checklists and procedures. This is to prepare for the start of a new system where the Animal Welfare Unit would appoint directly private veterinarians to carry out inspections on animal welfare in slaughterhouses, in addition to the official veterinarians of the FASFC. This revision will take into account the non-compliances detected by veterinarians working in the slaughterhouse and prioritise the less compliant establishments for visits by the Animal Welfare Unit. The appointed private veterinarians will start at the end of October 2020. They will daily check animal welfare in every slaughterhouse for a

The Walloon competent authority indicated that the shortage of resources limits their activities and for the time being they depend on the FASFC checks in the slaughterhouses and informed the audit team that: Its new plan is that its Animal Welfare Unit will do three controls per year for large scale slaughterhouses and one for the others. They did not provide a starting date. It has recently produced a new checklist for their Animal Welfare Unit. In March 2020, based on the protocol signed with FASFC, it issued new instructions for the FASFC official veterinarians.

The absence of risk-based method for establishing the frequency for official controls does not allow the Flemish and Walloon competent authorities to set the frequency of their controls based on risk and to ensure the level of compliance expected in different situations. This decreases the efficiency of their official controls to target problematic establishments.

The measures that Brussels-Capital regional authority put in place in its red meat slaughterhouse paid off. They improved animal welfare, in particular during slaughter without stunning. The use of video surveillance by the operator and authorities proved useful to improve the welfare of animals and to enforce the legislation. The current arrangements where the officials can only review the video footage from the establishment is a lost opportunity for the authorities for e.g. keep their controls on the slaughterhouse during the Covid-19 restrictions.

In response to Recommendation 2 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7057 - to take account of previous inspection results when establishing the risk basis for controls - the Belgian competent authorities provided in their action plan a summary of the system for controls in place after regionalisation, indicating that: Wallonia and Flanders analyse the reports of the FASFC official veterinarians to establish a benchmarking between slaughterhouses. That would allow the regions to prioritise certain slaughterhouses or specific items for their inspections.

The audit team noted that, for 2017, 2018 and 2019, there was no evidence that the analysis for benchmarking to prioritise between slaughterhouses had been carried out. The Flemish and Walloon authorities agreed that a systematic risk analysis had not been carried out in those years.

The slaughterhouse of Brussels-Capital region installed video cameras after the request from the regional competent authority following an animal welfare incident. The authority uses them (see paragraphs 26 to 28) to complement on-site inspections and to monitor critical points during slaughtering. The audit team noted that the regional competent authority officials have to review the recordings of the cameras on site. Due to the COVID-19 restrictions on on­site visits, they could not reach the frequency of video checks planned for the year. The animal welfare officer indicated that following the use of video footage, the staff performance, and the public image of the company have improved.

label_heading: Conclusions on animal welfare officer and training of slaughter staff
paragraph_text: The Walloon competent authority has not yet fully addressed recommendation 1 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059, as it has not yet published the necessary legislation to approve the training programme, and it has therefore not fulfilled its responsibilities as designated competent authority.

Since 1 July 2014, the government delegated to its three regions the responsibility to organise and perform official controls and other official activities for the requirements on the welfare of animals. Since 1 January 2015, Flemish, Walloon and Brussels- Capital Regional governments fully took on this responsibility in their territories and were given competence to adopt their own legislation. Each Region has a separate inspection unit dedicated to animal welfare - the Animal Welfare Unit.

The audit team verified the actions taken to address Recommendation 1 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059 - on improving the system for providing certificates of competence, by publishing the necessary legislation, targeting the animal welfare officer and covering tasks in slaughterhouses which present particular risks for animal welfare such as slaughter without stunning. The respective competent authorities stated that: In Flanders, the legislation approving the training programme has been published. The competent authority also indicated that although there is an examination module on slaughter without stunning available for cattle and for sheep and goats, the module on slaughter without

The competent authorities with poultry slaughterhouses (Flanders and Wallonia) have not addressed recommendation 6 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059. The monitoring of welfare indicators in poultry slaughterhouses is insufficient to allow the competent authorities to take enforcement actions on farms when and where necessary. With the absence of data on daily mortality rates the veterinarians in the slaughterhouses lose a valuable tool to evaluate at what stage of the birds' life the animal welfare problems have occurred. 5.6.3 Criteria for the use of increased stocking density in broiler farms.

Recommendation 6 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059 requested the competent authorities to put in place a system for monitoring in the slaughterhouse the welfare of broilers in the farm of origin, in line with the requirements from Annex III to Council Directive 2007/43/EC.

The competent authorities have not addressed recommendation 7 of audit report DG (SANTE) 2014-7059. The absence of procedures to check compliance in producers operating at the higher stocking densities, together with the absence of monitoring signs of welfare problems at slaughterhouse level, leaves unmonitored the welfare of broilers from the farms presenting the greatest risks.

The protocol signed with the certifying body has not been implemented which leaves the regional competent authorities unaware of any possible shortcomings and welfare problems at farms. This impedes them to take effective action to solve existing issues.

The regional competent authorities cannot confirm compliance in the farms operating at the higher stocking densities. This creates the potential risk that broilers are kept at stocking densities under which the housing and management conditions are not able to ensure their welfare. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION There has been limited progress since the previous audit in November 2014. The regional authorities (Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital) have taken the legal responsibility for animal welfare from January 2015. The 2018-2020 MANCP does not contain objectives for animal welfare in the three regions. This, together with the absence of information from the regional competent authorities to t

Audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059 recommended (Recommendation 7) setting up a procedure to ensure that the checks by a certifying body confirm that producers operating at the higher stocking densities comply with Directive 2007/43/EC.

In response to the pre-audit questionnaire for this audit, the competent authorities of the regions with broilers' farms (Flanders and Wallonia) indicated that they had signed a protocol with the certifying body. This protocol includes that this certifying body has to notify the Animal Welfare Units if it notices severe animal welfare infringements. The Animal Welfare Units will then follow up and carry out an inspection of its own.

The audit team noticed that: The certifying body provided a document of August 2020 with the items that they inspect and the way they carry out the inspections. In this document, the certifying body has grouped together, from the previous checklist, the animal welfare requirements laid down in Directive 2007/43/EC, to provide better information to the regional competent authorities and farmers. The two regional competent authorities have not yet analysed this document. The two regional competent authorities indicated that they do not have access to the database of the checklists completed by the certifying body and commented that if they had received the complete checklist, it would have bee

label_heading: Conclusions on management of official controls
paragraph_text: The Competent Authorities' approach to the setting of objectives in the MANCP is mainly operational with no defined targets, indicators or measurement of progress and, as such, they are insufficient to bring about measureable change.

label_heading: Conclusions on management of official controls
paragraph_text: There is a good well-developed prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources even though these do not link to clear objectives or targets in the MANCP or annual inspection plans.

label_heading: Conclusions on management of official controls
paragraph_text: Planning of cross compliance and animal welfare controls are well formulated on a demonstrable risk profiling basis using a range of risk criteria that target official resources to inspecting the potentially worst offenders. However, the introduction of post-mortem indicators as a risk criterion to target broiler farm inspections has had no impact on improving animal welfare outcomes for footpad dermatitis over a three- year period.

The Czech Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP) (2016-2018 - latest version), section 3.3, Strategic Objectives, includes a policy objective relevant for animal welfare: Objective two: "Ensure a high level of protection of human and consumer interests, animal health, animal welfare and plant health." There is no further description of what the SVA considers a high level of protection or how this should be measured.

The first operational objective of the MANCP related to on farm controls aims to ensure the keeping of farm animals in accordance with the minimal requirements - ensuring compliance with the requirements of the national and EU legislation.

The second operational objective of the MANCP focuses on raising awareness about the activities and powers of the competent authorities; responsibilities of breeders and general public involvement. A third aims for more effective procedures and enhanced cooperation between competent authorities: SVA, Regional Veterinary Authorities (RVAs) and Municipalities with extended powers (those that are legally entitled to enforce and sanction legislative requirements for farm welfare laws).

As the first MANCP operational objective on farm welfare solely reflects basic monitoring of compliance, there is no link between the planned prioritisation of controls and the allocation of resources to reflect strategic objective two of the MANCP described in paragraph 1 of this report or any of the operational objectives described in paragraphs 2 and 3 of this report. This is not in line with article 110 (2) (a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 that requires the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect the strategic objectives of the MANCP.

There are no baselines set to measure if outcomes for animal welfare meet strategic or operational objectives. For example, the SVA has been monitoring post-mortem indicators in broiler slaughterhouses from each production unit (flock and house) since 2011. From 2013 this data was used to target the poorest performing farms and from 2017 it started including also the incidence of footpad dermatitis (FPD). According to the SVA thresholds, the data indicate unsatisfactory scores for lesions of approximately 75% of flocks sent to slaughter in 2017, 2018 and 2019. The SVA had access to full data from the end of 2018. The use of the indicators to target inspections has had no impact on the outcom

There are no specific, measureable strategic or operational objectives or targets indicated in the MANCP on what the Czech Republic wants to achieve for animal welfare outcomes. Examples could include: reduce incidence of tail docking by x%; reduce FPD levels by x%; decrease lameness levels in cattle by x% through official controls and related actions. These could include targeted training for poorly performing sectors, 3 targeted enforcement campaigns on certain issues or; liaison with the relevant sector to set agreed targets for improvement, etc.

The assessment of non-compliances detected during cross-compliance controls gives a clearer picture of animal welfare problems as it gives conclusions on the severity, 10 extent, permanence and recurrence of the non-compliance. The planning of other animal welfare controls could benefit from the use of this methodology. 5.3 ANIMAL WELFARE INDICATORS A Commission funded project: "Welfare Quality", has developed principles and indicators for assessing the welfare of farm animals (4). The Welfare Quality Principles require housing, feeding, health and behaviour to be included in any on-farm assessment of animal welfare. The project concluded that animal-based indicators are better for measuring

There are no official control procedures for animal welfare controls on pig or broiler farms. There are no procedures for assessing documentation accompanying broiler flocks to slaughter. There is some specific guidance on measuring microclimate on broiler farms and a specific instruction on the assessment of FPD and a requirement to follow up on unsatisfactory scores. The SVA has made available information documents relating to tail docking of pigs but these are not procedures for official controls. The Methodology does not provide mandatory compliance criteria. Although farmers are taking some actions, it is insufficient to comply with the legal requirements relating 5 to risks for tail biting. The lack of binding criteria and detailed procedures for inspectors does not enable them to reliably, and consistently, address the legal requirements relating to risks for tail biting and the effectiveness of improvement measures. As a result inspectors cannot effectively enforce Point 8 of Annex I, Chapter I to Council Directive 2008/120/EC as to whether the mutilation should have been carried out in the first place.

For example: the pig premises visited was part of a larger group structure and fattened tail docked pigs received from its breeding premises. Tail biting on the fattening farm was extremely low (0.08%). The company carried out a trial of rearing pigs with intact tails in one batch on one of the four breeding farm locations in the group. This resulted in poor production results and increased tail biting compared to the docked pigs on site. However, the company did not substantially alter farm conditions prior to the trial. However, the procedures do not indicate when to take enforcement action for unsatisfactory results. It requires that "unsatisfactory" FPD scores should be included in the "feedback report" sent to the official services in charge of supervising the farm of origin. This had not been necessary for any flock slaughtered in the slaughterhouse visited in the last 3 years. The animal welfare fields in the SVA information system for animal welfare checks at the slaughterhouse can indicate "compliant", "not compliant" or "not checked". However, for a number of the parameters evaluated, such as "mortality" (birds dead on arrival), or "fitness and condition of the animal", or "unloading" there is no objective guidance or instruction on how compliance should be assessed. Individual OVs at each slaughterhouse are responsible for deciding what is "compliant" or "non-compliant" and for when they should take enforcement action.

RVAs used different formats for reporting animal welfare inspections on pig farms in the two regions visited. In the first region, inspectors used a template form with prepopulated areas for inspection findings printed on the form and expanded these with free text when they noted non-compliances. The other region used a free text style that had no standard reporting format, leaving the option to individual inspectors to complete the findings. The lack of standard report templates and procedures for carrying out and reporting on inspections does not ensure consistent implementation of controls, scope of inspections and reporting, and calls into question the consistency of the data reported fo

The Annual Report on implementation of the MANCP and the report on animal welfare required under Regulation (EU) 2019/723 provide a partial analysis of the results of official controls on animal welfare. The former does not address whether the activities are suitable to reach the strategic and operational objectives and ensure effective operation of the MANCP, even if it does include enforcement action and its results. The latter does not provide measureable, focussed actions to target recurrent non-compliances in specific areas.

The annual report on the MANCP gives statistics on compliance for each of the areas covered by Regulation (EU) 2019/723. However, although it does contain enforcement action and its results, it does not indicate the measures taken to ensure effective operation of the MANCP, as required under Article 113 (1) (d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

However, the SVA did not analyse why inspections on pig or calf farms resulted in higher rates of non-compliance than equivalent inspections on holdings for laying hens (18% for pigs and 9% for calves compared to 2-4% for laying hens). There is no indication as to why there were much higher percentages of serious non-compliances in category C for pigs and calves and not in other categories, or what can and should be done to address them.

There is potentially useful data within this framework but the reporting is not always reliable. For example, the report indicated that there was 100% compliance for the category "mutilations" in pigs. This is not the case as: approximately 99% pigs are routinely tail docked; the incidence of tail biting reported on farm and at slaughter was very low (from the sample reviewed); and only rudimentary efforts are being made in terms of complying with minimum requirements; including risk assessment, improvement measures, and enforcement.

The SVA explained that the inspection plan prioritised pig farms with fattening pigs for inspection. It considers that farms receiving tail-docked piglets are compliant with tail docking provision. However, the requirements of Point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I to Directive 2008/120/EC on the prohibition of routine tail docking apply to all pigs on either breeding or fattening farms. Even fattening farms that receive piglets already tail docked must have evidence that: there was tail biting on the fattening farm; they have taken improvement measures which attempted to improve the situation and attempted rearing full tailed pigs on site not at another farm under different conditions. Holdings selected for cross compliance inspections on animal welfare are identified using a number of risk criteria including animal-based indicators such as post-mortem lesions in ruminants and numbers of animals sent to rendering plants. Indications of severity, duration and frequency are used when assessing and reporting welfare non- compliances detected during cross compliance inspections, and the information is used to establish payment reductions as required by EU legislation.

One quality assurance (QA) scheme for pigs and cattle has recently started in the Czech Republic and includes mainly on-farm resource requirements. For example, in the case of pigs keepers must provide partially solid flooring or mats for pigs up until weaning no earlier than 28 days. The QA company audits the slaughterhouses who in turn audit the suppliers' compliance with the QA standard. There is no monitoring of animal-based indicators in the standard.

paragraph_text: DAFM has not translated its objectives into operational objectives and there is no indication on how the prioritisation of official controls and allocation of resources reflect those objectives. Most recently introduced (November 2020), the Intact Tails Programme aims to address the issue of routine tail docking in Irish pig farms. Nearly all commercial herds in Ireland rear pigs with docked tails contrary to the requirements of Directive 8 2008/120/EC. A new ante mortem/post mortem system will provide data for herds presenting pigs with docked tails for slaughter. DAFM envisage that in the future, these data will inform the risk-based approach applied to regulatory visits. At the moment, since the number of commercial pig herds in Ireland is not large, a randomised, area- based approach is used for selecting herds for Intact Tails visits.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: Documented procedures do not provide the necessary instructions for port inspectors on how to verify all the relevant legal requirements as part of a practical official control of a livestock vessel. In particular, these instructions are generally inadequate to support the port inspectors in verifying compliance with the specific technical requirements of the Regulation during official controls for approval of livestock vessels.

label_heading: Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport
paragraph_text: The effectiveness of controls of livestock vessels is dependent on the experience of the port inspectors. Nonetheless, official controls are not adequately verifying all the requirements, and this could have implications for animal welfare during sea journeys. paragraph_text: The official control on the handling and storage of wild boar carcases in general and on the destruction of carcases resulted positive to ASF in particular has improved since the FVS became responsible for this control in 2019. However, its efficiency is limited until official controls are more representative.

Since February 2019, the FVS has been responsible for the control of wild boar carcases in processing rooms and storage facilities of hunting grounds (chillers, freezers or other equipment), where wild boar carcases are stored while ASF test results are awaited. To date, the FVS does not have an overview of the facilities available for each hunting ground. When the FVS started to carry out official controls on hunting grounds, they set, mainly due to staff constraints, an objective for 2019 of inspecting 10% of the hunting grounds (the same objective of 10% for 2020), and a minimum number of carcases based on a statistical approach. label_heading: Conclusions on traceability and trade restrictions
paragraph_text: The official controls at the point of hunting, including for biosecurity, which remain under the competence of the State Forest Service, are still a very weak point in the control of ASF in Latvia and they increase the potential risk of spread of ASF 9 infection not only within the country but also in other Member States. 5.2 MEASURES IN CASE OF SUSPICION/CONFIRMATION OF ASF IN DOMESTIC PIGS Legal requirements Articles 4-5 and 8-11 of Directive 2002/60/EC; Article 1of Commission Decision 2003/422/EC. Findings

The objective of the State Forest Service for the current hunting season is to inspect 1,200 hunting grounds (they had inspected around 1,000 so far this season). Inspections are unannounced and, contrary to a legal requirement in force a few years ago, hunters do not have to inform the State Forest Service offices in advance of when they plan to hunt. For this reason, and according to the information provided to the audit team, inspectors have not been able to perform their tasks in half of the visits, as no hunting activities were taking place. In addition, inspections do not target any specific species so only in approximately 300 out of the 1,000 inspections wild boar was being hunted.

According to the State Forest Service, when wild boar is being hunted, inspectors must focus on biosecurity aspects. These are, for example, checking the presence of disinfectant at the point of hunting, the burial of offal if wild boars are gutted on the spot or the transport of offal to a watertight container or that carcases do not get in contact. However, inspectors have not received any specific training on biosecurity and there are no instructions or guidelines available to them.

The State Forest Service has prepared a checklist for the inspections, but it does not contain any detail on the biosecurity aspects checked (only yes/no). There is an online application to report the inspection results, but it does not contain details on the species that were hunted during the inspection therefore there is no overview of the wild boar hunting grounds visited. The State Forest Service assumed that there was hunting of wild boar if biosecurity was reported.

According to the data contained in the online application, inspectors have never found any non-compliance on biosecurity. An inspector clarified that although not reported, in cases of shortcomings, they normally prefer to instruct hunters to improve their awareness regarding biosecurity. 8 5.1.4 Control of ABPs of domestic and feral pigs Legal requirements Articles 2, 7 and 10 of Decision 2014/709/EU. Findings

The recruitment of almost 3,000 authorised veterinarians extends the veterinary authorities' capacity to monitor non-commercial (backyard) establishments. However, the lack of enforceable biosecurity requirements or limits on keeping breeding animals on these establishments means that they continue to play an active role in the persistence and circulation of disease.

The veterinary authorities do not have the full support and commitment of hunters or the hunting authorities to apply rigorously the measures needed to control the wild boar population and to eliminate the disease from affected meta-populations. As a result, these animals act as an important reservoir of disease, which can spill over into inadequately protected pig establishments.

The supervision and audit arrangements in place provide the veterinary authorities with reliable and up-to-date information on the completion of planned controls and activities. However, they do not systematically use this information to identify and tackle the issues that are impeding progress in tackling the disease. 9 6 FINDINGS ON PREVENTIVE MEASURES The combination of an up-to-date pig database and veterinary personnel deployed at local level provides the means to raise animal health standards on non-commercial establishments. BACKGROUND Controls on residues and contaminants and the use of veterinary medicinal products in Hungary were previously audited by the Commission in 2012 (2) and the 2012 report concluded that the system of residue monitoring was in compliance with EU legislation. However, the overall effectiveness of the residue monitoring plan was compromised by weaknesses in laboratory performance and, in particular, by deficiencies in implementation and a lack of effective supervision thereof. All five audit report recommendations were satisfactorily addressed.

label_heading: Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts
paragraph_text: The Border Inspection Post has been re-designated following the introduction of the OCR. The facilities, equipment and arrangements in place concerning animals and goods of animal origin for which the BCP was designated are satisfactory.

label_heading: Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts
paragraph_text: However, there were shortcomings in the facilities and arrangements in place concerning products of non-animal origin for human, and non-human consumption, and in the abbreviations used to indicate the categories of goods for which the BCP had been designated. Although the volume of imports through the BCP is low, the shortcomings identified may have an adverse impact on the hygienic handling and storage of goods for which the BCP has been designated. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a comprehensive system of official controls for animals and goods entering the Union through the BCP in the Czech Republic. Those controls were performed by well- trained officials, supported by detailed guidance,

The facilities are shared for food and feed of non-animal origin. CAFIA and CISTA informed the audit team that arrangements are in place to prevent risks, which may result in cross-contamination, in particular, time separation is used between the handling of different goods and the inspection facilities are cleaned and disinfected between consignments in line with Article 3(9)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team noted that the facilities and equipment at the BCP did not meet the minimum requirements for performing official controls of food and feed of non-animal origin. There are no dedicated storage rooms for commodities to be kept frozen or at ambient temperature under control of CISTA, and the arrangements in place for the shared facilities do not guarantee that CISTA and CAFIA have dedicated storage available to detain food and feed of non-animal origin under their control, in line with Article 64 of the OCR and Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. CAFIA did not have information available on the location of the dedicated storage rooms.

However, there were weaknesses in the notification of import and the implementation of certain documentary checks and reduced frequency of physical checks. While these were not sufficient to affect the validity of the decision to allow importation, the document checks for feed of non-animal origin are not carried out at the BCP as required. 15 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

The SVA and CISTA perform the documentary checks at the BCP while CAFIA indicated that their documentary checks for consignments of food of non-animal origin subject to special import conditions, are carried out at their office in Prague and not at the BCP, which is not in line with Article 49(1) of the OCR.

The audit team noted that the facilities and equipment used for official controls of animals and goods of animal origin meet the minimum requirements with the exception of the facilities for porcine animals at the live animal inspection centre. The audit team noted that the quarantine and housing facilities have in parts, walls constructed with rough concrete blocks, which together with the wall/ceiling junction, are not easy to clean, in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The ASV informed the audit team that this non-conformity had been identified before the facilities became operational, but that no changes had been made by the operator at the time of the audit.

The audit team noted that the inspection and storage areas for products of non-animal origin were not in fully in-line with the requirements of Articles 3(1)(c) and 4(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. SECULIM provided detailed floorplans and photographs of a new facility `Inspection zone 3 FNAO' which was planned to be operational by early 2021. The audit team noted that the proposed facilities would, if completed as planned, be compliant with the above requirements. Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts

The implementation of official controls on imported consignments of products of non-animal origin was based on valid Common Entry Documents (CEDs), selected by the competent authority. 11 5.2.1 Prior notification of arrival of consignments and systems to ensure they are presented for import controls

All pigs are imported from authorised third countries, territories or part thereof and listed approved bodies in line with Article 3a(1) of Commission Regulation (EU) 206/2010 and are moved to an approved body, institute or centre in Luxembourg. The audit team noted that one rejected consignment of products of animal origin was re- dispatched to the country of origin within 60 days of rejection, via an airport other than the one (BCP) of entry. The consignment was moved between airports under a customs procedure without SVA approval. Customs and the SVA subsequently confirmed that a consignment landed at one airport may be transported by road to another airport (destination) without the need for a customs transit document (T1) under a road-feeder service (`Luftfrachtersatzverkehr'). The air transport document (Air Waybill) indicates the airport of destination. The audit team noted that the procedure was not in line with the requirem

A number of shortcomings were noted with respect to the implementation of official controls, in particular the late notification of arrival of consignments and the performance of documentary checks for food of non-animal origin, other than upon arrival of the consignment at a designated BCP, which undermine the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls and their overall compliance with Union legislation. 14 6.2 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

The EHD stated that due to a lack of staff, documentary checks for consignments of food of non-animal origin or kitchenware are carried out at the central office of the EHD, and not at the BCP, which for goods referred to in Article 47(1)(d) and (e) of the OCR, is not in line with Article 49(1) of that Regulation.

However, the lack of documented procedures and necessary arrangements, updated as appropriate, and delays in finalising and implementing the monitoring plan, have an adverse impact on both the effectiveness of the organisation of official controls on imports of animals and goods, and its compliance with Union legislation. The lack of recent internal audits or verification checks of the official controls for such imports, represent possible missed opportunities to identify and address those issues.

The VRD informed the audit team that no guidelines or documented procedures had been issued at the time of the audit for performing import controls on feed of non- animal origin and hay and straw. Prior to the UK's withdrawal from the EU such goods were not imported. The VRD confirmed at the closing meeting (see section 8 below) that documented procedures for the control of feed of non-animal origin, hay and straw would be in place by 31 May 2021. As a result of that action, the VRD will have by that date, documented procedures in place that include the relevant subjects 7 specified in Chapter II of Annex II to the OCR, and which have been updated as appropriate, in line with Article 12(3)(b

However a number of shortcomings were noted in the application of the prior notification of arrival of consignments and the implementation of certain documentary and physical checks. The authorities have taken immediate action, or plan to take action, to address the majority of those, however the documentary checks of glazed foods carried out in-line with internal guidelines do not ensure consistency between the entry document and documents accompanying the consignment. 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

The audit team noted that the documentary checks had not identified certain minor errors in a small number of entry documents. The errors in the documents were not sufficient to affect the validity of the decision to allow importation of the animals or goods concerned. In light of that finding, the Chief Veterinary Officer issued an instruction to BVIs on 18 December 2020, to take measures to minimise errors and inconsistencies in the entry documents and accompanying documents. The VI also confirmed that Section 5 of the BIP Manual concerning documentary checks would be revised and that the issue would be included in future training programmes for border inspectors, in line with Article 12(3

The audit team also noted that the net weight declared in the CVED accompanying a consignment of frozen prawns, included the weight of the ice-glaze, although the 16 accompanying health certificate indicated the net weight without the ice-glaze, which in this case amounted to a difference of 3,584 kg. The VI informed the audit team that in- line with internal guidance, it was acceptable for the declared weight to be inclusive of glaze, and therefore the CVED was not rejected. The audit team noted that such guidance is not consistent with the clarification previously provided by DG Health and Food Safety to Member States, that in order to ensure consistency between Regulation (EU) No 1169/201

label_heading: Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts
paragraph_text: The absence of appropriate storage rooms or areas at one rail BCP is not in line with EU legislation and may have an adverse impact on the official controls and the hygienic handling of products for which that BCP has been designated. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION There is a comprehensive system of official controls for animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Poland. Those controls were carried out by well-trained officials, supported by detailed guidance, and were generally implemented in line with documented procedures, planned arrangements, and relevant Union legislation. However specific shortcomings were identified in the implementation of certain documentary and physical checks and in

The audit team noted that no storage facilities are available at the rail location at BCP Dorohusk/Dorohusku. The competent authorities confirmed that storage in the means of transport in which the goods were brought to the BCP is permitted under their control 18 instead, in line with Article 3(13) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014, and that in their view, there is no need for storage areas or rooms.

The audit team noted that while such storage is permitted, Article 3(13) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 does not derogate from the requirement for BCPs to have fixed storage areas or rooms, appropriate to the categories of goods for which the post has been designated, in line with Articles 3(1)(c), 3(2) and 6(2) of that Regulation. label_heading: Conclusion on the structure of the official control system
paragraph_text: The VRD has staff shortages in several of its Units, including the FSCU and its ABP Section. This has resulted in a higher workload for the ABP Section and failure to meet the annual targets for control frequencies. The situation is impaired by frequent staff turnover in the ABP Section, lack of specific procedures for some ABP control areas and lack of training on ABP organised in the last five years. At the time of the audit there were 11 unfilled posts for veterinary officers at the VRD, and to manage the workload, several officers had taken on additional duties, working only half time for their original job description without having been provided with specific training for their new tasks. The ABP Section has undergone frequent staff changes in recent years and two of the three officers in the ABP Section (one is on long term leave) are dividing their working time between controls on feedingstuffs and ABP.

paragraph_text: The arrangements in place for (internal) audits, official control procedures and instructions, are not fit for purpose and do not support the implementation of effective official controls along the entire chain of collection, transport, use and disposal of ABP and DP. 5.2 Registration, approval and listing of ABP plants, establishments and operators

label_heading: Conclusions on planning and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The Maltese competent authorities have neglected the conduct of official controls on ABP and DP in recent years and the evidence seen on the spot in the establishments visited by the audit team suggests that recent official controls are not effective in detecting and preventing inappropriate processing, handling and use of ABP and DP. Considering the numerous shortcomings in relation to the registration/approval and listing of ABP plants, establishments and operators, the overall picture is not consistent with a well-functioning system of official controls. 16 5.4 Overall Conclusions The central competent authority, the VRD, has staff shortages in several of its functional units including th

The VRD has incorporated controls on ABP in its multi-annual national control plan (MANCP) of 2017-2021. The ABP Section is responsible for establishing annual work plans on the sector which includes targets for the number of inspections. No such plans were presented to the audit team regarding controls on ABP for the years 2017-2020. The head of the ABP Section stated that the target is to inspect the ABP plants and establishments at least once a year, regardless of the risk and type of the establishment or plant. The few written records of official controls available for the establishments and plants visited at the end of 2019 or beginning of 2020 were very short and overall superficial - a number of non-compliances identified by the audit team had not been detected during the competent authority's controls in 2019 and 2020. 5.3.3.1 Official controls in the ABP plants

The official controls on ABP plants had not noted any serious shortcomings in relation to general hygiene conditions, operation and maintenance. However, the audit team still noted some shortcomings in the high-capacity incineration plant visited: a) The solid components of wastewater (Category 1 material) were pumped out to an approved site instead of disposing it using the methods allowed for this material under Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. If this shortcoming existed at the time of the previous inspection in 2016, it was not recorded in the report of said inspection. b) The meat and bone meal resulting from the thermal treatment preceding incineration was stored in large op

Regarding controls on requirements on general hygiene, the audit team noted some shortcomings that had not been picked up during previous official controls: a) In the poultry slaughterhouse, blood was collected in vats to be disposed of in the high-capacity incinerator plant. However, blood ended up also in the drain of the slaughter hall and some of it was leaking out from the floor to the slaughterhouse surroundings. This is contrary to requirements laid in point 6 of Section 2 of Chapter I of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, which prohibits disposal of blood through the waste stream. This had not been recorded as a shortcoming in the two annual control reports seen, the latest of

In the dairy establishment visited the permanent procedures based on the HACCP principles regarding ABP disposal included disposal of separator sludge and white wash water into the drains, instead of applying the methods provided for in Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. This had not been noted as a shortcoming in the report of an inspection carried out in 2019.

The official controls on ABP covered identification of ABP. The ABP storage plants and food business operators had arrangements in place to collect and identify ABP. Nonetheless, the audit team noted the following shortcomings in relation to identification of ABP which had not been identified in the records of official controls: a) Some of the containers designated and vehicles registered for transport of ABP to the high-capacity incinerator plant were not correctly identified and labelled; and b) In one of the cutting plants visited, ABP was collected in containers that were not correctly identified and labelled. 14 All the above are not in line with point 2 of Chapter II of Annex VIII to R

For example, in the dairy establishment visited, no commercial documents were available for the former foodstuffs and other ABP sent to landfill, which is contrary to the requirement of Article 21(2) and Article 22(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. There was no evidence that the official controls had i

The visited ABP storage plant for fallen stock had an adequate register in place which ensured traceability of the fallen stock. However, copies of commercial documents were not available for some consignments that had arrived (e.g. for spent hens) and in an ABP plant approved for storage of Category 3 hides the operator had commenced issuing commercial documents only in December 2019.

Several containers designated for transport of ABP seen by the audit team at the sites visited were not identified and labelled in line with the requirements of point 2 of Chapter II of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. This shortcoming was not noted in any of the inspection reports seen by the audit team, some of which were recent (official controls carried out at the end of 2019 or in January 2020). 15 5.3.4 Implementation of official sampling and testing programmes

paragraph_text: Inaccurate statuses recorded in the lists of approved ABP operators, plants and establishments indicate that despite changes in the activities of individual operators the information contained in the lists remain unchanged. label_heading: Conclusions on the structure of the official control system
paragraph_text: While adequate procedures exist for registration and approval of ABP operators, plants and establishments, inaccuracies in their implementation, identified in processing plants in relation to the assessment of the processing method 7 validation, 8 weaken their effectiveness.

paragraph_text: The SVFA has established a procedure for approval of ABP plants which meets the requirements of Article 44 of Regulation (EU) No 1069/2009. Despite applying the procedure during the approval process, in two out of five ABP plants visited the available approval-related documentation did not demonstrate that the competent authority had checked if the plant operators had carried out validation of processing in accordance with all of the procedures and indicators required by Section 2 of Chapter 1 of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. For example: An ABP plant processing Category 3 material had received an approval even though the operator's documentation did not clearly demonstrate that

label_heading: Conclusions on the structure of the official control system
paragraph_text: Most of the inspectors interviewed by the audit team were not aware about the sampling requirements for validation of the processing method 7 provided for in point G of Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 142/2011 and thus were unable to carry out the checks required by Section 2 of Chapter 1 of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 prior to granting the approval.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: While the inspection frequencies are established without taking into account the past performance of the operator, this deficiency is largely mitigated by the effective follow-up actions, including additional inspections and sampling where relevant, taken when cases of non-compliance are identified during routine inspections.

The SVFA decides on the inspection frequencies based on risk factors such as the intended use of the commodity (e.g. feed or for technical use), seasonality (or not) of production and size of the establishment. The inspectors at district level can increase the inspection frequency if they consider it justified based on their local risk assessment. The methodological instructions contain guidance on the risk factors to be taken into account for this purpose. Contrary to Article 9(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the 9 compliance history of the establishment is not included in the risk factors. The audit team noted that in none of the establishments visited had the shortcomings detected duri

label_heading: Conclusions on planning and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Although relatively frequent, the official controls on certain topics are superficial and ineffective in identifying non-compliances in relation to the general hygiene requirements, the permanent written procedures based on the HACCP principles, some areas of own checks and traceability and record keeping.

Regarding the general hygiene checks, the installations and equipment seen in the plants visited were in adequate condition and the general hygiene requirements were complied with, with the exception of an ABP plant processing Category 3 material where the audit team noted certain shortcomings that had not been recorded in earlier inspection reports. In particular, some of the plastic containers used were very dirty and broken and the clean area was insufficiently protected against rodents and pests (the doors were not properly fitted and as a consequence there were gaps allowing entering of insects and mice), contrary to Article 25(1)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

Concerning the official controls on the effective implementation of the permanent written procedure based on the HACCP principles, including operator's own checks and the standards of the products after processing, the audit team noted that all plants 11 visited established such procedures and carried out own controls and these were checked by the inspectors.

The audit team examined several inspection reports and noted that these had not identified a number of shortcomings in relation to the permanent written procedure based on the HACCP principles in the two plants processing Category 3 material visited. The procedures were not in line with the requirements of Article 29 of Regulation (EU) No 1069/2009 regarding the following points: In line with point 1(a) of Section 4 of Chapter II of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, in one of the processing plants, the size of the raw material particles before feeding into the cooker was identified as a CCP. However, the CCP was checked by the operator (`monitored') only once a year. This is contrary

The sampling and testing regimes and the procedure followed for ABP sampling of the final products as part of the operators' own checks were largely satisfactory in the plants visited. The laboratory results of the examinations assessed by the audit team were also satisfactory. However, the audit team noted that the procedures for microbiological sampling as part of own checks were not compliant with the requirements of Chapter I of Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 and this was not noted during previous official controls: Only one sample of the end product destined as feed material for analysis of Salmonella was taken instead of the five required. In one of the Category 3 ABP processin

In one of the plants processing Category 3 material, the PAP destined for production of petfood contained small but clearly visible plastic particles originating from plastic 12 wrapping or otherwise packaging materials. The audit team noted that the operator had in place a sieve which allowed for capturing particles of a bigger size. The presence of packaging materials in feedstuffs is contrary to the requirements of Article 6 and Point 7 of Chapter I of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council and was not detected by the inspectors during previous controls.

Concerning the checks on storage conditions, the audit team noted that in one of the plants processing Category 3 material, the raw ABP comprising raw meat and fats from slaughterhouses (including ABP from other Member States) destined for production of processed petfood was stored in rooms without temperature control. The operator stated that the raw material would be processed within 24 hours and considered that no cooling was necessary. However, the fact that the ABP was undergoing fermentation suggests that the products were stored at ambient temperature for longer than 24 hours from their delivery to the plant. The lack of suitable temperature-controlled storage facilities for incoming

However, the audit team noted that the official controls in some of the establishments visited have not included the checks on records or, when they covered the record keeping, did not detect a number of non- compliances with Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and the relevant requirements of Chapter III

The records of previous inspections in the OF/SI plant visited did not contain any remarks on record keeping, even though in line with Section 7 of Chapter III of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, official controls of OF/SI plants must always include a check on the records kept by the operator. The audit team noted that the operator does not keep any register of incoming and outgoing materials or commercial documents for consignments of raw ABP received from another Member State, contrary to the requirements of Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and point 2 of Chapter III of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. These non-compliances were not noted during previous inspec

In the ABP storage plant visited, a register of incoming ABP was available. However, the number of copies of commercial documents issued at the place of ABP origin kept in the register was lower than the number of ABP consignments handled by the storage plant. The inspector responsible for the controls explained that, in most cases, commercial documents were forwarded directly to the head office of the storage plant. The inspector did not however verify if the commercial documents are indeed available at the head office, contrary to Article 32(2) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, which requires that official controls must include checks on the keeping of records, including other documents.

MoRA is also responsible for the allocation of sufficient budget for controls and for the supervision of the control and certification tasks conferred to EAB and VFB. Supervision must take place once every five years in accordance with national rules. It is carried out either by MoRA´s internal audit team or by outsourcing it to external companies. The audit team found that the internal audit carried out of EAB by MoRA was well- structured and detailed and with good follow-up which allowed for the closing of most of the recommendations. However, its scope did not cover the most relevant aspects of the tasks conferred to this CtrlA. For example, the effectiveness of inspections, sampling and laboratory testing and the certification activities were not covered. It also did not include on-the-spot activities at operators to observe inspections performed by EAB. However, the audit team considered that documentary checks only would not allow MoRA to evaluate how controls are carried out, as the inspection reports, in particular EAB´s, lack

However, the reports issued by EAB inspectors lack detail on how verification takes place, with no objective evidence attached to the reports except in cases of non-compliance. The reports consist of a digital template where inspectors tick off the aspects verified with no further description of, or references made, to the documents or records checked.

For example, the audit team reviewed a report of an additional inspection carried out at an operator who runs conventional and organic units as described in paragraph 35 above. The inspector stated that she focused on the verification of proper cleaning of the harvesting machinery and equipment shared between the conventional and organic units. The inspector also stated that she followed the guidance in the handbook of procedures and monitored the purchase and use of inputs, as well as the balance between the organic products harvested against their sales, to confirm that only the products sold as organic were those produced in the organic unit. However, these statements were not supported b

The audit team noted that the manner in which inspections are announced to operators differ between EAB and VFB. VFB generally carries out all inspections unannounced while EAB allows for short prior warning of up to 48 hours being given to farmers, even for additional inspections that according to Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 should be primarily unannounced. Although the audit team fully understood the reasons given by EAB that in some cases it is difficult to carry out an inspection at farmers without prior warning, this should be the exception (for duly justified cases) rather than the rule. 9 As a consequence of this shortcoming, Estonia is not in the position to fulfil t

Additional inspections are planned at the beginning of the year by EAB and VFB. The audit team noted that both CtrlAs generally achieve the number of inspections planned. However, the manner in which EAB and VFB select operators for additional inspections differ greatly. VFB follows the working document agreed by Member States and issued by the European Commission, which instructs how to classify operators in risk categories following risk assessment made of them all. VFB thus uses a number of criteria (e.g quantities produced or traded, past non-conformities, potential of exchange of products, e-commerce, sales or pre-packed or unpacked products, subcontracted operations).

Every operator is rated for each criterion and given a final score based on the aggregated scores. The operators are selected for additional inspections in descending order starting with the one with the highest score. There are also additional factors that can be taken into account but not rated with points (e.g. textual remarks from the inspector, operator under control of EAB and VFB).

EAB sets up the risk criteria annually, with some criteria being used each year (e.g. past irregularities, risk of mixing organic and non-organic products) while others are introduced based on a thematic approach for the year in question (e.g. small potato growers with land area between 10-50 hectares for which complaints were received). EAB 10 then groups the operators under each of the criteria. Operators may be selected for additional controls based on one criterion only, also taking into account input from inspectors. This not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, as no individual assessment is made to determine the risk profile defined for each operator, taking into

Even if selecting the operators based on one criterion only can be useful to detect non- compliant operators, the inspections carried out on this basis should not be counted as part of the minimum, required by Article 92c(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, of 10% of operators that must be subject to additional inspections based on their risk profile.

VFB generally carries out all inspections unannounced while EAB allows for short prior warning of up to 48 hours being given to farmers, even for additional inspections that according to Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 should be primarily unannounced. The audit team noted that according to the Organic Farming Act, samples may be taken in the framework of horizontal controls and not necessarily with the purpose of verifying compliance of operators with the requirements of the organic regulation. For example, VFB elaborates its sampling plan in the framework of food safety controls, which generally include testing for the detection of multi-residues of plant protection products.

When the products sampled happen to be organic, the samples are counted for the 5% target required by article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The products selected for sampling are categorised according to pre-defined criteria (products most commonly purchased by Estonian consumers, results of samples from the previous years, OFIS (Organic Farming Information System) notifications and internal detections, risk of use 14 of substances extensively used in conventional production, products not tested before) and covering all stages of the food chain). However, VFB does not use the risk assessment described in paragraphs 36 and 37 to select the operators, which is not in line with the said

Moreover, VFB also counts the samples of products of animal origin, taken by VFB at primary producers in the framework of food safety controls, towards the 5%. This is not correct as the legal requirement refers to the taking of samples at operators under organic controls (and according to risk assessment under organic legislation) and not under food safety controls. VFB does not know the risk profile of primary producers as they are not under its control and this information is not shared by EAB.

EAB selects the operators based on the risk assessment implemented for deciding on additional inspections. However, as described in paragraph 38, the assessment is not fit for purpose and does not serve to identify the operators who pose the highest risk.

Moreover, EAB takes samples from final products intended for consumption and rarely from soil or non-edible plant parts. This and the fact that many samples are taken during storage of harvested products (e.g. 40% in 2020) reduces the likelihood of detecting substances not authorised in organic production. This is because the presence of residues of plant protection products decreases from the moment of application, and even faster from fruits than from plant parts or soil. Furthermore, if the sample is positive, it may be more difficult to determine from a sample taken from storage whether the cause was spray drift from neighbouring fields or use on the field itself, since it normally canno

The fact that samples are not taken at the most risky operators or at the most suitable time and place can explain the low number of samples that have tested positive for the presence of unauthorised products in the 2020 and 2019 campaigns. As an example, there were only four positive results in 2020 out of 147 samples taken. Of these, two were taken on suspicion by the EAB inspector and one taken by VFB at catering facilities not in the control system).

Moreover, the procedures for the taking of samples mentioned in paragraph 53 do not contain detailed guidance on how to collect samples from the fields or to evaluate the results of the samples taken. Both CtrlAs stated that any presence of unauthorised substances is considered as a potential irregularity and an investigation is launched in all cases. As an example of this, the audit team was shown a case where an operator raised a complaint to EAB against a wheat producer following the analytical results of a sample taken during the operator's own checks. EAB launched an investigation including a visit to the wheat producer, who attributed the presence of the residue to spray drift from a n

The case above shows good internal co-operation within EAB and enabled it to take a correct ad-hoc decision. However, it alone cannot ensure that an appropriate decision is made in all cases without a specific sampling methodology allowing for the assessment of the laboratory results to conclude that the presence of the unauthorised substance was the result of its use or spray drift. paragraph_text: The use of alternative, and as yet, un-validated test methods, different to those as stipulated in the Annex of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191, may undermine the effectiveness of the emergency measures.

With regards selected methodologies for the detection of ToBRFV, the Virology Laboratory only uses one of the prescribed test methods as laid down in the Annex to the Regulation (EU) 2020/1191 (International Seed Federation (ISF) protocol (2020), with their own modifications to thermal cycling parameters and decreased 5 concentrations of primer and probe). The method of Ling et al. (2019)1, not prescribed in the Annex, is used as the second, confirmatory test due to, in the laboratory's stated experience, superior method specificity. Neither of these methods are formally validated.

label_heading: Conclusions on the measures concerning the confirmed presence of ToBRFV
paragraph_text: The current practice of reporting the outbreaks is not in line with the requirements of the EU legislation. Any delayed reporting may have prevented a full overview of the current state of play of outbreaks in the Netherlands. It could prevent MS from assessing any indirect risk for them and so could negatively influence the related controls. 5.4 CONTROLS ON MOVEMENT OF SPECIFIED PLANTS FOR PLANTING WITHIN THE EU Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Findings

ToBRFV was first found in the Netherlands in a tomato fruit producing crop in October 2019. The production site was checked during the annual survey. Samples of symptomatic plants were tested positive with the ELISA method and were later confirmed by RT-PCR and next generation sequencing methods. Up to the time of the audit, the presence of the virus was identified in tomato fruit crops at 27 production sites.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls on movement of specified seeds within the EU
paragraph_text: A considerable part of the specified seed lots which were in storage prior to 15 August 2020 were not tested with the molecular method. Although many lots have been tested with ELISA method, the potential plant health risk is only partially addressed due to the lower sensitivity of those tests.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls on movement of specified seeds within the EU
paragraph_text: The supervision of the ToBRFV tests carried out by the seed companies by annual audits provides a level of guarantee. However, the sampling for those tests is not supervised adequately in all cases and therefore the associated plant health risk is not addressed. In addition, the CAs do not have comprehensive information about whether the test results reflect the plant health status of each specified seed lot. 5.6 CONTROLS ON THE INTRODUCTION INTO THE EU OF SPECIFIED PLANTS FOR PLANTING Legal requirements Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Currently there is no obligation for the seed companies to report to the CAs the number of samples and the methods used for the tests they carried out on seed lots and batches in stock. The controls of imported seeds are generally in line with EU requirements. However, the selection of consignments for laboratory tests does not take into consideration all known risk factors and no measures are implemented to prevent the free circulation of imported seeds before the laboratory analysis is completed. These issues compromise the effectiveness of EU measures to protect against the introduction of ToBRFV in seeds. 5.8 ADDITIONAL MEASURES IN RELATION TO TOBRFV Legal requirements Articles 29, 31 and 52 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Findings 5.8.1 Controls at the packaging houses

The NVWA stated that coated tomato and pepper seeds are excluded from the sampling regime as coating may affect the tests. In particular, chemicals in the coating could influence the RNA extraction or inhibit the PCR process. Currently there are no validated laboratory protocols for coated seeds. The majority of the seeds are imported as minimally processed. The growers use chemicals during the extraction and dry the seeds before the dispatch.

Consignments or seed lots of Capsicum spp., for which the AD on the PC certifies that the variety is resistant, are accepted for import. NVWA stated that there are uncertainties about which genes ensure the resistance. During their monitoring activity for ToBRFV the NVWA tested positive pepper seed lots, which had been declared to be ToBRFV resistant. Resistance of a variety could be linked to only one of the two parental lines. Hence, a contamination of the hybrid seed may only be related to the parents whereas the seed itself is still resistant.

At the time of the audit, the inspection bodies selected consignments for sampling randomly, without taking into consideration the existing risk such as countries, exporters and varieties with ToBRFV interception history. The NVWA is of the opinion that ToBRFV is much wider distributed in the world than officially recorded. Therefore, 21 third countries were evenly targeted, to avoid overlooking potential risky pathways. The audit team considers that a non-targeted sampling reduces the effectiveness of the test in preventing the entry of infected seed lots to the EU territory. If the consignment was sampled, the importer receives a notification about the sampled lot. The company is then informed about the test results in writing. Therefore, the exemption provided by Article 4(9) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130 does not apply and the consignments cannot be released for free circulation before the test results are available. label_heading: Conclusions on early detection and surveillance
paragraph_text: The very limited implementation of surveillance for ASF cannot provide adequate guarantees that this activity is suitable to detect rapidly an incursion of the disease in the wild boar population, notably in the high-risk areas in the north of the country. While testing of wild boar found dead has hardly contributed to that surveillance, plans for active surveillance of hunted animals included in the 2020 National ASF control and eradication programme are far from being fulfilled. Nevertheless, the competent authorities have taken additional action to incentivise and increase surveillance activities before the end of 2020 in order to address those shortcomings.

label_heading: Conclusions on early detection and surveillance
paragraph_text: Surveillance has not been complemented with the implementation of risk-based active surveillance, e.g. regularly testing dead pigs, while the planned serological sampling included in the 2020 National ASF control and eradication programme for commercial holdings has not yet been carried out.

During 2020, samples from 13 wild boars notified as found dead were tested; samples from 11 had been tested in 2019. In 2020, ten of the wild boars were from two regions, i.e. Central Macedonia and East Macedonia and Thrace. In the 2020 National ASF control and eradication programme, the competent authorities had estimated that, given the size of the wild boar population in Greece, a target of 780 wild boar found dead to be sampled as part of this component of ASF surveillance would be reasonable.

In the 2020 National ASF control and eradication programme, the competent authorities have included targets for active surveillance of wild boar in the areas included in Part I of the Annex to Decision 2014/709/EU that covers partially the territory under the responsibility of five regional units with an estimated wild boar population of 50,000. At the time of the audit, 73 out of an overall target of 980 hunted wild boar had been sampled.

According to data provided by the competent authorities, between January and September 2020, they have investigated suspicions of ASF in 30 pig holdings (including sampling and testing of 35 pigs). Those suspicions occurred throughout those months but mainly until the end of June, with only three investigated since then. All investigated holdings were situated in only two regions, i.e., Central Macedonia and East Macedonia 19 and Thrace. In the 2020 National ASF control and eradication programme, the competent authorities have included an estimated national target for passive surveillance in domestic pigs of 193 pigs from 69 holdings. Active surveillance in pigs

Data provided by the competent authorities on the application of active surveillance in domestic pigs confirm that the plan mentioned above has not yet been implemented. Those data include some 1,700 samples tested by the NRL in Athens (mostly serological testing and some 100 samples tested with a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) method) and 1,118 samples tested (serology) in the laboratory in Thessaloniki. All of them were tested between the date of confirmation of the ASF outbreak and mid-April, when the restrictions were lifted (see more information in section 5.3.3). Those samples were taken in the context of testing activities required within the protection and surveillance zones establi

paragraph_text: The competent authorities have developed some operational arrangements in their preparedness system, for instance on animal depopulation and disposal of carcasses. However, they have still to address important shortcomings in order to enhance that contingency system to respond rapidly and effectively to outbreaks of ASF in commercial pig holdings and to contain its spread if the wild boar population is affected. 5.5 VERIFICATION AND SUPERVISION Legal requirements Articles 4.2, 5.1, 6, 12.2 and 12.3(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings

Representatives of the central competent authority informed the audit team that the Ministry of Rural Development and Food has contacted the Ministry of Interior on the need for the municipalities to get ready to help the veterinary services to respond to animal disease outbreaks, i

This included information campaigns for farmers, hunters and the public, as well as increased surveillance for the disease. Those measures were reinforced since November 2019 once the Euro

However, the above evaluation did not make any recommendations or corrective actions as required by Article 12.3(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 on the fact that the specific frequency of "weekly" clinical inspections specified in the Circular detailing the duties of the additional veterinary staff had not been respected, nor that all regions and regional units should use the same checklist and reporting format to inspect the holdings and report their results (see section 5.2.3).

The central competent authority has not verified, as required by Article 12.2 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, the implementation of Circular (ref.: 458/50853, dated 13.02.2020) laying down instructions for all regions and regional units in Greece, including the nine regions which did not receive additional veterinary staff, to develop a system of surveillance of pig holdings by means of field visits with a specific frequency.

paragraph_text: The inspections at the places of production of tomato and pepper seeds, the necessary tracing back and forward of seed lots are carried out in line with the EU legislation. The approach taken to carry out the epidemiological investigations was not standardised or consistent along the epizootic, and there was a persistent lack of quality and completeness of the data obtained. This, in many cases, did not allow the competent authorities to investigate all the elements contained in points (a) to (d) of Article 6(2) of Directive 2005/94/EC.
