label_heading: Conclusions on diagnosis of avian influenza
paragraph_text: The competent authorities detected 24 outbreaks during pre-movement testing: 23 of them in movements granted for direct slaughter and one to force-feeding. The competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team on the risk assessments required by Article 33 of Directive 2005/94/EC that the competent authorities should have undertaken prior to these movements being authorised or on possible epidemiological links to previous outbreaks.

label_heading: Conclusions on repopulation of affected holdings
paragraph_text: The impressive amount of PCR tests carried out during the epizootic, in excess of 30,000 (approximately 70% between 25 March and 8 June), used for testing some 130,000 swabs from live poultry and tissues from poultry carcasses, cast doubts on the alleged limited analytical capacity of the NRL in that respect. As indicated in the report of the previous audit, the numerous derogations granted to holdings in the restricted zones overstretch significantly the testing capacity of the NRL (i.e. in 2020, derogations required PCR testing of tens of thousands of samples). This is not in line with Annex X (point 8) to Directive 2005/94/EC. 25
Sustained monitoring of the depopulated holdings ensures compliance with registration requirements, thereby preventing the resurgence of illegal activities.

The practical and financial challenges that the new biosecurity rules present for family farms that exceed the new stocking limits mean that enforcing compliance on these establishments is a priority.

On the other hand, the operation of private laboratories without the oversight of the national reference laboratory for ASF calls into question their role in the performance of diagnostic and pre-movement tests for the disease.
The decision to suspend control and eradication measures in the areas surrounding confirmed ASF cases in wild boar increases the likelihood that the disease will persist and spread.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: As, in general, the classification of production areas is consistent with the EU classification requirements and supported by recommendations from sanitary surveys, there is confidence that the level of contamination of molluscs harvested corresponds to the value expected according to their classification. The provisional classification based on a reduced number of results may overestimate the microbiological quality of mollusc.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The few cases where the results of the microbiological monitoring of class B production areas do not provide an exact result (number) pose a challenge to the decisions for reclassification and/or closure of these production areas.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The fact that IPMA: i) does not close or reclassify the production area when certain regulatory limits for microbiological quality are exceeded; ii) reverts the classification downgrade without an evaluation of the results for the review period; iii) excludes unexpected results without conclusive investigation, may result in the placing on the market of bivalve molluscs that exceed the health standards.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The current monitoring programme for biotoxins covers most of the requirements of EU legislation but the fact that the IPMA does not fully respect the sampling points and frequencies diminishes its value.

The classification of production, included in the IPMA procedure MB 01, foresees three types of classification: permanent, provisional and not classified, depending on the number of results available during the review period. The audit team noted that: For provisional classification, a reduced number of sampling results (between 12 and 23) in three years is sufficient for IPMA to classify provisionally a specific species in a production area with a better class than other species in the same area. The audit team considered that less than 24 results in three years does not ensure that results are representative of a production area, as required in Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Nonet

According to the procedure MB 02, laboratory reports have to include the Most Probable Result (MPR) of E. coli per 100 grams. However, the number of dilutions made during the analyses of samples from class B production areas is not enough to provide an exact number when results are > 18,000. Therefore, it is not possible to determine if these areas exceed the limit of 46,000 established in Article 54.3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 for class B production, and decisions for reclassification and/or closure of production areas cannot be adequately taken. b) For the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water

According to the procedure MB 03, and in line with Article 61.4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the indicator species shall be sampled on a weekly basis (other species only when testing of indicator species result is over the limits for biotoxins). However, for different reasons (e g. indicator species not available, weather conditions, etc.) IPMA does not always respect this frequency. IPMA does not always take the samples at the points designated in the procedure according to Article 61.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Indicator species are sometimes sampled in other locations or other species are sampled instead and used as indicator.

The decisions following results over the limits are included in the procedure MB 01, but it has a number of deviations from the legislation: a) For microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs The procedure does not foresee the closure or reclassification of production areas when health standards for live bivalve molluscs are not met (i.e. between 230 and 700 E. coli NMP/100 g for class A production areas, between 4,600 and 46,000 E. coli NMP/100 g for class B production areas), contrary to Article 62.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. IPMA reclassifies production areas when monitoring results are >700 E. coli NMP/100 g for class A production areas and closes production areas when monitoring

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The IPMA's intention to formalise the procedure for sampling of classified production areas by non-official staff is essential to ensure that samples taken in the context of official monitoring are reliable.

IPMA analyses all monitoring samples in its laboratories and there is a dedicated budget line to pay for these analyses. IPMA staff take monitoring samples, but also individual harvesters, harvesters' associations or aquaculture production companies with a contract with IPMA (there is no financial compensation for the sampling activities or for the samples themselves). Since 2015, IPMA has enhanced the content of contracts for 10 The guidance document of the EU Reference Laboratory for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs ("Good Practice Guide; issue 7", December 2018). 5 sampling to make them more comprehensive, to include a training session from IPMA staff

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The results of microbiological analysis using non-accredited testing methods are not 11 reliable and thus they generate the risk of misclassification of the areas. However, this risk is limited to only some of the monitoring samples of two of the 39 classified production areas.

Although the IPMA laboratory for lipophilic toxins routinely uses the EU analytical reference method to determine these toxins, the use of a non-recognised method on certain occasions means that the result in this biotoxin group, could be sporadically 15 non-reliable or underestimated. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Regarding official controls in production areas, there is a significant improvement since the previous audit. The system is now well structured and documented, and the official laboratories that support official control provide high quality and reliable results. There are some shortcomings, mainly on the classification of production areas and the decision that authorities take after gettin

According to the procedure MB 02, monitoring samples have to be analysed using a method recognised by the National Reference Laboratory that should preferably be standardised. The audit team saw that the analyses of a certain number of samples from two production areas (they are remoter therefore more difficult to transport the samples on time) deviated from the method accredited and their analyses started more than 24 hours after collection. Accordingly, laboratory reports do not display the accreditation logo. However, IPMA used these results for classification and for decisions following monitoring. IPMA informed the audit team of an ongoing project to estimate the difference in results w

The head of the biotoxins laboratories presented the facilities and equipment of the laboratories. The facilities of the three laboratories are appropriate. The equipment of the ASP and PSP laboratories is also adequate. There was only one piece of equipment validated for lipophilic toxins. In case of breakdown or regular maintenance (which is regularly required for this type of equipment), samples were analysed using a screening test which does not comply with the requirements of Chapter III.B of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. In addition, this test only detects two of the regulated compounds (OA and DTX) so the total toxicity of the lipophilic toxin group can be underestimated.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The flow of information regarding monitoring results and the prompt update of available information helps the system to avoid mistakes due to delays. However, the current improvable cooperation between authorities and the absence of designated authorities for some parts of the food chain create the risk of molluscs that could pose a risk for consumers reaching and staying on the market.

The decisions taken by IPMA following results over the limits apply only from the moment when they are formalised (e.g. some days after the sample was taken). Similarly to the previous audit, the audit team noted that Portugal has not designated an authority responsible for withdrawing from the market those bivalve molluscs harvested between the day when the sample was taken and the day when the results are available. In the worst-case scenario, this period can be up to three days. As an example, the audit team noted one case where wedge clams were harvested in a production area closed on the same day due to lipophilic toxins. These clams, destined to another Member State, were sampled at th

The exchange of information between the two competent authorities audited has clearly improved since the previous audit. IPMA presented evidence of regular and ad-hoc meetings with DGRMA and with other authorities. However, a significant lack of cooperation seems to persist in relation to the investigations derived from RASFFs notifications when they relate to health standards (i.e. microbiology and biotoxins). According to IPMA, except in one case, the contact point for RASFF (i.e. the DGAV) has never informed them of any notification or request any further investigation/explanation from them. This is not the case for RASFF notifications related to traceability: DGRM stated that DGAV referr

Marine gastropods (except limpets) for human consumption, which can be harvested outside classified production areas, are not subject to the official controls required by Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. At the time of the audit, Portugal has not designated an authority responsible for these controls. 5.1.6 Movement of live bivalve molluscs and registration document accompanying batches

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: The official control system is able to identify and rectify shortcomings of processors of FNAO. However, the lack of sufficiently detailed guidance for the use of existing checklists for controls of primary producers, compromises the consistency of official controls aimed at verifying that operators have taken appropriate measures to minimise microbiological risks, pre-farm gate. This hinders the capacity of the CA to identify and react to non-compliances. 15

The CA has procedures, instructions and checklists that enable the CAs to perform official controls of FNAO establishments and for establishments seeking approval, in a uniform fashion. However, checklists lack sufficient guidance to address specific measures taken by operators to prevent microbiological risks pre-farm gate. This can compromise the consistent performance of official controls by the inspectors. 5.3 RAPID ALERT SYSTEM FOR FOOD AND FEED (RASFF) Legal requirements Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 66(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Chapter 3, Section I of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. Findings

The audit team noted that the checklist for primary producers covers both sprout- producing establishments and other primary producers of FNAO. The audit team noted that this checklist has included the general questions from Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 for primary production (questions 5(a) to (g) of part A.II on hygiene provisions). However, these general questions have not been deployed into more specific control points and inspectors lack of criteria regarding the suitability of measures to be implemented by operators to address microbiological risks.

The inspectors interviewed during the audit were aware of the guidance document on addressing microbiological risks in fresh fruits and vegetables at primary production through good hygiene (2017/C 163/01 (2)). However, the CA has not availed of the opportunity to deploy this guidance document into the inspection procedure. Inspectors have not received formal training regarding this guidance, and no specific guide or instruction has been given to set clear criteria to have a common and consistent understanding on what measures are expected to be found in primary production establishments and how to assess their suitability for reducing microbiological risks. Seeds for sprouting and sprout-pr

The audit team noted that control points within the checklist for primary producers of FNAO are not detailed enough to guide the inspector in the type of measures that are expected to be implemented by primary producers to reduce microbiological risks associated with activities prior to and during harvest. As such, this checklist does not specifically address, among others, the need for "field toilets" and "handwashing facilities" for farms growing crops to be eaten raw and considered of high risk (see paragraphs 54 and 55). As such, and in the absence of specific notes uploaded to the system, it is not possible to corroborate whether such measures have been systematically verified during th

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: The CA has properly included in the official controls the monitoring of environmental samples to detect Listeria monocytogenes. However, its acceptance of monitoring plans from FBO where positive results had been found which proposed only a marginal increase in the frequency of tests (and moreover much lower than frequencies suggested in national guidance), calls into question the appropriateness of its measures to ensure that operator effectively remedies the situation and demonstrates effective preventive measures, as required by Art. 138(1) of Regulation (EU) No 2019/625. This, in turn, impacts on the overall effectiveness of the official controls. 5.2.5 Official sampling Legal requiremen

In two of these FBOs, some of the test results showed positive findings for Listeria monocytogenes, and operators were requested to take measures to address this problem. Operators agreed to carry out deep cleaning and sanitation and additional samples were taken with negative results. According to the recorded information on the official control reports, own-check monitoring plans were amended, increasing the number of environmental samples to detect Listeria monocytogenes from once a year to once every quarter. In another case, the frequency set by the FBO was twice a year. These proposed FBOs' own-control plans were accepted by the CA.

However, this is not in line with an expert opinion on surface sampling which is embedded in the Estonian document "Guidance on planning and reporting on sampling and reporting of microbiology and gluten-free labelled food during monitoring in 2021". This Estonian expert opinion indicates that if there is a positive Listeria monocytogenes result, the frequencies for analysis (environmental sample, end-product) should be much higher i.e. once a week. Other Control Systems

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and scope of official controls
paragraph_text: In primary production, the system of official controls covers both chemical (PPP) and microbiological risks, with greater attention being given to the former. As a result, the likelihood of detecting non-compliances with microbiological requirements is lower. In addition, non-compliances detected during the controls are not considered for future planning. This could lead to associated food safety risks being underestimated, weakening the system of official controls and thus the enforcement of EU legislation in this area. 5.2.4 Implementation of official controls over FBO obligations Legal requirements Articles 9(1)(d), 14 and 44(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 4 to 8, and Annexes I

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: Regarding primary production, official controls are not consistently implemented. When implemented, the official controls partially targeted microbiological risks and are focusing mainly on chemical risks (PPP). This is not in line with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: In addition, the specific checklist for microbiological inspections at primary production is not systematically used and when used not always documented, thus official controls are not carried out in a coherent and uniform way and are not effectively targeting microbiological risks.

For audits, if the FBO has a Private Quality Assurance Scheme (PQS) certified according to BRC, IFS, FSSC 22000, the frequency of audits could be reduced. Audits do not apply to primary production and having a PQS is not taken into account for reducing the frequency of official controls at this stage. Details are in the following table. In primary production, controls are in the form of special projects, that take place with the aim of obtaining information on the whole sector regarding microbiological risks of produce.

For these "special projects", each year, a crop category is identified and a limited number of FBOs is randomly selected (see table in paragraph 61) for microbiological inspections. Regardless of the outcome of the project, a different category is chosen for the following year, without continuity and without having a plan of when the FBO / category will be inspected further (see table in paragraph 54).

The prioritisation of these projects and controls is mainly based on the risks associated with pesticides and, to a minor extent, the risks of microbial contamination (i.e. EFSA opinion regarding crops posing particular risks).

The inspectors interviewed stated that a better balance between chemical and microbiological risks in prioritising official controls is advisable and it should be reflected in the official control risk-based plan. The inspectors informed the audit team that controls over hygiene at primary production is still a relatively new task.

The CCA informed the audit team that the approach in place aims to optimise the resources available. However, the team leader of the primary production area acknowledged that, based on the current state of implementation of projects, it is more likely to identify systematic deficiencies and to improve the sector for pesticides, whereas this is not possible for microbiological risks. The CCA informed the audit team that: a) in 2017, for this project, 80% of implementation. Half of the inspected PP were PQS certified and there were no significant differences in the outcome of the inspections; b) in 2018, implementation stopped at 60% mainly due to other priorities related to official controls and difficulties in having the selected FBO with the targeted crop at the time of the inspection; c) in 2019, only 19 crops posing particular risks out of 69 inspected fell within the scope of this audit (implementation drop to 19%), mainly due to difficulties in having the selected FBO with the targeted crop at the time of the inspection; d) in 2020, no inspections were carried out

The inspectors interviewed confirmed to the audit team that official controls are implemented at the primary producers in the scope of the specific project. However, the driving force to perform inspections is still pesticides residues; microbiological risks could also be part of the inspections.

Inspectors informed the audit team that due to time constraints the specific checklist (see paragraph 63) is not used systematically. The assessments of hygiene requirements can also differ, depending on the experience and on the knowledge that an inspector may have of an FBO. Thus, official controls are not systematically carried out in a coherent and uniform way, so are not effectively targeting microbiological risks.

When non-compliances were identified, corrective actions were systematically required but evidence of follow-up was not systematically available. Moreover, inspectors confirmed that non-compliances are not yet taken into account for future planning.

Generally, checklists were not part of the reports and were not stored / archived. Therefore, the traceability of the official controls depended on what was noted in the report, where usually, only non-compliances were recorded. Aspects related to PPP were well described and supported by solid evidence in the reports, which was not the case for microbiological risks related issues. Sprout-producing establishments

paragraph_text: However, NVWA Guideline 85 allows the reduction of the final product sampling frequency in sprout-producing establishments classified as small and therefore the minimum sampling frequency established in Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 is not ensured. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Designation of competent authorities and resources for official controls Legal requirements Articles 4, 5 and 6 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: A reduction in the sampling frequency on the final product in sprout-producing establishments has been granted by the CCA to FBOs in accordance with their Guideline 85. This is not in line with EU legislation.

Guideline 85 contains provisions for "small" sprout-producing establishments (with a production of less than 50 tonnes per year). In this case, and contrary to the establish requirements the guideline allows FBOs to reduce by half the minimum sampling frequency established in Chapter 3, Section 3.3, Part A of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Conclusions on relevant national legislation and guidelines

An inspector informed the audit team that they are in the process of evaluating, according to NVWA Guideline 85, the request of a small sprout-producing establishment for a frequency reduction in the final product analyses.

The CCA informed the audit team that based on NVWA Guideline 85, they have already granted the permission to 1 out of the 8 sprout producers, to reduce the frequency of sampling final products. Processing Plants

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: Whilst the official controls relating to sprout-producing establishments identify regularly non compliances and did not adequately cover the legal requirements of import certificate for seeds from third countries, which could result in contaminated product being placed on the market.

The CA has procedures, instructions and checklists that enable the CAs to perform official controls of FNAO establishments and for establishments seeking approval, in a uniform fashion. However, the generic checklists in use up until the end of 2020 for sprout-producing establishments, in conjunction with the fact that in primary production the checklist was not systematically used, prevent inspectors from carrying out official controls in a consistent manner.

Regarding controls at sprout-producing establishments, the checklists used were the same as those used for processors of FNAO (which are also the same as those used for food of animal origin). Not all elements related to the specific legislation for sprouts were included 17 (i.e. import certificate requirements are not indicated). The inspectors confirmed that such a generic checklist could not provide guidance to inspectors during official controls at sprout-producing establishments.

In the reports examined by the audit team, as well as in the summary of non-compliances provided by the CCA, there was no evidence of non-compliances having been identified during official controls related to import certificates of seeds for sprouting.

When reviewing the outcome of official controls of sprout-producing establishments, the audit team noted that evidence of what was checked during official controls, regarding import certificates of seeds for sprouting imported from third countries, was rarely traceable.

The inspectors confirmed that the generic checklist that was in use up until the end of 2020, made it difficult to provide evidence of official controls over import certificates of seeds for sprouting controls.

The inspectors confirmed to the audit team that a specific checklist is now in place (since the start of 2021), which includes all of the specific requirements of the EU legislation for sprouts and seeds for sprouting. This checklist was assessed as satisfactory by the audit team.

However, shortcomings in the use of this new checklist were observed, mainly related to the fact that inspectors limited the assessment of compliance to the import certificates requirement based on the statement of FBOs, instead of seeking evidence (i.e. presence of the import certificate).

In one case, the audit team observed that the import certificate requirements for mung bean had been assessed as satisfactory without having had the certificate available. The team leader inspector (CA) informed the audit team that this was his usual method, but in the 18 future he will ensure to check for the physical presence of the certificate and its compliance with EU legislation.
Furthermore, at the request of the audit team, the CA requested the certificate from the operator. The operator was unable to provide it by the end of this audit.

The fact that the system of supervision in place does not include documented on-site verifications of inspectors affects the CAs' capability to assess the appropriateness and consistency of inspections, and to identify any shortcomings in their performance. 5.2.2 Registration/approval of food establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Articles 10(2), 138(1), 138(2)(c)-(j), 138(3), 138(4) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings Registration of primary producers of FNAO

There are no mechanisms in place that can effectively identify, and correct, shortcomings of the official control system, in a timely manner. This affects the CAs' capability to assess the effectiveness and appropriateness of inspections, and to identify any shortcomings in their performance. 5.3 RAPID ALERT SYSTEM FOR FOOD AND FEED (RASFF) Legal requirements Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 66(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Chapter 3, Section I of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. Findings

The CCA informed the audit team that supervision activities of inspectors, including on- the-spot visit of FBOs, could be carried out yearly by a senior inspector (team leader) if the capacity allows. However, there are no procedures or instructions in place for these supervisory activities. In addition, no records are kept of these activities so there is no evidence available of whether results are taken into account or how they are used in order to improve the system of official controls.

The CCA acknowledge that an effective system of verification on-the-spot of the implementation of training, procedures, instructions and use of checklists could improve the entire system of official controls. For example, if such a mechanism of supervision was in place, the CCA could have identified deficiencies in the controls of import 8 certificate requirements (see paragraphs 88, 93, 95 and 96) and consistency in the use of specific checklists during official controls on primary production (see paragraph 84), and could have corrected them in a timely manner.

However, shortcomings in the use of checklists at primary production and at sprout- producing establishments were observed by the audit team. These deficiencies were identified by the audit team and brought to the attention of the CCA which acknowledged 23 that the current procedures in place for supervision (overseeing of inspections), which are based only on desk studies and training activities, do not allow for the identification of such shortcomings (see paragraphs 29, 30, 31, 32 and 34).

The anonymous sampling procedure in cases of sampling projects, does not fully respect the right of the FBO to a second expert opinion, which is not in line with Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.2.6 Laboratory performance Legal requirements Articles 5(1)(d), 34 to 42, 100 and 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 21 Findings

The sampling carried out as part of the sampling projects at retail level, is carried out anonymously, thus preventing the FBO from exercising her/his right to a counter sample 20 for the purposes of obtaining a second expert opinion. In the case of positive results, the CA requires the FBO to take measures to ensure food safety.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: Insufficient knowledge of the CA regarding appropriate actions and practices to manage Lm contamination hinders the capacity of the authority to verify that FBOs take the appropriate preventative and corrective measures to ensure that only safe product is placed on the market. 5.2.5 Official sampling Legal requirements Articles 34 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Annex I, Chapter 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

However, the audit team noted that the FNAO inspectors have not received guidance to perform Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) environmental tests and/or to verify if and how FBOs carry out environmental samples to investigate Lm occurrence in their establishments. Supervision and Audit

The audit team noted that FNAO inspectors do not check if FBOs have an environmental sampling plan in place and effective procedures to detect Lm, as indicated by "The European guideline on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Lm, version 3, August 2012 (3) as well as by EFSA Scientific Opinion on "The public health risk posed by Lm in frozen fruit and vegetables including herbs, blanched during processing" (4).

The CAs did not request the FBO to investigate the cause of contamination. The CCA informed the audit team that, up until now, a root cause analysis for Lm contamination is not required from the FBOs and in this case the FBO did not perform a root cause analysis.

label_heading: Conclusion on organisation and scope of official controls
paragraph_text: The risk-based official control system is weakened by the fact that the information available concerning the majority of primary producers is insufficient to take into account higher risks of microbiological contamination of certain produce. This, along with the fact that inspections regarding FNAO microbiological risks do not cover the pre-harvest and harvest stages of the majority of primary producers, hampers the effectiveness of the official control system. 5.2.4 Implementation of official controls over FBO obligations Legal requirements Articles 9(1)(d), 14 and 44(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 4 to 8, and Annexes I and II to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 18 of Regulati

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: The official control system is able to identify and rectify shortcomings only at a limited number of primary producers.

However, since 2016, these controls were performed only for producers of fruits and vegetables that also have storage and/or processing activities of FNAO and are registered as such. There were 77 producers registered in 2020 and 69 inspections were planned and carried out. Ten non-compliances were detected regarding, for example: the periodic medical evaluation of staff; missing water analysis; pest control; lack of procedures and records on sanitation; analytical reports made in the own-control programme were not available. However, there were no non-conformities reported related to the checks before or during harvest.

As regards other primary producers of FNAO, NSVFSA did not carry out controls with regard to microbial contamination until the end of 2020. As a result, different risk levels for different products are only partly taken into account, contrary to the provisions of Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 9

The county staff informed the audit team that official controls are only implemented at the primary producers of fruits and vegetables that also have storage and/or processing activities of FNAO and are registered as such. Furthermore, the county staff stated that the current registration system does not allow the inspectors to identify the other farms.

There is a system of supervision in place, however it was not able to identify important shortcomings relating to non-compliances with EU legislation. This limits the CAs to improve the official control system. 6 5.2.2 Registration/approval of food establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Articles 10(2), 138(1), 138(2)(c)-(j), 138(3), 138(4) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings Registration of primary producers of FNAO

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls over FBO obligations
paragraph_text: Official controls of sprouting establishments are not verifying compliance with all the relevant legal requirements. Shortcomings in relation to the verification of compliance with traceability, import certificates, own microbiological analyses (frequency) and granting an unjustified derogation regarding "preliminary tests of seeds for sprouting" weaken the official control system, which could result in contaminated product being placed on the market.

Although the supervision system made it possible to identify shortcomings in the detection and enforcement of non-conformities by local CAs, it was not able to identify other important shortcomings relating to non-compliances with EU legislation, such as import certificate requirement for seeds in sprout-producing establishments, as well as shortcomings in the official environmental sampling relating to Lm (see also findings 60, 61 and 62).

When reviewing the outcome of one of the official controls of a sprout-producing establishment, the audit team noted that no checks were performed regarding import certificates of seeds for sprouting that had been imported from third countries. The CCA stated that for mung beans produced in third countries, certificates accompanying the consignments to the sprouting establishments are not required by the inspectors. This is not in line with Regulation (EU) No 208/2013.

The CCA explained to the audit team that they provided clear instructions to the counties about checking the fitness of seeds for sprouting. However, one of the county inspectors explained to the audit team that he considered an organic certificate for seeds sufficient as evidence for the fitness of the seeds for sprouting. This was not in line with instructions of the CCA and Regulation (EU) No 208/2013.

One of the counties granted a derogation to one sprout producer from preliminary testing of batches of seeds for sprouting, based on Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Part B of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The derogation was granted on the basis of samples that consisted of a mix of seeds from different batches. Additionally, the CCA explained to the audit team that the FBO had not been following the required monthly frequency of tests of the final product even before they had been granted this derogation. The CCA provided written evidence during the audit that the derogation was withdrawn by the county authorities and a financial penalty was imposed to the FBO for not following legal obligations rega

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: Several national measures regulate the production of dairy products in establishments availing of the flexibility possibilities provided for in EU legislation. BACKGROUND The last two audits in Poland, in order to evaluate the official controls related to, inter alia, the safety of milk and dairy products were carried out in 2008 (ref. DG(SANCO)/2008-7810) and 2013 (ref. DG(SANCO)/2013-6874). The reports of these audits are available at the following links: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=2224 https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=3268. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/620 recognises Poland as officially free from Brucella abortus, Brucella melitensis and tuberculosis. The CCA provided the following data on the dairy herds in Poland: Cattle Sheep / Goat Buff

No procedures are in place to ensure that inspectors responsible for controls of dairy establishments and holdings have adequate knowledge of the specific requirements to ensure food safety of milk and dairy products. A training system is in place for the officials but no specific training has been organised and provided centrally in recent years in relation to the specific requirements and particularities of the dairy sector. This could have an impact on the level of competence of staff responsible for official controls of the dairy sector.

According to the CCA, during the periodic controls, the general hygiene requirements for holdings are documented on the basis of checklists drawn up at local level. The audit team saw some examples of inspections reports in which these requirements were covered. The CCA also provided general data on the non-conformities detected annually at national level. However, no such checklists were used by the DVIs assessed by the audit team.

The results of raw milk sampling and testing from the dairy companies and MCCs were not available on the dairy holdings and were not included in the documentation assessed by the official inspectors during their controls. The audit team was informed that farmers usually only receive the results as text messages to their mobile phones.

In relation to the controls on milk traceability, there is not a formal requirement for the farmer to keep data on the fate of raw milk that is not in 14 compliance with the raw milk criteria and therefore cannot be placed in the market (e.g. due to residues of antibiotics). In the case examined by the audit team it was stated by the DVI interviewed that a farmer's oral declaration, on the actions taken in relation to non-compliant milk, is sufficient.

According to the CVO Instructions, the DVOs have to assess the operation of the raw milk laboratories used by the FBOs for raw milk analysis during their official controls6. However, there were no guidelines available to the DVOs, detailing, for example, the standards against which they assess the laboratory procedures or the laboratory methods used. The practical value of the instruction is thus limited and the understanding of the DVI inspectors interviewed by the audit team on the relevant requirements and the necessary controls to be carried out was insufficient. The guidelines do not cover coagulase positive Staphylococci and not all regions have a policy to test such samples in line with the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The constitutional structure of Finland allows the local CAs to operate with very substantial autonomy. The central and regional CAs have no enforcement powers over the local CAs in relation to controls on dairy hygiene and the CCA have very limited oversight to verify the effectiveness, consistency and uniformity of the official controls.

At the time of the audit, the central and regional CAs had restricted access to the main control database VATI intended to support the controls system. Limited training has been organised for the local CAs on its use. The official controls are further hampered by the complexity, and difficulties in use, of IT applications and databases and problems related to transfer of dairy holding control data from old databases, which impairs the reliability of the data5.

The Finnish constitution enables the local CAs, which are the main implementing authorities with regard to food safety, to operate with very substantial autonomy. According to Article 32 of the Food Act they must carry out food controls within their territory as provided for in the Act and submit notifications and reports to the regional CAs and CCA in accordance with the food regulations. Furthermore, they are to advise FBOs and consumers and provide information on matters covered by the Food Act.

Although evidence of flows of information from top-down and vice versa between the central, regional and local CAs was provided to the audit team, the change of IT tools has resulted in gaps of information flows (see paragraph 32). At the time of the audit the FA had crude data available on the official controls carried out at national level and the percentage of performance (Oivahymy) scores given during dairy inspections. However, they had no real-time information readily available on the planned official controls and sampling of the local CAs that could be used for national planning of the official controls.

The CAs involved in food safety and veterinary controls use several IT tools for data input and to support planning and analysis of different activities and new information systems have been developed in recent years. At the time of the audit the new IT system VATI (keskitetty valvontatietojärjestelmä) had been introduced. The central, regional and local CAs have, dependent on the IT tool, different access rights: KUTI (kunnallinen tietojärjestelmä) was used in 2013-2018 to enable the regional and central CAs to collect and browse information on controls of establishments and holdings (on holdings only since 2016) from three different IT tools used by different municipalities. label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on milk and production holdings
paragraph_text: The official controls on dairy hygiene cover the topics listed in the CCA's guidelines. Based on the reports seen and discussions with the inspectors the grading of shortcomings and the use of emoticons is not strictly in line with the guidelines - a more lenient approach is followed. The system is further weakened by not reaching the annual inspection targets and by the fact that the results in VATI are not necessarily reliable.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation of official controls
paragraph_text: Based on the interviews of the CAs and documentary review, evidence was available that the dairy inspectors do not apply the scoring system as rigorously and in line with the guidance document and are hesitating to use enforcement measures. The operation in practice of the emoticon and scoring system intended to provide public information about the level of compliance of establishments resulted, at least in a number of the files reviewed, in an inaccurate reflection of that level of compliance. Furthermore, the annual inspection targets are not reached for all dairy establishments. 5.7 OFFICIAL SAMPLING PROGRAMMES AND LABORATORIES Legal requirements Articles 5(d), 14(g) and (h), 34, 37, 38,

At national level, the annual target of inspecting 20 % of dairy holdings was not reached in 2018-2020. For example, one of the regional CAs interviewed reported that 10% of the dairy holdings were inspected in 2019.

In the regions examined by the audit team, some local CAs had not reached their annual inspection targets for dairy holdings and some local CAs had not carried out any inspections within a year. The authorities had carried out 13 inspections in 2019, none in 2020 and so far 6 in 2021. Nearly all raw milk in the country is collected by 36 operators, which were all registered by the COKZ until 2020. In 2020, the COKZ requested such operators with storage facilities to apply for approval as milk collection centres, in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Four FBOs applied, of which one was approved in 2020, one received a conditional approval in September 2021 and one is still active without an approval. The fourth contacted operator did not need a specific approval because it is using the storage facilities of another operator.

One of the milk collection centres moved to new premises in 2021 and had applied for an approval, which was granted one month after the inspection by the COKZ official as a final approval. No information was collected by COKZ to ascertain that no activities related to storage of milk had been carried out in the interim period, taking into account the same activity carried out by the FBO at its previous location (collection and storage of raw milk to deliver milk in specific quantities and quality according to client specifications).

The audit team noted that the validity of conditional approval is generally extended to the maximum of 6 months without a follow-up inspection being carried out at the end of the first 3-month period, as required by Article 148(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In some cases, the conditional approval of the FBO was retained for more than 6 months (in one case for 18 months).

Visits by COKZ inspectors on FBOs seeking approval were documented. However, the inspection reports did not mention this specific scope of the inspection, nor the final assessment of the inspector in relation to the approval.

The system of official controls covers the entire dairy sector and is based on procedures and instructions aimed at ensuring consistency and uniformity of official controls. label_heading: Conclusions on system of supervision and internal audits
paragraph_text: Audits on delegated authorities are performed regularly, although not sufficiently in identifying all relevant shortcomings and enforcing the correction of the ones identified, as the recommendations of the audit reports had not or not comprehensively been addressed and followed-up.

The NVWA performs annual audits at COKZ to test the performance of the delegated tasks, in line with the requirements of Article 33(a) of the OCR; this is also laid down in the Working Agreement between NVWA and COKZ. Three NVWA audits to COKZ were carried out in the period 2018-2020: the audits in 2018 and 2019 have been completed, whilst the 2020 audit was performed as a remote assessment of the follow-up of audit recommendations made in the 2018 and 2019 reports, due to the restrictions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The report of 2018 made 16 recommendations to COKZ, among which the following are considered relevant for the sector being audited: · re-inspections to be timely carried ou

The audit team noted that the conclusions of the follow-up of the previous NVWA audits were in contrast with the finding of the DG Health and Food Safety audit as the recommendations of the previous NVWA audits were although the effectiveness of the measures adopted by COKZ had not been fully comprehensive. Moreover, serious non- compliances with regard to approval procedures were not taken into account.

paragraph_text: Italy has issued national and regional legislation and guidelines necessary to ensure implementation and/or enforcement of the EU requirements applicable to the bovine meat sector and, from a summary analysis, they are largely in line with EU legislation. However, certain procedures/guidelines were not up-to-date and, as a result, contrary to certain provisions in the EU legislation. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 6, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. label_heading: Conclusion on recommendation No 1 of the beef audit
paragraph_text: The actions, provided in the AP for addressing Recommendation No 1, have not been implemented. On the contrary, the reduction of the staff in the CAs leads to a further reduction of the supervision over the official controls at different levels and, in particular the supervision over a now substantially increased number of AVs. This further compromises assurances about the correct and effective implementation of official controls. 5.2 RECOMMENDATION NO 2 OF THE BEEF AND POULTRY AUDITS "To ensure impartiality, quality and consistency of the official controls and that staff carrying out official controls, including authorised veterinarians, are free from any conflict of interest, as required b

The draft Act, announced in the AP, has been suspended due to the high financial impact of the project. This Act was to include: · further wage increases for official staff in the CAs; · an increase in the number of official veterinarians (OVs) supervising slaughterhouses; · additional increases in the number of staff at the level of DVIs (i.e. aimed at increasing district veterinary officers' (DVOs) supervision capacity of official controls carried out by authorised veterinarians (AVs)).

The CCA provided data that shows that the number of AVs has increased considerably since the beef audit (from around 3 300 AVs in 2019 to 5 800 in 2021), while the number of official staff in the CAs has decreased slightly.

The audit team found evidence demonstrating the importance of the supervisory role of the CAs (see paragraph 6 on targeted controls on the AVs' performance and paragraphs 43, 57 and 58 on DVOs' inspections and GVI's audits carried out in some poultry slaughterhouses). label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: FSAI and DAFM have mechanisms in place to ensure that EU provisions are subject to official controls and enforced at national level. However, delays occur in making the changes in national rules required to bring them into full compliance with EU legislation, which may affect controls over, and enforcement of, requirements applicable to FBOs and, as established during this audit, the correct and timely implementation of EU requirements in respect of CA controls.

The overall operational control framework in LA does not match that of DAFM, either in terms of available resources, training of staff (while performing equivalent (OV) duties), arrangements to avoid/address possible conflict of interest, or supervision of the performance of controls. The considerable differences between the two CAs in respect of the above are detrimental to ensuring consistent official controls over, and enforcement in, the same type of establishments, including of comparable sizes. This results in diverging outcomes of DAFM and LA controls over equally applicable EU requirements, and inadequacies in the LA controls of such establishments.

A number of the above issues have been identified and recognised by the FSAI, which has made proposals aimed at addressing the challenges at LA level and the future delivery of LA controls. The absence of decisions in this respect at the time of the audit impacts on the country's ability to arrive at, and ensure, consistency between DAFM and LA official controls and enforcement of the same legal framework. 5.3 APPROVAL OF ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 11 Articles 10(2), 138(2)(j) and 148 of the OCR. AMI of bovine animals on the holding of provenance, for reasons other than emergency slaughter, is carried out by private veterinary practitioners, not by OVs. When it takes place, the system for emergency slaughter is used (see paragraphs 93 and 94). No arrangements are in place to give effect to the requirements of Chapter VIa of Section I, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, and the provision of Article 31(c) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2235 in respect of the model certificate to be used for such slaughter, is not implemented.

Nonetheless, the procedures require the private veterinarian (not an OV) to carry out the AMI at the holding of provenance. This is not in line with Article 5(2)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. DAFM has not yet assigned OVs for this task, and LA veterinarians are not legally authorised to access farms. If the AMI is favourable, the private veterinarian or slaughterhouse staff holding the required certificate of competence, performs the emergency slaughter. 18

The official certificate for emergency slaughter used nationally differs from the model set out in Chapter 5 of Annex IV \ to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2235, as do the arrangements in place. For example, the signing veterinarian is not an OV, and is neither required to declare the date and time of slaughter, nor that the slaughter and bleeding were carried out correctly. label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The AMI and PMI at slaughterhouse level are organised to cover the relevant elements for bovine slaughter (including of cull cows) and poultry. Some long-term arrangements that do not allow adequate performance of AMI and PMI had been accepted by the LAs, with divergent DAFM and LA assessments of the same arrangements.

In DAFM plants, TAOs perform certain tasks that, according to Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 are tasks of an OA. For example, verification of FCI, identification checks, and some welfare checks. They inform the TVI/VI of their findings. Nonetheless, contrary to the requirements of the same Article; · the OV does not regularly verify that TAOs carry out their practical tasks properly. TAOs' work is supervised by SAOs. DAFM does not consider TAOs to be OAs for the purpose of AMI; · TAOs perform the practical tasks for all bovine animals (e.g. including those from herds that have not been declared officially free of tuberculosis).

The DAFM TVIs and VIs interviewed were aware of the relevant requirements for AMI and PMI of bovine animals and of the decisions to be taken, including for findings that are more frequently seen in cull cows. In two of the LA plants, the LA TVIs were not available to be interviewed by the audit team. The reports of the DAFM visits in one of these plants noted, amongst other, inadequate arrangements to conduct AMI, due to difficult access to the limited sized lairage pens, with the FBO reading the animal tags in the trailers. The LAVI had repeatedly highlighted inadequate lairage facilities for AMI as 15 an issue, which is also mentioned in the FSAI-LA reports and corrective action requests.

LA procedures describe the identification requirements and checks that are to be carried out by the TVI/VI. Animals must be accompanied by the movement permission issued by AIM (ER 106 form). Carcases are not health-marked if this form is missing. TVIs check whether ear tags match the ER 106 form, in 5% of the animals. TVIs have no access to the database, although LA staff may have. There is no LA procedure for TVIs/LAVIs to deal with identification issues.

In DAFM plants, TAOs check the FCI and record the results on the AMI record used by the TVI. In LA plants, TVIs carry out FCI checks. The report of a DAFM visit in one of the LA plants mentions that the FBO was not aware of her/his role in checking the FCI prior to presentation of the animals for AMI. This (longstanding) non-compliance had not been previously identified by the LAs.

DAFM has procedures in place to arrange for sampling for residues when AMI and/or PMI findings lead TVI to suspect breaches of legislation on chemical residues or contaminants. This did not happen in the LA examined by the audit team, as the LA TVIs are not authorised to take samples and the LAVI, authorised to take samples, may not be available to do so. AMI procedures for poultry

The TVI may contact the LAVI to carry out controls and sample detained carcases (e.g. for Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) testing, detection of tuberculosis lesions); some exchanges in this regard were presented to the audit team. However, as regards residues sampling, this did not happen in one of the LA interviewed, and which attributed this to the LAVI not being present (TVIs are not authorised to take samples for residues). Under the circumstance, the LA did not fully apply the requirements of Article 14(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 on laboratory testing for reaching a definitive diagnosis of a suspected hazard or detecting the presence of chemical residues.

That enforcement action, initiated in 2020, was not fully effective: the report of a visit by DAFM in the same plant in 2021 still identified issues preventing PMI to be performed correctly (final carcase inspection in congested chiller without access to higher parts, livers discarded and gastro-intestinal tract removed before being presented for PMI). 17

In another LA plant, the DAFM report also noted, amongst others, "very significant concerns" linked to PMI: unsatisfactory facilities for inspection of offal - no dedicated inspection point on red offal rail, not all red offal presented for inspection, no knife steriliser for the TVI; TVI attempting to conduct inspection under conditions giving rise to health and safety concerns.

The LAVIs for these plants clarified that in the first plant the DAFM findings had been addressed, while in the second the LAVI considered that, notwithstanding the challenging conditions, all aspects of PMI were compliant. The FBO of this plant had presented plans for construction (halted due to COVID-19 restrictions) with a view to, amongst others, increase space for red and green offal handling and inspection. PMI procedures for poultry

There is a system in place aimed at granting approval to establishments in line with the EU requirements. Although both CAs follow the procedures in place, there are significant differences in the outcomes of DAFM and LAVS assessments of compliance with the approval conditions, in the same establishments. This highlights a lack of consistency between DAFM and LA controls but also, and taken together with the FSAI's own findings, that the LA cannot consistently ensure that the approval of establishments is adequately kept under review. In one case reviewed, this resulted in an establishment continuing to operate under LA supervision for years although deemed non-compliant by DAFM, and under w

Both DAFM VIs and LAVIs are required to keep the approval of establishments under review. Examples of addition or removal of approved activities from the list following CA controls were made available to the audit team. However, the two medium size bovine slaughterhouses under the supervision of the LAs and reviewed by the audit team received DAFM visits in the context of (possible) transfer of official controls requested by the LAs based on their increasing throughput: · The DAFM report, following the visit in one of these establishments, raised very significant concerns in relation to the plant's capacity (slaughter line inadequate for current throughput, see paragraph 98). This was also t

DAFM has the overall organisation, resources, overall training of staff, as well supervision mechanisms in place to ensure that official controls in establishments under its remit are carried out consistently and in line with EU legislation, and that corrective actions are taken when needed. Nonetheless, DAFM does not supervise the animal welfare controls in establishments under LA supervision, which undermines its ability to perform effectively its task of ensuring consistency and effectiveness of animal welfare controls. In respect of ensuring absence of conflict of interest on the part of TVI, the arrangements are more robust in poultry and certain export establishments, than in other est

The overall operational control framework in LA does not match that of DAFM, either in terms of available resources, training of staff (while performing equivalent (OV) duties), arrangements to avoid/address possible conflict of interest, or supervision of the performance of controls. The considerable differences between the two CAs in respect of the above are detrimental to ensuring consistent official controls over, and enforcement in, the same type of establishments, including of comparable sizes. This results in diverging outcomes of DAFM and LA controls over equally applicable EU requirements, and inadequacies in the LA controls of such establishments.

The delays in effectively using the existing FSAI coordination mechanisms and in CAs decision-making undermine the (effective) implementation of a number of horizontal EU requirements notably at LA level, such as the designation for certain official tasks and related derogation conditions, training requirements for staff involved in official controls, and safeguarding conflict of interest, which are of particular relevance for LA controls and the associated findings of this audit.

A number of the above issues have been identified and recognised by the FSAI, which has made proposals aimed at addressing the challenges at LA level and the future delivery of LA controls. The absence of decisions in this respect at the time of the audit impacts on the country's ability to arrive at, and ensure, consistency between DAFM and LA official controls and enforcement of the same legal framework. 5.3 APPROVAL OF ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 11 Articles 10(2), 138(2)(j) and 148 of the OCR. Findings

There is a system in place aimed at granting approval to establishments in line with the EU requirements. Although both CAs follow the procedures in place, there are significant differences in the outcomes of DAFM and LAVS assessments of compliance with the approval conditions, in the same establishments. This highlights a lack of consistency between DAFM and LA controls but also, and taken together with the FSAI's own findings, that the LA cannot consistently ensure that the approval of establishments is adequately kept under review. In one case reviewed, this resulted in an establishment continuing to operate under LA supervision for years although deemed non-compliant by DAFM, and under w

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Animal welfare requirements at slaughter and during transport are enforced, but to a lesser extent in slaughterhouses under LA supervision. There is a lack of consistency between the DAFM and LA controls (and between controls in LAs) over animal welfare, and a lack of supervision by DAFM over these controls at LA level, but also in respect of FBOs' compliance with hygiene and ABP rules. The effectiveness of LA controls had not been adequately ensured in the LAs under review, as highlighted by the shortcomings identified in the organisation and operation of LA controls both during this audit and by the FSAI.

At central level, in brief: · The FSAI delivers its overall responsibility for the enforcement of food safety legislation on the production chain of bovine meat (after primary production), through service contracts with DAFM and LAs. It is also responsible for co-ordinating control activities between DAFM and LAs, and for ensuring consistent performance of controls; · DAFM is responsible for developing policy and legislation, as well as implementing EU rules in national law. It is also responsible for official controls in medium and large bovine and poultry slaughterhouses, delivered through its regional and local staff; · FSAI responsibilities do not cover animal health and animal welfare c

There is no regional or central structure for LAs. Some LAVS perform official controls in more than one county. In most cases, one person per county/group of counties is in 5 charge of the official controls as the CA (see also paragraph 42). Official controls in bovine and poultry slaughterhouses are implemented by 24 LAVS, under service contracts with FSAI. The Local Authority Veterinary Inspectors (LAVIs), employed to perform OV duties, are not required to be present during slaughter. They carry out audits and inspections of the FBO as well as oversight over TVIs. The TVIs carry out the AMI and PMI.

At the time of the audit, discussions on points i. to iii. remained inconclusive and, as a result, outstanding issues related to these points had not been addressed. 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest

The audit found that differences in the staffing levels of DAFM compared to LAs are maintained when plants under LA supervision grow to sizes comparable to those of plants under DAFM supervision. In two comparable facilities, DAFM availed of a permanently present VI, three TVIs, a TAO and visiting SAO and RSVI, while the LA employed two TVIs and a visiting LAVI. The last internal audit (see paragraph 37) of this LA identified a lack of sufficient manpower to carry out all necessary official controls.

The same LA audit report highlighted that controls, other than AMI, PMI and sampling, were carried out on a reactive rather than a proactive basis, and concluded that, due to the lack of a strategic approach and sufficient manpower, controls in line with the requirements were not necessarily ensured. At the time of the current audit, one LAVI continued to carry out all the veterinary controls in the LA, except AMI and PMI.

Although the CAs mentioned resource constraints linked to Brexit and the COVID-19 pandemic, the overall figures for controls in establishments in the scope of this audit suggest that the planned controls were largely implemented in the past 2 years; sometimes, additional controls were carried out. LAs reviewed by the audit team attributed the current audit's findings on the lack of consistency and in some cases of the effectiveness of controls, to resource issues. 7

The official control staff interviewed during this audit indicated an overall adequate understanding of their responsibilities, according to the procedures in place, and of the legal requirements on the topics on which they were questioned. Nonetheless, reports following FSAI and DAFM visits in LA plants indicate that certain non-compliances went undetected or that certain requirements were not adequately enforced (see paragraphs 72, 77, 87, 88, 97 to 100 and 109 to 112). 5.2.5 Supervision and Audits

The work of LAVIs is not routinely supervised. LAs' internal audits by another LA - meant to cover all areas of activity under the OCR within a five-year cycle - are peer- review exercises, given that each LA is considered a CA. There are significant differences between the reports produced by different LAs, which suggests that the approach is not standardised. The FSAI highlighted that there is ongoing work to harmonise the approach of the internal audits performed by LAVS.

The FSAI carries out audits of the official controls carried out by DAFM and LAs, as well as targeted audits on selected topics. The overview of FSAI audits of LAs' official controls indicates that, on average, LAs received one official control audit in the past 10 years, with some receiving 2 audits, and some none. In addition, some LAs participated in joint compliance reviews with FSAI, and/or received targeted audits.

FSAI's most recent audits on topics relevant for the scope of this audit were: on traceability and controls thereof (in 2016 and 2017); on LAs' controls over FBOs' implementation of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (in 2019, 2016 and 2015); on DAFM controls of approved poultry slaughterhouses, and on 2 LAs' controls over on- farm emergency slaughter (2013).

The FSAI, based on the outcome of its own audits, FSAI joint compliance reviews, LA inspections, as well as DG Health and Food Safety audits, raised concerns about the consistency and effectiveness of official controls at some LAVS-supervised establishments with the County and City Management Association (representing the Chief Executives of the LAs) in 2019.

It highlighted instances of: a) incorrect application of approval procedures (establishments being approved which should not be); b) non-compliances not being detected; c) regulatory responses being insufficient to secure compliance; d) official controls not in line with the SOPs developed by the LAVS with FSAI support, nor with the requirements of the service contracts or EU legislation on official controls. 9

In 2020, FSAI suggested that structural changes to the system could be key to improving the service, and to render it more robust and consistent in its enforcement activity. It also identified other actions, including changes to the service contract. In 2021, FSAI made a submission on LAVS reforms that it deems necessary, highlighting limitations in the efficiency/effectiveness of LAs oversight of slaughterhouses and cutting plants: · no LA veterinary technical supervision of the work of LAVI in most cases, affecting the LA's ability to verify correct and effective delivery of the controls (illustrated by examples of non-compliances gone undetected or not met with an adequate response, and o
At the time of this audit, no definitive policy decisions on the future delivery of official controls by LAs or the proposals made by the FSAI had yet been taken.

FSAI audits and support mechanisms do not cover animal welfare or animal health. DAFM established a Liaison Committee with the LAVS to discuss animal welfare and animal health control aspects, but its activities do not ensure supervision of the LA controls over animal health and welfare. DAFM controls in LA plants and one of the two LA internal audit reports reviewed by the audit team found ineffective welfare controls (see paragraphs 109-112). 5.2.6 Actions in case of non-compliance

Both DAFM and LAs interviewed by the audit team provided examples of different enforcement actions taken in case of non-compliances. Nonetheless, when DAFM visited slaughterhouses under LA supervision - in the context of possible transfer of control responsibilities from LA to DAFM - the outcome was significantly different (see paragraph 56). The non-compliances identified by DAFM had either not been previously identified by LAs, or their correction not effectively enforced to prevent their reoccurrence (see paragraphs 5, 72, 77, 87, 88, 97-100 and 109-112). While the LAs acted upon most of the non-compliances identified by DAFM, they did not fully agree with all DAFM findings. 10 Conclusion

Both DAFM VIs and LAVIs are required to keep the approval of establishments under review. Examples of addition or removal of approved activities from the list following CA controls were made available to the audit team. However, the two medium size bovine slaughterhouses under the supervision of the LAs and reviewed by the audit team received DAFM visits in the context of (possible) transfer of official controls requested by the LAs based on their increasing throughput: · The DAFM report, following the visit in one of these establishments, raised very significant concerns in relation to the plant's capacity (slaughter line inadequate for current throughput, see paragraph 98). This was also t
DAFM visits concluded that one of these establishments did not comply with DAFM standards, and that the other one did not comply with the approval conditions under S.I. 22/2020. 12

DAFM explained its policy of requiring that non-compliances have been addressed at the time of approval, and prior to it taking over the official controls. Consequently, a transfer to DAFM may take as long as it takes for DAFM to deem an establishment to meet the approval standards: in one establishment, the transfer had not yet taken place despite repeated LA requests, since 2015. FSAI intends to address the transfer to DAFM of LA establishments exceeding the throughputs for which they were originally approved, in a Guidance Note.

Although the outcome of follow-up visits by the LAVI following the enforcement actions was considered satisfactory, a DAFM visit which took place some months later identified, amongst others, certain similar hygiene issues as well as inadequate handling of specified risk material. This suggests that, at least for some of the breaches, the corrective actions were not sufficiently effective, although deemed satisfactory by the LAVI.

In the other LA plant, the DAFM report identified issues which it deemed to be of very significant concern, amongst others in relation to/stemming from the daily numbers permitted by the LA for slaughter, for which the slaughter line and associated ancillary areas were not designed. The FBO had presented plans for extending the slaughter-line cutting capacity but, pending their completion, throughputs had not been affected.

The DAFM report also identified shortcomings not previously noted by the LAs, e.g. contamination of green offal (used for petfood - Category 3 ABP) with washings from the carcases splitting saw (Category 1 ABP); lack of changing facilities, and use of mobile toilets at the external perimeter of the premises for staff use, without adjacent hand- washing facilities.

The LAVIs reported to have taken the required action and that most of the findings reported by DAFM had been solved, including in relation to the procedures for dealing with ABP. Nonetheless, the gravity of some of these findings and their recurring character suggest that LA controls and enforcement in these plants had not been sufficiently effective.

DAFM started to enforce welfare during transport directly with the transporter at slaughterhouse level in 2019, but the VIs' approach was not yet uniform. One of the VIs interviewed and his RSVI were not aware of this DAFM approach and raised welfare 20 issues related to transport with the slaughterhouse operator, while the VI in another DAFM plant initiated enforcement action against the transporter. However, DAFM did not check whether the same transporter had been associated with non-compliances identified in other slaughterhouses when deciding whether a non-compliance was not repeated.

While in DAFM plants official controls staff may be present at the time of unloading and are present at the time of slaughter, this is not a requirement in most LAs. In practice, the TVIs may come to perform AMI, leave for other private tasks and return to perform delayed PMI. LAs did not report any animal welfare issues in the last 2 years. In the two LAs under review, the LAVI last notified DAFM in 2018 regarding an animal welfare incident during transport.

In one of the two LA slaughterhouses for which animal welfare controls were assessed, the LAVI had used the animal welfare checklists on an annual basis and, although certain non-compliances (e.g. no FBO checks of absence of life before dressing) were identified, the outcome of these controls was considered satisfactory. Nonetheless, when DAFM visited the same establishment, it identified animal welfare breaches which it deemed to warrant suspension of the FBOs' licence to slaughter. The LA acted upon these findings, took enforcement action and followed up the measures put in place by the FBO.

Following this incident, the LA requested DAFM to perform a dedicated animal welfare audit in the same establishment. The DAFM visit found, amongst other deficiencies, no evidence of monitoring/verification of the process of sticking/bleeding; a continued, considerable risk that head removal would commence before the animal's death (as noted in the previous DAFM visit); that the Animal Welfare Officer did not hold a certificate of competence; that the SOPs on animal intake and welfare from unloading to death did not adequately describe the process; and that the kill box and race were not fit for purpose.

Following the DAFM audit, the LA issued an improvement notice, followed by a suspension of the approval to slaughter given the FBO's inadequate progress. Nonetheless, in this case the LA's ability to identify and/or adequately assess the gravity of welfare non-compliances and to effectively enforce the relevant animal welfare requirements, was seriously called into question.

In the other slaughterhouse under LA supervision, the last report of an internal LA audit identified "significant weaknesses in the operating procedures of the slaughterhouse, particularly with regard to the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009" which had not been detected by the controls. The VI acted upon these findings. Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls

Officials on the ground have support/legal powers to perform the controls and, more importantly, to enforce the relevant legal requirements. However, regarding transporters, who are considered as primarily responsible for animals unfit for transport, current limitations in national legislation hinder proper enforcement. 5.3 APPROVAL OF ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6(3) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council.
