label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There are procedures and guidelines in place for official staff for the relevant controls, which include guidance on how to act in different scenarios with regard to the handling of animals unfit for transport. Yet, the non-existence of emergency slaughters at farm level, combined with the findings regarding the condition of some animals arriving at slaughterhouses, implies that bovine animals are transported to the slaughterhouse irrespective of their fitness for transport. Official controls at slaughterhouses identify animals unfit for transport, however, as those animals have already been certified by the local DVMs , no further investigation is carried out nor any enforcement implemented

Transporters are considered primarily accountable in the case of animals unfit for transport. However, due to limitations in the national legislation in relation to imposing and receiving payments of administrative fines, (the fines must be imposed and paid on- the-spot) no administrative sanctions have been imposed to date. The CCA is currently working on an amendment of this legislation. Conclusions on competent authorities

Movement declarations were also granted for animals that were unfit for transport (see paragraph 75); even though the existing procedures clearly indicate that such animals should not be transported (see paragraph 97). Once the local DVM's OVs have issued the 12 movement declaration, OVs at slaughterhouses accept the animals without questioning their fitness for transport.

None of the OVs in the 3 slaughterhouses mentioned identifying cases of bovine animals that were considered as unfit of transport and should have been slaughtered at farm. It should be noted that the movement declaration contains a specific clause that explicitly mentions that animals covered by the movement declaration are fit for transport, in line with Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

Even though the local DVM's OVs responsible for issuing the movement declaration would indicate on the document that the animal(s) listed is/are destined for emergency slaughter (the reason of injury was not always indicated), the ante-mortem records rarely indicated any issues with the animals concerned. Similarly, there was no reference made to this in the accompanying FCI documents.

By examining the available records the audit team observed the following: · There is no consistency in the way that the OVs at the slaughterhouses classify these animals upon arrival to the slaughterhouse, in the application that they use. In several cases, although the cattle had been classified as emergency by the DVM's OV issuing the movement declaration, this was not indicated in the system nor was any further detail documented as to the reasons for the emergency, or the findings identified during the AMI (see paragraph 72). This was attributed, based on the explanations provided by the CCA, to mistakes or omissions due to workload. · Based on documents provided by the CAs and reviewed b

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Cross-checks carried out revealed significant under-reporting of events in the database, both for slaughters and deaths, which prevents reliable and timely reconciliation of the existing records; this, in turn, hinders the identification of possible non compliances.

With regard to updating the CBD, farmers have the possibility to directly enter the births of bovine animals of their holdings up to 27 days after birth (i.e. up to 20 days to ear tag new-borns and up to another 7 days to notify). If a farmer is not able to enter the information her/himself, (s)he can request the local DVM to do it. Any other changes are notified in the CBD by the local DVMs, after farmers have informed them of such. This 10 concerns movements and deaths, which need to be notified by the famers within 7 days of the actual event. Generally, as was explained by the CAs, since this is quite demanding it is possible that there can be delays by the DVMs in updating the database.

There is no integration of the database with the collection companies for dead animals. Each company may keep records of the ears tags that it collects but that information is not cross-checked with that of the CBD. This information is communicated to the RUs/DVMs.

With regard to slaughtered bovine animals, in 2019 the CCA performed cross-checks between the bovine database and a database used by slaughterhouse operators to report 11 the classification of the carcases (see paragraph 17) and identified that a number of slaughtered animals were not notified by the OVs in the CBD as having been slaughtered. Based on the information collected by the CCA, around 10% of the bovines slaughtered were not recorded in the bovine database.

The CCA attributed this to understaffing and the workload of the OVs, who, in addition to their other tasks, are also expected to enter the ear tag numbers of the animals slaughtered into the database. Based on the outcome of that cross-check, the CCA sent out a reminder letter to the RUs of their obligations to notify the CBD. A similar cross- check, to be carried out in 2020, did not materialise.

In relation to fallen bovine animals, cross-checks carried out by the audit team in one RU between CBD data and those held by the company appointed for the collection of fallen stock, revealed an underreporting of fallen animals in the CBD. 5.4.2 Official controls at establishment level (slaughterhouses) Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Articles 10 to 19, 29, 30, 33, 34 and 43 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Article 7 of Council Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. paragraph_text: The high mortality rate of cows, as indicated is another factor highlighting the need for better plausibility checks and the necessity to consider this fact in the risk assessment for the selection of the holdings to be inspected. The official controls do not cover the possible causes of the high mortality rates. 18

label_heading: Conclusion on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: The CAs have issued national legislation and guidelines necessary to ensure the implementation and/or enforcement of EU requirements applicable to the bovine meat sector. From a summary analysis, they are in line with EU legislation and mostly adequate, with the exception of those dealing with cases of bovine animals with traceability issues. 3 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 6, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Findings 5.2.1 Structure and organisation

While the audit team did not carry out a comprehensive review of these guidelines, it was noted that they cover all of the food chain and controls related to the production of beef. However, the audit team noted that the "Instruction on procedures to be followed in slaughterhouses" does not provide sufficient information for the OVs on how to act appropriately in case of bovine animals with traceability issues (e.g. lost ear tags) detected at AMI. This has a negative impact on the official controls on bovine traceability. (See also paragraphs 79 and 81).

As part of the AMI, the OV verifies the identification of animals in the bovine database (see paragraph 72). If any non-compliances are detected in relation to the traceability of animals, the OV should follow the procedures laid down in the relevant VS instruction (see paragraph 4). The audit team noted that this instruction refers to the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1053/2010, which requires that if the keeper of an animal cannot prove its identification and traceability, the CA shall, where appropriate, on the basis of an assessment of the animal health and food safety risks, order the destruction of the animal without compensation.

One of the OVs interviewed explained that where the traceability of a bovine animal is not established (e.g. lost ear tag(s)), it will be slaughtered and the carcass will be detained and tested for antibiotic residues. If the result of the analysis is negative, the meat is declared fit for human consumption. The audit team noted that these actions were the initiatives of the OV, as they are not included in the VS instruction. The audit team was provided with examples of such cases and noted that a 400 fine was imposed on the farmers in each case.

In addition, the audit team reviewed a case when a bovine animal arrived at the slaughterhouse with one ear tag. After verification of the identification of this animal in the CBD, the OV ascertained that this ear tag belonged to an animal which, according to the data in the CBD, had already been declared dead. Despite the fact that the traceability of this animal was clearly not established, its meat was released for human consumption by the OV. The CA imposed a 400 fine on the farmer. A representative from the VPHD informed the audit team that the procedure included in the instruction does not provide sufficient information to direct OVs to act appropriately in such situations and that the

Cooperation and coordination arrangements between and within the CAs involved in the controls for the areas covered by this audit are in place. The mechanisms in place (such as documented procedures and training) give the CAs a reasonable level of assurance that controls are carried out uniformly and consistently. However, the contracted OVs are not included in the CAs' training system, which could have an impact on the sustained level of competence of contracted staff responsible for official controls of the bovine sector.

The prerequisites for private veterinarians to be contracted as OVs are previous experience and training. The audit team was informed by the VPHD that the last training sessions, provided by the VS for contracted staff, were in 2019. These included, among others, training on AMI, PMI and slaughterhouse inspection. However, the audit team also noted that the contracted OVs are not included in the CA`s training plan, therefore the VS do not provide them with regular training.

The cooperation and coordination arrangements between and within the CA(s) are satisfactory for the performance of official controls and enforcement, apart from the provision of feedback information to slaughterhouse OVs that report welfare-related 10 issues to the department dealing with farms and primary production, and which in one of the ACs was not in place.

The procedures of communication regarding animal welfare issues between the Health and Agriculture departments in one of the ACs were not satisfactory, resulting in a lack of feedback from Agriculture of the impact of the actions taken by the OVs working for the Health department at slaughterhouse level. This does not allow the OVs to understand how effective their work is or, potentially, to learn from mistakes. 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest,

Both CAs have procedures to train, support and control the OVs delivering official controls on a regular basis, but neither have a specific and structured procedure for those veterinarians that work for them occasionally.

Neither of the two CAs have a specific and structured training procedure for those veterinarians that work for them occasionally, covering absences of permanent OVs. The audit found evidence of some problems related to PMI in two out of six establishments, in both ACs, where the resident OV was not present and a locum one was in charge.

Equally, private veterinarians doing AMI on farm for ES are not included in these training activities. As mentioned in paragraph 15, one of the CAs has already taken steps to resolve this. 9 5.2.5 Supervision and audits
The two ACs have a system of internal audits and checks to monitor the performance of their OVs and ensure they deliver official controls adequately.

In one of the ACs, there are no arrangements to ensure that, following the approval process, a suitably short period of time for newly approved establishments other than slaughterhouses is established in which to carry out an FBO's audit or an operational inspection.

The system for review of approvals does not currently ensure, in one of the ACs, that the establishments maintain the approval for only those activities that are relevant or that the approval conditions for activities not carried out, continue to be met. 5.4 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.4.1 Official controls on cattle identification and movements of animals Legal requirements Articles 3, 5, 6, 7, and 9a of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Findings On farm/dealer control

In one of the ACs, for establishments other than slaughterhouses, there is no set procedure to regulate when the first inspection or audit of the establishment has to take place after approval and once the activity has started. As a result, the CA might not inspect a new establishment for a long period of time and cannot assess compliance with legislation and FBO's own checks.

Both CAs have procedures to review the approval status of the establishments in their territory on a regular basis, in order to ensure that it reflects the activities that the FBO carries out. However, one of the slaughterhouses reviewed by the audit team was still approved to slaughter a species that had not been processed for the last five years. The controls did not review if this slaughterhouse still met the conditions for this species. Conclusions on approval of establishments

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The implementation of the official controls does not ensure that PMI of all carcases and offal takes place in accordance with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.
According to the OVs' explanations and descriptions of the activities, in two of the six slaughterhouses audited (one in each AC), the PMI was not carried out in accordance with the legislation.

In one of them, the OV stated to have passed as fit for human consumption the carcase of an ES bovine without having inspected the lungs and green offal, as the FBO staff did not present them for inspection.

In the other slaughterhouse, where only one veterinarian is normally present, the OV explained that they would not be able to inspect the green offal (which would go directly to the gut room) of the carcases processed during the time they would spend in the lairage for AMI reasons as the slaughtering line would not stop. Nevertheless, those carcases would be health marked and passed as fit for human consumption. This is not in line with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.
In both cases, the OVs explained that, if any doubt, the slaughterhouse staff know what is fit and unfit for human consumption and would save for them any offal with signs of being unfit.

It has to be noted that, in the second AC and in order to address the fact that the PMI was not carried out in accordance with the EU requirements, management at central level took immediate action and arranged for a second and more experienced OV to be deployed to the slaughterhouse as a support mechanism.

Also in two of the six slaughterhouses, the FBO staff carried out the removal of the spinal cord, which is classed as a specified risk material, after the carcases had been inspected and health marked as fit for human consumption. This is not in line with Article 45 (q) to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Procedures for poultry

paragraph_text: The residue monitoring plan is generally implemented in accordance with planned arrangements. However, some identified shortcomings (i.e. inconsistencies regarding announcement of sampling visits to farms, delays sending samples to laboratories, the lack of supervision from the central and regional competent authorities to ensure that sampling in aquaculture takes place at all stages of production and, for other commodities, that repeated sampling of the same producer is avoided), cumulatively have a negative bearing on the effectiveness of official controls on residues. 5.4. Nevertheless, while instructions stated, in line with the requirements (15), that sampling visits should be unannounced, in some situations sampling staff were obliged to announce visits for practical reasons (e.g. to ensure farmers were present and that livestock could be restrained for sampling). In these cases, in the absence of specific instructions on how to make such announcements, practices among the staff met by the audit team varied. Notwithstanding the fact that all of the laboratories are duly accredited, operate methods included in their respective scopes of accreditation and that the laboratories' performance in proficiency tests has been generally satisfactory, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods and in the implementation of internal quality control procedures, combined with the absence of designation of sub-contracted laboratories and lack of temperature controls on incoming samples, weaken confidence in the reliability of analytical results and thus the effectiveness of the residue control system. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION In general, arrangements in place in Estonia for planning, implementation and f

Pending dispatch to the laboratory, samples can be stored in fridges or freezers, depending on the matrix and analyte concerned, under the control of the official sampler. Interviewed officials indicated that samples taken at slaughterhouses were sometimes be placed into the transportation boxes without preceding chilling/freezing.

National instructions do not specify any time limit between sampling and sample dispatch to the laboratory and, at the time of the audit, the time taken between sampling and dispatch was not actively monitoring by the AFB or Regional Specialists. Data requested by the audit team showed that, although most samples arrived at the laboratories on the day of sampling or one to two days afterwards, in some cases the time between sampling was much longer (up to 42 days). The AFB immediately responded to this new information, identified the main source of the delays and put in place corrective action.

The audit team checked the acceptance/rejection system for incoming samples by the three national laboratories and saw that this generally addressed control of the accompanying documentation, checks of the seals and general condition of the samples. Temperature of the samples at the time of reception was not controlled in any of the laboratories thus the provisions established by EU legislation (25) to ensure the samples' legal, scientific and technical validity were not fully addressed. During the audit, representatives of two national laboratories stated that temperature control of all incoming samples would commence from 1 October 2021 and that a pertinent quality control document was und

For aquaculture, instructions indicate that for samples to be analysed for group A substances, juvenile fish should also be sampled. The degree to which this instruction is followed was not actively verified by the AFB or Regional Specialists, and it was therefore not possible to verify the extent to which all stages of production were covered by the residue monitoring sampling.

Notwithstanding the fact that all of the laboratories are duly accredited, operate methods included in their respective scopes of accreditation and that the laboratories' performance in proficiency tests has been generally satisfactory, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods and in the implementation of internal quality control procedures, combined with the absence of designation of sub-contracted laboratories and lack of temperature controls on incoming samples, weaken confidence in the reliability of analytical results and thus the effectiveness of the residue control system. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION In general, arrangements in place in Estonia for planning, implementation and f

The audit team noted that the designation of the national official laboratories was in line with the requirements of EU legislation (22). Contrary to that, none of the three laboratories located in other EU Member States was designated as an official laboratory by the Estonian central competent authority.

Notwithstanding the fact that all of the laboratories are duly accredited, operate methods included in their respective scopes of accreditation and that the laboratories' performance in proficiency tests has been generally satisfactory, deficiencies in the validation of analytical methods and in the implementation of internal quality control procedures, combined with the absence of designation of sub-contracted laboratories and lack of temperature controls on incoming samples, weaken confidence in the reliability of analytical results and thus the effectiveness of the residue control system. 6. The screening method for aminoglycosides in muscle was initially validated as a confirmatory method in line with pertinent EU requirements (26). However, due to consistently and unacceptably high reproducibility levels, the conclusion stated that the method would be used only as a semi-quantitative screening method. The audit team noted that no further elaboration/evidence was provided in a documented traceable manner to demonstrate that the method had a false compliant rate lower than or equal to 5 % ( error) (27).

The screening method for antibacterial agents in kidney was verified in line with applicable EU provisions (28). However, the documentation submitted for the screening method for antibacterial substances in milk suggested that only 12 samples (per concentration) were used for the verification, which did not correspond to the minimum number of 20 samples required to ensure that the method had a false compliant rate lower than or equal to 5 % ( error) (27).

The documentation submitted regarding the method for hormones in urine and serum demonstrated that the repeatability and reproducibility values were consistently identical which is not in line with EU requirements (29). These phenomena were not commented on or discussed in the validation report and the method was considered fit for purpose as a confirmatory method. The situation with non-commented identical repeatability and reproducibility values was seen for certain fortification levels in several other validation files scrutinised by the audit team, questioning the validity of the laboratory's conclusion that said methods were fit for their intended use.

The audit team noted numerous occasions where recovery or/and reproducibility values exceeded the ranges established in the EU legislation (30), e.g. for diclazuril and salinomycin in the coccidiostats confirmatory method. These occurrences were largely not evaluated/discussed in the validation files and consequently not taken into account for the decisions on methods' fitness for purpose.

The audit team noted that in all of the validation files scrutinised, stability was mentioned as a performance characteristic. However, the procedure for its assessment was substantially different from the protocol suggested in EU law (31) and essentially not adequate to provide sufficient knowledge on the stability of analytes, in particular in matrix. Combined with the absence of a temperature check on the incoming samples (see finding 51), this might influence the test results. The audit team scrutinised the implementation of internal quality controls for four samples (analysed in 2020-2021 by the largest national laboratory) where measurable quantities of veterinary medicinal products were found. In two of the four samples (diclofenac in bovine muscle and antibacterial substances in raw milk, both from 2020), the audit team observed that no matrix-based `positive control' samples were included in the analytical runs, which is not fully in line with EU requirements (33). The laboratory representative explained that this was due to absence of pertinent control samples and that this practice was discontinued since the beginning of 2021.

The audit team observed the control charts for the methods used for the four samples scrutinised and found that: a. in the control chart for penicillin V, the trueness based on results of more than 30 analytical runs was 184%, which substantially exceeds the range established in EU law (80-120%) (34). While the laboratory representative was aware about that breach, no action had been taken to address the situation. b. for the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs method, very few points were available due to the low number of analytical series (since the relevant samples are collected during a narrow time window to ensure that the laboratory processes those in one go). This precluded the cre

For the screening method for antibacterial substances in milk, no sufficient evidence was submitted that quality control samples had been regularly used for the purpose of verifying ongoing method performance, which contradicts pertinent EU requirements (33).

For the same method, the audit team noted that once a suspect non-compliant result was identified, the same sample was run up to three times more before a decision was made to confirm the screened positive result with a chemical confirmatory method. This practice may lead to the situation where non-compliant results would not be identified due to false-compliant outcome of screening testing, is not in line with legal requirements (27), and contradicts the bioassay manual.

All laboratories are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025 and overall, have systems in place to ensure their effective performance and the reliability of analytical results. Methods are generally appropriately validated, however shortcomings were identified concerning the sensitivity and scope of validation of some methods with respect to EU requirements. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION The planning and implementation of residue monitoring in Germany is effective, underpinned by a well-functioning competent authority, comprehensive follow-up investigations and notwithstanding some shortcomings concerning method validation in one laboratory, a well-performing laboratory network. 7. The system in place for collection, use and disposal of ABP and DP is largely adequate. For ABP derived from some species (fish, horses), the entire territory of Finland has been defined as a `remote area'. However, such designation is not justified since operational means of collection, disposal and use of ABP are available throughout the entire country. In practice, despite the absence of a risk assessment carried out by the competent authority, the impact of this shortcoming is probably limited and the quantities of ABP that might be disposed of by burial or landfilling are likely to be small, as most operators seem to make use of the existing collection arrangements. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROL

Domestic legislation defines the areas that have been categorised as `remote' under Article 19(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. For ABP derived from some species, the entire territory of Finland is considered a remote area. In particular, ABP from slaughtering of horses and from aquatic animals can be disposed of by burial or landfilling throughout Finland, when authorised under environmental rules. However, according to the FFA, operators do not routinely avail of these possibilities.

This was confirmed during interviews held in a region where fish processing is an important economic activity. The audit team noted that, while this area was categorised as `remote' for ABP from aquatic animals, there were arrangements in place for collection and use of such ABP, in particular for feeding to fur animals or for other purposes outside the feed chain. Some of the inspection reports of food operators processing fish in other parts of Finland indicated similar collection arrangements for ABP.

The audit team noted that slaughtering of horses usually takes place in multi-species slaughterhouses, the majority of which are located in areas where ABP of the other species slaughtered are collected. ABP from horses can therefore be collected from such slaughterhouses. This was confirmed during the interview of an official veterinarian, who was substituting for other official veterinarians in several slaughterhouses, some of which were slaughtering horses.

Based on the above-mentioned, the audit team noted that there are viable collection and transport arrangements in areas that have been categorised as `remote' and consequently such areas do not meet the definition of a `remote area', as laid down in Article 3(23) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

FFA representatives stated that for those species for which the entire territory of Finland is categorised as a `remote area', the risk assessments referred to in point (d) of Section 2 of Chapter III of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 were not carried out. 5 Conclusion on the system in place for collection, use and disposal on ABP and DP

label_heading: Conclusion on registration, approval and listing
paragraph_text: Arrangements in place for registration, approval and listing provide assurance that the vast majority of operators active along the chain of ABP and DP are known, which facilitates the implementation of official controls. However, an incomplete and, currently, not reliable registration of fur farms concerned with intra-species recycling prevents the system from being fully in line with Union rules. 5.3.2 Planning of official controls

The FFA has implemented a system for registration of fur animal farms where the feeding of fur animals (foxes and racoon dogs) with proteins derived from animal of the same species can take place (such feeding is hereafter referred to as `intra-species recycling'). An accurate and complete registration of farm is important for the purpose of official controls, as operators must comply with specific requirements (Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011). Farms where intra-species recycling take place are registered in the animal keepers' register with an indication of the concerned species (for other farms there is a statement that intra-species recycling is not carried out). 6

The FFA, despite efforts to spread the information to fur animal farmers, noted that around 50% of all fur animal farms are currently registered for intra-species recycling, which is believed to be far below the percentage of farms actually involved in intra- species recycling. This incomplete registration was confirmed during the interview of RVO of a region where most of the fur animals are located.

The audit team noted that inspections of fur animal farms must verify that these are correctly registered for intra-species recycling, if applicable. However, some MVO interviewed stated that they usually rely on the farmers statement that they are registered (or not) rather than checking the register. This led to situations where, when comparing register information and the corresponding inspection reports, the audit team noted contradictory information.

The audit team also noted that the information contained in the register was not fully reliable. The FFA explained that the migration of data between the previous and current IT system supporting the animal keepers' register resulted in inconsistencies in the information recorded. The FFA stated that the data contained in the register would be corrected.

RVO carry out checks on animal welfare, including at fur farms, during which is it required that the information contained in the animal keepers' register is checked (in general and not only for intra-species recycling). Some RVO interviewed stated that during such checks, in case of incorrect registration, the farmer is asked to update the register and that this is usually done orally. As a consequence, the FFA could not provide evidence of such checks or that follow-up had taken place in case of incorrect registration (which, in any case, would prove difficult in the absence of official records).

Based on the above-mentioned gaps, the ability of the current system to ensure that the register of fur animal farms (where intra-species recycling occurs) is updated over time is rather limited and this register is likely to remain incomplete. This does not ensure that the requirements of point 3(a)(i) of Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 are fulfilled. Conclusion on registration, approval and listing

The DGAL informed the audit team that BCP staff have access to guidance documents and instructions via its quality assurance intranet websites. The documents include three vade mecums respectively for import controls on animals, goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin. The DGAL staff also have access to the IMPADON database for further information to support documentary checks. With the exception of the vade mecum for live animals, the guidance documents and instructions have yet to be updated in order to take account of EU legislation which entered in force as of 14 December 2019.

The DGAL "guide d'inspection" contains general instructions for the performance of official controls at BCPs by its staff. It includes measures to be taken in the case of non- compliant consignments, in particular, destruction, redispatch and special treatment. This guide has also yet to be updated to take account of the measures provided for in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR.

The DGAL stated that the reasons for not having updated these instructions were due the prioritisation of staff resources in the preparations for the withdrawal of United Kingdom from the EU and the management of business continuity during the Covid-19 pandemic. The DGAL confirmed they would update the documented procedures in the period 2022-2023.

The competent authorities have documented procedures and guidance for the performance of official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU, 8 in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR. However these have not been updated as appropriate, which is not in line with Article 12(3)(b) of that Regulation.

However, a number of shortcomings were noted in the implementation of official controls. They concerned, for example, prior notification of arrival of consignments, documentary checks, transhipment and transit, and decisions on consignments and, in addition, the performance of documentary checks for food of non-animal origin other than upon arrival of the consignment at designated BCPs. These shortcomings collectively undermine the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the Union. 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

The audit team noted that, for consignments of animals and goods of animal origin intended for transhipment within the transhipment period, the DGAL stated that it requires TRACES-NT to be used for the notification of such consignments, in line with Article 16(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. The DGAL further stated that each BCP must set up a local procedure to monitor the notified information before the transhipment period expires. The DGAL informed the audit team however that, in practice, the BCPs do not have systematic access to customs declarations or manifest data (other than roll- on roll-off ferry manifests). As a consequence, the BCP staff can only rely on operators' notifications

The audit team evaluated one CHED-P authorised for transhipment at a port BCP. For this consignment, there was a five-month delay in notification of the arrival. The CHED- P for this consignment was, following a documentary check only, finalised as a transhipment to a third country. In reality, this consignment was stored for at least five months at the terminal. The competent authority, although having a transhipment procedure in place, was not aware of this consignment until its notification in TRACES.

All consignments notified at an airport BCP were subjected to at least a documentary check and an identity check, even in cases where the transhipment period was not exceeded. However, for 19 of these consignments, no date of departure was indicated in part I of the CHED-P, thus not allowing calculation of the transhipment period. In 17 of 21 cases where a physical check was not done, it was stated that the reason for not performing the physical check was `reduced checks'. For three of the five consignments 14 on which physical checks were performed, the transhipment period had not been exceeded.

The DGAL technical instruction for transhipped consignments does not require any pre- notification or checks other than in cases where the transhipment period has been exceeded. In such cases, those consignments should be subject to a documentary check, and with an identity and physical check only in cases of suspicion of non-compliance.

The DGAL could not provide evidence that the BCPs of transhipment acted in line with their instruction. In addition, as noted in section 5.1.5, BCPs do not have systematic access to customs declarations or manifest data, and as a consequence, BCPs only rely on the operator's notification of transhipment.

The audit team noted that the procedure in place does not ensure that, in the event that a transhipment takes place, it is done in line with Articles 13 and 16 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. 5.2.3 Transit and ship supply procedures

During the current audit cycle, five audits were planned in 2017, whereas six were carried out, and in 2018, three out of six planned audits were carried out. No audits took place between 2019 and 2021, with none planned for the remainder of 2021. The DGAL explained that during this period, audits could not be carried out for resource reasons, activities related to the preparedness for the withdrawal of United Kingdom from the EU and the COVID-19 pandemic.

The audits are concluded with individual audit reports, detailing the objectives, scope, findings and conclusions, and recommendations if applicable. Follow-up of previous audit recommendations is carried out by desk-based assessment or during the subsequent on-the-spot audit. As no audits have taken place since 2018 for above-mentioned reasons, follow-up on the 2018 audits is still outstanding.

The General Inspectorate of Services of the DGCCRF also carries out internal audits and verification checks. The prioritisation of these internal audits is based on an analysis of risk factors which leads to the establishment of a multi-year program for 2016-2020. The audit of official controls on imports of food of non-animal origin and food contact materials, which was scheduled for 2020, did not take place. The DGCCRF stated that this was due in part to the COVID-19 pandemic and the transfer of responsibilities to the DGDDI).

The DGCCRF stated that the multiannual audit programme is currently being revised, but that there are no plans to integrate import control audits in view of the transfer (see section 5.1.1). The DGDDI stated that it did not yet plan any audits for the same reason.

The audit team noted that the competent authorities have procedures in place to verify the effectiveness of their controls and carry out internal audits in line with Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1) and 12(2) of the OCR. However, there has been a shortfall in its implementation as no such internal audits have been carried since 2018, prior to the entry into force of the OCR. Examination of the documentary checks showed that the discrepancies in part I were either not detected or corrected, and that the outcome of those checks had been recorded as satisfactory. These CHEDs had subsequently been validated and the corresponding consignments accepted for entry into the EU, which is not in line with Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

In addition in four out of the eight CHED-As evaluated, the impact of the transport on animals was not completed in part II, which is not in line with Article 56(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 40(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715.

All but three consignments of goods of animal origin intended for import, evaluated by the audit team, were subject to documentary checks and identity checks. Identity checks were either full identity checks or checks on seals in accordance with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. With the three exceptions (see section 5.2.5), the frequency 16 rate for identity checks was in line with the baseline frequency rate set out in Article 5 and Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2129.

The audit team noted discrepancies in the relevant parts of the CHED-Ps evaluated, which were either not fully or correctly completed, and that the information included in part I of the evaluated CHED-Ps did not match the information in the accompanying certificates or attestations in 10 out of 28 CHED-Ps verified, which is not in line with Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. However, the CHED-Ps were subsequently finalised and the corresponding consignments accepted for entry into the EU, which is not in line with Article 55 of the OCR.

Following their evaluation of examples of imports of consignments of food of non- animal origin subject to a temporary increase of official controls or emergency measures, the audit team noted that the laboratory results had been delivered in a timely manner in line with Article 37(4)(d) of the OCR. The audit team noted however that, in three out of six cases, the inspector's conclusion of the laboratory tests was not recorded in TRACES-NT, which is not in line with Article 56(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 40(2)(b) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. In the remaining cases, the details of the analyses, such as for example, the test method and detailed results, were not fully

The audit team found that, in the case of a consignment of fishery products where the cold chain was not maintained, the competent authority at the BCP permitted the operator to subject the consignment to special treatment to alter the best before date of the goods by reducing it by six months to 18 months. This neither ensured compliance with the rules referred to in Article 1(2) of the OCR, nor was in line with the DGAL procedures.

The audit team noted, that a consignment of meat products, which was notified by the operator at the BCP of entry, was refused for reasons of a missing health certificate without being subjected to a documentary, identity or physical check. The health certificate was, however, uploaded in TRACES-NT. At the same BCP, but without being sent to the dedicated inspection centre used for controls of fishery products, the inspectors at this centre refused for similar reasons two consignments of fishery products without subjecting them to mandatory controls. The DGAL explained that the three consignments formed part of a `groupage' load. The operator did not present a health certificate for two cons

The audit team found that the decisions on these three consignments were not taken following the performance of official controls, including documentary checks and, where necessary, identity checks and physical checks, indicating whether the consignment is in compliance with the rules referred to in Article 1(2) of the OCR, which 18 is not in line with Article 55 of the said Regulation. The DGAL informed the team that it had since taken corrective action to ensure that consignments are only refused following the performance of official controls which indicate that the consignment is not in compliance with the applicable rules.

The audit team found that decisions on consignments were not always taken in line with Article 55 of the OCR. Conclusions on the implementation of official controls on imports/transits of animals and goods

paragraph_text: None of the BCPs evaluated are fully compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals and goods for which they have been designated. Consequently the French authorities cannot guarantee the appropriate handling of animals and goods, the proper verification of compliance of those animals and goods and the prevention of the risk of cross contamination in these facilities. However, the competent authority has already initiated corrective actions in the BCPs concerned during this audit which, when completed, should go some way to achieving compliance in these BCPs. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a system of official controls in place for animals and goods of animal

The audit team found that none of the evaluated BCPs met the minimum and detailed rules on minimum requirements for BCPs laid down in article 64 of the OCR and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

In the case of the selected BCPs which are designated for products of non-animal origin, categories PNAO-HC(food) and PNAO-NHC(feed), none had the pre-requisite areas or rooms for unloading, inspection or storage of goods, which is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

However, the audit team found that the proposed commercial storage facility did not meet the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The audit team made the following main observations: a. the flow of goods did not facilitate their proper handling and prevention of risks which may result from cross contamination; 20 b. the dedicated inspection areas did not have a supply of hot and cold running water or facilities for washing and drying of hands, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; and c. the ambient storage facilities were not appropriate to the categories of food of non- animal origin for which

Regarding the BCP Nantes Saint-Nazaire designated for goods of animal origin, the audit team found, inter alia, that appropriate arrangements were not in place for the proper handling of packed and unpacked goods and to prevent risks which may result from cross contamination. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(h) of the OCR and Article 3(9)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team found that, inter alia, in respect of the inspection centre Fécamp at BCP Le Havre which is listed for liquid fish oils and fats only, there was no procedure in place for cleaning and disinfection of the special pipes used for the unloading of bulk liquids of animal origin. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(h) and (i) of the OCR. In addition, the specification in the list of BCPs did not limit the use of this inspection centre for liquid in bulk only, despite the inspection centre availing of derogations laid down in Article 3(5) and 6(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 for such goods.

Regarding the selected airport BCP for live animals (categories LA-E, LA-U and LA- O), the audit team observed that the changing room with shower facilities, unloading, inspection and housing facilities for other live animals, category LA-O, do not constitute one integrated and whole working unit, which is not in line with the minimum requirement laid down in Article 5(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

In addition, the audit team found that the facilities for categories LA-E and LA-U do not have restraining equipment in place for equidae, and that the restraining equipment for ungulates other than equidae are stored in a separate room to the inspection area, which is not in line with Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

For BCPs Port de Saint-Nazaire Montoire, Nantes Saint-Nazaire and inspection centre Fécamp, the DGAL and the DGCCRF did not provide information on suitable 21 arrangements in place at all of the BCPs to ensure the smooth operation of official controls and to apply measures as provided for by Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(e) of that Regulation. label_heading: Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts
paragraph_text: The BCPs evaluated satisfy the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals and goods of animal origin for which they had been designated. However, there 14 are significant shortcomings in the facilities for performing official controls and in particular for storing non-compliant consignments of products of non-animal origin, which has an adverse impact on the capacity to implement of official controls and ensure the appropriate handling of such products for which those BCPs were designated. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a framework in place for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU though BCPs in Cyprus, which are generally carried out in line

As detailed in section 5.3 below, there are no arrangements in place at the BCPs for the Public Health Services to apply measures as provided for by Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR for non-compliant consignments of food of non-animal origin, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(d) and (e) of that Regulation. The Public Health Services stated that such consignments would be transferred to a designated Control Point, where measures, including re-dispatch or rejection would be applied. Such movements are not in line with Article 66(1) of the OCR, or the rules in Article 2 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2123.

The audit team noted however that there was a lack of the required inspection and storage facilities at those BCPs for the categories of products of non-animal origin for which they had been designated by the Department of Agriculture and the Public Health Services.

The Public Health Services confirmed that they do not have access to facilities to detain consignments at the BCPs in case of unsatisfactory documentary checks. Those BCPs therefore do not comply with the minimum requirements for BCPs, in particular Article 64(3)(c) and (d) of the OCR and Article 3(1)(b) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The Department of Agriculture stated that there were no consignments of feed of non- animal origin under the emergency measures in 2020 and 2021. In the event that such consignments would arrive, the Department of Agriculture staff would carry out official controls in the facilities designated for products of plant origin (plants, plant products and wood packaging materials). However, no arrangements and risk-analyses were in place in this respect at the time of audit. Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts

However, the lack of documented procedures for the performance of official controls on food of non-animal origin, has the potential to undermine assurances that such controls are sufficient to minimise, as far as possible, the introduction of non-compliant consignments into the Union. 11 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTS/TRANSITS OF ANIMALS AND GOODS

The NFCSO-DPPSCA has issued two specific documented procedures for the official controls on imports of consignments of food of non-animal origin for the presence of aflatoxins and unauthorised genetically modified organisms in rice products originating in China. No documented procedures or instructions for performing official controls on imports of other food of non-animal origin had been issued at the time of the audit, which is not in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR.

The NFCSO-DPPSCA informed the audit team that it was in the process of updating its Authority's Guide, which is aimed at controls on food of non-animal origin in the Single Market, to include guidance on performing official controls on imports of such products listed in Annexes I and II.1 to Regulation (EU) 2019/1793. The NFCSO-DPPSCA stated that the update was due to be completed by January 2022.

The competent authorities are allowing movements of live pigs from areas situated in Part III without ensuring that they meet the necessary conditions. This could facilitate the spread of ASF and jeopardise its control.

Slovakia has established a very good framework for the control system of ASF at national level with appropriate legislation, control plans and staff instructions. The veterinary authorities have suitable contingency plans, equipment and the capacity to deal with confirmed ASF outbreaks and to control cases in wild boar. This has been confirmed by the fact that the authorities have successfully controlled 28 outbreaks of ASF in pig holdings since July 2019. Epidemiological inquiries of outbreaks provided limited added value to understand the origin and potential further transmission of the disease in the affected holdings and geographical areas where they happened.

Laboratory testing for ASF meets, with some exceptions, the standards to provide sound and technically valid results. There has been a sub-optimal collaboration with the EU reference laboratory for ASF (EURL) in relation to validation of the new molecular test used for confirmation of the disease and the NRL could not yet confirm the reliability of that test participating in the annual inter-laboratory test organised by the EURL.

The implementation of measures to enhance surveillance has been satisfactory in commercial holdings but sub-optimal in non-commercial ones, notably on the thousands of pigs slaughtered on-farm. Therefore, surveillance for ASF in commercial holdings is probably sensitive enough, but there is considerable uncertainty with the capacity of surveillance to detect promptly the disease in the non-commercial sub-population.

paragraph_text: The DVFA does not follow the sanitary surveys' recommendations for sampling points and has not established a monitoring programme following them. Consequently, the validity of the sampling points for microbiological quality and their representativeness for production areas is questionable and so is the classification of production areas.

However, the remaining active production areas (or parts of them) are classified on a weekly basis (see Appendix 1 for further details) based on single results instead of on data from a review period, which is contrary to Article 52(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. paragraph_text: The DVFA does not monitor production areas (and consequently has not drawn up sampling plans) to check the microbiological quality of bivalve molluscs, the presence of toxin-producing plankton in seawater, and the presence of biotoxins and heavy metals in bivalve molluscs. This poses a risk that live bivalve with high levels of E. coli contamination, or with biotoxins and heavy metals content above the regulated limits, might be placed on the market.

The national legislation, which is the basis for the control system of live bivalve molluscs (Order No 1793 of 2 December 2020 and Guideline No 9042 of 29 January 2021 concerning food hygiene), deviates from almost all the EU requirements for bivalve molluscs (this report describes those deviations in detail).

Regarding the production areas and aquaculture farms with permanent classification: · The competent authority has fixed a review period of three years for sampling data in order to determine compliance with the requirements for class A, B and C areas, as required in Article 52(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. · According to national legislation, the DVFA can classify production areas and aquaculture farms only if there are at least 24 analytical results in the previous three years, as foreseen in the community guide 7 and in the guidance document of the European Union Reference Laboratory (EURL) for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs 8. · Every year (except

As required by Article 56(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the DVFA has completed sanitary surveys for all of the production areas (this is one of the two recommendations of the previous audit report still pending). By request of the DVFA, the DTU has carried out sanitary surveys, grouping all the production areas according to the water basins where they are located (fourteen sanitary surveys in total), and has published them on its website. The DTU plans to revise all sanitary surveys in a 5-year period (2021-2025). The audit team noted that: · The DTU informed that the revision will not include all the content but most of it and that it does not plan to carry out annual reviews (recommended

Contrary to Article 59 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the DVFA does not monitor production areas to check the microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs, the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water and the biotoxins and chemical contaminants in live bivalve molluscs.
Consequently, contrary to Article 61(1), the DVFA does not draw up sampling plans for the purpose of the checks mentioned in the previous point.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The DVFA takes decisions based on results of checks carried out by harvesters, but without taking all necessary steps to ensure their reliability. The heat treatment of most of the samples, the lack of training of samplers, absence of control and supervision of samplers, sampling points not representative of the area, etc. diminish the trustworthiness of these results. This poses a risk that live bivalve molluscs with high levels of E. coli contamination, or with biotoxins and heavy metals content above the regulated limits, might be placed on the market.

paragraph_text: The absence of an NRL for biotoxins and the fact that one of the NRLs for E. coli is not designated and that they do not fulfil all their responsibilities and tasks, is an important shortcoming that diminishes the reliability of results in an official system that is based on results from (a number of) private laboratories.

The absence of a NRL for biotoxins and the existence of NRLs for E coli, which do not fulfil all the NRL responsibilities and tasks, negatively affect the harmonisation and improvement in the performance of testing methods by other official and private laboratories. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION 19 The official control system in place does not meet the requirements of EU legislation in most of the relevant parts. The classification and monitoring of production areas, and the decisions that the authority takes are inadequate. The absence of oversight over laboratories and the shortcomings in analytical methods, particularly for biotoxins, constitute a serious limitation for the authorities to rely on

Two laboratories share the role of National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for E. coli, the DVFA and the DTU laboratories. The DVFA does not consider necessary to designate the DTU as NRL, which is not in line with Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The DVFA provided to the audit team the service contract that was in place between the DVFA and the DTU for the period 2017-2020, which included the list of tasks to be done. It also provided the list of NRLs (based on repealed EU legislation, Regulation (EC) No 882/2004), indicating the responsibilities of each one6. However, tasks required analysis for the parameters E. coli, biotoxins, and potentially toxic algae. 4 in Article 101(1)(b) a

Contrary to Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, there is no NRL for biotoxins in Denmark. The DVFA explained that the DTU laboratory was the NRL until the end of 2020; the new one, the DVFA laboratory, was in the process of setting up the biotoxins methods. 5.1.1 Classification of production areas

As described in paragraph 8, and contrary to Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, there is no NRL for biotoxins. The NRL's tasks established in Article 101(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are not carried out. Taking into account the results in 16 participation in proficiency testing (described in paragraph 45 and 46 below), the implementation of Article 101(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, regarding the appropriate follow-up of these tests by an NRL is of utmost importance.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: Significant delays in obtaining laboratory test results for some biotoxins lower the effectiveness of weekly monitoring, delays area closures and can increase the risk of placing unsafe product on the market.

The monitoring programme indicates that biotoxins monitoring results that exceed the limits established in in Annex III, Section VII, Chapter V Point 2 to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, trigger an immediate closure of production areas and, in one autonomous community, an increased sampling of water and bivalve molluscs in the adjacent production areas. Only one of the autonomous communities had a closure in the last two years due to exceedance of biotoxins. Closure of the production area, and withdrawal and recall of bivalve molluscs already placed on the market, was correctly implemented but there was a significant delay (7 days from the date of sampling) in the availability of test results (

The audit team noted significant delays in the issuing of laboratory test results to both autonomous communities, requiring often four to six days for ASP and lipophilic toxins and seven to ten working days in the case of PSP, instead of the three days commonly needed. The legally required, Art. 37(4)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, timely delivery of test results is not achieved. Conclusions on laboratories

The audit team was informed that in Spain these controls are performed by food safety/public health authorities at auction halls, dispatch centres and processing 9 establishment. The controls are documental, on identity, and on results of sampling performed by operators. However, some autonomous communities do not take official samples to verify compliance with the health standards laid down in Chapter V of Section VII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 5.1.6 Movement of live bivalve molluscs and registration document accompanying batches

The absence of national reference laboratories for biotoxins and E.coli at primary production, with the consequent gap on their tasks and responsibilities, is an important shortcoming in a control system for which laboratory performance has high impact.

The competent authority has not designated National Reference Laboratories either for E. coli or for biotoxins testing of live bivalve molluscs sampled at primary production level for the monitoring of production areas, contrary to the requirements of Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Due to the above currently there is no coordination of activities of the official laboratories involved in testing of live bivalve molluscs sampled at primary production level. Nor organisation of proficiency testing and respective follow up for those laboratories or of any of the other tasks under the responsibility of a national reference laboratory, contrary to the required by Article 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The designation of official control laboratories does not yet include all relevant laboratories, and is lacking in details to ensure timely provision of results, and efficient and effective coordination and supervision. As a consequence laboratory underperformance or failures may be detected with delay, or go undetected, negatively impacting on the quality of official controls.

One of the laboratories for biotoxins could be evaluated and was determined to be providing reliable results for the ASP and lipophilic toxins testing it performs. The other laboratory could not be fully evaluated and the data received causes doubts on PSP method validation and accuracy, and on PSP proficiency testing. Therefore, quality and reliability of the testing it performs is doubtful. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The control systems in place in Spain generally meet the requirements of the relevant EU legislation and are correctly implemented. The more relevant shortcomings identified concern national reference laboratories and designation of official control laboratories. Production area clo

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The competent authority has established the location and boundaries of "production zones", monitors them individually for microbiological quality and classifies them. They conform to the EU concept of production areas, but the use of the term "production zones" is misleading.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The current classification of production areas (or "production zones" in those production areas that are further divided) is not in line with the EU requirements. This poses certain doubts that the level of contamination of molluscs harvested corresponds to the value expected according to their classification. In addition, as the plan does not consider sampling other mollusc species available in the same geographical location, this generates a risk of misclassification of the corresponding areas.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The lack of sanitary surveys questions the validity of the designated sampling points for microbiological monitoring and their representativeness for production areas, which has direct implications in the adequate classification of production areas.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs

paragraph_text: The current monitoring programme for toxin-producing plankton is not adequate as an 11 early warning system for the appearance of biotoxins in molluscs. In addition, the fact that the official control system does not foresee any decisions following this monitoring, makes it of no value.

The monitoring plan established the requirements for the sampling of water to check for the presence of toxin-producing plankton in production areas, as required in Article 59(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. paragraph_text: There are several factors that diminish the value of the monitoring programme for biotoxins for detecting biotoxins above the established limits in production areas: the plan does not include all "production zones"13, the sampling points may not be representative of the area monitored, and the most abundant specie, and not the most representative one, is sometimes used as indicator. Although biotoxin episodes can be therefore overlooked or underestimated during monitoring, the risk of presence of biotoxins in Croatian molluscs does not seems high as data from previous years show very few episodes of biotoxins in Croatian waters.

Laboratories provide, in principle, reliable results but there is certain risk of underestimation of biotoxins as laboratories did not find conclusive explanations for unsatisfactory and questionable results in proficiency tests.

Regarding the ASP laboratory reviewed: The laboratory validated and accredited this method in 2009 and it has not renewed the validation since then (according to the information provided, it was due to the considerable amount of certified reference material that it implied and the corresponding costs, and because there was no ASP in Croatian waters). This may have an impact on the testing results due to the potential matrix effect. The laboratory tested all the relevant PSP compounds, however the SOP did not reflect it (i.e. GTX 6 and C3, 4). paragraph_text: The national legislation that incorporates the EU requirements is obsolete and does not correctly interpret some of these requirements, which is of particular relevance in relation to the decisions that the competent authority takes subsequent to the monitoring of production areas for microbiological quality. The MoA, which designs the monitoring plan that is the basis for the official control of production areas, has a reduced oversight of the sector. This is partly due to the currently significant lack of input from NRLs into the monitoring plan. All this has a negative impact in the effectiveness of the control of production areas.

The NRL for biotoxins is not entirely fulfilling all its responsibilities and tasks, which can affect negatively the harmonisation and improvement in the performance of testing methods by other official laboratories and the competence of staff when using these complex analytical methods. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The national legislation that incorporates the EU requirements does not provide an adequate framework for the official control of production areas as it is obsolete and does not correctly interpret some of these requirements, particularly relevant in relation to the decisions subsequent to microbiological monitoring of production areas. label_heading: Conclusions on oral vaccination of foxes
paragraph_text: The absence of oral vaccination campaigns in 2018 had negative impact on rabies eradication, and resulted in a decrease of the wildlife population immunity and a higher risk of spread of the disease. Similar negative effect on the rabies eradication is likely to happen in 2021 due to the absence of campaign during the spring.

label_heading: Conclusions on oral vaccination of foxes
paragraph_text: The official controls on vaccine quality, its storage conditions, and manual and aerial distribution provided timely verification that the vaccine quality met the contract specifications, and that vaccine distribution was in line with the approved vaccination plan. The late implementation of the spring campaigns increases the risk of reducing the vaccine efficacy after their distribution. The authority and contractor took some actions to mitigate this risk but they had not verified their effectiveness. 5.1 MONITORING, AWARENESS AND SURVEILLANCE Legal requirements 8 Articles 10 to 13, 15, 18, 24, 26, 27, 31(1), 32(1), 34, 46, 57, 72 to 75, 77 to 79, 81 and 257(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 201

The central authority did not apply the programme in 2018, which had a negative effect on the progress of eradication. The national legislation on public procurement caused the authority to miss another spring vaccination campaign in 2021, with likely similar negative effect on the rabies eradication as in 2018 (See Table 1 in Annex 3). Therefore, it could not follow the recommendations of the 2015 EFSA report and the 2015 Commission guidelines advising vaccination continuation for at least two years after the last reported case of rabies. This is not line with Section 2 (point 1(a)) of Chapter 1 in Part 1 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

The spring campaigns in 2019 and 2020 started at the end of May or beginning of June and finished in July, when the outside temperature was higher. The regular late start and finish of spring campaigns were not in line with the 2015 Commission guidelines. 4

The central authority and contractor took some preventive actions to mitigate risk associated to high temperatures (e.g. reduce efficacy of the vaccine), in particular by adapting the vaccination plan and the daily vaccine distribution schedules prioritising distribution early in the morning and trying to avoid days where temperatures rose over 30ºC. But the authority had not verified their effectiveness, e.g. they had not monitored the virus titre of the vaccine baits after their distribution to confirm that their potency was not altered by the exposure to high temperatures for several days in the environment. This is not in line with Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and with Sec

This hinders the authority's capability to identify quickly the areas of the country at a higher risk of rabies spread where they need to focus additional prevention, surveillance and control efforts.

In 2019, the majority of counties sampled 4 or more animals /100 km2, therefore reaching their sampling targets. The percentage of the target reached varied between counties, ranging from 51.33% to 165.46 % (for the fluorescent antibody test (FAT) tests). Seven counties (out of 40) took less than 80 % of their targeted number of samples, with two counties presenting data well below their targets. Those counties sampled only two animals /100 km2 (just above 50% of their plans).

In 2020, the variation between the counties in the percentage of the target reached was similar to the one in the previous year, ranging from 48% to 153.09 % (for the FAT tests). 26 counties achieved their sampling targets. Nine counties reached less than 80 % of their planned number of samples, with four counties well below their targets (less than 60 %). One county, bordering Ukraine; i.e. with a high risk of rabies incursion from the adjacent infected area, was not able to reach 50 % of the planned sampling target (less than 2 animals /100 km2).

The audit team analysed data provided for 2019 and 2020 for some counties showing that there had been an uneven geographical distribution of the samples taken within their territories. Both aspects; i.e. some counties not analysing the necessary number of samples and the potentially biased sample taken only from some hunting grounds, can significantly reduce the representativeness and reliability of the results obtained from their analysis and the validity of the conclusions drawn up at county and national level on the levels of immunity reached.

The authority has access to estimates of the geographical distribution of the population of wild carnivores in Romania, including the yearly hunting quotas and the hunting bags obtained at the end of the season, broken down per species and for each hunting ground. The data (see Map 5 in Annex 3) show an increased density of the jackal population in the southern part of the country, even exceeding in some counties that of the fox population. However, the authority does not take into account the estimates of all population of wild carnivores to fine-tune the planning of the rabies monitoring activities; e.g. targeting the jackal population in the selected area to obtain a representative image

The authority designed the rabies monitoring activities in accordance with the approved rabies programme and with general obligations in that respect laid down in Articles 3(points 1(a)(iv) and (b)(ii)) and 4 (point 1(b)(i)) of Regulation (EU) 2020/689. However, they did not apply those activities as planned. This is not in line with the provisions of the rabies eradication programme, recommendations of the 2013 WHO report and of the 2015 Commission guidelines, and point 1(d), of Section 2 of Chapter 1 of Part I of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

Despite the activities mentioned above, the authorities still lack sufficient understanding of how different factors contribute to the weaknesses identified in some areas of the country, e.g. underperformance in monitoring vaccination effectiveness, low levels of 16 immunity in wildlife in certain counties and under-notification and investigation of suspect cases and indicator animals. They have not identified and shared good practices that resulted in the adequate application of those measures in some well performing counties.

label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring, awareness and surveillance
paragraph_text: Although there are well-tailored information campaigns to raise public awareness on the disease, there has been an obvious decrease in the reporting of suspect cases and indicator animals investigated to exclude the presence of rabies in the last two years. This prevents the authorities from having more accurate and up-to-date epidemiological information on the rabies incidence and its geographical distribution in wild carnivores in Romania. Consequently, they might not be able to apply the measures promptly and to adapt them to reduce the risk of spread of rabies.

label_heading: Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the plant health controls
paragraph_text: There is an established laboratory network for the implementation of official controls. However, the performance of the official testing for ToBRFV in official laboratories is not verified by the NRL, who does not organise ring tests for this purpose. The official laboratories do not participate either in ring tests, organised by other entities, to achieve the same verification. As a consequence, the CA has no information on how reliable these tests are in detecting the presence of the virus. Any 7 measure based on an unreliable laboratory result has negative influence on the controls. 5.2 SURVEYS ON THE PRESENCE OF TOBRFV Legal requirements Article 34(4) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Up until the time of the audit, the NRL provided technical and scientific assistance on request. However, it has not organised inter-laboratory comparative testing or proficiency tests between the official laboratories, although this is appropriate and therefore required by Article 101(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Almost each RPS has their own official laboratory where initial tests and the vast majority of confirmatory tests are carried out. The regional laboratories have experienced staff for working with molecular methods, and have already performed analysis with at least one of the methods listed in the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. The RPS laboratory is nominated as Regional Reference Laboratory in those regions where more than one laboratory carries out the tests of official samples. However, the proficiency of the official laboratories' ToBRFV analysis with the listed methods has never been assessed by ring tests.

paragraph_text: The survey protocol of the National Contingency Plan provides comprehensive guidance for the ACs for Xf surveys outside the DAs. However, no mechanism exists to verify whether the surveys are risk based and whether they are implemented consistently and effectively.
