label_heading: Conclusions on the contingency plans for Xf
paragraph_text: The National Contingency Plan was prepared and updated according to the provisions of the EU legislation and provides a general framework for the implementation of the necessary actions in the case of an outbreak. However, it does not contain specific provisions required by the EU legislation, which are within the competency of the 12 ACCAs. The absence of information on how these provisions are addressed by the regions calls into question the ability of ACs to control any future outbreaks.

The regional autonomy established in the Spanish Constitution means that the National Contingency Plan cannot specify the minimum resources for controls that each AC shall make available, including procedures for making additional resources available as necessary. Similarly, it cannot specify rules detailing how to identify the owners of plants subject to measures or how to notify the order of removal and powers to access private properties. These are specifically required by Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. These issues may be dealt at AC level and annexed to the national contingency plan. However, in the absence of appropriate regional measures, compliance with EU rules may not be e

In the IZs of the DA Alicante, only a part of the specified plants were removed and in the vast majority of the cases with substantial delays. The delayed completion of the works and the system of prioritisation of the removals are not in line with the EU legislation. The applied measures do not sufficiently control the spread of the disease and cannot result in eradication. There is a pronounced risk that the bacterium continues to spread within the DA and a there is a risk of further natural spread from the DA into the neighbouring areas. 21

The audit team noted that the laboratories of the ACs Balearic Islands and Madrid have sufficient capacity to test all official plant and insect samples collected in the AC. Although the capacity of the official laboratory of AC Valencia has increased since the last audit, it is still not sufficient for testing all official samples within the timeframe technically necessary. In particular, in 2020, there were substantial delays during testing plant samples from the DA. The ACCAs stated that requirements for personal distancing in the laboratory during the COVID-19 pandemic and a shortage of PCR reagents contributed to the delay. For 2021 the delays decreased, however the laboratory still nee

The ACCA stated that in the DA Alicante : · Since 2017, 4,694 plants were tested positive. After the establishment of a new IZ, the first priority is the removal of the positive tested plant as it is the proven source of any further spread by the vector. Until the time of the audit, 97.7% of the positives (4,588 plants) have been removed. In 2021, the average time elapsed between the test result and the removal of plants was 89 days. · For the removal of plants listed in Article 7(1)(a)to(e) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 (i.e. specified plants other than the positive), priorities are applied. The DA, where numerous overlapping IZs are surrounded by a common BZ of 2.5 km radius, was divided in

label_heading: Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the plant health controls
paragraph_text: The official controls and other official activities of the RPS regarding the application of the eradication and containment measures against A. chinensis, A. glabripennis and P. japonica are not sufficiently coordinated and there is a lack of procedures, which lead to inconsistent application of the control measures and decreases their effectiveness. 5.2 SPECIFIC SURVEYS AND NOTIFICATIONS Legal requirements Article 22 to 24 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Article 5 of Decision (EU) 2012/138. Article 6 of Decision (EU) 2015/893. Article 32(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. Findings

There are general documented procedures in place, but there are none regarding the application of the eradication and containment measures to be taken following official controls against A. chinensis, A. glabripennis and P. japonica, contrary to Article 12 (1) of Regulation 2017/625. This has contributed to the different implementation of the eradication measures in the regions (see also sections 5.5 and 5.6).

The CA does not have access to information about active orchards in DAs or elsewhere, and therefore cannot check that phytosanitary measures are carried out in orchards, as required. This potentially undermines the measures for eradication taken in a DA.

The DGAV informed the audit team that according to the national Decree Law, professional operators carrying out the activities referred to in Article 65(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, in Portugal, are obliged to be registered in a register kept by, or accessible by, the DGAV, and shared a summary list of registered operators to the audit team. Other operators, such as producers of citrus fruits (orchards) are registered under agricultural legislation, but the DGAV does not have direct access to those registers.

According to Article 65 referred to above, Member States may decide for further categories of operators to be registered if so justified by the pest risk presented by the plants that they grow. Portugal has not yet made use of that possibility, but the DGAV informed the audit team that this is currently being considered. 5.5.2 Measures in case of suspicion of Trioza erytreae

The DGAV informed the audit team that the DRAPs shall locate and map abandoned host trees and orchards in the BZ and in the surveillance zone. The DRAPs however do not have access to information about active orchards in the DAs. This was confirmed during an on-site visit in a DA, when the DRAP showed the audit team a citrus orchard which they knew of only because its owner reported a suspected case of infestation with T. erytreae to the DRAP. The suspicion was later confirmed, and measures such as phytosanitary treatments, pruning and placing of yellow traps were applied in the orchard. The orchard was in an existing DA when the owner reported the suspected finding.

The CA cannot immediately take measures to eradicate T. erytreae in private gardens unless the owners cooperate voluntarily. Given the large number of host plants present in private gardens, this situation potentially risks undermining efforts made by the CA and professional operators to eradicate the pest and increases the risk for its further spread. 5.6 MOVEMENT CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 41 and 78 to 84 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

The DGAV informed the audit team that national legislation provides the possibility to impose penalties on private individuals for not implementing the required eradication measures. However, the DRAPs do not have measures in place to enable them to immediately take the necessary phytosanitary measures in cases when these are not carried out by the owner or any other person on behalf of the owner. In such cases, the matter must first be taken to court, although the DGAV stated that they had never taken private individuals to court for failing to implement the eradication measures. paragraph_text: The revised NAP, in force since December 2017, contains objectives, detailed measures and actions to achieve a general reduction in the use and risk of PPPs. Although two key quantitative objectives have been defined, the lack of baselines and indicators does not allow to monitor the progress, and limits the possibility to define and achieve adequate targets for reduction of PPP use and risks, arising thereof. 5.3. TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION OF OPERATORS Legal Requirements Article 5 of Directive 2009/128/EC on training and certification Article 6 of Directive 2009/128/EC on pesticide sales Findings

The audit team noted the following: · There are only two key quantitative objectives specified in the NAP. The first is the reduction of `big movers' by 30% by 2025, and the second is the reduction of the use of PPP by 50% by 2030. However, the baseline period is not specified in either case. · The definition and the listing of AS called `big movers' is a measure under the NAP, and has been achieved by the publication of an official list of such AS2. However, the NAP does not contain any description of the indicators to monitor the progress of the reduction target. The same applies to the second objective (50% reduction in the use of PPPs). This is not in line with Article 4(1) of the SUD. ·

There is a system in place to provide the necessary training and certification to PPP operators. However, the process to build the system started only from late 2017 and certification was only mandatory since January 2021. This means that PPPs are being sold and used by operators, who do not have the necessary knowledge on the proper use of PPPs and the associated risks for the human health and the environment. 5.4. label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The CAs consider most of the relevant risks and have defined control frequencies for controls on the marketing and use of PPPs. However, the absence of up to date list(s) of all professional users of PPPs and the lack of control at some users, such as service providers for the application of PPPs in non-agricultural use areas, reduces the efficiency of controls on the use of PPPs.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls on the use of plant protection products
paragraph_text: Due to the absence of an up to date list of all professional users of PPPs and consequent lack of official controls at those users not claiming CAP payments, the CAs cannot ensure the overall effectiveness of the official controls on the use of PPPs.

There are no up-to-date list(s) at the disposal of TRD of all possible professional users of PPP, contrary to what is required by Article 10(2) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Given the high number of farmers/land owners in Malta (approximately 11 400 in 2005 audit report DG(SANCO)/7671/2005), the CA acknowledge during the audit that it is possible 6 that a significant proportion of professional users of PPPs are not known to the TRD, are not trained and certified as professional users, and are not subject to official controls. This is not in line with Article 9(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The CAs consider most of the relevant risks and have defined control frequencies for controls on the marketing and use of PPPs. However, the absence of up to date list(s) of all professional users of PPPs and the lack of control at some users, such as service providers for the application of PPPs in non-agricultural use areas, reduces the efficiency of controls on the use of PPPs.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls on the use of plant protection products
paragraph_text: Due to the absence of an up to date list of all professional users of PPPs and consequent lack of official controls at those users not claiming CAP payments, the CAs cannot ensure the overall effectiveness of the official controls on the use of PPPs.

The CA stated that these service providers are currently not covered by any official controls unless they are also CAP beneficiaries. This is not in line with Article 9(1) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which requires that official controls have to be performed at all operators regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The lack of exchange of some official control data between TRD and ARPA further reduces the effectiveness and efficiency of the official control.

The audit team noted that TRD does not communicate the results of official controls on PPP residues in domestic food and feed to ARPA to facilitate their planning of controls at user level. This is not in line with the Article 4(2) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires to ensure efficient and effective coordination between all authorities involved. In 2020, some 10% of samples taken from domestically grown products had exceedances of maximum residue limits (MRLs), while in 2019, the exceedance rate was almost 15%. According to the European Food Safety Authority report "The 2019 European Union report on pesticide residues in food" (https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/6491)

The absence of a designated laboratory for PPP formulation analyses limits the scope of official controls. Consequently, the CA cannot confirm that PPPs placed on the market are compliant with the authorisation requirements. 5.2. label_heading: Conclusions on controls on the marketing of plant protection products
paragraph_text: The low level of compliance with the requirements of Articles 5 and 6 of SUD raises concerns over the level of competency and training of the staff involved in the distribution of PPPs in Malta.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls on the use of plant protection products
paragraph_text: The low level of compliance with the requirements of Articles 5 and 6 of SUD raises concerns over the competencies and training of the staff purchasing and using PPPs in Malta.

As far as compliance with the requirements of Article 6(1) of the SUD on the certification off the staff of distributors is concerned, according to the data provided to the audit team by the CA, at the time of the audit only 24% of the 67 distributors selling products for professional users of PPP were compliant.

According to the information provided to the audit team, the main non-compliances detected in 2020 were related to the lack of valid certificates under Article 5(2) of the SUD (43% of operators selected in 2020, 57% in 2019), deficiencies with regard to IPM implementation, non-compliant use of authorised PPPs, inappropriate storage conditions and lack of up to date records on the application of PPPs.

paragraph_text: The high level of non-compliances identified during official controls indicate the need for more effective enforcement actions to ensure that the operators concerned remedy the non-compliances and that these do not recur. 6. paragraph_text: The administrative delays in providing formulation details to the formulation laboratory during 2020 delayed the timely delivery of analytical results, and weakened the overall effectiveness of the control programme.

In 2020, the laboratory processed samples in an average of 34 days from receipt of the sample to reporting the results. The laboratory explained that analysis can take considerably longer (up to six months) in a small number (circa. 5%) of cases. This occurs in cases where the laboratory requests the formulation details from MARD and there are delays in receiving this information. This information is necessary for the laboratory to conduct the most appropriate analysis and to determine if the analytical result demonstrates compliance. Conclusions on relevant national legislation and provisions

The INAO is responsible for the suspension/withdrawal of approval of CBs. The approval procedure is described in INAO-DIR-CAC-5-Rev. 4. CBs are approved by the INAO before they are formally accredited, on the condition that accreditation to ISO/IEC 17065:2012 is obtained within one year. This does require that the INAO receives from the COFRAC the operational admissibility of the CB's files, which is issued after the COFRAC has carried out a documentary check of all documents in the accreditation file. To obtain such operational admissibility from the COFRAC, the CB must have a control plan approved by the INAO. The COFRAC explained to the audit team that for them it is not acceptable to gra

The INAO provided to the audit team the most recent supervision reports for four CBs. The team noted that the instructions and the provisions in place for supervision of CBs were followed. In all cases, the report template was used. However, in two of the reports reviewed, there was no evidence that the inspectors had checked that the risk-based selection of operators for sampling was properly carried out by the CBs. As mentioned in chapter 5.2.4 below, the audit team found for the two CBs involved in the audit that the selection of operators for sampling and additional visits was not fully in line with the EU organic regulations, including for one of them that the risk assessment did not ta

The INAO did not take into account COFRAC's accreditation reports when supervising the CBs, which is not in line with Article 92c (1) of Regulation (EC) 889/2008. Conclusions on approval, supervision and withdrawal of CBs

The audit team noted that the documentary evidence that CBs issue in line with Article 29(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 was not available for some operators on the published list of operators. The CA stated that the CBs do not issue documentary evidence for operators in their first year of conversion. For these operators an attestation of conversion was granted stating that the operator is engaged in organic production but it is not allowed to market products with an organic reference. This attestation is not published, which is not in line with Article 92(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. In addition, this document is not in line with Article 29(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Ar

When operators move CB, the relevant elements of their file and the reports referred to in the second subparagraph of Article 63(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 must be transferred from the previous CB to the new CB. The audit team reviewed several cases of transfer of operators. However, while the relevant elements of the operator's files are transferred, the reports referred to in Article 63(2) are not transferred. This is not fully in line with Article 92(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on registration of operators

In addition, the two CBs visited have risk analysis procedures in place to select operators for additional visits. The CBs have a mixed risk assessment based on quantitative and qualitative factors. However, one CB did not have the volume of production as a risk factor in its procedure, which is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and the INAO Directive.

The two CBs also have procedures for sampling based on risk. The audit team noted that even if most of the operators selected for sampling are based on risk there is also an important number of operators that are randomly selected by the inspectors. Therefore, it 10 is very difficult for the CBs to have an overview to ensure that operators selected for sampling in the end are those posing the highest risk. In one CB, around 30 % and 40% operators classified as low risk were selected for sampling in 2019 and 2020 respectively. This is not in line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

At the beginning of the year, inspectors are given an indicative annual plan of inspections with the operators to inspect and, in the CB's database, inspectors have online access to all necessary information concerning previous controls of the operators, and any pending non-compliances. However, the two CBs could not provide evidence that inspectors have the information the operator must submit to the CB when engaged in organic production in line with Article 63 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 (a full description of the unit and of the precautionary measures).

The reports issued by the CB inspectors lack detail on how verification takes place, with no objective evidence attached to the reports. The reports consist of a template where inspectors tick off the aspects verified with little or no further description of, or references made, to the documents or records checked or any explanation to provide evidence that the item checked was in line with requirements.

For example, the audit team reviewed a report of an inspection carried out at an operator who has plant and livestock production. The inspector stated that the density of animals was in line with the requirements as were the records of veterinarian medicines and the 12 consumption of feed. The inspector also stated that the purchase and use of inputs and the quantity of feed produced and used was in line with requirements. However, these statements were not supported by evidence as the reports lack details on how the checks had been made. This lack of detail prevents effective supervision, as there is no evidence that can be objectively assessed. Nevertheless, in some instances, for example,

For example, to distinguish whether the presence of the substance is due to contamination from conventional neighbours or to the use of the substance by the operators themselves.

In all cases, the CB imposed sanctions on the operators in line with the catalogue of measures. However, deadlines for the investigation are not defined so it could take up to several months from the identification of the irregularity to resolve the case. In one particular case of Ethylene oxide contamination in sesame seeds originating in India, the CB only decided to take measures after a substantial delay even though the level of contamination was far above the maximum residue level. In addition, the CB informed the INAO about the case around 40 days after the detection of the substance. This constitutes significant misconduct on the part of the CB given there is an ongoing alert about Ethylene oxide contamination of sesame seeds and other products from India and there should be immediate exchange of information between the CBs and the CAs in order to enable the CAs to notify the Commission and other Member States through OFIS.

The audit team reviewed four cases related to OFIS notifications. There is a procedure to deal with notifications in OFIS. In the four cases investigated, the INAO and the CBs carried out investigations to identify the source of contamination. The CBs involved carried out inspection visits to the relevant operators and took samples. Other CBs involved were also informed. In two of the cases, the CB concluded that the contamination was accidental without providing robust evidence of that. The INAO provided information in OFIS respecting the established deadlines. These discrepancies are detailed in the relevant sections of the report. Conclusions on relevant national legislation and provisions

As stipulated in the national Rules on Organic Agriculture, Ekoagros applies a threshold for detected unauthorised substances below which, no contamination is recorded or investigation or other follow-up carried out. The threshold is formally 0.01 mg/kg, but since the measurement of uncertainty, which the laboratory is obliged to indicate (generally 50%), must also be added the threshold is in practice most often 0.02 mg/kg. Furthermore, this still applies if several substances are found, as long as the level of each substance is below the threshold. In 2019-2020, some 40% of the positive samples found in the risk-based surveys were below the threshold and in practice regarded as negative. P

The Rules on Organic Agriculture lay down the overall procedure and rights and obligations regarding particular types of irregularities, such as presence of an unauthorised substance. In cases of the latter, if the level of (each) unauthorised substance is above the threshold (see 62 above), the lot in question is blocked and the operator is given 5 days to request an investigation, for which he has to pay the additional analyses of samples. If the operator does not make such a request the lot is downgraded to conventional and if on a farm, the field is furthermore downgraded to conversion and the farmer loses the subsidy on the field for that year.

Order No 3D-370 of 22 May 2009 describes the procedure for the exchange of information of non-compliances with other Member States and the Commission in the OFIS system. The audit team examined examples of the follow-up done in response to notifications made by other Member States. One of them involved the finding of Glyphosate in oats exported by a grain trader in 2019. The lot was originally composed from 140 truckloads of oats from over 50 farmers. By analysing the samples referred to in paragraph 45 above, Glyphosate was confirmed in 121 of the 140 truckloads. Apart from the application of the threshold, the team noted that appropriate investigations and reporting were done in the examined OFIS cases.

As stipulated in Order No 3D-630, Ekoagros produces an annual activity report, which is also published. Furthermore, the national Rules on Organic Agriculture require that Ekoagros shall submit to the Ministry of Agriculture, by 1 March each year, a summary of the primary production by the certified operators in the previous year. The audit team noted that none of these reports fully give the summary of the control activities envisaged in Article 27(14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 to enable the competent authority to timely monitor the control activities. This is mitigated by the fact that the control activities are subject to annual audits by the AEOFD, as mentioned above.

Order No 3D-397 lays down the obligations and deadlines for communication about identified infringements between the bodies involved with inspections and control, i.e. SFVS, the State Plant Service and Ekoagros. The audit team noted that information to AEOFD is not covered in this order. Ekoagros and AEOFD stated that Ekoagros 7 nevertheless immediately notifies each case when an unauthorised substance is found as well as cases of fraud. However, other cases of non-compliance affecting the organic status of the product are only transmitted to AEOFD in summarised form once a month. This is not fully in line with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC)

The FPS-e is the central competent authority for controlling PDO/PGI/TSG products and GI spirit drinks on the market and their labelling in the entire country. Within the FPS-e, the Directorate-General for Economic Inspection (DGEI) is designated for this 5 purpose. However, the controls carried out are not systematic or risk based (see also section 5.2.5).

DGEI inspectors of FPS-e are responsible for carrying out labelling and traceability checks at retailers and distribution centres of products under all national quality schemes including PDO/PGI/TSG products and GI spirit drinks. The results of controls at retailer level are systematically reported to FPS-e. Non-compliances trigger further checks at producers or importers of PDO/PGI/TSG products and GI spirit drinks. Controls are also done of direct sales from producers. However, the market controls are not based on a national inspection plan or analysis of the associated risk of non-compliance or to the amounts of non-domestic PDO/PGI/TSG products and GI spirit drinks on the market. Cooperation and coordination arrangements between and within the CAs involved in the controls for the areas covered by this audit are in place. The mechanisms in place (such as documented procedures and training) give the CAs a reasonable level of assurance that controls are carried out uniformly and consistently. However, the audit team noted, in one of the three slaughterhouses, some weaknesses related to the knowledge of SVA staff on these documented procedures.

Most of the staff interviewed during this audit had a good knowledge of the tasks that they have to carry out and the applicable EU and national legislation. Findings

From 2017 to 2019, the NVWA performed annual audits on COZK controls over laying hen holdings, and establishments further along in the egg production and marketing chain. The audits included accompanying a few COKZ inspections on the spot at each of those establishments. None of the audits detected deficiencies with COKZ performance in relation to the tasks delegated by the NVWA. 19

The NVWA audits did not look into how COKZ performed the egg channelling after the imposition of restriction measures in laying hen holdings. NVWA did not detect that COKZ was imposing restrictions on the eggs, and/or recalling those eggs, only from the date of the positive test result instead of from the date of the sampling for that test. This could negatively affect the ability to identify the possible sources of disease and to implement forward and backward tracing correctly.

The effectiveness of ASF surveillance varies across the island, but data demonstrates a decline in the presence of ASF in the wild boar population and of seropositive pigs in farms. The temporal and spatial clustering of passive surveillance creates a risk of new cases not being detected quickly, in particular outside the defined infected area.

Inspectors do not verify the compliance with the other conditions set out in the product specifications with official on-site checks at the premises of operators (see also paragraph 43 above). This includes vineyards where the cultivation method and the vine varieties used are verified only by internal controls carried out by the ODGs. INAO stated that the specifications of a PGI wine product under the competence of CB2 do not contain specific requirements to be met and verified on-site. However, for the specific PGI wine product examined by the audit team, the verification of compliance with the conditions set out in the product specifications could not be based exclusively on documentary checks. CB2 stated that, in general, on-site checks are carried out in case of non-compliances identified during the documentary checks or at the request of an operator who appeals an unfavourable result of the organoleptic testing. This non-compliance identified by the audit team is somewhat mitigated by the intensive, but non-official,

Representatives of CB2 stated that the ODGs carry out internal checks, which include organoleptic and if necessary, analytical testing of all batches of PDO/PGI wines prior to packaging, whilst official external checks take place only after their packaging by organoleptic testing of all wine batches of circa 5% of operators. Representatives of CB3 stated that internal checks of PDO wines are carried out by the ODGs at 100% of wine batches prior to their marketing in bulk, where samples are taken for organoleptic and, if necessary, analytical testing. The same procedure is followed when different batches of PDO wines are destined for blending.

For CB1 and CB2, the official organoleptic and analytical testing is triggered by declarations of packaging and carried out only on wine that has already been packaged (bottled or bag in box). Either no official testing is carried out by these CBs on wines prior to their marketing in bulk or it is carried out only upon request of the operator, e.g. if he disagrees with non-compliances identified by the ODGs. INAO stated that the official organoleptic and analytical testing of the PDO/PGI wines is carried out after packaging to be as close as possible to the final product sold.

However, as the operators may continue their routine activities during official inspections carried out by the CBs, these batches can potentially already be on the market using the PDO/PGI designation, without having been blocked until the results of the official testing confirm that they comply with the conditions in the specification and possess all the appropriate characteristics of the PDO/PGI designation. Belgium has adopted IMSOC systems into their procedures for controls on imported regulated plants and plant products in line with EU requirements, ensuring a harmonised approach to the management of controls within the EU. Harmonisation of the system will be completed when the electronic signature is fully implemented.

Belgium is using TRACES for import of plants, plant products and other objects at all BCPs and CPs. FASFC staff, as well at LCUs as at BCPs, have reading and writing access to the system, while those posted working at the Regions have read-only access for CHED-PP parts I and II, and writing access for part III. Customs has reading access to TRACES. The system is also used to report non-compliant consignments. The CAs stated that although full implementation of the electronic signature is expected for the near future, it has not been fully implemented yet, contrary to the requirements of Article 39(1)(b)(c) and (d) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. 5.2.2Documented Control

paragraph_text: There are official laboratories with adequate capabilities for the ToBRFV tests. However, the practice used for the confirmation of positive or undefined sample of imported specified seeds is in not line with the EU legislation and the proficiency of the laboratory test was not verified, there is a risk of false results, which may compromise the controls. 5.2 SURVEYS ON THE PRESENCE OF TOBRFV Legal requirements Article 34(4) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. label_heading: Conclusions on the surveys on the presence of ToBRFV
paragraph_text: The annual surveys for ToBRFV concentrated on high-risk production sites, related to outbreaks and to the follow-up of contaminated seed lots. As the planned number of random surveys at tomato producers was not achieved, and pepper growers were not checked, the actual outbreak situation may not be entirely known, which could compromise the eradication efforts. 5.3 MEASURES RELATED TO THE CONFIRMED PRESENCE OF TOBRFV Legal requirements Articles 17, 29, 31 and 52 and Annex II Section 1 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Findings

In 2020 and 2021, the FASFC carried out annual surveys for the detection of ToBRFV, which were planned after a risk assessment, as required by Article 5(2) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Only tomato fruit growers were targeted. Growers of Capsicum sp. were included in the 2020 and 2021 survey programmes, but sampling was not carried out, on the assumption that pepper producers generally cultivate resistant varieties. Concerning the surveys on the market the FASFC stated that growers comply with the marketing standards, i.e., sort out of symptomatic fruits. Therefore, it is difficult to find symptomatic fruits on the market.

The controls at the places of production of specified plants for planting are in line with EU requirements and aimed at reducing the risk of introduction of the virus to fruit production establishments. As the timing of the inspections is not appropriate for each lot at sites with various growth periods, there is a risk of not detecting some infections. 5.5 CONTROLS ON MOVEMENT OF SPECIFIED SEEDS WITHIN THE EU Legal requirements Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Findings

The audit team noted that the inspection and sampling procedure of the production of specified plants for planting is in line with provisions of Article 6(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. However, the inspections which are carried out once a year per production site cannot cover those specified plants for planting which are not present during the official visit. For sites with continuous production of multiple crops with various sowing times, a single inspection may not be considered as appropriate to obtain comprehensive information about the status of the production site. Conclusions on the controls of the movement of specified plants for planting within the EU

The controls on imported specified seeds are generally in line with EU requirements. label_heading: Conclusions on the containment measures against A. glabripennis
paragraph_text: The intensive monitoring activity of the regional CAs within the DAs is suitable to detect the occurrence of any additional infested plants. Although the change to containment strategy was not in line with EU requirements, the measures implemented by the regional phytosanitary services are generally in line with the provisions of the EU legislation regarding containment. However, issues with the potential movement of green waste out of the DA in Centre-Val de Loire could decrease the effectiveness of the official measures.

Although the order of the prefect specifies that transport of plants and plant material of the specified plants from the DA is prohibited, compliance with this requirement is not ensured. The municipal green waste disposal site, where the public can bring pruned material or any green waste, is located outside the DA. The movement of such material is not controlled, which does not comply with Annex II section 3 (1)(d) of Decision (EU) 2012/138. 5.5.4 Tracing activity

label_heading: Conclusions on the registration of professional operators
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for the registration of professional operators as required by EU Regulations. This may result in the movement of plants without a valid plant passport within the EU. 5.3 AUTHORISATION AND SUPERVISION OF PROFESSIONAL OPERATORS FOR ISSUING PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 89 to 92 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 1 to 4 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Articles 1 and 2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 Findings 5.3.1 Authorisation procedures
The CA has not fully embraced the concept of the new system of plant passporting with the objective of placing greater responsibility on professional operators.

label_heading: Conclusions on issuance of plant passports, including record keeping
paragraph_text: The issuance of plant passports is generally in line with EU requirements with the exception of some isolated incidents, where there was misinterpretation of the EU plant passport requirements by both the CA and the operator. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON MOVEMENT OF PLANTS AND PLANT PRODUCTS WITH PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 69, 79 to 83, 88 and 93 to 95 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Articles 1 to 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 in its entirety Findings 5.6.1 Official controls on traceability

While traceability of regulated goods was demonstrated to the audit team by the authorised operator visited, it is not checked by the CA. Furthermore, checks on operators selling through distance contracts to the final consumer are largely excluded from official controls. This may result in the movement of plants without a plant passport or movement of plants without a plant passport linked to a traceability system, thus posing a risk to the integrity of the plant passport system in Romania. 5.7 ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS Legal requirements Articles 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Findings

The CA did not provide a clear legal basis to take enforcement action in the case of non-compliances with regard to EU plant passport requirements. This may result in the CA not having the legal powers to take action in the event of a non-compliance and without the appropriate guidance, therefore risking the spread of regulated pests into the EU. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Romania has a structure in place that provides a basis for the implementation of the EU requirements for the system of plant passporting which is led by a central authority and competent staff. Moreover, existing operating control procedures, manuals and guides do not provide sufficient instructions to staff to enable them to competently and consistently carry out their inspection duties on operators acting along the chain of ABP and DP. The lack of appropriate support, in terms of training and documented procedures, to the staff performing official controls along the ABP chain undermines the overall quality and effectiveness of these controls.

Moreover, all of the DVFA inspectors met stated that have not ever received a specific ABP training, except for rules on SRM, and they had to self-educate on the ABP rules, what was in their opinion challenging due to complexity of the ABP legislation. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: While since the last Commission audit of 2011 there has been a significant improvement across the country in the collection and disposal of ABP resulting from slaughter and from food establishments handling products of animal origin, the collection of fallen farmed animals has only improved in those few regions were the national collection programme has been operating the longest (since 2019) and even there, the huge variation between different animal species and between regions, illustrates that the implementation of the system is very much a work in progress. . 14

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Each of the ten regions manages the programme itself and, via a public tender, contracts operators collecting ABP and fallen farmed animals. This resulted in the signing of contracts by the regions at different times; consequently, regions are at different stages of the programme implementation. While some regions will soon begin the second round of the programme, some are still in the mid-phase of the first round and one region only recently (March 2022) initiated the first round and expects to begin the collection from April 2022 (see Table 1.). label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: According to the data reviewed by the audit team, the ten regions that implemented the programme collected 13,551 bovine animals, 15,304 small ruminants and 3,551 pigs (9).

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The public awareness of the programme varies between the regions. In two of the four regions visited, the regional authorities had actively informed animal keepers about the programme, using leaflets, local media and local administrations. In the other two, the information action had a much smaller scale. Consequently, farmers' awareness of the programme varies and is best in those regions where the programme is already being implemented.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Out of the nine regions currently implementing the programme, two have already achieved the foreseen target for collection of fallen bovine animals. In the remaining seven, the collection of fallen cattle ranges from almost half of the expected number of fallen animals (a region with a longer period of implementation) to zero (in a region where the programme has been implemented only since November 2021) (10). In those regions where the collection programme is not fully operational or has not started yet, farmers are burying fallen animals on their own lands (see finding 31).

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In two of the regions visited, the audit team visited large bovine holdings (keeping more than 300 animals) and noted that: a. In the region implementing the national collection programme for fallen stock, the farmer had abandoned the earlier practice of burying dead animals and notified all fallen animals to a collector contracted under the programme. The number of fallen animals notified to the collector matched the number of notifications to the national system for animal identification and registration (IVIS). b. In the region where the programme for collection was not yet operational, the farmer notified all dead animals to the system for animal identification and registration but conti

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The programme covers the collection of ABP and fallen animals of the following species: bovine, porcine, ovine and caprine. For all of these species, DGVS has estimated the annual collection target (i.e. the mortality rate) at 4% of the total population. The programme does not cover collection of other farmed species, e.g. poultry or equidae; however, regions may include these upon their own decision. While one of the four regions visited included poultry in the programme, another one excluded pigs. The RVS representatives from the region where the programme did not cover pigs, stated that this situation will change because operators of smaller scale pig holdings and backyard farmers have re

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The collection of pigs, sheep and goats is by far less effective than that of cattle. For pigs, the percentage of fallen stock collected (by region) ranges from zero to 29.71% of the expected number of fallen stock (4% of the population). The VS representatives met informed the audit team that in some regions, including those visited during the audit, the outbreaks of African swine fever happening in the recent years resulted in the issuing of a decision allowing for on-site burial of pigs to prevent further spread of the disease. Moreover, large pig farms usually have their own arrangements for collection and disposal of fallen animals directly by ABP processors. However, there are no data

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: For sheep and goats, the percentage of fallen animals collected (by region) remains far from the expected target (4% of the population) and ranges from 0.01 to 9.28% of the target. In the regions visited, the RVS officials met explained that sheep and goats spend more than half of the year free-grazing in mountainous areas with difficult access, where collection is practically not possible. This part of the year represents also the period with the highest proportion of deaths of small ruminants as losses usually happen around and shortly after the lambing season.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: With the exception of controls on low capacity incinerators and, more significantly, official sampling, official controls are mostly implemented as planned and are largely suitable to check operator compliance with the applicable Union requirements on ABP and DP. However, and similar to what has been seen in the plant approval process, in some instances official controls have erroneously concluded on operator compliance when in fact this is not the case, thus weakening confidence in the reliability of said controls.

In the regions visited, contrary to the requirement of Section 2 of Chapter III in Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, there were no regular (at least once a year) 8 official controls on low capacity incineration plants incinerating SRM. paragraph_text: With the exception of controls on low capacity incinerators and, more significantly, official sampling, official controls are mostly implemented as planned and are largely suitable to check operator compliance with the applicable Union requirements on ABP and DP. However, and similar to what has been seen in the plant approval process, in some instances official controls have erroneously concluded on operator compliance when in fact this is not the case, thus weakening confidence in the reliability of said controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team noted that official controls usually properly assessed compliance with infrastructural, equipment or hygiene-related requirements. However, for other types of requirements, official controls concluded on compliance even though: a. some of the ABP operators recorded the processing parameters in a way which did not allow to demonstrate compliance with permitted operating conditions (parameters were not recorded continuously against real time or information on the quantity of processed/incinerated material was missing), and; b. operators' documents and procedures often missed mention of or reference to: (i) cleaning procedures and their documentation, required by Article 25(3)(e)

label_heading: Conclusions on registration, approval and listing
paragraph_text: The registration of establishments and regular updating of the lists of establishments is effective and facilitates the planning of official controls. The national rules for approval of establishments are in line with EU requirements, however, the implementation of the rules is deficient resulting in a situation where an ABP plant whose conditional approval has expired, can continue to operate. This undermines an otherwise well-functioning approval process with resulting risks to public and animal health. 5.2.2 Planning of official controls

In several of the files, the conditional approval had expired well before the competent authority could perform the on-site visit necessary to either prolong the conditional approval or grant a full approval. This resulted in plants continuing their activities for several months without a valid approval, contrary to the requirements of Article 44(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls do not verify compliance with the requirements for milk-derived products used for feeding of farmed animals. This, combined with procedures for the authorisation of farms (using milk-derived products for feeding pigs) that do not include an assessment of the risks of feeding such ABP in the context of possible outbreak of epizootic diseases, could present a risk in case of an outbreak of such diseases, in particular foot-and-mouth disease. 10

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the dairy sector, official controls covering food hygiene requirements include checks on the disposal of ABP from the processing of milk. However, such controls do not cover the use of milk-derived products for the feeding of farmed animals contrary to the requirements of Article 4.3 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In particular, the audit team noted that there were no controls on sweet whey (a by-product of the manufacture of semi- hard cheeses) dispatched to farms for the feeding of pigs. As a result, such whey, which originates from the clotting of pasteurised milk but whose pH is not necessarily below six, was sent to farms that were not authorised to receive it on the basis of the r

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team noted that, while there is a process for the authorisation of such farms, it is incomplete as it does not require the abovementioned assessment. The process is based solely on a declaration by the farmer, which results in the registration of the farm. At the time of the audit, there were no farms registered for the use of milk-derived products for the feeding of animals (such as pigs) susceptible to foot and mouth disease.

label_heading: Conclusions on registration, approval and listing
paragraph_text: Although the national rules for approval of establishments are in line with EU requirements, they lack clarity with respect to the competent authority actions when significant alterations are made to the process in already approved ABP processing plants. label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls in ABP plants are, overall, effective in verifying compliance with most of the ABP requirements, and thus provide a satisfactory level of assurance in terms of the overall compliance of operators. However, controls on food operators from the meat producing sector acting along the ABP chain, although regular, do not pay sufficient attention to operators' obligations concerning the categorisation of ABP and information required in documents accompanying ABP consignments dispatched from meat producing establishments, and as a result, weaken confidence in the overall reliability of these controls and in the safe handling of ABP, and the use of DP.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the slaughterhouses visited, official controls on food hygiene covered ABP related requirements in a comprehensive manner. However, the audit team noted that these controls have in certain cases erroneously concluded on compliance with the applicable requirements while in fact the relevant requirements were not met. For example, the official controls have overlooked: a. Improper categorisation of some ABP, namely not-emptied intestines containing digestive track content (thus entirely consisting of Category 2 material) were categorised and collected as Category 3 material and as such dispatched to Category 3 processing plants producing PAP. b. Incorrect filling in of commercial documents,

The system in place for collection, treatment and disposal of ABP is largely capable of ensuring a safe management of ABP an DP. However, ABP from the treatment of hides are not disposed of in line with EU rules and some ABP from on-farm slaughter are disposed of by burial, while this is not authorised under EU rules for ABP.

Domestic legislation authorises, throughout the country, on-site burial of animal carcasses and Category 2 material, consisting of ABP from on-farm slaughter, provided that the amount does not exceed 40 kg a week. This is not in line with EU rules, in particular Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, which do not provide for any exemption for routinely burying these types of ABP (outside of remote areas).

For bovine animals, an authorisation from DGAV (regional services) is required before on-farm slaughter takes place; animals must be younger than 12 months and the number of slaughters is limited to two per year. As part of the authorisation process, DGAV must verify that ABP from such slaughter is collected by an authorised ABP operator. In one of the regions visited, where more than 800 authorisations were granted between 2019 and 2022, the abovementioned rules were enforced. DGAV informed the audit team that, to date, no solution had been found to process such material in Portugal. Category 3 (and Category 1) processing plants were not willing to accept these by- products from hides due to difficulties in processing them. label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls on collection and disposal of ABP are in place at food business operators. However, they are not effective enough to verify compliance with all applicable requirements and can either overlook incorrect disposal of ABP or not ensure timely correction by the operators. There is also an insufficient level of attention paid to the operators' documented procedures for management of ABP. Finally, no regular controls have been implemented to verify burial conditions in areas designated as remote. All of this weakens the guarantees that ABP and DP generated by food business operators are collected and disposed of in line with EU rules.

Whilst there is a framework in place for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, underpinned by systematic communication and cooperation between the relevant authorities, certain organisational aspects weaken the effectiveness of the control system. These include the lack of (updated) documented procedures and arrangements and the failure to develop and implement an appropriate monitoring plan. It is likely that the shortfall in the implementation of control verification procedures hindered the ability of the competent authority to identify and address those shortcomings. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU

The BFSA stated that, with limited exceptions, it did not have documented procedures in place for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods of animal origin entering the EU, including on transhipped consignments, consignments in transit and channelling of consignments, which is not in line with article 12(1) of the OCR.

The limited exceptions concern a documented procedure for the use of TRACES-NT in the case of unsatisfactory laboratory results for certain consignments of goods of animal origin, and a standard operating procedure for the sampling of food of animal origin, the latter of which the audit team noted had not been updated as appropriate in line with Article 12(3)(b) of the OCR.

In contrast to finding 15, the BFSA has documented procedures in place for official controls on food of non-animal origin entering the EU, for the onward transportation and transfer to control points of consignments of food and feed of non-animal origin, and for the exchange of information in iRASFF, which is in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR. A further procedure concerning the action to take for non-compliant consignments of (8) https://btsfacademy.eu/training/ 6 food of non-animal origin and food contact materials had not been updated as appropriate in line with Article 12(3)(b) of the OCR.

The BFSA also stated there are no documented arrangements in place for the implementation of measures on consignments of animals and goods referred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR, which is not in line with Article 12(1) and Article 64(3)(d) of the OCR.

The system in place ensures that consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are presented for official controls, and that controls with few exceptions are generally carried out in line with guidelines and documented procedures and Union legislation.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for meat inspection on bovine, ovine, porcine and poultry that covers most relevant aspects. However, the effectiveness of AMI and, to a larger extent, PMI is impacted by a number of systemic shortcomings. 5.4 RAPID ALERT SYSTEM FOR FOOD AND FEED (RASFF) Legal requirements Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715 (IMSOC Regulation). Findings

The CCA has adopted several legal acts and guidelines, relevant for the scope of this audit, in recent years. According to the CCA, the changes introduced by these are mainly updates to reflect changes made to EU legislation. The CAs and food business operators (FBOs) are implementing the updated legislation and guidance documents. However, · Guidance No 9504/2021 (on meat inspection), contains certain provisions for post- mortem inspection (PMI) in red meat slaughterhouses that are not in line with Regulation (EU) 2019/627 (see paragraphs 49 and 50). · Guideline No 9853/2017 (on microbiological criteria for foodstuffs) contains certain provisions that are not in line with Regulation (EC) No

There are cooperation and coordination mechanisms in place within DVFA's departments and a system of notification of other CAs when the non-compliances identified need follow-up by other CAs. The OVs at slaughterhouse level notify welfare and animal identification issues that may concern the transport or farm level. Nonetheless, the outcome of on the farm/database controls is not considered when making decisions on animal identification (see paragraphs 40 and 41). 4 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest

The CA considers that, the recommendation on enforcing provisions that animals are clean prior to slaughter, has been addressed. Nonetheless, the findings at the time of the current audit suggest that the recommendation was not adequately addressed. AMI in cattle did not include checking animal cleanliness (see paragraph 39). This was replaced by CA audits of FBOs' systems for dealing with dirty cattle. 5.2.6 Enforcement

In large slaughterhouses the OVs permanently present during slaughter perform AMI. In the small slaughterhouses, private veterinarians employed on a contract basis for AMI perform this task. AMI includes controls on most of the relevant aspects (e.g. health status, identification, food chain information and animal welfare). However, AMI does not include verification of FBOs compliance with their obligation to ensure that animals have a clean hide, skin or fleece, so as to avoid any unacceptable risk of contamination of the fresh meat during slaughter. This is not in line with Article 11(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Animal health and animal welfare findings of AMI are reported to the relevant services 9 and on-farm investigations are conducted when considered necessary. However, the OVs allow slaughter for human consumption of unidentified or incorrectly identified bovine animals in the absence of an adequate investigation to ascertain the identity of the animal.

When a bovine is presented for slaughter with eartags of an animal that appears as belonging to the category of stolen/dead on large grazing areas (and not found) in the central bovine database or is without eartags, the owner is allowed to make a sworn declaration for a change of details in the central bovine database. The CA allows slaughter for human consumption if the breed, sex and age of the animal matches the (new details) notified by the farmer and accepted by the database. The CA does not receive the outcome of a(possible) investigation before making the decision on the animal. (2)

In the cases assessed, the OVs were aware that red meat animals need to be inspected less than 24 hours after arrival and less than 24 hours before slaughter and had agreed arrangements with the FBOs to ensure this happens, including when animals were delivered during the weekend. AMI of all animals is documented. Nonetheless, should the agreed arrangements for the FBOs (to call the OV for AMI when new animals are presented for slaughter) fail to deliver, there is no reconciliation carried out between the number of animals passing AMI with the number passing PMI, nor are the OVs required to do so.

The CA has put provisions in place for AMI to be carried out at the holding of provenance. This option is used for emergency slaughter of animals and for animals that are difficult to handle. Approximately 350 private veterinarians have been designated as OVs for AMI on farms. The designation was not precluded by training or a system of measures to safeguard potential conflict of interest. The CA organised an information session and plans for more such sessions to be delivered to reach all designated OVs. Ante-mortem inspection - poultry

In the cases assessed there were sufficient OVs/OAs to cover all inspection posts during production and for all carcases to receive PMI. There are arrangements in place for PMI including official controls for Trichinella in pigs, tuberculosis and cysticercosis in bovines and pigs. The "in principle" standard are Articles 18-24 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, while in certain circumstances (e.g. for outdoor pigs) the inspection maintains the additional incisions and palpations as per previous Regulation (EC) No 854/2004. Nonetheless, certain provisions of Guidance 9504/2021 differ from the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 · The guidance allows carcases with certain pathology and contaminat

In addition, PMI does not check for the presence/safe removal of SRM, contrary to the requirements of Article 17(d)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Carcases with SRM are health-marked, contrary to the requirements of Article 45(q) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The OVs do not subsequently check if the FBO has removed SRM from all health-marked carcases either. The OVs check FBOs' procedures for SRM removal, during audits on related FBOs procedures, a few times a year.

The cows' udders were not inspected unless they went for human consumption and/or pet food in the case assessed. The OV explained this is in line with the clarification received from central level. However, this approach is contrary to the requirements of Article 19(1)(k) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

The audit team identified different additional gaps in PMI in the sheep and bovine slaughterhouses visited, contrary to the requirements of Articles 12(3), 17 and 45(r) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627: · In the large bovine slaughterhouse, the inadequate presentation of the spleen by the FBO (long highlighted by the OV, but not addressed) resulted in the spleen not being routinely inspected;. · In the small slaughterhouses, several gaps in PMI had been noted by the audit team, but not by the supervisor present that day [e.g. in the sheep slaughterhouse, the OV was not checking the lower part of the carcase (and therefore missing several carcases with contamination in the lower part), not palpati

The CA has arrangements in place for poultry PMI to be carried out by OVs and OAs as well as in some cases by authorised slaughterhouse staff under the supervision of the OV. The slaughterhouse staff is authorised to perform certain PMI tasks only after undergoing relevant training and passing an assessment by the CA. The arrangements for poultry PMI were found to be largely satisfactory in the case assessed, where slaughterhouse staff were performing PMI, apart from the absence of a system for the OV/OA to check viscera and body cavities on a representative sample for each flock, contrary to the requirements of Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 5.3.2 Official controls over food busine

The OVs check FBO procedures to ensure that only animals/batches of animals that are properly identified and traceable to origin are slaughtered and these checks have been satisfactory in the cases assessed, with FBOs bringing inadequately identified and unidentified animals to the attention of the OVs. Nonetheless, the action taken by the CA in these cases is not fully satisfactory (see paragraphs 40 and 41). General and specific hygiene requirements, including HACCP based procedures Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and Article 46 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 13 Findings

Health-marking is applied either by the OV or by the FBO under the supervision of the OV. In the case assessed, the health mark was kept under official control outside of working hours. Controls on the application of identification marks are included in the audit plan and are carried out at least once a year. However, contrary to the requirements of Article 48(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the health mark is also applied in certain cases when there are grounds for declaring the meat unfit for human consumption (see paragraphs 49-52).

paragraph_text: The CA notified the national derogations and adaptations. However, given that the notification of national measures on delayed PMI, carried out in accordance with the procedure laid down in Directive (EU) 2015/1535, was incomplete, the Commission has not granted the (already implemented) derogation. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 6, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. 3 Findings 5.2.1 Structure and organisation

In accordance with the same procedure, the CA notified the national derogation on increased (slaughterhouse capacity) thresholds for performing delayed PMI compared to those provided in point (a), (i) and (ii) of Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. However, the notification concerns 11 slaughterhouses whilst, at the time of the audit, delayed PMI was performed in most of the small slaughterhouses in the scope of the audit. Contrary to the requirements of Article 13(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the CA did not take into consideration, in the above notification, the combined annual production of the establishments where delayed PMI is performed. Conclusions on legislation and implemen

The CA structure, organisation and resources, including support, are adequate, overall, to deliver effective controls in large slaughterhouses. However, this is not the case for small slaughterhouses, where the system relies heavily on a small number of staff to perform audits, act as supervisors, determine training needs and deliver the training of OVs. This system has proved inadequate in terms of detecting poor hygiene practices as well as poor staff performance/knowledge gaps and has resulted in ineffective controls.

The CA provides training to the official control staff, including OVs and official auxiliaries (OAs). In the absence of a national system to deliver OV training in line with Article 13 and Chapter I of Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2019/624, the supervisors assess the training needs upon recruitment of an OV and deliver the training considered needed. The CA highlighted that a centrally developed/harmonised training is in the process of being developed. The training needs for OVs already active are identified during routine supervision and then custom made for the respective OV, sometimes also delivered by the supervisor. When the supervisor is not able to adequately detect knowledge gaps and

The training topics for a new OV (developed by one of the four supervisors of OVs in small slaughterhouses) did not cover aspects on which the OV is required to perform controls such as animal welfare and animal identification. In addition, no control procedure is available for the latter. The OV performing AMI, PMI and some animal welfare controls in one of the small slaughterhouses visited did not have a satisfactory knowledge of PMI requirements (see paragraph 52) and of certain animal welfare 5 requirements (e.g. 0.7- 0.8A for 15 seconds was considered better than the 1A for effective electric stun).

The OVs benefit from the technical support of the supervisors. The supervisors for the teams in large slaughterhouse met by the audit team were knowledgeable in the areas under review. Nonetheless, the audit team identified gaps in the knowledge of the supervisor for small slaughterhouses, met during the audit (e.g. as regards prevention of cross-contamination and PMI ­ see paragraphs 52, 60-62, 64). The supervisor also had an incorrect understanding of certain animal welfare requirements (e.g. considering captive bolt a stun-to-kill method for which effectiveness of stunning did not need to be checked).

As the supervisor is the only CA member of staff performing controls on FBOs' hygiene requirements, as well as supervision of OVs contracted for AMI, PMI and some animal welfare controls, these knowledge gaps have impacted the effectiveness of the controls in the small establishments visited during the current audit (see paragraphs 60-62, 64, 66). The same supervisor was in charge of controls in 25 small slaughterhouses, assessing the training needs, training and supervising the contracted OVs in these establishments. This questions the effectiveness of the controls in the remaining small slaughterhouses.

The design and implementation of the official control system does not provide assurance that controls over EU requirements and their enforcement are carried out correctly and uniformly across the 15 large and 44 low-capacity slaughterhouses. The system does not ensure that controls in respect of general hygiene requirements and welfare during slaughter actually take place with an appropriate frequency, or at all.

There are shortcomings in the identification, rating, action taken and follow-up of enforcement of non-compliances by the establishment OVs and in the CA supervision of those OVs that weaken the effectiveness of the enforcement that takes place.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The time dedicated to official controls by OVs in low-capacity slaughterhouses, other than to carry out AMI and PMI, is very limited and affects the OVs' capacity to observe and assess the slaughterhouse hygiene practices and take necessary enforcement action where and when required.

Senior Meat Inspection Unit officers carry out approximately six `assessment and guidance' visits to slaughterhouses annually, where meat inspection arrangements and controls by OVs are checked and assessed. Normally, two of these visits take place in large establishments, the rest in low-capacity ones. The Animal Welfare and Identification Unit also carries out control visits to slaughterhouses. Regional managers' visits focus on staff support and HR-style aspects but also on mentoring and advising staff on meat inspection and official controls matters.

Taking into account the number of approved establishments and the frequency of visits, large slaughterhouses should receive an `assessment and guidance' visit every seven or eight years, and a low-capacity establishment once every ten or eleven years.(2)

The system to prioritise slaughterhouses to be visited by senior officers considers aspects like issues identified by OVs and enforcement taken. Establishments where OVs identify no or very few non-compliances are given low priority.

There are no regular checks at central level in order to establish if the OVs in approved slaughterhouses have a system in place to ensure that all the required controls are carried out within the agreed three-year cycle. In all establishments reviewed by the audit team, there were some controls that had not been completed at all during the last three years. Examples included `compliance with requirements of approval' or `vermin control'.

Although the CA provided some good examples of suitable and timely enforcement that had achieved positive outcomes, the audit team observed several examples where non- compliances were not identified or inadequate rating was given to those non- compliances that had actually been found. As lower rating non-compliance do not require the FBO to produce an action plan to resolve them or the OV to follow them up, an inadequately rated non-compliance has an impact on the likelihood of it being satisfactorily resolved.

Equally, there was also evidence of lack of follow up actions by OVs in some instances that the rating of a non-compliance required it, to ensure the FBO remedied the identified problems and/ or prevented the recurrence of the problem. label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The delivery of official controls is adequate in preventing bovine animals unfit for (slaughter for) human consumption from entering the food chain. Nonetheless, the continued performance of AMI and PMI by OA without the presence of the OV in the slaughterhouse is contrary to EU requirements (except for PMI in low throughput slaughterhouses). The same applies to the absence of visual inspection of udders and its lymph nodes and the visual inspection of the gastro-intestinal tract and palpation of the gastric and mesenteric lymph nodes. It is necessary that the official controls verify that operators follow their existing procedures on dirty animals and carcases and that those are fit for pur

Currently, green offal and udders are not inspected as part of PMI. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 19 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The audit team was informed that the CCA is in the process of drafting a guideline clarifying the regulatory requirements, but noted that the requirements in question were already contained in EU legislation well preceding the above Regulation (i.e. in repealed Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council). Red offal including kidneys are examined during PMI, as required.

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: National legislation and guidelines necessary to ensure implementation and/or enforcement of the EU requirements applicable to the meat sector are in place and they are largely in line with EU legislation, with the exception of one guideline, which was not up-to-date and, as a result, certain provisions of its content are contrary to EU legislation.

However, the audit team noted that the guidance on ante-mortem inspection (AMI) of poultry at the holding of provenance (DGAV Order 23/G/2016) allows that "approved veterinarians" perform AMI at the holding of origin (EU legislation requires that AMI should be carried out by an official veterinarian (OV)). In this regard, DGAV informed the audit team that this document had been in place before the new EU legislation was applicable and it has not been updated as yet. They explained that the procedure was applied in the past, and in a small number of slaughterhouses due to the lack of available human resources. They added that this option is no longer practiced, as additional OVs have since be

According to national rules, AMI of poultry can be done at slaughterhouse by OVs or, when necessary, at the holding of origin by approved veterinarians. DGAV explained that "when necessary" means when the CAs detect a lack of OVs at a specific slaughterhouse for a particular day or period. In this regard, there is a specific procedure under Order 23/G/2016 (see paragraph 3), which describes the steps to follow and, among other things, requires OAs to perform a simplified AMI under the responsibility of the OV. DGAV added that at the time of this audit this procedure was not being applied in any slaughterhouse and AMI is always carried out by OVs at the slaughterhouse.

paragraph_text: The reporting by FBO to CABs of non-compliances concerning the quality of raw milk (PC and/or SCC), and detection of residues of antibiotics in raw milk, on a monthly basis only, hinders effective follow-up, which is further impacted by systemic delays at the level of the CAB. Equally, positive findings for residues of antibiotics/inhibitory substances are, in general, not timely followed up with official controls at holding level. This is not in line with Article 138.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 50.2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 5.5 CONTROLS ON RAW MILK Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.
