label_heading: Conclusions on controls on raw milk upon collection
paragraph_text: The FBOs' systems in place in relation to SCC and PC in raw co milk is generally implemented in line with the requirements with Section IX of Annex III, Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, whereas the verification and enforcement action by the CAs after notification of non-compliances in relation to these parameters and/or after detecting antibiotic residues in raw milk is not in line with Article 138.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 50.2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 as it is done with a delay.

Cases of non-compliances in relation to raw milk quality (PC, SCC or antibiotic residues/inhibitory substances) notified monthly by dairy establishments are usually followed up during the next planned inspection, and not immediately after the county veterinarians receive the reports from the CAB unit dealing with controls over the primary sector. This practice hampers the CAs efforts to take action to determine the origin and extent of the non-compliance in line with Article 138.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The immediate measures are left to the dairy establishments and comprise an immediate stop of further deliveries in case of antibiotic residues. Milk payment reduction is also used by 1

Although the presence of antibiotic residues was deemed a critical control point (CCP) in the HACCP plan of the third larger dairy plant visited by the audit team, the milk trucks were only tested once weekly randomly for inhibitory substances/antibiotic residues, and the test result of the raw milk silo was used to decide if the milk was fit for human consumption. This practice was in line with the branch guidelines. In addition, the use by FBOs of rapid tests that detect beta-lactams and tetracyclines only, implies that other possible antibiotic residues in raw milk would remain undetected.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls on raw milk upon collection
paragraph_text: The delays in the FBOs reporting of incidents where raw milk has tested positive of residues of VMPs, combined with the situation that allows the FBOs to use the raw milk silo as a testing point for antibiotic residues to determine if the milk is fit to be processed for human consumption, leads to situations where raw milk containing antibiotic residues could be processed into products for human consumption.

The CA have accepted the branch approach that the raw milk reception silo is the control point for inhibitory substances/antibiotic residues in raw milk (in combination with the system that milk from each holding is tested for antibiotic residues at least once monthly and testing of the raw milk from at least 3 trucks monthly) to determine if it can be processed for human consumption. At silo sampling stage, any possible antibiotic residue in raw milk is largely diluted and the probability of detecting it is very low. One of the dairy establishments visited (part of a chain) had chosen not to test the trucks for inhibitory substances, which is not in line with the industry guideline.

Although the presence of antibiotic residues was deemed a critical control point (CCP) in the HACCP plan of the third larger dairy plant visited by the audit team, the milk trucks were only tested once weekly randomly for inhibitory substances/antibiotic residues, and the test result of the raw milk silo was used to decide if the milk was fit for human consumption. This practice was in line with the branch guidelines. In addition, the use by FBOs of rapid tests that detect beta-lactams and tetracyclines only, implies that other possible antibiotic residues in raw milk would remain undetected.

The audit team noted that, if the overall assessment is "Favourable" or "Favourable with comments", no corrective action is requested or enforced for identified non-compliance. This is only triggered if the inspections are "Unfavourable", which means that lower grade (less severe) non-compliances are up to the operators' discretion to address. This is not in line with Article 138(1)(b) of the OCR.

According to the CA, a new checklist has been developed designed to allow for the follow up of identified non-compliances, in order to prevent these being neglected and perpetuated. The audit team noted that the above-mentioned checklist does not necessarily improve enforcement, in particular for less severe non-compliances, as: a) the system does not apply to BMO inspections. This means that non-compliances identified from BMOs are not subject to follow up if their inspections are assessed as "Favourable" or "Favourable with comments". b) The checklist deals with non-compliances assigned three or more points; those with one point are not followed up, irrespective of their total number.

The provision to allow operators to produce in approved establishments "under the approval" of another operator, and the way this is implemented, has a negative impact on ability of the control system to verify and ensure compliance with the legal requirements of all operators involved and, consequently, on the safety, hygiene and traceability of fishery products produced by those operators under such an arrangement.

In response to queries from the audit team in respect of the operation of the various official controls over operators working "under the approval" of an approval owner (option b(ii) above), the CA indicated these cases to be known, and fully within the scope of official controls: a) an applicant operator who plans to work with others in an "under the approval" arrangement, should indicate this on the floor plan with the approval application. b) All operators involved should be registered and have a registration number with an address of the establishment where the activity will take place. c) Operators that will work "under the approval" should apply to the LCU for approval using the applic

The audit team noted that: a) Question 45 of the "Frequently asked questions" in the section on approvals on the CA website is only explicit in terms of time/space separation of activities and products for cases of individual approval of all operators involved. It is therefore unclear why a prospective approval owner would need to indicate the intention to operate a working "under the approval" arrangement on the floor plan. Moreover, such an arrangement may be entered into at any time, even after the approval. 9 b) Although the approval application requires operators to indicate their intent to work "under the approval", it does not require an attestation or acknowledgement from the approva

The official control reports drafted did not include references to non-compliances identified in relation to the activities of these four operators, but do not clarify whether this was because they were compliant, or because they were not present and active during the official controls. Upon request by the audit team, the CA performed an official control in order to verify whether progress has been made towards compliance of the operator, during which two additional operators were identified o

Training programmes are in place and officials have in general sufficient knowledge and experience to perform official controls. However, the training provided was not sufficient to enable inspectors performing routine inspections to reliably check basic aspects of the FBO's HACCP.

SVA and CAFIA have put staff training arrangements in place, addressing one of the recommendations from the 2013 audit. Any newly recruited veterinary official in SVA is required to pass an attestation within three years, which includes generic knowledge on legislation, hygiene (including a two hour HACCP module) as well as animal welfare and animal health. SVA and CAFIA also provided examples of the staff participation in the European Commission Better Training for Safer Food programme.

SVA provides compulsory annual training on selected topics and asks staff to choose additional voluntary training from a catalogue of training topics. The training catalogue offered 106 courses in 2019, 112 in 2020 and 128 in 2020. The audit team noted that no specific training in fishery products or HACCP was available in the catalogue.

The Ministry of Agriculture organises online training since 2011, available to SVA and CAFIA officials, which includes module No. 9 on HACCP-based procedures. According to the CA, this module requires about 6 hours of self-study and a final test. This online training was followed by 88 and 79 officials in 2020 and 2021, respectively. 4

The audit team noted a solid HACCP knowledge in the officials performing the FBOs audits. These auditors receive compulsory training on basic HACCP (23 hours) to be lead auditors, and are offered voluntary training on advanced HACCP (15 hours). The audit team also reviewed the HACCP training provided in 2018 and new training sessions scheduled in 2022 and found these satisfactory.

According to SVA statement, within routine inspections, inspectors need basic knowledge about HAACP, as they must assess FBO HACCP basic elements such as layout, critical control points, surveillance records, corrective action taken, etc.

The audit team interviewed SVA inspectors from two RVAs, with different years of experience, taking part in routine inspections, noting that in some cases, inspectors lacked sufficient knowledge of the HACCP principles to perform the assigned tasks. This is not in line with Article 5.4(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in respect of the subject matter included in its Annex II, Chapter I points (5) and (7). Transparency and confidentiality

SVA publishes a list of Food establishments ­ according to EU specifications, including section: VIII Fishery Products7. The published list does not capture this information and as result, is not possible to know if a particular establishment from the approved list is in operation (subject to regular SVA checks) or not (SVA checks suspended).

As a consequence, there are approved establishments included in the list, without regular controls, on the basis that they are not in operation. SVA could not provide assurances that those establishments continue to comply with the approval requirements. This is not in line with Article 4(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and Articles 18(1) and 148(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

According to SVA, there is a system in place to keep track of the inoperative approved establishments with a record of this in the OIS information system, in the T02 list (self- discontinued establishments). SVA inspectors have access in the OIS system to establishments data such as address, list of individual establishments, whether or not they are active, list of approved/registered activities, etc. They have limited access to the OIS information system only as regards inspection findings. In one case, the approval (and the HACCP based procedures) covered one activity (freezing) that in practice was not being carried out at that establishment. The freezing activity was in fact taking place at a neighbouring establishment (also approved) but the activity was covered in the approval the first establishment. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 148(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In another case, the audit team noted that the MFCA had approved a collective facility despite the absence of: a) documented procedures indicating the activities carried out, including procedures to ensure traceability, b) a suitable HACCP plan; and, c) production records (see paragraph 72.d below). Since its first approval, MFCA did not control regularly this establishment (the control frequency was not followed). This is contrary to both the FFA and the EU rules concerning the approval of establishments of food business operators ­ Article 148(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/625 (6).

The controls over approved establishments are carried out using the OIVA guidance and are recorded in the VATI system. However, in half of the establishments visited, the control frequency determined for these establishments on the basis of the risk categorisation, was not followed.

According to the information provided by FFA and MFCAs, fishing vessels are not controlled within the set frequencies. Despite being included at national level in the Finnish MANCP, the audit team did not find evidence in the relevant MFCAs that their control plans follow the MANCP and include controls of fishing vessels (food safety requirements). From the 56 vessels (see section 4.2 above), in 2019, 11 fishing vessels (over 12 metres) were controlled, 14 in 2020, and 6 in 2021. paragraph_text: The official controls carried out by the MCFAs do not include all the relevant provisions set out in Chapter I of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Organoleptic examinations, random testing for histamine and risk-based parasite testing are not carried out as required. With regard to organoleptic examinations, the audit team noted that the MCFAs visited do not perform them, despite it being clearly requested in the FFA guidance that such examinations be carried out. FFA indicated that staff from ELY carries out some organoleptic examinations during the landing controls, however incidental records of those controls are not made available to the food control authorities. The audit team also noted that the FFA guidance document provides for generic descriptions of organoleptic characteristics as standards and not Regulation (EC) 2406/96 as indicated in Chapter I(A) of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Specifically for histamine, the FFA guidance indicates that "sampling for histamine shall be included in official controls, unless the activity is very small and the operator can demonstrate that self-monitoring is adequate". Additionally, for imported products tested at the EU border, it indicates that official sampling is not required.

In addition, the possibility of using laboratories not designated by the authority(ies) does not comply with the above requirements above. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The official control system in place is clearly organised and supported by extensive and detailed written instructions/guidance. There is a system in place for official controls of approved establishments. This failure to comply with frequencies of controls compromises the effectiveness of the official control system to achieve its objectives to verify compliance with EU rules.

There are 11 factory vessels approved in Greece. EFET stated that the risk associated with factory vessels was set, by default, as high risk. Consequently, the frequency of 11 controls should be from 6 to 18 months. From the data submitted by EFET, the audit team noted that the set frequency had not been respected, with the exception of two cases. For six of the vessels, the last inspection took place prior to 2012 (in one case the last inspection was in 2007). In another case, the last inspection was carried out in 2016 and for two others, in 2018. This is not in line with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and Article 67 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

The CAs responsible for the official control system over the production of fishery products are designated and their structure and organisation is suitable to perform their tasks. However, the significant shortage of staff and the limited risk criteria prevents the controls to be fully effective.

Controls at approved establishments are implemented and cover all applicable EU requirements. The stipulated frequencies, however, cannot be met due to the low staff numbers, which compromises the outcome of the risk-based assessment which the CA had carried out to determine an adequate frequency of controls, in line with Art. 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Up to 50% of the work of this staff is to handle and follow up incidents and notifications (8 424 notifications in 2021). The CCA stated that food safety topics are not included within the scope of the controls on this type of operator. This is not in line with Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The knowledge and currently available guidance does not allow the OVs to be aware or identify the correct course of action they should take in case of unfrequently presented situations related to cattle identification, in particular the presence of animals with only one ear tag.

Several of the OVs interviewed did not have a clear understanding of what actions to take in the small number of cases where farmers present cattle for AMI with only one ear tag, instead of the compulsory two. Some OVs considered that those bovine animals did not have suitable identification and therefore could not enter the human food chain.
The available guidance, in the form of methodological instructions issued by the 3 CCA, for OVs on AMI tasks and animal identification, is silent on how to handle animals with only one ear tag.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The CA has not enforced the requirement that pens in the lairages of approved slaughterhouses clearly display information on the the maximum number of animals that could be kept in them, as required by Regulation (EC) 1099/2009.

None of the slaughterhouse FBOs visited had clearly displayed the maximum number of animals that could be kept in each pen in the lairage, as required by Regulation (EC) 1099/2009 on the protection of animals at the time of killing.

paragraph_text: PMI is in general carried out in line with EU requirements but the practical inspection arrangements and facilities are, in some of the establishments, not fully suitable and can lead to contaminated carcases being passed as fit for human consumption.

Initial validation data for screening of stilbenes and steroids were revised by the laboratory in response to the findings made in the 2020 audit report (see finding 32 of that report) to eliminate most of the obvious discrepancies. However, some data at the lowest calibration levels still showed that the performance characteristics (e.g., identical repeatability and reproducibility values for methylboldenone and 17- clostebol chlorandrostenedione) were not in line with legal requirements (8). These shortcomings in the method performance characteristics were neither spotted nor evaluated by the laboratory. In addition, the calculation of CC was not in line with legal provisions (9).

In the method validation file for confirmation of thyrostats, a number of recoveries were outside the acceptable range laid down in EU legislation (10). This was not noticed by the laboratory and thus no assessment of the possible influence of that phenomenon on the suitability of the method had been carried out. The linearity of the calibration curve for propylthiouracil was below the criteria set by the laboratory ­ however, this was not reflected and concluded on in the validation documentation. The laboratory representative informed the audit team that the revalidation of the method was planned for 2025.

In the validation documentation for the screening and confirmatory method for beta- agonists, there was inadequate assessment of several method performance characteristics (e.g., recoveries outside the established range (10), reproducibilities identical to repeatabilities (8)).

At the time of the audit, the screening and confirmatory method for chloramphenicol, thiamphenicol and florfenicol was under validation. Consequently, no properly validated method was available in the laboratory for monitoring residues of these analytes.

The validation of the screening method for antibacterial substances was stated to be finalised just prior to the audit. The available documentation included only data on specificity and results of measurements at one fortification level for each analyte/matrix combination. This level was assumed as the CC with no justification for that decision. This is not in line with legal requirements (11). Since the validation did not address all of the performance characteristics required for quantitative screening methods (12), the method could not be considered as properly validated.

In the three TSUs visited, sampling was in most of the cases examined neither targeted nor performed without prior notice being given to the operator. Most of the samples were taken randomly by food inspectors (at slaughterhouses and from honey) and by veterinary inspectors (for eggs, milk, fish). This is not in line with EU requirements (25).

While national procedures clearly state that, in line with applicable EU legal requirements (26), RCP samples can only be taken by trained and authorised sampling officers, this was not always the case. In one TSU, samples were regularly taken by official veterinarians engaged in ante- and post-mortem inspection at slaughter. Whilst these veterinarians were likely capable of carrying out the sampling correctly, they had not been trained for the task. This is not in line with pertinent EU requirements (27).

Contrary to applicable EU requirements (21), the choice of animals to be sampled was not risk-based but random with no justification given. For aquaculture finfish, sampling was carried out exclusively at processing plants on fish ready to be placed on the market and not at all stages of production, as required by EU legislation, which stipulates that, for Group A (illegal) substances, samples must be taken from fish at all stages of farming (28).

The audit team noted that, in two visited TSUs, sometimes it happened that a single sample taken was registered in the records as several individual samples that were originally planned. Therefore, the number of samples actually collected was lower than the number indicated in the plan.

Although the authorities have made efforts to increase the sensitivity of surveillance for HPAI in both wild birds and domestic poultry, neither component was effective as an early warning system to better prevent the evolution of both epizootics. The authorities are aware of it and, in particular for domestic poultry, they are working on further strengthening that surveillance.

Surveillance for wild birds is regularly adapted according to the perceived risk of introduction of HPAI, and is enhanced in all territories where the level of risk increases, and in restricted zones around outbreaks. This resulted in a significantly higher number of samples taken from wild birds once the first outbreaks were confirmed, as that was considered a period with increased risk. However, at the time when the first few index outbreaks were detected in poultry in 2020, for which the authorities determined that introduction of the HPAI virus by wildlife was the most likely cause, the circulation of that HPAI virus had not yet been detected in wild birds in the affected areas.

The inability of the surveillance to detect promptly the virus in wild birds contrasts with the fact that the authorities considered circulation of the virus in them as the main cause for most of the initial outbreaks in the region. The NRL confirmed this a posteriori by virus phylogenetic studies. That sub-optimal effectiveness of the early warning system in wild birds cannot be considered in line with provisions laid down in Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the need to design and apply surveillance in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to the objectives pursued and to the risk factors involved in order to ensure the timely detection of the presence of

ANSES experts pointed out that passive surveillance alone had been sometimes ineffective to detect some of the outbreaks, due to a longer incubation period with excretion of virus for several days prior to the clinical stage of the disease. In areas with 9 a high density of poultry, this probably led to fast undetected spread of infection and an immediate overflow of cases that surpassed the disease management and control capacity.

Despite raised and maintained public awareness, the delayed notification of suspect cases by certain operators, as noted on the establishments visited by the audit team, likely contributed to the spread of the disease in areas with a high density of poultry.

The audit team reviewed files related to HPAI suspicions. In most cases, business operators and private veterinarians had notified quickly to the authority abnormal mortality rates and clinical signs. However, the audit team noted on two visited establishments, unnecessary delays, of three and one day, respectively. In second instance, although the establishment immediately notified a suspicion to a private veterinarian, he suspected bacteriological infection and only on following day he took correct decision to notify the suspicion to the authority. This delay occurred in the area with a high density of poultry during ongoing epizootic. That is not in line with requirements laid down in Art

Despite plenty of evidence on the inappropriate application of, and insufficient compliance with national requirements on biosecurity in poultry establishments in the areas affected by both HPAI epizootics, the competent authorities failed to correct those shortcomings (already noted in the previous report) and enforce those requirements before they started. This played a major role in facilitating the introduction of the disease and its further spread. The authorities only recently linked 14 the payment of compensation to compliance with biosecurity requirements, acknowledging that before the recent epizootics they had lost an opportunity to incentivise that compliance and to make HPAI prev

The recently published ANSES analysis of the epidemiological information obtained from the recent HPAI epizootics helps the authorities to understand the main risk factors present in the affected areas that contributed to the introduction and spread of the disease. The authorities have now sufficient information to tailor more effective risk-mitigating practices to better prevent the occurrence of HPAI epizootics in the future.

label_heading: Conclusions on repopulation of affected holdings
paragraph_text: The authorities allowed repopulation of establishments affected by outbreaks of HPAI only after verifying properly that there was no risk of residual infection. This contributed to prevent the resurgence of the disease in those establishments. However, as regards compliance with biosecurity measures to prevent reoccurrence of the disease, the authorities did not verify that lower biosecurity levels, often identified in epidemiological enquires as the most likely source of introduction and spread of the infection, were adequately addressed and strengthened. 5.2 OPERATION OF THE ANIMAL HEALTH EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS SYSTEM ­ APPLICATION OF THE SPECIFIC CONTINGENCY PLAN 5.2.1 Contingency plan ­

label_heading: Conclusions on the application of the specific contingency plan
paragraph_text: The authorities have repeatedly underlined the significant risk that the very high density of poultry represents for the areas affected by the two recent HPAI epizootics, but they have not acted accordingly to reduce it. This, coupled with the sub-optimal application of biosecurity measures to mitigate the prevailing risks of HPAI introduction and spread, raises concerns about their capability to prevent and control new HPAI epizootics.

It was only in September 2021 when the DGAL defined high-risk areas for the likely dissemination of HPAI after introduction of the disease by wild birds (areas at risk of virus spread), taking into account the density of poultry establishments and some other risk factors, mainly related to the presence of domestic waterfowl (see map 5 in Annex 2). In those areas, additional enhanced biosecurity and surveillance measures apply in instances of moderate and high risk of HPAI introduction. The delayed definition of those areas was not in line with Article 3 of Commission implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1136, that was adopted in August 2018 and applicable until 20 April 2021.

During the two recent HPAI epizootics, the low number of epidemiological investigations and their varying quality precluded the authorities from obtaining fundamental information to understand the likely spread of the disease and to identify contact establishments. Hence, they could not take the right decisions to rapidly contain the spread of the disease.

label_heading: Conclusions on the application of the specific contingency plan
paragraph_text: Despite the efforts of the disease control centres established during the epizootics at national and regional level to coordinate the application of the main control measures in the affected areas, they lacked adequate timely expertise, epidemiological analytical capacity and up-to-date knowledge about available resources, to take certain important decisions at critical times. Thus, they could not provide adequate and rapid advice to the departmental authorities in those areas so that they could prioritise their actions to contain and prevent the spread of HPAI effectively.

Similar to what happened in previous HPAI epizootics, due to the sudden increase in the number of outbreaks, the departmental authorities were able to carry out complete epidemiological enquires, mostly, only at the beginning of the two recent epizootics. The audit team estimated that in 70-80% of the cases, they did not carry out an in-depth 11 enquiry. In the most affected département in the south-west region (Landes), the departmental authorities conducted complete enquires for the first eight outbreaks. Later on, they carried out enquires on some additional outbreaks, adding up to 20 in total (there were 341 confirmed outbreaks in this area). A similar situation was noted in the Pays de

The significant delays in the killing and disposal of animals and of other products that could be contaminated with the HPAI virus undermined the effectiveness of other containment measures and likely contributed to the further spread of the disease during the worst of both epizootics. 5.1.2 Diagnosis of HPAI

The shortage of capacity to depopulate (including for preventive killing) animals, to dispose of their carcases and to quickly visit establishments within restricted zones, undermined the effectiveness of the control measures to contain the disease.

label_heading: Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control
paragraph_text: Since the previous Commission audit in 2019 the authorities had not taken adequate steps and had not made the necessary logistical arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity to collect and dispose safely of the carcases in establishments where the presence of HPAI was confirmed or as a preventive measure in areas affected by the disease. This caused significant delays in the depopulation of establishments and accumulation of carcases, which significantly undermined the effectiveness of other measures to contain the spread of the disease. 5.1.5 Cleaning and disinfection

label_heading: Conclusions on the application of the specific contingency plan
paragraph_text: The authorities did not fulfil the undertakings given in response to the previous audit to update and complete the national contingency plan for HPAI, to adequately reinforce the most important components of the emergency preparedness system for the high-risk areas affected by previous HPAI epizootics, and to assess, and improve if necessary, the level of preparedness of the departmental authorities to cope with an epizootic. Hence, they could not avail of sufficiently qualified and trained human resources with access to all necessary operational tools to succeed with the rapid and effective containment of the disease.

During both recent epizootics, as the number of new outbreaks sharply increased, the resources available for killing and disposal of carcasses were quickly depleted. Some establishments could only be culled three to four days after confirmation, even up to seven days at some stages in 2022 during the 2021/22 epizootic (see chart 4 in Annex 2). For example, in one of the establishments visited by the audit team, a prolonged keeping of live infected animals potentially shedding the virus, facilitated infection spread and caused some secondary outbreaks. In addition, due to high mortality and delays in killing, when killing started many birds had already died. These shortcomings are not in comp

However, in both epizootics, a large proportion of the flocks subject to pre-emptive culling were already infected, indicating that this culling arrived late. In the most affected département (Landes), during the 2020/21 HPAI epizootic, out of 160 depopulated establishments, 70 were already positive for HPAI.

The exponential increase in the number of outbreaks in the 2021/22 HPAI epizootic, and the subsequent overflow of carcasses to be disposed of, exceeded the available 17 processing capacity and made preventive killing no longer feasible, as noted in the most affected département in the Pays de la Loire region (Vendée).

The shortcomings mentioned in the previous points did not allow the competent authorities to accelerate the killing of susceptible poultry within the restricted zone when the epidemiological situation so required. The actions were not in line with provisions of Article 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

However, due to the rapid increase in the number of affected establishments and poultry in the Pays de la Loire region, the capacity of rendering plants in the area was quickly exceeded. This slowed down the killing process and postponed some of the activities until the accumulated amount of killed animals could be disposed of safely. To cope with the lack of capacity and to prevent further delays in killing of poultry, the authorities opted for burial on site of carcasses, which they did at purposely-made landfills in some of the establishments affected. They also stored ABP temporarily in some affected establishments and other designated sites. Representatives of the authorities met conced

At the time of the audit the departmental contingency plans had not yet been updated to anticipate and deal with such exceptional situations. They had not included details and pre-arrangements on the alternative methods of disposal of carcasses that can be used locally, e.g., a list of sites selected and authorised for storage or burial on site of carcasses.

The shortcomings highlighted in the previous points are not in line with requirements of Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities to take the necessary disease control measures, including disposal of animals that may contribute to the spread of the disease, in the event of an animal health crisis. Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control

In general, the departmental Plans for Sanitary Emergencies contain the necessary instructions and ready-to-use documentation for the authorities to act promptly in the event of a HPAI outbreak, in particular to handle the many administrative tasks involved in those situations. However, as demonstrated in the two recent HPAI epizootics, the authorities found challenging to apply some control measures effectively due to inadequate emergency preparedness. In this context some of the components of those plans were still either missing, not detailed enough or simply not guaranteeing a prompt and effective response (e.g., missing and/or inadequate quality of epidemiological enquires, inadequate e

Although the authorities established restricted zones rapidly once they confirmed the presence of HPAI in poultry establishments, they defined their size and shape without having enough information on the likely spread of the disease and without considering important criteria for doing that. In addition, they did not take full consideration of all appropriate epidemiological criteria for establishing further restricted zones and when they did establish them they did so late. Therefore, those restricted zones were not effective to stop the spread of the disease before it reached epizootic proportions and expanded far beyond the initially affected areas.

The slow start and the difficulty to apply preventive killing at early stages as planned, limited the contribution of that measure to reduce quickly the poultry population in high-risk areas. In some instances, the authorities eventually implemented preventive killing and in the end it contributed to reduce the number of birds and regain control of 20 the situation in some areas heavily affected by HPAI. However, the delayed testing of flocks moved to slaughterhouses meant that many of them were already infected, thus increasing the risk of spreading the infection during critical periods of the epizootics.

The competent authorities granted thousands of derogations to move animals and products of animal origin from restricted zones. Derogations granted for emergency slaughter contributed significantly to the reduction of susceptible animals in restricted areas. However, non-compliances with movement requirements, such as not taking certain risk-mitigating measures and not respecting certain procedural conditions before granting those derogations, compromised the health status of the areas of destination of those commodities. 5.1.4 Animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control 5.1.4.1 Animal welfare considerations

paragraph_text: The authorities did not fulfil the undertakings given in response to the previous audit to update and complete the national contingency plan for HPAI, to adequately reinforce the most important components of the emergency preparedness system for the high-risk areas affected by previous HPAI epizootics, and to assess, and improve if necessary, the level of preparedness of the departmental authorities to cope with an epizootic. Hence, they could not avail of sufficiently qualified and trained human resources with access to all necessary operational tools to succeed with the rapid and effective containment of the disease.

During the 2020/21 HPAI epizootic, the authorities established restricted zones based on the minimum radius required by EU legislation, i.e., a 3 km protection zone and a 10 km surveillance zone, taking also into consideration relevant municipal boundaries (e.g., a zone could be slightly expanded to cover the territory of a municipality until one of those boundaries). However, the authorities did not take into account other important factors, e.g., the disease profile (e.g., whether it was more or less virulent and transmissible depending on the species and production stage affected), the high density of poultry and the network of contacts, to determine if the boundaries and size of the rest

Although the authorities established restricted zones rapidly once they confirmed the presence of HPAI in poultry establishments, they defined their size and shape without having enough information on the likely spread of the disease and without considering important criteria for doing that. In addition, they did not take full consideration of all appropriate epidemiological criteria for establishing further restricted zones and when they did establish them they did so late. Therefore, those restricted zones were not effective to stop the spread of the disease before it reached epizootic proportions and expanded far beyond the initially affected areas.

As explained in section 5.1.3.1, during the 2021/22 HPAI epizootic, the central authority introduced a new strategy to immediately establish in the event of an outbreak further restricted zones in areas considered of high-risk for the introduction and spread of HPAI. When applied, this measure strengthened the application of control measures. Based on the epidemiological situation and the expected fast spread of infection, the departmental authorities, in coordination with the DGAL, established those further restricted zones even in some areas not defined as high-risk areas.

However, as mentioned in 5.1.3.1, those zones were not always applied as instructed. For example, the fast evolution of the epizootic in the Pays de la Loire region confirmed that the authorities did not properly consider the epidemiological situation when they defined the restricted zones and did not establish a further restricted zone immediately. This is not in accordance with Article 64(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 21(1)(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. 5.1.3.4 Derogations to measures applied in protection and surveillance zones

label_heading: Conclusions on the application of the specific contingency plan
paragraph_text: The presence of unregistered commercial establishments in restricted zones, alongside the lack of up-to-date information on the poultry population in the official databases used by the authorities to handle the HPAI outbreaks, increased the volume of control activities necessary to determine the census of poultry present in those zones at the expense of delaying other tasks that were more important to prevent the spread of the disease.

The authorities do not consider the databases fully updated. Notification of data to the BD Avicole database became obligatory only in 2021. The data kept in there, in particular for independent farmers and those collected from censuses in recent epizootics, show that not all commercial establishments are registered yet and, as confirmed by the 26 audit team in the départements visited, data in the database was not fully updated. For example, up to 5% of establishments registered in the database had ceased their operation, while that information had not been updated in the database. That complicates planning of official activities such as visits to establishments located in restricted zones

The shortcomings above had an impact on the application of control measures laid down in Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (Article 64(1) and (2)) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 (Chapters I and II of Part II) requiring the availability of accurate and updated inventories of poultry establishments in the event of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI to establish restricted zones, apply and regularly adapt those measures, and grant derogations therefrom.

However, it took the DGAL several years until this initiative resulted in an instruction and a published self-assessment tool, as they were available only since February 2021. The benchmarks included in the instruction should help the departmental authorities to better assess their preparedness for animal health emergencies, in particular regarding availability of material and human resources, and maintenance of the necessary technical and administrative skills. However, according to representatives of the authorities met, the presence of the HPAI epizootics in recent years precluded any analysis of the progress achieved with those self-assessment tools.

The DGAL presented to the audit team the main pillars of the new strategy they intend to follow in 2022, an action plan to tackle the shortcomings identified during the recent HPAI epizootics. They added that it will be the basis for updating their instructions, including the contingency plan to combat the disease.

paragraph_text: Despite the efforts of the disease control centres established during the epizootics at national and regional level to coordinate the application of the main control measures in the affected areas, they lacked adequate timely expertise, epidemiological analytical capacity and up-to-date knowledge about available resources, to take certain important decisions at critical times. Thus, they could not provide adequate and rapid advice to the departmental authorities in those areas so that they could prioritise their actions to contain and prevent the spread of HPAI effectively.

The authorities used information management tools that included planning and recording of the activities performed on a daily basis by the departmental disease control centres. They shared data retrieved from these centres which with experts of the ANSES and of some veterinary schools. However, during the 2020/21 HPAI epizootic they experienced difficulties to obtain and share some of the data with those experts. During the 2021/22 HPAI epizootic, although the sharing of data with experts improved, the fact that many data were fragmented in several databases and formats made still difficult their analysis, for those experts to contribute rapidly and effectively to the decision-making process

However, despite the improvements noted in this regard since the previous audit, the human resources available were not sufficient to perform timely all the control measures necessary to contain the disease rapidly (e.g., depopulation of affected establishments and pre-emptive killing, official visits to poultry establishments in the restricted zones, completion of epidemiological enquiries). That was not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 13(1)(a) and 43(2)(c)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on responsibilities of the competent authorities to have qualified personnel and an effective organisation to apply disease control measures effectively, and on application of the 29 contin

The effective systems to raise and maintain public awareness contribute to reinforce 10 prevention and surveillance for HPAI. The existing unofficial investigation of situations where there is a reason to suspect of the presence of HPAI potentially delay the establishment of measures to control the disease and prevent the authorities from having an actual overview of the effectiveness of surveillance for early detection of the disease.

According to representatives of several competent authorities, since those tests are not considered part of official controls or other official activities, they do not consider the above as their responsibility. Nevertheless, that is inconsistent with the fact that the unofficial testing activities described in the previous points are framed by the investigation obligations required by German legislation in those cases. Moreover, they are in contradiction with EU requirements laid down in Articles 18(1)(a) and 54(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the obligation to notify the competent authority of any suspicion of HPAI and on the means that the latter shall use for their investigation.

label_heading: Conclusions on diagnosis of avian influenza
paragraph_text: The authorities have not addressed recommendation No 2 of the previous audit report, and there is still use of non-officially designated laboratories to investigate situations where there are reasons to suspect of the presence of HPAI. The absence of official verification on those laboratories precludes the authorities to know whether they fulfil the requirements of an officially designated laboratory (e.g., freedom from any conflict of interest), the real ability of these laboratories to detect the presence of HPAI, and thus, if that is affecting the sensitivity of their surveillance for early detection of HPAI. 5.1.3 General measures in relation to protection and surveillance zones 5.1.3.1

The practice of having investigations by the private sector is a persistent shortcoming and it shows that the competent authorities have not taken action to address recommendation No 1 of the previous audit. This shortcoming is not in line with: Articles 18(1)(a) and 54(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and with Article 3(2)(c)(i) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. 8 5.1.1.2 Epidemiological enquiry ­ Additional control measures

The current use of non-officially designated laboratories for testing in the context of surveillance for early detection of HPAI, is not in compliance with: Articles 37(1) and 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, Article 54(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, Article 3(2)(c)(i) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 and Article 6(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/68. It also means that the authority has not yet addressed recommendation No 2 of the previous audit. 12 Conclusions on diagnosis of avian influenza

The competent authorities only lifted the disease control measures in the protection zones, after proper verification that there was no risk of disease transmission from poultry kept therein. The competent authorities lifted the restrictions in surveillance zones without having sufficient epidemiological evidence to prove absence of virus circulation in those zones. However, there is no evidence that this contributed to worsen the disease situation in areas with a high density of susceptible poultry. 5.1.7 Repopulation of affected establishments

During the 2021-22 HPAI epizootic, for the final lifting of restrictions from surveillance zones, the competent authorities based their decisions on the absence of notification of suspect cases and on clinical checks and tests carried out by official veterinarians in 16 establishments with derogations to move poultry or products. They were in the process of agreeing with the FLI on which type of visits and sampling activities would be suitable to provide sufficient evidence to confirm that the absence of HPAI virus circulation in surveillance zones and, thus, to update their contingency plan accordingly to align it fully with the provisions laid down in Article 55(1) (referring to Article 41

The audit team saw examples of how all competent authorities had updated the relevant contingency plans and operational manuals according to the lessons learnt from the 2016- 17 and 2020-21 epizootics, according to their specific circumstances at regional and district level. Save for a specific outstanding issue regarding official checks on establishments situated within surveillance zones (see section 5.1.6), this was in line with Article 43(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The system in place for the control of ASF in wild boar is effective. The constant reduction in wild boar density over the last three years should help the authorities to slow down the spread of the disease. The effective passive surveillance, the good testing and correct disposal of carcases helps preventing the spread of the disease from wild animals.

The authorities use unclear risk criteria to decide how many and which establishments the counties should target for their biosecurity inspections. Their control plan is poorly implemented and the authorities do not inspect the vast majority of small commercial establishments and non-commercial ones. Therefore, for these sectors, the authorities are not aware of level of compliance with basic 8 requirements, the degree of preparation to avoid the entry and spread of ASF and the awareness of operators regarding the disease. This is a major risk to prevent the disease entering such establishments and to detect the disease promptly if this happened.

The competent authority maintains that there are no "outdoor" pig establishments in Hungary as defined in the EU strategy for ASF, although they keep a list of "outdoor" pig establishments and there are establishments allowing pig access to outdoor pens. The absence of legal definition of "outdoor establishments" creates different interpretations between officials2. All this creates some uncertainty when evaluating the risk of introduction of ASF.

The contingency plans at county level are still incomplete, as they lack guidance for depopulation, information regarding availability of equipment and materials necessary for the effective control of the disease and provisions to dispose of the carcases safely and quickly. This compromises the readiness of Hungary to deal effectively with outbreaks in the event that ASF is confirmed in domestic pigs.

The competent authority is incorrectly certifying consignments of live pigs as compliant with the ASF Regulation, as they originate from establishments without approved biosecurity plans. Therefore, there is an unknown proportion of live pigs moving out of restricted zone II without complying with the requirements and their meat being placed on the intra-Union market. The risk of disease spread due to these shortcomings is partially mitigated by the systematic pre-movement testing.

The absence of verification activities over county authorities and approved veterinarians jeopardises the continuous improvement of the official control system and favours the persistence of non-compliances.

The low number of suspected ASF cases reported from establishments (i.e. pigs with clinical symptoms compatible with ASF) put in question the effectiveness of the awareness campaigns or the willingness of key stakeholders to notify. This might jeopardise early detection of ASF in domestic pigs.

Although the authorities have made efforts to increase the sensitivity of surveillance in both wild birds and domestic poultry, surveillance in the former was only partially effective as an early warning system to better prevent the outbreaks in both epizootics and to confirm epidemiological hypothesis on the source of infection in affected establishments.

The monitoring of HPAI in wild birds is based on reporting and sampling of fallen, or sick and killed animals. Prior to the epizootics, the SVA and the SBA reminded the public and ornithologists of the importance to report those findings to enhance 6 surveillance for HPAI in wild birds. Reports of observed morbidity and mortality in wild birds are analysed on a daily basis and a subset of the birds are submitted to SVA for analysis. As a result, between 400 and 500 wild birds are surveyed annually. However, neither the risk assessments of the SVA, nor the SBA, identified the relevance of adapting and strengthening that surveillance in certain areas of the country in close vicinity to some of

Therefore, that sub-optimal effectiveness of the surveillance in wild birds cannot be considered in line with provisions laid down in Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the need to design and apply surveillance in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to the objectives pursued and to the risk factors involved in order to ensure the timely detection of the presence of the targeted disease. In doing that, the competent authority shall as well comply with EU requirements establishing the Union surveillance programme for HPAI, as laid down in Articles 3(1)(a) and (b)(i), 4(1)(b)(i) and 10(2) of, and Annex II to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

The efforts to raise and maintain public awareness on the risks associated with HPAI contributed to the prompt notification of suspect cases and limited the spread of the disease. Some delays in certain cases to notify suspect cases had a limited impact since they occurred in areas with a low density of poultry.

However, the audit team saw two cases where the private veterinary practitioner had not done that on the establishment infected in both epizootics and there had been delays in passing the information to the SVA or to district veterinarians of the SBA in both instances. Representatives of the SBA indicated that it had happened during the 2020/21 epizootic because some operators were not yet familiar with the high risk related to HPAI; however, 7 one of the above-mentioned cases happened during the 2021/22 epizootic. That is not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 12(1) and 18(1)(a) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The lack of a system to adequately verify compliance of poultry establishments with HPAI preventive measures precludes that the SBA obtains accurate and up-to-date information on the actual implementation and effectiveness of their HPAI preventive policy. Despite evidence on the inappropriate application of, and insufficient compliance with national requirements on biosecurity in poultry establishments affected by the HPAI epizootics, the SBA failed to correct those shortcomings. This resulted in an unmitigated high risk of infection in certain types of establishments, which contributed to some of the outbreaks and, in certain cases, to recurrent infections in the same establishments in both

When reviewing one of the HPAI outbreaks, confirmed on 2 March 2021 in an establishment keeping pheasants for game re-stocking, the audit team noted that in January, i.e., once the SBA had raised the alert concerning the high risk of incursion of the disease, the business operator responsible for the establishment had re-captured previously released birds from the wild. The district veterinarians who dealt with the outbreak were aware of this practice, as they confirmed that it is common during that period of the year in several establishments from the area. However, neither them or other staff of the SBA had investigated the potential risk associated with that activity, and they had not tak

The SBA delegated inspections on biosecurity in establishments to the poultry meat and eggs sectoral associations. However, examples like the one explained in the previous point prove that at least some parts of the poultry industry had not adapted disease preventive measures properly to mitigate the specific risks associated with the presence of HPAI in wild birds in accordance with the requirements established by the SBA, as required until 20 April 2021 by Commission Decision 2018/1136 and, since that date, by provisions laid down in Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4) and (5), and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

In addition, the competent authorities had not adapted their official controls, or their procedures and/or arrangements to verify their effectiveness, to ensure that the biosecurity measures applied by the industry were suitable, implemented in compliance with their instructions, and that the inspections carried out by the sector itself were effective to achieve that. This is not line with Articles 5(1)(a), 9(1) and 33(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Surveillance

The results of most of the epidemiological enquiries indicated that the outbreaks were very likely caused by a separate primary introduction of the HPAI virus from wild birds. This was confirmed later by the SVA with phylogenetic analyses. Some epidemiological enquiries underlined weaknesses related to the application of biosecurity measures to prevent the introduction of HPAI. However, the SBA had not adequately investigated the possible influence of those weaknesses as a cause of infection, even recurrent in both epizootics, in certain establishments (e.g., in the turkey production sector).

The SBA allowed repopulation in affected establishments only after the final cleaning and disinfection was carried out. SBA staff verified establishments' compliance with 20 national requirements on biosecurity measures and that they were suitable to minimise the risks of introduction of HPAI. The audit team saw some examples where they gave recommendations to operators to address weaknesses identified in that respect. In one of the cases checked, an establishment that was infected in both epizootics, at the time of the second outbreak the operator had not addressed some of the recommendations given by SBA staff after the checks carried out after the first one. The inconsistent and slow analysis in many cases of the data and information collected by district veterinarians during the epidemiological enquiries, alongside the often inadequate documentation of its outcome, made it difficult for the SBA to take timely and appropriate risk-based control measures (e.g., identifying contact establishments, granting of derogations for separate epidemiological units and for movements in restricted zones). That slowed down the response to the disease, which was not as effective as it should have been to limit the impact of the outbreaks.

The district veterinarians responsible for the areas where the suspect cases were notified initiated the epidemiological enquiries at the time of suspicion. In most cases, they finished with them shortly after the disease had been confirmed. But some of them were incomplete, not providing all relevant epidemiological information/data, e.g., they did not include information on other establishments of the same owner, often sharing their machinery, which they did not identify as contact holdings. District veterinarians provided the collected information to the SBA. The SBA frequently relayed it to the SVA, which analysed it promptly in some cases. SBA and SVA experts visited most of the outbreaks to further evaluate the epidemiological situation on site, but they did that only once the establishments had been depopulated and the carcasses dispatched for their disposal5. That precluded that those experts could obtain important information on the routine operation of the establishment and from their own evaluation of the evolution of the disease in the affected poultry present in the establishment.

In some cases, the outcome of the analyses carried out by the SVA and the SBA served to establish the most likely time window for the infection of the flocks, the duration of the incubation period, and to obtain other relevant epidemiological information. That delayed often completion of the epidemiological inquiries for the same establishments. The audit team confirmed that in a large laying hen establishment infected at the beginning of 2021, as the district veterinarian could only complete the epidemiological enquiry 18 days after confirmation of the disease. The SBA did not consider necessary consulting the SVA before deciding on granting that derogation.

The measures applied immediately upon confirmation of HPAI outbreaks during both epizootics were adequate in most cases and helped to contain the spread of the disease. However, during the 2020/21 epizootic, the SBA granted certain derogations that postponed the killing of poultry in epidemiological units of affected establishments considered as separate. Those decisions proved to be not only unjustified, as most of those units got eventually infected by the same HPAI virus, but were also not based on a proper risk assessment to exclude any risk of spread of the disease, as required by EU legislation. The competent authority granted some derogations to move animals and products of animal origin from restricted zones without adequately ensuring that they would not endanger disease control, as required by EU legislation. Nevertheless, there was no evidence that those situations had any impact on the further spread of the disease or in delaying its containment. 5.1.4 Animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control 5.1.4.1 Animal welfare considerations

label_heading: Conclusions on the application of the specific contingency plan
paragraph_text: The disease control centres established at national and local level during the epizootics, in particular during the one in 2020/21, coordinated the response to most of the outbreaks effectively. However, they lacked some necessary information to take important decisions related to specific outbreaks. Although those decisions could have had important consequences (e.g., transmission of the disease locally, or elsewhere in the country via derogated movements), the low density of poultry in the affected areas and the low risk associated with commodities allowed to leave the restricted zones, helped to prevent the spread of the disease.

As indicated in the previous section, at the beginning of 2021, when some large establishments with several poultry houses got infected, the SBA granted a derogation from immediate killing of birds to some of them, in which the disease had not been confirmed, and that were considered separate production/epidemiological units. They did not only grant the derogation to not kill the poultry from the not (yet) affected units, but also allowed the dispatch of several consignments of hatching eggs from them to other establishments in Sweden (see also section 5.1.3.4 concerning that derogation). Those decisions were taken without carrying out a proper risk assessment and without considering either the epidemiological and laboratory analysis information mentioned in the pr

In the above cases, the disease was detected eventually in other epidemiological units, and all birds remaining on the establishments were subsequently killed. The few remaining units not yet clinically affected were preventively culled. However, the SBA did not take any samples to rule out the infection in those units, as required at the time by Article 10(3) of Directive 2005/94/EC and point 8.2 in Chapter IV of the Annex to Commission Decision 2006/437/EC. Nor did the SBA take any action to trace and destroy hatching eggs already dispatched to hatcheries in non-affected areas of the country from these preventively killed birds. All in all, the process to grant those derogations was not in

Before they could grant the derogation for those movements, district veterinarians performed checks on the health status of the poultry kept in the relevant establishments. 15 Beyond that, the SBA did not require any pre-movement sampling and laboratory testing since they did not consider it necessary. They argued that the HPAI viruses circulating in Sweden during both epizootics caused obvious clinical symptoms and high mortality in the poultry species kept, and thus, that they were easily and quickly detectable during the clinical examinations and checks on production records their staff carried out (e.g., no establishments with ducks or geese involved).

The audit team reviewed several examples where a derogation was granted. One of them, happening before 21 April 2021, involved dispatching hatching eggs from units of breeding establishments where a case of HPAI was confirmed, that the SBA considered as separate epidemiological units (see more details in section 5.1.1.3). However, they did that without taking and analyse first the standard samples from each of the production units involved in that activity, as required by point 8.10(c) of Chapter IV of the Annex to Commission Decision (EC) 2006/437, in accordance with the requirements of Article 26(1)(a) of Directive 2005/94/EC (applicable at the time of the outbreak).

In another case, happening in December 2021, the SBA granted a derogation to move poultry to a slaughterhouse from two establishments belonging to the same operator, in whose third establishment they had just confirmed an outbreak of HPAI (two days before). One of those two establishments was located in the protection zone established after the outbreak, less than two kilometres from the affected one, whereas the second one was within the surveillance zone. All three establishments shared some machinery, and the operator visited them regularly. paragraph_text: The authorities had taken adequate steps and made the necessary logistical arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity to collect and dispose safely of the carcases of dead and killed poultry in the event of outbreaks of HPAI affecting establishments of average size and not occurring in spatiotemporal clusters. However, that preparedness did not factor in the possibility of an outbreak in some exceptionally large establishments, where significant delays in applying those measures increased for weeks the risk of spread of the disease. Although the low density of poultry in the affected area mitigated that risk and no additional outbreak was confirmed in it, the authorities have not yet upscale

The competent authorities ensured that adequate cleaning and disinfection of most affected establishments contributed to the elimination of residual infection, except where the presence of contaminated materials precluded them to do so and caused delays, and when they could not supervise application of those measures. Although those 19 shortcomings increased temporarily the risk of spreading the infection in certain areas, there was no evidence that it had happened. 5.1.6 Lifting of restrictions

The SBA did not ensure that the objective of applying the final cleaning and disinfection on establishments affected by HPAI outbreaks, i.e., to minimise the risk of spread of the disease, was achieved in all cases before discontinuing the application of control measures in restricted zones. Although that non-compliance with EU rules increased temporarily that risk, there was no evidence that it had materialised in further outbreaks of the disease. 5.1.7 Repopulation of affected holdings

In most cases, collection and disposal of killed poultry operated swiftly and without delay. However, in the case of a large establishment affected by an outbreak in 2021, the authorities lacked sufficient collection and processing capacity. This was due to the exceptionally large number of poultry carcasses and an exceptionally large number of eggs. To cope with the situation and keep on killing the poultry, the SBA opted for the temporary storage of those ABP in specially designed big bags on the establishment until they were collected and processed as described above along the following four months. During that time, the SBA paid special attention to the application of biosecurity measure

The shortcomings highlighted in the previous point are not in line with requirements of Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities to take the necessary disease control measures, including disposal of animals that may contribute to the spread of a category A disease in the event of an animal health crisis, such as the 2020/21 HPAI epizootic.

At the time of the audit, and despite the lessons learnt from the case mentioned above, the contingency plan for HPAI had not yet been updated to anticipate and deal with such exceptional situation. However, the SBA amended their procedures to speed up the disposal of ABP from the average poultry establishment affected by a HPAI outbreak, e.g., starting preparations for collection and disposal of carcasses already at the time of suspicion. label_heading: Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control
paragraph_text: The SBA externalised the application of the preliminary cleaning and disinfection in affected establishments to private contractors, who, in most cases, did it within short deadlines once the poultry were killed and the carcasses disposed of. There were cases where the authorities had to postpone the application of both preliminary and final cleaning and disinfection because of the limited capacity of some of those contractors or as a consequence of delays in removal of dead bodies or killed animals. Thus, in some instances, because of those delays, the SBA lifted the restrictions in surveillance zones without having applied first the final cleaning and disinfection (see also section 5.1.6).

label_heading: Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control
paragraph_text: In a large establishment affected by an outbreak at the beginning of 2021, the SBA initially questioned the efficacy of applying the preliminary disinfection due to unfavourable weather conditions (low temperatures and snow fall), as they considered that the biocidal available was not going to be effective. After further consultation with the SVA, they decided to proceed with the disinfection. In addition, the final cleaning and disinfection was delayed for more than four months due to the presence of contaminated materials (for more see section 5.1.4.2).

label_heading: Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control
paragraph_text: Staff from the SBA at central level and some of the district veterinarians met confirmed that they had not supervised implementation of cleaning and disinfection activities in all affected establishments, as required by Article 48(a) of Directive 2005/94/EC (before 21 April 2021) and Article 57(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 (since 21 April 2021). label_heading: Conclusions on the application of the specific contingency plan
paragraph_text: The authorities have not fully updated and verified the functionality of the contingency plan and related operational manuals for HPAI in recent years, despite the recent epizootics and the recurrent risk of incursion via wild birds of HPAI. That missed opportunity to adequately reinforce all important components of their emergency preparedness system, including up-to-date training of district veterinarians, had a detrimental effect on the timeliness, selection and effectiveness of some of the measures applied to control the disease outbreaks, and could have had worse consequences resulting in the further spread of HPAI.

The SBA has not fully updated the contingency plan for HPAI in recent years, despite the recent epizootics and the recurrent risk of incursion via wild birds of HPAI in EU Member States. They have been developing for several years a new version of that contingency plan trying to adapt it to the one they developed for foot-and-mouth disease, but several parts still need to be amended and further developed, including some operational manuals.

In the last three years, there has been no simulation exercise on HPAI to test the emergency preparedness system. Nevertheless, the authorities provided evidence on several actions introduced in their animal health emergency preparedness system as a result of the lessons learnt from the 2020/2021 and 2021/2022 HPAI epizootics. Those 21 actions aim to increase the effectiveness of their system, e.g., on conducting of epidemiological enquiries, new arrangements for disposal of carcasses, on killing of poultry, including provisions on preventive killing, on raising awareness, and to streamline certain administrative procedures.

The improvements mentioned in the previous point go in the right direction, but the situation found at the time of both epizootics cannot be considered in line with EU requirements laid down in Article 62 of Directive 2005/94/EC (before 21 April 2021) and Article 43(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (since 21 April 2021), on the matters that contingency plans should at least cover. This does not allow to confirm whether the controls are effective in achieving their intended purpose, whether verification checks detect any issues and whether the authorities take timely corrective actions to improve the effectiveness of official controls when needed.

The competent authorities use the wide range of effective and proportionate enforcement actions available when non-compliances are detected. They promptly suspend transporters, drivers and/or vehicle certificates if necessary to bring operators to take the desired corrective actions and comply with EU animal welfare requirements. However, as the Irish authorities do not interpret Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 as creating a legal obligation to feed unweaned calves on a ferry journey from Ireland to neighbouring Member States, they do not enforce feeding the animals on the ferry. 6 FINDINGS ON FRAMEWORK FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS AND OTHER OFFICIAL ACTIVITIES The key strengths of the official control s

The national programme established as the main risk factors for animal welfare, firstly the transport of unweaned (and cull animals), secondly the transport over long journeys (and by sea) and thirdly transport during adverse weather conditions. Therefore, the ACCAs' risk-based checks should consider, and prioritised for official controls, the transport of unweaned calves over long journeys. However, this was not always the case and some autonomous communities failed to consider them within their control programme, resulting in the implementation of an official control system which was not aligned with the identified risk factors.
