label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring, awareness and surveillance
paragraph_text: The fact that some districts do not collect and analyse the necessary number of samples and the geographical bias (i.e. samples taken only from some hunting grounds), can reduce the representativeness and reliability of the results obtained from their analysis and the validity of the conclusions drawn up at regional and district level on the levels of immunity reached.

label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring, awareness and surveillance
paragraph_text: The values of sero-positivity in young foxes demonstrates that, in some regions, oral vaccination campaigns have not successfully reached the young fox population. There is an important variation between authorities regarding the use of hunting data. This likely means that the difference between districts regarding the quality of their planning and monitoring is increasing, with those using hunting data to fine-tune the actions planned in the eradication programme achieving better results.

label_heading: Conclusions on monitoring, awareness and surveillance
paragraph_text: The insufficient monitoring of vaccination effectiveness in some areas of the country weakens the authority's capability to detect promptly potential issues in the rabies eradication, in particular in oral vaccination of wild carnivores.

The audit team looked at more detailed data on monitoring. Those show important variations between the regions regarding the percentage of the target they were achieving. One region (Masovian) was constantly not reaching the targets. This indicates a persistent issue with sampling, in particular in one district that had reported a lower density of foxes. 10

There is a good system to minimise the risk of livestock vehicles having to wait long times at the port. However, when delays happen, the authorities do not unload, water and feed the animals after 4 hours, as the ports lack facilities for it and officials do not send them to the nearby facilities identified for this purpose unless the loading is delayed to the next day. This, together with the fact that drivers ignore the use of shaded parking leaving vehicles with animals in the sun, creates a risk of animals suffering when there are delays and/or temperatures are high.

Although the competent authorities have made considerable efforts to increase the sensitivity of surveillance for HPAI in wild birds, the tool however was not effective as an early warning system. That raises questions about the suitability of the design, the proper application, and the cost-effectiveness of that surveillance, as there is consensus among all relevant parties that the HPAI virus was circulating in wild birds in the affected areas before it was detected in poultry.

The inability of the surveillance to detect promptly the virus in wild birds (detection in wild birds happened after outbreaks in poultry establishments) contrasts with the fact that all competent authorities considered circulation of the virus in wild birds as the main cause for most of the initial outbreaks of the disease in both regions. The NRL confirmed this a posteriori by virus phylogenetic studies. That sub-optimal effectiveness cannot be considered in line with provisions laid down in Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the need to design and apply surveillance in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to the objectives pursued and to the risk factors

The effective systems to raise and maintain public awareness and the good laboratory support helped the authorities to identify and confirm most cases of HPAI in poultry quickly. The delayed notification of suspect cases by certain operators is still a cause for concern as it may facilitate the spread of the disease in areas with a high density of 13 poultry.

In the cases checked by the audit team, turkey producers notified suspect cases of HPAI quickly, in most cases timely. In contrast, the audit team saw examples of affected layer hen establishments where the operator had not notified the authorities despite experiencing mortality rates of four or five times the usual daily average for a few days, or of other significant deviations in other production parameters. That is not in line with 10 requirements laid down in Article 18(1)(a) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The competent authorities did not obtain timely the necessary information from the analysis of the epidemiological enquiries carried out in affected establishments to understand the likely spread of the disease, notably in areas with a high density of susceptible establishments exposed to a high level of environmental infection and frequency of contacts between them. Hence, they could not take the right decisions and adopt preliminary restrictions and additional control measures rapidly to contain the spread of the disease, as they had undertaken in response to a previous recommendation of the Commission services.

The competent authorities did not evaluate swiftly all relevant epidemiological criteria and establish immediately a further restricted zone in the area of Veneto where the epizootic began and which they considered of very high risk for the spread of HPAI. That delay undermined the effectiveness of the additional control measures they applied, which therefore were not sufficient to stop the spread of the disease before it reached epizootic proportions and expanded far beyond the initially affected area.

label_heading: Conclusions on the application of the specific contingency plan
paragraph_text: The disease control centres established at national, regional, and local level during the epizootic coordinated application of the main control measures in the affected areas effectively. However, they all failed to take certain important decisions at critical times, and thus, they did not prevent the spread of the disease effectively.

According to representatives of the field epidemiology teams and to SVL staff who performed those enquiries, the current model of epidemiological enquiry is too burdensome, and it requires gathering too much information, especially in the face of multiple outbreaks, and thus, it was not a suitable tool to inform quickly on the best possible measures mentioned above. That is not in line with general requirements laid down in Articles 5(1)(a) and 12(2) and (3) (read with point 5 in Chapter II of Annex II thereto) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, for the competent authorities to have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls and other 11 official activ

The shortcomings mentioned above did not allow the competent authorities to analyse quickly a sufficient number of records and information to ascertain quickly the likely spread of the disease and determine which preliminary disease control measures they had to take to prevent it. Thus, they could not fulfil the fundamental objectives of the epidemiological enquiries to inform decisions on application of control measures as provided for in Articles 55(1)(e) and (f), 56(a)(ii), 57(2)(e), 62(1) and 64(1)(f) and (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Articles 8(3), 9, 21(1)(c) and 23(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The competent authorities were aware of the dense and frequent network of contacts occurring between many of those establishments, especially because most of them belong to the same few companies. The fast evolution of the disease confirmed that those circumstances were not properly considered in accordance with Article 64(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 21(1)(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, when the authorities delimitated the boundaries and size of the restricted zones to contain the spread of the disease and did not establish a further restricted zone immediately, precisely to prevent that.

However, certain shortcomings, such as a) the lack of adequate epidemiological expertise to analyse the dynamics of the disease quickly, anticipate its evolution, and advice appropriately on actions to curtail its spread, b) the delays during the initial stages of the epizootic to decide on establishing a further restricted zone, and c) the incapability to find quickly adequate solutions to the problems experienced with application of animal depopulation, indicate that the operation of the national and regional disease control centres was not fully operational, which is not in line with Article 43(2)(a) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

label_heading: Conclusions on the application of the specific contingency plan
paragraph_text: The competent authorities have repeatedly underlined the significant risk that the very high density of poultry represents for the areas affected by the 2021-2022 HPAI epizootic, but they have not acted accordingly to reduce it. Moreover, evidence confirms that that density has even increased in some of those areas. This, coupled with the sub-optimal application of biosecurity measures at times unsuitable to mitigate the prevailing risks of HPAI introduction and spread, raises concerns about their capability to prevent and control new HPAI epizootics.

According to the analysis of the competent authorities, local airborne spread played a significant role in transmitting the infection in areas with a very high density of establishments (e.g., facilitated by the proximity between establishments and by the use of force ventilation), together with the risk of environmental infection associated with wild birds. However, the industry had not adapted disease preventive measures properly to mitigate the impact of those critical risk factors, and the competent authorities had not adapted their verification activities to ensure that the measures applied by the industry were suitable for that purpose. Therefore, all that evidence had not been properl

The official controls, despite their extensive application and largely positive outcome, did not contribute sufficiently to correct the shortcomings related to biosecurity that likely facilitated the spread of the disease during the 2021-2022 epizootic. Hence, they could not take the right decisions and adopt preliminary restrictions and additional control measures rapidly to contain the spread of the disease, as they had undertaken in response to a previous recommendation of the Commission services.

The competent authorities did not evaluate swiftly all relevant epidemiological criteria and establish immediately a further restricted zone in the area of Veneto where the epizootic began and which they considered of very high risk for the spread of HPAI. That delay undermined the effectiveness of the additional control measures they applied, which therefore were not sufficient to stop the spread of the disease before it reached epizootic proportions and expanded far beyond the initially affected area.

According to representatives of the field epidemiology teams and to SVL staff who performed those enquiries, the current model of epidemiological enquiry is too burdensome, and it requires gathering too much information, especially in the face of multiple outbreaks, and thus, it was not a suitable tool to inform quickly on the best possible measures mentioned above. That is not in line with general requirements laid down in Articles 5(1)(a) and 12(2) and (3) (read with point 5 in Chapter II of Annex II thereto) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, for the competent authorities to have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls and other 11 official activ

The shortcomings mentioned above did not allow the competent authorities to analyse quickly a sufficient number of records and information to ascertain quickly the likely spread of the disease and determine which preliminary disease control measures they had to take to prevent it. Thus, they could not fulfil the fundamental objectives of the epidemiological enquiries to inform decisions on application of control measures as provided for in Articles 55(1)(e) and (f), 56(a)(ii), 57(2)(e), 62(1) and 64(1)(f) and (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Articles 8(3), 9, 21(1)(c) and 23(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The competent authorities were aware of the dense and frequent network of contacts occurring between many of those establishments, especially because most of them belong to the same few companies. The fast evolution of the disease confirmed that those circumstances were not properly considered in accordance with Article 64(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 21(1)(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, when the authorities delimitated the boundaries and size of the restricted zones to contain the spread of the disease and did not establish a further restricted zone immediately, precisely to prevent that.

The competent authorities did not obtain timely the necessary information from the analysis of the epidemiological enquiries carried out in affected establishments to understand the likely spread of the disease, notably in areas with a high density of susceptible establishments exposed to a high level of environmental infection and frequency of contacts between them. Hence, they could not take the right decisions and adopt preliminary restrictions and additional control measures rapidly to contain the spread of the disease, as they had undertaken in response to a previous recommendation of the Commission services.

The increasing delays in the killing and disposal of animals and of other products that may be contaminated, gradually undermined the effectiveness of other containment measures and was one of the main drivers of the further spread of the disease during the worst of the epizootic. 5.1.2Diagnosis of HPAI

Although the competent authorities established restricted zones rapidly once they confirmed the presence of HPAI in poultry establishments, other shortcomings, such as the limited availability of means to apply animal depopulation and carcass disposal and the shortage of personnel to visit quickly high-risk establishments within those zones, undermined the quick application of measures to contain the disease and the prevention of its spread.

The application of preventive killing to sufficiently reduce the poultry population in high-risk areas quickly and stop the spread of the disease was not possible due to resource constraints as all animal depopulation capacity was compromised by the numerous affected establishments the. The impact of that shortcoming was partially mitigated by the decisive action of the competent authorities and the cooperation of the industry to send for slaughter as many poultry as possible from establishments situated within restricted zones.

label_heading: Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control
paragraph_text: The competent authorities had not taken adequate administrative steps and made the necessary logistical arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity to collect and dispose safely of the carcases of dead and killed poultry in establishments where the presence of HPAI was confirmed or as a preventive measure in areas affected by the disease. This was even more evident in the region of Veneto and caused significant delays in the depopulation of establishments and accumulation of carcases, which significantly undermined the effectiveness of other measures to contain the spread of the disease. 5.1.5Cleaning and disinfection

Considering that that was the preferred choice of the competent authorities based on their experience and the analysis of the situation, that cannot be considered fully in line with provisions of Article 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2020/687. 5.1.3.3 Further restricted zones

The shortcomings highlighted in the previous points are not in line with requirements of Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities and equipment and to have an effective organisation to be capable to take the necessary disease control measures, including disposal of animals that may be contaminated or contribute to the spread of the disease, in the event of an animal health crisis like the recent HPAI epizootic.

However, certain shortcomings, such as a) the lack of adequate epidemiological expertise to analyse the dynamics of the disease quickly, anticipate its evolution, and advice appropriately on actions to curtail its spread, b) the delays during the initial stages of the epizootic to decide on establishing a further restricted zone, and c) the incapability to find quickly adequate solutions to the problems experienced with application of animal depopulation, indicate that the operation of the national and regional disease control centres was not fully operational, which is not in line with Article 43(2)(a) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Neither the national nor the regional disease control centres reacted quickly enough to make available sufficient additional staff to attend the demands of that SVL during the worst weeks of the epizootic. That was not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 13(1)(a) and 43(2)(c)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on responsibilities of the competent authorities to have qualified personnel and an effective organisation to apply disease control measures effectively, and on application of the contingency plan for HPAI. 5.2.5 Availability of equipment and materials

Once the number of outbreaks in the main affected areas became very high, some of the SVL in both regions could not carry out the quick official visits to all poultry establishments situated in the protection zones, as required by provisions laid down in Article 26(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. The main reason for that was the temporary shortage of staff (see also 5.2.4).

The lack of checks in those establishments situated in protection zones, by definition at a high-risk of infection, precluded verification that they were applying proper biosecurity measures and implementing additional surveillance to identify the further spread of the disease from affected establishments quickly. This is not in line with the provisions laid down in Article 25(1)(b), (d) and (e) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Those limitations also applied to large establishments situated in some of those protection zones.

paragraph_text: The absence of internal audits to check the compliance and suitability of the animal health emergency preparedness systems in the regions repeatedly affected by HPAI epizootics favoured the persistence of shortcomings in those systems, notably in Veneto. paragraph_text: Authorised operators met by the audit team do not carry out meticulous examinations to verify that their plants fulfil the EU requirements, therefore their examinations do not provide sufficient guarantee for the issuance of plant passports.

The GVI declared that the current system in place to impose penalties to operators that use or trade VMPs is not always efficient. label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: CISTA has prepared guidance on official sampling, including a sampling report template, based on the requirements laid down in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections
paragraph_text: The audit team observed official sampling being conducted in three compound feed manufacturers visited (the matrix and parameters to be controlled were suggested by the audit team). In all of the establishments, the feed inspectors sampled for analytes likely to be non- uniformly distributed in the matrix. The audit team noted that all of the inspectors adequately implemented the pertinent legal requirements, as established in Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. However, during the preparation of the final samples, none of the inspectors used a divider (and did not have one), as required by part 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

label_heading: Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at ABP plants are largely effective to verify infrastructural and hygiene requirements. However, they are usually notified in advance and they do not pay sufficient attention to the implementation of HACCP-based procedures and the operators' own checks. Similarly, checks on the validation of processing plants remain limited or poorly documented. All of this limits the ability of the competent authorities to verify whether ABP and DP are handled and processed to the high safety standards provided for in EU legislation.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: All district veterinary inspectors met confirmed that inspections of ABP plants are carried out with prior notification and that unannounced inspections are the exception. In some cases, inspections are announced one or two days before the due date and, in other cases, up to a week in advance, when the inspectors prepare their weekly schedule of activities. Routine prior notification of inspections in not in line with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: For operators under veterinary supervision (meat establishments), official controls on ABP generated in such food establishments are largely effective, except for controls on the marking of specified risk material.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In one processing plant for Category 1 material visited, the audit team noted, in the raw material received from domestic slaughterhouses, the presence of heads of adult bovine animals (specified risk material) that were not stained with a dye or otherwise marked, contrary to the requirements of point 3 of Annex V to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. According to the operator of the processing plant, there was an agreement with slaughterhouses not to mark specified risk material as this resulted in staining of the processing equipment. Officials from the province visited confirmed that specified risk material was usually not stained on removal.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: In contrast, for food business operators under supervision of the food inspectorates (e.g. milk, eggs, fish and retail sectors) official controls are inadequate, mainly due to 13 insufficient knowledge of ABP requirements, to monitor the correct handling, use and disposal of such materials. This weakens the guarantees that ABP and DP generated by food business operators are collected and disposed of in line with EU rules.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The food inspectors met stated that they had not received training on ABP and that in the absence of knowledge of the rules applicable to ABP, they were not able to critically assess the degree of compliance of the food operators in this area. They stated that their main point of attention was to verify that food and waste (this included ABP for the food inspectors) were adequately separated and that there was no contamination of food by waste.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team reviewed several records of inspections carried out by food inspectors at randomly chosen food operators. From these records, it was visible that some information was available on the type of ABP produced by the operators and the operators collecting them. However, the food inspectors met stated that such information was collected but not assessed. For instance, they did not check the presence of commercial documentation or if the operator collecting such ABP was approved for handling these types of ABP.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team reviewed some cases where non-conformities were identified in relation to ABP at some operators under the supervision of food inspectors. These cases were either identified by the inspectors or were investigated following complaints. From the discussion held with the audit team, it was clear that in the few cases where food inspectors had some knowledge of ABP or had investigated ABP-related complaints, they were able to adequately follow-up on such issues, in particular by liaising with the veterinary inspectors in charge of controls at ABP operators.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The food inspectors met stated that, at retailers, they verified that meat and meat products not fit for human consumption (e.g., products with expired shelf life or spoiled meat) were kept separated from food. They also verified that unsold food of animal origin was not given to farmers for feeding their animals. They confirmed that no other checks were carried out to ascertain the destination of ABP as this was, in their opinion, the responsibility of the business operator to dispose of them in line with the applicable rules.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Based on the above findings, the audit team noted that official controls carried by food inspectors at food business operators are not suitable to verify compliance with ABP rules, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(3) of Regulation No 1069/2009.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: In contrast, for food business operators under supervision of the food inspectorates (e.g. milk, eggs, fish and retail sectors) official controls are inadequate, mainly due to 13 insufficient knowledge of ABP requirements, to monitor the correct handling, use and disposal of such materials. This weakens the guarantees that ABP and DP generated by food business operators are collected and disposed of in line with EU rules.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the milk processing plant visited (a large-scale cheese manufacturing plant), official controls overlooked that some cheese considered unfit for human consumption (e.g. mouldy cheese) was disposed of as waste, without ABP documentation, collected by a waste management company that was not approved as an ABP operator. Similarly, according to the operator, whey, if not used as feed material, could be disposed of through the wastewater treatment system. These ways of disposing of milk derived ABP (Category 3 material) are not in line with Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at the milk processing plant visited did not cover the treatment applied to milk-derived products supplied to farms for feeding pigs. The whey sent to two pig farms from this dairy plant was obtained from pasteurised milk and there was no monitoring of pH to ensure that it would be kept under pH<6 for at least an hour before being dispatched to the pig farm. According to the operator, the whey pH was certainly below 6 but no records were available to demonstrate it. Such whey, in line with Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, should only be sent to farms that have been authorised based on a risk assessment. However, contrary to the requirements of point 3(b)(i) of Part I

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team noted that farms receiving milk-derived products for feeding farmed animals were registered in VIS by the district veterinary authorities. However, in the provinces visited, as explained in the above paragraphs, such registration did not consider the different requirements applicable to the farms, based on the type of treatment applied to the milk-derived products, as set out in Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. These farms, once authorised, are subject to inspections carried out as part of cross-compliance checks that verify their registration to use milk derived by- products but do not cover specific ABP requirements, such as commercial documents or possible restrictio

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at ABP plants are largely effective to verify infrastructural and hygiene requirements. However, they are usually notified in advance and they do not pay sufficient attention to the implementation of HACCP-based procedures and the operators' own checks. Similarly, checks on the validation of processing plants remain limited or poorly documented. All of this limits the ability of the competent authorities to verify whether ABP and DP are handled and processed to the high safety standards provided for in EU legislation.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the ABP plants visited, official controls often overlooked shortcomings in the implementation of Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) based 11 procedures (1). In some cases, these procedures were not maintained (biogas plant, petfood plant) contrary to the requirements of Article 29(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 or were incomplete (one of the Category 1 processing plants visited) and thus not in compliance with the requirements of Article 29(2) of said Regulation.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Whilst official controls on food business operators include verification of compliance with ABP requirements, they are not effective in verifying said operators' compliance with the requirements concerning the correct categorisation and disposal of ABP.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In relation to categorisation and handling of ABP, past inspections carried out at the two slaughterhouses visited (one for poultry and one for ungulates) overlooked the following: (a) categorisation of unemptied pig digestive tracts and material collected from unclean sections (floor) of slaughterhouses as Category 3 material, contrary to the requirements of Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, (b) disposal of large amount of pig blood through the waste water treatment, contrary to the requirements of Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and, (c) absence of traps with mesh size of no more than 6 mm in areas where specified risk material (SRM) is removed and more generally for th

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Contrary to EU requirements, SRM is not stained or otherwise marked after its removal, thus limiting the ability of the competent authority (and the operator) to identify possible unintentional or deliberate cases of contamination of food or other categories of ABP by SRM.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Controls on removal and disposal of SRM are in place. However, contrary to the operator's procedures, in one of the slaughterhouses visited, SRM were not stained with a dye or otherwise marked following their removal. SFVS representatives informed the audit team that the current guidelines for slaughterhouses and instructions for carrying out inspections at slaughterhouses do not require staining or marking of SRM. According to these instructions, placing of SRM in containers labelled as Category 1 material is considered sufficient. The absence of staining of SRM with a dye or, as appropriate, marking (with another marker) is not in line with the requirements of point 3 of Annex V to Regulat

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at ABP plants where EU rules require that HACCP-based procedures are implemented are not adequate to verify the operators' level of compliance with all of the key requirements of these procedures.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the ABP plants visited, official controls overlooked shortcomings in the implementation of HACCP-based procedures. These procedures were in place but often incorrectly implemented and thus not in compliance with the requirements of Article 29(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Deficiencies noted by the audit team concerned: (a) process flow diagrams not reflecting all processing steps (petfood plant), (b) incorrect definition of critical control points (biogas plants and processing plant for Category 2 material) and, (c) absence or inadequate monitoring arrangements for critical control points (petfood plant, biogas plant and processing plant for Category 2 material).

The CAs are designated for the performance of official controls throughout the production chain, except for public health controls at aquaculture farms. Consequently, in the controls in the aquaculture area there is a reliance on controls that are designed and carried out primarily for animal health purposes.

The audit team identified a designation gap concerning the competencies on public health controls for aquaculture farms that are not formally assigned in the service contracts from FSAI to MI or DAFM. According to MI, they are the CA for the implementation of aquatic animal health controls and have no role in public health. This designation gap is not in line with Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The MI documented procedures for aquaculture farms are designed for fish health controls and not for public health. Nonetheless, the current checks for biosecurity in fish health broadly cover the public health requirements for primary production (e.g. hygiene and disinfection, waste removal, staff training, excessive mortality etc.). However, in the absence of dedicated public health procedures (e.g. checklists), from a cursory review of documentation the audit team could not readily verify to what extent public health issues are taken into account during controls nor of the obligation to do so.

According to DAFM inspectors, they never check and or ask the operator to check the core temperature of the fishery products. The audit team noted several boxes of smoked salmon labelled "refrigerated 0-4°C". The expiry date on the label was exceeded by five months at the time of the visit. According to DAFM and SFPA the product was received chilled, and blast frozen at the owner's request.

The salmon's producer sets a use-by period of 28 days for refrigerated smoked salmon. If the salmon is later frozen, they would relabel the product, modifying the batch code to add 9 "defrosted" and indicating a new use-by period of 21 days after thawing. In the meanwhile, the product is kept in the cold store with the old label, even if the date has expired, with no indication of the maximum period that it can be kept frozen.

The actions taken by DAFM and SFPA officials to investigate this finding, at the audit team's request, were satisfactory. According to the information provided by the CA, the operator did not avail of a validated shelf study to demonstrate compliance with the relevant microbiological criteria set out in Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 (supporting the 21 days period for the use-by date of the thawed smoked salmon, after being frozen and defrosted). 5.3.1.6 Freezer and factory vessels

In three of four establishments visited, the operators set CCPs with a critical limit not in line with the EU requirements, which had been accepted by the inspectors. A critical limit of -12°C was set for the reception of frozen products by the supplier and a critical limit of 8 +4°C for fresh and chilled products, the latter being in line with the instructions for official control (see paragraph 8).

The majority of SFPA inspections are carried out with prior notice, despite the fact that this is contrary to their own instructions and that unannounced visits could be readily performed on land-based establishments. This can negatively impact the effectiveness of official controls.

DAFM, SFPA and MI have the required powers to access on-land premises. Regarding vessels, SFPA shall be informed of any vessel calling to a port with a four-hour prior notice and can perform ad-hoc visits regarding their fisheries competencies. SFPA's inspectors make case-by-case arrangements with the vessel's owner to perform an announced public health inspection. The SFPA has the power to inspect vessels when berthed.

SFPA performs inspections, generally with prior notice, which should cover all the relevant requirements during the year. In the two SFPA regions visited, 84% of inspections in one and 80% in the other, in 2022, were performed with prior notice. Up to 64% of the operators only received inspections with prior notice. The audit team identified 4 operators in different SFPA regions that underwent prior notice inspections for a period of 3 years 7 (covering up to 9 inspections) without having been "duly justified", as required by Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

According to officials, the main reason for prior notice inspections is to guarantee that the premises are in operation and those responsible are available, especially in remote areas. However, the establishments visited (mainly subject to prior notice) were not in remote locations, had predictable working shifts and the responsible staff (e.g. the quality manager) was present on a daily basis during operation. 5.3.1.2 Primary production fishing vessels

According to officials, the inspections take place with prior notice after consultation with the owner, usually when the vessel is not in operation. Inspections are generally avoided during landing to reduce the extra burden on operators and, in some regions, are clustered during low season. The audit team noted unannounced inspections at the time of berthing, despite the fact that operators did not consistently provide the four-hours prior notice of arrival.

SFA is responsible for the approval of the establishments. SFA performs an on-site visit and grants full approval before starting the operation, therefore in the absence of HACCP records. Thus, SFA cannot verify that the FBO meets the other relevant requirements of the food law. This is not in line with Article 148(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Three months after the full approval is granted, SFA performs a new on-site visit, to assess the HACCP records generated during this period. SFA informed the audit team that a new procedure was under development, to grant conditional approval on the first visit and full approval after the three-month visit.

The audit team identified the following issues during the visits to approved establishments: a. The audit team noted that some recently approved establishments did not meet certain approval requirements laid down in Regulations (EC) Nos 852/2004 and 853/2004, such as temperature recording devices for cold chambers, temperature displays or the avoidance of inappropriate product flows. Inspectors were not aware of these requirements. b. During the approval process, relevant information is not recorded, such as blueprints. It is unclear which parts of the premises and which activities are included in the approval. The audit team visited a cold room located in a separate building. The municipali

While SFA approval procedures include provisions for establishments where there have been significative modifications (including activities or equipment), the interpretation of these procedures was unclear for municipality representatives. They were not certain if a reapproval should be carried out in these cases and if it was, by whom (SFA or municipalities). 6 Conclusions on registration/approval of food business operator establishments

CABs are not performing regular check on the hygiene conditions at landing as laid down in Article 67 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. A similar conclusion was detected in the previous audit (ref. DG(SANCO) 2015-7462) leading to the issuance of a specific recommendation (7).

The controls of the landing are under the responsibility of CABs. According to CABs, new items were added to the checklist of fishing vessels. After the closing meeting, CABs provided the only available control in which a check on a landing site was included. However, CABs are not in a position to demonstrate the performance of regular checks on the hygiene conditions of landing as indicated in Article 67 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Facilities handling fishery products

The approval conditions are not consistently kept under review. The verification of FBO's documents by officials is partially missing, as it relies on the FBO's verbal statements. This impacts the effectiveness and consistency of the official controls to verify compliance with EU rules.

Officials do not consistently assess HACCP plans, validation studies and/or verification of the production processes. As a result, the CA cannot verify that the HACCP plans are suitable for purpose. This impacts the effectiveness of the official controls.

SFA cannot verify that factory vessels implement and maintain permanent procedures based on HACCP principles and that they comply with the specific requirements for cooking shrimp on board. This impacts the effectiveness, and consistency of the official controls.

Inspectors (mainly in municipalities) overlook hygiene situations in the FBOs, that can be a direct risk for ready-to-eat products. This impacts the effectiveness of the official control. 5.3.2 Official controls of fishery products Legal requirements Council Regulation (EC) No 2406/96. Article 1 and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915. Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 70, 71 and Chapter I and II of Annex VI to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627. (7) In response to the draft report, the CA confirmed that , "Regular checks of the hygiene conditions at landing have been initiated". 11 Findings

However, there is not a systematic approach to guarantee that all control-areas are fully covered over the 3 to 4-year inspection cycle and in accordance with the results of the risk classification, notability in the municipalities. Therefore, the CA cannot verify that the approval conditions are kept under review and that official controls include verification of compliance according to Article 67 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Factory vessels produce fresh and cooked shrimp. The fishing association developed "guidelines for shrimp operation" in 2007. SFA inspectors accept the guidelines as appropriate to comply with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Inspectors verify that they are adhered to by the FBO during inspections.

label_heading: Conclusion on official controls of fishery products
paragraph_text: Official controls of fishery products include all the relevant elements, except for PAHs. This impacts the capacity of the CA to monitor certain risks associated with smoking activities. 5.4 FOLLOW UP OF IRASFF NOTIFICATIONS Legal requirements Articles 50(5) and 52 of Section 1 Chapter IV to Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council. Articles 1(a), 2, 4, 12 to 22 and 25 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. Findings

During the audit, SFA, municipalities or CABs did not provide evidence of official sampling for PAHs. This is not in line with Article 70 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Conclusion on official controls of fishery products

Verification procedures do not cover the official controls on transport of unweaned calves. This, coupled with the prolonged omission of this area in the audit program, results in missed opportunities for the competent authority to identify shortcomings in the official controls, to get insights for improvement and to provide stakeholders with assurances of compliance with animal welfare legislation. 6 FINDINGS ON FRAMEWORK FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS AND OTHER OFFICIAL ACTIVITIES The key strengths of the official control system were the instructions and guidance which enable the consistent and effective implementation of most requirements, the measures taken on non-compliance (suspension/withdraw

The departmental services of DGAL approve the control posts after having checked and issued an approval number to each control post. The approval is limited to species and categories establishing which control posts are approved for handling unweaned calves. The instructions for approval do not contain specific provisions other than the general requirements and an adaptation to the categories of kept animals.

In some cases, DGAL departmental services plan their controls considering risk factors, for example, past compliance records of the operators, notifications from other competent authorities, activities under the control of operator (e.g., involvement in intracommunity trade), weather conditions (extreme heat) and species (e.g., bovine animals). In other cases, the departments conduct official controls on ad hoc basis, for example following up on complaints relating to animal welfare. Although some departmental have targeted the transport of unweaned claves in planning their controls, the planning procedure and its implementation have not consistently considered risks associated to the transp

In addition, the internal audit and sectoral evaluation systems and related procedures are in place to supervise the activities carried out by official staff. However, slaughter hygiene and meat inspection have not been subject to sectoral evaluations in depth and frequency to provide the CA with a reasonable level of confidence that controls at establishment level are, as required by Article 5 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, effective and that non-compliances are identified, and corrective action taken if/when necessary. The lack of a direct supervision of staff performance undermines the capability of the CA to provide guarantees about the effectiveness of the official controls.

There has been one sectoral evaluation covering slaughter hygiene in 2018 and the most recent one, in August 2023, covering post-mortem inspection of adult bovine animals that has not yet been completed at the time of this DG Health and Food Safety audit. The audit team noted that the 2018 sectoral evaluation report identified some weaknesses. Some of the conclusions are: The slaughter hygiene checks are insufficiently carried out and/or the results of the checks are not recorded in accordance with established procedures, operators do not comply with requirements set in the precepts (i.e. an order to correct a non-compliance), RDs' specialists have not set deadlines correctly in the precepts

The audit team noted that one of the main conclusions of the above-mentioned sectoral evaluation report was that "the effectiveness of controls depend solely on the controller". No corrective actions/follow up activities to address this issue were included in the sectoral evaluation report. In addition, the CA explained that the current system in place does not include a direct supervision of OVs and OAs in order to verify the effectiveness and efficiency of the controls they carry out and to ensure that these controls are carried out in a harmonised and consistent way. 5.2.6 Enforcement

The competent authority has made significant improvements to increase the registration of non-commercial pig establishments in the national register system. It also made improvements in the system to facilitate the use of information to plan certain official controls for ASF. However, the fact that the system does not always keep records of the number of pigs present in certain establishments (i.e., one pig farms) prevents the accurate 5 and risk-based planning of official controls, both during peace time and during disease outbreaks.

The national plan to reduce the wild porcine population seems to have been effective in recent years. The strategy is based on reliable data. However, the population is still high and even increasing in certain areas of the country. The competent authority acknowledges the need to develop a national action plan to continuously manage the wild porcine animals' population to avoid the spread of ASF, in line with Annex IV of the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/594 by 17 September 2023.

The competent authorities implement both passive and active surveillance of hunted and dead wild boar. There is no evidence that the authorities systematically verify the implementation of these official control and thus, confirm that all wild porcine meat intended for human consumption originates from carcases with negative results.
The laboratory network provides reliable and consistent support for the implementation of ASF control programme.
Home slaughter is not always reported to the authorities in order to supervise it, not allowing the competent authority to comply with their approved eradication programme.

The competent authority informed the audit team that the target to inspect 100% of home slaughters is not feasible for the capacity of the SVFA and that this issue will be discussed with policy makers colleagues in the European Commission. 14 System is in place Surveillance in wild porcine animals to test all wild porcine animals 35. There are financial incentives to hunt, report and dispose of dead wild hunted that are porcine animals. intended for human 36. According to the SVFA, in free, buffer and restricted zones I, all dead and consumption in sick wild porcine suspected of infection with ASF virus, should be tested Restriction zones with Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) test and serolog

The epidemiological enquiries do not always include the required information. This prevents the competent authority from taking informed decisions to implement adequate prevention and control measures to avoid the spreading and ensure the eradication of the disease.

There are unnecessary delays in confirming ASF in domestic pigs, resulting in the setting of restriction areas five days after the suspicion of the disease was reported. This creates an unnecessary time window during which the infection can be spread to both domestic pigs and wild porcine animals.

The confirmation of disease in suspect cases was delayed. The audit team assessed two epidemiological linked outbreaks. The officials visited the first reported suspect and took samples on the same day of the epidemiological investigation report. However, the competent authority did not give any urgency to the samples. And the laboratory did not process them until four days later. The direct linked establishment was neither investigated nor sampled until four days after the initial suspicion. By SVFA's decision, the NRL was not (and still is not) operational during weekends. This resulted in the confirmation of these outbreaks four and five days after the initial suspicion was reported. In t

The system implemented by the competent authorities to verify that official controls are planned on a risk basis (e.g., identification and registration; biosecurity measures, surveillance), and are implemented with appropriate frequency to ensure that the objectives of the legislations are effectively achieve is weak.
The veterinary authorities have suitable contingency plans, equipment, and the capacity to deal with confirmed ASF outbreaks.

The last internal audit report issued in March 2023 included nine recommendations and a deadline of 10 working days for the creation of an action plan to address those recommendations. Up until the closing meeting of this audit (4 July), no action plan had been created and no reminder had been issued. The competent authority did not provide evidence that they have officially addressed those important shortcomings and weakens the prevention and control system for ASF in the country. 6 PREVENTIVE MEASURES The compliance with registration of pig establishments and data on the national database is generally good. There is a definition of "commercial" or "non-commercial" pig establishments. Howev

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures.
paragraph_text: A number of establishments make use of the derogation of PMI under the responsibility of the OV that are above the legally permitted throughput threshold. 3 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 6, 9, 12, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Findings 5.2.1 Structure and organisation

According to the data provided by the CCA, of the approximately 430 red meat approved slaughterhouses in the country, there are 18 establishments that apply the derogation of the timing of post-mortem inspection (PMI) and 96 where PMI is carried out under the responsibility of the official veterinarian (OV). During the preparation for the audit, the CCA identified that some of those establishments were not in compliance with EU legislation as their annual throughput was above the permitted threshold for these derogations. Some CAs took immediate action and, as consequence, some establishments have now reverted to PMI with the presence of an OV on-site fulltime. The CCA is considering next st

label_heading: Conclusion on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: The lack of legal instruments for the CA to impose economic sanctions limits the efficiency of official controls. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 6, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Findings 5.2.1 Structure and organisation

Furthermore, when FBO fails to take corrective action, the lack of an option to impose economic sanctions (other than through penal courts) reduces the ability of the CCA to ensure that the FBO remedies the situation. 5.3 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Official controls at slaughterhouse level Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Articles 10 to 21, 23 to 25, 29, 30, 31, 33, 34 and 43 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings Ante-mortem inspection-red meat and poultry

The law of 28 July 2018 on the system of controls and of sanctions regarding foodstuffs, is the main law governing controls applicable to the establishments within the scope of this audit. This national legislation does not provide the possibility for the CA to impose administrative fines. This is a longstanding issue, already identified in previous Commission audits including DG(SANCO) 2011-8856 and DG(SANCO) 2014-7219. The CA explained that a solution to this has been in preparation for a number of years and that a draft bill was currently being studied. 1 EU legal texts quoted in this document refer to the last amended version 2

The Law of 28 July 2018 established a control system and sanctions relating to foodstuffs, covering all steps of the production chain. As previously explained, this legal 5 instrument does not give the possibility to the CA to impose economic penalties to FBOs other than through a penal process2. Conclusions on competent authorities
There were shortcomings in the CA identifying non-compliances and/or taking appropriate measures to ensure that the operator resolved and prevented the recurrence of those non-compliances.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The shortcomings identified in how the OVs deal with contamination on carcases, with lack of enforcement to ensure that FBOs monitor the hygiene of operations and take suitable and timely action before carcases are presented for PMI with visible contamination.
FBO staff regularly presented carcases with visible contamination for PMI, which created extra work for the vacataires, some of which were busy removing the contamination during PMI.

The audit team did not observe, in any of the two establishments, any FBO staff checking on carcase contamination and taking suitable corrective action (i.e. immediately removing all visible contamination, before presenting those carcases for PMI). The official staff had taken up the task of removing the contamination before declaring the carcases fit for human consumption. HACCP Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Findings

The FBOs food safety management systems checked by the audit team included sufficient controls on animal identification, FCI and on the cleanliness and the state of health of the livestock. In relation to carcase monitoring for the presence of contamination, the FBOs had decided to set a frequency of two checks per week.

The CA accepted this frequency of controls over FBO monitoring of carcass contamination as sufficient. At the time of the visits, especially during cattle production, the OVs and vacataires were seen to be busy removing visible faecal contamination from 9 a significant number of carcases. No monitoring by the FBO on the carcases presented for PMI was observed, nor any action to avoid or to eliminate the contamination on those carcases. Microbiological criteria Legal requirements Articles 35 and 36 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings
The lack of documented procedures or guidance affects the effectiveness of delivery of official controls and results in some controls not fully carried out or not carried out in a consistent manner.

There are several official checklists that the CCA have created and are used during the day-to-day activities at the establishments and also during yearly audits. The daily checklist includes pre-operational checks and animal welfare checks. There are no checklists, nor documented procedures in place for other official controls, including operational hygiene related activities. For those cases, the system relies on verbal instructions and guidance and support from central office staff.

Occasionally different officers gave very different deadlines to similar non-compliances. This was evident when comparing several yearly audit reports. As explained by the CA, this has improved as a result to recent changes in the official controls team, with the current team providing more realistic and suitable enforcement.

Despite these daily checks, in some instances, the OVs didn't manage to identify some problems concerning lack of cleanliness that were later identified during the yearly audit carried out by central office staff.
There are no dedicated checklists or written guidance to aid the OVs when monitoring the hygiene standards during the slaughter operation.
In relation to the operational hygiene requirements, the OV controls did not identify a number of generalised and recurrent unhygienic practices (see p.20) which were observed during the audit.

According to the records checked and discussions with CA staff, the establishment OVs had not identified any problems in relation to FBO's own sampling. However, the audit team found that the sampling programmes were not fully in line with legislation. Issues including the fact that FBOs do not take the samples randomly during production but tend to sample batches or the use of alternative sampling arrangements without demonstration of equivalence (i.e. chicken tested before chilling or beef tested during chilling).

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The post-mortem inspection arrangements in the slaughterhouse that makes use of the time of inspection derogation is not in line with EU law which requires correlation of carcases and offal irrespective of the delay in PMI. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The organisation and structure of the CA and its control system provide a largely adequate framework for the delivery of official controls, which are delivered at the established frequency and generally cover the relevant aspects. Some systemic weaknesses have, however, an impact on their effectiveness: The current legal instrument does not provide the possibility to impose fines. This is a longstanding issue, already identified in previous DG (SANTE)

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: National legislation and guidelines, necessary to ensure implementation and/or enforcement of the EU requirements applicable to the meat sector, are in place and they are largely in line with EU legislation, with the exception of one guideline, which was not up-to-date and, as a result, certain provisions of its content are contrary to EU legislation.

However, the audit team noted that the guidance on ante-mortem inspection (AMI) of poultry at the holding of provenance (NSVFSA Service Note 25901/12.04.2019) allows that "designated veterinarians" perform AMI at the holding of origin (EU legislation requires that AMI should be carried out by an OV). In this regard, NSVFSA informed the audit team that this document had been in place before the new EU legislation was applicable and it has not been updated as yet. In addition, NSVFSA stated that they intend to amend the provisions contained in this document in order to bring them in line with EU requirements.

According to national rules, AMI of poultry is carried out at the holding of origin by "designated veterinarians". In this regard, there is a specific procedure under the Service Note 25901/12.04.2019 (see paragraph 3), which describes the steps to follow and, among other things, requires OVs or OAs (under the supervision of the OV) to perform a simplified AMI at the slaughterhouse.

Conversely, the effectiveness of early detection may be compromised by delays in notifying cases where there are reasons to suspect the presence of ASF to the competent authority. Testing to rule out the disease in those cases, although not yet as part of an official investi- gation, is performed in official laboratories. However, in such instances, the delays, beyond the authorities' control, hinder the swift confirmation of ASF and implementation of restric- tive measures in suspected establishments.

The competent authorities have appropriately controlled confirmed outbreaks of ASF in domestic pigs in four different federal states. All restriction measures had been success- fully lifted by the time of this audit. Despite administrative delays in some cases, the au- thorities effectively implemented measures to eliminate the infection.

However, in some instances, official veterinarians tasked with controlling food business operators do not receive all the necessary documentary guarantees on compliance of the 7 farms of origin with all specific conditions to grant derogations for movement of fresh meat from restricted zones II. That deficiency, which should not increase the risk of spreading ASF, as official controls on those farms are satisfactory, precludes that those officials can properly certify, or guarantee, compliance of that fresh meat with those spe- cific conditions, including with those necessary to apply the health mark to be placed on the EU market.

There are inadequate administrative arrangements and limited official verification to guarantee compliance with rules on the private domestic use of wild boar meat obtained in restricted zones II. Nevertheless, other measures in place mitigate the potential risk of spreading ASF associated with that practice.

The certification of pigs from establishments not complying with the relevant requirements for movement derogations and located in restricted zones II and III, leads to meat which should be restricted to the national market being marked with an oval stamp and considered suitable for the EU market.

The absence of planned checks to ensure the suitability of biosecurity measures on hunting grounds prevent the competent authority to properly identify and address potential sources of infection, to adequately assess risk and monitor disease transmission, to check the level of understanding of the hunting community regarding ASF and to control the pathways of ASF transmission.

The absence of effective verification of the implementation of the official controls related to the certification of pigs from establishments in restricted zones II and III prevents the competent authority to demonstrate the quality, consistency and effectiveness of controls and to ensure that movement of pigs occurs as intended and in line with the rules. In this context, the absence of effective verification lead to incorrect certification of compliance with Regulation 2021/605 not being detected. 6 PREVENTIVE MEASURES The compliance with registration of pig establishments and data on the national database is generally good. There is no legal definition of "commercial" or "non-commercial"

paragraph_text: The interpretation and implementation of "marginal, localised and restricted activity" in the Food Hygiene Direct Marketing Ordinance is not in line with the provisions of Article 1, paragraph 5, point b(ii) of Regulation (EC) N 853/2004. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of, and Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings

The main national legislation covering the safety of milk and dairy products comprises: a. The Food Safety and Consumer Protection Act (Lebensmittesicherheits- und Verbraucherschutzgesetz), as amended, provides the CAs with powers to carry out inspections and audits, and to initiate enforcement measures. b. The Raw milk Ordinance (Rohmilchverordnung) regulates the direct sale of raw milk and cream by the keeper of the animals for immediate human consumption by the final consumer or to retail for immediate sale to the final consumer. It prohibits the sale of raw milk/cream to schools and creches. Other types of catering companies can only use it after effective heat treatment. Raw milk can al
The exchange of information between the veterinary service and public health service at Land level has some gaps that reduce the effectivity of the controls (see paragraphs 37 and 59).

The information flow between the veterinary and food authorities in case of suspicion of bovine tuberculosis and in relation to detection of residues of veterinary medicinal products at Land level demonstrated some gaps (see paragraphs 37 and 59).

The audit team checked a file regarding a bovine milk production holding which was suspected to have animals infected with M. caprae. The actions taken were in line with the legal requirements of the Bovine Tuberculosis Ordinance (Rinder- Tuberkuloseverordnung). Evidence was available that milk from the holding, derived from suspect animals, was sent either to a composting or a biogas plant as category 2 animal by-product (ABP). The information flow between the veterinary and food control authorities in case of suspicion revealed some gaps. The dairy that had received the milk before the suspicion had refused to receive the milk from clinically healthy animals after the suspicion was known.

In Styria and Tyrol, information regarding residues of VMPs detected in raw milk is provided only to the veterinary services. The food inspector from Styria interviewed stated they had requested to also receive this information, as they are responsible for the control of direct sales from the holdings.
The Approval Ordinance is not fully in line with the equivalent EU legislation.

The CAs do not keep the approvals under review in a fully effective manner, and consequently are not aware of all changes in FBOs' activities. 5.4 CONTROLS OVER MILK AND COLOSTRUM PRODUCTION HOLDINGS Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 3 of, and Chapter I of Section IX, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 49 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

Contrary to the requirements of Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 the national legislation permits the issuing of a temporary approval up to 6 months in one step, and the audit team noted this possibility had been used in one establishment file examined.

The approvals issued by the Länder vary in format. Some (e.g. Styria and Upper Austria) include the products range in the approval, some don't (e.g. Tyrol), and some do it for more recent approvals. In Tyrol some long existing FBOs had approvals that were dated back to the 1990s and where the legal basis was old, revoked legislation. The food inspectors interviewed stated that they would know the product range by going through the files of the establishments in the databases. However, the general checklist for dairy inspections did not include a verification of the approval against the activities on the spot. The inspector in one Land stated to use his own checklist for his purpose.

The audit team found a deep freezer in one dairy establishment, used by farmers to deposit colostrum for a dairy FBO located in another Member State. The deep freezer was owned by the foreign dairy and the CA responsible for the controls of the establishment visited was unaware of this activity, which was not subject to an official or own control. Another establishment produced a non-dairy product, which was not included in the approval; the responsible CA was not aware of this activity.

label_heading: Conclusion on controls over milk and colostrum production holdings
paragraph_text: The verification of compliance with hygiene regulatory requirements is carried out on a limited percentage of holdings and the CCA has no overview of the situation, especially in relation to goat and sheep milk production holdings. 5.5 CONTROLS ON RAW MILK UPON COLLECTION Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 3 of, and Chapter I, Part III, Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 50 of, and Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

No harmonised programme is in place for verification of hygiene of primary milk production. The organisation of controls on the hygiene on milk and colostrum on dairy holdings is left to the Länder and the CCA had no overview of the situation, especially regarding goat and sheep dairy production holdings. The Länder Upper and Lower Austria, Styria, and Burgenland use AGES to select the holdings to be visited based on certain risk criteria, the other Länder choose the holdings to be inspected themselves. The controls are usually combined with other controls, e.g. cross-compliance controls, controls on animal welfare, on the use of veterinary medicinal products (VMPs) or animal health controls

The national statistics on inspections of dairy goat and sheep holdings did not match the data from the Länder (for example, in 2021 the number of inspections planned and carried out on goat and sheep dairy holdings was 42 in the national statistics, whereas the number of inspections in Upper Austria was 69 planned and 25 carried out and in Styria there were 10 planned and 5 carried out). Although no inspections of dairy sheep and goat holdings were planned for 2019,2020 and 2021 in Tyrol, the number of annual inspections carried out was 4, 15 and 5, respectively. The CA of Upper Austria stated that no training has been organised on this topic (2). (2) In their response to the draft report,

label_heading: Conclusions on controls on raw milk upon collection
paragraph_text: The central and Land CAs do not have an oversight on how the raw milk quality control system is implemented: for first purchasers who receive 24 000 kg or less raw cow milk annually, milk producers in the agricultural sector who market their milk directly, farms that produce sheep and goat milk and first purchasers of sheep and goat milk.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls on raw milk upon collection
paragraph_text: The methods in place regarding testing of raw milk for antibiotic residues detects only a limited range of residues and the way the testing is implemented cannot guarantee that raw milk containing antibiotic residues is not entering into the production of dairy products for human consumption. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OVER FOOD BUSINESS OPERATORS' COMPLIANCE WITH HYGIENE RULES Legal requirements Articles 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 137, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Articles 3 and 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings 5.6.1 General organisation of official controls

The method used in the AMA-listed laboratories for detection of residues of VMPs at farm tank level (random sampling once a month per producer) is the Brilliant Black- Reductase test (BRT-Test) which had been validated. The method detects beta-lactam antibiotics as well as other groups of antibiotics but the limit of detection is above the maximum residue limit for trimethoprim, lincomycin, sulfadimidine, gentamycin, erythromycin, tetracycline, oxytetracycline and cefquinome. 11

The tests used for testing of raw milk delivered to the dairies for residues of VMPs in the framework of the producers' own controls, was limited to beta-lactams in the dairies visited by the audit team, leaving other possibly used antibiotics undetected in raw milk. The rapid commercial tests were done either at truck and trailer level or truck compartment level by the driver. If the truck/trailer and/or compartment tested positive, the test was repeated as a confirmatory test using an automated reader and the result of this test was decisive.

A large dairy group was processing milk that had tested positive for residues of VMPs with the BRT test, and had used another commercial test for confirmation. The range of antibiotic residues with the second test did not cover all the types of beta-lactams that the first test did. This procedure had, in one dairy, led to 30 340 litres of milk that had tested positive in the first test but negative in the second test to be processed for human consumption in 2020-2022 (in total 49 cases). The FBOs opinion was this milk had been tested as false positive in the first test. The CAs in different Länder had accepted this approach.

A recent Ministerial decree in 2022 has consolidated biosecurity rules for pig establishments, taking into account requirements of the EU ASF Regulation and strengthening protection of establishments against the infection. A new dedicated IT tool is available for categorisation of establishments and selection for official controls. The system is however still under development, and the frequency of regular official controls to verify operators' compliance is not clear yet, even for restricted and infected zones. Hence results from the above efforts to increase biosecurity are yet to yield.

The laboratory network provides reliable and consistent support for the implementation of the ASF control programme. The competent authorities need to ensure that all regional laboratories which carry out confirmatory tests are accredited for the test method used as required by Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Audits of the Regional authorities on the implementation of control measures take place but focus more on procedures rather than on operational activities, thus not fully ensuring that official controls ensure compliance with animal health regulations. 6 PREVENTIVE MEASURES The compliance with registration of pig establishments and data kept on the national database is generally good and allows the competent authorities a good overview of establishments keeping pigs. The authorities have recently strengthened biosecurity rules for all pig establishments and hunting activities. However, the verification of operator compliance with the new rules, in particular the general frequency of controls

Data submitted on the inspections carried out show that the competent authorities followed so far in general the 1 % approach which is the same as 11 Repopulation will for official controls on registration and identification. One Region only be allowed (Piedmonte) visited had increased it to 3% in the free zone, other Regions when biosecurity reportedly apply still higher frequencies. In the restricted zones, the competent requirements are authorities had carried out inspections on biosecurity in all establishments, as adhered to. requested by the decrees of the Ministry of Health, without delay. It remained unclear however, at the time of the audit what the system of regular official contro

The results of the biosecurity inspections varied in the Regions visited, some local health units (ASLs) reported a high number of non-compliances in 2022, following the new rules, but also in 2023. The audit team visited one newly registered establishment, and one existing, located in restricted zone II, which had upgraded their biosecurity measures to the standard as requested following official controls. In both cases, the authorities had approved the biosecurity plans before the establishments could start or continue their activities; the audit team assessed that both plans were generally in compliance with Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2023/594.

The CAs considered that understaffing and work prioritisation had resulted in the reduction of participation in staff training.

Some of the RVUs in the regions visited were understaffed. In one region, only 30 of the 55 posts detailed in the organigram were occupied. In some regions, the regional EFET directorates perform all controls in dairy establishments while in other regions the RVDs and RVUs perform a part of these controls under regional EFET coordination. There are procedures in place for the registration and approval of dairy FBOs. However, the RVU/RVD assessment at the time of approval/update of the approval is not fully effective. label_heading: Conclusions on Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF)
paragraph_text: The CA has designated a national contact point for RASFF and issued procedures for managing RASFF notifications. However, the notifications are not immediately transmitted to the local CAs, which delays the CAs in carrying out appropriate actions on-the-spot.

Five alerts related to milk and dairy products of Greek origin had been notified in RASFF between 2019 and 2022. The audit team reviewed the CA action in two RASFF cases issued after detection of pathogens in cheese. The national contact point communicated the information on RASFF to local level one week after its receipt in the first case and after 3 days in the second case. This is not in line with Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. The CCA explained that a management signature is required, which delays the communication to local level.

label_heading: Conclusion on controls on raw milk upon collection
paragraph_text: A raw milk sampling and testing framework in line with the EU legal requirements is in place. The compliance of raw milk with PC requirements has improved compared to the previous audit. However, the measures in place had not been effective to 9 improve the raw cow milk compliance with SCC requirements as approximately 30% of the raw cow milk does not comply with the SCC requirements. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OVER FOOD BUSINESS OPERATORS' COMPLIANCE WITH HYGIENE RULES Legal requirements Articles 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 137, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The RVUs in general follow up through letters to the farmers and, for recurring high levels of non-compliance, sometimes also on-farm visits. However, contrary to the requirements of Section IX, Chapter I, Part III (5) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, the FBOs do not routinely notify the CA of the 8 (non-compliant) results.
