The CA performing controls in the dairy establishments either did not check whether the FBOs notify the non-compliant results for SCC, PC and antibiotic residues or, when this was checked, the shortcoming did not trigger enforcement ­ the CA recommended the FBO to notify the CA. The option for suspension of milk collection provided by Article 50(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 is not generally used by FBOs and is not required by CAs as the milk is pasteurised. The results for SCC and/or PC testing of many holdings (amongst those with non-compliant results) showed very high counts, repeatedly each month, during a selected period of 12 consecutive months.

Summary statistics provided by ELGO Dimitra for the 2020-2022 timeframe indicate that between 97.4% and 99.3% of the sheep and goat milk collected from milk production holdings had satisfactory results at PC testing. At the time of the previous audit, over 96% of the sheep and goat milk was compliant whereas the level of compliance for raw bovine milk was of approximately 80% for PC and 70% for SCC. Regarding cow milk received in the establishments, the compliance levels reached in recent years (rolling geometrical averages over a two- and three-month period, respectively) were the following: a. label_heading: Conclusions on controls over milk and colostrum production holdings
paragraph_text: Official controls on holdings are planned on a risk basis. However, the implementation of these controls was not harmonised between regions and the CAs verify compliance with hygiene requirements on a small number of holdings (the targets for these controls are not reached). While the assessed (performed) controls detected shortcomings, these shortcomings were not enforced in all regions which may further limit the impact of the on-farm controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on controls over milk and colostrum production holdings
paragraph_text: The CAs put measures in place in case of tuberculosis and/or brucellosis in dairy farms and those measures also concern the destination of the milk from the respective herds. However, the measures were not effective to timely prevent milk from positive animals from entering the food chain in the case assessed by the audit team. 5.5 CONTROLS ON RAW MILK Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. The CA stated this was a result of limited staff availability and in 2020 was also due to challenges faced because of the COVID-19 pandemic. 5.4.1 Health requirements for raw milk and colostrum

The audit team assessed the action taken by the CA after detection of brucellosis in a bovine herd. The RVU had imposed the measures outlined by the procedures in place that aim to ensure the safety of milk obtained from the holding after receiving a positive blood test result. The CA had also required the FBO to sign a sworn statement that they would comply with these measures. However, the actions were not effective to adequately/timely prevent that the milk from positive animals does not enter the food chain, contrary to the requirements of Section IX, Chapter I, Part I(4) and (5) of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. a. In one of the regions visited the scope of the hygiene controls on holdings was comprehensive, the RVU/RVD used the CCA's and locally developed targeted checklist and implemented the inspections largely as planned. The CAs documented their controls and detected relevant non-compliances, except for the lack of protection against vermin of the milk storage premises in the farm visited by the audit team. However, in this region the CA performed an advisory role and had not used enforcement on farms.

In the other region visited, the CAs had recently started to use the checklist issued by the CCA when carrying out on-farm controls. The CAs met explained that previous hygiene controls had not been documented. Overall, the RVUs performed a small number of on- farm controls due to resource limitations (see paragraph 20). In this region, enforcement measures had been taken for shortcomings noted during dairy farm controls.

The RVUs' farm inspections include checks on compliance with the rules for administration of veterinary drugs. label_heading: Conclusion on system of supervision and internal audits
paragraph_text: Internal audits are in place and identify relevant aspects on the performance of dairy controls. However, the audit sample is limited to one region. The audits have not triggered systemic improvements although similar issues persist in other regions. This limits the overall impact. The measures to verify the effectiveness of the official controls were not fully effective. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The structure and organisation of the CAs responsible for official controls over the production of milk and dairy products provides, in principle, for an adequate framework for the performance of their tasks. The official controls are planned on a risk basis. However, their effectiveness is impacted by

The frequency of the dairy internal audits by EFET is approximately once every 5 years. Each audit assesses the CCA and one regional CA. The systemic findings of one audit (in a region) do not trigger actions in the other regions nor an enquiry into whether the same problems arise in other regions, nor related measures to be taken if so needed. The audit team had access to different audit reports that identify similar problems in different regions, but these were in different audit cycles and therefore years apart. label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: There is no system of official controls of bivalve molluscs and marine gastropods at primary production level in Bulgaria and the majority of the requirement of EU legislation are not met. Although there are certain official controls in place after primary production (carried out at establishments), they are insufficient to provide adequate food safety assurances if the primary production is not controlled. 5 5.3 LABORATORIES Legal requirements Articles 5(1), 18(2)(d)(iv), 34, 37 to 39, 100 and 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Bulgaria has not fixed the location and boundaries of production areas, contrary to Article 52(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The BFSA stated that each mussel farm is considered as an individual production area, and that the BFSA's Directorate of Animal Health and Welfare has a register of mussels' aquaculture farms publicly available at the BFSA website, with the farm location and boundaries coordinates provided by the Black Sea Basin Directorate.

Bulgaria has not carried out the sanitary surveys required in Article 56 of the same Regulation. Consequently, it has not classified them, contrary to the requirements of Articles 52(2) and (3) of the same Regulation.

At the time of the audit, there was no monitoring of production areas (or aquaculture farms if they are individually considered, see paragraph 4) for microbiological, chemical contaminants, biotoxins or phytoplankton, contrary to the requirements of Articles 57 to 61 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Consequently, there is neither management of production areas nor record and exchange of information to interested parties, which conditions are established respectively in Articles 61 and 62, and 66 of the same Regulation, with the exception of the BFSA's register of mussels' aquaculture farms (see paragraph 4), which could partially meet the recording of information required in Article 66(a) of that Regulation.

As required by Article 64 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the BFSA has in place a sampling programme of final products of bivalve molluscs' origin, either at establishments or at retail level. Official samples of mussels and wedge clams are tested for biotoxins at the NRL and for E. coli and salmonella at the regional official control laboratories. Non- compliant results trigger the recall and withdraw from the market of the batch of bivalve molluscs tested. 5.2.2 Official controls of certain bivalve molluscs harvested outside classified production areas

In 2021, the NRL in Spain processed 1,225 samples from wild birds, of which two were positive. In 2022, there were 3,040 such samples of which 144 were positives.

There were major delays in confirming the infection (Table A) for the positive samples taken either by active or passive surveillance of wild birds (172 from September 2020 to April 2023). Nearly 99% of all cases were confirmed more than three days after sampling, and 50% of them were confirmed two weeks after sampling. The timescales were due to the involvement of two laboratories in the diagnosis of the disease ­ the Autonomous Community laboratory where the generic Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test is carried out and the national reference laboratory where the virus is subtyped and its pathogenicity determined. The authorities explained that in many of those cases, confirmation was not

The authorities took samples of dead and sick wild birds reported under passive surveillance in the same areas where the first cases of poultry were confirmed a few days after (January and February 2022). However, the fact that those wild birds' samples were processed and confirmed several days after the poultry cases were detected, prevented the competent authority from implementing the enhanced surveillance in poultry, that should have been triggered after confirmation of the infection in wild birds. This is not in line with Section 2, paragraph 2(a)of Annex II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/689.

During passive and active surveillance, the NRL detected six positives to avian influenza virus other than H5 or H7 in 2020, 43 positives to other than H5 or H7 avian influenza virus in 2021 and, 67 non H5 and no H7 avian influenza virus in 2022. All these were detected in wild birds. Laboratory capacity- Diagnostics used for general early detection.

In the event of suspicion of HPAI in poultry, the competent authority set restrictions on the suspected establishments without delay. However, the initial veterinary investigation and sampling was delayed in several cases. Although in most cases, informal communications with the national disease crisis centre occurred immediately, there were delays in the regional authorities conducting the required investigation to confirm or rule out the presence of HPAI. This is not in line with Article 54 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The authorities granted a total of 752 movement derogations from restricted zones to free areas. The great majority (740) were direct movements to slaughter. The remaining 12 movements were granted from hatcheries in the restricted zone to other neighbouring areas outside the restricted zone. 12

These movements were carried out in line with the majority of requirements, e.g., clinical inspections, testing, sealed transports, best available routes to avoid cross contamination, and they were all under official supervision. But the audit team saw evidence that the authorities did not carry out an adequate risk assessment before they authorised those movements considering all relevant EU requirements. There is no protocol or instructions to carry out this risk assessment taking into account relevant legislation. This is not in line with Article 28(1) and 43(1) of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. E.g. during this epidemic in Spain, there was evidence that some neighbour

The competent authorities need to update the contingency plan, together with the epidemiological inquiry to be used for the investigation of aquatic diseases, taking into account the new provisions set by the AHL. This would allow the competent authorities to act, in line with the EU legislation, if a Category A disease is occurring in the country.

The competent authority has a contingency plan on how to contain and manage outbreaks of listed or emerging Category A diseases in aquaculture animals. The contingency plan is available on the intranet of the DVFA. However, the last version of the contingency plan is dated 2010 and the DVFA is planning to update it in 2024, together with a new format for the epidemiological inquiry that the Team Aqua has to use to investigate aquatic diseases.

label_heading: Conclusions on registration and approval of aquaculture establishments
paragraph_text: The competent authority have implemented effectively the new process of registration and approval of the aquaculture establishments, according to the AHL, with clear guidelines and instructions for the correct implementation from the VIU. However, in some cases the Team Aqua has assessed the risk of the approved establishments not taking into account all the criteria listed in Annex VI to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689. This may increase the risk of not detecting the IHN during the regular health visits carried out by the Team Aqua.

The audit team visited one trout establishment approved and ranked as medium risk by the Team Aqua, since aquatic animals are sent to put and take lakes only. However, the competent authority didn't consider the high risk of infection due to the close proximity to an angling lake next to it, the recurrence of the IHN infection with two outbreaks occurred respectively in 2021 and 2022 and the high number of movements in and out the establishment. This is not in line with Chapter 2 a) and b), Part I of Annex VI to Regulation (EU) 2020/689, as regards the risk ranking to be applied in certain approved aquaculture establishments in this regard.

The audit team visited another trout establishment approved and ranked as medium risk, which has been infected with IHN in September 2022. Fish is kept for approximately three months, from 200 to 500 grams. The operator is consigning to more than 50 establishments, of which approximately 70 % are put and take lakes, and it is receiving from other 20 establishments. Nevertheless, the competent authority didn't consider the high risk of infection due to the high number of movements going in and out the establishment. This is not in line with Regulation (EU) 2020/689, as mentioned in the previous finding. The competent authority agreed with the audit team on the need to review the risk assessme

The official veterinarians of the Team Aqua are implementing, in particular, the risk-based health surveillance in all approved aquaculture establishments, as foreseen by Chapter 1, Part III, Annex VI of Regulation (EU) 2020/689. The frequency of the health visits and possible sampling depends on the risk of the approved aquaculture establishment, determined by the DVFA as high, medium or low. However, the DVFA ranked some of the establishments visited by the audit team, as explained in previous findings 36 and 37, with a risk ranking (i.e. "medium" instead of "high) which is resulting in a frequency of health visits too low.

The competent authorities implemented the certification for the trade of aquatic animals from Denmark to other Member States as required by EU legislation. However, the competent authority deemed transportation of aquatic animals, transiting through a water exchange point in Denmark without proper disinfection procedures, as the possible cause of the transmission of IHN to another Member State This is not in line with the EU legislation, that requires that the competent authorities must certify that animals are not transported under conditions that jeopardize their health status.

The competent authorities in Finland notified an IHN outbreak in June 2022, following a consignment of aquatic animals received from Denmark. The DVFA traced and tested, with negative results, the two establishments delivering respectively eggs and fishes to the confirmed outbreak in Finland, explaining to the audit team that a possible transmission of the disease was 24 due to the transit through one of the two water exchange points registered in Denmark. As a consequence, the DVFA established a specific procedure for the cleaning and disinfection of one of the two water exchange points, with all transporters requested to transit that specific water exchange point when delivering fish for i

The competent authorities have approved the procedures for the cleaning and disinfection of the transporters, one water exchange point, and for all the other documents foreseen by the EU legislation. However, they are not applying regular official controls on transporters and water exchange points, on a risk basis, to verify compliance with the approved procedures and the activities under the control of operators. This is not in line with the EU legislation, and it is not assuring the absence of risk of transmission of IHN or other aquatic diseases with the 25 movement of aquatic animals. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The competent authorities have established a system with effective coordination a

The VIUs are carrying out spot-checks of transporters according to Regulation (EU) 1/2005, for animal welfare. However, they are not carrying out the official controls of the transporters registered in the Country. This is not in line with the provisions of paragraph 1 of Articles 9, 10 and 20 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (Official Controls Regulation - OCR), regarding the regular risk based official controls on all operators, including transporters, at any stage of production, processing and distribution of animals, products of animal origin and germinal products. Those official controls would need to address, as well, the activities under the control of operators, i.e., the general obligati

Official personnel at central and local levels are clearly designated. They have followed comprehensive training on aquaculture animal health and the EU requirements. However, in the Federal States visited, the Fish Health Services and private veterinarians and/or aquatic animal health professionals, perform certain tasks related to other official activities, such as the health visits and sampling that are part of the risk-based health surveillance that is designed and should be conducted by the competent authority. The competent authorities have not formally delegated those responsibilities, or audited or inspected the Fish Health Services and/or private professionals, to verify that they p

Those veterinarians and professionals are providing animal health services, but neither them nor the Fish Health Services can carry out the official controls required by Article 5 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/160 and Article 3 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/671. They count also on the support of private designated and accredited 6 laboratories to investigate situations where they are notified by operators and need to take samples for examination in accordance with Article 18(1)(c) of the AHL. The authorities of the Federal States visited have not delegated formally to the Fish Health Services (that are not part of their organisation) or to private veterinaria

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls of live bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The classification of production areas would be consistent with the EU classification requirements if harvesting is officially allowed exclusively during the summer (harvesting period). If harvesting is allowed during the whole year, the absence of appropriate frequency for sampling does not allow the authorities to ensure the same level of health and safety guarantees for the mollusc harvested outside this period.

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls of live bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: The current design of the monitoring programme for microbiological quality seems adequate for the harvesting period, but the programmes for the presence of biotoxins and phytoplankton are not fully aligned with EU requirements and are not fully implemented. This could compromise the ability of the competent authority to detect possible exceedances of biotoxins limits. The delays in obtaining laboratory test results lower the effectiveness of the monitoring.

According to the relevant procedures, competent authorities periodically monitor classified production areas in order to check the microbiological quality of LBM, and the presence of marine biotoxins and chemical contaminants in LBM and, since recently, for the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water, as required respectively in Article 59(b)(c) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The monitoring in one of the production areas was very limited, therefore not meeting these requirements. a) For microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs

According to the relevant procedure, all points have to sampled once per month, which comply with the requirements of Article 61(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627; however, in practice, this frequency is only implemented during the harvesting period and the months immediately prior and subsequent to it (see section 4 and paragraph 9, regarding seasonal harvesting), which could be sufficient if harvesting was officially allowed exclusively during this part of the year, which was not the case at the time of the audit.

According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency that varies between once per week (during the harvesting season) to once per month (from October to April), which would be in line with Article 61(1) an (4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 if harvesting was officially allowed exclusively during part of the year. However, at the time of the audit, this frequency was not met. According to the information provided to the audit team, there were different factors that prevented the sampling plan to be fulfilled (e.g., availability of vessels and other logistic problems, rough weather conditions), or that undermined the usefulness of complying with these frequencies

According to the relevant procedure, monitoring has to be carried out with a frequency similar to the biotoxins; therefore, the same observations made above (paragraph 17) regarding required frequencies and the difficulties faced by counties CA are relevant here.

They consider its effectiveness is limited value due to several reasons: the same sampling locations are used for water and LBM, there are no additional water sampling locations for early warning, the long turnarounds times for results established in national legislation, and delays from laboratories results for biotoxins and phytopla

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls of live bivalve molluscs
paragraph_text: In addition, the monitoring programme for biotoxins does not include marine gastropods, and there are no data that compare the rate of accumulation of biotoxins with the indicator species. This poses a risk that marine gastropods with biotoxins content above the regulated limits might be placed on the market.

Although NRLs for E. coli and biotoxins are designated, the fact that they do not always fulfil the conditions of EU legislation for this designation or that they do not carry out all the tasks and responsibilities prescribed can have an impact in the quality and consistency of the results delivered.

The designation of official control laboratories includes all relevant laboratories (except for phytoplankton). As these laboratories do not always fulfil all the conditions for their designation and the designation does not always include all the necessary details to ensure timely and quality provision of results, this can have a negative impact in the quality of official controls over LBM and affect their efficient and effective supervision.

The technical competence and capacity of the official control laboratories for E. coli and phytoplankton, their fitness for purpose and their generally adequate analytical methods, instils confidence in the reliability of their results. This supports the authorities in the monitoring of production areas, allowing them to make informed decisions to safeguard the safety of molluscs.

Despite the technical competence and capacity of the official control laboratory for biotoxins, the fact that the validation of ASP and PSP testing methods is not internationally recognised, makes the reliability and accuracy of the results produced questionable for these two biotoxins. In addition, the fact that the laboratory for lipophilic toxins cannot analyse a number of compounds of this group (although it uses the EU reference method, internally validated and accredited) raises concern about the risk of underestimation of this biotoxin.
The absence of participation of official control laboratories in proficiency testing prevent the authorities to demonstrate the reliability of their results.

The long turnarounds times established in national legislation, together with the laboratories delays in providing timely results, have a negative impact on the quality of 13 official controls. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Although the official system for controlling bivalve molluscs and marine gastropods was only established in 2019, the authorities at different levels show good understanding of legislative requirements, and willingness to solve the deficiencies and to improve the system. The control system in place generally aligns with EU provisions, but it is implemented in full only during the harvesting period. Therefore, it would be consistent with the EU requirements if harvesting is officia

The competent authority has designated NRLs for E. coli and for biotoxins in LBM, as required in Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. However, at the time of the audit, the NRL for biotoxins did not meet certain legislative requirements (i.e., Article 100(2) and (3)(c)(e)). 10

The audit team showed evidence of the implementation of part of the tasks established in Article 101(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 by the NRL for E. coli (e.g., participation in proficiency testing organised by the EURL, provision of training and support to official control laboratories); however, this laboratory has not been able to organise an inter-laboratory comparative testing or a proficiency test between official control laboratories (there are only a few of them in the country) (required in Article 101(1)(c) of the same Regulation).
At the time of the audit, the NRL for biotoxins was not in a position to comply with most of the responsibilities and tasks established in Article 101(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The competent authorities have designated official control laboratories, as required in Article 37(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In particular, they have designated three laboratories for E. coli (two testing LBM from production areas and one testing final products from dispatch centres) and one for biotoxins. However, designations do not include all the details required by Article 37(3) and, in the case of biotoxins laboratory, it does not require to use testing methods in line with EU requirements (see paragraph 57). At the time of the audit the laboratory testing for phytoplankton had not yet been designated as it did not comply with part of the national requirements for designation.

With regard to supervision of the designated laboratories, the CCA, in collaboration with the NRL for E. coli, carries out audits of these laboratories at county level, as required in Article 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, although limited to the conditions described in the previous paragraph. However, the CCA informed the audit team that a similar type of supervision cannot be carried out over central level laboratories designated for official controls; therefore, audits required by Article 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 are not performed over the biotoxins laboratory. 5.3.1 Laboratories for microbiology
These laboratories regularly participate in proficiency testing but they have never participated in a proficiency testing with LBM sample matrix. 11 5.3.2 Laboratory for phytoplankton
There are two analysts qualified for the identification and quantification of plankton species. Both were internally trained and have plans to participate in external training in 2024.

The laboratory consistently conducts internal quality controls, with every sample being analysed by the two analysts by default to ensure the accuracy and consistency of phytoplankton results. The laboratory has never participated in a proficiency testing, but it intends to participate in one in 2024.

At the time of the audit, the long turnarounds times established in national legislation, together with the length of the analysis in this laboratory, limited the value of this monitoring for the competent authorities. 5.3.3 Laboratories for biotoxins

The official control laboratory for PSP and ASP uses testing methods which validation has not been internationally recognised, therefore they do not meet the requirements of Chapters I(A) and (B) and II(A) and (B) of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627, respectively.

The laboratory for lipophilic toxins uses the EU reference method established in Chapter III(A) of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. It mostly follows the EU reference laboratory standard operational procedure with a few deviations (e.g., it does not include part of the certified reference materials, certain quality control criteria, recovery correction and matrix correction). It is accredited by the national accreditation body, as required in Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The laboratory has carried out an internal validation for mussel matrix, as this is the species routinely analysed in this laboratory. However, the validation was not carried out for all the relevant tox

According to the information provided to the audit team, biotoxins results are normally issued in 4-5 days; however, it most of the laboratory reports assessed, the reporting time was one week. Despite the fact this is within the deadline established in national legislation, this provides limited value to the competent authorities to adequately manage production areas, therefore it cannot be considered as a timely delivery of test results as required in Article 37(4)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Regarding the BCPs designated by AFSVSPP for food and feed of non-animal origin, the facilities were in general not compliant at the BCP Luka Koper port. At the BCP Ljubljana Brnik airport the facilities for controls on consignments of goods of animal origin were shared with controls of food and feed of non-animal origin. The audit team noted that the unloading and storage facilities for food and feed of non-animal origin at the BCP Luka Koper port did not have adequate drainage and most floors were constructed of tarmac which is not easy to clean and disinfect. This is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team noted that both BCPs designated by HIRS for controls on food contact materials and food supplements were not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs due to a lack of facilities and equipment. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) and (c) of the OCR and Articles 3 and 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In the absence of BCP control facilities, the documentary controls are carried out in regional offices outside the port or airport. The identity and physical checks take place in the storage facilities within the BCP Luka Koper port which do not meet the minimum requirements (see finding 48) or at Ljubljana airport, which also did not have adequate drainage.

The identity and physical checks take place in the storage facilities within the BCP Luka Koper port which do not meet the minimum requirements (see finding 48) or at Ljubljana airport, which also did not have adequate drainage.

While the evaluated BCPs were generally compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals and goods of animal origin for which they had been designated, shortcomings were identified with respect to the facilities in place at three BCPs, for the storage of goods of non-animal origin intended for human consumption for which the BCPs had been designated, which have the potential to reduce the overall effectiveness of the official control system. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The audit found that there is a comprehensive system of official controls in place for animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the Union through BCPs in Portugal, which is supported b

The audit team noted that the facilities in place for official controls on live animals and goods of animal origin at the BCP Lisbon airport were generally compliant with the requirements for BCP's, in line with Article 64(3) of the OCR and Articles 3, 4, 5 and 6 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. However, the team found that the facilities in place for official controls on goods of non-animal origin were not compliant with those minimum requirements, and noted the following shortcomings: · there were no storage facilities for food of non-animal origin, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · adjacent commercial storage facilities of cargo handlers were used for

The following shortcomings were noted during the visits to the two inspection centres: 12 · both inspection centres did not have adequate drainage in the unloading, inspection and storage areas or rooms, which is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · at the inspection centre Sotagus, the storage room for ambient goods of animal origin intended for human consumption was not easy to clean and disinfect due

The system in place ensures that consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are presented for official controls, and that those controls are, generally carried out in line with guidelines, documented procedures and Union legislation. A limited number of shortcomings were identified, the most significant of which related to the performance of physical checks on consignments of animals in transit, which are based on a visual check rather than a clinical examination as required.

The SFVS stated that consignments of bovine animals in transit are not partially or fully unloaded for identity and physical checks at the BCP of arrival, but that they conduct a visual check of the animals on the means of transport, using fixed platforms. The audit team noted that this does not allow an appropriate clinical examination of the selected 10 animals to be performed, which is not in line with Article 4(3) and Part II of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

paragraph_text: The CAs consider almost all relevant risks when developing the plan of controls on the marketing and use of PPPs, however the pesticide residues monitoring programme does not feed into the development of the professional user control plan as required by Article 24 (2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and entities for national controls are chosen at random.

It was confirmed that the Czech Agriculture and Food Inspection Authority (CAFIA) cross report MRL exceedances to CISTA and this in turn triggers extraordinary controls on professional users. However, the results of the annual residue monitoring programme are not used to enhance the risk based elements of choosing which professional users to inspect as required by Article 24 (2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at professional user level with the exception of extraordinary controls, are performed with prior notice, as are the majority of official controls carried out at PPP manufacturing and distribution level, thus taking away from the overall effectiveness of the control programme.

The official controls are routinely performed with up to two or three days prior notice being given which is in conflict with Article 9 (4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires no prior notice be given before controls are carried out except where particular circumstances require that notice is given. This was further confirmed by the inspectors from the regional departments. However, official controls are carried out in a way that minimises disruption or administrative burden to the entities inspected as required by Article 9 (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 10

Controls are generally carried out with at least some level of prior notice. This can be as little as twenty-four hours or as much as a few weeks depending on the circumstances. It is more routine that two to three days' notice is given to the entity being inspected which is not coherent the requirement laid down by Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Importation of PPPs for use in other MSs or third countries

The audit team observed 3 routine controls of professional users of PPPs and all incorporated the use of both control questionnaires mentioned in the preceding paragraphs. Two of the controls involved farming companies and the other control was carried out on a company involved in managing and maintaining private and public spaces. The same main process was used in all three controls by different inspectors. To avoid wasted journeys and wasting time it is routine that controls are announced in advance. label_heading: Conclusions on controls on the marketing of plant protection products
paragraph_text: The CISTA has lists for all entities marketing PPPs, thereby having the necessary information on which to base controls, however, some of these lists provided to the audit team were found to be somewhat incomplete, resulting in the stores of some distributors being less subject to control than others.

The CISTA provided the audit team with a comprehensive set of lists which act as a basis for the PPP marketing control programme. It was explained during the course of the audit that the lists do contain some overlaps, which is understandable as some operators may function in multiple ways. However, it is conceivable that a manufacturer, not registered as a professional use PPP distributor will not be automatically inspected annually. They may be picked for inspection each year, but this is dependent on each individual regional department. It is also the case that some of the manufacturers and other operators offer products for sale on-line, but yet do not appear on the "on-line" list. Never

The CISTA operates a system that requires all distributors of professional use PPPs to be notified to them. This enables the CISTA to have a working list from which to base their control plan. This is a good practice and having lists of entities to control is a fundamental basis on which to build a control plan. There are lists of distributors, re- packers, manufacturers, importers and online sellers maintained by the DAIC of the CISTA, however, during the course of the audit it was found that in some cases the lists were incomplete or at very least not up to date.

One such example is where the actual full list of premises associated with at least three distributors was not up to date. It was observed during the two distributor inspections, where each premises visited was also acting as a PPP store on contract for another 15 entity. Therefore, the premises that we visited should have been listed for a number of different legal entities but was not. Furthermore, the PPPs that were owned by those third party entities and present in the same store as the entity being inspected, were not considered or subjected to the control the audit team observed. The information kept in the database makes possible full traceability of PDO and PGI wines. CAFIA verifies the origin and the quality of PDO wines and issues administrative decisions for the classification and marketing of PDO wines. Such controls are not required for wines intended to be marketed as PGI (see also paragraphs 33, 46 and 66 below). The eligibility for using PDO/PGI designations is also checked when the products are placed on the market, particularly in the retailers' chain.

Operators wishing to market their wine as PDO have to request the classification of every batch of wine produced by CAFIA. This is achieved at the expense of an administrative fee paid to CAFIA, which becomes income of the state budget. The classification procedure is based on the verification of grapes and on analytical and organoleptic testing. The wine classification carried out by CAFIA ensures the traceability of the origin and the quality of every batch of wine intended to be marketed as PDO (e.g. "quality wine" or "quality wine with an attribute"). However, such a system is not in place for PGI wines.

The authenticity of the marketed wines is verified through official analytical testing carried out in the laboratory of CAFIA. The sensory commission of CAFIA carries out organoleptic testing. Where the traceability of sampled wines cannot be otherwise verified, the laboratory is requested to carry out isotopic analysis of wine samples. However, the examination of the authenticity is not an option for PGI wines, as no classification involving at least sampling for analytical testing is carried out for wine batches intended to be marketed as PGI products. paragraph_text: The combination of a clear legal framework, CAs with clearly defined responsibilities and allocation of resources provides a solid foundation for the eradication of the outbreaks of OFF in Italy. The lack of verification of the work of non-accredited laboratories via proficiency tests organised by the NRL increases the risk of incorrect diagnostics of OFF. 5.2 CONTINGENCY AND ACTION PLANS Legal requirements Article 25, 26 and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The Plant Protection Laboratory (PPL) is the national reference laboratory (NRL) for plant health for Cyprus. The PPL exchanges information with the CA on the sampling procedure and carries out the examination and analysis of samples required for the identification of S. frugiperda, D. citri and C. Liberibacter. PPL is accredited in accordance with EN ISO/IEC 17025 standard, however methods used for testing for these pests are not within the scope of the accreditation, as required by Article 100(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The initial positive results concerning both pests presence was confirmed by an EU reference laboratory (EURL). All subsequent testing is carried out by the NRL. 7

The "Contingency plan for the control of C. Liberibacter", is currently in draft format. According to the CA, this document is also considered to serve as the action plan for its control, should the pest be detected in the future. The document includes details about the biology and vectors of the pest, the measures to be taken in case of suspected or confirmed findings of C. Liberibacter and the establishment of DAs and measures to be taken within i.e. destruction of all host plants in nurseries and garden centres and orchards. Following the first confirmed finding of S. frugiperda in January 2023, the CA did not immediately establish a demarcated area, as the first finding was found in a light trap on the property of a private citizen and was not associated with a growing crop or located near host species. On 14 March 2023, the CA issued instructions in the form of an action plan to delimit an area of 5 km around the site where the pests was found. However, the CA did carry out intensive surveys assisted by trapping to detect the pest in the vicinity of the outbreak, in accordance with the action plan.

In July 2023, the second finding occurred, where one S. frugiperda larva was detected in a maize crop in Larnaca district and then again in September 2023, the CA reported the third official detection of the pest in a maize crop in Nicosia. According to the first Europhyt update (ref: 01/2023-07-26) on the outbreak, the CA stated that they demarcated a 100 m infested area and a 100 km buffer zone around the outbreak site, and in effect demarcating the entire island. Contrary to the Europhyt update, the audit team noted during the site visits, that the infested zones were considered to be the field or plot of land where the infestation occurred but did not include a radius of 100 m around the

According to the CA, maize, peppers and aubergines are considered to be a risk among those specified plants referred to in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/638, which was in force up until 30 June 2023. Furthermore, the CA stated, that at the time, it did not consider other host plants listed in the ESFA pest survey card for S. frugiperda (June 2020) to be a risk, even though according to the document, they are liable to become infested. Crops such as potatoes, certain cereal crops and brassicas which are grown throughout Cyprus where the pest is not known to occur are excluded. 5.3.2 Establishment of DAs due to the presence of Diaphorina citri

Similar to the procedure for S. frugiperda, the CA established the infested zone to be the citrus orchard or plot infested with D. citri, without taking into consideration other citrus orchards in close proximity to the source of infestation. The audit team visited a number of outbreak sites, where there were other citrus orchards adjacent to the infested plots. According to the CA, since there was no evidence of infestation in these plots, they did not include them in the infested zone. If established, the buffer zone can form the basis for measures such as surveys and restrictions on movement of plants or additional controls. Following the first finding of S. frugiperda, the CA conducted intensive surveys with the assistance of trapping in the vicinity of this finding, focusing their efforts on production sites of host plants of maize, peppers and aubergines considered to be a risk for the presence of the pest (see paragraph 22). However, according to the EFSA pest survey card, delimiting surveys should cover all host species in the survey area. Surveys are not carried out in line with Articles 19(1) and 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, which requires that surveys shall take account of scientific and technical evidence, and any other appropriate information, concerning the presence of the pests concerned.

At the time of the second finding in a maize crop, Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 applied, with regards to the requirements for surveys in demarcated areas. According to the action plan of 14 March 2023, surveillance and sampling for the presence of S. frugiperda, a mix of seven funnel and delta pheromone traps were to be placed within the 5 km buffer zone. These were checked once or twice a week, 11 respectively, and the insect samples were sent to the PPL for analysis. In the update to the action plan (12 September 2023), it provided instructions for the placement of a further 17 funnel and delta traps in the Nicosia, Limassol, Larnaca, and the Paphos areas, which were to be checke

On 12 June 2023, Annex 1 to Regulation (EU) 2023/1134, provided an extended list of host plants, including certain Solanum spp. and Brassicaceae. However, following the second finding of the pest, the CA maintained their survey focus on the three crops referred to in paragraph 27, without full consideration for the other hosts listed in the annex to the above Regulation or the EFSA pest survey card. This is not fully in line with Article 7(b) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134, which requires scouting in sites of production where host plants are grown.

In the update to the action plan (12 September 2023) when Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 applied, there was no survey design or sampling scheme developed, which should provide guidelines on being able to identify with at least a 95 % level of confidence, a 1 % a level of presence of the specified pest. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 7(c) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134.

As a result of the surveys and trapping, the pest was detected in multiple locations across the island. According to the CA, there are 16 infested production sites spread across the whole island. As a result of these findings the CA demarcated the whole island (see section 4.3). The audit team noted that ADOs staff displayed good knowledge for recognising the late larval stages of the pest and signs or symptoms for their presence, particularly on maize crops. 5.4.2 Surveys for Diaphorina citri

The CA carries out regular surveys in the demarcated areas for D. citri in parallel with the survey for C. Liberibacter. These surveys are focused on production sites of citrus fruit, nurseries and garden centres with host plants including citrus and Murraya spp. plants. However, as a result of the buffer zone not being clearly defined (see paragraphs 23 and 24), these surveys were conducted all over Cyprus.

The audit team noted that citrus trees were abundant all over Cyprus however, abandoned orchards, private properties and urban areas with bitter orange (Citrus aurantium) trees growing on the footpaths, are not included in the scope of the survey. According to the CA, this was due to the lack of resources. Furthermore, the CA requires permission to access private properties and if refused it would require a court order to gain access, which was too complicated, so it was not done. This is not in line with Articles 19(1) and 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, which requires that the survey shall be carried out in all appropriate locations and be based on sound scientific and technical princi

The ADO staff informed the audit team that surveys are in general based on visual examination of plant material of trees grown in orchards, for detecting symptoms caused by D. citri adults or nymphs. They also stated that as a result of the information 12 campaign raised by the Department of Agriculture for D. citri, the producers frequently report suspicious symptoms concerning its presence.

ADO staff have been instructed to focus the survey on citrus trees in places of production at the time of new flushing, in spring, mid-summer and late autumn. The ADO staff follow an "S-shape" course within the citrus orchards and focus on the recently developed flushes of young stems and leaves of trees. However, this is not always possible, in particular for the developing upper parts of the tree canopy and surveillance efforts are mostly limited to leaves growing within the lower interior central part of the trees.

According to the statement of the ADOs staff, one yellow sticky trap is deployed per citrus orchard regardless of its size. However, out of the six citrus orchards visited, only one yellow sticky trap was spotted by the audit team in an orchard located in the Asomatos Limassol area where the presence of D. citri was first reported. Also, in the nurseries and garden centres visited, close to infested zones, the audit team noted that yellow sticky traps were not deployed for the detection of D. citri, as there was no requirement or recommendation to do so.

However, the document recommends that visual examinations for C. Liberibacter should be complemented with a sampling programme for symptomatic and asymptomatic plant material.

Surveys for C. Where the pest is found to be present, operators are instructed to implement increased frequency of pesticide applications by spraying for the control of S. frugiperda. According to the CA, at the stage when larvae were detected, it was largely ineffective due to inappropriate timing of applications as the caterpillar was already protected in the plant. According to the CA, the option of burning of the crops is not possible during the hot summer months due to the risk of wildfires.

The EFSA pest risk assessment for S. frugiperda (section 4.2)7 states that "if this pest were to arrive and become a pest of maize in Europe, it is likely that the existing available tools could be used to control it effectively". However, the CA has not defined official procedures for treatment against the pest (see paragraph 13). Treatment methods, such as the use of chemical pesticides at other growth stages (flight season of adult moths, young larvae stages), the use of biological control agents, destruction or deep burial of infested material and other host plants, burning of plant material in other seasons, soil cultivation, have not been assessed or defined as official treatment proce

Operators are advised that the movement of the upper layer of soil from infested plots is prohibited and they are to apply strict hygiene measures with regards to the movement of machinery and equipment in and out of infested areas. However, the implementation of these measures is not supervised or verified by the CA.

Furthermore, the CA have not introduced restrictions on the cultivation, harvesting or movement of possibly infested plant material from infested plots. Maize cobs for human consumption and plant material for animal feed are permitted to move out of these infested plots and are traded all over Cyprus.

Risk management measures targeting prevention and elimination of infestation are outlined in Annex II, section 1 point 1 (b) and (c) to Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 as provided for in Article 17(1) in the same Regulation. This provides for measures regarding restrictions on the cultivation and use of the infested plants and movement of machinery in order to limit the spread of the pest. Furthermore, EPPO standard on guidelines on the design and implementation of a bufferzone (PM 5/10), recommends to restrict the spread of the pest by preventing the movement out of the infested area and buffer zone. 7 EFSA PRA Spodoptera.pdf 15 5.5.2 Measures for eradication of Diaphorina citri

The planning and implementation of veterinary controls that the NVWA carries out is appropriate to verify compliance with most of the requirements of the VMPR under the scope of this audit, and therefore largely contributes to a more prudent use of antimicrobials. However, the NVWA allow veterinarians to use old antimicrobials outside of the terms of their marketing authorisation. 5.3 ACTIONS IN CASE OF NON-COMPLIANCE Legal requirements Article 135(1). Observations and findings The audit team noted the following:

The competent authorities declared their view that the marketing authorisations for certain old antimicrobials are no longer in line with the most recent scientific knowledge, in that they often indicate doses that are too low and are administered for periods that are too long.

For old antimicrobials and for specific cases laid down in the prescription guidelines for the veterinary profession, the competent authorities allow veterinarians to deviate, the dose and duration of the treatment, from the terms of the corresponding marketing authorisations. The competent authorities declared that their goal is that when decisions for such a deviation are taken by veterinarians, these are based on scientific knowledge, and always follow a consistent approach. In order to do that, the guidelines detail the extent of deviation allowed for each condition, antimicrobial and animal species. label_heading: Conclusions on sampling framework and analysis
paragraph_text: Late implementation of the plans for 2022 and 2023 resulted in an uneven distribution of the samples over the year, negatively impacting the representativeness of the data.

A review of the AMR sampling programme revealed the following: i. The planned sample sizes did not take into account the estimated prevalence of the bacterial species monitored in order to obtain the required number of isolates, which is not in line with point 3.1(b) of Part A of the Annex to the EU Decision. ii. There are limitations to the randomness of sampling, because of the instruction to sample from Monday to Wednesday to allow for delivery to the laboratory. Plans take stratified sampling into account and emphasise not repeating the epidemiological unit. iii. The instruction is to send the samples to the laboratory within 36 hours of sampling. Samples are kept chilled during storage

label_heading: Conclusions on sampling framework and analysis
paragraph_text: The lack of adequate sampling at slaughterhouse, retail level and BCPs has resulted in Greece not achieving the planned number of samples since 2021. As a consequence, there was also a low number of isolates available for AST at this level in 2021 and 2023. Additionally, no AST was performed in 2022, resulting in no test data available for transmission to EFSA.

label_heading: Conclusions on sampling framework and analysis
paragraph_text: The lack of information available for 2022 combined with incomplete data set for the years 2021 to 2023, raises a concern regarding the gap in AMR information and affects the representativeness of Greek data and its comparability across the EU. 5.3 OFFICIAL LABORATORIES Legal requirements Article 10 of Directive 2003/99/EC, Article 3 of and Annex (points 4 to 7 of Part A) to the EU Decision, and Articles 37 to 39, 100 and 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings The audit team noted the following: Designation

The laboratories involved in AMR monitoring are properly designated, have quality systems in place and participate in proficiency tests with overall satisfactory results. The laboratory performance and reliability of the results provided can be considered satisfactory. However, the continuing pressure on equipment and resources represents a potential risk to the monitoring programme.

There were several instances where AST was not conducted on available isolates (nor reported to EFSA) due to extreme delays in procurement of laboratory consumables. This negatively affects the representativeness of the Greek data. 5.4 ASSESSING AND REPORTING OF AMR Legal requirements Article 9 of and Annex IV to Directive 2003/99/EC, and Article 5 of and Annex (Part B) to the EU Decision. Findings The audit team noted the following:

Regarding Salmonella spp. isolates obtained from the SNCP in 2022: i. Isolates were obtained from samples collected from the populations of laying hens, broilers and fattening turkeys in the framework of the national control plans provided for in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. ii. Official and operator samples are analysed in 4 official laboratories and 29 private laboratories in Greece, designated as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003. National designated laboratories are obliged to provide Salmonella spp. isolates to the NRL. iii. A total of 40 isolates were obtained from laying hen flocks, mostly from official laboratories, and were referred to the NRL.

However, minor differences in the application of some plant passport requirements and the insufficient training for inspectors mean that the CAs do not ensure that the plant passport system is implemented in a consistent manner and fully in line with EU requirements.

The DGAL issued a technical instruction containing detailed procedures regarding the registration of professional operators, their authorisation to issue plant passports, the visual examination of plants, the issuance of plant passports and the official controls on professional operators as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The instruction contains guidance on how to practically implement the requirements, and examples of major and minor non-compliances. The instruction is directly used by the SRALs and the CTIFL. The FAM has developed its own procedures based on the DGAL technical instruction. The SEMAE has developed its own instructions based on international control a

However, in a small number of cases, and in line with the technical instruction issued by the DGAL (see also finding 4), the SRALs grant provisional authorisation. In these cases, there is no on-site official control and documents regarding the traceability system and the format of plant passports intended to be issued are verified remotely. Operators which receive provisional authorisation are allowed to issue plant passports until the first on-site official control, after which the final authorisation can be granted. In these cases, the SRALs do not verify whether operators possess the necessary knowledge concerning the signs, symptoms, and the means to prevent the spread of regulated pest

During the official controls observed by the audit team, the inspectors used checklists containing all relevant elements of the technical instruction issued by the DGAL to verify whether authorised operators comply with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. These controls were broadly effective. However, the audit team noted the following: · All inspectors verified the content, format and attachment of issued and received plant passports. This was done correctly in all cases and resulted in inspectors finding non-compliant plant passports. Non-compliant plant passports were issued by two visited authorised operators and were present in the garden centre (see also finding 29). · Inspect

Authorised operators are required to keep all plant passport related records for at least three years. The plant passports provided to the audit team were generally compliant with EU requirements. However, the following examples did not comply with the requirements of Article 83(2) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 since they did not contain some required elements or contained additional information. · Plant passports contained references to traceability information outside of the plant passport, but on the same substrate, instead of having the traceability code on the plant passport itself. · Plant passports with a hole on the label which removed part of the botanical name. · After the c

Furthermore, the CAs tolerate some forms of non-compliant plant passports: · The use of pre-printed plant passports with hand-written amendments is tolerated by the SRALs. In general, such plant passports often do not comply with Article 83(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 based on which the plant passports must be clearly legible, and the information on them must be unchangeable and durable. However, the CAs verify if plant passports available at the time of the official control and containing hand-written entries are legible, unchangeable and visible. · Contrary to the Annex of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/2313 ­ which provides that the required flag of the Union may be prin

Plant passports are attached to the trade units, replaced or invalidated by the authorised operators. However, the SRALs accept that the plant passport is only an accompanying document and is not attached to the trade units in the case of logs and plants moved in bulk, which is not in line with Article 88 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.5.5 Application of the exemptions provided for in EU law

National legislation provides a legal basis for enforcement actions in case of non- compliances with plant health requirements. When such non-compliances are detected, operators are ordered to take corrective actions. If the necessary corrective actions are not taken, the CA issues a formal notice containing the possibility of withdrawal or suspension of the authorisation for issuing plant passports. When appropriate actions are still not taken, the CA withdraws or suspends the authorisation to issue plant passports and may apply financial penalties. At Federal level, there are procedures in place to ensure the effectiveness, quality and consistency of official controls as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The compendium of phytosanitary controls provides general information on all areas of the plant health system, including basic work instructions and procedures. In the context of plant passports, it contains instructions for registering operators and checklists for conducting controls on authorised operators. Both Länder visited had developed detailed templates for conducting controls based on the templates in the compendium. However, they had not developed sufficiently detailed instructions for inspector

While these checklists address all legal requirements of authorised operators, the controls observed by the audit team did not verify if authorised operators comply with relevant requirements outlined in paragraph 21 as required by Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. This was due to insufficiently detailed instructions for inspectors as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (paragraph 5), with the result that inspectors did not perform high quality controls effectively and consistently, as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The checklist used by inspectors when conducting official controls at authorised operators includes a question on traceability. However, due to the lack of clear guidance for inspectors as described in paragraph 31, these controls do not systematically check if authorised operators have traceability systems within and between their premises as required by Article 70 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 15 5.6.2 Official controls on sales through distance contracts

The system of authorisation of professional operators to issue plant passports follows rules established in EU legislation. However, the CA has neither provided authorised operators with the information needed to carry out meticulous inspections independent- ly and at critical points, nor has it required them to keep records of such inspections. Moreover, there is no requirement in the guidelines for the CA to verify compliance to the abovementioned criteria. These shortcomings increase the risk that operators do not carry out their inspections meticulously, and that they place plants on the market, in- fested with regulated pests. 5.4 EXAMINATIONS FOR THE ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS Legal r

The audit team noted that compliance of professional operators with the requirements of Article 1(b)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827, such as competence to conduct plant health examinations and to apply best practices and measures to prevent the presence and spread of plant pests, is not verified during the authorisation process. This is not in line with Article 89(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

For compliance with Article 2 (a)(b)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827, SBA has provided operators some information on their website, mainly for priority pests and for some EU quarantine pests such as regulated potato pests. For other pests, links to the EPPO global database were made available (information is in English only). The CA has not provided operators information on modalities of visual inspections as required by Article (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 and information on best practices and measures to prevent pest presences as required by Article (2)(c) of the same Regulation. 5.3.2 Official supervision of professional operators and verification of their actions

As inspection guidelines and checklists do not require verification of the authorised op- erators' compliance with the requirements of Articles 87 and 90 on the appropriateness of authorised operators' examinations and obligation to keep records on examinations, compliance with these requirements was not included in any of the observed inspections. This is not in line with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports:

Operators met by the audit team stated that they check their plants constantly as they go about their work, even though formally not required to do so by the SBA. However, as operators visited had never documented this activity, as required by Article 87(3)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, the audit team could not verify that authorised operators conduct meticulous examinations in line with Article 87(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 prior to issuing plant passports. In addition, only one of the operators met by 8 the audit team had defined their critical points and the list of pests for monitoring pur- poses as required by Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. No records are kept on mo

The official controls on sales through distance contracts are undertaken at those opera- tors who had registered this specific activity in the national plant health registry. The of- ficial controls at operators issuing plant passports are undertaken as described under sec- tions 5.3 to 5.5, with the inspection scope focusing mainly on the format and attachment of the plant passports and traceability. Authorised operators' compliance with the re- quirements of Articles 87 and 90 on the appropriateness of authorised operators' exami- nations and obligation to keep records on examinations is not verified by the CA. The inspection frequency for 2022 and 2023 was met and no non-compliances were

The audit team verified the application of enforcement action for a case where the pro- tected zone pest Bemisia tabaci was found during the annual inspection for plant pass- 12 port purposes in September 2023. Although the operator was ordered to apply insecti- cides and a deadline of approximately 10 days was provided, no follow up inspection was conducted to verify if the pest eradication measures were applied and had been ef- fective. According to the SBA, the follow up as an additional inspection to the annual plant passport inspection was scheduled for February 2024.2 A similar approach was ob- served for the finding of Bemisia tabaci in one of the authorised operator's facilities in S

In general, sanctions appear to be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive thereby help- ing to ensure that professional operators comply with their legal obligations. However, in cases where the presence of a pest was confirmed, the long period of time before the implementation of eradication measures applied by the authorised operator is verified increases the risk that plants for which plant passports have been issued in the mean- time are not free of the relevant pests. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Sweden has implemented the concept of EU legislation on plant passports by authorizing professional operators to issue plant passports. The competent authorities conduct controls over the activities

The roles and responsibilities of the different CAs are clearly regulated, with detailed procedures to assist inspectors providing a good basis for the effective implementation of EU legislation. Minor differences in the application of some plant passport requirements mean that Slovenia does not implement all the rules in line with the requirements established by EU legislation.

Weaknesses in the annual official controls weaken the level of assurance that authorised operators fully meet the requirements for issuing plant passports. The PPQCFFV Directorate and the CLPQ do not have a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff in the area of plant health as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The BFSA stated that there are five staff in the PPQCFFV Directorate and 21 staff in the CLPQ dealing with plant health, with 64 plant health inspectors in the 28 RFSDs. The BFSA noted that the number of staff dealing with plant health matters had halved in the previous ten years, despite an increase in the workload. These numbers include both technical and administrative staff and include staff responsible for implementing all aspects of plant health legislation. The BFSA gave concrete example

The BFSA does not have appropriate and properly maintained Information Technology (IT) facilities and equipment as required by Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. It has not had an IT system to plan and to record all plant health survey activity since 2007. Instead, information on each survey is recorded in each RFSD using spreadsheets. This information is subsequently compiled by the relevant report rapporteur for priority pests or the PPQCFFV Directorate for other pests. For example, S. frugiperda is surveyed under three separate annual survey programmes ­ for vegetables, for ornamental plants, and for other plants. The resulting data from each of these three surveys is compiled s

The multi-annual survey programme for 155 Union quarantine pests (including 18 priority pests) provides a sound basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests. However, at least two thirds of Union quarantine pests, some of which could establish in Bulgaria, are not surveyed, giving rise to the risk that some of these pests could establish, and remain undetected until such time as their eradication would be impossible.

Under the 2021-2023 programme, the BFSA planned and conducted surveys on 155 pests, comprising 18 priority pests and 137 Union quarantine pests, under a range of crop-specific surveys. The remaining Union quarantine pests (more than 240) were neither included in, nor excluded with a justification from, the programme, which is not in compliance with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

As was the case for the 2021-2023 programme, 240 or more Union quarantine pests are neither included in, nor excluded with a justification from, the 2024-2028 multi-annual survey programme, which is not in compliance with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

The multi-annual survey programme for 155 Union quarantine pests (including 18 priority pests) provides a sound basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests. However, at least two thirds of Union quarantine pests, some of which could establish in Bulgaria, are not surveyed, giving rise to the risk that some of these pests could establish, and remain undetected until such time as their eradication would be impossible.

Thirty-seven pests are excluded from the 2024-2028 multi-annual survey programme with a clear justification. In the majority of these cases, the justification relates to the ecoclimatic conditions or to the absence of the host species as permitted under Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. However, in 40% of cases, the justification is either that official controls take place at the point of import, or that there is a proposal to deregulate the pest, or that the risk of the pest establishing in Bulgaria is low, none of which are permitted as valid reasons for excluding pests from multi-annual survey programmes under Article 22(1) of that Regulation. 6 5.2.2 Planning annual statistical

The implementation of the annual risk-based survey programme for priority pests provides a high level of assurance that any outbreaks of these pests will be detected promptly. However, the failure to develop the required statistically based annual survey programme for X. fastidiosa means that the level of confidence the current risk-based survey programme for this pest provides is unknown.

Bulgaria did not establish (i.e. did not plan to conduct) a statistically based survey programme for X. fastidiosa in 2023 and 2024 as required by Article 2(4) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201, primarily due to a lack of human resources. However, some requirements laid down in Article 2 of this Regulation are complied with in the annual survey programmes for X. fastidiosa, as described in findings 21, 22 and 23. 5.2.3 Planning annual risk-based survey programmes for priority pests

The failure to report survey results for the vast majority of Union quarantine pests surveyed each year means that this important information is not easily accessible to the Commission and to other MS.

Bulgaria generally reports the results of the annual surveys of priority pests to the Commission and to other MS, by the deadline of 30 April for the preceding year as required by Article 24(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Article 2(8) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 regarding X. fastidiosa and Article 12(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 as regards S. frugiperda. In 2022 and 2023, Bulgaria reported results on 23 and 28 of the 137 pests surveyed to the Commission and to other MS, which is not in line with Article 22(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The BFSA attributed the failure to report results for the vast majority of Union quarantine pests surveyed to difficulties

Bulgaria is not sufficiently prepared to eradicate outbreaks of priority pests. Of the 15 required contingency plans, four remain to be drafted, with no clear deadline for their completion, while the published contingency plans lack the necessary detail to help the authorities rapidly and effectively eradicate any established priority pests. 11 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The relatively limited number of staff dealing with plant health, and inefficiencies arising from deficiencies in IT systems means that Bulgaria is unable to comply with a number of legal requirements relating to surveys and contingency plans. Bulgaria has implemented a multi-annual survey programme for 155 Union quarantine pests,

Bulgaria has drawn up pest-specific contingency plans for 11 of the 15 priority pests which are capable of entering into and becoming established in its territory. These plans were communicated to the Commission and to other MS as required by Article 25(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 by uploading them to internet Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (iRASFF) plant health portal on 26 August 2024, some eight months after the legal deadline. The BFSA stated that work was ongoing on one of the four remaining 10 required plans at the time of the audit in September 2024, but acknowledged that there was no clear time schedule to conclude this work. Finally, it acknowledged that it had not consult

The published contingency plans all share a common format. The audit team examined the contingency plans for S. frugiperda and X. fastidiosa as a representative sample. Based on this examination, the plans comply with most, but not all, requirements of Article 25(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Article 4(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 and Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. Specifically, the plans lack sufficient detail regarding CAs' access to laboratories, equipment, personnel, external expertise and resources necessary for the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of the priority pest concerned as required by Article 25(2)(c) of

The available laboratory capacity provides sufficient support to the CAs for the early detection of relevant priority pests. However, a small proportion of samples are tested in official laboratories which are neither accredited, nor meeting the criteria for the derogation from accreditation, which increases the risk that results from these laboratories may not be accurate. 5.2 SURVEY PROGRAMMES Legal requirements and international standards Articles 22, 23 and 24 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Article 1 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/1702 Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Article 2 and 35(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 Article 3 of 12(a) Implementing Regulati

The MRDF stated that these laboratories are not accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025, and that they do not meet all the criteria set out in Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 that an official laboratory must comply with to avail of the derogation from the condition for mandatory accreditation. The MDRF attributes this due to the low priority which DREVs give to plant health survey work, rather than insufficient staff resources. The MRDF and BPI monitor implementation of the survey programme on an ongoing basis, and when implementation falls behind schedule, MRFD issues letters to the DREVs to emphasise

The BPI estimates that in 2025 (Year 2 of the multi-annual survey programme), the survey workload will increase by 15% and by a further 20% in 2026 (Year 3).
