Greece does not conduct surveys for priority pests in line with the requirements of Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and for all relevant Union quarantine pests in line with the requirements of Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Finally, it does not conduct surveys for X. fastidiosa in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. This is because while surveys are conducted by knowledgeable inspectors, at appropriate locations and appropriate times, the DREVs consistently fail to implement a sufficiently high number of visual examinations, sampling and testing as appropriate for each priority pest, and as outlined in the annual survey p

Greece has yet to complete the required contingency plans for relevant priority pests, or to undertake any simulation exercises concerning their implementation. This raises doubts that Greece is sufficiently prepared to take effective actions to eradicate any outbreaks of priority pests, in line with EU requirements. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION In 2024, Greece started to implement a multi-annual survey programme for all relevant Union quarantine pests, four years after the deadline for doing so. The planning of both the multi-annual survey programme and annual surveys is well organised, with very detailed survey plans and guidance for inspectors. Surveys are implemented and recorded by knowledgeabl

Greece had not drawn up all required contingency plans nor had they been communicated to the Commission and other MS and published on the internet by 14 December 2023 contrary to Article 25(1), (4) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Greece completed and provided 11 contingency plans to the Commission just a few weeks prior to this audit in October 2024. The MRDF stated that a further four plans would be finalised by the end of 2024, and that the final four plans would be completed in 2025.

Given that Greece only completed the first 11 of the 19 required contingency plans in the weeks prior to the audit, it did not have an opportunity to carry out simulation exercises concerning the implementation of the contingency plans as required by Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 by the time of the audit in October 2024. There is a risk of delays in applying effective and efficient measures in the case of priority pest outbreaks in Finland as none of the ten required contingency plans have been completed and no simulation exercises have been carried out. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Since 2021, the CAs of Finland are implementing a five-year multi-annual survey programme for the 67 Union quarantine pests which have been assessed as being capable of establishing, spreading and having a significant impact within its territory. With regard to the risk-based planning criteria the programme requires the regional CAs to choose a number of risk criteria from a list. In CLM, the regional control programmes for 2022 and 2023 reviewed by the audit team included annual controls of 550 agricultural holdings. In both programmes, they were planned across risk categories in line with the percentages specified in the national pro- gramme. The criteria used to classify agricultural holdings were essentially the crops cul- tivated and the size of the holding, therefore, in line, as well, with the indications provid- ed in the national programme, although not in line with Article 24 (2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (see paragraph 53).

In VC, the 2022 and 2023 regional control programmes on agricultural holdings set a target of 314 annual controls and the specific number for each province. In both pro- grammes, the controls were planned across risk categories in line with the percentages specified in the national programme. The main criteria to classify agricultural holdings were the crops cultivated, the size of the holding and its location with respect to the risk of nitrate loss, therefore, in line, as well, with the indications provided in the national programme, although not in line with article 24 (2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (see paragraph 53).

In one of the two main Länder visited by the audit team, the annual plan of controls includes a fixed number of traders (retailers, wholesalers and online traders) to be inspected (around 20% of the 15 total number), in the other one, traders selling exclusively to non-professional users (e.g. garden centres) are inspected annually. label_heading: Conclusions on controls on the marketing of plant protection products
paragraph_text: The system of official controls at import and of PPP traders is implemented in a coordinated manner, according to the risk-based control priorities agreed at national level and by sufficiently knowledgeable inspectors from the Länder who, generally, follow the control methods laid down in the national control manual. This represents a solid and harmonised basis to ensure that only authorised PPPs are placed on the national market. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of system is partly weakened by the fact that a limited number of controls of PPP manufacturers have been carried out, so far, and insufficient attention has been paid to ensure that PPPs not authorised in Germany are actually exporte

The audit team visited a PPP operator carrying out manufacturing activities on behalf of various PPP authorisation holders. This manufacturer had not been inspected previously by the CA from the relevant Land and was only visited in 2020 to take a sample. The inspection observed by the audit team, which was carried out by inspectors from the relevant Land and a representative from BVL, was comprehensive. Nonetheless, the audit team noted that the CAs were not aware that the manufacturer was exporting PPPs not authorised in Germany from this plant and that no checks were carried out to ensure that such PPPs were actually exported to the place of destination, which is not in line with Article

label_heading: Conclusions on authorisation of plant protection products
paragraph_text: Emergency authorisations may each include multiple crops and/or targets or extend to a total period beyond 120 days. This is not in line with Article 53 of Regulation No (EC) 1107/2009. Furthermore, emergency authorisations generally involve approved active substances and PPPs authorised elsewhere. The dangers these authorisations are addressing could therefore, at least in the medium term, be contained by the regular authorisation procedures laid down in Articles 33, 40, or 51 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Using emergency authorisations repeatedly instead, waters down the integrity of the authorisation system. 5.2. ORGANISATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE MARKETING AND USE OF PLANT PROTE

Tukes has a rule of thumb that emergency authorisations should not be given for more than five years, but exceptions have been made and the audit team noted cases of repeated emergency authorisations for many years (e.g. in one case, 8 years, so far). The audit team considered that these applications would be more correctly accommodated within the conventional authorisation framework maintaining the system's integrity as referred to in Commission Staff Working Document on emergency situations according to Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. This is especially so because Tukes only grants emergency authorisations for PPPs that contain approved active substances, as mentioned above, an

Furthermore, the audit team noted that the CA had considered as a single emergency authorisation in 2023 a use granted for two non-consecutive periods of two months (April to May and September to October), which is not in line with Article 53 of Regulation (EC) 1107/2009. In addition, there are cases of single emergency authorisations granted for multiple crops or targets, which is also not in line with the said Article.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The CAs plan controls to define broad areas of controls at national level, based to an extent on risk. However, the lack of a clear and complete universe for control, the lack of risk assessment to target the relatively few inspections at regional level and the prior notifications of inspections may reduce the general effectiveness of controls. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

As a general rule, samples are taken from distributors' warehouses and retailers. Finland aims to control about 20 PPPs annually, which is around 5% of PPPs authorised in Finland. In order to collect the samples, the only two inspectors doing controls on marketing of PPPs select the operators to be visited randomly, as they do not have operators classified based on risk. Furthermore, retailers selling only PPPs for non- professional use are usually not included. This system is not fully in line with Article 9(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Inadequate risk assessment for prioritisation of inspections was also noted in the 2014 audit.

According to information provided by Tukes inspectors, three large companies, which have approximately 130 outlets (based on the information available from open sources) supply the majority of the Finnish market of PPPs for professional use. In addition, there is an unknown number of retailers (also mainly outlets of larger chains) selling only PPPs for non-professional use. Retailers do not need to register with Tukes, so precise numbers cannot be given, and Tukes does not keep the up-to-date list of operators required by Article 10(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 10

Each centre selects the operators to be controlled for PPP use. However, the ELY centres have not been provided with risk criteria from the FFA for this. The audit team interviewed staff from three ELY centres. They stated that they select operators based on their own criteria and while they have knowledge of the farmers that receive subsidies under the Common Agricultural Policy or under other national schemes, they do not have a full overview of the universe to be controlled. In particular, the number of non- agricultural users is not known. In one ELY centre, the operators are randomly selected, in the second, the potential contamination of ground water was mentioned as a potential criter

Moreover, the results of the PPP residue and water status monitoring programmes are not taken into consideration for the programming of controls which is not in line with Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The CAs plan controls to define broad areas of controls at national level, based to an extent on risk. However, the lack of a clear and complete universe for control, the lack of risk assessment to target the relatively few inspections at regional level and the prior notifications of inspections may reduce the general effectiveness of controls. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

The official controls for the use of PPPs are always announced in advance. The instructions stipulate that notice should be `as short as possible' The FFA stated that controls cannot be carried out without the presence of the farmer, as they also need to check the farmer's records on the use of PPPs. In addition, given the long distances between inspection sites, the advance notice helps to prevent wasted resources by ensuring the farmer is present at the agreed time. The audit team considered that such general use of prior notifications is not in line with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. This issue was also noted in the 2014 audit.

The FFA laboratory is the designated laboratory for PPP formulation analyses, and it is accredited to ISO 17025. This provides the basis for ensuring reliable results of tests and analyses. However, not including analyses for unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities in the sampling programme reduces the overall capability of the control system to ensure the safety of the PPPs placed on the market. 5.3. IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE MARKETING AND USE OF PLANT PROTECTION PRODUCTS Controls on the marketing of plant protection products Legal Requirements Articles 10 to 14, 24, and 137 to 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Article 28, 29, 31, 52, 64, 65, 67(1), 68 and 72 of R

The analyses focus on identifying the content of active substances and certain physical and chemical properties of PPPs. They do not cover co-formulants and impurities. Consequently, the CAs are unable to verify the absence of unacceptable co-formulants in PPPs, as outlined in Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and listed in its Annex IIII. They are also unable to determine whether certain impurities exceed the maximum content permitted in the approval of the relevant active substances, as referred to in Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. This is not in line with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The CA stated that the technical capabilities for detecting impurities, co-formulants and auxiliary substances do exist, since the laboratory is equipped with suitable analytical tools. However due to a lack of validated methods, the results cannot be reported in compliance with general standards of good laboratory practices or used for enforcement. 12

Disease control measures on suspected cases were generally adequate. However, the lack of routine sampling and testing in suspected cases may have delayed outbreak confirmation, and potentially increased the viral load in the farm, or weakened the basis for ruling out suspected cases.

For confirmed cases, the authorities implemented appropriate control measures, except they fail to trace animal products dispatched from infected farms. Although the oversight is unknown, it could have led to the unintentional spread of sheep pox 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/official-controls-and-enforcement/legislation-official-controls/better- training-safer-food_en. 4 to other farms and regions, presenting inconsistent risk-mitigation measures and hampering the assurance provided by the disease containment measures.

Belgian legislation (Royal decrees of 5 May 2008 and of 20 May 2022) requires mandatory registration of: i. all commercial poultry establishments regardless of the number of birds kept, ii. all poultry traders, iii. all "hobby keepers" with more than 200 hobby poultry, 4 iv. and all "hobby keepers" who wish to participate in or trade hobby poultry through public events such as a local weekly market. So called "hobby keepers" with less than 200 birds can attend competitions or exhibitions without having to register, and can sell directly to other hobby keepers, but if they supply the food chain or are involved in any commercial activities they must also be registered. In the event of particip

"Hobby poultry" is defined in a guidance document for the public as the most common poultry species, including chicken, ducks, turkeys etc that are not intended for the food chain or for restocking supplies of game; they are then considered to be "captive birds". This definition, and the national provisions applied, are not entirely in line with the Animal Health Law (AHL), which defines poultry as birds kept or reared in captivity for production (of eggs, meat or other products). Furthermore, Articles 84 and 85 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 3 of Commission Implementing Regulation 2022/1345, which provides for exceptions for registration of establishments, require among other that

In Belgium there are several wildlife rehabilitation centres (around 25) which shelter injured or abandoned animals until they can be released into the wild again. The audit team interviewed a manager of one of these centres, located near the coast. The capacity of that centre could reach up to of approximately 5,000 birds annually. In some cases, the centre can keep birds for up to few months, especially when dealing with young birds, before they can be released in the wild again. These centres are currently not registered with veterinary authorities, despite keeping birds for an extended period and 5 therefore falling under the definition of an establishment according to Article 4 (27) of

When a farm veterinarian notifies the suspicion, authorities instruct the private veterinarian to take samples and to carry out the clinical assessment of the birds present at the establishment. The audit team noted a case, when the private veterinarian had a suspicion during his animal health check visit, and therefore took samples based on a general instruction document (available at the FASFC website) and sent them to a regional laboratory for further dispatch to the NRL. The practitioner then informed the LCU of the suspicion by email, including a clinical assessment of the animals present, as requested by Article 6 (2) of Delegated Regulation 2020/687. During the audit, the competent au

LCUs contact registered establishments in the restricted zones, asking them to do an inventory of birds kept and to send it back, in the protection zone within 24 hours and in the surveillance zone within 48 hours. They also contact mayors asking them to forward publish information on restriction measures on local channels, to ensure that hobby keepers that are not registered receive information. All commercial establishments within the protection zone are visited by their private veterinarians within 24 hours. During these visits the veterinarians perform clinical examinations, checking health and production parameters' records, and taking samples for laboratory analysis as necessary. 17

The restriction zones established following an outbreak of HPAI are lifted as follows: i. The protection zone is lifted 21 days after it is established, provided hat clinical examinations on commercial holdings within the zone--conducted every four days--show no signs of concern. Once lifted, the area becomes part of the surveillance zone. ii. The surveillance zone is lifted 30 days after it is established, provided that no new outbreaks have been detected and all registered poultry establishments have undergone clinical examinations by a farm veterinarian and sampling as per FASFC instructions. The zone is lifted once all samples collected have been favourably tested using PCR testing by DG

Temporary official veterinarians ("seasonal veterinarians") have been hired to implement ASF measures in four areas of higher risk. During their work they also detected a significant number of not registered non-commercial farms. Since 2023, the number of small pig farms has decreased significantly in Greece as many did not meet minimum biosecurity standards and a depopulation programme was put in place. Nevertheless, there are gaps as regards the registration of non-commercial farms. Incomplete entries and delays in updating the national pig database as well as the farm registers do not allow the competent authority to have a reliable overview of the pig population for animal health control

Despite a national plan for implementing official controls on biosecurity measures during hunting activities, the competent authority does not carry out such controls as planned; related activities have also not produced any impact so far. In addition, the national plan is not well established as regards scope, inspection records and addressing non-compliances. This means that the competent authority has limited control over the risk of the virus spreading by hunted wild boar.

Passive surveillance of the domestic pig population is implemented through testing of dead animals notified to authorities by farmers. The level of notifications is overall satisfactory for larger establishments, whereas absent or incomplete mortality records in smaller farms make verification of compliance in these operations difficult to estimate.

The number of reported wild boar found dead by hunters is very low compared to the hunting bag (total number of wild boars hunted per year). This is compounded by underreporting and thus a lack of testing of carcasses hunted in restricted areas and destined for private consumption. As a result, the competent authority misses important information on the epidemiological status of the disease. Although the hunting community has comprehensive knowledge of the wild boar population and its dynamics, it has failed to achieve the targets set by the competent authority for reducing the wild porcine animal population. 6

The performance of the NRL in ASF testing allows for reliable detection of the virus. In some cases, however, there have been delays in the timely availability of results due to delays in the dispatch of samples by regional units and the lab's capacity limitations over weekends.

Pig operators located in restricted zones, sending pigs for immediate slaughter are not always in compliance with requirements for movement derogations regarding biosecurity and continuous surveillance. This can increase the risk of spreading ASF virus.

paragraph_text: Internal audits are carried out as planned. However, the audit team noted that there is no established procedure for such supervision: in some CGOs this is limited to the evaluation of the percentage of completion of the control plan (without investigating their effectiveness), whilst, in others, some either observe inspections or carry out follow-up inspections to evaluate the performance of DGO and/or CGO staff. In the establishments visited this sampling was carried out after cleaning and disinfection (before processing) only. The global figures for Italy show that overall 19% of the primary production fishing fleet was controlled in 2022 (1 148 out of 5 964 registered fishing operators (mainly fishing vessels)), which can be considered as being equivalent to one control every 5 years). 15 However, taking also into account the EUROSTAT figures, this percentage of cover drops to less than 10%.

The control procedures, on the use of sulphites by operators of primary production fishing vessels, do not cover all the relevant EU rules, in particular with regard to the maximum admissible levels for such additives, and are therefore not adequately checked by the competent authorities.

With regard to the addition of sulphites on board primary production fishing vessels, the audit team noted that the guidance document on Regulations Nos 852/2004 and 853/2004 (see paragraph 19 above) allows this practice under certain conditions: recording by the fisherman of the use of the additive; indication on the landing document of the use of the additive; and, existence of a label, or a specific indication, to be kept up to retail and sale to the final consumer.
Overall, the control system is implemented as planned, except for fishing (primary production) and freezer vessels.

The different levels of the authorities indicated that, in general, the number of staff available for the control tasks is adequate. However, in certain cases not all tasks are carried out as per the defined deadlines (in particular, those related to the approval of establishments and vessels, and official controls of approved vessels), mainly due to work overload linked with certification for exports and the displacement to international ports (for approved vessels).

The national competent authority indicated that the frequency for the controls of certain approved vessels (mainly freezer) is not respected due to the shortage of staff available for those controls, the remote location of the ports where the vessels may land, and the unpredictable working pattern of the vessels.

The national competent authority did not control this freezer vessel as required by the Italian procedures and by Article 67(b)(i) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Moreover, this vessel changed ownership in 2020 and the approval was transferred to the new owner 16 without an on-the-spot visit to ascertain that the initial approval conditions are still respected and have not been changed.

The national competent authority indicated that the situation, described in paragraph 51 above, is shared by many operators of crustacean freezer vessels and that the Italian rules will preclude the option to suspend the approval. According to these rules, a suspension of the approval is limited to a certain amount of time, after which the approval is either reinstated or is withdrawn. While understanding the limitations of the Italian provision, the audit team also considers that the current situation is not in line with the EU rules, namely Article 67 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 and Article 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. label_heading: Conclusions on recommendation No 2 of the 2021 audit
paragraph_text: As regard the remuneration system of staff performing official tasks in slaughterhouses with automatic conveyor belt, the measures announced in the AP, and that will address the relevant part of the recommendation, have not been introduced. No deadline is foreseen for solving this long-standing situation. Furthermore, it is particularly worrying that the scale of this non-compliance appears to affect most of the slaughterhouses in the country. 5.3 RECOMMENDATION NO 3 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure the correct application of Article 79 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 in respect of the collection of fees or charges to cover the costs occasioned by official controls". Findings

The changes in the national legislation on the remuneration system of AVs supervising the slaughter of animals announced in the AP have been partially introduced: in slaughterhouses without automatic conveyor belt the AVs are paid per hour. However, in slaughterhouses with automatic conveyor belt it still depends on the number of animals slaughtered. This is not in line with Art. 5(1)(b) of Reg. label_heading: Conclusions on recommendation No 5 of the 2021 audit
paragraph_text: Despite nearly all the actions from the AP being implemented and GVI's' efforts to strengthen enforcement measures for non-compliance with animal welfare rules, significant progress has not been made. Many cases are still being dismissed or rejected by enforcement authorities. According to the Polish legal system, the VI has no competence on this matter. 9 5.6 RECOMMENDATION NO 6 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure that approved establishments meet the relevant requirements of food law and that those requirements are kept under review when carrying out official controls in order to comply with Article 148(3) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Particular attention should be paid to the assessment

The CVO received feedback from the NPO in February 2024. The document indicated that from 2020 to October 2023, the prosecutor's offices handled 1 928 cases concerning the violation of the animal welfare law. All these cases were initiated by the VI, and following their verification were discontinued at their initial stage. The primary reason for not proceeding with the cases was that the acts in question did not constitute a criminal offense. The audit team noted that the document lacked detailed analyses or explanations to help the DVOs understand the reasons behind the dismissals and prevent similar situations from occurring in the future.

During the meetings the audit team had with the DVOs and RVOs they noted that it is difficult to monitor the prosecutors' duties, as they are independent from any other governmental body, and explain that they usually do not receive information about the follow up of the cases they transmitted to the NPO. One of the DVOs met provided figures of the number of cases transmitted to the enforcement authorities and number of cases 8 dismissed/rejected during the investigation phase (e.g. in 2023, 180 cases were notified, 80 cases dismissed/rejected and no information on 29 cases). The DVO lodged 19 complaints for the refusal to open an investigation or closure of the case at the pre-trial stage.

According to the DVO and RVO when they identify non-compliance related to animal welfare, they do not take into account whether the same operator has repeatedly committed these breaches, nor do they maintain any records. Consequently, they lack awareness of whether an FBO has a history of repeated offenses and are unable to include this information in their notifications to the NPO.

label_heading: Conclusions on recommendation No 8 of the 2021 audit
paragraph_text: Although the measures from the action plan were implemented and improvements have been observed since the 2021 audit, the actions are not effective or do not have the expected results. They often fail to identify the source of contamination or prevent its recurrence, suggesting that the measures taken by the FBOs to address this recommendation are not adequate and/or sufficient. 5.9 RECOMMENDATION NO 9 OF THE 2021 AUDIT "To ensure that in case of suspicion of non-compliance (e.g. reliability of Salmonella test results provided by some private laboratories), the competent authorities perform an inves- tigation to confirm or to eliminate the suspicion, as prescribed by Article 137(2) of Regula

In all the poultry slaughterhouses visited the implementation of the measures and corrective actions provided in the HACCP plans in case of Salmonella detection could not identify the source of the contamination and prevent recurrence. It was noted that the FBO's actions and investigations were repeatedly focused on primary production (e.g. visits to farms and verification of the biosecurity measures) and did not pay attention, for example, to possible cross contamination points or production shortcomings at establishment level.

During the DVO visits, they confirm the FBOs' actions implemented to identify the source of the contamination and prevent recurrences. However, they did not assess the adequacy of these actions, as there was no comprehensive evaluation of the establishment's HACCP systems. For instance, the audit team found in two slaughterhouses where Salmonella spp was found in chicken fillets, the FBOs' investigations overlooked potential cross- contamination risks during the slaughter and cutting processes (see also paragraph 36). This issue was neither identified nor documented during the DVO's inspections. Conclusions on recommendation No 8 of the 2021 audit

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures.
paragraph_text: The official control system is supported by national legislation covering the relevant as- pects within the scope of the audit. However, the absence of guidance docu- ments/instructions for the official staff compromises the guarantees that official controls are effective and are carried out in a uniform and consistent way.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: An official control plan, based on risk, is implemented by the CA. However, the limited 14 detection and/or recording of non-compliances at establishment level and, consequently, the lack of enforcement actions to correct the non-compliant situations compromise the effectiveness of the control system in place. In this regard, significant shortcomings in relation to the sanitary conditions and to the animal welfare conditions were noted that had not been previously identified or recorded in any level of official control.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Certain official controls at slaughterhouse level are not carried out in line with the EU requirements. In particular, the serious deviations from the legally required practical ar- rangements concerning PMI and the controls on HACCP-based procedures undermine the reliability of the OVs' decision on the fitness of meat for human consumption.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The AMI and the controls on FCI, animal identification and traceability are in general in line with the EU requirements. However, the lack of procedures for suitable recording and communication of AMI and PMI results by the OVs has, as a consequence, that no feedback is provided to the competent authorities and operators at primary production level in order to take appropriate actions when these inspections reveal a disease or con- dition that might affect human or animal health or animal welfare. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The structure and organisation of the Competent Authority are adequate and provide a suita- ble basis for the performance of its tasks in the areas covered by this audit. The cur- rent instructions on post-mortem inspection (PMI), have not been updated to take into account the last changes in EU legislation. The audit team noted that the checklists have not been up- dated since 2014 and they are not usually used by the OVs during their controls. The au- dit team assessed one checklist for official controls in poultry slaughterhouses and noted that it mainly reported the requirements laid down in Regulations (EC) Nos 853/2004 and 854/2004 and did not provide technical assistance to the OVs. 5.2.4 Training

Animal welfare checks were also included in the planned thematic controls (see also paragraph 43) with a mini- mum frequency of two controls per year. In all but one of the establishments visited the cleanliness of live animals before slaugh- ter was not taken into consideration in the HACCP plans. This was monitored in one of the establishments even though that procedure was not included in the HACCP plan, which also did not include clear instructions or corrective actions. This establishment was approved in 2022 and, in this regard, no observations were noted by the CA.

According to the information provided by the CA, and in addition to the RFSD audits, the FBOs own-checks are evaluated during the OV's thematic inspections. The audit and inspection reports the CA shared with the audit team did not include any remark con- cerning the above-mentioned aspects. The BFSA explained that there are no guidelines concerning assessment of HACCP systems available for the regional inspectors or the OVs. Microbiological criteria Legal requirements Article 35 and 36 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

All the FBOs at the establishments visited had a microbiological sampling plan in place. This plan is verified by the OVs during their thematic controls. There are no official in- structions in place to assist the OVs on this verification and on the subsequent official actions needed in case of non-compliance.

A training system is in place however the findings of this audit indicate that this training is not effective or sufficient to ensure adequate knowledge of official inspectors respon- sible for the official controls in slaughterhouses.

The audit team noted during the on-the-spot visits that the officials did not have a suffi- cient level of knowledge of specific legal requirements to perform their duties properly, in particular concerning PMI, hazard analysis and critical control point (HACCP) sys- tems and the protection of animals at the time of killing (see also paragraphs 33, 36, 38, 48, 49 and 50). 5.2.5 Supervision and audits

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures.
paragraph_text: The official control system is supported by national legislation covering the relevant as- pects within the scope of the audit. However, the absence of guidance docu- ments/instructions for the official staff compromises the guarantees that official controls are effective and are carried out in a uniform and consistent way.

Mechanisms are in place to provide guarantees about the effectiveness of the official controls. However, these mechanisms are not working properly because the supervision system over the OVs' performance is not able to uncover the weaknesses in the official controls and, when shortcomings are identified during the internal audits, these remain unsolved.

No further checks were carried out by the OV/OA to ensure that the rectification of the carcase had been performed satisfactorily; · Lack of lockable facilities for the refrigerated storage of detained meat in one of the establishments visited. The audit team observed several unhygienic practices taking place during the visits, some of them systematically occurring in several establishments. They included the overuse of drop hoses by operatives to clean themselves and the equipment, causing a risk of cross-contamination to nearby carcases by uncontrolled splashing. It was noted that staff could not make use of apron washes or other suitable alternatives as no apron washing cabinets were available in the majority of the slaughterhouses visited. Also, some water pipes and hand-wash basins on working platforms were not properly ducted, which facilitated the pooling of water and thereby created a risk of contamination of dirty water sp

Although there is an enforcement system in place, which is clearly designed and could work satisfactorily, some weaknesses in the delivery (mainly linked to the deadlines and follow-ups) limit its impact and undermine its efficacy to ensure that FBOs resolve the identified deficiencies and prevent their recurrence.

At the establishments visited, the OVs had already detected some of the non- compliances observed by the audit team and had started taking action to address them. The audit team identified that: · Several of the deficiencies were of a long-standing nature and had been under enforcement for a considerable length of time, without having achieved the required results; · In some cases, the deadlines for the rectification of these issues had expired and a new deadline had been given without indication of further consequences, or the follow-up had been planned/taken place a considerable time after the deadline had expired (at times, a year later, at the time of the next planned audit/inspection).

Nevertheless, in one of the establishments, the maintenance and cleaning status of some of the wall surfaces near and in one of the chillers were not satisfactory. Although the FBO had begun a refurbishment to remedy the situation, the enforcement process had lasted several years and had not produced suitable and timely results; some areas where refurbishment was in progress (e.g. corridors, buffer areas between cattle and sheep slaughter lines) were not suitably isolated to avoid risks of cross-contamination of carcases and offal intended for human consumption. 13

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There is a system in place for AMI and PMI covering most of the relevant aspects. The performance of AMI by the OVs was considered as fully satisfactory and some establishments showed elements of good practices to ensure that animals were not slaughtered without inspection. PMI was carried out in accordance with the legislation, in the majority of cases. However, the current arrangements in place do not guarantee that the health mark will only be applied to carcases that have undergone full PMI and where there are no grounds for declaring the carcase (or part of it) unfit for human consumption. In the poultry slaughterhouse, the PMI procedures did not include the cavity inspection of the car

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The delayed PMI in establishments without permanent supervision is frequently carried out by OAs and not by OVs as required by Article 13(1) of EU Regs 2019/ 627

According to the information provided by the SFA, the derogation on the timing of PMI in the context of Article 13 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627, in establishments without permanent official supervision, is applied in 70 red meat slaughterhouses.

At these low-capacity slaughterhouses without permanent official supervision, the delayed PMI is sometimes carried out by OAs and not by OVs. This happened, according to the CA's figures, 22% of the time in 2023.

label_heading: Conclusions on legislation and implementing measures
paragraph_text: National legislation and guidelines, necessary to ensure implementation and/or enforcement of the EU requirements applicable to the meat sector, are in place and they largely ensure compliance with EU legislation, except for some provisions regarding the own-check sampling of carcasses. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4, 5, 6, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The official control system in place also includes taking official samples for microbiological analyses in order to guarantee the safety of red meat and poultry meat. However, the effectiveness of the system is weakened by the inconsistencies noted by the audit team in relation to CA` verification of FBOs` compliance with microbiological criteria. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The official control system over the production and placing on the market of red meat and poultry meat comprises all the required elements, largely fulfils the legal requirements of the Official Controls Regulation, and its implementation is well organised and in general is effective in identifying relevant non-compliances. Non

However, the audit team noted that the Royal Decree (RD) of 30 November 2015 on the hygiene of foodstuffs of animal origin states that Food Business Operators (FBOs) of slaughterhouses of domestic ungulates should take their own-check carcass samples "at the end of the slaughter line or in the chiller but in any case, within two to four hours after slaughter".

As a result, the audit team noted in the four domestic ungulates' large capacity slaughterhouses visited that FBOs took these samples within two to four hours after slaughter when the carcasses already underwent blast-chilling. This is not in line with the provisions of Chapter II of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 which requires that such samples should be taken after dressing but before chilling. Article 5(5) of the mentioned Regulation allows that FBOs may use other sampling and testing procedures, if they can demonstrate to the satisfaction of the CA that these procedures provide at least equivalent guarantees. The FASFC confirmed to the audit team that no such study had been car

The audit team noted that the analytical method used by the FBOs are not consistently verified during official controls. In some cases, it was neither clear from the FBOs procedures nor from the analytical results whether the reference method or an alternative method was used by the FBO. Moreover, some of the LCU inspectors informed the audit team that they do not verify if the analytical method used by the FBO was in line with the requirements of points 1 and 5 of Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and/or were not aware of the availability of the list of the validated methods on the CA`s website. They were satisfied with the fact that the laboratory performed the analyses was accredi

The mechanisms in place (such as documented procedures, training, and several IT applications) give the CAs a reasonable level of assurance that controls are carried out uniformly and consistently. However, the staff knowledge in relation to implementation of PMI requirements, which suggest a need for further training, does not ensure that the PMI requirements are apply fully in line with the EU requirements.

label_heading: Conclusions on organisation and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: In general, AMI both for domestic ungulates and poultry and PMI of poultry are organised in line with the relevant EU requirements. However, the implementation of PMI has some systemic shortcomings, in particular, related to the obligatory incisions to be made during PMI of bovine animals (see also paragraph 48).

Although the audit team was provided with evidence of VOAs` training in all slaughterhouses visited and noted that procedures are available which describe the palpations and incisions that must be made during the PMI, non-compliances with Articles 19, 20 and 23 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 were noted by the audit team in the slaughterhouses of domestic ungulates visited (see more under paragraph 65).

Although training and guidance documents are available to the VOAs performing PMI, the audit team noted some deficiencies in relation to the implementation of PMI in most of the slaughterhouses for ungulates visited: · pig testicles were not subject to visual inspection as required by point 1(h) of Article 23 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, · masseters of adult bovines were not systematically incised (only one incision in the external masseter instead of the required two) as required by point 1(a) of Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, · the lymph nodes (i.e. retropharyngeal, bronchial, and mediastinal) of adult bovines were not systematically incised as required by points 1(a) and 1(b) of

In addition, in a small slaughterhouse implementing the derogation on the timing of PMI, the PMI of the gastro-intestinal tract was not carried out properly as the VOA carried out such inspection in small buckets/bins that did not allow a proper inspection (only a small surface of the tract was visible).

The system in place provides official staff with legal powers for the performance of 9 official controls and the enforcement of legal requirements. However, the enforcement system is weakened by the fact that some non-compliances are not always followed up in a manner which ensures swift corrective action by the FBO. 5.3 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Official controls at slaughterhouse level Legal requirements Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CCA informed the audit team that follow up of non-compliances detected during inspections where the result is "favourable with remarks" is carried out during the next planned inspection visit by the LCU inspector. In these cases, no deadline for correction is given to the FBO and the non-compliances are expected to be corrected by the following CA visit (which can be in 3 or 6 months depending on the planned inspection frequency). Although the VOAs are permanently present at the slaughterhouses, the FASFC procedure does not require them to perform such follow up controls.

The audit team also noted some inconsistencies regarding the deadlines given to rectify non-compliances which could have been eliminated by an immediate action, in order to comply with the requirements of Article 137(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In two slaughterhouses visited the deadlines given to the FBO to remedy the issues related to knife sterilisers (insufficient contact time with the disinfectant used to sterilize knives) was around two months (in one of the cases the deadline was extended). In other slaughterhouses an immediate action was requested by the LCU inspector in similar situations.
The training systems are not able to deliver specific competency to staff, which has an impact on the implementation of official controls.

However, the inspectors were not adequately trained and provided with specific tools to properly identify all non-compliances and to register them in the official reports (see paragraphs 52 to 55). PHS

This is not in line with Article 1(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which states that official controls in the area food and food safety, integrity and wholesomeness must be performed at any stage of production, processing and distribution of food, including primary production.

Regarding DAA, for many years the official controls on fruit and vegetables throughout Denmark have been carried out by the same team of two inspectors (30 official inspec- tions/year). The two inspectors informed the audit team that they had not received any specific training on official controls at primary production relating to microbiological risks.

Employees are introduced to relevant legislation and educated in practical skills and aca- demic subjects to the extent required. Some inspectors participate in other relevant courses outside DVFA such as Better Training for Safer Food (BTSF). However, there was no evidence of any cascade course activity in order to share experiences and knowledge from BTSF courses with other colleagues.

During official inspections observed by the audit team, both DAA and DVFA inspectors and their supervisors demonstrated clear deficiencies in identifying non-compliances. Only when the audit team highlighted evidence of several very critical deficiencies over- looked during official inspections (e.g. cross-contamination and staff misconduct) did inspectors and supervisors acknowledge that these deficiencies represent a real risk for food safety (see paragraphs 19, 20, 35, 48, 49, 52, 57, 65, 66 and 67). Presence of birds inside greenhouses and food handling areas, inconsistent use of gloves by harvesting personnel, potential cross-contamination of harvested strawberries either by placing crates directly on the ground or by unhygienic worker practices, excessive presence of cobwebs in all packaging/storage areas of a primary FBO, were not identi- fied as non-compliance by either the inspectors or their supervisor.

There was no evidence that the above-mentioned non-compliances had ever been identi- fied and registered in previous inspections, including during the annual screening on "marketing standards" (see paragraph 38). In addition, the review of previous inspection reports detected very few non-compliances which gives the impression of compliance throughout the country, when this was not the case.

DVFA informed the audit team that their procedures provide inspectors with the power to require corrective action to be taken. However, during the audit, neither the FBOs, nor the inspectors, nor the supervisor took/requested immediate action to segregate potential- ly contaminated products observed by the audit team. Sprout-producing establishment

The inspectors correctly assessed the certification requirements for mung beans imported from a specific third country as seeds for sprouting but neither the inspectors nor the su- pervisor identify that the FBO also sprout imported seeds from other third countries. Therefore, the requirements (e.g. health certificates) for other seeds imported from other third countries have never been verified meaning, DVFA has never fully enforced this requirement.

However, other major non-compliances such as other areas of the establishment where condensation water was dropping on the food, a worker touching dirty surfaces and then product without changing gloves and rust/oil on two electric motors above the produc- tion line were overlooked by inspectors and their supervisor. In the last three years (six official inspections) there was no evidence that the inspectors or supervisor had detected or recorded similar non-compliances requiring correction.

During the debriefing with the FBO the inspectors, with the agreement of the supervisor, concluded that the official report will contain a minor non-conformity related to rusty pipes. Non-conformities regarding direct contamination of the product, even when de- tected by inspectors (condensation falling on the product), were not planned to be docu- mented in the official report. The audit team observed inspections being carried out at the high care areas (cutting, slicing, chopping area). In one case, even though several non-compliances were detected and recorded by the inspectors, condensation issues (even over the exposed foodstuff), rust and dirt on the ceiling and flaking paint on some equipment was overlooked.

When guided by the audit team, the inspectors identified inadequate cleaning of machin- ery, which the FBO considered as clean and ready to be used. However, there was no ev- idence (official reports) that similar non-compliances had ever been identified in previ- ous inspections as in other processors of FNAO.

The inspectors and the supervisor confirmed to the audit team that, during inspection, non-compliances, like the one observed by the audit team during these official inspec- tions, are usually communicated orally to the FBOs rather than documented in the offi- cial reports.

The competent authorities carried out official controls to sprout producers with overall an adequate scope. However, the verification of compliance that seeds produced in the EU stored and used in these establishments are suitable for production of sprout has been systematically overlooked during official controls. This undermines the effectiveness of such official controls.

However, the inspectors did not properly cover the suitability of the seeds of EU origin to be used for sprouting. In all visited establishments, there were bags of seeds of different species stored which were labelled as seeds for sowing, with no indication of suitability for sprouting, neither in the labels, nor in the associated documentation such as invoices or delivery notes. Inspectors did not require evidence that the seeds were appropriate for producing sprouts, and that had been obtained in compliance with the requirements of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

The CAs do verify that operators carry out microbiological testing as set out in Regulation (EC) 2073/2005. However, there is no control of whether the methods used are in line with Article 5(5) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. This lack of assessment to challenge the reliability of the own controls carried out by operators weakens the effectiveness of the official controls.

The latest available Multi-annual National Control Plan (MANCP) covered the period 2018-2020. Since then, also due to the COVID pandemic, the official control system 11 has been implemented following single annual control plans. In 2022, the CCA stated that the MANCP for the period 2023­2027 was under development. The new deadline currently defined for the approval of the MANCP is the end of 2024(2). This is not in line with the requirements of Article 109 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which stipulates that the official controls shall be carried out on the basis of a MANCP.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Whilst official controls are performed on the ABP operators supplying the petfood industry and those manufacturing petfood, they are ineffective, as evidenced by the numerous non-compliances identified by the audit team in establishments deemed to be compliant by the competent authority. The fact that these issues had not been identified in the context of the regular supervisory activities or in the DAFM internal audit of the sector, additionally raises concerns about the operation of the official control system in this sector. paragraph_text: The audit team examined documents accompanying consignments of ABP destined for the manufacture of petfood. On the evidence provided, the team inferred that the official controls in some of the meat-producing establishments supplying raw material to the petfood industry were ineffective given the observed non-compliances with the requirements for commercial documents and health certificates, identification and categorisation of ABP, and the collection and transport of ABP. Examples included: a. label_heading: Conclusions on the planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the petfood plants, the audit team examined the operators' compliance with the requirements regarding commercial documents and health certificates, identification, the collection and transport of ABP and traceability and compared what they saw with what 9 was recorded in the inspection reports. The reports omitted the following non- compliances: a. For the manufacture of petfood, operators accepted ABP arriving either without or with incomplete commercial documents/health certificates (see finding 36.a). label_heading: Conclusions on the planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team also noted that as regards the overall hygiene, cleanliness and maintenance of the plant equipment, the reports of the official controls indicated that these aspects were compliant, in marked contrast to what the audit team encountered in the establishments. It found (i) dirty containers used for collection of ABP resulting from the plant operations, (ii) dirty crates and racks used for the handling of ABP destined for thermal treatment and (iii) dirty chambers used for thermal treatment.

paragraph_text: With regard to the operators' written procedures based on HACCP principles, the reports of the official controls did not indicate any particular issues, whereas the audit team noted that: a. Some petfood operators had in place HACCP-based procedures that were generic and not reflective of the practices taking place in the plant. For example, whilst the transport temperature for arriving ABP was considered as a critical control point (CCP), it was not monitored by the operator and the storage temperature limit which would trigger an alarm was at a much higher temperature than the limit established as a CCP. b. In all of the petfood plants visited, the HACCP-based procedures were deficient wit

paragraph_text: With regard to the official assessments of the operators' own-checks, in some of the petfood plants, the inspection reports did not record non-compliances identified by the audit team: a. Sampling for Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae did not follow the appropriate sampling protocol ­ the operator collected one instead of five samples. 10 b. Notwithstanding the above, the operators also incorrectly interpreted the examination results when determining the compliance of the sampled batch of petfood, contrary to the requirements laid down in point 5 (dogchews) and point 6 (raw petfood) of Chapter II of Annex XIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. For instance, the operators did not consider a res

label_heading: Conclusions on the planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The one ABP plant visited which was processing Category 3 material and supplying derived products (processed animal proteins of mixed species) to the petfood industry was subject to bi-annual controls (see finding 30) and daily controls were performed by the DAFM official who is present in this particular plant on a daily basis (see finding 24). The reports of these controls indicated that the plant was compliant. However, the audit team identified numerous non-compliances related to the categorisation of ABP. The overall cleanliness and hygiene in the plant was poor as was the maintenance of the processing equipment.

label_heading: Conclusions on the planning of official controls
paragraph_text: With respect to the categorisation of ABP, the audit team noted that Category 2 material was being used for production of mixed processed animal proteins: a. ABP from slaughterhouses arriving as Category 3, contained Category 2 material such as (i) digestive tracts with their contents, (ii) animals' heads with attached plastic eartags, (iii) animal tissues mixed with plastic and paper and (iv) by- products in a state of decomposition. b. Category 2 material originating in the processing plant was recycled into the Category 3 processing line. This Category 2 material consisted of (i) the sludge collected from water traps, (ii) ABP from another line processing material of poultry origin, and r

label_heading: Conclusions on the planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The issues on incorrect categorisation of ABP identified in the finding above were also seen in the 2018 audit report (DG SANTE 2018-6334) and on which a recommendation (#4) was made. The actions taken by DAFM have not been effective given the recurrence of the issue.

label_heading: Conclusions on registration, approval, and listing
paragraph_text: There are arrangements in place for the registration, approval, and listing which should provide assurances that the operators active along the chain of petfood production are known and thus facilitate the implementation of official controls throughout this supply chain. However, the fact that the registration/approval data are not kept up to date (as evidenced by the disparity between the data in the national list and TRACES-NT), weakens an otherwise satisfactory system for approval and registration. 5.2.2 Planning of official controls

label_heading: Conclusions on the structural elements of the official control system
paragraph_text: The audit team noted that the national list of approved and registered petfood plants published on the Ministry of Health website did not contain information on the product types placed on the market, contrary to the Commission technical specifications (4) and the requirements of Article 20a(a) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

label_heading: Conclusions on the structural elements of the official control system
paragraph_text: The list of Italian petfood plants on the Commission's Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES NT) was not up to date; 125 plants were listed vs. 184 on the website of the Ministry of Health. Thus, the requirements of Article 20a(b) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 are not met.

label_heading: Conclusions on the structural elements of the official control system
paragraph_text: Based on the review of documents submitted by the Ministry of Health, the audit team noted that, in several regions, petfood plants that had stopped their activities for a long while were still present on the published list of petfood plants, despite several reminders sent by the Ministry of Health to RVS to ensure the timely removal of inactive operators from the national lists. Therefore, it cannot be considered that the list of petfood plant is kept up-to-date as required by Article 47(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Conclusions on registration, approval, and listing

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Notwithstanding these positive aspects, the official controls are not effective in verify- ing operator compliance with some of the applicable requirements as evidenced by the serious non-compliances identified by the audit team in establishments and plants visit- ed. These concerned the unsuitability of raw material used for the production of petfood (including lack of or incomplete commercial documents for any such raw material used), serious breaches of hygiene rules and absence of required own-testing of final product or absence of corrective actions by the operators following non-compliant own- testing results.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In both of the raw petfood plants, the operators had received (and accepted) incomplete commercial documents for incoming Category 3 materials. These documents did not contain information demonstrating that, as required by Article 35(aa)(iii) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the ABP consisted of exclusively Category 3 material of the sub- categories defined in Article 10(a),(b)(i) and/or (ii) of the said Regulation, which are the only sub-categories allowed for the production of raw petfood in the EU.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The internal procedures of both operators did not mention any restrictions on the sub- categories of Category 3 material that could be used for production of raw petfood.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In one of the raw petfood plants, some raw materials of animal origin were not accom- panied by any ABP commercial documentation, contrary to the requirements of Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The operator stated that such raw materials were considered food and, in its opinion, ABP documentation was not necessary. How- ever, by definition, in accordance with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, these raw materials are ABP and must be accompanied by ABP commercial documents.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The incompleteness and absence of commercial documentation for ABP dispatched from food establishments (such as slaughterhouses and cutting plants) is also an indica- tion that official controls at food business operators where these ABP originate have not effectively verified compliance with ABP requirements. 5.2.3.2 Official controls in ABP plants

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Firstly, storage conditions for PAP destined for use in petfood were unhygienic. Before bagging or dispatch in bulk, PAP were stored on an unclean and damaged concrete floor contrary to the requirements of Article 25(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and point C of Section I of Chapter II of Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Secondly, Category 3 material used for the production of PAP were stored on the floor before processing, mixed with dirt from cleaning operations. Pits in which these materi- als were subsequently placed prior to their processing, were unclean and with remains of ABP from previous days. The raw materials used in production during the visit were highly contaminated with foreign bodies and therefore they should have been catego- rised as Category 2 material (Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009) and not used for production of PAP (Article 31(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009). Company staff were removing foreign bodies from the raw materials before their shredding but, in spite of the

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: Thirdly, materials recovered from cleaning the processing equipment were recycled into processing. Such materials included sludge and remains of spoiled ABP that stayed in the unclean processing equipment for several days. Such materials should have been categorised as Category 2 material (Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009) and not used for production of PAP (Article 31(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009).

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the raw petfood plants visited, the reports of the inspections reviewed by the audit team made no reference to the following serious non-compliances. In one of the plants, the operator did not carry out own testing for Enterobacteriaceae (hygiene criteria). On- ly a subset of this family of microorganisms was tested for. Testing by operator of raw petfood for Enterobacteriaceae is a requirement under EU rules (Point 6 of Chapter II of Annex XIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011) as it provides an assessment of the overall hygienic conditions at the plant. The same operator carried out analyses for Salmonella in raw petfood but only on one sample, instead of five, contrary to the aforementio

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In the other plant, the audit team reviewed the operator's own-check Enterobacteriaceae results from 2023 to date. Several results were non-compliant (there were three or more samples with a bacterial count between 500 and 5000 colony forming units in 1 gramme of raw petfood). However, the operator did not consider the results to be non-compliant and therefore did not take any corrective actions to improve the hygienic conditions of the process, contrary to the requirement of Point 6 of Chapter II of Annex XIII to Regu- lation (EU) No 142/2011. This was not detected during official inspections carried out in that plant.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The competent authority has allowed the use of raw fish and ABP derived from fish for the manufacture of raw petfood at approved petfood plants, contrary to the EU require- ments. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Whilst all of the structural elements of a control system for petfood are in place, including supervisory audits by the regional and central competent authorities, the official controls are nevertheless not effective in verifying operators' compliance with some of the applicable requirements. The audit team identified in the establishments and plants visited serious non- 10 compliances which had not been detected by the officials during their regular controls. label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team noted that ABP consisting of raw fish were used for production of raw petfood in the two petfood plants visited. In January 2024, the Ministry of Health made use of a derogation laid down in Article 16(g) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 to au- thorise the use of raw fish and other fish derived ABP, under specific conditions and on- ly for direct sale to the final consumer within the territory of Italy. ABP from raw fish to 9 be used in the manufacture of raw petfood must not show signs of alterations (from an organoleptic point of view) and be subjected to freezing at -20°C for at least 24 hours.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: For petfood placed on the market, Article 35(a)(iii) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 states that raw petfood must derive only from material referred to in Article 10(a) and (b)(i) and (ii) of that Regulation. As fish-derived ABP fall under Article 10(i) and (j), they cannot be used for the production of raw petfood in an approved petfood plant. 5.2.3.3 Actions taken in the event of non-compliance and follow-up

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls at ABP plants cover HACCP-based procedures when required but they are not sufficient to reliably verify the operators' level of compliance with all of the key requirements of these procedures, resulting in incomplete identification of hazards by ABP operators.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The petfood and processing plants visited maintained HACCP-based procedures as re- quired by Article 29 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. However, the audit team noted that these procedures were deficient in several areas: (a) incomplete process flow dia- gram, (b) insufficient monitoring arrangement for critical control points or (c) missing critical control points required by EU rules on ABP and DP for processing plants im- plementing continuous processing methods. These issues were overlooked during past official controls.

label_heading: Conclusions on implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: Official controls verify that operators use the correct category and types of ABP for manufacturing petfood. However, such controls are not sufficient to identify instances of incorrect categorisation and handling of ABP by some operators. This resulted in limited quantities of ABP being used for the production of feed or petfood while they are not allowed for such use under EU rules.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: The audit team noted that commercial documents accompany ABP and DP during transport, as required by Article 17 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. In most cases, they contained the necessary information. However, in one of the petfood plant visited (raw petfood), ABP commercial documents were missing for most of the category 3 materials used in the production of petfood. The audit team noted that GVI had taken action to avoid that such situation is widespread and had informed (by means of circular letters) all food business operators where ABP are generated and collected that ABP commer- cial documentation should be used in all cases. In addition, the audit team noted that all inspectors met we

paragraph_text: In relation to categorisation and handling of ABP, past inspections carried out in some of the petfood and intermediate plants visited overlooked that, contrary to the require- ments of Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, operators considered as Category 3 material the following materials: (a) material of animal origin collected from unclean sections (floor) and (b) Category 3 material containing foreign bodies. Some of these in- correctly categorised materials were recycled in the production of petfood or dispatched to processing plants for Category 3 material from which derived products may be used in feed. The audit team noted that the quantities of ABP incorrectly categorised as C

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: During the review of files concerning actions taken by DVIs in cases of petfood contam- inated with Salmonella or exceeding the acceptable values for Enterobacteriaceae, the audit team noted that some of these non-compliant petfood (Category 2 material) was disposed of accompanied by commercial documentation stating these were Category 3 material, contrary to the provisions of Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. However, despite this incorrect categorisation, the audit team noted that such petfood had been processed in Category 1 and 2 processing plants, which prevented their diver- sion back into the feed chain.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning of official controls
paragraph_text: In one of the petfood plant visited (canned petfood), the audit team noted that the opera- tor's procedures for dealing with ABP that were unfit for production of petfood (e.g. Category 2 material) were very succinct and did not allow for an unequivocal identifica- tion of the crates to be used for collecting such ABP. As a result, the audit team noted that containers of various colours were used, some being identified with paper labels that could easily be removed. In particular, crates for storing raw material fit for use and material unfit for production of petfood were identical, except for a paper label glued on the crate and bearing the mention `kat. 2'. The frequency varies between once every 7 years (very low) to three times per year (high). FeBOs dealing with medicated feed are also included in the risk-based planning. The assessed labels did not contain information on the added amount of active substances contained in the veterinary medicinal products, information on the adequate disposal of the medicated feed, information on any contra-indications and instructions for use in line with the veterinary prescription. These are not in line with the requirement of points 3, 4, 5, 8 and 10 of Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2019/4. These non-compliances had not been identified in the reports of the previous official controls.

There is a system of official controls in place for animals and goods of animal and non- animal origin entering the EU though BCPs in Romania, which is supported by information technology systems and cooperation and communication within and between the competent authorities. However, shortcomings related to the lack of up-to-date documented procedures and arrangements in place and a shortage of staff have an adverse impact on the effectiveness of implementation of official import controls. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU The audit team evaluated the implementation of official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU through BC

The audit team noted that the majority of the documented procedures had not been updated to reflect the requirements of the OCR and could not therefore ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, which is not in line with Article 5(1)(a) and 12(3)(b)of the OCR. For example, the competent authorities do not have up- to-date documented procedures for prior notification, the performance of documentary, identity and physical checks, including the frequency rates, on consignments of animals and goods and official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit (see section 5.2).

The audit team also noted that the arrangements in place for the implementation of the measures referred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR and contingency arrangements are incomplete, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(d) and(e) respectively of the OCR.

The system of official controls on animals and goods entering the Union though BCPs in Romania showed significant shortcomings in the frequencies at which identity and physical checks are performed on goods of animal origin and in the performance of official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit. Other shortcomings were noted concerning the implementation of official controls on certain consignments of animals and goods of non-animal origin. Collectively, these shortcomings significantly undermine the overall effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the EU. 5.3 COMPLIANCE OF BORDER CON

At one BCP of introduction visited, the BCP staff stated that in case of official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit, the vehicles or transport containers in which such consignments leave the BCP were not sealed by the BCP staff, which is not in line with Article 19(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. This practice was further confirmed to the audit team during subsequent meetings with staff at other Romanian BCPs.

During the visit to a port BCP of exit, the BCP staff stated that they did not perform an identity check to ensure that consignment of goods leaving the EU through this BCP corresponded to the consignment referred to in the associated CHED. This is not in line with Article 33 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. The staff at this BCP of exit explained that part III of the CHEDs was completed solely based on receiving copies of CHEDs from the relevant customs agents. According to TRACES-NT, this port BCP accounted for 8 402 out of a total of 12 317 consignments exiting in transit through Romanian BCPs of which about 7 000 have part III completed. 10

During their visit to the approved warehouse, the audit team noted that the competent authority did not confirm the arrival of the consignments at the warehouse in part III of the CHED, which is not in line with Article 26(4)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124.

The audit team also noted that the competent authority did not ensure that the operator responsible for the consignments leaving the warehouse submitted a CHED in TRACES- NT and consequently failed to authorise the movement by finalising the CHED which must accompany consignments leaving the warehouses to third countries, other warehouses and disposal places. The competent authority instead completed part III of the CHED which accompanied the consignment upon arrival at the warehouse. This is not in line with Article 28(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124.
