The audit team noted that the frequency of physical checks performed on goods of animal origin was not in line with the baseline frequency rate set out in Articles 4(1) and 11 5(1) and Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2129. This finding predominantly relates to consignments of poultry meat from Ukraine entering the EU; approximately 3 000 consignments of poultry meat in 2023 were subjected to physical checks at a rate of 3% compared to the required minimum frequency of 30%. 5.2.4.3 Checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin

However, identity and physical checks on consignments subject to measures set out in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1158 had not been carried out in line with the minimum frequency rate set out in Article 5(2) of that Regulation. Based on data provided by the competent authorities, approximately 1.7% (4 out of 240) of such consignments in 2023 were subjected to identity and physical checks compared to the required minimum frequency of 20%.

The evaluated BCPs, except for a suspended BCP for animals, had the minimum facilities and equipment in place for the categories of animals and goods of animal origin for which they had been designated, but the three BCPs visited were not well maintained. In addition, the Romanian authorities perform official controls on consignments of food contact materials entering the EU without having designated BCPs for this category of goods. The control point visited does not comply with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of goods for which it has been designated. These shortcomings have the potential to reduce the overall effectiveness of the official control system. 5.4 FOLLOW ­ U

The audit team noted that no BCPs have been designated and listed for food contact materials, (i.e. category PNAO-NHC(other)), and that official controls on consignments of food contact materials entering the EU are instead performed at the importers' warehouses, which is not in line with Article 49(1) of the OCR.

The audit team found that facilities and equipment at the port BCPs Constana North and Constana South and the airport BCP Bucharest Henri Coand were generally compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of goods for which they had been designated. However, the loading and storage facilities for goods of animal and non-animal origin at these three BCPs, and the inspection facilities at the airport BCP Bucharest Henri Coand, were not maintained and thus not easy to clean and disinfect. This is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 and 64(3) of the OCR.

The audit team visited one control point used for identity and physical checks on consignments of non-animal origin. The audit team found that the control point was not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Article 53(1)(a) of the OCR. There were no clearly dedicated unloading, inspection and storage areas, there was no drainage in these areas, and the floors of these areas were poorly maintained and thus not easy to clean and disinfect. In addition, the inspection area did not have a supply of hot and cold running water and hand washing facilities and it was equipped with a table that was not easy to clean and disinfect. The audit team noted therefore, that the documented procedures do not include all of the subject areas set out in Chapter II of Annex II to the OCR, which is not in line with Arti- cle 12(1) of that regulation. The Romanian authorities made resolute efforts in recent years to increase among backyards' operators the levels of awareness about, and compliance with requirements on animal traceability. However, despite introducing new legislation and strengthening official controls on the matter, the inadequate powers available to officials to enforce those new provisions keep holding back progress in this area.

An undetermined, but still significant number of illegal movements in the backyards population, and the underreporting to the national database of other events from those establishments (e.g., on-site slaughter), have an uncertain impact on surveillance for ASF and keep impairing epidemiological investigations when the disease is suspected or confirmed.

When ASF outbreaks occur in backyards, authorities do not always take effective measures to mitigate the risk of local disease spread. Persistent shortcomings in animal traceability and biosecurity allow the virus to circulate between backyards, leading to clusters of outbreaks that last longer than expected, even when the number of primary cases is limited.

Implementation of surveillance for ASF in wild boar varies significantly between counties, but it confronts since the 2021/22 hunting season increasing challenges to find and test dead animals, which became a rare event in many of them4. Besides, the reluctance of the competent authorities to enforce requirements on ASF surveillance in hunting grounds, and delays in approving new legal provisions to introduce economic incentives to encourage searching for and testing of wild boars, keep impairing early detection and control of the disease.

The national action plan and legal framework to manage wild boar populations for ASF control, alongside the natural impact of the disease, led to a steady population decline until spring 2023. However, disagreements with part of the hunting community in some areas of the country, resulting in weak compliance with and enforcement of hunting quotas, exacerbated by recent climatic and environmental challenges, contributed to reverse that trend. While many hunting grounds apply biosecurity measures effectively, inconsistencies in population management and limited enforcement of ASF control policies create uncertainty about long-term disease control.

However, the authorities do not keep properly updated the list of those designated food business operators and their activities, that should be accessible to the Commission and to the other Member States to facilitate their verification activities on compliance with EU trade rules. Nevertheless, despite the inaccuracies present on that list for some operators, this deficiency was not increasing the risk of transmitting ASF outside of Romania, as they comply with the activities for which they are designated.

Although the new instructions to conduct controls on the use of VMPs include the need to check whether antimicrobials in the reserved list have been prescribed, the competent authorities responsible for these types of checks have not been designated yet. Therefore, recommendation 1 of report DG(SANTE) 2023-7694 has not been addressed. 4.2 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON THE USE OF ANTIMICROBIALS Legal requirements Articles 105(1) to (3), (5)(m) and (6), 106(1), 107(1) to (5) and (7) to (9), 108, 112 to 114, and 123. 2 Observations and findings Report DG(SANTE) 2023-7694 concluded that even though checks done in accordance with national legislation enacted before 2019 covered the trade and use of VMPs,

According to personnel from the General Veterinary Inspectorate (GVI), the designation of the competent authority responsible for checking that antimicrobials reserved for the treatment of certain infections in humans are not prescribed for animals is contingent on having national legislation in place incorporating the requirements of the VMPR. Work is still in progress in that regard, and it is expected to be finished during the first half of 2026. This is not in line with Article 137(1).

label_heading: Conclusion on actions in case of non-compliance
paragraph_text: Despite the number of veterinarians referred to the relevant regional veterinary chambers, the lack of national legislation still prevents GVI to impose dissuasive penalties applicable to infringements of the VMPR. Therefore, recommendation 3 of report DG(SANTE) 2023-7694 has not been addressed. 4 5 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There has been noticeable and significant progress in designing and implementing suitable controls to check compliance with the prudent use requirements of the Veterinary Medicinal Products Regulation (VMPR). However, there continues to be: i) a lack of designation of the competent authority responsible for checking that antimicrobials reserved for the treatment of certain inf

According to personnel from GVI, they will not be able to impose efficient penalties applicable to infringements of the VMPR until national legislation is in place, incorporating the requirements of the VMPR, which is not expected to happen before the first half of 2026 (see point 1). This is not in line with Article 135(1).

Despite initial challenges which provoked the quick spread of ASF, authorities controlled affectively outbreaks on pig establishments using all required measures. The epidemics highlighted resource challenges for the authorities, who did not perform complete epidemiological investigations for all outbreaks and could not carry out quick final disinfections of all affected premises.

The clear rules for biosecurity measures and surveillance for domestic pigs contribute to prevent the entry and spread of AFS. However, the fact that many outbreaks were detected by continuous passive surveillance without notification of suspicions indicates important gaps in awareness or notification.

Official controls as implemented are not identifying and/or recording a range of readily apparent non-compliances in HACCP based plans, maintenance, hygiene, cold chain, pest control, traceability and labelling. Additionally, when non-compliances are detected, the CA is reluctant to use enforcement measures.

In the absence of on-the-spot verification of officials' performance when carrying out official controls, the VS is not aware of the situation described above, and that official 11 controls, as systematically inadequately implemented, cannot ensure the compliance of operators and processing of fishery products with food safety requirements as already noted during the previous DG SANTE audits on the same topic. 5.3.2 Official controls of fishery products Legal requirements Council Regulation (EC) No 2406/96. The VS has an internal audit system, and the fishery sector was covered in 2013. The VS monitors the implementation of the official control plans by receiving the completed checklists and the DVOs' reports every six and twelve months. When serious non- compliances at operators are detected, joint inspections can be carried out, but in these cases, evaluation of the performance of the individual officers is not included. The aforementioned tools are not adequate to allow the CA to have an overview of the effectiveness and appropriateness of the controls as set out in Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Additionally, the VS does not have in place control verification procedures in lin

The audit team reviewed the approvals of several on-land establishments and noted that in general the procedure described above was followed. However, the timelines between conditional and final approvals were not always respected and exceeded a total of six months. This is not in line with Article 148(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team noted that when new premises were built to replace the old one, in the same location with the same activity, there was not a new approval carried out. According to the CA, the current national approval procedure is not clear in this kind of case.

The procedure described above is not in line with Article 148(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires that after three months, the CA must either extend the conditional approval (for a period not exceeding a total of six months) or issue a final approval. The exception (i.e. the possibility to extend conditional approval to a total of 12 months) applies only to factory and freezer vessels.

The audit team noted that even the current procedure is not always followed with regard to the deadlines set: one of the RVs was conditionally approved in 2020 and has not yet been granted with a final approval.

The audit team carried out a desk-based assessment of the documented controls over RVs. The planned inspection frequency has not been respected and was consequently extended to six years instead of four years. The audit team noted that HACCP plans did not cover all relevant areas e.g. temperatures in the holds and fishery product traceability.

HACCP-based procedures are assessed by the central level at the time of approval. The DVO officials explained that they only check recordings and sampling by the operator related to HACCP and they do not review the HACCP plans themselves during inspections. Consequently, none of the reports included remarks of any non-compliances 9 in the operators' HACCP plans (see findings in paragraphs 49 and 50 on HACCP non- compliances).

The audit team noted that in many cases the operators had used external consultants to produce their HACCP plans. When reviewing the plans, the audit team noted discrepancies in relation to current processes and EU legislation. Furthermore, the HACCP plans were not always updated, when changes in activities and/or equipment occurred.

The audit team noted that in many cases HACCP hazard analysis did not include all possible hazards (no physical and chemical hazards included), critical control points had critical limits (temperatures) not in line with EU rules, monitoring of critical limits was not adequately determined, and in case of failures to comply with a critical limit (mainly related to temperatures of frozen fishery products), adequate corrective actions were not defined properly. When questioned, the operators did not have knowledge and ownership over their HACCP plans.

In addition to the findings related to HACCP-based procedures, the audit team noted non- compliances in many other areas, which were either not covered during official controls or, if checked, non-compliances were not detected and/or not recorded in the reports (see below paragraphs 52 - 59). The audit team did not find any evidence of enforcement measures used as defined in Articles 137 and 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. When questioned, the officials explained that due to the good cooperation with the operators, and because the use of enforcement measures is too much workload and time consuming, there has not been willingness to take measures. Unfortunately, many of the findings in this

Regarding non-compliances in the cold chain, the audit team noted the following during the visits: storage temperature records for chambers with frozen fishery products showed consistently temperatures above -18, temperature recording devices were not in place, not properly recording or not in a place where it can be easily read, locations of temperature sensors were unknown or not situated in the area of the highest temperature, temperatures measured from frozen fishery products were above the EU limits (starting from -12) and cold chambers with products stored up to the doors preventing access and proper air circulation. Those non compliances were not identified by the operators and the of

Freezing of fishery products was carried out for whole wrapped fish, such as tuna, in a cold store with no criteria for rapid freezing and/or controlling the freezing process. In another case, fishery products frozen two weeks ago were found to have a core temperature of -12, while the temperature recording display showed -23 (at the time of the visit the blast freezer was used as a storage facility for polystyrene boxes). 10

Significant non-compliances in general hygiene were noted in areas where chilled fresh fish was processed as well as the excessive use of water resulting in spillage to floor instead of being directing to a drain. The audit team noted condensation above unprotected fishery products. In one case, bins used for the transport of farmed fish were dirty and had a bad odour as they were only flushed briefly after use and then stored outside at high ambient temperature waiting to be washed later before use. These bins (washed and filled with some ice), were still dirty. Officials were unaware of this situation.

Maintenance issues, some significant, were detected in several premises. In some cases, it was explained to the audit team that verbal orders have been given, and some corrective actions had been taken by the operators.
Deficiencies in pest control were noted due to the gaps around doors and fans. Live ants and flies were detected in some establishments.

Traceability was not ensured when fishery products were found in cold storage without any labels. During one traceability exercise, the operator was not able to show evidence of the origin of the raw material.

Hygiene of water was not ensured when seawater, added to bins with ice, was taken from the dock. In addition, the ice machine checked by the audit team was rusty, the room had dirty walls and ceiling and the process of loading ice into transport bins was unhygienic. In another case, the water treatment system with an ultraviolet lamp for river water had not been maintained since 2010. In addition, the analysis did not include all relevant chemical parameters.

The audit team identified non-compliances on the labelling of fishery products with regard to identification marking, mandatory information of origin, references to aquaculture/wild catch, latin names of species, storage temperatures, and when relevant, a warning on potential gastrointestinal effects of consuming oilfish (Ruvettus pretiosus). Conclusions on official controls on the production and placing on the market

The official control system covers land-based establishments, aquaculture farms and to some extent, RVs and primary production fishing vessels above 12 meters in length. Official controls are performed using documented procedures covering the required aspects. However, landing sites and primary production fishing vessels below 12 meters in length are omitted from the official control planning and, thus a significant proportion of the production chain is not subject to official controls.

Vessels below 12 meters in length belonging to categories A and B are currently not included in the annual control plans. This is not in line with Article 67(b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The VS informed the audit team that they have been excluded 8 from the controls mainly due to lack of resources, difficulty to reach the vessels and they do not need a certificate of compliance to operate. The VS added that they can be inspected on a random basis, if available and if an inspection to a landing site takes place (see paragraph 43). During an on-site visit to one landing site, two such vessels came back from a fishing trip. The DVO official inspected these vessels and detected t

Based on information provided, controls of landing sites have not been planned and consequently not carried out since 2020. This is not in line with Article 67(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Contrary to the EU rules, ALVA is not providing the Commission services with information necessary for the functioning of TRACES, in particular, it has not provided the lists of food business establishments approved in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 in the fishery products sector. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Official controls on the production and placing on the market Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament a

A list of approved food business establishments is made available on the ALVA website on a "Fiche Informative". This list does not adequately follow the technical specifications of issued by DG Health and Food Safety (5) as required by Article 45(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. Establishments are categorised in the above list according to their main commercial activity with additional activities (and potentially those of a higher risk from a food safety perspective) presented in a separate column. It is the operator who decides on the category when registering the establishment in the "MyGuichet.lu" web platform.

ALVA does not maintain and keep in TRACES an up-to-date list of approved fishery products establishments contrary to the requirement of Article 45(1)(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. ALVA indicated that staff had not been assigned for this purpose.

label_heading: Conclusion on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: While there is a clear designation of competent authorities and distribution of the tasks, and the sampling officials are adequately trained and equipped, the overall effectiveness of the residue control plans for pharmacologically active substances and contaminants is seriously undermined by incomplete implementation of the plans combined with uneven distribution of the sampling over the year. 5.5. Follow-up of non-compliant results and enforcement

In recent years, the implementation of residue control started only in the second half of the year, which is not in line with EU requirements (20) and did not allow the fulfilment of the plans and of the minimum sampling frequencies laid down in EU legislation (21), even if the competent authority always planned 0.5% more samples than required by EU legislation.
In 2023, only 4077 (62%) of the 6574 planned samples were taken, out of which 3588 samples were analysed by the laboratories, therefore only 55% of the samples planned were taken and analysed.

In 2024, the sampling plans were transmitted to the regional offices in September, and 4911 (74%) of the 6654 planned samples were taken, and 4631 samples were analysed, therefore only 70% of the samples planned were taken and analysed. In addition, 70% of all samples were taken in October and November, which is not in line with EU legislation (22) to ensure an even spread of sampling throughout the year.

A total of 280 taken samples in 2024 could not be analysed in the laboratory analysing most samples. For four of the 280 samples, transport-related matters were indicated as the reason, for 70 ­ sampling-related obstacles and for 206 ­ the laboratory highlighted breakdowns of the technical equipment and staff holidays and shortages. In June 2025, the competent authority cancelled the request of analysis for 44 samples taken in 2024, as the analyses had still not started.

For both years 2023 and 2024, the auditors observed that, in addition to the sampling carried out largely in the second half of those years, in several cases, multiple sampling was performed to fulfil the requested sample numbers, especially during the last weeks of the respective years. This multiple sampling was not always performed in line with EU legal requirements which set the conditions to be respected for double sampling. Notably, no specific identification of the operator could be found, nor any risk-based justification. This appeared to be done only to improve overall sample numbers at the end of the year. There was no other justification (23).
Other deficiencies in the implementation of the plan, such as incorrect matrices sampled, could not be corrected on time, as they were only discovered when the sampling year was already over.

In addition, the turn-around times between the arrival of the sample and the availability of the analytical result from the laboratory in charge of most analyses, exceeded, for most of the samples, the 30 days agreed with the competent authority. In the 2023 and 2024 sample files verified by the auditors, several delays of 6-8 months were observed before the analytical result was available. At the time of the audit, there was no systematic verification by the competent authority regarding the turn-around times of samples in the laboratory.

For 2025, the sampling plans were distributed to the regional offices by email on 5 May 2025. Until the time of the audit, 2552 (39%) of the 6506 samples planned were taken by 6 October 2025, out of which 746 were registered as analysed. In the same laboratory, as mentioned in the previous finding, the auditors were informed that for 324 of the 1572 analysed samples (all plans), the turn-around time already exceeded 30 days. The laboratory explained the reasons for these delays as linked to staff holidays, staff shortages and breakdowns of technical equipment. paragraph_text: However, registered businesses are allowed to trade their products in the whole territory of Croatia, which is not in line with the requirements of Article 1.5.(b).(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of, and Annex II to OCR. Findings
Limited and insufficient training impact the technical knowledge of the control staff and, ultimately, on the effectiveness of official controls.

The lack of adequate supervision (internal audit) and the limited coordination between CAs do not provide sufficient guarantees that consistent enforcement and actions are always carried out. 5.3 APPROVAL AND REGISTRATION OF OPERATORS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Articles 10(2), 138(2)(j) and 148 of OCR. Findings

The central office of SI ­ Independent Internal Audit Service (staffed with 3 auditors) also carries out the supervision of the work of the DBs entrusted with official controls: supervision is carried out by documentary checks at the DB headquarters, with a limited component performed by witness audit in the field. No internal audit in the dairy sector had been performed in the recent years (the last audit in the veterinary field was carried out in 2024 on official sampling of poultry caecum, involving 10 DBs and 1 witness au- dit in the field).

Staff of DBs had not been provided with specific training since a long time: some years ago an online training on HACCP in dairy had been provided but not sufficiently de- tailed on the verification/validation of the milk heat-treatment process. Moreover, AVs of DBs have to deal with a large number of FBOs involved in the processing of different commodities (meat, milk, fish, retail, etc.), making it hard to be specialised in any of them. Due to this lack of training and of some specific knowledge required in the dairy processing sector, the effectiveness of the official controls carried out by DBs is also sometimes questionable.
The SI organises at least twice a year a co-ordination meeting between Veterinary and Sanitary Inspection. Coordination activities between VFSI and VFSD had not been doc- umented.

The VFSD have a formal computerised reporting system in place for the outcome of official controls (approval/registration processes, animal health controls) called VetIs, to which also the VFSI has access. This latter uses its own database e-Inspector for reporting of official controls, for its exclusive use (the VFSD has no access to this database). Conclusions on competent authorities

label_heading: Conclusion on approval and listing of establishments
paragraph_text: The provisions and procedures in place for the registration and/or approval of dairy businesses are adequate to maintain oversight over the approval conditions. However, the current approvals granted to FBOs do not always ensure that all activities and struc- tures are covered by a valid approval. 5.4 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON MILK PRODUCTION HOLDINGS Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 3 of, and Chapter I of Section IX, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 49 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

All visited establishments had a valid approval at the time of the audit team visit. How- ever, also discrepancies were noted: a. some FBOs had not informed the CAs about relevant changes that had occurred in the structure/equipment/activities, as required by Article 6.2 of Reg. 852/2004, and by Article 9 of Rules on the registration and approval of establishments and registration of operators in food businesses (OG 123/19). No specific sanctions had been applied by the VFSI staff in such cases; b. in one of the holdings visited, the operator had not informed the CA on the ceased operation of sale of raw milk through 3 vending machines: the operator has been sanctioned by VFSI Decision on 18

label_heading: Conclusion on raw milk criteria for export to the EU
paragraph_text: Official controls over raw milk criteria ensure that these latter are generally correctly and timely enforced by the FBOs. However, the obligation of FBO to notify the CAs about non-compliances is not always consistently enforced. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OVER FOOD BUSINESS OPERATORS' COMPLIANCE WITH HYGIENE RULES AT ESTABLISHMENT LEVEL Legal requirements Articles 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 137, 138 and 139 of OCR. Articles 3 and 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 14 Findings 5.6.1 General organisation of controls

The procedures and mechanisms in place ensure that controls are carried out uniformly and consistently, but do not guarantee that the controls are sufficiently thorough and in depth to detect shortcomings.

The supervision arrangements are not robust enough and have covered only narrow scopes and thus have not fully ensured the effectiveness, appropriateness, and quality of official controls, as required by Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.3 REGISTRATION AND APPROVAL OF FOOD BUSINESS ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. 5 Articles 10(2), 138(2)(j) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on controls over milk and colostrum production holdings
paragraph_text: The official controls on compliance of dairy holdings with the legal requirements on an- imal health and welfare, identification and registration as well as the use of VMPs and milking hygiene are adequate and, with some exceptions, carried out correctly and well documented. 5.5 CONTROLS ON RAW MILK UPON COLLECTION Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 3 of, and Chapter I, Part III, Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 50 of, and Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on FBOs' compliance with hygiene rules
paragraph_text: The controls were not sufficiently in-depth in two of the four regions visited to detect all relevant shortcomings and/or, if detected, not recorded. In one establishment visited the enforcement measures available had not been applied although the plant had long- standing shortcomings and was not in compliance with EU requirements and its prod- ucts could pose a food safety risk. In another establishment, there were significant short- comings in relation to traceability and the categorisation of a large amount of products. These had not been covered by official controls and lacked the guarantees of being safe for human consumption.

The findings of the audit team in two establishments visited compared with the inspec- tions reports of the inspections/audits carried out by the regional milk specialists in two of the four regions visited (see chapter 5.6) indicate that the supervision by the central level (as foreseen in Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625) has not been sufficient to detect weaknesses in the control system.

The audit team visited three dairy cow and one dairy sheep farm which had been in- spected by official veterinarians quite recently. The inspection reports reflected the ob- servations of the audit team related to three farms, where the conditions of milking hy- giene and use of VMPs and records kept were assessed as satisfactory. However, in one farm, milking hygiene was not complying with all requirements of Regulation (EC) No 7 852/2004. This was not recorded in the inspection report and consequently no corrective actions were requested. The CA ensured that an additional inspection would take place, and the necessary measures will be taken. Conclusions on controls over milk and colostrum

Some of the shortcomings noted by the DG(SANTE) audit team had not been identi- fied/recorded during previous inspections in relation to premises, hygiene, HACCP- based procedures, microbiological criteria, traceability and labelling (more details be- low). 5.6.3 General and specific hygiene requirements Legal requirements Article 4 of, and Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 3 of, and Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Findings

Major maintenance and general hygiene issues were noted by the audit team in one dairy establishment visited (producing ready-to-eat dairy products). The inspector had not recorded any non-compliances in the reports. The CCA accompanying the audit team in- formed on-spot that immediate actions are taken to suspend its activities.

Another dairy establishment visited was storing dairy products in a warehouse which had not been inspected by the milk specialist. The blueprint seen by the audit team did not indicate it was used for storing of milk products. 5.6.4 Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points based systems Legal requirements Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Findings

The audit team noted that the pest control programme in one establishment visited was insufficient. The inspection reports showed constant rodent activity but there was no root cause analysis to detect the reason (which was probably the access of rodents to milk powders in the storage containers for milk powder samples). 5.6.5 Microbiological criteria for foodstuffs Legal requirements Articles 3 and 4, and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

In one establishment visited, the audit team noticed that raw material packages (cheese in vacuum) in big carton boxes did not bear an identification mark and thus lacked relia- ble traceability. The operator stated, based on the accompanying documents, that these cheeses had been cut (sometimes also sliced or graded) and repacked in an approved es- tablishment. The later did not appear on the list of milk establishments, but on the list for packing establishments (see also paragraph 27) (2). The CA agreed to take measures regarding the non-compliant identification marking.

In one of the establishments visited, a dry store that had not been inspected by the re- gional milk specialist had approximately 50 tonnes of different types of milk and milk products powders without traceability or any other clear indication of their content as well as the purpose for use (for human consumption, feed or destruction). Some of the packages had passed their best before dates. In the same establishment, the audit team detected two milk powder packages in the main storage facility for which traceability could not be provided. The CA initiated investigations and measures immediately. Conclusions on official controls on FBOs' compliance with hygiene rules

label_heading: Conclusions on official controls on FBOs' compliance with hygiene rules
paragraph_text: The controls have not been thorough enough in order to ensure that operators' sampling schemes for Listeria provide reliable results regarding the safety of ready-to-eat food. 2 In their response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that according to the implementation guide for Regulation (EC) 853/2004, operations related to the unpacking and repackaging of products of animal origin (slicing and cutting) may take place at the repackaging plant. 14 5.7 OFFICIAL SAMPLING PROGRAMMES AND LABORATORIES Legal requirements Articles 5(d), 14(g) and (h), 34, 37, 38, 39 and 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Part III of Chapter I, of Section IX, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. F

The audit team noted the following shortcoming in relation to requirements of Regula- tion (EC) No 2073/2005 on sampling and testing for Listeria monocytogenes (L. mono- cytogenes): a) Only one product (five subsamples) once in a year was send for detection of L. mon- ocytogenes while the operator produces a wide range of ready-to-eat products. label_heading: Conclusions on Registration and approval of food business operators
paragraph_text: There are procedures in place to ensure that FBOs of FNAO are registered and are known to CAs which have the possibility to access to different sources of registers. However, the lack of direct access to relevant information and proper coordination between CAs prevents regional and therefore, local CAs to avail updated information of farms growing crops potentially posing higher microbial risk, thus limiting the adequate prioritisation of official controls in accordance with Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

However, these registers do not include relevant information on the crops being grown. Different strategies have been followed by the regional CAs to overcome the lack of detailed information in the register: · In some cases, regional CAs have got access to the data bases of the Chambers of Commerce. These databases only provide for general activity groups, which in the case of primary production comprises permanent crops and other general activities such as "cereals", or "horticulture". · In Sicily, there are 53 000 farms dedicated to primary production of FNAO, including permanent and non-permanent crops. The regional CAs of Sicily indicated that 8 000 farms were dedicated to horticulture.

label_heading: Conclusions on planning and implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: There is not a reliable official system to identify growers producing seeds for sprouting, and therefore they are not subject to official controls to verify compliance with hygiene requirements to address microbiological risks. Regarding seeds for sprouting, the current available registers do not provide information on the farms producing this type of product. However, this was an initiative of the local SIAN that it has not been systematically taken by the rest of local, regional or central CAs to identify the farms producing seeds for sprouting. paragraph_text: The audit team visited one FBO placing seeds for sprouting in the market. This FBO has an internal system in place for controlling growers producing seeds. paragraph_text: In Campania, there are 39 000 classified as non-permanent crops (therefore including cereals, fruits and vegetables). The official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Belgium are generally carried out in line with relevant EU legislation, documented procedures and planned arrangements. However, some shortcomings were noted in the performance of official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit, which potentially weaken the guarantee that only compliant goods enter the Union. 5.3 COMPLIANCE OF BORDER CONTROL POSTS WITH MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS The audit team carried out on-the-spot visits to nine inspection centres located in the BCPs Zeebrugge Port, Brussels Airport and Antwerp Port, and one control point not located in a BCP from the lists published on the Commiss

The audit team noted, according to data in TRACES-NT for 2024, that in the vast ma- jority (over 90%) of cases of consignments in transit, confirmation of arrival and compli- ance of consignments had been completed in part III of the relevant CHEDs at either the BCPs of exit or the approved warehouses. However, at the warehouse visited, the audit team observed that the identity check on arrival of consignments at this warehouse was mainly based on information provided by the operator rather than the performance of an identity check, which was not in line with Article 26(4)(a) and (b) of Delegated Regula- tion (EU) 2019/2124 nor has the FASFC exempted consignments from those checks or updated

For consignments of goods of animal origin in transit to United States' army bases locat- ed in the EU, the staff at one BCP allow the identity checks to be carried out based in part by information provided by the terminal operator on such consignments. This prac- tice is not in line with Article 49(1) of the OCR and Article 3(1) and (2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

Regarding the evaluated cases of consignments of goods in transit to vessels located in ports in other Member States, the audit team noted that an official certificate in accord- ance with the model laid down in Part I of the Annex to Commission Implementing Reg- ulation (EU) 2019/2128 had been issued in each case. The certificates, however, were not always completed in line with the requirements set out in Article 5 and Part 2 of the An- nex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2128.

At one BCP, the arrival of the consignments of goods in transit to vessels had not been confirmed for the 25 certificates issued in 2024 and follow-up measures were not ap- plied, which is not in line with Articles 30 and 31(5) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124, although BCP staff had sent several reminders to the warehouse operator.

The audit team further noted that the FASFC did not ensure that the warehouse operator did submit a CHED in TRACES-NT for consignments transported from the warehouse to exit BCPs to be delivered to supply vessels in ports in third countries, and consequently failed to authorise the movement by finalising the CHEDs which must accompany con- signments. This delegation is subject to compliance with the delegated conditions laid down in Article 30, (applied mutatis mutandis), being fulfilled. Official veterinarians use a standard template to carry out the epidemiological enquiries of outbreaks. The template follows the requirements of Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Most outbreak investigations concluded that wild birds were the source of infection. However, they did not consistently include detail on possible biosecurity breaches. For instance, in one case, minks that had got into the hen house had killed laying hens, but this was not further examined or linked to biosecurity breaches.

The DVFA did not document the tracing back and forward of all possible sources (people, vehicles or otherwise) that may have led to the introduction of the virus to the outbreak or to other possible epidemiological links of the outbreaks. The DVFA acknowledged the lack of records and expressed that there are plans to develop a system to record the steps and conclusions of the investigations of all possible epidemiological links to the cases. This was not in line with Article 57(2) and Article 62 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. 13

The DVFA consistently documented certain verification steps, such as movement derogation reviews and disinfection validations. At the time of the audit, the authorities did not have plans to establish regular biosecurity controls, enforce these proportionally, or delegate and supervise private veterinarians tasked with carrying out official activities. 16 4.2.2 Conclusions on control and eradication

Most operators have the necessary knowledge and motivation to ensure proper animal welfare at slaughter. Improvements in animal welfare at slaughter are driven by that, supported by effective official control activities with adequate follow-up actions from operators. However, administratively burdensome and lengthy sanctioning process reduce the dissuasive effect of enforcement when operators are reluctant to comply. Sanctioning procedures are not dissuasive, risking repeated or prolonged animal suffering.

The area surveyed, compared to the average area planted with main host plants (see section 4.3, Table 1), represent less than 10% of the area occupied by cultivated main host of D. ciliatus (see paragraph 29). The CA did not have reliable data on the secondary and wild hosts area surveyed (See paragraph 27). This is not in line with Article 22(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see paragraphs 18 and 21).

According to the information reported by the CA during the remote meetings of the audit, the total area surveyed in 2024 for the main four host plants were 62.78 ha of which, the presence of D. ciliatus was detected in 25.76 ha. The area surveyed, compared to the average area planted with main host plants (see section 4.3, Table 1), represent less than 10% of the area occupied by cultivated main host of D. ciliatus (see paragraph 29). The CA did not have reliable data on the secondary and wild hosts area surveyed (See paragraph 27). This is not in line with Article 22(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see paragraphs 18 and 21).

During the field assessments, staff from Ammochostos ADO and LCS informed the PHMSAPS that in this district, about 95% of main host producers and many secondary host plots were surveyed during the 2024 season. In the Larnaca District, officials from the ADO and LCS units informed the audit team that out of the five cultivation cycles of cucumbers per year, between two and three of these cycles per professional growers were surveyed in 2024. Officials also implemented some surveys on secondary host crops (see section 4.6) when present in the same professional operator farm.

During discussions between the LCS and ADO in the districts of Ammochostos, Larnaca and Limassol, the audit team verified that some of this information was kept in field books and not uploaded timely during the 2024 season. In the case of Ammochostos district, some of this information was reported by the LCS official to the PHMSAPS office by phone and not transferred to the spread sheets of the CA until the end of the audit (see paragraph 29). These delays in the survey data reporting represent weaknesses in the coordination and cooperation between the Units of the CA. Furthermore, this 9 practice is not in line with the requirements of point 12 (IV) of the action plan against D. ciliatus. T
This lack of up-to-date information concerning the surveys has a strong impact on the capacity of the CA to to immediately communicate the DAs to the Commission and MS.

By the end of the audit and based on the survey information collected by the district Units during 2024, the CA provided the audit team with updated information on the area surveyed for the main host plants during this year. In accordance with this latest information provided by the LCSs, the overall area surveyed of main host plants of D. ciliatus during 2024 was approximately 190 ha, which is equivalent to one quarter of the total area planted with main host crops in 2023 (see section 4.1, table 1). Of this area, D. ciliatus was found in approximately one third of this area (63.8 ha). This data significantly differs from the data reported in update number two of 10 March for Europhyt Outbr

According to the EFSA pest survey card6 for Tephritidae, detection surveys should focus mainly on Cucurbitaceae and Solanaceae cultivated as commercial crops and found as ornamentals or cultivated non-commercially in residential areas. Delimiting surveys following a detection could include all Cucurbitaceae and Solanaceae and all other species described as hosts for the detected species, that are found in the surveyed area as crops, ornamentals or naturally occurring wild plants.

The eradication measures are listed in Annex III to the action plan and include; · prohibition of movement of infested fruits outside the IZ and their disposal in black plastic bags, 7 https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/DACUCI/datasheet 11 · application of contact insecticides in the plots and weeds in the area up to 10 meters around the infested plot, and · placements of yellow sticky traps or feed traps for mass trapping.

Prior to the issuance of the action plan, LCS and ADO officials provided verbal instructions to professional operators affected by D. ciliatus. The audit team could verify this information during the field assessments and were informed by the professional operators visited that the measures listed in the action plan were immediately implemented in 2024.

The CA stated that all exports of host plants of D. ciliatus are subject to 100% phytosanitary controls by the CA before being exported, and trade to EU destinations outside the island. No non-compliances due to the presence of this pest were reported by the importing country or another MS.

Control verification procedure is carried out by two means. Firstly, by the PHMSAPS by remotely checking the information provided by the liaison officers of each LCSs on the CA shared IT files. Secondly, for the on-site control verification procedures of LCS and ADO officials which is to be carried out jointly by the Heads of the PHMSAPS and LCS. However, no such verification has been implemented yet. This is not fully in line with Article 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

label_heading: Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the plant health controls
paragraph_text: There is sufficient testing capacity in the network of designated laboratories under supervision of the NRL. Most samples tested are taken for surveys. A small number of samples are taken for official controls, and the testing of these samples in laboratories, which are not accredited to ISO 17025, does not provide the level of quality assurance required by EU legislation.

All official laboratories designated for the analysis of samples for PWN are exempt from mandatory accreditation under Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA also indicated that all designated laboratories are under the official supervision of the NRL and will participate in proficiency tests for PWN in 2025. Data provided by the CA show that some laboratories have participated in proficiency tests in the past, such as the Centro de Sanidad Forestal Calabazanos in 2010. Additionally, some laboratories have organized inter-laboratory collaborative studies on PWN, including the Laboratorio Agrario y Fitopatológico de Galicia and Centro de Sanidad Forestal Calabazanos in 5 April 2

Authorisation is required prior to the movement of specified wood outside the DA in the AC Extremadura. This process also includes official sampling of the wood. In the AC Galicia, official samples for PWN are taken during the annual official control visits to operators authorised to issue plant passports. Additionally, an official sample was taken at a suspended operator to confirm his compliance with requirements to issue the ISPM mark (see details in section 5.8, point 61). Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 defines that official control means activities in order to verify compliance by operators and goods with plant health legislation. Therefore, the samples described above were ta

While the CA has started to supervise delegated bodies, the limited activity completed to date indicates that these bodies don't consistently adhere to the guidance on surveys, which impacts negatively on the quality and consistency of surveys.

The AFSVSPP has no schedule of audits or inspections on delegated bodies as required by Article 33(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. However, in 2024, for the first time, it inspected four delegated bodies to verify if they were conducting surveys in line with the Survey Guidelines. These controls identified a range of weaknesses common to all four bodies. These weaknesses included failing to consider all relevant risks in choosing surveys sites and incorrectly entering survey data into the UVH-apl/ISI database. The AFSVSPP subsequently organised specific training in 2025 to help address these weaknesses.

The failure to inspect grassland and soil for the presence of P. japonica larvae in the vicinity of trap findings, means that the CA cannot satisfactorily demonstrate that the source of the trap findings are isolated findings of hitchhikers, rather than beetles emerging from soil (indicating that the pest has established), in which case Slovenia should have established demarcated areas around the trap findings.

In 2024, adult P. japonica beetles were captured in traps at two motorway service stations/lorry rest areas along the A1 highway coming from Italy (there are outbreaks of P. japonica in Italy, including one in the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia, which borders Slovenia). At the first site (Lukovica), six beetles were found in the same trap over five separate dates in July and August. Following the first detection, a total of eight extra traps were placed at this site in 2024, but there were no findings in any of these additional traps. At the second site (Barje), one beetle was found in a trap on 17 July and one on 5 September. The PHPRMD explained that these service stations are

Slovenia did not establish demarcated areas in response to these findings. The PHPRMD explained that it took this approach because all findings were in traps and visual inspections in a 1km radius showed no evidence of pest damage to host plants. On this basis, it concluded that the pest had not multiplied and that these were isolated findings, so it could avail of the derogation to avoid establishing demarcated areas as permitted under Article 6(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1584. 12

The PHPRMD implements the measures required under Article 6(2) of the same Regulation (i.e. for MS availing of the derogation to establish demarcated areas), with one exception. It immediately intensified the number of traps and the frequency with which the traps were checked in a 1km radius of findings. It also intensified visual examination for the presence of adults and raised public awareness of the pest in the local areas. However, it does not inspect grassland and soil for the presence of larvae as required by Article 6(2)(c). It explained that as no beetles have ever been found outside traps, it sees no scientific reason to meet this requirement. This breach is significant, because it

The failure to conduct simulation exercises to test the robustness of contingency plans means that the CA cannot demonstrate that it will be able to access the necessary resources to ensure the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of any larger outbreaks of priority pests, if and when these are detected. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The planning and implementation of the comprehensive multi-annual survey programme covering all relevant Union quarantine pests and pests subject to emergency measures gives a solid basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests and provides a reasonable level of assurance that these pests have not established in Slovenia. Th

Slovenia does not comply with Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 which requires MS to carry out simulation exercises concerning the implementation of all contingency plans within a reasonable period of time, except in cases where the MS concerned has recently taken measures for the eradication of the pest or pests concerned. Slovenia has undertaken just one formal simulation exercise, a field-based exercise conducted by the FIS and the SFS in 2020 focusing on A. planipennis. The PHPRMD added that it has gained valuable experience through dealing with a suspected case of A. chinensis in 2022 and the trap findings of P. japonica in 2024. The PHPRMD has no schedule of planned simulation

The PHPRMD, in discussions with the audit team, expressed confidence that its planned response to pest outbreaks, as outlined in its contingency plans, means that it is sufficiently prepared for relatively small pest outbreaks. However, it acknowledged that by not conducting simulation exercises, in particular for larger outbreaks, to test the robustness of these plans, there is a risk that it may not be able to access sufficient laboratories, equipment, personnel, external expertise and resources necessary for the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of larger outbreaks of priority pests, as required by Article 25(2)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions

At an operational level, there is clear, legally binding guidance for the planning and implementation of surveys, but deficiencies in the IT system used means that the central competent authority is unable to monitor the implementation of surveys by the regions.

In the context of surveys, the CAs do not have appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment to perform surveys efficiently and effectively as required by Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The National Plant Health Service uses the Monitoring of Harmful Pests (MORGANA) IT system to plan and record surveys, to send samples to laboratories, and to manage the resultant data. Sixteen of the 21 RPSs input survey data directly into MORGANA, while the remaining five use their own systems and transfer relevant data into MORGANA periodically throughout the year. The MAFF explained that deficiencies in MORGANA make it very difficult to extract data from the system. As a pract

The system for planning the multi-annual and annual survey programmes, as currently in operation, does not ensure that the resultant plans comprise a sufficient number of risk- based surveys, to be carried out in all appropriate locations, and based on sound scientific and technical principles, to ensure the timely detection of any outbreaks of these pests.

While Italy's multi-annual survey programme includes all (approximately 400) relevant pests, significant weaknesses in the planning (and subsequent implementation) of the annual risk-based survey programme, including for priority pests, means that the resultant surveys do not provide a reasonable level of assurance that these pests have not established in Italy.

The three RPSs met by the audit team stated that they propose survey numbers for risk- based surveys for all Union quarantine pests (including priority pests) and pests provisionally qualifying as Union quarantine pests based on available resources, rather than phytosanitary risks. The MAFF acknowledged that the majority of RPSs follow this same approach. The MAFF and CREA-DC stated that they do not have the human resources to critically analyse the survey proposals of the RPSs (in terms of numbers of planned surveys, locations for surveys and survey methodology) as foreseen under the structures described in findings 4 and 5, with the result that the proposals of the RPSs are aggregated to f

The multi-annual risk-based survey programme is drawn up by the CREA-DC based on proposals from the RPSs. CREA-DC explained that annual survey plans are also drawn up using this approach. Due to the weaknesses described in finding 9, the resultant risk- based (as distinct from statistically-based) survey programmes for Union quarantine pests and pests provisionally qualifying as Union quarantine pests are not risk-based, not carried out in all appropriate locations, nor based on sound scientific and technical principles as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. In addition, in the case of priority pests, surveys do not include a sufficiently high number of visual examination

The number of planned and completed visual examinations and traps under the S. frugiperda risk-based survey programme in Italy (as recorded in MORGANA) are summarised in Table 1. CREA-DC and the three RPSs met by the audit team stated that visual examinations refer exclusively to examining plants, rather than examining the contents of traps. The planned numbers and types (visual examinations or traps) of surveys are based on the proposals of the RPSs. The three RPSs met by the audit team acknowledged that their proposed survey numbers for S. frugiperda are based on the available resources as described in finding 9. Table 1. Surveys are not planned (and subsequently implemented) based on risk as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and by Article 3(2)(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134. Article 3(2)(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 requires MS to conduct risk-based surveys in line with the the EFSA pest survey card, in particular at areas where host plants enter the EU, where they are handled and repacked, and where their waste is disposed of, at airports and seaports, and at nurseries, garden centres and retail shops, as appropriate. The EFSA pest survey card suggests placing traps in fields of host plants and at storage and handling facilities dealing with host plants. T

Sicily has 4 000 ha of tomatoes and 1 400 ha of peppers and aubergines. Solanum lycopersicum L. (tomatoes) are listed as host plants in Annex I, while Capsicum L. (peppers) are listed as specified plants in Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134. It has approximately 5 000 nurseries. It also has five international airports (four civilian and one military) and four commercial seaports. The RPS in Sicily has not determined the number of traps needed, but in July 2025, it established two traps and had conducted three visual examinations at the time of the audit in September. Calabria has 1 500 ha of tomatoes and almost 400 nurseries. It has three international airports and four commercial seapo

Surveys for S. frugiperda are not planned based on the scientific and technical information referred to in the EFSA pest survey card as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134. The EFSA pest survey card for S. frugiperda clearly states that "detection surveys to substantiate pest freedom should be based on a trapping strategy" while Article 3(3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 states that surveys shall consists of traps, and where appropriate, visual examinations. In both 2024 and 2025, approximately 1 000 - 1 100 visual examinations and 220 traps were planned throughout Italy for S. frugiperda. The three RPSs met by the audit team explained that they prioritise visua

Surveys for B. dorsalis and B. zonata are not planned based on "the scientific and technical information" in the EFSA pest survey cards as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2025/311. Both pest survey cards clearly state that "trapping is the recommended method for surveillance and detection". In addition, Article 3(2)(c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/311 states that surveys for B. dorsalis and B. zonata shall be conducted by trapping and makes no reference to visual examinations in the case of routine surveys. Finally, the OTSS guidance documents for B. dorsalis and B. zonata state that surveys should be predominantly based on monitoring with traps.

In the 2021-2024 period, the ratio of traps to visual examinations for B. dorsalis (detailed in Table 2) ranged from 1:6 to 1:10 at national level. The ratio of traps to visual examinations is broadly similar for B. zonata and for other years. The three RPSs met by the audit team explained that they prioritise visual inspections due to a lack of staff. They explained that inspectors can observe up to 30 pests in fruit orchards in a single visit. On 14 the other hand, traps are pest specific, and they plan to check them every 7-10 days, which is much more demanding on staff resources. However, they acknowledged that it is not possible to identify the four relevant species of fruit flies by vi

Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2025/311 requires surveys for B. dorsalis and B. zonata to be based on EFSA's General guidelines for statistically sound and risk-based surveys and the scientific and technical information referred to in relevant EFSA pest survey cards. The EFSA pest survey card for B. dorsalis identifies citrus and prunus species (particularly peach and nectarine) as the primary host species for detection surveys (these are also listed as host plants in Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2025/311). Sicily has about 70 000 ha of these host plants (62 000 ha citrus and 7 000 ha of peaches and nectarine). Calabria has about 35 000 ha (32 000 ha citrus and 3 200 ha of peaches and nectari

The EFSA pest survey card for B. zonata identifies Prunus persica (peaches and nectarines) as the primary host species for detection surveys (these are also listed as host plants in Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2025/311). Sicily has about 7 000 ha of peaches and nectarines. Calabria has about 3 200 ha of peaches and nectarines and Lazio has about 600 ha peaches and 50 ha nectarines. The EFSA pest survey card for B. zonata refers to the ISPM 26, and on that basis, recommends 1 trap/100 ha in production areas, with higher trap densities in higher risk areas. The OTSS for B. zonata also uses the values in ISPM 26 for recommended trap densities. 15 Table 4. Numbers of traps for B. zonata Area of R

In the case of A. ludens, surveys should be risk-based, carried out in all appropriate locations, and based on sound scientific and technical principles as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. In addition, surveys should include a sufficiently high number of visual examinations, sampling and testing, to ensure, as far as it is possible given the respective biology of each priority pest and the ecoclimatic conditions, with a high degree of confidence, the timely detection of the pest as required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The OTSS for A. ludens identifies citrus species as the primary host species for surveys and recommends 0.25-1trap/100 ha in productio

The huge variation between regions in the intensity of surveys for specific pests is a result of the weakness in risk-based planning under Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 16 This results in an inconsistent approach to surveys in different regions which can be seen by comparing Lazio to Sicily and Calabria in Tables 3, 4 and 5.

In addition, in the case of priority pests, surveys do not include a sufficiently high number of visual examination

The failure to finalise three quarters of the required contingency plans almost two years after the legal deadline means that Italy has yet to establish a solid starting point to deal with outbreaks for the majority of priority pests.

At the time of the audit in September 2025, Italy had finished the process of drawing up contingency plans for just four of the 20 priority pests which are capable of entering into and becoming established in its territory on the basis of Article 25(1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 (X. fastidiosa), Article 4 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1584 (P. japonica) and Article 4 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/311 (B. dorsalis and B. zonata). The finalised contingency plans relate to X. fastidiosa, P. japonica and a combined contingency plan for B. dorsalis and B. zonata. (In all cases, Italy has outbreaks of the pests).

In the case of the contingency plans for the remaining 16 pests, CREA-DC had drawn up 15 of these plans, which had subsequently been approved by the NPC. The MAFF stated that the final step of the process, a series of Decrees of the MAFF to formally adopt these plans were under preparation. The NPC was working on the contingency plan for S. frugiperda, with a view to finalising it by the end of 2025.

At the time of the audit in September 2025, the four completed contingency plans were published at https://www.protezionedellepiante.it/. However, these plans had not been communicated to the Commission and to other MS, as requested by the Commission in a letter to Italy in March 2024, by uploading them to the internet Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (iRASFF) plant health portal, as required by Article 25(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

In the absence of contingency plans, the CAs have not conducted simulation exercises for relevant pests and therefore cannot demonstrate that they will be able to eradicate or, where appropriate, contain outbreaks of these priority pests, if and when they are detected. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS Surveys are conducted for all relevant pests, but the number and type of surveys are determined based on staff resources, rather than risk. In all three regions visited by the audit team, the numbers of risk-based surveys planned and completed for all pests (including priority pests) fall far below that required by both EU and national guidelines to detect any pest outbreaks in a timely fashion. Therefore

MS are not required to carry out simulation exercises in cases where they have recently taken measures to eradicate the pest(s) concerned, given what they have learned from the practical experiences gained ­ this applies to six of the 20 priority pests in the case of Italy. Therefore, Italy is obliged to carry out simulation exercises for 14 priority pests. The MAFF stated that Italy has not completed any simulation exercises to date and has no documented plans to conduct such exercises, which is not in line with Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 23 Conclusions on contingency plans

The NRL has a quality assurance system in place. This laboratory is accredited and has participated in interlaboratory testing for the determination of some priority and EU quarantine pests. Nevertheless, the incomplete accreditation for the remaining methods required for the multi-annual survey programme, reduces the level of assurance in their respective survey results. 5.2 SURVEY PROGRAMMES Legal requirements Articles 2 of Implementing Decision 2012/535/EU Articles 22, 23 and 24 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Article 1 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/1702 Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Articles 2, 3 and 35(1) and Annex IV of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 Annex

The NRL is EN ISO/IEC 17025 accredited for the determination of the following organisms; A. chinensis, Citrus tristeza virus, Clavibacter sepedonicus, Globodera rostochiensis and G. pallida, Phyllosticta citricarpa, Phytophthora ramorum, Plum pox virus, Ralstonia solanacearum and Thrips palmi. It has participated in interlaboratory testing for PWN in 2020 and 2023, P. japonica in 2023, and for Spodoptera frugiperda, T. palmi and Agrilus planipennis in 2024. For the multi-annual survey programme which includes more than 400 species (see Chapter 5.2), the limited number of pests included in the accreditation is not fully in line with the requirements of Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017

The multi-annual survey programme for the relevant Union quarantine pests (including relevant priority pests) provides a basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests. The small number of shortcomings identified do not have a critical impact on the outcome of the survey programmes.

The CAAF informed the audit team that several counties of Croatia which have X. fastidiosa host plants, but environmental conditions with a low risk, are not taken into account in the survey for this pest. The design of the survey system practically assigns a zero risk to these areas, rather than a low risk. This is not in line with the environmental suitability factors, as described in the EFSA Guidelines and therefore, not fully in line with Article 2(3) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 which, requires that surveys shall be performed on the basis of the level of risk. Additionally, islands which have difficult access are not part of the survey programme for the presence of X. fastidios

The SI also surveys in Croatia for the presence of X. fastidiosa. Planning of these surveys is done by assigning the staff available to maximise the number of inspections. The responsible staff from the SI informed the audit team that these surveys are not statistically based, contrary to the requirements of Article 2(4) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. The SI surveys garden centres and nurseries in four inland counties. Urban areas and crops are surveyed in another five counties. For the 2024 survey season, the SI planned to survey 36 nurseries and garden centres, 28 urban areas and 17 fields, taking a total of 105 samples. For the current 2025 season, the SI is planning to survey

For the implementation of the 2024 annual survey plan for X. fastidiosa, the PHD reported that CAAF and SI have implemented 408 visual inspections, 35 of which were implemented in nurseries. The same CAs took 297 samples during the 2024 season, of these 115 were taken in garden centres. Although the sampling target was fully achieved, concerning the number of sites visited and samples taken (see paragraph 22 and 23), it is not possible to determine the confidence level achieved by this survey at national level (see paragraph 21 and 23).

The multi-annual survey programme for the relevant Union quarantine pests (including relevant priority pests) provides a basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests. The small number of shortcomings identified do not have a critical impact on the outcome of the survey programmes.

The CAAF has 20 pheromone traps to capture beetles of the genus Monochamus sp. while the CFRI has 28. The beetles captured are tested at the CFRI (see paragraph 3) to determine whether they belong to any non-European species, which are EU quarantine pests. However, they are not examined for the presence of PWN, contrary to the requirements of Article 2(1) of Implementing Decision 2012/535/EU which requires that, MS shall annually conduct surveys for Bursaphelenchus xylophilus on the vector.

For the 2024 annual survey for PWN, the CFRI visited seven counties, and performed 2 610 visual examinations of individual trees. Field inspectors visited 32 forest units and took 28 samples of wood, exceeding the annual plan. The CFRI reported that surveys focussed on symptomatic trees of Pinus halepensis by the coastal counties and Pinus sylvestris in the non-coastal ones. CFRI captured 130 Monochamus sp. beetles in the 29 pheromone traps placed. These beetles were analysed at the CFRI laboratory to determine whether they belonged to non-European species. However, they were not tested for the presence of PWN (see paragraph 30).

In 2024, the CAAF visited 5 counties and took 25 samples of wood from forest stands and public areas near ports. This CA reported captured 10 Monochamus sp. beetles which were examined with the same objective as the beetles captured by the CFRI.

By developing all required contingency plans, Croatia has laid down a solid basis to eradicate any outbreak of relevant EU priority pests. Once the shortcomings identified in the simulation exercises are addressed, the CAs will be able to rapidly implement eradication measures in the case of an outbreak of a priority pest. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Since 2021, the CAs of Croatia are implementing a multi-annual survey programme. This programme initially covered seven years but has has recently been extended to a ten year period. The plan covers all EU quarantine and priority pests, except eleven for which the competent authorities assessed that they are not capable of establishing, spreading and h

The contingency plans are overall in line with the requirements of Article 25(2) of Regulations (EU) 2016/2031. All CAs participated in the drafting of the plans (see paragraph 2 and 3) however, they have not consulted the relevant stakeholders in the process of drawing up and keeping up to date the contingency plans. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 25(1) of Regulations (EU) 2016/2031.

The CAs informed the audit team that they are considering how to amend the national legislation to address these issues. Once they are addressed, the CAs can review these plans, which is a requirement under Article 25(4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on contingency plans

label_heading: Conclusions on the organisation of official controls on GMOs
paragraph_text: The procedures and arrangements on which controls on trials and food are based provide a sound basis for ensuring the consistent implementation of legislation on GMOs in these areas. Deficiencies in the checklists used by inspectors in the feed area mean that there is no documentary evidence that controls relating to labelling, traceability and the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds are performed.

label_heading: Conclusions on the organisation of official controls on GMOs
paragraph_text: Sampling of seed lots, which forms the basis of the control system for seeds, is not performed consistently due to significant deficiencies in the procedures provided to inspectors, which compromises the reliability of the control system on seeds. 5.2 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Articles 4(5) and 21 of Directive 2001/18/EC Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 Findings

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: While considerable operational resources are invested in controlling seeds, there are significant weaknesses relating to sampling and analysis, with the result that the control system does not provide reasonable assurances that seeds sown in Italy are free from GMOs. The importance of establishing an effective control system is demonstrated by the fact that in 2024, notwithstanding the weaknesses in controls, 3% of samples of imported soya seeds and almost 4% of soya seed samples tested under own-controls contained GMOs.

label_heading: Conclusions on the implementation of official controls
paragraph_text: The system of official controls in feed is weakened by the failure to satisfactorily address risks linked to imported feed materials, the failure to test all samples for all relevant GM events, and the absence of documentary evidence demonstrating controls on labelling and traceability requirements, and the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds. Consequently, official controls do not provide a satisfactory level of assurance that feed marketed in Italy complies with EU requirements regarding GMOs.

There are insufficient procedures and arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls in the areas of feed and seed contrary to Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.
